The Śṛṅgāraprakāśa composed by the illustrious King Bhoja, the Great Conqueror;
the first manifestation.
May the body of the Enemy of Tripura protect you— his waistband unloosened, his lips not yet attained, the luster of his face moistened by tears,
his form mingled with that of his beloved, as if he had established a kinship between the states of separation and union.

May that Lord Gaṇeśa, the master of the hosts, be for the destruction of obstacles— he by whose feet the minds of seekers, when cleansed of their dust, attain the stainless clarity of a mirror’s surface, and in which the most exalted riches of word and meaning flash forth.
They say that the excellence of qualities established in the self, characterized by egoity, is the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), which is the very life of the self-born [poetry].

Because it is to be relished by the power of the self, it possesses the nature of "rasa" (flavor); for this reason, there is the popular saying: "He who possesses this is a connoisseur (rasika). || 3 ||

There exists in the hearts of beings a certain transformation consisting of pride, born from the excellence of stainless qualities that delight the virtuous; arising from latent impressions (vāsanā) shattered by the destruction of other births, it is the sole cause for the supreme emergence of all personal perfections throughout the world. (4)

In speech, it is the intended meaning alone that is relished; in poetry, it is suggestion alone; in the excellence of qualities, it is charm alone for a lover; in the body of a woman, it is symmetry alone; and in the heart of a person possessed by love, it is the erotic sentiment alone. (5)

The wise have traditionally enumerated ten aesthetic flavors (rasas) by name— erotic, heroic, pathetic, marvelous, furious, comic, loathsome, tender, terrifying, and peaceful— but we, because it is that which tastes, recognize only the erotic as the true flavor.

Furthermore, as for the well-established presence of rasa in the heroic, the marvelous, and other such [sentiments], which appears here like a fig tree growing from a seedless branch—this effort of ours is undertaken to restrain this [notion] which has gained currency in the world through mere conformity to popular custom. (7)

In this context, self-consciousness (*abhimāna*)—which, by not being contrary to the mind, causes the joy of the heart and is the cause for the experience of consciousness—is to be known as *rasa* because it is that which is relished through its own power. However, the expression "rasa" applied to the abundance of love (*rati*) and the like is merely figurative. (8)

The one hundred and four emotions, beginning with *rati* (love), each being distinct and giving rise to various other states, surround the essence of *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment) and augment it, like masses of light surrounding the seven-flamed fire. || 9 ||
That state which is cultivated in the mind by people through meditation with one-pointed concentration until its manifestation is called *bhāva*.
But that aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) which, having transcended the path of meditation, unfolds within the heart accompanied by ego-consciousness, is the supreme. (10)
If *rati* and the others were indeed aesthetic flavors (*rasa*), what offense would be committed by *harṣa* (joy) and the rest, which differ from them?
If you say that they are not lasting, then tell me: how long do fear, disgust, sorrow, anger, and so forth persist? 11.

If it is argued that stability [of the emotion] here is due to the excellence of the object, then from what source would anxiety and the like arise? Or, if it is by the power of one's nature, that nature would be equally present in oneself. Alternatively, if it is due to the stimulation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), then that is the same in both cases. 12.

Therefore, this is established: the forty-nine *bhāvas*, beginning with love (*rati*), arise solely from the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*); the heroic and other sentiments are merely false claims; and the erotic sentiment alone is the single cause of all sentiments. Because it is accessible only through personal experience and because its object is beyond the scope of the senses, it is difficult to ascertain; yet, when properly manifested by skilled actors on the stage, it is apprehended by the audience, or when accurately described by great poets in their compositions, it enters the depths of the minds of the wise.

In this regard, objects do not provide such delight when perceived through direct perception as they do when communicated by the words of eloquent speakers. Thus it is said: "The specific meanings of things do not produce such mental expansion when truly described as they do when they blossom forth through the well-uttered verses of poets. Therefore, we hold poets in higher esteem than actors, and the poetic work itself in higher esteem than the performance.

Furthermore, they maintain that this is the conjunction (*sāhitya*) of word and meaning, as in the statement: "Poetry is the conjunction of word and meaning. What, then, is the word? That which is conveyed by the word. And it is twelvefold: action, time, grammatical relation (*kāraka*), person (*puruṣa*), qualification (*upādhi*), the primary sense (*pradhāna*), the sense of embellishment (*upaskārārtha*), the sense of the nominal stem (*pratipadikārtha*), the sense of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*), the sense of the verbal derivative (*vṛttyartha*), and the sense of the sentence (*vākyārtha*). What is conjunction? It is the relationship between word and meaning.

And that [poetic expression] is twelvefold: intention (*vivakṣā*), purport (*tātparya*), differentiation (*pravibhāga*), mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*), syntactic connection (*anvaya*), unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), elimination of defects (*doṣahāna*), adoption of excellences (*guṇopādāna*), and employment of ornaments (*alaṅkārayoga*).

In this regard, although there is a rule of usage stating that "neither the base alone nor the suffix alone should be employed," nevertheless, for the sake of regulating the properties [of words] within the technical practice of grammatical analysis (*prakriyā*), they designate as "base" (*prakṛti*) that which is presented—like a primary material cause—at the very outset of the productive process (*bhāvanā*) of word-meaning, through the conceptual division of base and suffix. That [base] is threefold: consisting of a verbal root (*dhātu*), consisting of a suffix (*pratyaya*), consisting of a suffixal element (*pratyayāṅga*), and consisting of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

In that regard, verbal roots (*dhātu*) are classified as sixfold: those explicitly listed (*paripaṭhita*), those not listed (*aparipaṭhita*), those both listed and not listed (*paripaṭhitāparipaṭhita*), derivative roots (*pratyayadhātu*), nominal roots (*nāmadhātu*), and roots consisting of both suffixes and nouns (*pratyayanāmadhātu*). Among these, the explicitly listed are *bhū* and so forth, such as: "May birth in their family be yours; may prosperity attend them, for seekers accept as their own that which they consider to be theirs. "The poet creates poems; the virtuous cherish them in their hearts."

The ocean produces pearls, and the breasts of young women exude them; yet you do not restrain the collection of your senses, nor do you hearken to the words of your teacher, nor do you acquire friends—how then can you seize the wealth of your enemies?

The unrecited forms such as *āndalayati* and others are used, as in: "Just as it does not merely sway the boat, so does it swing my mind; the wind, fanning the quarters, utterly uproots the hope of pride. "The lightning seems to stitch the quarters together; the peacocks find no comfort in the summer; the monsoon winds dispel the heat that has entered the sighs of travelers. "Clouds meet in the quarters and the planets roam in the sky; the rainy season extinguishes the fever, and the calamities of the Kali age are overcome."

Those roots which are recited only in the Sūtras and not in the *bhūvādi* (first) class are called "recited and non-recited" (*paripaṭitāparipaṭitāḥ*), such as *skṛ* and others. For example: "O messenger, do not forget my offenses, for even in spring one might forget insults; therefore, run quickly! Love desires to cause you to live. "With the slaps of her pestle and her shouts of 'hum', Love seems to thresh your ears while propping up the expanse of your breasts. "The minds of young men, prone to falling [in love], are eager to seize them; by a single form, women become a source of torment to them."

The elements of cognition have long since reached their end; for example: "You contemplate the scriptures, yet you do not fulfill the needs of those who seek your help; you do not protect the terrified—why do you wander about so haughtily? "She acts like the sun with her rays of moonlight; she acts like a denizen of hell in the Nandana grove. Desiring you with all her heart, though she lives, she acts as if dead. "Her cheeks grow red; her tearful eyes act as if weeping. O slender-limbed one, desiring the salutations of your beloved, why do you endure such hardship?"

Verbs such as *kaṇḍūyati* are denominative roots (*nāmadhātu*); for example: "He who does not scratch his own vital parts, who does not seek to bend what is unbendable; he who wards off anger and heals the kingdom—he is a true king. "He who does not strut like one who is wicked, nor envy the virtuous, nor find fault with one worthy of honor—he is honored among the great. "What would the sacrificers desire? What would the panegyrists sing of? What would the seekers of wealth strive for, while Rāma ranges through the forest?"

How, then, can *kaḍḍhvādi* be both a noun-base (*nāman*) and a verbal root (*dhātu*)? Because it occurs in the section on roots, it is a root; and because of the attachment of the suffix *kvi*, it is a noun. As it is said: "I consider this long [form] to be a verbal root that has been explained. Those from which the suffixes *kvip* and so forth are elided—either for the sake of establishing the status of a noun from already-recited roots, or for the sake of establishing the status of a root from nouns—are both nouns and roots by virtue of that suffix; these are the *pratyayanāmadhātus*, such as *hoḍa*, *ḍambha*, *klība*, and others, just like *giraḥ*.

You are the source of speech and sacred prayer, the fulfiller of desires and the bestower of fortune; you are the head of enemies and the arm that protects friends—may you be united with these bonds. You are clever among the simple, yet you do not pride yourself on the arrogant; you are discerning among the foolish, yet you do not show off your boldness before the timid. When the mind is enslaved by pleasure or pain, the sun acts like the moon, and the moon acts like the sun; likewise, nights act like days, and days act like nights.

Thus, one who narrates the slaying of Kaṃsa is said to "cause Kaṃsa to be slain" (kaṃsaṃ ghātayati); one who narrates the passing of the night is said to "cause the night to pass" (rātriṃ vivāsayati); one who knows the conjunction of the moon with the Puṣya asterism is said to "join the moon with Puṣya" (puṣyeṇa candraṃ yojayati); and one who, having set out from Ujjayinī, reaches sunrise at Māhiṣmatī is said to "cause the sun to rise at Māhiṣmatī" (māhiṣmatyāṃ sūryam udgamayati).

In this context, it is traditionally taught: "The suffix *ṇac* is applied after a verbal derivative (*kṛdanta*) to express that which the derivative describes"; "There is elision of the *kṛt*-suffix, the restoration of the original form (*prakṛti*), and the grammatical function (*kāraka*) remains as in the original"; "The prefix *āṅ* is elided when expressing a limit (*maryādā*) involving continuous duration of time"; "The suffix *jñi* is applied in connection with a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*)"; and "The suffix *prap* is applied in the sense of causing wonder. This original form (*prakṛti*) has been described as being of six types, consisting of verbal roots (*dhātu*). Now, the original form consisting of suffixes (*pratyaya*) is likewise described as being of six types.

For suffixes (*pratyaya*) are of six types, distinguished as: nominal endings (*sup*), verbal endings (*tiṅ*), primary suffixes (*kṛt*), secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), verbal roots (*dhātu*), and feminine suffixes (*strīpratyaya*). A stem (*prakṛti*) that ends in such a suffix likewise becomes sixfold in form, according to the type of suffix it possesses. Examples of stems ending in nominal suffixes (*sup*) are: *ahaṃyuḥ*, *śubhaṃyuḥ*, *sāyamatanam*, *ciranatanam*, *tvayakā*, *mayakā*, *āmuṣyāṇaḥ*, *apsavyaḥ*, *prahṇetarām*, *pragetarām*, *pūrvāhṇetanam*, and *samāṃsamīnā*.

Examples of words ending in *tiṅ* suffixes are: *pacatitarām*, *gacchatitamām*, *spṛśati rūpam*, *jalpatikalpam*, *jighratidheśyam*, *paśyatideśīyam*, *āstikaḥ*, *nāstikaḥ*, *pacataki*, *bhindhaki*, *pacatabhṛjjatā*, and *khādatamodatā*. Examples of words ending in *kṛt* suffixes are: *kṛtrimam*, *bhṛtrimaṃ*, *sekimam*, *sāṅkūṭinam*, *sāṃrāviṇam*, *vyāvakrośī*, *vyāvahāsī*, *śyenampātā*, *tailampātā*, *jitvarī*, and *āḍhyamkaraṇī*.

Examples of words ending in *taddhita* suffixes include: *gārgyāyaṇaḥ*, *dākṣāyaṇaḥ*, *vāṣryāyaṇukaḥ*, *vāṣryayaṇīyaḥ*, *phāṇṭāhṛtāyaniḥ*, *ābhidityaḥ*, *kauñjāyaṇaḥ*, *kutastyaḥ*, *tatratyaḥ*, *pacatitarām*, and *pacatitamām*. Examples of words ending in suffixes that receive the designation *dhātu* (verbal root) include: *tikīrṣā*, *kaṇḍyā*, *putrūyā*, *kāraṇā*, *miśraṇā*, *mṛdayā*, *aṭāṭyā*, *sāsahiḥ*, *yāyavaraḥ*, *yāyajūkaḥ*, *cikīrṣuḥ*, and *caṅkramaṇaḥ*.

Examples of [patronymics] ending in *stri* (the feminine suffix) are: *gāṅgeyaḥ*, *saudāmeyaḥ*, *kārīṣagandheyaḥ*, *draupadeyaḥ*, *gaureyaḥ*, *śāṅgaraveyaḥ*, *kādraveyaḥ*, *kāmaṇḍaleyaḥ*, *yauvateyaḥ*, *saurabheyaḥ*, *bahusetrīkaḥ*, and *suvathadhūkaḥ*. Now, how is it that *yauvateyaḥ* is cited as an example for the base of the suffix, given that by the technical designation *taddhita*, the form *yūnaḥ* [from Pāṇini 4.1.79, *yūnasti*] is itself a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)?

That is true; however, there exists another verbal root (*prakṛti*) for the word *yuvati* which is a synonym for the general term *strī* (woman), as it has been said: "A man should study the *Kāmasūtra* and its auxiliary rules without obstructing his duty, wealth, limbs, ordinances, or time; likewise, a woman [should study] before her youth. Thus, [the term *yuvati* refers to a young woman].

From that [base], either from *yūnaḥ* itself or from *yūnaḥ* with the optional suffix *ti* (i.e., *yūnti*), the suffix *ḍhak* arises according to the rule *eraktinaḥ*, as in *āditeyaḥ* and *saurabheyaḥ*. But how is it in the case of *kādraveyaḥ* and *kāmaṇḍaleyaḥ*? For even though the feminine suffixes *ṅī* and *āp* are not nominal stems (*aprātipadika*), the suffix *ḍhak* applies because of the specific rule *ṅyāpprātipadikāt*; however, while the suffix *ti* in *yūnti* allows for the subsequent addition of case-endings (*sub*) since it is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), the suffix *ūṅ* does not achieve this result because it is a primary suffix (*pratyaya*), and a secondary derivative requires a semantically related base.

It must be so; it will occur because of the status of having a final element (*antavadbhāva*). For instance, in *brahmabandhūḥ* and similar forms, by the rule "a long vowel replaces [a short vowel] before a homogeneous vowel" (*akaḥ savarṇe dīrghaḥ*), the two become as if one. If this were the case, the suffix *ḍhak* in the rule "from *satrū* and others, *ḍhak*" would not be established; however, that too will be established through the status of being like the initial (*ādivadbhāva*). Furthermore, based on the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule "she whose deity is she" (*sā'sāya devatā*), the addition of the suffix *vāsu* occurs even prior to the production of the feminine suffix *ūṅ*. Thus, these sixteen types of bases have been described, including those consisting of suffixes.

Now, therefore, the nature of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is described in six ways. [This is] the section on the nominal stem as the base. In this regard, nouns, indeclinables, *kṛt* formations, *taddhita* formations, and compounds are nominal stems; as it is said: "That which possesses meaning, which is not a verbal root, and is not a suffix, is a nominal stem," and "as well as those consisting of *kṛt*, *taddhita*, and compounds. Among these, by the inclusion of "that which possesses meaning" (*arthavat*), nouns, indeclinables, and *kṛt* formations are grasped, while *taddhita* formations and compounds are mentioned explicitly. But are not these also indeed possessors of meaning?

This is true; however, since *kṛt* and *taddhita* suffixes are included [in the definition of a nominal stem], they would not attain the status of *prātipadika* because they are not explicitly mentioned in the rule for *prātipadikas*. Therefore, by the inclusion of the term *kṛttaddhita*, he encompasses them. By the inclusion of the term *samāsa*, however, he indicates that only a compound which is a meaningful aggregate is intended, thereby excluding this [status] from such a sentence. In that regard, nouns (*nāman*) are those words whose formation is independent of other words and which denote entities that have attained existence (*sattvabhūta*).

These [words] are of two kinds: those whose gender is manifested (*āviṣṭaliṅga*) and those whose gender is not manifested (*anāviṣṭaliṅga*). Among them, those that denote genus (*jāti*), substance (*dravya*), and measure (*parimāṇa*) are those whose gender is manifested. Therein, genus is twofold: that manifested by form (*ākṛti*) and that manifested by instruction (*upadeśa*). Of these two, the first is as follows: cow, deer, animal, snake, lion, tree, girl, pot, woman, man, neuter.

The second [category] is as follows: a Brāhmaṇa, a Gārgya, a Kaṭha, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, a Mūrdhābhiṣikta, an Ambaṣṭha, a Pāraśava, a Sūta, a Vaidehaka, and a Caṇḍāla. Substance is twofold: dependent and independent. Of these two, the first is as follows: a teacher, a father, a son, a brother, a son-in-law, a friend, a mother, a sister, a daughter, a wife's sister, a husband's sister, a wife, and so forth.

The second [category] is, for example: Caitra, Maitra, Indra, Upendra, Sūrya, Kāla, Ākāśa, Prācī, Praticī, Śacī, and Lakṣmī. Measure is twofold: determinate and indeterminate. Of these two, the first is, for example: a *droṇa*, a *kharī*, a *pala*, a *bhāra*, a *krośa*, a *yojana*, a *nipartana*, a *nalva*, a *paṇa*, a *purāṇa*, a *gaṇa*, and an *akṣauhiṇī*.

The second [type] is, for example: *saṃgha*, *pūga*, *sārtha*, *samāja*, *varga*, *śroṇi*, *kuṭumba*, *pariṣad*, *paṅkti*, *yūtha*, *vana*, and *senā*. [There are also] words expressing qualities (*guṇa*), numbers (*saṃkhyā*), and pronouns (*sarvanāman*) that do not undergo gender change (*anāviṣṭaliṅga*); among these, a quality (*guṇa*) is of two kinds: that which colors [the object] (*anurañjaka*) and that which does not color it (*ananurañjaka*).

Among these, those resulting from the conjunction of the *anurañjaka* (pleasing) with the *udātta* (exalted) are as follows: white, sweet, swift, slow, long, short, straight, crooked, soft, hard, young, and old. Those resulting from the conjunction of the *ananurañjaka* (unpleasing) with the *udātta* are the opposites of those, as follows: spotted, crooked, dull, wise, wicked, virtuous, affectionate, cruel, brave, timid, light, and heavy.

Number is of two kinds: that which possesses gender and that which is genderless. Of these, the first is as follows: *ekaḥ*, *ekā*, *ekam*; *dvau*, *dve*, *dve*; *ubhau*, *ubhe*, *ubhe*; *trayaḥ*, *tisraḥ*, *trīṇi*; *catvāraḥ*, *catastraḥ*, *catvāri*. Thus it is.

The second [type] is as follows: the five meanings of nominal stems (*prātipadika*), the five modes of occurrence (*vṛtti*), the five classes of words (*padajāti*), the six suffixes (*vidhvaṣaya*), the six cognitions (*buddhi*), the six sense organs (*indriya*), the eight Vasus, the eight forms (*mūrti*), the eight places of articulation (*varṇasthāna*), the ten directions (*diś*), the sixteen categories of existence (*padārtha*), and the eighteen Purāṇas.

All nouns are of two kinds: those beginning with *sarva* and those not beginning with *sarva*. Among them, the first group is as follows: *śarvaḥ*, *viśvaḥ*, *anyaḥ*, *itaraḥ*, *katamaḥ*, *yaḥ*, *saḥ*, *eṣaḥ*, *ayam*, *tvam*, and *aham*. The second group is as follows: *prathamaḥ*, *caramaḥ*, *alpaḥ*, *katipayaḥ*, *pūrvaḥ*, *paraḥ*, *aparaḥ*, *dakṣiṇaḥ*, *uttaraḥ*, *svaḥ*, *antaraḥ*, *sakalaḥ*, and *kṛtsnaḥ*. Generally, these [nouns] are indeclinables (*avyaya*) that lack gender, number, and case-role (*śakti*).

These [indeclinables] are of six types, distinguished as: avyaya (indeclinable), nipāta (particle), gati (governing particle), upasarga (preverb), karmapravacanīya (governing preposition), and those resembling case-endings (*vibhaktipratirūpaka*). Among them, indeclinables such as *svar* and others generally possess both gender and number; as it is said: "That which does not vary across the three genders, all case-endings, and all numbers—that is an indeclinable. These are of two kinds: those possessing a trace of gender (*sattvagandhin*) and those lacking a trace of gender (*asattvagandhin*).

Among those, the words denoting sentient beings (*sattvagandhi*) are of six kinds: those having the form of substances (*dravya*), those having the form of qualities (*guṇa*), those having the form of actions (*kriyā*), those having the form of universals (*jāti*), those having the form of names (*saṃjñā*), and those having the form of relations (*saṃbandhin*). Those not denoting sentient beings (*asattvagandhi*) are likewise of six kinds: those dependent on an action (*kriyāpekṣin*), those dependent on an action and a substance (*kriyādravyāpekṣin*), adverbs (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), [adjectives] qualifying an action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), qualifiers of both an action and a substance (*kriyādravyaviśeṣaṇa*), those whose form is permeated by action (*kriyāviṣṭarūpa*), and those whose form is permeated by both action and substance (*kriyādravyāviṣṭarūpa*).

Among those varieties characterized by the quality of being (*sattvagandhibheda*), the forms consisting of substance (*dravyarūpa*) are as follows: *śvaḥ*, *divaḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, *vihāyasā*, *rodasī*, *āpaḥ*, *bhūḥ*, *ṛcaḥ*, *ṣam*, *mahaḥ*, *tapaḥ*, *hāhā*, *hūhū*; the forms consisting of action (*giṇarūpa*) are as follows: *śaśvat*, *āvat*, *nṛvat*, *kūpat*, *kuvat*, *sāmi*, *sāci*, *drāk*, *strāk*, *jyok*, *manāk*, *āṣat*; and the forms consisting of activity (*kriyārūpa*) are as follows: *namaḥ*, *svasti*, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *śrauṣaṭ*, *hanta*, *accha*, *vavam*, *vave*, *bhāva*.

Examples of forms based on genus (*jāti*) are: *kam*, *śam*, *yoḥ*, *mayaḥ*, *sāyam*, *prataḥ*, *astam*, *naktam*, *divā*, *doṣā*, *hyaḥ*, *śvaḥ*. Examples of forms based on technical names (*saṃjñā*) are: *kkip*, *saḥ*, *om*, *svāhā*, *hnāṃ*, *hnīṃ*, *klīṃ*, *brūṃ*, *diṅ*, *hleṅ*, *ṛṅ*, *juṅ*, *duṅ*. Examples of forms based on relations (*saṃbandha*) are: *antaḥ*, *antarā*, *ūdhrvam*, *bahiḥ*, *pāre*, *madhye*, *samāyā*, *nikaṣā*, *ārāt*, *viṣvak*, *puraḥ*, *paścāt*.

Those dependent on action (kriyā) in the case of non-sentient objects (*asattva*) and in distinctions of conjunction (*dvandva*) are: *yathā-dvandvam*, *yathā-yatham*, *mithaḥ*, *anyo'nyam*, *parasparam*, *itaretarām*, *paroparām*, *uttarādharam*, and *adharottaram*. Those dependent on both action and substance (*kriyā-dravya*) are: *śākam*, *sārdham*, *saha*, *samam*, *amā*, *vinā*, *ṛte*, *pṛthak*, and *nānā*. Adverbs (*kriyā-viśeṣaṇa*) are: *abhīkṣṇam*, *alam*, *balavat*, *suṣṭhu*, *mṛṣā*, *vṛthā*, *mithyā*, *mudhā*, *addhā*, *ṛdhak*, and *uccaiḥ*.

"Nucaiḥ" (softly), etc.; those whose form is entered by action (*kriyā*) are, for example: *śaśvat*, *sapadi*, *saṃprati*, *purā*, *asaṃprati*, *sanā*, *sāṃpratam*, *jātu*, *hāḍham*, *phāṇaṭam*, *svayam*, *kāmam*, *iti*; those whose form is entered by both action and substance (*kriyā-dravya*) are, for example: *āviḥ*, *prādiḥ*, *tiraḥ*, *sāśrāt*, *alam*, *prādhvam*, *sat*, *asat*, *dhik*, *hiruk*, *tūṣṇīm*, *joṣam*, *iti*.

The particles (*nipāta*), such as *ca* and others, are indeed a specific class of indeclinables (*avyaya*), because they denote objects that are non-substantial by virtue of causing the application of [grammatical categories] such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth; they are devoid of attachment to gender and number, and they fall upon various high and low objects. As it is said: "The particles beginning with *ca*, when not denoting a substance (*asattve*)."

Indeed, those [words] have the following purposes: the purpose of injunction (*vidhi*), the purpose of explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), the purpose of restatement (*anuvāda*), the purpose of prohibition (*niṣedha*), the purpose of both injunction and prohibition, and the purpose of neither injunction nor prohibition. Injunction consists of: command, censure, praise, despondency, joy, envy, and wonder. Explanatory praise consists of: recollection, comparison, admission, inquiry, the deeds of others, and ancient lore. Restatement consists of: prohibition, dismissal, removal, envy, reproach, and restraint. Prohibition consists of these.

For instance: *adhyom*, *adhyoḍhā*, *adhyeva jhaṭiti*, *ācchādayati*, and *mācchidat*. However, the prohibition of such substitutions as the subsequent form applies in the following cases: *eve cāniyoge*, *nāmreḍitasyāntyasya tu vā*, and *na māṅyoge*. For example: *adhaidava gaccha* (where *eva* is used in its restrictive sense), *ihaiva ihaiva tiṣṭha*, *paṭat*, *paṭaditi karoti*, *mā kārṣīt*, *mā sma kārṣīt*, and *mā sma karot*.

The prohibition of *saṃhitā* (euphonic combination) applies according to the rules: *“nipāta ekājanāṅ”* [Pāṇini 1.1.14], *“ot”* [1.1.15], and *“saṃbuddhau śākalyasyetāvanārṣe”* [1.1.16]; for example: *avehi*, *i indraṃ paśya*, *u uttiṣṭha*, *ā evaṃ nu manyase*, *aho*, *āścaryam*, *bhāno*.

The prohibition of word-substitutions and similar operations applies according to the rules: *“na cavāhāhaivayukte”* [8.1.24], *“nānejrñaḥ”* [8.2.3], and *“samāse'nañpūrve ktvo lyapa”* [7.1.37]; for example: *grāme yuṣmākaṃ ca grāmo'smākaṃ ca*, *grāmo yuṣmākameva grāmo'smākam eva*, *putram anijijñāsati*, and *snātvā bhuṅkte*.

There is a prohibition of *nighāta* (the loss of accentuation) according to the rules: “*nipātair yadyadīhantakuvinnecceccaṇkañcidyatrayuktam*,” “*cādiṣu ca*,” and “*cavāyoge prathamā*” [Pāṇini 8.1.30–34]. For example: *yad devadattaḥ pacati*, *yadi devadattaḥ pacati*, *devadattaḥ pacati ca khādati ca*, *devadattaḥ pacati vā khādati vā*, *gardabhāṃś ca kālayati vīṇāṃ ca parivādayati*, and *gardabhān vā kālayati vīṇāṃ vā parivādayati*.

Only a few particles (*nipāta*) are eligible for composition (*samāsa*), namely those listed as *gati*s: "the words beginning with *pra* when used in connection with a verb" (*prādayaḥ kriyāyoge*); "words beginning with *ūri*, as well as those ending in *cvi* and *ḍāc*" (*ūryādicviḍācaśca*); "an imitation [of a sound] provided it does not end in *iti*" (*anukaraṇaṃ cānitiparam*); "*kaṇe* and *manas* when there is a lack of faith" (*kaṇemanasī śraddhāpratīghāte*); "*puras* as an indeclinable" (*puro'vyayam*); "and *astas*" (*astaṃ ca*); "*acchas* in connection with verbs meaning 'to go' or 'to speak'" (*accha gatyarthavadeṣu*); "*adas* when not indicating instruction" (*ado'nupadeśe*); "*tiras* in the sense of disappearance" (*tiro'ntardhau*); "optionally before the root *kṛ*" (*vibhāṣā kṛñi*); "*upāje* and *anvāje*" (*upāje'nvāje*); "the group beginning with *sākṣāt*" (*sākṣātprabhṛtīni ca*); "*uras* and *manas* when not meaning 'to place upon'" (*anatyādhāna urasimanasī*); "also *madhye*, *pade*, and *nivacane*" (*madhyepadenivatane ca*); and "always... (*nityam*).

"Hasta" and "pāṇi" [are used] in the sense of taking by the hand; "prādhvam" in the sense of binding; "jīvikā" and "upaniṣad" in the sense of resemblance; "those two" (i.e., *gati* and *upasarga*) [occur] before the verbal root; [in] Vedic usage (*chandas*), they may also occur after [the root]; and they may also be separated [from the root] by other words.

Now, these are examples [of forms] used with the suffix *kṛt* (in the sense of making): *prapaciti*, *parākareti*, *kārikākaroti*, *śuklīkaroti*, *paṭapaṭākareti*, *paṭatkaroti*, *khāṭ karoti*, *satkaroti*, *asatkaroti*, *alaṃkṛtya*, *antahratya*, *kaṇepatya*, *manohatya*, *puraskṛtya*, *astaṃgatya*, *acchagatya*, *acchodhya*, *adaḥkṛtya*, *tirobhūya*, *tiraskṛtvā*, *tiraskṛtya*, *upojekṛtvā*, *upājekṛtya*, *anvāje kṛtvā*, *anvājekṛtya*, *sākṣāt kṛtvā*.

Having realized; having made false, *mithyākṛtvā*, *mithyākṛtya*; having placed upon the chest, *urasikṛtvā*, *urasikṛtya*; having placed in the mind, *manasikṛtvā*, *manasikṛtya*, *manasikṛtya*; having placed in the middle, *madhyekṛtvā*, *madhyekṛtya*; having placed on the foot, *padekṛtvā*, *padekṛtya*; having placed in the speech, *nivacanekṛtvā*, *nivacanekṛtya*; having placed in the hand, *hastekṛtya*, *pāṇaikṛtya*; having made favorable, *prādhvaṃkṛtya*, *prādhvaṃkṛtya*; having made a livelihood, *jīvikākṛtya*; having made a secret doctrine, *upaniṣatkṛtya*, *upaniṣatkṛtam*, "that which he makes a secret doctrine," *yadupanuṣatkaroti*, "that which he makes a secret doctrine."

The prefixes (*pra* and so forth) are indeed *upasargas* (prepositions/prefixes) that indicate a modification of motion. *Pra*, *para*, *apa*, *sam*, *anu*, *ava*, *ni*, *dus*, *vi*, *āṅ*, *ni*, *adhi*, as well as *ati*, *su*, *dur*, and *abhi*—these should be recognized along with *prati*; here, the definition applies to *pari* and *upa* as well. Bhāguri maintains the elision (*lopa*) of the initial vowel of these prefixes when followed by *ava* and *api*. In the case of *hitādi* and similar words, there is the elision of the *m* of *sam*, and here *śrat* is read between *antara* and *upa*. Thus, these twenty prefixes, together with *vaṣi*, *saścat*, *antar*, and *bhiḥ*, become twenty-five.

These [compounds] indeed are classified into six types: denoters (*vācaka*), illuminators (*dyotaka*), qualifiers (*viśeṣaka*), co-expressors (*sahābhidhāyaka*), those whose meaning is based on grammatical operation (*kāryārthaka*), and those that are meaningless (*nirarthaka*). Among these, the denoters are as follows: *pragatā ṛṣabhā asmād vanāt* (the bulls have departed from this forest) becomes *prarṣabhaṃ vanam*; *parāgatā asava asya* (his life-breaths have departed) becomes *parāsuḥ*; *apagato manyurasya* (his anger has departed) becomes *apamanyuḥ*; *saṅgatamakṣeṇa* (joined with the eye) becomes *samakṣam*; *anuprāptonāsikām* (reached the nose) becomes *anunāsikaḥ*; *avakruṣṭaḥ kokilayā* (called out by a cuckoo) becomes *avakokilaḥ*; and *abhāvo makṣikāṇām* (the absence of flies) becomes *nirmakṣikam*.

The absence of power among the Yavanas is *duryavana*; an opposing side is *vipakṣa*; that with which one fights by taking hold of it is *āyudha*; the absence of wind is *nivāta*; that which has not been reached by the eye is *adhyakṣa*; that in which the *śala* tree is covered is *apiśala*; a boar that has passed beyond hearing is *atiśrva*; the abundance of auspicious things is *subhadra*; that which has risen excessively is *uttama*; that which has its face directed toward something is *abhimukha*; a body that is to be repelled is *pratikāya*; [the word] for study is *parigrahaṇa*.

From *paryadhyayana* comes *upādhyāya*, for one approaches and studies from him; likewise, from *avagata-vām-koṭa* comes *vateṭa*; from *apihita-kāyin* comes *apika*; from *saṃpanna-brahman* comes *sabrahma* among the descendants of Bābhrava; from *śraddhīyate* comes *śraddhā*; and from *antardhīyate* comes *antardhi*. Thus [it is explained].

The indicatory letters (*dyotaka*) are as follows: *pratiṣṭhate*, *parākramate*, *apakaroti*, *saṃkrīḍati*, *anukampate*, *avadhatte*, *nirviveśa*, *durlalitaḥ*, *vyādadāti*, *āhvayate*, *niśamayati*, *adhikuruṣva*, *apidadhāti*, *atiśete surabhiḥ*, *ullāpayati*, *abhidhatte*, *pratīkṣate*, *pariṇamate*, *upāyaṃsta*, *evaṃ vadhate*, *pidhatte*, *śraddhatte*, *sahitaḥ*, and *antardadhāti*.

There are qualifiers (*viśeṣaka*); they are twofold: qualifiers of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) and qualifiers of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*). Examples of qualifiers of the meaning of the base are: *pravardhate*, *palāyate*, *apavadate*, *saṃsarati*, *anumanyate*, *avalokate*, *subhavati*, *udbhavati*, *abhyeti*, *pratipadyate*, *parigaṇayati*, *upadadhāti*; likewise: *vataṃsaḥ*, *pinaddhavān*, *satatam*, *śraddhaḥ*, and *antarbhavati*.

The suffixes that specify the meaning of the object (*pratyayārtha-viśeṣaka*) are as follows: *manasvī* becomes *sumanāyate*, *durmanāyate*; likewise, *abhimanyate*; he raises his tail—*utpucchayate*; he spreads it out—*vipucchayate*; he turns it around—*paripucchayate*; he arranges his belongings—*saṃbhāṇḍayate*; he gathers his robe—*saṃcīvarayate*; he throws with the hand—*apahastayati*; he arms himself—*saṃvarmayati*; he fastens with a noose—*saṃpāśayati*.

He scatters with powders, he covers; he winnows with cotton, he fans; he cuts with a razor, he shaves; he praises with verses, he flatters; he strokes the hair, he combs; he unties the snares, he releases; he beats the chaff, he winnows; he gazes at the form, he looks intently; he puts on a garment, he clothes; he removes the saddle, he unsaddles—thus [it is said].

But why do these [words] not also become denoters of specific actions? For whatever is understood from the employment of a word is its denotation. This is not so; because by rules such as "after *bhṛśa* and others, when *bhū* follows, except for *acvi*," the suffix arises only in the sense of becoming (*bhavati*) and so forth.

Do not speak thus; I do not ask about the *kyaj*-anta [derivative], but rather the *ṇij*-anta. In that case, the rule "after *śabda*, *vaira*, *kalaha*, *abhra*, *kaṇva*, and *medha*, when the sense is 'instrument' (*karaṇa*)" applies. Consequently, since the suffixes *ṇiṅ* and *ṇic* are prescribed to denote the general meaning of the verbal root—characterized by the sense of "doing"—in expressions such as *utpucchyate* ("he performs the lifting up of the tail") and *abhiṣeṇayati* ("he makes an attack with an army"), these words possess denotative power (*vācakatva*) because the suffix expresses the sense of "doing," while the prefix expresses specific actions such as "lifting up" or "attack."

It will be so. It is said in response: here, by the word *karaṇa* ("instrument"), it is not the general action (*kriyāsāmānya*) that accompanies the meaning of all verbal roots (*dhātu*) which is indicated; rather, it refers specifically to particular actions such as shaving (*udvapanā*), mixing (*miśraṇa*), and so forth, whose specific natures have not yet been determined.

If one asks how this is known, the activity of the Teacher (*ācārya*) makes it known: he provides examples for the suffix [denoting] the instrument alone after the roots *muṇḍ*, *miśra*, *ślakṣṇa*, and *lavaṇa*. For instance: *muṇḍayati* (he shaves), similarly *miśrayati* (he mixes), *ślakṣṇayati* (he smoothes), and *lavaṇayati* (he seasons with salt).

From *hala*, *kali*, *kṛta*, and *tvaca*, [the suffix *ṇic* is applied] when the sense is "to seize" (*grahaṇa*), specifically in its various nuances: as in *halam agrahīt* → *ajahalat*, *kalim agrahīt* → *acakalat*, *kṛtaṃ gṛhṇāti* → *kṛtayati*, and *tvacaṃ gṛhṇāti* → *tvacayati*. From *varṇa*, *satya*, *artha*, and *veda*, [the suffix *ṇic* is applied] when the meaning of the verbal root is qualified by a prefix (*upasarga*) in the sense of "he describes" (*ācaṣṭe*): as in *varṇam ācaṣṭe* → *varṇayati*, *satyam ācaṣṭe* → *satyāpayati*, *arthāpayati*, and *vedam ācaṣṭe* → *vedāpayati*. From *vrata*, [the suffix *ṇic* is applied] in the sense of eating (*bhojana*) and the cessation thereof (*tannivṛtti*).

Just as one says "he vows milk" (*payo vratayati*) or "he vows the food of a low-born man" (*vṛṣalānnaṃ vratayati*), it is understood from this that the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), whose specific nature has not yet been determined, is taken up as the object denoted by the suffix in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa*).

If that were the case, then since the specific action qualified by its adjunct would already have been expressed by the suffix, the employment of prefixes (*upasarga*) in forms such as *abhiṣeṇayati* would not be possible—just as in *śyenāyate* (he acts like a hawk), *bāṣpāyate* (he emits steam), *hastayate* (he grasps with the hand), and *pādayate* (he protects). This [objection] would hold true where there is only a single meaning for the suffix, as in the rules: "after a word denoting a standard of comparison, [the suffix *kyac* is added] in the sense of 'acting like'"; "after *bāṣpa* and *ūṣman*, in the sense of 'emitting'"; and "after a body part, in the sense of 'expelling'."

In this case, however, there are many meanings of the suffix (*pratyaya*), such as: "after *puccha*, [the suffix *ṇic* is applied] in the sense of biting and spreading," "after *bhāṇḍa*, in the sense of collecting and dividing," "after *cīvara*, in the sense of acquiring and wearing," and "after *muṇḍa* and so forth, in the senses of 'one does that,' 'one describes that,' 'one overcomes by means of that,' or 'one has gone by means of that. In those instances, even though a specific action is included [in the rule], because its form is common [to other actions], it cannot be determined solely from the suffix; therefore, a specific prefix (*upasarga*) is employed to delimit it, just as in the view where the prefix qualifies the meaning of the suffix.

Since the suffix *kyaṅ* itself arises from the word *manas* and expresses the meaning of the root *bhū* as qualified by the sense of the prefix (*upasarga*), the prefixes *su*, *dur*, and *abhi* are employed [separately] in forms such as *sumanāyate*, *durmanāyate*, and *abhimanāyate*. If that were the case, then just as in *hastinā atikrāmati* → *atihastayati* and so forth, one would expect the employment of the prefix *āṅ* in cases such as *aśvam ācaṣṭe* → *āśvayati*. This is not so; for in these instances, the prefix *āṅ* is expressed as being inherent [to the verbal base].

For, unlike [words such as] *krāmati* and so forth, a solitary word like *caṣṭe* does not possess the capacity to convey its own meaning; therefore, these [suffixes] function solely as qualifiers (*viśeṣaka*) and are not denotative (*vācaka*).

Now, along with their respective verbal suffixes (abhidhāyaka), they are as follows: *praṇute*, *praṇiti*, *prapañcati*, *prāpnoti*, *saṃgrāmayate*, *saṃcaṣṭe*, *saṃrambhate*, *saṃdhukṣayati*, *anurudhyate*, *viklavate*, *vilokate*, *viśrāṇayati*, *ācaṣṭe*, *āśāste*, *ācāmati*, *ātaṅkayati*, *nidrāyati*, *niyamayate*, *adhīte*, *adhyeti*, *abhivādayate*, *pariṣvajate*, *ujjāsayati*, and *uttaṃsayati*.

Examples of [roots] used for the sake of the object (*kāryārtha*) are: *vijayate*, *parājayate*, *nyavikṣata*, *samagaṃsta*, *anvakarot*, *parākarot*, *virarāma*, *upararāma*, *udasiṣyati*, *udasiṣyate*, *apaskirate*, *praticaskāra*, *upaskurute*, *plāyate*, *prārṣabhīyati*, *niṣṭapati*, *abhiṣṭauti*, *viṣahate*, *pariṣvajate*, *viṣvaṇati*, *prahiṇoti*, *praṇaśyati*, *pariṇeṣyati*, *antarṇayati*. Thus [ends the section].

They are meaningless when used as follows: *prārabhate*, *pralambate*, *prasūyate*, *prayacchati*, *apaharati*, *apahnute*, *apatrapate*, *abhiṣuṇoti*, *nimīlati*, *nivāryate*, *niṣṭhīvati*, *nimajjati*, *nikhañjati*, *vigāhate*, *virājate*, *vijānāti*, *vinaśyati*, *vikatthate*, *vidīryate*, *āśrayati*, *āśliṣyati*, *saṃyujyate*, *adhyāgacchati*, and *paryāgacchati*.

The *prādayaḥ* (prefixes and particles beginning with *pra*) alone, when they serve as the cause for delimiting a relationship produced by a specific action, are called *karmapravacanīya*. As it has been said: "In the manifestation of relationships produced by specific actions, those [particles] determined to be the cause [of that manifestation] are *karmapravacanīya*."

What, then, is the restriction regarding these? Within the governing rule for the designation *karmapravacanīya*, there are eleven words beginning with *anu* and twenty-two meanings beginning with *lakṣaṇa*. They are as follows: “*anu* [is used] in the sense of a mark (*lakṣaṇa*)”; “in the sense of the third case (*tṛtīyārtha*)”; “in the sense of inferiority (*hīna*)”; “*upa* [is used] in the sense of superiority (*adhika*) and [inferiority]”; “*apa* and *pari* [are used] in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*)”; “*āṅ* [is used] in the sense of a limit (*maryādā*)”; “*prati*, *pari*, and *anu* [are used] in the senses of a mark, description of a state (*itthaṃbhūtākhyāna*), share (*bhāga*), and distribution (*vīpsā*)”; “*adhi* and *pari* [are used] when they are meaningless (*anarthaka*)”; “*su-* [is used] in the sense of praise (*pūjā*)”; “*ati-* [is used] in the sense of exceeding (*atikramaṇa*) and [surpassing]”; “*api-*...”

[The prepositions *anu*, *upa*, *apa*, *pari*, *āṅ*, *prati*, *abhi*, *adhi*, *su*, *ati*, *api* signify] "possibility of a thing" (*padārthasaṃbhāvanā*), "permission" (*anvavasarga*), "reproach" (*garhā*), and "conjunction" (*samuccaya*) [according to Pāṇini 1.4.90]; "over" (*adhi*) and "around" (*pari*) [signify the sense of] "sovereignty" (*aiśvarya*) [according to 1.4.97]; and [the suffix] *kṛt* [is used] optionally [after these] [according to 1.4.98]. Thus, there are eleven words: *anu*, *upa*, *apa*, *pari*, *āṅ*, *prati*, *abhi*, *adhi*, *su*, *ati*, and *api*. There are twenty-two meanings: the definition of a cause (*hetulakṣaṇa*), the sense of accompaniment (*sahārtha*), inferiority (*hīnatā*), superiority (*ādhikya*), exclusion (*varjana*), futility (*ānarthakya*), honor (*pūjā*), transgression (*ātikramaṇa*), the meaning of a word (*padārtha*), possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*), permission (*anvavasarga*), reproach (*garhā*), conjunction (*samuccaya*), ownership (*svāmya*), and authority (*adhikāra*).

In this regard, *anu* has seven meanings; *prati* and *pari* have six meanings each; *api* has five meanings; *adhi* and *abhi* have three meanings each; *upa* and *ati* have two meanings each; and *āṅ* and *apa* have one meaning each.

In these cases, *anu* is a *karmapravacanīya* when it signifies cause (*hetu*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), accompaniment (*sahārtha*), deficiency (*hīnatālakṣaṇa*), description of a state (*itthaṃbhūtākhyāna*), portion (*bhāga*), and distribution (*vīpsā*); and in connection with it, the second case ending is employed. Examples are as follows: *śākalyasya saṃhitāmanu prāvarṣat* (it rained after [in accordance with] Śākalya’s recitation of the *saṃhitā*); *parvatamanvavasitā senā* (the army encamped along the mountain); *anuśākaṭāyanaṃ vaiyākaraṇāḥ* (the grammarians follow Śākaṭāyana); *vṛkṣamanu vidyotate vidyut* (the lightning flashes across the tree); *sādhardevadatto mātaramanu* (Devadatta is inferior to his mother); *yadatra māmanu syāt* (whatever may be equal to me here); *vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣamanu tiṣṭhati* (he stands at every tree).

This [particle *anu*] is neither an indicator of an action (*kriyā*) nor an expresser of a relation (*saṃbandha*); nor does it imply a verbal root for action; rather, it is a differentiator of a relation. For instance, in the case of "It rained after Śākalya’s *saṃhitā*" (*śākalyasya saṃhitāmanuprāvarṣat*), the relationship between the cause and the effect—the *saṃhitā* and the rain—is one of the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and this is made manifest by the particle *anu*, as in: "Having heard Śākalya’s *saṃhitā*, it rained. This should be understood in other cases as well. Thus, *anu* has seven meanings.

The particle *pari* is used in the senses of indication (*lakṣaṇa*), description of a state (*itthaṃbhūtākhyāna*), division (*bhāga*), exclusion (*vīpsā*), and rejection (*avarjana*). It likewise governs the accusative case in four instances and the ablative case in two: as in *vṛkṣaṃ pari vidyotate* (it flashes around the tree), *sādhur devadatto mātaraṃ pari* (Devadatta is kind toward his mother), *yad atra māṃ pari syāt* (whatever may be left over for me here), *vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣaṃ pari sekaḥ* (watering each and every tree), *paripari trigartebhyo vṛṣṭo devaḥ* (the rain fell on all sides around the Trigartas), and *“viśrvapsniyā viśrvataspari”* (all-encompassing on every side). Thus ends the section on *pari*. Regarding *prati*, there are six [instances].

The particle *api* is used in the senses of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*), permission (*anvavasarga*), censure (*garhā*), and conjunction (*samuccaya*). In these cases, its designation as a prefix (*upasarga*) is set aside. Here, "word-meaning" (*padārtha*) refers to the meaning of another word that is not explicitly employed. For example: *sarpiṣo 'pi syāt*, *madhuno 'pi syāt* ("there might be even a bit of ghee," "there might be even a bit of honey"). In this sense, the word *api* functions to express a small measure, a drop, or a little. Possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*) is the manifestation of the non-obstruction of power through the expression of an additional meaning. Examples include: *api siñcen mūlakasahasram* ("one might even water a thousand radishes") and *api stuyād rājānam* ("one might even praise the king").

The suffix *api* signifies permission to act at will (*kāmacārānujñāna*) when used as a prefix (*upasarga*). For example: *api siñca*, "you may water [it]"; *api stuhi*, "you may praise. It also signifies censure (*nindā*), which is a form of reproach (*garhā*). Thus, *stuhi api* means "praise [him] even [if he is blameworthy]" and *siñca api* means "water [it] even [if it is unworthy]. Because the designation as a prefix (*upasarga-saṃjñā*) is sublated, the change to the sibilant *ṣ* (ṣatva) does not occur. Thus, *api* has five meanings.

In the section concerning the meaninglessness of *adhi*, it is treated as a *karmapravacanīya* with respect to other [meanings]. In its first two senses—namely, "motion" (*gati*) and "attainment" (*prāpti*)—it does not undergo elision of accent (*nighāta*) and so forth, because it subverts the technical designations of "motion" (*gati*) and "preverb" (*upasarga*) by the rules "in the case of motion and attainment" (*gatiprāptau*) and "when followed by a verb ending with an acute accent" (*tiṅi codāttavati*). For example: *kuto 'dhyāgacchati* ("whence does he come from? and *yad atra mām adhikariṣyati* ("that which will appoint me here"). But in the sense of "lordship" (*svāmya*), when used in conjunction with *adhi*, the locative case sometimes occurs for the lord (*svāmin*), and sometimes for the subject (*sva*). For example: *adhi brahmadatte pañcālāḥ* ("the Pañcālas are under Brahmadatta's rule") and *adhi pañcāleṣu brahmadattaḥ* ("Brahmadatta is the lord over the Pañcālas").

The preposition *abhi* is used twice to express three meanings: indication (*lakṣaṇa*), description of a state (*itthaṃbhūtākhyāna*), and repetition (*vīpsā*). For example: *vṛkṣam abhi vidyotate* (It lightens toward the tree), *sādhur devadatto mātaram abhi* (Devadatta is kind toward his mother), and *vṛkṣaṃ vṛkṣam abhi siñcati* (He waters tree after tree). Thus, *adhi* and *abhi* each have three meanings.

The preposition *upa* is used with two meanings: inferiority (*hīna*) and proximity (*adhika*). In these cases, the second and seventh case endings are applied respectively, as in *upārjunam yoddhāraḥ* ("the warriors are inferior to Arjuna") and *upa khāryāṃ droṇaḥ* ("a *droṇa* measure is close to a *khārī*"). The preposition *ati* is used in the senses of honor (*pūjā*) and transgression (*atikramaṇa*). In the sense of honor—that is, praise—it is as in *bhavatā ati siktam etat* ("this has been well-watered by you"). Because [in this context] it is designated as an *upasarga*, the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* does not occur. Thus, *upa* and *ati* have two meanings each. The preposition *āṅ* is used when expressing a limit (*maryādā*), and it causes the fifth case ending to be employed, as in *ā pāṭaliputrād vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("it rained as far as Pāṭaliputra").

By the mention of the word "vacana" (speech/utterance), inclusive limit (*abhividhi*) is also included; in that case as well, this very same example applies. The word *apa* causes the fifth case (*pañcamī*) to arise in the sense of exclusion (*varjana*): *apa trigartebhyo vṛṣṭo devaḥ* ("the god has rained away from the Trigartas"). The word *su* in the sense of praise (*pūjā*) subverts its designation as a prefix (*upasarga*); thus, in *sustutaṃ bhavatā* ("well-praised by you") and *susiktaṃ bhavatā* ("well-sprinkled by you"), the change to *ṣ* does not occur. Thus, *āṅ*, *apa*, and *su* have identical meanings [in these specific contexts].

Indeclinables (*avyaya*) are imitations of words ending in nominal or verbal suffixes that resemble case-endings; they are each sixfold: those whose meaning is the base (*prakṛti*), those whose meaning is the suffix (*pratyaya*), those whose meaning is both, those whose meaning is neither, those whose meaning is that of another base, and those whose meaning is that of another suffix.

Among those, those ending in sup (nouns) have meanings belonging to the base (*prakṛti*), such as *uccais*, *nīcais*, *cirāya*, and *vihāyasā*; those having meanings belonging to the suffix (*pratyaya*), such as *ārāt*, *akasmāt*, *ekapade*, and *prage*; and those having meanings belonging to both, such as *śāyam*, *svayam*, *pāre*, and *madhye*. Those ending in tiṅ (verbs) have meanings belonging to the base, such as *manye*, *śaṅke*, *aye*, and *āma*; those having meanings belonging to the suffix, such as *ehi*, *apehi*, *paśya*, and *paśyata*; and those having meanings belonging to both, such as *asti*, *asmi*, and *brūhi*.

Those [words] whose meaning pertains to neither [of the two categories] are, for example: *yāti*, *na yāti*, *vartate*, *na vartate*. Those whose meaning pertains to another base (*prakṛti*) are, for example: *astu*, *bhavatu*, *pūryate*, *āsa*. Those whose meaning pertains to another suffix (*pratyaya*) are, for example: *āha*, *syāt*, *stuyāt*, *bhūyāt*. In the section on indeclinables, under the rule "that which begins with a vowel and is listed [in the Gaṇapāṭha] is an indeclinable" (*svarādinipātam avyayam*), the following are recited: "a form ending in a kṛt-suffix that ends in -e or -ai is an indeclinable" (*kṛnmejantaḥ*), "forms in -ktvā, -tosun, and -kasun are indeclinables" (*ktvātosunkasunaḥ*), "a taddhita suffix that does not take all case-endings is an indeclinable" (*taddhitaś cāsarvavibhaktiḥ*), and "an avyayībhāva compound is an indeclinable" (*avyayībhāvaś ca*)."

In that regard, there are six types of *kṛt* suffixes used in the spoken language (*bhāṣā*): *ām*, *ktvā*, *lyap*, *tumun*, *ṇamul*, and *svañ*. These *kṛt* suffixes function as: (1) the form of the action itself (*kriyārūpa*), (2) the form of the result of the action (*kriyāphalarūpa*), (3) the form of an adverbial modifier of the action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇarūpa*), (4) the form of a limit of the action (*kriyāvadhirūpa*), (5) the form of the object of the action (*kriyākarmarūpa*), and (6) the form of the agent of the action (*kriyākartṛrūpa*). Among these, examples of those that are the form of the action itself (*kriyārūpa*) are: *cakāsāñcakāra*, *kārayāmāsa*, *bibharāṃbabhūva*, *vidāṃkurvantu*, *alaṃ kṛtvā*, *khalu kṛtvā*, *alamālapya*, *khalvālapya*, *alaṃ bhoktum*, and *kālo bhoktum*.

[The following illustrate] the forms of adverbs of manner (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*): *sahate*, "he endures"; *bhoktum bhuṅkte*, "he eats in order to eat"; *paktum pacati*, "he cooks in order to cook"; *bhoktum glāyati*, "he is weary of eating"; *bhoktum prabhavati*, "he is able to eat. [Examples of such forms include: *yathetthakāram*, "in this way"; *anyathākāram*, "otherwise"; *yathākāram*, "as it is"; *tathākāram*, "so"; *uccaiḥkāram*, "loudly"; *tiryakkāram*, "sideways"; *mukhataḥkāram*, "from the mouth"; *nānābhāvam*, "in various ways"; *dvidhābhāvam*, "twofold"; *tūṣṇīmbhāvam*, "silently"; *anvagbhāvam*, "following after. [The following illustrate] the forms of adverbs of limit (*kriyāvadhi*): *bhikṣitvā vrajati*, "having begged, he goes"; *apamitya yajate*, "having borrowed, he sacrifices"; *agre-bhojam vrajati*, "he goes while eating first"; *dvyahātyāyam gāḥ*, "cows that have been kept for two days."

He causes [her] to drink; when there is an increase of two finger-breadths, he cuts the pieces of sugar-cane; rising from his bed, he goes to the king’s gate; at the sight of a maiden, he chooses her as a bride; he feeds the Brahmins according to the Veda; as long as one is able to eat throughout life, so too one *dhṛṣṇoti* (dares), *bhoktum* (to eat); one *jānāti* (knows how) to eat; one *pārayati* (is able/perfects) to eat; one *prakramate* (sets out/undertakes) to eat; one *labhate* (obtains/is entitled) to eat; one *arhati* (deserves) to eat; one *icchati* (wishes) to eat; one *kāmayate* (desires) to eat; thus, one wishes to seek (*eṣitum icchati*) and desires to desire (*kamitum kāmayate*).

An example of [an accusative] having the form of an action-part (*kriyāvayava*) is as follows: "He eats with radish-sides" (*mūlakopadaṃśaṃ bhuṅkte*), "he drives the cows by striking them with a staff" (*daṇḍopadhātaṃ gāḥ kālayati*), "he sleeps pressing against his side" (*pārśvopavīḍaṃ śete*), "he lets the cows graze blocking the path" (*vrajoparodhaṃ gāḥ sādayati*), "he raises him up pulling him by the hand" (*pāṇyupakarṣam utthāpayati*), "they fight seizing each other by the hair" (*keśagrāhaṃ yudhyante*), "he talks knitting his brows" (*bhrūvikṣepaṃ jalpati*), "he sits entering the house" (*gehānupraveśam āste*), "he calls him by name" (*nāmagrāham ākārayati*), "he reviles him calling him a thief" (*coraṃkāram ākrośati*), "he eats making it tasty" (*svāduṃkāraṃ bhuṅkte*), or "he eats having made it tasty" (*svādūkṛtya bhuṅkte*).

Furthermore, there are indeed instances where the form of a verbal root occurs as a member of a compound denoting the object of an action (*krayākarma*): for example, *śvapoṣaṃ puṣyati* (he nourishes [himself] by rearing dogs), *ātmapeṣaṃ puṣṇāti* (he nourishes [himself] by grinding for himself), *gopoṣaṃ puṣyati* (he nourishes [himself] by rearing cows), *raipāṣaṃ puṣṇāti* (he nourishes [himself] by tending cattle); *nimusakāṣaṃ kaṣati* (he scrapes [it] down to the roots), *samūlaghātaṃ hanti* (he kills [them] by destroying them root and branch), *pāṇighātaṃ vedimāhanti* (he strikes the altar with a blow of the hand); *śuṣkapeṣaṃ pinaṣṭi* (he grinds dryly), *cūrṇapeṣaṃ pinaṣṭi* (he grinds into powder), *rūkṣapeṣaṃ pinaṣṭi* (he grinds coarsely), *udapeṣaṃ pinaṣṭi* (he grinds with water); *akṛtakāraṃ karoti* (he does what has not been done), *jīvagrāhaṃ gṛhṇāti* (he seizes [him] alive), *hastagrāhaṃ gṛhṇāti* (he seizes him by the hand), *hastavarte vartayati* (he turns him around by the hand).

The crest has perished; gold was deposited as a treasure; the rice-porridge was cooked; he was bound in the "crane-knot" (krauñcabandha); he perishes with the loss of his livelihood; he carries a man's load; the parrot is dried at the top; it is filled to the brim at the top. Thus.

In the Vedic language (*chandas*), there are twenty-four remaining [kṛt suffixes], namely: *eś*, *ken*, *tavai*, *ke*, *se*, *kem*, *ase*, *asen*, *kse*, *kasem*, *adhyai*, *adhyain*, *kadhyai*, *kadhyain*, *śadhyai*, *śadhyain*, *taveṅ*, *kai*, *iṣyai*, *ṇamul*, *kamul*, *tosun*, and *kasun*. Among these, *eś* and *ken* are used in the sense of the gerundive (*kṛtya*): for example, *avacakṣe* (with *eś*) and *nāvagāhe* (with *ken*).

The *kṛtya* suffixes are used in the sense of the verbal noun (*kṛtyārtha*) and in the sense of the infinitive (*tum-artha*). For example, in the sense of the verbal noun: *paridhātavai*, *paristaritavai*; in the sense of the infinitive: *somam indrāya pātave*, *anvetave*. There are seventeen [suffixes] beginning with *kā* used in the sense of the infinitive (*tum-artha*). Among them, ten are as follows: *viśvāya sūryam vikhye tvā harāmi*, *se vakṣe rāyaḥ*, *sen tā vāmeṣe rathānām*, *ase kratve dakṣāya jīvase*, *kasem apy evaṃrīpaḥ*. There is a difference in accent (*svara*). *Adhyai* is used in the sense of "to desire" (*kāmam upācaradhyai*); *adhyai* is also of this form, but there is a difference in accent.

The distinction is this: "When shall Indra and Agni be invoked for the sake of offering? When shall they be praised for the sake of glory? For the sake of drinking, for the sake of exhilaration, and for the sake of rejoicing together? For thee, in the tenth month, so that [the Soma] may be pressed; for thee, O Indra, so that the Soma may be drunk? To go to the worlds of light, to perform [the sacrifice], and to carry it away; for what purpose? To proceed toward the gods, for the impelling of the waters and the growth of the plants—for their non-falling away; that is to say, for their growth and for their stability."

The suffixes *ṇamul* and *kamul* are used precisely in the sense of possibility (*śaki*). For example: "O gods, we were not able to divide the fire. Regarding the suffixes *tosun* and *kasun* used in the sense of capability (*īśvare*): "They sit down so as to know the ritual arrangement," "It is to be established before the rising of the sun," "For the purpose of driving away the calves at a later time," "One must offer into the fire before it begins to roar," "One must offer in the Āgnīdhra shed before the [sacrificial] procession begins," "He stands vigilant until the offering is made," "He stands worshipping until the [oblation] is consumed," "We shall come together until the [enemy] is struck down," "Before the spreading of the cruel [weapon]," "Before..."

From the *jatru* [section], the *ātṛga* [section follows]. Regarding the secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) that do not end in case endings (*al-arvavibhakti*), there is the rule: "The suffixes beginning with *tasil* and ending before *pāśap*, those ending before the *samāsānta* suffixes, those ending in *m*, those having the sense of *kṛtvas*, and *tas*, *vat*, *nānā*, and *añ*"—for example: *yataḥ*, *tatra*, *iha*, *kva*, *ekadā*, *etarhi*, *adhunā*, *idānīm*, *sadyaḥ*, *parut*, *parāri*, *aiṣamaḥ*, *adya*, *paredyavi*, *pūrvedyuḥ*, *sarvathā*, *itthām*, *purastāt*, *prāk*, *adhaḥ*, *upari*, *upariṣṭāt*, *puraḥ*, *paścāt*, *dakṣiṇāt*.

*dakṣiṇā*, *dakṣiṇāhi*, *dakṣiṇena*, *dakṣiṇataḥ*; *dvidhā*, *dvaidhā*, *dvaidham*; *aikadhyam*; *bahuśo dehi* (give many times); *vāsudevataḥ prati*; *śuklībhavati* (becomes white); *agnisāt saṃpadyate* (is reduced to fire); *devatrāgacchati* (goes among the gods); *paṭapaṭākaroti* (makes a clattering sound); *paṭatitarām* (more clatteringly); *bahukṛtvo bhuṅkte* (eats many times), *dvirbhuṅkte* (eats twice), *sakṛdbhuṅkte* (eats once); *bahudhā bhuṅkte* (eats in many ways); *ādito bhavati* (comes from the beginning); *brāhmaṇavad bravīti* (speaks like a Brāhmaṇa); *vinā devadattam* (without Devadatta); *nānā devadattam* (apart from Devadatta)—the *avyayībhāva* compound is thus twofold.

The meaning consisting of a sentient being (*sattvabhūtārtha*) and the meaning not consisting of a sentient being (*asattvabhūtārtha*). Of these two, the meaning consisting of a sentient being is, for example: *upakumbham* (near the jar), *sumadram* (well-Madra), *duryavanm* (ill-Yavana), *nirmakṣikam* (free from flies), *niśītam* (without cold), *sabrahma* (together with Brahmā), *bahirgrāmam* (outside the village), *supapratim* (good at reciting), *madhyesamudram* (in the middle of the ocean), *dvimuni* (two sages), *pañcanadam* (five rivers), and *lohitagaṅgam* (the red Ganges).

An object that does not exist as a real entity [is expressed] as follows: *pratyurasam* (against the chest), *anuratham* (alongside the chariot), *pratyartham* (for each object), *yathāśakti* (according to one's power), *sacakram* (with the wheel), *yāvadamatram* (as much as a vessel holds), *paritrigartam* (all around Trigarta), *āpāṭaliputram* (as far as Pāṭaliputra), *abhyagni* (toward the fire), *dvipari* (twice over), and *anugaṅgaṃ vāraṇasī* (Vārāṇasī along the Gaṅgā). Mimicry (*anukaraṇa*) is the designation of a word by means of its own form. Furthermore, mimicries are expressions characterized by a resemblance to manifest or unmanifest phonemes, words, and sentences.

In that regard, an example of the expression of similarity through distinct phonemes (*vyaktavarṇasādṛśya*) is as follows: "When [Rāvaṇa’s] head, severed and falling into the fire, was forcibly addressed by Hara with the words 'Sva! and 'He!', she became Svāhā herself—this is that very Rāvaṇa. An example of the expression of similarity through distinct words (*vyaktapadasādṛśya*) is as follows: "O beloved of mine, desiring your welfare, I wish to speak; but as you depart, words of refusal issue from my mouth. 'Do not go'—what can I do?"

An example of a statement based on similarity to distinct words is as follows: "You are my life, you are my second heart; you are the moonlight for my eyes, you are nectar for my limbs. Having won over that charming girl with hundreds of such endearments, she was then at peace—or rather, what is the use of anything further? An example of a statement based on similarity to indistinct phonemes is as follows: "When midnight has passed, those clouds of the rainy season thunder very softly..."

The night, like a cow, lowed "hum" at that lunar orb as it appeared like her calf. An example of an expression using words with indistinct phonetic similarity (*avyakta-pada-sādṛśya*) is as follows: "Purify [the world]—the fire born from the friction of the five-pronged discus against the chest of Hari, the king of the enemies of the gods, as it strikes with a *caṭañ-caṭit* sound upon the skin, a *ñcit* sound upon the quivering blood, a *dhagad-dhagit* sound upon the fat, and a *ṣṭhāgit* sound upon the bones."

An example of speech resembling an unintelligible utterance is as follows: "Pipipriya! Sasasvayam! Give me mumumukhāsava! Tatatya-ja! Dududrutam! Bhabhabhabhājam! Kāṇṭanam! Kāñcanam! This faltering chatter of the fawn-eyed woman, intoxicated by wine at dawn, was studied by her companions for the sake of laughter.

By this, the correctness (*sādhutva*) of those words which are correct and meaningful, those which are to be cooked (i.e., derived), that form of speech which is incorrect due to incapacity, those corrupt forms (*apabhraṃśa*), those phonemes which are meaningless, and those utterances of unmanifest phonemes, words, and sentences—as well as the imitation thereof—is established.

Now, is it not the case that imitation results in correctness (*sādhutva*)—whether it be the imitation of the learned in acts such as giving or studying, or of the unlearned in acts such as laughing or clearing one's throat, provided these are not prohibited? It does not result from the imitation of what is prohibited; for instance, if one were to cut down a plantain trunk while imitating someone who says, "He kills a Brahmin," I do not think he would thereby become an outcast (*patita*). Furthermore, an imitation is not itself an incorrect word (*apaśabda*), for if it were, it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that every other [instance] would likewise be an incorrect word.

Furthermore, one who employs an incorrect word (*apaśabda*) while imitating another who has employed such an incorrect word in its denotative meanings becomes, indeed, a user of incorrect words themselves. The verbal roots and suffixes that denote action (*bhāva*) and grammatical participant (*kāraka*)—namely, the *kṛt* suffixes—are of six types of indicators (*liṅgin*): those with different indicators, those with their own indicators, those without indicators, those dependent on capacity (*śakti*), and those dependent on subsequent application (*anuprayoga*), and so forth.

Among these, those denoting substances (*dravyavacana*) such as *aṇ* and others possess their own gender (*liṅgin*), as in: *kumbhakāraḥ*, *paṅkajam*, *dhātrī*, *dātram*, *kārūḥ*, and *kṛkavākuḥ*. Those denoting qualities (*guṇavacana*) such as *ṇvul* and others take the gender of another word (*anyaliṅgin*), as in: *kārakaḥ*, *kārikā*, *kārakam*, *darśanīyaḥ*, *darśanīyā*, and *darśanīyam*. Those whose gender is fixed by the very nature of their formation, such as those formed by the rule "the suffix *ktin* is used for feminine" (*striyāṃ ktin*), possess the feminine gender (*striliṅgin*), as in: *paktiḥ*, *pacanam*, *pākaḥ*, *vrajaḥ*, *śayyā*, and *suptam*.

However, suffixes such as *tumun* and others, which do not grasp the capacity for gender and number because their meaning is not that of a sentient being (*asattvabhūta*), are themselves devoid of gender; for example: *kālo bhoktum*, *alaṃ kṛtvā*, *khalu prahṛtya*, *nāvagāhe*, *īśvaro 'bhicetitoḥ*, and *īśvaro vilikhaḥ*.

The suffixes *śatṛ* and others depend upon potentiality (*śakti*), cause (*hetu*), and the expectation of implied action (*lakṣyakriyā*) and so forth; they depend on potentiality and the like, as in: *vrajatā kṛtam* ("done by one who is going"), *kriyamāṇaṃ paśya* ("see it being done"), *ārjayam vasati* ("he dwells while earning"), *caṅkramyamāṇo'dhīte* ("he studies while walking about"), *pakṣyam vrajati* ("he goes intending to cook"), and *bhojake vrajati* ("he goes to the feeder"). Similarly, the suffixes *ṇamul*, *lu*, and others depend on the connection with subsequent application (*anuprayoga*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and so forth; they depend on such subsequent applications, as in: *raipoṣaṃ puṣyati* ("he thrives with the thriving of wealth"), *coraṃkāram ākrośati* ("he reviles him calling him a thief"), *kārayāñcakāra* ("he caused to do repeatedly"), *kṛtrimam* ("artificially made"), *vyāvakrośī* ("reviling excessively"), and *sāṃrāviṇam* ("resounding everywhere").

Taddhita suffixes are those affixes that are not verbal roots (*dhātu*) and which express their own meaning as related to an agent (*kāraka*), a state (*bhāva*), or a connection (*saṃbandhin*). They are of six types: those that cause elision (*lepin*), those that cause partial elision (*lopin*), those that cause total elision (*sarvalopin*), those that cause substitution (*ādeśin*), those that cause partial substitution (*pradeśin*), and those that cause no substitution (*apradeśin*). Among these, those with the markers *m* and *ṛ* as indicatory letters (*it*) are "non-eliding" (*alopin*), such as: *aśvakaḥ*, *aśvatthāmaḥ*, *sabhyaḥ*, *sakhyam*, and *devadattarūpyaḥ*.

Those [suffixes] that undergo elision (*lopin*) along with their subsequent elements (*sānubandha*) are as follows: *brāhmaṇyam*, *mṛttikā*, *dākṣiḥ*, *vaiyākaraṇaḥ*, *steyam*, *kaidāryam*; those for whom the *kim*-suffix does not remain due to *luk*, *lup*, and other such operations are all *lopins*, such as *gargāḥ*, *carakāḥ*, *pañcalāḥ*, *cañcā*, *gārgī*, *sāmagrī*. Those for whom *āyan* and others are prescribed as substitutes (*ādeśa*) are the *ādeśins*, such as *aitikāyanaḥ*, *kāpeyam*, *ātmanīyam*, *aśvīyam*, *kṣatriyaḥ*, *śāśvatikam*.

Those situated at the beginning, middle, or end of a *prakṛti* (base form) are "with parts" (*pradeśin*), such as: *bahutṛṇam*, *bahurājā*, *sarvakaḥ*, *uñcakaiḥ*, *tvayakā*, and *pacataki*. Those which constitute the final constituent parts of that very same [base] are "without parts" (*apradeśin*), such as: *pākyavacam*, *pratyurasam*, *keśākeśi*, *yuvajīniḥ*, *sarajasam*, and *niṣpravāṇiḥ*.

*Samāsa* (compound) is the state of words having distinct meanings becoming a single meaning; it is sixfold: by two *sup*-ending words, by two *suptiṅ*-ending words, by a *sup*-ending word and a verbal root, by two *sup*-ending nouns, and by two nouns. Among these, examples of compounds formed by two *sup*-ending words are: *upakumbham*, *rājapuruṣaḥ*, *nīlotpalam*, *aṣṭakapālaḥ*, *citraguḥ*, and *dhavakhadirau*. Here, because of the rule "A grammatical operation concerning words applies when there is semantic expectancy (*sāmarthya*)," the compound occurs when semantic expectancy exists. And semantic expectancy is [the presence of] a relationship.

And that [relation] is expressed in two ways—by being denoted and by being implied—and it is twofold according to the status of the subordinate and the principal. When it is denoted, it involves the use of the ablative case when there is a difference of substratum (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), as in "near the jar" (*kumbhasya samīpam*) or "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*). In those cases, *upakumbham* is an *avyayībhāva* compound where the first member is predominant, while *rājapuruṣaḥ* is a *tatpuruṣa* compound where the final member is predominant.

The principal (pradhāna) is denoted by the first case-ending (*prathamā*) when its own meaning is not displaced; the subordinate (*upasarjana*), however, which assumes a distinct grammatical relation for the sake of favoring the principal, is expressed by the sixth case-ending (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and so forth. And this occurs only when [the word] ends in a nominal suffix (*subanta*). When there is co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with an implied [word] having the same case-ending, as in "the blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam ca* = *nīlotpalam*), or as in "prepared on eight potsherds" (*aṣṭasu kapāleṣu saṃskṛtaḥ* = *aṣṭākapālaḥ*).

And this is a *karmadhāraya* compound according to the rule “the qualifier [is compounded] with the qualified” (*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*). Furthermore, the status of a *dvigu*—according to the rules “preceded by a numeral” (*saṃkhyāpūrvaḥ*) and “for the sake of a secondary derivative” (*taddhitārtha*)—is prescribed when there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the subordinate and the principal elements as they are perceived through the relation of qualifier and qualified; and that [coreferentiality] would occur only when there is identity of case-ending, which exists precisely when both members end in a nominal suffix (*subanta*).

And when it is a *bahuvrīhi*—characterized by the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the qualifier and the qualified because it is directed toward another referent (*anyapadārtha*) in the sense that "he whose cows are variegated"—then too, that expressed meaning becomes included within the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Thus, in the state of the compound (*vṛtti*), contrary to the sentence, the subordinate element "his variegated cows" (*citragavo 'sya*) comes to possess the status of the primary element as "this [person] belonging to the variegated cows" (*citragavām ayam*). And since it ends in either the genitive or the nominative case, it would indeed be a form ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*).

And when, in the case of "dhavaśca khadiraśca" (the *dhava* and the *khadira*), whether it refers to the primary elements (*pradhāna*) or the secondary elements (*apradhāna*) such as actions and so forth, the *dvandva* compound expresses their simultaneous co-occurrence in a single substratum (*itaretarayoga*), even then neither primacy nor non-primacy is perceived without the equality of their case-endings (*tulyavibhaktitva*). Furthermore, this equality of case-endings occurs only when both members are *suptanta* (ending in a nominal suffix). Therefore, it is traditionally taught that "in all cases, a *suptanta* is compounded with another *suptanta*."

Examples of compounds formed from two finite verbs (*tiṅanta*) include *aśṛṇuta-pibata*, *khādata-modata*, *pacata-bhṛjjata*, *unmṛja-avamṛja*, *āvapa-nivapa*, and *ehi-reyāhi*. Here, the compounding of finite verbs is prescribed by the rule "a finite verb is compounded with another finite verb to express continuity of action" (*ākhyātam ākhyātena kriyāsātatye*), as they are included in the list beginning with *mayūra-vyaṃsaka*. Those actions in which [the acts of] "listening and drinking," and so forth, occur continuously are expressed in this manner.

The principle that "that which falls within the scope of a rule is included by the mention of that [rule]" applies here; thus, the verbal nature (*ākhyātatva*) belongs both to the items beginning with *ud* and to *re*. Examples of words ending in *sup* and *tiṅ* are: *apacasi*, *prāvarṣat*, *anuvyacalat*, *astikṣīrā*, *ehivāṇijā*, and *jahistambam*. In this context, although the sense of "together" (*saha*) is already implied by the instrumental case in the rule *saha supā*, the explicit mention of *saha* allows for an additional application of the rule through a separate syntactical split (*yogavibhāga*), whereby a compound is formed between words ending in *sup* and words ending in *tiṅ*.

And thus, [the following rules] become applicable: "The elision of 'na' occurs before a finite verb (tiṅ) when used in a sense of contempt"; "With a finite verb that possesses an udātta accent and expresses motion"; "Under the heading of 'sub', there is the mention of 'astikṣīrā' and so forth"; "Compounds such as 'ehīḍā' and others are formed with another word as their referent"; and "The verb 'jahi' is frequently compounded with its object to express repetition, and it denotes the agent."

Therefore, this meaning is consistent: "You are censured; you do not cook, even though you have been addressed as 'vṛṣala'," or "Come, merchant"—wherein there is an action qualified by the merchant being addressed; or "Kill, kill the pillar," where the agent who is designated is spoken of in this way. As for the [formation of] *sub* from roots, it is as in *śaṃgrāmayate*, *anurīdhyete*, *śraddhā*, *antardhiḥ*, *paramaniyau*, and *pratibhuvau*. In these cases, the reading is of the two [roots] in their combined form: *saṃgrāma* in the sense of "battle" (*yuddhe*) and *anurīdha* in the sense of "desire" (*kāme*).

Regarding the rules for the suffixes *aṅ* and *ki*, namely *ātaścopasarge* and *upasarge ghoḥ kiḥ*, there is an extension (*upasaṅkhyāna*) to include *pra*, *adhi*, *anu*, *ava*, *ni*, *vi*, *ā*, *ud*, *upa*, *sam*, and *pari*. This is for the sake of accomplishing grammatical operations such as *aci śnudhātubhruvāṃ yvoriyaṅuvaṅau*; since a word ending in *kvip* is not inherently a verbal root (*dhātu*), it must be treated as a root to achieve these results. Consequently, a compound can occur with both *sib* and *tati*. Examples of compounds formed from words ending in *sup* (nouns) and *nāman* (proper names) are: *dadhisek* (one who sprinkles curds), *carmakrīti* (one who buys leather), *dhanakrītā* (a woman bought for wealth), *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī* (one who recites for a Brahmin), and *sarasijam* (a lotus).

In this context, by the inclusion of the term *atiṅ* in the rule *“kugatiprādayaḥ”*—which is explained as being supplementary to both rules including *“upapadamatiṅ”*—the word *sup* (referring to nominal suffixes) is excluded. Furthermore, in the rule *“kartṛkaraṇe kṛtā bahulam,”* since the composition of the agent (*kartṛ*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*) with a *kṛt*-derived suffix is prescribed, the status of the subsequent member as ending in a *kṛt* suffix is already established; however, because of the explicit mention of the word *kṛt*, the composition is permitted even when that suffix is not present, provided the compound is in its state of being formed (*tadantāvasthāyām*), whereby the word *sup* is also excluded.

Furthermore, it is taught that the compounding of words denoting motion (*gati*), verbal roots (*kāraka*), and upapadas with *kṛt*-affixes occurs even prior to the production of case-endings (*sub*), because the inclusion of the term "variously" (*bahulam*) serves the purpose of indicating such desired cases. This [compounding] is determined in some instances by nouns (*naman*) and in others by words ending in case-endings (*subanta*).

In this regard, in the example *dadhi-seka*, the word ending in a case-suffix is employed so that the prohibition of the *ṣatva* (the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*)—which is based on the condition of being at the beginning of a word (*padādi*) as prescribed by the rule *sātpadādyoḥ*—may be established for the final member; whereas in *carmakāra*, the word ending in a case-suffix is used for the sake of the elision of *n* (*nalopa*), which is conditioned by its being at the end of a word (*padānta*) for the preceding member.

In the case of *carmakrītī*, the preceding member (*pūrvapada*) is a word ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*) solely for the purpose of eliding the *n* (in *carman*), while the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is treated as a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Consequently, by the rule "after *krīta* preceded by an instrument [expressed in the first member], provided it does not end in *a*," the fact that *krīta* ends in *a* would be negated, thereby preventing the application of the suffix *ṅīṣ*. However, in the case of *dhanakrītā*, as seen in the usage of the learned, such as "For she was purchased by him with wealth, dearer even than his own life," the subsequent member undergoes the production of a case-suffix; because it thus ends in *ā* due to the production of the suffix *ṭāp*, the suffix *ṅīṣ* does not arise.

In the case of *brāhmaṇācchaṃsī* and *sarasijam*, there is the direct hearing of the nominative suffix (*sip*) in the two preceding members; however, in the two subsequent members, the case-suffix does not arise due to the absence of a purpose. Regarding the two nouns *aśvakrītī* and *dhanakrītī*, just as before, when the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* arises, there is no contradiction regarding their status as instruments even without the arising of a case-suffix, according to the view that the meaning of a nominal stem consists of five factors.

In the case of *pravāpiṇī* and *māṣavāpiṇī*, however, since the compound is formed prior to the addition of the nominal suffix (*sup*), the final element of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) ends in the letter *n*. Consequently, by the rule "prātipadikāntanumvibhaktiṣu ca," the substitution of *ṇ* for *n* occurs. If, however, the compound were formed from two words already ending in nominal suffixes, the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would arise first because it is an internal operation (*antaraṅga*). In that case, since the negative particle *nañ* is connected with the action denoted by the root *sūrya* (to see), there is no mutual connection between *nañ* and *sūrya*; thus, due to a lack of semantic expectancy (*sāmarthya*), the case-suffix (*vibhakti*) would not occur. For in this context, the phrase "they do not even see the sun" implies that *nañ* has the act of seeing the sun as its object.

It requires the action of seeing (*darśana-kriyā*), not the existence of the sun; for according to the rule "in *asūrya* and *lalāṭa* when used with *dṛś* and *tap*, [the suffix *kha* is applied]," a compound occurs even in the absence of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*) between two nouns alone. By this, *kṛtapūrvī* is also explained; for here too, in the analysis "he previously made a mat" (*kṛtaṃ pūrve kaṭo'nena*), since the word *kṛta* requires an object (*karman*) and thus lacks connection with the word *pūrva*, there is semantic incompetency. Nevertheless, by the rules "from *pūrva*, [the suffix] *ini*" and "also after [a word] preceded by another," it is established that a compound occurs between *kṛta* and *pūrva* themselves, even though they are not nominal stems (*asubanta*).
