In this context, the dual number in expressions such as "by two inflected words" (*subantābhyām*) is intended as an illustration; therefore, just as it occurs with two, so too does compound formation occur with three or many. Among these, the *avyayībhāva* and the *karmadhāraya* compounds consist of two members, as in *adhistri*, *śākaprati*, *pañcamūlāni*, and *puruṣavyāghraḥ*. The *tatpuruṣa* compound—characterized by the genitive case or by the measurement of time—consists of either two or three members.

As in the cases of *rājagavīkṣīram* (the milk of a royal cow), *rājagokṣīram* (the milk of the king’s cow), *dvyahajātaḥ* (born after two days), and *dvyahnajātaḥ* (born after two days). Here, when [the compound] is analyzed as "the milk of a cow that belongs to a king" (*rājñaḥ gauḥ rājagavī*, tasyāḥ kṣīram*), then it consists of two [words]; but when it is analyzed as "the milk of the king’s cow" (*rājño goḥ kṣīram rājagokṣīram*), then it consists of three [words]. Thus it has been said: "In the case of *rājagavīkṣīra*, there would be the contingency of it being a *dvigusamāsa* because of the existence of the number 'two' [in *dvyahajāta*]; however, it is established [as a *tatpuruṣa*] because of its connection with the milk of a cow qualified by the king," namely *rājagavīkṣīram* and *rājagokṣīram*.

But surely, one could say "cow's milk" (*gokṣīram*) and "the king's cow's milk" (*rājagokṣīram*); this will be possible under the second alternative. It is not so, because of the difference in meaning. Just as one strives for [milk] from a cow and does not settle for the mere milk of a buffalo or other animals, so too one strives for [a specific cow] belonging to the king—namely, "the milk of that cow which belongs to the king. And this is not established by that [second alternative], for in that case, it would be understood that the king is related to any mere cow's milk obtained from anywhere whatsoever.

But how can there be a compound of *goḥ* (of the cow) with *kṣīram* (milk), when [the cow] depends on the milk, and of *rājñaḥ* (of the king) with *rājānam* (the king), when [the king] depends on the king? It is said in reply: the cow does not depend on the milk in the same way that the king [depends on the cow], because the cow is not subordinate (*apradhānatvāt*). Nor does the milk depend on the cow with such eagerness (*autsukyena*) as the cow depends on the milk; for the milk, having its own meaning unaltered, lacks that intensity of dependence, whereas the cow, due to the emergence of a distinct relational state, possesses that eagerness.

Thus, because it conveys meaning when there is compatibility and dependence upon a principal word, a compound indeed occurs, as in *devadattagurukulam* (Devadatta’s teacher’s family) and *rājarṣibhāryā* (the king’s seer-wife). As it has been said: "A compound does indeed occur even when the principal word is dependent. Likewise, when the compound *dvyahaḥ* (two days) is formed from two days joined together (*dve ahanī samāhṛte*), then [the rule] applies with two [words]; but when the compound is *dvyahnajāta* (born after two days), meaning "two days born of," then it applies with three [words].

If it is argued that, because of the rule "sub supā" (Pāṇini 2.1.4), a compound occurs only between two words, we say no; for since the plural number is employed in the rule "kālāḥ parimāṇinā" (Pāṇini 2.1.29), the number is not intended to be significant even in the subordinate member "sub supā. Thus, when compounding is permitted among all three words, since the word *dvi* denotes time by counting time, in the analysis *dve ahanī jātasya*, the two words *dvi* and *ahan*—both denoting time—are compounded with the word *jāta*, which is the possessor of the measure (*parimāṇin*).

Because the designation *tatpuruṣa*—which is conditioned by the subsequent member—is applied to the preceding member, and because there is no prohibition by the rule "not [after] a numeral, etc., in a collective compound" (*na saṃkhyādeḥ samāhāre*), the compound-final suffix is established by the rule "for *ahan*, [substitute] *ahna-* after these [words]" (*ahno'hn etebhyaḥ*). Thus, the intended form *dvyahnaja* (born after two days) is successfully established. Now, why is there not likewise a compound-final suffix in the case of *rājagokṣīram* (the king’s cow-milk)? Because the word *go* lacks semantic competency (*asāmarthya*) when it simultaneously depends upon both the preceding and the subsequent members.

If it is argued that this is the same case for the expression *dvyahnajātaḥ* ("born two days ago"), that is not so; for a *dvigu* compound is prescribed only when joined with a subsequent word (*uttarapada*). Furthermore, in the phrase *dve avanī*, both words end in the nominative case, while in *rājño goḥ*, both end in the genitive case. Moreover, there is a distinction between what ends in the nominative and what ends in the genitive: the nominative, because its distinctness [from other relations] has not yet arisen, is free from longing and does not depend on anything else; the genitive, however, because its distinctness has already emerged, proceeds with a longing to assist others.

It does not cease its activity until it has achieved its purpose. If it is asked how a compound can exist when there is a lack of capacity due to such mutual dependence, the answer is that it occurs because the meaning is intelligible (*gamakatvāt*). For example: "The king's wives do not see even the sun" (*asūryampaśyā rājadārāḥ*); "Verses that are not sung by men" (*apumgīyāḥ ślokāḥ*); "A Brahmin who does not eat at a funeral feast" (*aśrāddhabhojī brāhmaṇaḥ*), or "one who does not eat the food of a Śūdra" (*aśūdrānnabhojī*), likewise "one who does not eat salt" (*alavaṇabhojī*); "nineteen" (*ekānnaviṃśatiḥ*); and "this behavior of yours is like that of a mongoose in a heated pan" (*avataptenakulasthitam*). Thus, the compound is formed.

In the case of *bahuvrīhi* and *dvandva* compounds, they are formed by two, three, or many [words], as in: *citraguḥ* (one who has variegated cows), *kaṇṭhekālaḥ* (one on whose neck Kāla resides), *plakṣanyagrodhau* (the *plakṣa* and *nyagrodha* trees), *pāṇipādam* (hands and feet), *pañcagavadhanaḥ* (one whose wealth consists of five cows), *mattabahumātaṅgam* (one with many rutting elephants), *śaṅkhadundubhivīṇāḥ* (the conch, drum, and lute), and *dhavakhadirapalāśam* (the *dhava*, *khadira*, and *palāśa* trees). Regarding these, the traditional rule (*smṛti*) states: "The *bahuvrīhi* occurs when multiple [words] refer to another object," and "The *dvandva* occurs in the sense of conjunction (*cārthe*). And it is said: "By him whose hair was matted like beautiful grass, who wore a fine deerskin garment..."

In the case of *samāhāra-dvandva*, the formation is not established by means of the *samanta-śitirandhra* (the rule for all [other] cases), because the *dvandva* is not accomplished through two [words]. In that [type of *dvandva*], predominance belongs to as many [members] as were employed; however, in *itaretara-yoga*, [predominance] belongs to the individual members, whereas in *samāhāra*, it belongs to the aggregate.

Now, one might object: these are *bahuvrīhi* compounds containing within them *karmadhāraya* compounds—namely, "one whose matted hair (*jaṭā*) and locks (*keśa*) are beautiful and fine" (*su-śūkṣma-jaṭa-keśa*), "one whose garment is a beautiful and well-made deer-skin" (*su-nata-ajina-vāsas*), and "one in whose extremities white pores have arisen" (*sañjātāny anteṣu śiti-randhrāṇi asya*). In these cases, why is a *bahuvrīhi* not formed for both [the first two] by first establishing a *karmadhāraya* between the middle member and either the subsequent or the preceding member (i.e., *su-śūkṣma-jaṭa* and *keśa*, or *su-nata-ajina* and *vāsas*), and then forming a *saptamī-tatpuruṣa* for the last [term] with its subsequent member (*anteṣu śiti-randhrāṇi*), before finally applying the *bahuvrīhi*?

It is said that in the case of the two preceding [words], a *karmadhāraya* compound is untenable because they lack grammatical coreferentiality (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*); for there is no coreferentiality between two qualifiers.

However, by the subsequent rule "the qualifier [is compounded] with the qualified," a *karmadhāraya* occurs in a state of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); yet, at that later stage, the accomplishment of the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*)—which was intended—is not established. For if that were the case, the beauty of the hair would be perceived as being based solely on its connection with fine matted locks rather than being inherent, and the loveliness of the deerskin garment would be understood as having only the [hair] as its cause rather than being natural.

In the case of the word *antye* (in the final), because the compound *pumaranteṣu* (in the ends of the men) is dependent [on another word] and thus lacks syntactic independence (*asāmarthya*), a locative tatpuruṣa compound with the subsequent member is not possible. For if one were to say "the nine apertures are at the ends," there would be an expectation of "at whose ends? And that [expectation] is satisfied only within a bahuvrīhi compound arising for the sake of the word *śiti* (nine), namely: "those in whose ends subtle apertures have gathered," but not in a masculine tatpuruṣa.

But surely, a compound is observed even when both members are qualifiers, as for example: *khañjakubjaḥ* (both lame and humpbacked), or *bhrāturbhāryā devadattasya* (the brother’s wife of Devadatta). Regarding this, it has been stated by the Teachers: what was stated? It was said that since one person is known to be lame and another to be humpbacked, the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) indeed occurs because of their status as primary and subordinate; moreover, every relative term always functions dependently.

In its usage, this [compound] does not lose its dependence on its own meaning, just as in the case of "the father of Devadatta’s father," where he is called the grandfather. However, in this instance, the expression *sūkṣmajaṭaḥ* is taught as having the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) alone as its meaning; yet even the word *tamaḥ*, because it denotes an action and is thus a quality-word (*guṇavacana*), remains dependent.

The word *su*—this very term—is again mentioned here as being compounded when used in the sense of "excellent" (*śobhana*). Regarding this, there is a dispute as to whether it denotes a substance (*dravyavacana*) or a quality (*guṇavacana*), because indeclinables (*avyaya*) are traditionally held to denote non-substantial entities (*asattvārtha*). However, some further dispute even on that point, asserting that these [indeclinables] are merely indicators (*dyotaka*) and not denoters (*vācaka*). And a compound formed by the rule *sup supā* occurs even in the case of indicators.

Let it not be that there is a *karmadhāraya* in the first two cases; however, in the last case, since the word *anta* is a relative term (*saṃbandhiśabda*), why is it not a *tatpuruṣa*, as in the case of *bhrātṛbhāryā* (the wife of a brother)? It is said in reply: although relative terms are compounded even when they possess a requirement for a correlative, their formation occurs only where no doubt, misconception, or the like arises. In this case, however, when one says *antaśitirandhrāṇi*, a doubt arises: does it mean "its apertures are at the ends" (*anteṣu śitirandhrāṇy asya*), or "the apertures are dark and without gaps at the end" (*antaśitinīrandhrāṇi*)?

Now, when the analysis [of the compound] is "he whose hair (keśāḥ) has very fine roots (su-sūkṣma-jaṭāḥ)," then there ought to be a *karmadhāraya* of the two preceding members. But it should not be so. Why? Because there would be a fault regarding the accent (*svara*). In a *bahuvrīhi*, setting aside the original accent of the preceding member (*pūrvapada-prakṛtisvara*), the rule "the end of a compound is acute" (*samāsasyānta udāttaḥ*) applies because it is a general rule for compounds; thus, the accent of the subordinate compound (*avayavasamāsasvara*) would result. Therefore, he says: "In cases such as *susūkṣmajatakeśa*, if [the first part] is a constituent of the compound..."

In that case, because it is *antaraṅga*, the accent of the member (*avayavasvara*) would be the sublater; however, this is not desired. What, then, is the justification for the sublation of the *karmadhāraya* [accent] here? It is simply the inclusion of the term *bahulam* (in various cases) in the rule “*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa bahulam*” (P. 2.1.57). And it has been said: “That designation which is based on general principles, and that which pertains to specific instances—due to the inclusion of *bahulam*, there is no application of either of these two.”

Therefore, where both members [of the compound] are specific terms (*viśeṣasaṃjñā*), there the *dvigu* and *dvandva* compounds necessarily occur in the final member; for example, *pañcadravapriyaḥ* ("fond of five fruits") and *chatropānahapriyaḥ* ("fond of umbrella and sandals"). Where one member is a general term and the other is a specific term, there it occurs optionally, as in *rājagavīkṣīram* ("milk of the king's cow") or *rājagokṣīram*.

Where there is a general term on one side and a specific term on the other, [the former] does not occur at all; for example, in the case of *śuśūkṣmajaṭakeśena sunatājina-vāsasā* (by one with very fine matted hair and wearing a well-tanned deer-skin), here, since it is a *bahuvrīhi*, when there is the designation of a "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*) in relation to the "qualified" (*viśeṣya*) by the rule "*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa bahulam*," that designation of a compound (*samāsa*) is called a "general designation" (*sāmānya-saṃjñā*) because it does not indicate the specific divisions such as *tatpuruṣa* and so forth, which are indicated by the rule "*sup-supā*."

Objection: Is it not the case that the author of the Mahābhāṣya-vārttika states, "In the case of *dvandva* and *tatpuruṣa* compounds, the rule for obligatory composition applies when there is a final member (*uttarapada*)"? Since this [compound] is indeed a *tatpuruṣa*, why does composition not occur here as well? Response: Because of the inclusion of the term "final member" (*uttarapada*), it is only in the context of a final member that the rule is traditionally taught; therefore, in this instance, only that [type of] *tatpuruṣa* should be understood, such as in *dvyahnajātaḥ* ("born after two days") and *pañcagavadhanaḥ* ("possessing wealth of five cows"). A *dvandva*, however, occurs only when there is a subsequent member; thus, by the term "final member," all [types of compounds] are included within the scope of the *bahuvrīhi*.

Why, then, is this stated, since it is already established by the inclusion of the word "bahula" (variously)? [The answer is: so that when there is the application (*vṛtti*) of the whole, there might never be a non-application (*avṛtti*) of its parts. Even so, it need not be stated; for in this case there are two positions: the position of application and the position of non-application. When there is application, there is the application of all; but when there is no application, there is the non-application of all.

This is not so; there is a distinction here. To explain: in expressions such as *pañcagavapriya* ("one for whom five cows are dear"), it is neither the mere number five that is dear, nor merely the cows themselves. Rather, it is certain cows characterized by the number five—just as in the cases of "five mangoes" (*pañcāmrāḥ*) or "the seven sages" (*saptarṣayaḥ*). And this [meaning] would be difficult to establish if the *dvigu* compound did not exist beforehand.

By this [principle], in examples such as *chatropānahapriya* ("fond of umbrella and sandals"), the word *priya* does not denote a beloved number five, nor does it denote cattle in general; rather, it refers to certain cows characterized by the number five, just as in the cases of "five mangoes" (*pañcāmrāḥ*) or "the seven sages" (*saptarṣayaḥ*). And that [usage] would be difficult to justify in a *dvigu* compound if the prior member did not exist [to indicate plurality]. By this, the example *chatropānahapriya* is also explained; for there too, without a *dvandva* compound expressing simultaneous location (*yugapadadhikaraṇavacana*), the desired result cannot be achieved.

For it is not only the sandals that are dear to him, but the umbrella as well; and the word *priya* heard immediately following the word *upānah* (sandals) is unable to include the umbrella without a *dvandva* compound. Therefore, there is no elliptical extension (*anākṣepa*). Furthermore, by [the analysis of] "a forest with intoxicated, many elephants" as "one whose hair is very fine and matted," it is stated that even in such cases there is only a single word. In this case too, the form *mattabahumātaṅgāḥ* does not occur.

What is the reason? Because the word *bahu* denotes a number, according to the rule: "The words *bahu*, *gaṇa*, *vat*, *uḍ*, *ḍat*, *ḍati*, and *saṃkhyā* [are called numbers]"; and because a *karmadhāraya* compound preceded by a number becomes a *dvigu*; and because a *dvigu* occurs only when there is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), or a collective (*samāhāra*), as in *pañcakapālaḥ*, *trilokahamryam*, and *pañcapūlī*. How then are [compounds] such as *saptarṣayaḥ* and *pañcāmrāḥ* formed? They occur only when it is a proper name (*saṃjñā*), according to the rule: "Directional words and numbers [form a *tatpuruṣa*] when they constitute a proper name."

But surely, there was neither a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix nor a subsequent member (*uttarapada*); nevertheless, it will form a collective compound (*samāhāra*) as *bahumātaṅgam*, meaning "many *mātaṅgas* brought together. Then, from that, the term *mattabahumātaṅga*—meaning "in this forest there are intoxicated many *mātaṅgas*"—will become a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*). It may be asked: what is the meaning of the word "collection" (*samāhāra*)? Indeed, it is derived from the root *hṛ* preceded by the prefix *sam-*, with the suffix *ghañ* in the sense of the object; thus, that which is gathered together (*samāhriyate*) is a "collection" (*samāhāra*).

If this is so, then in the case of *pañcakumāri* (five maidens) and *daśakumārī* (ten maidens), where five or ten maidens have been collected (*samāhṛtāḥ*), the shortening [of the final vowel] prescribed by the rule "the feminine ending of a word denoting a herd or a subordinate member" would not apply; for since the meaning of the compound is manifold, the rule "a *dvigu* compound takes the singular number" would also have to be stated. In that case, it will be a formation based on the abstract state (*bhāvasādhana*): the act of collecting is "collection" (*samāhāra*). But what is expressed by a formation based on the abstract state? That which is the state of being placed one above the other (*auttarādharya*).

Furthermore, what is the "collection" (*samāhāra*) of cows and other animals in expressions such as "a group of five" (*pañcāvaṃ*) or "a bundle of five" (*pañcapūlī*), which consists of their acquisition, purchase, begging, or bringing together? If this were so, it would not apply when cows are grazing among scattered bundles of grass. In that case, "collection" must be the act of bringing them into proximity. Even so, there is an inconsistency regarding expressions such as "a group of five villages" (*pañcagrāmī*) or "a group of six cities" (*ṣaṇṇagarī*). Why? Because "collection" is defined as the act of bringing into proximity.

In the word *samiti*, the prefix *sam-* functions in the sense of "all around" (*abhividhi*), while *āṅ* signifies "towards" (*abhimukhya*), and the root *harati* signifies "bringing to another place. However, the root *harati* does not necessarily function only in the sense of bringing to another location. What then? It is also used in the sense of similarity, as in "he imitates his mother" (*māturanuharati*) or "he follows his father" (*pituranuharati*). Alternatively, in cases such as *pañcagrāmī* ("a collection of five villages") or *ṣaṇṇagarī* ("a collection of six cities"), the term does not stop at this much alone; for it necessarily requires something more than that—either an action or a quality—and that which it requires is the single composite whole (*samāhāra*).

In that case, if it is understood as denoting an action (*bhāva-sādhana*), there is this fault: when one says, "Let the *pañcapūlī* (a bundle of five) be brought," the bringing of the substance itself would not be achieved. This is not a fault. For example, when it is enjoined regarding the genus (*jāti*)—"A cow is to be sacrificed; a goat [is to be sacrificed] to Agni-Soma"—because those actions are impossible with respect to the genus, the acts of touching, sprinkling, and slaughtering take place with respect to the substance. Here too, because the action cannot be performed upon the genus, the bringing of the substance will occur. Or rather, because there is no difference: for the aggregate characterized as a collection is not distinct from the individual members of that collection.

It occurs thus. If that is so, then in the case of *bahumātaṅgam* as a collective (*samāhāra*), this fault arises: because of the rule "a *dvigu* compound whose final member ends in short *a* is stated to be feminine," it would result in ending in long *ū*, like *pañcapūlī*. Nor is this [term *mātaṅga*] recited among the items beginning with *pātra*, by which—like *cakṣuṣpātra* or *tribhuvana*—its [feminine application] would be prohibited. Nor does it end in *ān*, by which an option might be possible, such as *pañcakhaṭvī* or *pañcakhaṭvam*.

But surely, the vowel *i* is not seen even in a *dvigu* compound, as in *ekaputraḥ* or *ekabhikṣā*. This is not a *dvigu*. What then? It is a *karmadhāraya* by the rule beginning with "words denoting prior time, *eka*, *sarva*, *jara*, *purāṇa*, etc. Furthermore, why would a *dvigu* not be formed even when preceded by a numeral? Certainly; because that [term] occurs only in the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), in a compound where the final member is a word (*uttarapada*), or in a collective (*samāhāra*). And here, neither a secondary derivative meaning nor a final member is being analyzed, nor is a collection of one thing possible.

But when, due to an excellence of capacity (*sāmarthyātiśaya*), there is a superimposition (*samūhāropaṇa*) upon even a single entity, then it indeed occurs, as in *ekāpūpī* ("a single cake") and *ekaśācī* ("a single garment"). Now, does the designation *dvigu* apply to the suffix (*pratyaya*) and the final member (*uttarapada*) [of the compound]? It is so, for the time being. However, in this case, there is a lack of establishment (*aprasiddhi*) because of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). How is there mutual dependence? [It is because] the suffix and the final member are the cause for the *dvigu* designation, and the *dvigu* designation is the cause for the suffix and the final member. If that is the case, then I shall state: "when the meaning [is present]."

If [the suffix] is for the sake of the meaning, there would be no production of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*), as in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound. In that regard, just as in "citraguḥ" (one who has brindled cows) or "śabalaguḥ" (one who has variegated cows), because the sense is already expressed by the *bahuvrīhi*, the production of a secondary derivative such as *-mat* or *-tva* does not occur. Suppose you accept it as you wish; let it be that the suffix occurs after the subsequent member of the compound. [Objection: But was it not said that there is no established usage because of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*)? [Reply: This is not a fault. This is not equal to other cases of mutual dependence, because words are non-eternal (*anitya*). [Objection: But the technical name (*saṃjñā*) is not eternal; what is, then? Words.

If a designation were to be understood in this way as something yet to come into being—for example, as when a weaver says, "Weave a cloth from this thread"—he would see that if it is not a cloth, it must be woven, but if it is to be woven, it is not yet a cloth; thus, "the cloth is to be woven" is a contradiction. However, what is intended here is a designation for something yet to come into being; he thinks that when it has been woven, it will consist of what is called a "cloth."

In the same way here as well, that *dvigu* compound occurs for which, once it has been formed, these two designations—*uttarapada* and so forth—will apply. Or rather, let it be that [the word] refers to the meaning (*artha*). But was it not said that if it refers to the meaning, there would be no production of a *taddhita* suffix because of the rule regarding the *bahuvrīhi*? This is not a fault; the word *artha* does not necessarily denote only the "thing expressed" (*abhidheya*). What then? It may also refer to the "sense" (*syāt-artha*). For example, a *dvigu* is used in the sense of "wives" (*dāra-arthe*), and thus a *taddhita* suffix may occur.

The statement regarding the elision (*luk*) [of the suffix] after a *dvigu* compound is an indicator (*jñapaka*); namely, that since this rule—"there is elision of the secondary suffix (*taddhita*) after a *dvigu*, except for those denoting a descendant"—teaches the elision of a *taddhita* suffix following a *dvigu*, it indicates that a *taddhita* suffix is indeed produced after a *dvigu*.

If this is so, then since there is no distinction between a *samāhāra* (a collective) and a *samūha* (a group), the mention of *samāhāra* is redundant; for the meaning of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) in the rule "its group" (*tasya samūhaḥ*) already establishes this, since these two meanings—*samāhāra* and *samūha*—are indistinguishable. In that case, just as with a *samūha*, a *dvigu* compound will apply to a *samāhāra* as well when it falls within the scope of a secondary derivative. If it is said that a *dvigu* occurs in the sense of a secondary derivative, then the production of the secondary suffix would follow. Let it be produced; there will be its elision (*luk*). But then the grammatical operations conditioned by the elision would follow.

What, then, are those cases? In the case of *pañcapūlī* and *daśapūlī*, the prohibition of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* by the rule "na taddhitaluki" would apply; in the case of *pañcagavam* and *daśagavam*, the suffix *ṭac* by the rule "gorataddhitaluki" would not apply.

This is not a fault. Having stated that the suffix *ṅīp* occurs after a *dvigu* compound without qualification, I shall state: "after [words ending in] *aparimāṇa*, *vitta*, *acita*, and *kambalya*, [the suffix *ṅīp* occurs] when it denotes a collective (*samāhāra*). And having stated that the suffix *ṣṭuc* occurs after a *go* [ending *dvigu*] without qualification, I shall state: "after a *dvigu*, [the suffix *ṣṭuc* occurs] when it denotes a collective. Both of these will serve as restrictive rules (*niyamārtha*), meaning that [the suffixes occur] only in the sense of a collective and not otherwise. If that is so, then the mention of "collective" (*samāhāra*) is for the purpose of denotation; it is so that there may be denotation by means of the collective, and not by means of the secondary derivative meaning (*taddhitārtha*).

If it were so, what fault would there be? The production of secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) would result [as an undesirable consequence]. Let it result; there will be elision (*luk*). But then the operations dependent on elision would apply. All [faults] have been avoided. They have not all been avoided; for in the case of *pañcakumārī* and *daśakumārī*, the elision of the feminine suffix *ṅīp* would result by the rule "elision of *ṅīp* when a secondary suffix has been elided" (*luk taddhitaluki*).

But surely, if it is stated that a *dvigu* compound occurs when there is the sense of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), then in cases such as *pañcakhaṭvaḥ* ("five beds") and *daśakhaṭvaḥ* ("ten beds"), the designation of *dvigu* would apply even in the sense of possession (*matvartha*), and consequently, the suffix *-ī* would be required by the rule "after a *dvigu*. [Objection: This will not occur because the designation of *dvigu* is superseded by the designation of *bahuvrīhi*; for a *bahuvrīhi* occurs in the sense of possession when the members are in apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). [Reply: If it is intended that the *dvigu* occurs when there is a subsequent member (*uttarapada*), then the mention of "subsequent member" must be explicitly stated.

This is called "the statement regarding the formation of a *dvigu* compound with a word denoting the thing measured as the final member": for example, *dvimāsajātaḥ* ("born two months ago"), meaning "one for whom two months have passed since birth," and *dvyahnajātaḥ* ("born two days ago"), meaning "one for whom two days have passed since birth. Why is it said that [the rule applies] only with a word denoting the thing measured (*parimāṇin*), and not elsewhere? For instance, in cases such as *pañcagavapriyaḥ* ("fond of five cows") and *pañcagavadhanaḥ* ("possessing wealth of five cows").

In other cases, because the compound is a *bahuvrīhi*, the final member is indeed well-known; for it is stated that "many [words] are compounded when another word's meaning is intended," and thus a *bahuvrīhi* compound is formed. Now, what about the *dvandva*? The *dvandva* will be explained specifically later on. Furthermore, a *bahuvrīhi* is formed by many words, as in: "whose pair of thighs was crushed by the blows of a fierce mace whirled by swinging arms."

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "his pair of temples was completely crushed by the impact of a fierce mace that had been whirled around by his two swinging arms. Nor should it be argued that a *bahuvrīhi* compound occurs only when its members share the same grammatical substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*); for, by the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi*, [the word ending in] the seventh case [is placed first] when it is a qualifier" (*saptamīviśeṣaṇe bahuvrīhau*), the tradition teaches that a *bahuvrīhi* may occur even when there is a difference of substratum (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).

By this, the *dvandva* compound, in which all members are equally principal, is also explained, as in: "May the Sun, Fire, Wind, the Moon, Kubera, Śakra, the Lord of the Dead, and Varuṇa be the object of our compassion. Now, it is traditionally taught that a *bahuvrīhi* compound has as its referent a meaning external to the constituent words; in such cases, for example, in the phrase "Devadatta is the one who possesses brindled cows" (*citragur devadattaḥ*), the subsequent application of the word "Devadatta" would not be appropriate. For once Caitra and others have been determined through the use of the word "Caitra," the word "Caitra" is not used again.

It is not so; the word *citragu* denotes the general state of being the owner of those who possess brindled cows. In that case, one who seeks a specific [referent] must necessarily employ a specific term, such as "Who is the owner of the brindled cows? Devadatta. However, where the compound itself consists of a unique qualifier and so forth, there is no subsequent application [of another word], as in "The brindled-cow-possessor is everything" (*citragu sarvam*) or "The brindled-cow-possessor is the universe" (*citragu viśvam*).

Just as a universal (*sāmānya*) may function as a particular (*viśe�ṣa*), so it is: for instance, in the case of "these variegated cows belong to Devadatta" (*citragavo 'sya devadattasya*), because the meaning of the genitive is expressed by the compound, the genitive case-ending is not employed; yet, since the related entity (*saṃbandhin*) is not included within the compound, it is employed [as a separate word]. If this is so, then a *bahuvrīhi* word that expresses the meaning of a case-ending would not achieve grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with substance-words such as "Devadatta. [Reply: This will be possible through the elision of the possessive suffix *matup*.

It is not so; since the suffix *matup* also has the sense of a relation, there is indeed no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words denoting substances. Furthermore, it is impossible to enjoin the suffix *matup* as expressing the meaning of a case-ending within a *bahuvrīhi*, for that suffix is enjoined as having "existence" (*asti*) as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) following a word in the nominative case; and a *bahuvrīhi* term, which functions to express a case-meaning, cannot have a connection through coreferentiality with verbs such as "exists."

Now, it might be argued that once that meaning has been expressed, it becomes included within the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and thus grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) will be established. That is not so; for even when expressed, it will not abandon its own essential nature, just as in the case of [the locative] "in which" (*yatra*) and so forth.

In that case, just as when an operation prescribed for the universal (*jāti*)—which is the denoted meaning of a word—is applied to the individuals associated with it because [the operation] is impossible for the universal itself, so too, when an operation such as grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), connection with a verb, and so forth, is employed regarding the relation which is the meaning of a *bahuvrīhi*, it will apply to the substratum [of that relation]. And thus, when the relata possessing a metaphorical relation (expressed as "this is that") are denoted by *bahuvrīhi* words, the gender and number [of the compound] will not be in conflict, just as the gender and number of qualifiers like "white" do not conflict due to their dependence on the substratum.

Alternatively, because of the force of the inclusion of the word "meaning" (*artha*) in the phrase "a meaning other than a word-meaning" (*avanyapadārtha*), there will be the inclusion of that which possesses substance, gender, and number, and not merely the sense of the case-ending.

But how is this meaning obtained through the inclusion of the word *artha* (meaning)? Listen: if it were stated simply as *anyapade* ("in another word"), since a function (*vṛtti*) is impossible for a mere word, the word *pada* would either indicate some measure of meaning associated with the word, or it would convey the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*), which is closely related as the cause for the status of being a "word" (*padatva*). Since this desired result is already achieved in this way, the fact that he includes the word *artha* indicates this: that the meaning which is the object of the word, as far as it is apprehended through its linguistic expression (*artha-śruti*), [is what is intended].

It is taken up for the sake of delimitation; for meanings, which are generally applicable to roots and so forth, are delimited by the word, and thus the meaning delimited by the word is what should be adopted. In this regard, just as there is no recourse to the sentence-meaning because it is excessive, so too there is none to even a portion of the word-meaning because it is deficient.

Thus, because of the capacity for grasping the meaning, a word-meaning (*padārtha*) that possesses gender, number, and substance is taken as the efficient factor; accordingly, suffixes such as *sva* and others which denote number, or suffixes such as *ṭāp* and others which denote gender, would not be employed, nor would suffixes such as *sva* denoting number or suffixes such as *ṭāp* denoting gender be perceived [as distinct].

It is said: although number is expressed by the members of a compound just as it is by words such as "one" (*eka*) and so forth, it will not effect the grammatical operations associated with number. For, unlike the rule for the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) and others, there is no governing heading (*adhikāra*) regarding the "unexpressed" (*anabhihita*) in the rules for verbal suffixes (*vacana*). Furthermore, since the specific kārakas such as the object (*karman*) must be conveyed, the second case (*dvitīyā*) and others necessarily have to be prescribed. However, as for the nominative (*prathamā*), by the force of the mention of "verbal suffix" (*vacana-grahaṇa*), the rule that "the base alone should not be used" will apply either through convention or as a primary alternative.

It might be argued that just as the expressed [qualities] such as oneness (*ekatva*) and so forth serve as the basis for the application of the grammatical numbers (*vacana*), so too the expressed relation (*saṃbandha*) serves as the basis for the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*). This is incorrect, because of the rule *anabhihite* ("when not already expressed"). Furthermore, the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), with the relation as its subordinate element, is denoted by the word ending in the primary suffix (*vṛtti-śabda*); and this is not the domain of the genitive, because the genitive is prescribed when the relation is subordinate to the meaning of the nominal stem.

The suffixes *ṭāp* and so forth, however, occur even when the gender has already been expressed because they are *svārthika* (denotative of their own meaning); as it has been said: "But it is established that *ṭāp* and the others occur in their own meaning, because the feminine [suffix] is a qualifier of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*)."

Alternatively, the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*) may be distinct from the meaning of the compound (*vṛttyartha*); for instance, in the sentence "citragavo 'sya" ("these variegated cows belong to him"), the variegated cows are denoted by the sentence as being subordinate to the referent of another word (the possessor). However, in the compound "citraguḥ," the owner is perceived as having the cows subordinate to his own meaning. In this regard, when the referent of another word is employed to specify a particular owner of those cows whose dependence on another is already established—as in "these cows belong to him"—then it is not a *bahuvrīhi*. But when those variegated cows are used to denote a specific distinction regarding the owner...

When it is reflected upon that "this one is the owner of these cows," then a *bahuvrīhi* compound occurs, such as *citraguḥ* (one who has brindled cows) or *śabalaguḥ* (one who has dappled cows). And making that very state of being a qualifier of the owner clear, they illustrate it by saying: "he whose cows are brindled is *citraguḥ*; he whose [cows] are dappled is *śabalaguḥ*."

And here, the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an indicator); therefore, it should be stated that a *bahuvrīhi* compound may also be formed with words other than the nominative when they denote the object or the agent. For example: *ūḍharatho 'naḍvān* ("an ox by whom a chariot has been drawn"), *uddhṛtaudanā sthālī* ("a pot from which rice has been taken out"), *upahṛtapaśū rudraḥ* ("Rudra to whom an animal has been offered"), and *siddhāsādhakā vidyā* ("knowledge by which a practitioner has attained success"). Now, for what purpose is the phrase "other than the nominative" (*aprathamāyāḥ*) used? It is so that [the compound] does not occur here: *vṛṣṭe deve gataḥ* ("he went while it was raining").

Now, why does this not occur here: "vṛṣṭe deve gataṃ paśya" (See that which has gone while it was raining)? Because here, the non-nominative case is external (*bahir-aṅga*). If that is so, then since the genitive and others are internal (*antaraṅga*) [in a compound], why do the genitive and other cases not recur in examples such as "citragor devadattasya" (Devadatta’s [owner] of the brindled cow), and likewise, why do the ablative and locative cases not occur after words such as *yataḥ* and *yatra*? It is replied: the meaning expressed by the ablative, locative, and so forth, through suffixes such as *tasil* and *tral*, is not included within [the compound].

In the case of *citragu* and similar compounds, however, that meaning expressed by the *bahuvrīhi* becomes internalized and results in being the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). Now, why does a *bahuvrīhi* not occur here in the expression "pañcabhir bhuktam asya" (five have been eaten by him)? Because it is traditionally taught that a *bahuvrīhi* occurs only when the members are in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*).

If that were so, then the designation of *bahuvrīhi* would not apply to the following: *astikṣīrā*, *uṣṭramukhaḥ*, *abhāryaḥ*, *praparṇaḥ*, *uṣṭragramukhaḥ*, *candravadanā*, *keśacūḍaḥ*, *suvarṇālaṅkāraḥ*, *candraśekharaḥ*, *śūlapāṇiḥ*, *kaṇṭhekālaḥ*, and *urasilomā*. For in the first four cases, the prior member is an indeclinable (*avyaya*); because it is non-substantial (*asattvavācin*), it lacks grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with substantial (*sattvabhūta*) words such as "milk" (*kṣīra*). This is likewise true for those in the middle group.

Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not possible because the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) is untenable; moreover, in the case of the latter [type of compounds], the lack of co-referentiality between the locative and nominative endings is quite evident. This is not so, for co-referentiality is indeed possible even in these cases.

In this context, the particle *asti* is a substitute for a case-ending (*vibhakti-pratirūpaka*); it does not deviate from [indicating] tense, person, number, or grammatical relation (*sādhana*). Furthermore, the word *uccais* is seen to denote a substantive (*sattvavacana*), as in the expression: "How much more so he who is thus exalted (*tathoñcaiḥ*)? For this very reason, in the domain of compound formation (*vṛtti-viṣaya*), these two [words] should be understood as having an optional application (*asthitavibhāṣā*). Consequently, the following meanings are established: *asty asyāḥ kṣīram* becomes *astikṣīrā gauḥ* ("a cow that has milk"); *uccam mukham asya* becomes *uccairmukhaḥ maitreyaḥ* ("Maitreya, whose face is high"); and *avidyamānā bhāryā asya* becomes *abhāryaḥ* ("one who has no wife").

Or, one whose wife is not present is *avidyamānabhārya*; one from whom the leaves have fallen is *praparṇa*, or one whose leaves have fallen off. However, in the cases of *uṣṭramukha* ("camel-faced") and *candravadanā* ("moon-faced"), the words *uṣṭra* and *candra* function metaphorically (*gauṇī vṛtti*), serving as qualifiers for the face through the figurative identification (*abhedopacāra*) based on an excellence in the similarity of their constituent parts. Now, what is the mutual similarity between a camel and a face? Here, by the word *uṣṭra*, the camel’s face is denoted; one should understand that this is a figurative usage (*upacāra*) where a part is treated as if it were the whole.

In the cases of *keśacūḍa* (hair-tuft) and *suvarṇālaṅkāra* (golden ornament), the word "hair" (*keśa*) and the word "gold" (*suvarṇa*) are used [metaphorically] for their respective modifications, because the effect is figuratively designated by the name of its cause. In the expressions *candraśekhara* (moon-crested) and *śūlapāṇi* (trident-handed), the words "moon" and "trident" denote the crest and the hand as characterized by the moon and the trident, just as one says, "Bring in the spears," or "Bring in the staffs."

Regarding the two examples *kaṇṭhekālaḥ* (black-throated) and *urasilomā* (hair-chested), one must supply additional words within the compounds, such as "those who are black reside in his throat" (*kaṇṭhe sthitāḥ kālāḥ asya*) and "whose hair is born on his chest" (*urasi jātāni lomāny asya*). This is just as when the word *dvāram* (door) is uttered twice, one must supply either "let it be opened" (*apāvriyatām*) or "let it be closed" (*saṃvriyatām*).

By this principle, there is no need to state the following rules: "Under the heading of *su*, the addition of *astikṣīra* etc. should be mentioned"; "A *bahuvrīhi* compound of indeclinables should be stated"; "When the first member consists of a locative or a standard of comparison, there is elision of the second member"; "And [the genitive] expressing a whole or a modification [is compounded]"; and "After *pra* and other prefixes, [the suffix] is optionally applied to a verbal derivative."

[Objection: "But surely this must be stated even for the sake of enumeration. [Response: It is not so; for even when an enumeration is made, a *bahuvrīhi* compound does not occur where there is no denotation [of the meaning], as in the case: "he for whom five have eaten" (*pañca bhuktavanto 'sya*).

If that is the case, then the inclusion of the sense of possession (*matvartha*) will be made, such that a *bahuvrīhi* compound occurs in the sense of possession for words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*). Even so, there would still be problems: *ūḍharatha anaṅgavān* ("one who has carried a chariot, [but] is not a horse"); *dakṣiṇasyāśca pūrvasyāśca diśo yad antarālaṃ sā dakṣiṇapūrvā* ("that which is between the southern and eastern directions is the south-eastern direction"); *putreṇa saha saputraḥ* ("together with his son, he is 'with-son'"); *keśeṣu keśeṣu ca gṛhītvā pravṛttaṃ yuddhaṃ keśākeśi* ("a battle that has proceeded by seizing each other by the hair is 'hair-to-hair'"); *daṇḍaiśca daṇḍaiśca prahṛtya daṇḍādaṇḍi* ("striking with staffs against staffs is 'staff-to-staff'"); and *trirdaśa ete tridaśāḥ* ("these thirty are the 'thrice-ten'").

By such arguments as these, pervasion (*vyāpti*) alone [is established]. Therefore, even going to great lengths, one must resort to direct denotation (*abhidhāna*) itself; for it is stated that "primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds (*samāsa*) are characterized by direct denotation," so there is no need for further enumeration. Now, what is the analysis (*vigraha*) of the word *tridaśāḥ*? It is: "these ten [plus] three are the *tridaśāḥ*. According to the rule, "in a compound of numbers, the designation 'number' applies to that which ends in the suffix *suc* for the sake of subsequent grammatical operations," yet there is no number ending in *suc*. Let the analysis then be this: "these are the *tridaśāḥ* because they consist of thirteen (*trayo daśataḥ*)."

Even so, the designation "number" (saṃkhyā) for that which ends in *at* [i.e., *pañcat*] remains unestablished; furthermore, we do not see the suffix *suc* here in the compound (*samāsa*). What then? It is seen in the sentence (*vākya*). But why is *suc* seen in the sentence? Because its meaning has been expressed (*abhihitatvāt*); the meaning of *suc* has been expressed. By what? By the compound. Furthermore, is the compound stated to express the meaning of *suc*? No, it is not so; rather, the meaning of *suc* is understood here by virtue of semantic competency (*sāmarthyāt*).

How so? Since it is enumerated [as a number], and since that [number] has been stated by way of a compound for the purpose of repeating an action, the suffix *suj* will not occur. The base (*prakṛti*) has already been described as being of the nature of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*). Now, the forms of the affixes (*pratyaya*) and so forth are explained individually. In this context, an "affix" (*pratyaya*) is so called because meaning is understood (*pratīyate*) by means of it; it is threefold: an affix of a verbal root (*dhātu-pratyaya*), an affix of an affix (*pratyaya-pratyaya*), and an affix of a nominal stem (*prātipadika-pratyaya*).

Among these, the distinctions of verbal suffixes (*dhātupratyaya*) are: *san* and so forth, *tun* and *na* and so forth, *tavya* and so forth, *ṇvul* and so forth, and *uṇ* and so forth. Among them, those suffixes that are prescribed for the expression of desire, immediate action, repetition of an action, and the like—because they denote an action, they require another suffix just like the roots beginning with *bhū*—are *san* and so forth; for example: *cikīrṣati*, *adhyāpayati*, *pāpacyate*, *gopāyati*, *ṛtīyate*, *kāmayate*.

Those suffixes such as *tiP* and others, which are prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*), the object (*karman*), and the action (*kriyā*)—functioning as designators of the action that has attained the form of a verbal root (*sādhyarūpāpannakriyābhidhāyitvena*)—do not require any other suffix; for example: *vrajati devadattaḥ* (Devadatta goes), *pacyate odanaḥ* (the rice is being cooked), *rajyati vastram* (the cloth is being dyed), *sūyeta kedāraḥ* (the field ought to be sown), *corasya rujati* (it pains the thief), and *āsyate yuṣmābhiḥ* (you are sitting).

Those suffixes beginning with *tumun* which are prescribed when there is a state to be accomplished (*sādhyabhāva*), denoting an action whose sequence is not grasped and whose meaning is non-substantial (*asattvabhūtārtha*), are as follows: for example, *paktum icchati*, *bhuktvā vrajati*, *adhītya śete*, *pāyaṃpāyam āste*, *coraṃkāram ākrośati*, and *cakāsāñcakāra*.

Generally, those suffixes beginning with *tavya* which are prescribed in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), as well as in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth, are as follows: for example, *gantavyaṃ bhavatā*, *karaṇīyaḥ kaṭaḥ*, *kṛto bhavatā*, *lūyamānaḥ kedāraḥ*, *durgamo mārgaḥ*, and *vāstavyo lokaḥ*.

Generally, those suffixes such as *ṇvul* and others which are prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*) and for the object (*karman*) and so forth are as follows: "the man who cooks" (*pācakaḥ pumān*), "purifying the Soma" (*somaṃ pavamānaḥ*), "cooking the gruel" (*pacantyavāgūm*), "desirous of adorning the maiden" (*kanyāmalaṅkariṣṇuḥ*), "mud that carries away the feet" (*pādahārakaḥ paṅkaḥ*), and "the habit of doing what is dear" (*priyaṃkaraṇaṃ śīlam*).

Those suffixes which, when applied to all grammatical factors (*kāraka*) and to established states (*siddhabhāva*), generally acquire the status of denoting substances (*dravyavacanatva*) are the *uṇādi* suffixes; for example: "the wind is cold," "the nurse is affectionate," "the sickle is sharp," "the teacher is old," "the palace is beautiful," and "cooking is taking place. These include various types of suffixes and sub-suffixes, such as *yat* and so forth, *gha* and so forth, *man* and so forth, *phan* and so forth, *yuc* and so forth, and *ḍhak* and so forth.

Those suffixes beginning with *yat* that arise from nominal bases (*subanta*) such as those denoting existence, offspring, self-interest, or maturation—namely *bhava*, *apatya*, *svārtha*, and *matvartha*—are called *yadādi*. Examples are: *apsavyaḥ*, *pūrvāhṇetanaḥ*, *cirantanaḥ*, *āmuṣyāyaṇaḥ*, *tvayakā*, and *śubhaṃyuḥ*. Those suffixes beginning with *gha* that arise from verbal bases (*tiṅanta*) to express excellence, deficiency, reproach, praise, and so forth, are called *ghādi*. Examples are: *pacatitarām*, *gacchatitamām*, *jalpatikalpam*, *spṛśatideśyam*, *pacatiki*, and *pacatirūpam*.

The suffixes *ma* and so forth are those that are produced after primary derivatives (*kṛt*) when the sense of the root’s own meaning has ceased—as in the case of the suffixes expressing the sense of "possessing" (*matvartha*) and the like—such as: *kṛtrimam*, *pākimam*, *sāṃrāviṇam*, *gacchatitamām*, *jalpatikalpam*, *spṛśatideśyam*, *pacataki*, and *pacatirīpam*.

Those suffixes beginning with *phak* which arise after words ending in secondary (*taddhita*) suffixes such as *apatya* (offspring), when [the base word] signifies "living," "lineage," "praised," "despised," or "one's own interest"—as in *gārgyāyaṇaḥ*, *dākṣāyaṇaḥ*, *vāṣryāyaṇīyaḥ*, *vāṣryāyaṇikaḥ*, *ābhijityaḥ*, and *kauñjāyanyaḥ*. Those suffixes beginning with *yuc* which arise after verbal roots ending in *ṇic* and so forth, when [the action] signifies "accomplishment," "habitual nature," or "qualification for agency" and so on—as in *kāraṇā*, *aṭāṭyā*, *yāyajūkaḥ*, *sāsahiḥ*, *yāyāvaraḥ*, and *cikīrṣuḥ*.

The suffixes *ḍhak* and others which arise from feminine-stem endings (*strīpratyayānta*) in the senses of offspring and so forth, as well as in the senses of self, capacity, number, and the like, are as follows: for example, *gāṅgeyaḥ*, *yauvateyaḥ*, *vārāṇaseyaḥ*, *suvadhukaḥ*; [and in the senses of] "in a river" (*nadyām*), "on a bed" (*khaṭvāyām*), and "young women" (*yuvatayaḥ*). Furthermore, there are the various types of nominal stem suffixes (*prātipadikapratyaya*), namely: the *ṭāp* and others, the *sva* and others, the *tasil* and others, the *ka* and others, the *aṇ* and others, and the *kyac* and others.

Among those, the suffixes beginning with *ṭāp*—such as *khaṭvā*, *sudāmā*, *kārīṣagandhyā*, *brahmabandhūḥ*, *kumārī*, and *yuvatiḥ*—arise directly from the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that expresses the gender inherent in its base meaning (*prakṛtiliṅga*). The suffixes beginning with *su*—such as *kuṇḍam*, *kuṇḍe*, *kuṇḍābhyām*, *kuṇḍebhyaḥ*, *kuṇḍayoḥ*, and *kuṇḍeṣu*—arise directly from the nominal stem itself that expresses the number belonging to the base meaning (*prakṛtyarthasaṃkhyā*).

Those suffixes beginning with *tasil* which arise after nominal stems (*prātipadika*) ending in case-terminations (*subanta*), denoting either mere capacity (*śaktimātra*) or capacity accompanied by a limiting adjunct (*sopādhiśakti*), [function] in their own meanings (*svārtha*) and so forth; for example: *yataḥ*, *yatra*, *kadā*, *purastāt*, *bahuśaḥ*, and *purutrā vasati*.

Those suffixes beginning with *ka* which arise from nominal stems (*prātipadika*) ending in case-terminations (*subanta*), whether they possess conditions such as contempt, praise, excellence, non-excellence, and so forth, or lack such conditions, are used in the sense of the stem's own meaning (*svārtha*) and the like; for example: *aśvakaḥ*, *yuṣmakābhiḥ*, *vaiyākaraṇarūpaḥ*, *paṭutaraḥ*, *kutīraḥ*, and *tārtīyīkam*. Those suffixes beginning with *aṇ* which arise from nominal stems expressing a quality (*mala*), in the sense of a relationship (*saṃbandha*), a grammatical participant (*kāraka*), or an abstract state (*bhāva*), are used in those senses; for example: *aupagavaḥ*, *tāvakīnaḥ*, *ākṣikaḥ*, *vāmadevyam*, *brāhmaṇatvam*, and *paurohityam*.

The suffixes beginning with *kyac* arise from nominal stems (*prātipadika*) that are capable of expressing meanings such as the desire for an action characterized by factors like the agent (*kāraka*), or the performance of an act, as in the examples: *citrīyate*, *putrakāmyati*, *śyenāyate*, *lohitāyati*, *kaṇḍūyate*, and *muṇḍayati*. The term *upaskāra* refers to the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of bases (*prakṛti*) and suffixes (*pratyaya*), consisting of elision (*apāya*), augmentation (*upajana*), substitution (*āgama*), deletion (*lopa*), modification of phonemes (*varṇavikāra*), and the introduction of verbal roots (*vikaraṇa*). This refinement is threefold: refinement of the base, refinement of the suffix, and refinement of both.

Furthermore, these [suffixes] are each of six types, distinguished by ornamentation (*bhūṣaṇa*), combination (*samavāya*), addition (*adhyāhāra*), modification (*vaikṛta*), effort (*yatna*), and counter-effort (*pratiyatna*). Among these, those of the nature of ornamentation belonging to the *prakṛti* (base form) include the *nirarthaka*, *upalarga*, *svārthika*, *vaikalpika*, and so forth; for example: *adhyāgacchati*, *paryāgacchati*, *pralambete*, *nikhañjati*; *yāvakaḥ*, *ṣāḍguṇyam*, *aupayikam*, *mānasam*; and *ālī*, *mṛdvī*, *kamaṇḍaluḥ*, *cañcūḥ*.

The examples of *samavāya-ripa* (forms resulting from the combination [of roots with prefixes]) include those with meaningful prefixes (*sārthaka-upasarga*) and those with *san*, *ky-aṅ*, and so forth, such as: *yathāśāste*, *pratiṣṭhate*, *sumanāyate*, *durmanāyate*; *jugupsate*, *gopāyate*, *ṛtīyate*, *kāmayate*; *putrīyati*, *putrakāmyati*, *śyenāyate*, *muṇḍayati*.

Those of the nature of ellipsis include the co-utterance of prefixes, reduplication, and the augment *suṭ*, such as: *adhīte*, *adhyeti*, *anurudhyate*, *saṃgrāmayate*; *jañjapyate*, *saṃpanīpadyate*, *arāryate*, *undidiṣati*; *ipaskurute*, *apaptat*, *āsthat*, *madhvasyati*.

*Vaikṛta-rūpas* (forms resulting from modification) consist of the transposition, reversal, elision, and so forth of phonemes (*varṇa*), such as: *niṣiñcati*, *praṇayati*, *yanti*, *uśanti*; *tarūḥ*, *siṃhaḥ*, *sikātā*, *saktavaḥ*; and *santi*, *ghnanti*, *dyanti*, *samagata*. *Yatna-rūpas* (forms resulting from effort) consist of contraction (*saṃvṛti*), expansion (*vivṛti*), production (*prasava*), and so forth, such as: *yauti*, *medyati*, *dīvyati*, *nigūhati*; *kīryate*, *pūryate*, *saudhātakiḥ*, *svāyaṃbhuvam*; and *āsta*, *āste*, *avocat*, *ghaṭayati*.

The specific rules of prescription, prohibition, and so forth are of a nature requiring little effort, as for example: *aghāsat*, *vadhyāt*, *adhyagīṣmahi*; *japyaḥ*, *pitryam*, *gavyam*, *nāvyam*; *titauḥ*, *praugam*, *kokūyate*, *kathayati*.

The terrifying forms of suffixes (*pratyaya*) include *iṭ*, *ḍ*, *t*, *dh*, *suk*, *īk*, *ka*, and so forth; for example: *śahitā*, *varitā*, *bhruvai*, *bhrūṇām*, *devāsaḥ*, *pārayāmasi*, *tāriṣat*, *bhavāti*, *tārtīyīkam*, *pītvāya*, *tvayakā*, and *pacataki*. The collective forms include *sy*, *sic*, *us*, *īyus*, and so forth; for example: *kariṣyati*, *akariṣyat*, *vaktī*, and *bravīti*.

The suffixes such as *pra*, *upa*, *sam*, and *tara* are of the nature of ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), serving to qualify the meaning of the suffix; for example: *sumanāyate*, *durmanāyate*, *abhimanāyate*, *abhiṣeṇayati*; likewise, *kṛtrimam*, *sāṃrāviṇam*, *vyāvahāsī*, *kauñjāyanyaḥ*; and *pacatitarām*, *pacamānaḥ*, *sarveṣām*, *vṛkṣāṇām*.

The modified forms (*vaikṛtarūpa*) include those resulting from partial substitution (*ādeśa*), total substitution (*sarvādeśa*), and the substitution of suffixes (*pratyayādeśa*), such as: *gāgryāyaṇaḥ*, *cāndramasāyaniḥ*, *gaudheraḥ*, *kauleyakaḥ*; *pavanaḥ*, *pāvakaḥ*, *vṛkṣasya*, *vṛkṣaiḥ*; *veda*, *viveda*, *vidvan*, *viddhi*; *dadṛśe*, *adrākṣīt*, *kārakaḥ*, *kāmaṇḍaleyaḥ*; *agnicit*, *śubhaṃyāḥ*, *mūlakhāḥ*, *aśvati*; *udapādi*, *rāṣṭriyaḥ*, *āgneyaḥ*, *straiṇam*; *subhrūḥ*, *supreyasī*.

"They laugh together" (*vyatihasanti*) and "they go together" (*vyatigacchanti*). The forms beginning with *yuṣmad* and so forth serve as ornaments for both [the agent and the object], such as: "you cook" (*tvaṃ pacasi*), "you two cook" (*yuvāṃ pacathaḥ*), "you all cook" (*yūyaṃ pacatha*), "I cook" (*ahaṃ pacāmi*), "we two cook" (*āvāṃ pacāvaḥ*), and "we all cook" (*vayaṃ pacāmaḥ*). Likewise: "the wind blows" (*vāyurvāti*), "the god rains" (*devo varṣati*), "the scripture breaks of its own accord" (*śāstraṃ svayameva bhajyate*), "the elephant scatters [dust] of its own accord" (*hastī svayameva avakirate*), "the maiden terrifies herself" (*kanyā svayameva bhīṣayate*), and "the story tells itself" (*kathā svayameva brūte*).

The *vikaraṇas* and other such elements consist of the form of *samavāya* (inherent connection), as in: *bhavati*, *corayati*, *dīvyati*, *sunoti*, *tudati*, *tanoti*, *ruṇaddhi*, *kriṇāti*, *svayaṃ namate*, *svayaṃ dugdhe*, *tapyate tapaḥ*, and *lūyate kedāraḥ*.

Forms consisting of ellipsis include reduplication and the like, such as: *pāyaṃ pāyam* (drinking repeatedly), *pacati pacati* (cooking repeatedly), *grāmo grāmo ramaṇīyaḥ* (every village is beautiful), *mūle mūle sthūlāḥ* (thick at every root), *agre agre sūkṣmāḥ* (fine at every tip), *pūrvaṃ pūrvaṃ puṣyati* (it nourishes each preceding one), *prathamaṃ prathamaṃ pacyate* (each first one is cooked), *jyeṣṭhaṃ jyeṣṭham uveśaya* (lay down each eldest one), *māṣaṃ māṣaṃ dehi* (give me bean after bean), *upary upary āste* (he sits higher and higher), and *ahir ahiḥ budhyasva* (snake after snake, wake up!).

Words of modified form (*vaikṛtarūpa*) include *vām*, *nau*, and so forth; for example: *grāmo vām*, *grāmo vaḥ*, *grāmo naḥ*, *grāmo me*, *grāmastvā rakṣat*, *grāmo mā rakṣat*, *haiyaṅgavīnam*, *mātulaḥ*, *kṣatriyaḥ*, and *śrotriyaḥ*.

Words of effortful form (*yatnarūpa*) include those involving suffixes such as *-sāt* and others; for example: *agnisāt saṃpadyate*, *bhasmasād bhavati*, *brāhmaṇasāt syāt*, *devatrā karoti*, *matryatrā gacchati*, *manuṣyatrā vasati*, *śuklībhavati*, *paṭapaṭākaroti*, *cakāsāṃcakāra*, *kārayāmāsa*, *bibhaṃbabhūva*, and *vidāṃkurvantu*.

Forms that appear to require special effort include the application of a root after a verbal prefix (vidhyanuprayoga) and others, such as: *raipoṣaṃ puṣyati* (he prospers with abundant nourishment), *samūlakāṣaṃ kaṣati* (he eradicates [it] root and branch), *jīvagrāhaṃ gṛhṇāti* (he captures [him] alive), *purūṣavāhaṃ vahati* (he carries [him] manfully), *ūrdhvaśoṣaṃ śuṣkaḥ* (dried up until it withered from the top), *cūḍakanāśaṃ naṣṭaḥ* (perished until the crest was lost), *odanapākaṃ pakvaḥ* (cooked until the rice was done), *suvarṇanidhāyaṃ nihitaḥ* (deposited until the gold was laid down), *lunīhi lunīhityevāyaṃ lunāti* (he cuts while saying "cut, cut!"), *adhīṣvādhīṣvetyevāyamadhīte* (he studies while saying "study, study!"), *rāṣṭramaṭa maṭhamaṭa dūramaṭetyevāyamaṭati* (he wanders while saying "wander through the kingdom, wander through the monastery, wander far!"), and *sakatūn piba dhānāḥ svāda odanam* (drink the groats, eat the parched grains, taste the rice!).

"He eats," thus he consumes; this is [the definition of] an *upapada*. A word uttered in proximity to a verbal root (*prakṛti*) is an *upapada*, and it is of three kinds: a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*) as an *upapada*, a primary derivative suffix (*kṛt*) as an *upapada*, and a nominal suffix (*su*) as an *upapada*. Among these, the first [type] consists of: that which has the form of an action (*kriyārūpa*), that which has the form of a case-role (*kārakarūpa*), that which has the form of a noun (*nāmarūpa*), that which has the form of an indeclinable (*avyayarūpa*), that which has the form of a particle (*nipātarūpa*), and that which has the form of a prefix (*upasargarūpa*). Among those, an example of that which has the form of an action is: "Come, I think you will go by chariot," "I do not tolerate that your honor [should act]," or "He should cause a low-born man (*vṛṣala*) to sacrifice."

The form of a *kāraka* (agent/grammatical relation) is, for example: "he travels by horse," "he gives with a female slave. The form of a *nāman* (noun/proper name) is, for example: "the time when you might eat," "the occasion when you might eat," "the hour when you might eat. The form of an indeclinable (*avyaya*) is, for example: "how indeed could his honor cause a low-caste man to sacrifice? "the staff bows down of its own accord. The form of a particle (*nipāta*) is, for example: "when he eats," "he goes before [that]," "the eater goes," "the giver of cows goes," "he desires to do."

The form of the agent (*kāraka-rūpa*) is, for example: *kumbhakāraḥ* (potter), *uttānaśayaḥ* (one who lies on his back), *śayyotthāyam* (rising from bed), *mūlakopadaṃśam* (with radish as a side-dish). The form of the noun (*nāma-rūpa*) is, for example: *kālo bhoktum* (it is time to eat), *samaye bhoktum* (it is the occasion to eat), *brahmabhūyam* (becoming Brahman), *brahmodyam* (a riddle concerning Brahman). The form of the indeclinable (*avyaya-rūpa*) is, for example: *divākaraḥ* (maker of the day), *doṣākaraḥ* (maker of the night), *mṛṣodyam* (false speech), *īṣatpānaḥ* (drinking slightly).

The form of a particle (*nipātarūpa*) is as follows: *alam* having been used, *khalu* having been used, up to *vedam*, *anyathākāram*, the form of a case-role (*kārakarūpa*), the form of a name (*nāmarūpa*), the form of an indeclinable (*avyayarūpa*), and the form of a particle (*nipātarūpa*): "He went while the cows were being milked" (*goṣu duhyamānāsu gataḥ*); "He renounced the world while [they] were crying" (*krośataḥ prāvrājīt*). The form of a case-role (*kārakarūpa*) is as follows: "One kills a leopard for its skin; one kills an elephant for its two tusks; one kills a yak for its hair; a muskrat is killed at the boundary. (*carmaṇi dvīpinaṃ hanti dantayorhanti kuñjaram| keśeṣu camarīṃ hanti sīmni puṣkalako hataḥ||*)

[The case of] attachment: "He is attached to his hair"; [the case of] simultaneous action: "While the Brahmins are eating, the *vṛṣalas* sit," and "While the *vṛṣalas* are sitting, the Brahmins eat. [The case of] name and form (*nāmarūpa*): "The owner of the cows," "He dwells for the sake of food," "Resembling his father," and "Welfare for the subjects. [The case of] indeclinable form (*avyaya*): "To the village by means of peace," "Together with the student," "Salutation to the gods," and "To the south of the village."

The form of a particle (*nipāta*) is illustrated as: *he devadatta*, *hā devadattam*, *vinā viṣṇumitreṇa*, and *ṛte yajñadattāt*. The form of a karmapravacanīya is illustrated as: *vṛkṣamanu vidyotate* (it lightens near the tree), *upārjunam yoddhāraḥ* (the warriors are inferior to Arjuna), *adhi brahmadatte pañcālāḥ* (the Pañcālas are subordinate to Brahmadatta), and *adhi pañcāleṣu brahmadattaḥ* (Brahmadatta rules over the Pañcālas). Thus, the base forms, suffixes, and grammatical embellishments have been shown. In due order, the nature of the upapada has also been described. The indeclinables (*avyaya*), particles (*nipāta*), and prefixes (*gati*) have been examined.

The *karmapravacanīyas* along with their prefixes have also been elucidated. Here, neither the verbal root (*prakṛti*) alone is employed, nor are the nominal suffixes (*sup*), verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), primary suffixes (*aṇ*), secondary suffixes (*kyac*), and so forth used in isolation. An embellishment (*upaskāra*) occurs here; indeed, a complement (*upapada*) is employed for the sake of the meaning of the word itself. Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Elucidation of the Root and Other Elements," in the *Śṛṅgāraprakāśa* composed by the Great Emperor, the illustrious Bhojadeva.
The second [section] is the exposition of nominal stems (*prātipadika*) and so forth.

A nominal stem is threefold: consisting of parts that are inflected (*vibhaktāvayava*), consisting of parts that are not inflected (*avibhaktāvayava*), and imitation words (*anukaraṇa*). Among these, those consisting of parts that are inflected are threefold: the form of primary derivatives (*kṛt*), the form of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and the form of compounds (*samāsa*). Among these, the *kṛt* suffixes are those that denote action (*bhāva*) or grammatical relations (*kāraka*). Therein, "action" (*bhāva*) is simply the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*) itself, existing as a sequence of prior and posterior stages; as it has been said: "That form of the meaning of the root which follows time and is called 'action' (*kriyā*), and which is delimited on all sides—that is declared to be 'action' (*bhāva*)."

In this context, it (the *bhāva*) manifests in six ways: as *siddha* (established), *sādhya* (to be accomplished), *siddhāsamāpta* (partially established), *sādhyāsamāpta* (partially to be accomplished), *siddhasādhya* (established-to-be-accomplished), and *sādhyasiddha* (to-be-accomplished-established). Among these, the *siddha* is that which, by virtue of having the aspect of a fully manifested cognition (*udbhūtapratyayāṃśatva*), lacks an excess of action (*kriyānudreka*) and thus possesses the nature of a substantive entity (*sattvabhūtatva*); it is the cause for the genitive case of relation prescribed by the rule "kartṛkarmaṇoḥ kṛti," and it takes on gender, number, and so forth. Examples are: "the cooking of rice for the sake of the Ācārya" (*ācāryasyedaṃ odanasya pākaḥ*), "the appearance of Brāhmaṇas" (*brāhmaṇānāṃ ca prādurbhāvaḥ*), and "Devadatta’s splitting of the wood" (*bhedikā kāṣṭhānāṃ devadattasya*).

In the example *cikīrṣā yajñadattasya kaṭasya* ("Yajñadatta’s desire to make a mat"), although there is a rule stating that when both [agent and object] are possible, the genitive occurs only for the object (*karmaṇy eva*), this is because the commentary explains it as "in which [suffix] both are possible" (*ubhayoḥ prāptir yasmin kṛti*). Furthermore, since the restriction is prohibited for suffixes ending in *a* and *ā*, the genitive occurs even for the agent; thus, it indicates the state of the action as something already accomplished (*siddhatām*).

Because of the predominance of the verbal action (*kriyā*) due to its being a highly manifest aspect of its own nature (*udbhataprakṛtyaṃśatva*), and because it is not yet an accomplished entity (*asattvabhūtatva*), the *sādhya* (the object to be accomplished) does not admit gender, number, and so forth; rather, it is the cause for the case endings (*kārakavibhakti*) of the agent and the object, as in: "he goes to eat rice" (*odanaṃ bhoktuṃ yāti*), "he studies his own portion" (*svādhyāyam adhīte*), and "he sits drinking milk again and again" (*payaḥ pāyaṃ pāyam āste*). For this very reason, the genitive case is prohibited by the rule "na loka... (*Pāṇini 2.3.69*). That which is connected with secondary suffixes (*taddhita*) is already established (*siddha*), yet it remains incomplete (*asamāpta*) in its accomplishment, as in: "one who cries out while moving" (*vyāvakrośī*), "one who intends to deceive" (*sāṅkūṭinam*), and "that which is artificial" (*kṛtrimam*).

In this regard, just as in examples such as *ābhijityaḥ* and *kauñjāyanyaḥ*, the meaning of "offspring" (*apatya*), though already expressed by the suffixes *aṇ* and others, is not fully realized; and just as in examples such as *taittirīyāḥ* and *chāgaleyinaḥ*, the meaning of "proclaimed by" (*prokta*), though already expressed by the suffixes *thaṇ* and others, is not completed without the production of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) whose scope concerns the student or knower of that [text]—so too, the abstract state (*bhāva*), whether expressed by the suffix *ṇac* (in *vyatihāra*) and *ini* and *uṇ* (under the conditions of *abhividhi*), or expressed by the pure *kṛtya* suffixes, even when established, is not complete without the production of a secondary derivative whose purpose is to exclude its own original meaning (*svārthika-vanivṛttārtha*).

"Is completed" means that it becomes one whose completion is established. That which is connected to a subsequent usage while still being in the state of being accomplished is "incomplete in its accomplishment" (*sādhyāsamāpta*), as in *cakāsāñcakāra*, *vidāṅkurvantu*, and *raipoṣaṃ puṣyati*.

In this regard, just as in cases such as *śuklībhavati* ("it becomes white") and *paṭapaṭākaroti* ("he makes a clattering sound"), where forms ending in * cvi* and other suffixes denote the transition from one state to another (*abhūtatadbhāva*), or in cases such as *lunīhi lunīhīty evāyaṃ lunāti* ("he cuts repeatedly, saying 'cut, cut'!"), *rāṣṭramaṭa aṭhamaṭa dūramaṭety evāyam aṭati* ("he wanders, saying 'wander through the kingdom, wander through the forest, wander through the distance'!"), and so forth—where forms ending in *soḍaḍḍatdhnta* (the *yaṅ* suffix) denote the intensification of an action (*kriyāsamabhihāra*) and the like, they remain incomplete because their meaning is not fully manifested; thus, they require the subsequent application of roots such as *kṛ*, *bhū*, and others, according to the rule "the subsequent application follows the original form" (*yathāvidhyanuprayoga*). In the same way, this applies to forms ending in *ām* and *ṇamul*.

Furthermore, because its meaning has not yet been fully manifested, the verbal root (*bhāva*) remains incomplete in its state as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*); thus, for the sake of manifesting its own meaning, it requires the subsequent application of a verb such as *kṛ*, *bhū*, or *as*, as well as the subsequent application [of the original verb] according to its specific rule. This is what is meant by saying that the *bhāva* is "incomplete in its accomplishment. Regarding this, he says: "Since the suffix *ṇamul* also possesses an incomplete sense—just like the suffix *ām*—its subsequent application is already established, as in the case of *caṅ* and others; however, the statement regarding 'according to the rule' (*yathāvidhi*) applies to cases such as *kaṣādiṣu* where there is subsequent application according to the rule."

By the statement "tena cakāsāṃcakāra" and so forth, this meaning arises: [he] shone, let them know, nourishing wealth, he nourishes that [person]. For this very reason, since the matter is established by the adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) alone, some do not even begin the section on the suffix *ṇamul*. Now, one might object: "Adverbial modifiers possess the status of an object (*karman*) and are neuter; how then can 'nourishing' (*puṣi*) itself be the object of the root *puṣ*? For a thing cannot be pervaded by itself, nor can even a well-trained boy mount his own shoulder."

It is not so; for in such cases as "one should live according to the conduct of a city-dweller" (*nāgarakaṃ vṛttaṃ varteta*) or "one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit" (*viśvajitā yajeta*), because the universal and the particular are perceived through their non-identity in terms of pervasion and delimitation, the action belonging to the universal constituent itself becomes the action belonging to the individual constituent.

Nor is there a rule that qualifiers of an action must necessarily be objects (*karman*); for just as an action is an object because it is being accomplished (*sādhyamānatva*), so too it is an agent (*kartṛ*) because it is coming into being (*utpadyamānatva*). Therefore, qualifiers of an action are employed in both ways: as in *raipoṣaṃ kṛtvā puṣyati* ("having brought about the nourishment of cattle, he prospers"), meaning "he prospers in such a way that the nourishment of cattle occurs."

The connection with a property that is already established is "established-sādhyā" (*siddhasādhya*). For example: "Wondrous indeed is the milking of cows by one who is not a cowherd," "Excellent indeed is the drinking of milk by Yajñadatta," and "Marvelous indeed is the composition of the Sūtras by Pāṇini. In these cases, since it is prescribed that when both [agent and object] are possible, the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) applies only to the object, the fact that the agent takes the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) indicates that even what is established becomes "to be accomplished" (*sādhya*) according to the speaker's intention.

Others, however, describe the "accomplished" (*siddha*) and the "to-be-accomplished" (*sādhya*) differently, as in the examples: *uṣṭrāsikām āste* ("he sits like a camel"), *pañca vārān bhuṅkte* ("he eats five times"), and *pañca prayogān pacati* ("he cooks five applications"). Here, because the camel-sitting, the times, and the applications are not distinct from the nature of the performance of specific actions through repetition, and because no accusative case is seen for those things designated as actions, it is understood—due to the intention to express non-difference—that even though they are accomplished, they possess the status of being "to-be-accomplished" just like the action itself. Thus he says: "Because of its specific nature, the camel-sitting is not something else that is not pervaded [by the action]."

However, when they are to be accomplished (*sādhya*), they are called "actions" (*karman*) because they result in identity with the substrate (*āsana*). Since there is non-difference between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) due to the relation of "this is that," the status of being something to be accomplished does not conflict for the *vāra* and other such terms, just as it does not for the action itself. Therefore, in expressions such as *uṣṭrāsikām āste*, the meaning is: "he sits like a camel," "he performs the act of eating five times," or "he accomplishes five acts of cooking."

That which possesses a property yet to be established (*siddha-dharma-yogin*) is "established as something to be accomplished" (*sādhya-siddha*), such as in the examples *kartavyaṃ bhavataḥ* ("it is to be done by you") and *kāryaṃ bhavataḥ* ("it is to be performed by you"). Here, because the affixes beginning with *la* (the verbal suffixes) denote a state yet to be accomplished (*sādhya-artha*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) for the agent and the object is prohibited by the rule *na lokāvyayaniṣṭhākhalarthatṛnām*. However, by the subsequent rules—"the optionality of the genitive for the agent in the case of kṛtya-affixes," "the genitive for the past passive participle (*kta*) when referring to the present," and the supplementary rule (*upasaṃkhyāna*) "the genitive for the neuter abstract action"—the genitive is again prescribed optionally according to the speaker's intention.

It is understood that the state of denoting an accomplished fact (*siddhārtha*) is what is intended here; thus, the meaning stated [by the rule] results in the accomplishment of the goal (*sādhya*). Furthermore, no prohibition of *kṛtya* suffixes is heard in this context, because in the rule *khasarthatṛnām*, the term *khal-artha* includes *kṛtya*, *akta*, *khal-artha*, as well as *śatṛ*, *śāna*, *añ*, and *cvi*, whereas the term *tṛn* includes only the *tṛn* suffix itself.

For this very reason, just as with a state denoted by a past passive participle (*niṣṭhā*), the genitive case is not employed for the object even when the suffix denotes a future obligation (*kṛtya*); for example: "The deer-eyed woman must come to a state of relaxation, just as the sun has set and just as the moon has risen. (tatā manina śaithilyam āgantavyaṃ mṛgīddaśaḥ).

But how can there be an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) after a transitive verb? For by that [rule], it should arise from an intransitive verb; as it is said: "The *l*-suffixes occur in the sense of the object and in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) after intransitives," and "The *kṛtya*, *kta*, and *khal* suffixes occur only in those two senses" (Pāṇini 3.4.70). Indeed, one does not say, "The mat was made by Devadatta."

It is said: this is not an internal object (*antar-aṅga-karman*), but rather, according to the rule "time, distance, state, and the destination are known as objects for roots whose primary meaning is 'to go' when they do not have [another] object," the object characterized by the destination is an external object (*bahir-aṅga-karman*) among the external objects such as time and so forth. And its status as external is known from the fact that the second case ending is mentioned again in the rule "in connection with time and distance when there is continuous contact" (*kālādhvanor atyantasaṃyoge*); otherwise, since the second case would already be established for an object, he would have simply said "the fourth case ending [is used] for the object of roots meaning 'to go'."

When a verbal root is intransitive because its internal object (*antaraṅga-karman*) is absent, it becomes transitive precisely when that same object exists as an abstract state (*bhāva*); therefore, even though the object consisting of time (*kāla*) and so forth exists, it does not obstruct the designation "intransitive.
