Since this is a matter of words, and because [the formation of a compound] is impossible in the case of the word itself, the operation will be understood as applying to the meaning.

This being established, the purpose for which he employs the term "ratha" (chariot) is so that it may be understood that [the compound] occurs even when the sense is already accomplished. But what is the "accomplished sense"? It is *samuccaya* (aggregation), *anvācaya* (conjunction), *itaretarayoga* (mutual connection), and *samāhāra* (collective totality). Regarding these, it has been demonstrated by the author of the treatise (*pustakṛt*) that a compound does not occur between two [words] because they are mutually dependent, whereas it does occur between two [words] when they are independent.

But if this were so, then in the case of *plakṣanyagrodhau*—where the meaning is "the *plakṣa* tree and the *nyagrodha* tree"—the analysis (*vigraha*) would have to be *plakṣaśca nyagrodhaśca*. For even when it is said *plakṣaśca nyagrodhaśca*, it is understood that the *plakṣa* is accompanied by the *nyagrodha*, and the *nyagrodha* is also accompanied by the *plakṣa*. What fault would there be in that? [The answer is: what was stated—that it should be *plakṣau ca nyagrodhau ca*—is not tenable.

This [sūtra] is intended merely to demonstrate the expression of things residing in a common locus simultaneously; however, this is not the ultimate truth. For if it were done in this way, then *ekā ca viṃśatiś ca* would result in *ekaviṃśatiḥ*, and *dvau ca viṃśatiś ca* would result in *dvāviṃśatiḥ*; thus, the dual and plural number endings would follow. But are words such as *ekaviṃśatiḥ* and so forth compounds (*dvandva*)? Certainly they are.

For if one adopts the position that it is "twenty-one," the accent on the number would not be obtained; since that [accent] should not apply to a genitive compound such as *śatasahasram*, only the *dvandva* compound is permitted. If this were so, then in the case of mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*), there would be dual number, whereas in the case of collective aggregation (*samāhāra*), neuter gender would result. This is not so; for according to the rule, "Gender is not to be prescribed, as it depends on common usage," neuter gender will not occur even in the case of collective aggregation.

Now, why does a collective compound (*samāhāra*) not also occur here in the case of *dvādaśa* ("twelve")? Numbers up to ten function only as numerable entities; therefore, when there is a collection whose constituent parts are prominent, only a copulative compound (*itaretarayoga*) is applicable, as in the rule "and when the extent of the substratum is indicated," for example: "these ten are drummers and cymbal players. Thus, this [nominal stem] has been explained as threefold—distinguished by primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and compounds (*samāsa*)—with its constituent parts being distinct. Now, that which has undivided constituent parts is described.

That *nāmarūpa* (name-and-form) is also threefold: *avyayarūpa* (indeclinable form), *nipātarūpa* (particle form), and *nāma* (noun). Among these, *nāmas* are those that do not depend on etymological derivation and denote entities that are sentient beings (*sattvabhūta*). These are of three types: those with a single meaning, those with multiple meanings, and those with both single and multiple meanings. Among them, examples of those with a single meaning are: *vṛkṣaḥ* (tree), *kuṇḍam* (pot), *kumārī* (maiden), *ḍitthah* (a proper name), *śuklaḥ* (white), *śīghraḥ* (swift), *indraḥ* (Indra), *śukraḥ* (Venus/the bright one), *purandaraḥ* (Indra/the destroyer of cities), *koṣṭhaḥ* (granary), and *kusūlaḥ* (storehouse).

Words with multiple meanings are, for example: *akṣāḥ*, *māṣāḥ*, *pādāḥ*, *avayaḥ*, *harayaḥ*, *gāvaḥ*, *bhūtayaḥ*, *puṇḍarīkam*, *puṣkaram*, *sāma*, and *lalāmam*. Words with both single and multiple meanings are, for example: *dastrau*, *nāsatyau*, *puṣpavantau*, *ubhau*, *rodasī*, *rodasyai*, *dārāḥ*, *varṣāḥ*, *āpaḥ*, *vanam*, and *senā*.

The indeclinables (*avyaya*) are primarily [divided into] those expressing number, gender, and power; among them, those denoting substance (*dravyavacana*) are as follows: *śvas*, *prātar*, *divā*, *doṣā*, *naktam*, *sāyam*, *vihāyasā*, *bhūḥ*, *śam*, *saṃyoḥ*, *mayaḥ*; those denoting quality (*guṇavacana*) are as follows: *uccaiḥ*, *nīcaiḥ*, *suṣṭhu*, *apaṣṭhu*, *mudhā*, *addhā*, *mṛṣā*, *mithyā*, *alam*, *balavat*, *pṛthak*, *viṣvak*.

Words expressing relation (*saṃbandhavacana*) are, for example: *śamayā*, *nikaṣā*, *bahiḥ*, *antaḥ*, *antareṇa*, *ṛte*, *ārāt*, *yugapat*, *sākam*, *sārdham*, *amā*, and *saha*. Furthermore, particles (*nipāta*) such as *ca* and others denote non-substance (*asattva*). These are also of three kinds: independent (*svatantra*), dependent on another (*paratantra*), and dependent on a qualifier (*viśeṣaparatantra*). Among these, the verbs beginning with *as* (the root *as*) are independent, such as: *asti*, *asi*, *asmi*, *ehi*, *brūhi*, *mṛduhi*, *manye*, *jāne*, *paśya*, *paśyata*, and *syāt*.

The *karmapravacanīyas* beginning with *ca* are dependent [on other words], as in: *vṛkṣam anu vidyotate* (it lightens in the direction of the tree), *upārjunam yoddhāraḥ* (the warriors are inferior to Arjuna), *apa trigartebhyo vṛṣṭo devaḥ* (it rained away from the Trigartas), *abhimanyur arjunataḥ prati* (Abhimanyu is a match for Arjuna), *yad atra mām prati syāt* (whatever may befall me here), *adhi brahmadatte pañcālāḥ* (the Pañcālas are subordinate to Brahmadatta), *ahaṃ ca tvaṃ ca vṛtrahan* (both I and you, O slayer of Vṛtra), “*vāyurvā tvā manurvā tvā*” (either Vāyu or Manu [has chosen] you), “*ahameva paśūnām īśe*” (I alone am the lord of animals), *sarojam iva te mukham* (your face is like a lotus), “*na nūnam ati no śvaḥ*” (neither now nor tomorrow), and “*kaḥ svid ekākī carati*” (who indeed wanders alone?).

The *gati*s and *prādi*s are dependent upon specific meanings, such as: *prakaroti*, *parākaroti*, *ūrīkaroti*, *gulugudhākaroti*, *kārikākareti*, *khāṭkaroti*, *paṭapaṭākaroti*, *tiraskaroti*, *pulaskaroti*, *śraddhā*, and *antardhiḥ*. Now, regarding imitation (*anukaraṇa*): that too is of exactly three kinds—imitation of a correct form (*sādhu*), imitation of an incorrect form (*asādhu*), and imitation of an indistinct sound (*avyakta*). Among these, the first [the correct] is both meaningful (*pārthaka*) and meaningless (*nirarthaka*).

An example of these two [types of] meaningful [utterances] is as follows: "He says *pacatu* twice," "He says *agni*," and "He says *pacati*. Because these are meaningful, there is no *nighāta* (anudātta accent) by the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*; there is *pragṛhya* status by the rule *īdūdeddvivacanam*; and because they end in a *tiṅ* suffix, they are not *prātipadikas*, so there is no subsequent derivation of case endings (*sub*).

Meaningless [utterances] are, for example: "suḥ pūjāyām" (the prefix *su-* is used in the sense of honor), "apiḥ padārthasaṃbhāvanā'nvavasargagarhāsamuccayeṣu" (the particle *api* is used in the senses of possibility regarding word-meanings, permission, reproach, and conjunction), and "caḥ samuccaye" (the particle *ca* is used in the sense of conjunction). In these cases, because the meaning is being imitated and because they possess their own formal identity (*svasvarūpatva*), they are treated as nominal stems (*prātipadika*); consequently, the case endings (*sup*) are heard [in the utterance]. The second type is that which arises from incapacity (*aśaktija*) and is corrupt speech (*apabhraṃśa*). Among these, an example of that arising from incapacity is: when one ought to say "aho ṛtaka," the Asuras were defeated while saying "helayo helaya."

The third [type of suffix] is either *nirullekha* (without distinct expression) or *sollakha* (with distinct expression). Of these two, an example of *nirullekha* is: *paṭat-paṭat* he makes it, or *paṭapaṭāyate*. An example of *sollakha* is: "This very same speech of the Dawn repeats: 'O giver, give!'; 'You shall give!'; 'Give!'; 'Be merciful!'"—therefore, one should learn this triad: self-restraint (*dama*), giving (*dāna*), and compassion (*dayā*). A case-ending (*vibhakti*) is precisely a specific suffix that effects the distinction between power (*śakti*) and number (*saṃkhyā*).

That [inflection] is threefold: the *tiṅ*-inflection, the *sup*-inflection, and the indeclinable (*avyaya*) inflection. Among these, the *tiṅ*-inflection is sixfold: the *parasmaipada* inflection, the *ātmanepada* inflection, the *sārvadhātuka* inflection, the *ārdhadhātuka* inflection, the inflection with manifest tense (*vyaktakāla*), and the inflection with unmanifest tense (*avyaktakāla*). Among these, the *parasmaipada* inflection is, for example: *pacati*, *pacataḥ*, *pacanti*; the *ātmanepada* inflection is, for example: *pacyate*, *pacyete*, *pacyante*; the *sārvadhātuka* inflection is, for example: [etc.]

The [forms] *vyapacyata*, *vyacyetām*, and *vyapacyanta* illustrate the *ārdhadhātuka* verbal suffixes, as in *papāca*, *paktā*, and *pakṣyati*. Those with manifest tense-suffixes (*vyaktakālavibhakti*) are, for example, *apākṣīt*, *apacat*, and *pakṣyate*. Those with unmanifest tense-suffixes (*avyaktakālavibhakti*) are, for example, *pacatu*, *pacat*, and *apakṣyata*.

The case-inflection (*vibhakti*) is also sixfold: the agentive case (*kāraka-vibhakti*), the residual case (*śeṣa-vibhakti*), the adverbial case (*upapada-vibhakti*), the primary case (*pradhāna-vibhakti*), and the vocative case (*saṃbodhana-vibhakti*). Among these, the agentive case is, for example: *kaṭaṃ karoti* (he makes a mat), *dātreṇa lunāti* (he cuts with a sickle), *brāhmaṇāya dadāti* (he gives to a Brahmin). The genitive case of relation is, for example: *vidyayā yajñaḥ* (sacrifice by means of knowledge), *yūpāya dāru* (wood for a sacrificial post), *gavāṃ kṛṣṇā saṃpannakṣīratamā* (among cows, the black one has the most abundant milk). The residual case is, for example: *mātuḥ smarati* (he remembers his mother), *vṛkṣasya parṇaṃ patati* (the leaf of the tree falls), [and] *māṇavakasya* (of the boy).

The case of inquiry is, for example, "he asks the father about the path. The case of relation (*upapada-vibhakti*) is, for example, "the lightning flashes toward the tree," "salutation to the gods," and "except for Devadatta. The primary case (*pradhāna-vibhakti*) is, for example, "Devadatta cooks," "it is cooked by Caitra," and "the man is a hero. The case of address (*saṃbodhana-vibhakti*) is, for example, "O Devadatta! "I am going, Devadatta! and "Come here, Devadatta! The indeclinable case (*avyaya-vibhakti*) is a specific type of *taddhita* suffix.

That [term] is twofold: functioning as a case-ending (*vibhakti*) and not functioning as a case-ending. That which functions as a case-ending is governed by the rule *prāgdiśo vibhaktiḥ*. It is threefold: consisting of substitutes for case-endings, consisting of substitutes for suffixes, and consisting of suffixes themselves. Among these, those consisting of substitutes for case-endings are, for example: *pañcamyāstasil*, *saptamyāstral*, *idamo haḥ*, *kimo't*; and in connection with the words *bhavān*, *dīrghāyus*, *āyuṣmant*, and *devānāmpriya*, the rule *te'nyāsām ca* applies, as in *sarvasmāt*.

From *sarvataḥ*, *yasmin*, *yatra*, *taṃ bhavantam*, *tato bhavantam*, *etena dīrghāyuṣā*, *atra dīrghāyuṣā*, *ihāyuṣmate*, *asmai āyuṣmate*, *kasya devānāṃ priyasya*, and *kva devānāṃ priyasya*—the forms [ending] in *tasi* according to the rule "pratyayadeśarūpā ‘teseśca’" [Pāṇini 6.3.35].

And that [suffix] occurs as follows: "The suffix *tasi* is used for the ablative case when it expresses the sense of 'in opposition to' (*pratiyoga*)," "also when expressing the *apādāna* (ablative) case, except after the roots *hā* and *ruh*," "the third case ending is used for the instrumental case when expressing 'overpowering,' 'afflicting,' or 'reproaching,' provided it does not denote the agent," "the sixth case ending is used when expressing 'dependence on' (*vyāśraya*)," and "from words beginning with *ādi*, all case endings are used. For example: *abhimanyur arjunataḥ prati* ("Abhimanyu is the rival of Arjuna"), *śailato'vatarati* ("he descends from the mountain"), *śīlato'tigṛhyate* ("he is overcome because of his character"), *devā arjunato'bhavan* ("the gods were inferior to Arjuna"), *ādau* or *āditaḥ* ("in the beginning"), and *pramāṇena* or *pramāṇataḥ* ("by measure"). Furthermore, the form of the suffix is given by the rules: "*thā* is used in the sense of cause in the Vedic language" (*thā hetau ca chandasi*) and "*amu* is substituted for *idam*" (*idamasthamuḥ*).

[The suffixes are prescribed] by the rules: *imorhil*, *prakāravacane thāl*, *thā hetau ca cchandasi*, *idamasthamuḥ*, and *kimaśca*; as in the examples: *śarvadā*, *etarhi*, *sarvathā*, *prakathā*, *itthaṃ*, and *kathaṃ*.

Even the operation of case endings (*avibhaktikārya*) is stated in three ways: by word (*śabdoktā*), by meaning (*arthoktā*), and by usage (*prayogoktā*). Among these, that which is stated by word is as follows: "The suffix *tāti* [is applied] after the seventh, fifth, and first cases," and "After *deva*, *manuṣya*, *puruṣa*, *purumat*, and *martya*, [the suffixes] the second and seventh cases are diversely applied. For example: *purastād vasati* (he dwells in front), *purastād āgataḥ* (he has come from in front), *purastād ramaṇīyam* (it is beautiful in front); *devatrā gacchati* (he goes among the gods), *manuṣyatrā vasati* (he dwells among men), *puruṣatrābhiniviśete* (they two settle among men). Similarly: "He behaves like fire" is expressed as *agninā tulyam ayam vartate* or *agnivat*; likewise, *devam iva*.

"I see you as a god" (*devavat*); "he is given to him like a Brahmin" (*brahmaṇavat*); "he fears him like a tiger" (*vyāghravat*); "the palaces in Pāṭaliputra are like those in Mathurā" (*madhurāvat*); "his teeth are white like those of a Vedic scholar" (*śrotriyavat*). While it would have been sufficient to say "the secondary derivative suffixes" (*taddhita-vibhakti*), the inclusion of the term "indeclinable" (*avyaya*) is for the purpose of including such forms as *adhistri*, *pratyurasaṃ*, *pāregaṅgaṃ*, *purā*, and *sākṣāt*.

“That which is designated first in a compound is the *upasarjana* (subordinate member), and that which has a single case-ending is so when it does not occur as the prior member. That [subordinate] is threefold: having the nature of a substantive (*viśeṣyarūpa*), having the nature of an adjective (*viśeṣaṇarūpa*), and having the nature of an equivalent (*tulyarūpa*). Among these, an example of having the nature of a substantive is: this man is like a tiger—a *puruṣavyāghra*; a honored horse—an *aśvakuñjara*; a pregnant cow—a *gogarbhiṇī*; a small fire—an *agnistoka*; the front part of the body—a *pūrvakāya*; half of a *pippalī* fruit—an *ardhapippalī*. An example of having the nature of an adjective is as follows:

The king’s man is *rājapuruṣaḥ*; the king of teeth is *rājadantaḥ*; one who has resorted to hardship is *kaṣṭaśritaḥ*; one who has attained a livelihood is *āpannajīvikaḥ*; a blue lotus is *nīlotpalam*; the best of men is *puruṣottamaḥ*. Examples of similar forms are: dark as a sword-blade is *śastrīśyāmā*; both lame and hunchbacked is *khañjakubjaḥ*; gone out from Kauśāmbī is *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*; he whose cows are variegated is *citraguḥ*; half and a third of these are *ardhatṛtīyāḥ*. Who?

[The question is: "What is his fellow-celibate? [The answer is: "A fellow-celibate. But surely, in the case of the expression *ardha-tṛtīyam eṣām* ("half of a third of these"), the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*) is not applicable; for that would only occur where there is a compound of certain words and the meaning belongs to a word other than those. This is not a fault. The analysis (*vigraha*) is by means of a part, while the meaning of the compound (*samāsārtha*) is the whole. But if this were so, how do you explain: "Pāṇḍu followed, having no second," or "May the strength of Kṛṣṇa, who has Saṅkarṣaṇa as his second, increase"?

In cases such as *idam* and so forth, the dual number would apply because there are two things; however, this is not so. For in the expression "one whose second is a bee" (*alirdvitīyo yasya*), only a single entity is expressed through the sense of the external referent (*anyapadārtha*). This is just as in the phrase, "Janārdana himself as his fourth. Alternatively, the word *dvitīya* exists both as a numeral ending in *-tīya* meaning "completing a count," and as an uninflected (*avyutpanna*) term meaning "accompanied by"; here, the latter is intended, so that *asudvitīyaḥ* means "having no companion" (*asisahāya*).

Regarding the compound *ātmacaturtha*: what kind of compound is this? Is it not the case that the self (*ātman*) is the fourth member of something else, thus [forming a bahuvrīhi]? Why does it not become a *tatpuruṣa* compound, such as *ātmānā caturthaḥ* ("the fourth with the self")? Because of the rule "ātmanaśca pūraṇe" (Pāṇini 6.3.6), there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-elision (*aluk*) of the instrumental ending. If this is so, then the non-elision need not be stated; there will be the analytical sentence (*vākya*) "ātmānā caturthaḥ," and the compound form (*vṛtti*) "ātmacaturthaḥ. Furthermore, when "ātma-caturthaḥ" is uttered—whether it be a bahuvrīhi or a tatpuruṣa—no difference in meaning exists, since in both cases a collective group characterized by the number four is understood.

It is not so; for if this were the case, when it is said "the king’s friend" (*rājasakhaḥ*), one would necessarily infer from the connection that "surely the king is his friend," and when it is said "the king-friend" (*rājasakha*), one would have to understand that "this person is the king’s friend. Consequently, neither the *bahuvrīhi* nor the *tatpuruṣa* compound would be applicable. This is not so; there is a distinction here: in a *tatpuruṣa*, a compound-ending suffix (*samāsānta*) occurs, as in "Hail to you, O friend of Soma! (*svasti somasakhāya te*), whereas in a *bahuvrīhi*, it does not occur, as in "Slay Vṛtra, O friend of the Maruts! (*vṛtraṃ jahi marutsakhe*).

In this case as well, there is indeed a distinction: in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, this is to be accomplished with oneself as the fourth; in a *bahuvrīhi* compound, this is to be accomplished with oneself as the fourth. Furthermore, the comprehension of an object through perception is of one kind, while that through inference is of another kind. In that regard, "this is the king's friend, himself being the fourth" is known through perception, because a relationship resides in both parties. Surely the king also [is included] in this group, and thus it is in the singular number because they share a single purpose; likewise with "two and a half."

Why does this [rule] not also apply here? For other collective groups (*samudāya*) also have the same single referent (*ekārtha*), such as "a hundred," "a herd," or "a forest. This is an unequal comparison; for in the case of *ātmacaturtha* ("with himself as the fourth"), by means of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, Janārdana—who is denoted by the expressive power of the word *ātmacaturtha* which is subordinate and has a perceived correlative number as its coreferential—becomes the meaning of the second member of the compound (*anya-pada*) as "one who has this [Janārdana] as one [of his companions]. But here, in the case of *ardhatṛtīya*, three numerables (*saṃkhyeya*) are denoted by the expressive power of the word *ardhatṛtīya*.

In that case, if the singular number occurs in the sentence or in the compound (*vṛtti*), of what would that [singular] be half and a third? But even so, in the expression "two and a half *droṇas*," the word *droṇa* applies to the aggregate and does not apply to the half. This is not a fault; words that apply to aggregates also apply to their constituent parts, as for example: "the eastern Pañcālas" or "the northern Kurus. Alternatively, one might argue that two *droṇas* and half an *āḍhaka* should be expressed as "two and a half *droṇas*. It need not be so expressed.

Words that function for a whole apply to its constituent parts; thus, if the analysis *tṛtīyam anayoḥ* ("the third of these two") were made, what fault would there be? The sense of the genitive case would not be tenable, for how could there be a "third half" belonging to two things? You too, being asked, should explain this.

Now, in the case of "Devadatta’s brother," what is the meaning of the relationship? If it is argued that it means "manifestation from one [source]," that is false; for example, when members of a Śārtika family who share a single dwelling depart in different directions upon rising in the morning, no mutual relationship whatsoever exists between them—such is the nature of so-called "brotherhood. If the sense of the genitive case is observed to be appropriate there, then let it be observed as appropriate here as well; for a third person becomes the younger sibling of two.

Furthermore, a connection between two things by means of a third is observed elsewhere as well; for example: "In this [place], these two—Śrī and Sarasvatī—who have naturally distinct abodes yet dwell together, are worthy [of you] through their beauty, speech, and nobility; O auspicious lady, you alone are the third between them. Now, if this were so, then in the case of the command, "Let two and a half be brought," the bringing of a half would not be possible, nor would the use of the plural number be justified.

This is not a fault, for in a *bahuvrīhi* compound there is indeed "cognition of its qualities" (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*) as well. For example, in the cases "bring the one who wears white clothes" (*śuklavāsasamānaya*) and "the priests wearing red turbans proceed with the ritual" (*lohitoṣṇīṣā ṛtvijaḥ pracaranti*), that which possesses those qualities is brought, and those possessing those qualities proceed. As for the plural number, it is justified in the same way as [the plural] in "two or three" (*dvitrādi*). In that regard, just as when one says "let them be brought," the plural is justified even in the case of bringing two, just as it would be for three; so too will it be here.

This is an unequal comparison. For in that case, when "two" is said, "three" is understood; and when "three" is said, "two" is understood. This speech is based on five referents within the same grammatical core (*samānādhikaraṇa*), and thus the plural is appropriate there. However, in this case, although it is understood from the statement "the half is the third of these two" that the third completes a triad, nevertheless, because the compound refers to something other than its constituent members (*anyapadārtha*), only two are denoted; therefore, the plural does not arise.

The inclusion of the quality (*tadguṇasaṃvijñāna*) is only possible under the view that the compound expresses a single unified meaning; and a compound occurs only when there is semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*), while semantic capacity consists in the identity of meaning between the derivative form (*vṛtti*) and the analytical sentence (*vākya*). This identity arises only if, just as in the derivative form, the plural number is also employed for the referent of the compound within the analytical sentences. Now, regarding the expression *kiṃsabrahmacārī*, what kind of compound is this? It is [the analysis] *ke sabrahmacāriṇo 'syeti* ("whose fellow-students are these?").

Why does the compound *sabrahmacārī* not become a *karmadhāraya* [meaning "one who is himself a fellow-student"]? It would indeed be so, provided that a disparagement (*kṣepa*) is understood—as in "What kind of king is he who does not protect? or "What kind of ox is it that does not pull?"—[in which case it means "one who is a fellow-student in name only"]. If, on the other hand, it is a *tatpuruṣa* [meaning "a fellow-student of someone"], then why is the response "Kaṭha" not appropriate? For one thing asked should not be answered with something else; therefore, the response ought to have been "of the Kaṭhas."

This is equally true for the *bahuvrīhi* compound as well; for even there, when asked "Who are his fellow-students? (*ke sabrahmacāriṇo 'sya?*), the answer cannot be "Kaṭha" in the singular. This is not a fault, for it will be resolved by the principle of "I shall perform [the action] in the fire" (*agnau karavāṇi*). For example, when someone says, "I wish to perform something in the fire," and the other replies "Do so," once the agent is authorized, the action itself is also authorized.

In this way, when it is asked, "Who are his fellow religious practitioners (*sabrahmacārin*)? and the reply is given, "The Kaṭhas," it is understood from that connection that he too is a Kaṭha; likewise, when "Kaṭha" is said, it should be understood from that connection that they too are Kaṭhas. However, it is impossible to indicate them by a compound, for in that case there would be two subordinate members (*upasarjana*). A compound (*samāsa*) is a single word. It is of three kinds: that with an expressed action (*upaśliṣṭākriya*), that with an implied action (*gamitakriya*), and that without an action (*akriya*).

Among these, the compound with an implied action (*upaśliṣṭākriya*) is of two kinds: that in which the action resides in both members and that in which the action resides in only one. An example of the former, where the action resides in both, is: *kṛtākṛtam* (done and not done), *kliṣṭākliṣṭam* (afflicted and unafflicted), *snātānuliptaḥ* (bathed and anointed), *bhraṣṭaluñcitaḥ* (fallen and plucked), *kṛṣṭātikṛṣṭam* (ploughed and over-ploughed), and *krayākrayikā* (buying and selling). An example of the latter, where the action resides in only one member, is: *bhojyeṣṇaḥ* (eager for food), *prāptajīvukaḥ* (one who has obtained livelihood), *āhitāgniḥ* (one who has established the sacred fires), *kaṣṭaśrutaḥ* (one who has mastered difficult texts), *kākapeyā* (drinkable even by crows—i.e., very shallow), and *idhmapravraścanaḥ* (one who cuts fuel-sticks). The compound with an implied object (*gamitakriya*) is also of two kinds: that in which the agent performs both actions and that in which the agent performs only one.

An example of that which is produced by both [factors] is as follows: rice mixed with curds is *dadhyodana*; roasted grains mixed with molasses are *guḍadhānā*; a piece cut with a knife is *śaṅkulākhaṇḍa*; one who is addicted to dice is *akṣaśauṇḍa*; one whose time (death) is fixed in the throat is *kaṇṭhekāla*; and what is prepared in five bowls is *pañcakapāla*.

An example of a compound formed with one member as the principal element (*anyatarakāraka*) is as follows: *pragata ācāryaḥ* becomes *prācāryaḥ*; *atikrānto mālām* becomes *atimālaḥ*; *avakraṣṭaḥ kokilayā* becomes *avakesilaḥ*; *pariglāno 'dhyayanāya* becomes *paryadhyayanaḥ*; *niśkrāntaḥ kauśāmbyāḥ* becomes *niṣkauśāmbiḥ*; and *prapatitāni palāśāny asya* becomes *prapalāśaḥ*. Negation (*nañ*) is of two kinds: that which has the form of a real entity (*vasturūpa*) and that which does not have the form of a real entity (*avasturūpa*).

Of these two, the *vasturūpa* (substantive form) is, for example: *upakumbham* (near the jar), *tribhuvanam* (the three worlds), *nālotpalam* (a lotus with a stalk), *rājapuruṣaḥ* (the king’s man), *citraguḥ* (one who has spotted cows), and *dhavakhadirau* (the *dhava* and *khadira* trees). The *avasturūpa* (non-substantive form) is, for example: *adhistri* (concerning a woman), *pratyurasam* (upon the chest), *yathāśakti* (according to ability), *yāvadamatram* (as much as the vessel holds), *pārogaṅgam* (as far as the Gaṅgā), and *madhyesamudram* (in the middle of the ocean). This [type of compound], moreover, is either one whose action is attached (*upaśliṣṭakriya*) or one whose action is implied (*gamitakriya*). For example: *āyatīgavam āgacchati* (he comes while the cows are coming), *ātiṣṭhadgū patiṣṭhate* (he stands while the bull is standing); or: *nikucya karṇe śārdūlaḥ* (having tucked his ears, the tiger), *apohya pucchī pradhāvati* (having thrust out his tail, he runs).

And just as a game of dice with four-sided pieces may be played even with a single die, observe that when the procedure is reversed, it arises even from the palms and so forth. Some maintain that [compounds] such as *keśākeśi*, *bāhūbāhavi*, *daṇḍādaṇḍi*, and *muṣṭīmuṣṭi* convey an action whose nature is non-substantial (*asattva*). For example: "Out of a fit of rage, two men, having suddenly encountered one another face-to-face and called each other by name, engaged in a wrestling match limb-to-limb (*bāhūbāhavi*), like boxers, striking with blows to the temples after breaking their weapons."

Some, however, assert that this [suffix] has the nature of a substantive (*vasturūpa*), as in the examples: *daṇḍād daṇḍī* (one who possesses a staff) and *na kurvanti na kacākaci kokilāḥ* (the cuckoos do not engage in mutual pulling of hair). Nevertheless, by these very words alone, the three worlds have been conquered. But how can it be that at one time *daṇḍin*, *adaṇḍin*, and so forth, have the nature of existence (*sattvarūpa*), while at another time they have the nature of non-existence (*asattvarūpa*)? This is due to the different interpretations of the rule (*sūtra*) "In that case, with that, this [is expressed] when the forms are identical" (*tatra tenedam iti sarūpe*).

In this regard, the meaning of this sūtra is as follows: two word-forms (*śabdarūpa*) of identical form are compounded when they refer to another referent (*anyapadārtha*), [expressing] "therein" (*tatra*) and "by that" (*tena*). But what here is the "other referent"? Some say: because the word *iti* expresses a mode (*prakāra*), there is the nature of a quality (*sattvarūpatā*) in the subsequent [word], since the nature of a real entity (*vasturūpa*) is referred to by the pronoun *idam*.

Furthermore, what is the meaning of the word *iha* (here) in this context? It refers to that action which takes the form of a procedure (*itikartavyatā*) following the sense of "this," occurring either in the locative sense as "there" (*tatra*) or in the instrumental sense as "by that" (*tena*), such as "having seized there" or "having struck with that. The referent of the pronouns *yat* and *tat*—that is, the battle or similar activity to be accomplished through actions such as seizing and striking—is what is denoted by the term *tad*. Thus Candragomin says: "Having seized there and having struck with that in battle, the words of identical form [become a compound] when two nouns (*sup*) stand in a single sense (*ekārthe*)."

What is this that must be stated? It need not be stated. How is it understood even when not explicitly stated? By the fact that the mention of two locatives and two instruments at the same time serves as an exception to the rule of *ekaśeṣa* for "homogeneous" (*sarūpa*) items. For indeed, without the operation of two counter-correlatives of equal strength, there can be no simultaneous mention of two locatives or two instruments. Nevertheless, the restriction regarding battle and so forth is not obtained.

Who, moreover, says that this is a restrictive rule (*niyama*)? For [the compound] is employed even in cases other than those involving battle and so forth; for example, "hand-to-hand" (*hastāhasti*), as in "having grasped hand in hand, he hands over his son to Mitra," and "insult-to-insult" (*gālīgāli*), as in "the joke proceeded by insulting each other with insults."

But surely, if it is stated that a *bahuvrīhi* compound occurs when another word-meaning (*anyapadārtha*) is intended, then how would it apply to general compounds such as *vispaṣṭapaṭur vaṭuḥ* (a boy clear and clever), *punarutsyūtaṃ vāsaḥ* (a garment sewn again), and *paraśśatāḥ śaradaḥ* (more than a hundred autumns); to specific compounds such as *svayaṃdhautau pādau* (feet washed by oneself), *sāmibhuktam annam* (food half-eaten), and *śreṇīkṛtāḥ pattayaḥ* (soldiers formed into a line); to attributive compounds such as *vinirvṛttaprarūḍho vṛkṣaḥ* (a tree grown out of its place), *kṛṣṇapiṅgalo grāvā* (a blackish-brown stone), and *īṣatkaḍāro 'śmā* (a slightly ruddy rock); and to [compounds] such as *avakokilaṃ vanam* (a forest where cuckoos have departed), *paryadhyayanaś chātraḥ* (a student who has ceased studying), and *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* (one who has gone out from Kauśāmbī)?

"An caravan" (*sārthaḥ*) is an example of a *pradi*-compound; "Devadatta is as dark as a sword-blade" (*śastrīśyāmā devadattā*), "this [act] of yours is like a snake placed in a heated vessel" (*avataptenakulasthitam tavedam*), and "the boy is like a frog in a well" (*kūpamaṇḍūkaḥ māṇavakaḥ*) are examples of compounds with an upamāna (standard of comparison). "Vallabhī is dear to the king" (*rājavallabhā vallabhī*), "a maiden to be given as a boon" (*varapradeyā kanyā*), and "a month has passed since he was born" (*māso jāto 'syeti*) are examples of genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compounds. "A foe who has resorted to hardship" (*kaṣṭaśrito ripuḥ*), "a deer afraid of a wolf" (*vṛkabhīto nyaṅkuḥ*), and "a youth broken by a wooden wedge" (*śaṅkulākhaṇḍaḥ pogaṇḍaḥ*) are examples of compounds based on grammatical relations (*kāraka*). "A Brāhmaṇa who does not eat at a funeral feast" (*aśrāddhabhojī brāhmaṇaḥ*) and "an individual who is not one [but many]" (*pumān anekaḥ padārthaḥ*) are further examples.

Thus, it might follow that negative compounds (*nañ-samāsa*) would receive the designation of *bahuvrīhi*. This is not so; for in these cases, the status of having another word as their referent (*anyapadārthatva*) is not produced by the compound itself, but rather by their nature as qualifiers (*guṇavacanatva*). Whatever gender, number, or meaning belongs to the substance when it is qualified by that quality, those same characteristics belong to the compound as well. For example: *śuklaṃ vastram* (a white cloth), *śuklā śāṭī* (a white garment), *śuklaḥ kambalaḥ* (a white blanket), *śuklau paṭau* (two white cloths), *śuklāḥ paṭāḥ* (white cloths).

But how, then, can there be a general designation of *samāsa* for words such as *vispaṣṭa* and *paṭu*? Since the understanding of a *samāsa* [in these cases] occurs through the indicative rule (*jñāpaka*) "vispaṣṭādīni guṇavacaneṣu" (P. 2.1.48), which implies that no specific *samāsa* designation applies, and since a *samāsa* is accepted by the rule "saha supā" (P. 2.1.4), one must rely on the *samāsa* designation provided by the rule "prāk ḍārāt samāsaḥ" (P. 2.1.3).

How is it that *svayaṃdhauta* and the like constitute a "compound with a qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*)? Because, although there is a difference between the compound and the analytical sentence for the words *svayaṃ* and *sāmi*—as in the rules “*svayaṃ ktena*” and “*sāmi*” [Pāṇini 2.1.27]—the formation of the compound is undertaken solely for the sake of establishing a single word-form (*ekapada*) with its specific accent. Furthermore, in the case of “*śreṇyādayaḥ kṛtādibhiḥ*” and “*cvyarthe*” [Pāṇini 2.1.59], within the compound (*vṛtti*), there is no relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*).

But surely, when something is cut, it is not then grown; and when it is grown, it is not then cut. Therefore, how can there be a relationship of qualifier and qualified characterized by grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇa*) between two objects that do not coalesce with one another? [The answer is: because of the synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*) that "that very thing which was cut is this same thing which is grown. Now, how is it so in the case of "a black-and-tawny animal" (*kṛṣṇapiṅgala*)? For that part of it which is black is not tawny, and that which is tawny is not black.

Words that function with respect to wholes (samudāya) also function with respect to their parts (avayava), as in the cases "the eastern Pañcālas" or "the northern Kurus. Alternatively, through connection with a black part, that very thing is "black," and through connection with a bull-like part, that very thing is a "bull"; thus, grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) is established. Now, what is qualified by the word "īṣat"? It is the object endowed with the quality of being brownish-red. But how can indeclinables, which denote non-existence, serve as qualifiers of objects that possess existence? This is because they function as qualifiers of an action (kriyā).

What, then, is the operation here? It is the connection with the quality of *kaḍāra* (tawny). Or rather, since some indeclinables possess a trace of substantiality (*sattvagandhitva*), a property of substance such as the possession of power is observed; for example: "the day was considered a night," or "the night was considered a day. As it is said: "He who looks upon the darkness in caves as if it were daylight, like one afraid of the day. And: "O you who possess a planet [or seize the mind], you who take away friends—you are not a woman, you are a fault (*doṣa*)."

In this way, by qualifying the quality through its connection with the substance (*sattvagandhitva*), this [word] will also qualify the substance. But why does it not qualify the substance itself directly, as in the cases of *kaḍāram* (tawny) or *iṣṭatantreṇa kātantram* (the Kātantra by means of the desired rule)? If that were the case, the state of being "slight" (*īṣadbhāva*) would not be obtained for the quality; as it has been said: "by the expression 'possessing a slight indication' (*īṣadbhaṇavatvacanena*)."

Now, how can there be a compound of the prefixes (*prādayaḥ*) with words denoting substances (*dravyavacana*)? For it is only where some word expressing an action (*kriyāvācin*) is employed that the employment of the prefixes occurs. It is said in reply: this must be understood from usage itself; surely, in such cases, a word fit for employment is not actually used, by virtue of which the prefix possesses its functional capacity (*sāmarthya*). For example, upon seeing smoke, it is understood that "fire is here," and upon seeing a *triviṣṭabdhaka* (a specific posture), it is understood that "this is a wandering mendicant."

Which words, then, are suitable for application here? Those that end in *kṛt* suffixes and denote both the object and the agent (*karmakartṛ*), such as: *avakokilaṃ* (called by the cuckoo), *paryadhyayanaḥ* (exhausted with regard to study), and *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* (departed from Kauśāmbī). Now, how are compounds such as *śāstrīśyāmā* (dark like a female teacher) logically formed? They are established by rules such as "Comparisons [are compounded] with words expressing common properties" (*upamānāni sāmānyavacanaiḥ*).

If this is so, then the rule "In the case of *iva*, there is no elision of the case-ending, and the preceding word retains its original accent" need not be stated; for usages such as *vāsasī iva* (like two garments) and *kanye iva* (like two maidens) are already established by the rule "The standard of comparison [is compounded] with words expressing common properties. Furthermore, the mere non-elision of the case-ending would have to be stated again in the section on *aluk*. It is replied: This word *iva* is not itself expressive of a common property (*sāmānyavācin*), but rather it is an indicator (*dyotaka*) of a common property. For example, when it is said, "The eyes are blue lotuses," qualities such as having the same shape or color are understood.

In cases such as *śastriśyāmā* ("sword-dark"), the word *śyāmā*, which directly denotes a general quality, is employed. Now, how is it in the case of *avataptenakulasthitam* ("like a mongoose in hot ashes")? For this is not used in the sense of a simile (*upamā*), but rather in the sense of censure (*kṣepa*). Here, censure is understood through the standard of comparison: "This fickleness of yours remains like that of a mongoose in hot ashes. Just as a mongoose does not remain for long in hot ashes, so too one who, having begun a task, does not persist in it for long is described thus: "This [fickleness] of yours remains like that of a mongoose in hot ashes."

By this, the expression "the frog in the well" is also explained: just as a frog in a well, not emerging outside the well, does not know the affairs of other lands, so too this person, not emerging outside his own home, is not a knower of the affairs of other lands; thus he is called "this frog in the well."

Now, how are compounds such as *rājavallabhā* (the king’s favorite) and others formed as genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) compounds? Why does *rājavallabhā* not become a possessive (*bahuvrīhi*) compound in the sense of "she whose favorite is the king"? Because, being insentient, a woman cannot possess the state of being a favorite [in that specific sense]; however, the expression *rājño vallabhā* ("the king’s favorite") is indeed possible.

In this context, the meaning of the word *rājñaḥ* (of the king) is as follows: it has deviated from its own nature as a universal (*sāmānya*) because a universal, being established in its generality, is incapable of acting as an agent; it depends upon a related universal, or rather, it depends upon a related universal because it functions for the purpose of excluding other relations; and although the relation itself resides in both relata, since it is employed for the sake of another, that which ends in the genitive case expressing a manifested relation is employed.
Principal words whose meanings are not yet determined are joined with the nominative case-ending alone; for example: "Where, then, was this recited? [It was] the verses known as the *Bhrāja*.

Consequently, because its meaning is not yet determined, the word *vallabhāḥ*, while not deviating from its own primary sense (*svārtha*) in order to designate the self, functions by its very nature as a qualifier (*viśeṣavṛtti*), since even when there is a desire for something else, only the qualities are perceived. Then, seeking the status of being "this" (*idam-kāram*) from another, it is restricted to a specific meaning of its own by means of a related term whose meaning is already determined; thus, its eagerness subsiding, it proceeds with indifference.

In that context, the genitive case expresses a relation that has difference as its substratum. When this [genitive] is heard residing in the word for the quality (*guṇapada*), it is qualified by another word expressing the correlate which possesses a requirement for a related term; this is because a compound has a specific object as its domain. Furthermore, qualities function by internalizing the relation—which has difference as its substratum—once difference has ceased, as they bring about the primary meaning while subordinating their own meaning.

In that case, when "beloved of the king" (*rājavallabhā*) is being reduced to the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) referring to it—which has ceased by its very nature but was generally applicable for the sake of grammatical operation—is either excluded or explained away by the rule "supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.71). Now, as for the phrase "a maiden to whom a boon is to be given" (*varapradeyā kanyā*), what kind of compound is this? It is precisely a genitive tatpuruṣa (*ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*), just like "a flower to be offered to the god" (*devadeyam puṣpam*) or "wealth to be given to a Brahmin" (*brāhmaṇadeyam dhanam*).

But if this is so, why do these not become *caturthī*-compounds? [One might object] because that [type of compound] is enumerated only among those [categories] beginning with "for its sake" (*tadartha*) in the rule: "A word in the dative case forms a compound with words meaning 'for its sake' (*tadartha*), 'benefit' (*artha*), 'offering' (*bali*), 'good for' (*hita*), 'pleasure' (*sukha*), and 'protected' (*rakṣita*). [Reply: In that case, let the compounds occur only when there is the state of being "for its sake" (*tādathrya*). For whatever is given to someone is indeed for the sake of that person. [Objection: Not so. A word in the dative case does not form a compound merely on account of the state of being "for its sake. For example, as in the case of "an *ulūkhala* for threshing" (*avahananāyolūkhalam*).

Rather, [the fourth case suffix] is used when there is a relationship of identity between the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikāra*). For example, wood is the material cause of the modification that takes the form of a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), as in the expression *yūpāya dāru* ("wood for the sacrificial post"). But is it not the case that the term "material cause and modification" is not explicitly mentioned here, and yet we see [the usage of the fourth case] even in the absence of such a relationship—as in *aśvaghāsaḥ* ("horse fodder"), *śvaśrūsuraṃ* ("mother-in-law and father-in-law"), and the compound *athāto dharmajijñāsā* ("now, therefore, the desire to know dharma")? How then can it be said that the capacity of the fourth case is restricted solely to the relationship of material cause and modification? The Teacher [Patañjali], by his own conduct, provides the indication (*jñāpaka*) that this is so...

The mention of "bali-rakṣita" (sacrificial offering and protected) applies to compounds of those items that are of such a nature that the mention of "bali-rakṣita" is appropriate; thus, the compound consists of items of that same nature. The mention of "bali-rakṣita" applies specifically to modified forms (*vikṛti*) ending in the dative case when compounded with their primary materials (*prakṛti*), and not merely to the state of being for the sake of something else (*tādarthya*). As for *aśvaghāsa* and similar terms, they will be genitive compounds (*ṣaṣṭhī-samāsa*). For when one thing exists for the sake of another, this relationship of "this belongs to that" (*tasyedaṃ*) is also present there.

For example, as in the expression "this is for the teacher," where it means "that which is for the sake of the teacher. This "being-for-the-sake-of" (*tādarthya*) is also a specific type of relationship, and wherever there is a particularity, a generality necessarily exists within it. Nor is this not observed even in the case of [grammatical] operations (*karma* and so forth), as in: "One should eat beans," or "All of this has been heard by you."

But surely, if a maiden is to be given as a gift (*varapradeyā*), then even in the construction involving the act of giving (*dadāti-prayoga*), she would not be the recipient (*saṃpradāna*); and if she is not the recipient, the dative case (*caturthī*) would not occur after the word *saṃpradāne*. What, then, will be the distinction between those two cases? Who, moreover, says that there is no recipient here? This genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of the dative; for we observe the use of both the genitive and the dative without distinction in reference to the recipient and so forth. For example: "The elephant of the Himalayas" (*himavato hastī*), "A hymn for a man, [a song] for the moon" (*puruṣam ṛk candramase*), and "Or rather, it is not out of desire for his wife... (*na vā are jāyāyai kāmāya*).

"The wife becomes dear for the sake of one's own desire; the wife becomes dear [for the sake of] long-lasting sight, for the sake of long-lasting vision: 'Ghee with rice-porridge, śāli rice, curd, and milk-rice—these please me'; 'Cooked food indeed pleases me, as does milk that has been boiled and cooled, with sugar. Now, in the expression 'this one who is a month-born,' what is the governing element of this compound? It is that which emphasizes the meaning of the final member (*uttarapadārthapradhāna*). By virtue of its similarity to this, it must be like other compounds that emphasize the meaning of the final member."

In other cases where the subsequent member of the compound is predominant, whatever case-ending occurs within the compound is heard even when it is compounded; for example, *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the king’s servant) and *puruṣo rājñaḥ* (the servant of the king). Here, however, there is the genitive case in the sentence, but the nominative in the compound.

Is it not the case that this is so? That connection which exists between the month and the one born is dissolved in the compound; that meaning, having been expressed, becomes internalized and results in the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). In that case, the nominative occurs by the rule "the nominative is used for the meaning of the nominal stem. But then, why does the form *māsajātasya* (of the one born in the month) not occur now? It will occur with respect to an external correlate. But is it not the case that this compound is formed by the rule "time-measures [are compounded] with that which possesses the measure"?

Nor is the month the measure of one who has been born; rather, it is the measure of thirty nights. Just as in the expression "Devadatta’s *droṇa* of jujube fruits," the *droṇa* is not the measure of Devadatta, but rather of the jujube fruits; thus it is said: "Because that with which time is compounded is itself immeasurable, there is no designation [of its measure]. What, then, do you consider time to be, by which the increase and decrease of material forms are perceived?

In that case, for one who is connected with a certain action, there arises the notion of "day," "year," and "night. By what action? By the movement of the sun. By that very movement, when repeated, there arises the notion of "month" and "year. If this is so, then just as one says "a month has passed for the newborn," one would also have to say "two months have passed for the newborn" or "three months have passed for the newborn. However, [the usage] "a month for the newborn" is intended to mean "a month measured by the newborn. But [if your logic holds], it would follow that "two months for the newborn" or "three months for the newborn" would also apply.

It is not so; for when "born after one month" (*māsajātaḥ*) is said, no specific number such as two or more is perceived. However, where there is a basis for perception, [the compound] certainly occurs, as in "born after two months" (*dvimāsajātaḥ*) or likewise "born after three months" (*trimāsajātaḥ*). But how is the compounding of the factors of action (*kāraka*) justified? For their connection is indeed with the action alone, and that which denotes an action does not possess the status of being a *subanta* (a word ending in a nominal suffix).

If it is argued that [the relation] will occur between two nominal stems (*subanta*) in which specific actions are already included, this is not so; for the connection of substances with action constitutes the domain of the "residual" (*śeṣa*), not the domain of the "factors of action" (*kāraka*). Indeed, a substance established by its own nature, when expressed as an accomplished entity, has no further expectation toward another substance upon attaining its own identity, and thus does not assume the status of an object (*karman*) or other *kāraka* roles. Furthermore, there is no rule stating that *kārakas* are compounded within the section on compounds (*samāsa-prakaraṇa*).

It is said: let there be no explicit statement; however, it is understood by implication, as when it is stated that "the second case [ending] is compounded with words such as *śrita* (resorted to)," as in *kaṣṭaśritaḥ* ("one who has resorted to hardship"). In this context, the agent (*kartṛ*)—defined by the specific action denoted by the word *śrita*—is capable of being connected to another action involving the relationship between means and end, which has been internalized. Even though he is already in a state of unified coexistence with other powers directed toward his own substratum, he requires external factors such as "hardship" (*kaṣṭa*) through the subordinate action of "resorting."

Furthermore, because of its connection with the action of "resorting" (*āśrayati*), the word *kaṣṭa* possesses the status of an object (*karman*); thus, there arises a relationship between *kaṣṭa* and *śrita* preceded by the action of resorting. When that new meaning has emerged—sustained by the power of the meanings of its constituent parts as they function within themselves—the word denoting it receives the designation of a compound (*samāsa*).

Thus, in the case of *vṛkabhītaḥ* (“fearing the wolf”), although the rule *pañcamī bhayena* (Pāṇini 2.1.37) applies because the wolf is the cause of fear—since the rule *bhītrārthānāṃ bhayahetuḥ* (Pāṇini 1.4.25) establishes its status as an *apādāna* (ablative)—the entire compound, which possesses semantic coherence (*sāmarthya*) and whose internal relationship between action and its factors is included within itself, receives the designation of a *samāsa*. Now, one might object: the wolf does not possess the status of an *apādāna* with respect to the act of becoming (*bhūta*), but rather with respect to fear, terror, and so forth.

It is said: just as in the expression "a month for one born," the collection of actions known as a "month" serves as a delimiter by way of being the limit for the birth called the first separation from the womb, or rather, it depends upon the one born by encompassing the existence obtained at birth; so too here, this term "ablative" (*apādāna*) will serve as a delimiter of fear alone, not of that which has already occurred.

Alternatively, just as in the case of *kaṣṭaśritaḥ* ("rested in hardship"), where *kaṣṭa* possesses the status of an object (*karman*) due to its connection with the action of resting (*śrayati*) implied therein—and thus connects with *kaṣṭa* preceded by the action of resting—so too here, the agent, delimited by the implied action of fearing, possesses the status of an ablative (*apādāna*) for the wolf (*vṛka*) due to its connection with the action of fearing; thus, it connects with the wolf preceded by the action of fearing.

Let it be so where there is an explicit mention of the action even though it is subordinate; but where the action is not heard, as in the case of *śaṅkulākhaṇḍa*, how is it to be understood? It will be understood through implication (*pratīyamāna*); for when one says *śaṅkulākhaṇḍaḥ*, it is understood that [the action] has been performed (*kṛta*). Indicating this very point, [Pāṇini] says: "The third case-affix is used with a quality-word (*guṇavacana*) denoting that which is produced by it (*tatkṛta*)."

If it is argued that the statement is redundant because [the meaning] is established by logic (*nyāya*), we say no; for the statement serves a restrictive purpose (*niyamārtha*). It is understood that the compound occurs only where [the action] has been performed, and so forth, so that it may not occur elsewhere. Thus, when there is a third-case ending denoting the instrument or the agent—such as *śaṅkulā* (a mallet)—which is governed by the implied action of "doing" (*karoti*) and expresses a quality such as being broken (*khaṇḍa*) through the elision of the suffix *-mat* (*matublopa*), and when the semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) exists because the state of being produced by that which is signified by the third case is present—as in "blind in one eye because of the axle" (*akṣṇā kāṇaḥ*) or "lame in the foot" (*pādena khañjaḥ*)—then the compound is established.

Thus, in this way, the meaning of the word *khaṇḍa*—which is delimited by the implied action of "making" (*karoti*) and is thus capable of being connected with another action—is connected with the wedges (*śaṅkulā*) and so forth, which function either as instruments (*karaṇa*) or as agents (*kartṛ*), while depending on the action of "making" that has become a subordinate factor (*upasarjanībhūta*). Furthermore, it is a collection (*samudāya*) whose internal connection between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka-sambandha*) constitutes a compound (*samāsa*). Now, why does this not occur here in cases such as *dadhnā paṭuḥ* ("clever because of yogurt") or *ghṛtena paṭuḥ* ("clever because of ghee")? Because there is a lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*).

What is incapacity (*asāmarthya*)? That which is dependent is incapable; for curd has no capacity with respect to a cloth. What then? [The phrase] "he eats with curd" is used with respect to the act of eating (*bhujinā*). In that case, it would not apply here either in the expression "a fragment from a *śaṅkulā*," because even here the *śaṅkulā* has no capacity with respect to the fragment. What then? [It means] "a fragment made by the *śaṅkulā*," [using] the word "made" (*kṛta*). It will be so by virtue of the rule stating "by that which is made by it" (*tatkṛtena*).

If it is argued that [the term "guṇavacana" means] "by virtue of expressing a quality," then when it is stated here "by a guṇavacana," how is it understood that it refers to a substance-word such as "khaṇḍa" (sugar-candy) through the elision of the possessive suffix *matup*? It is because of the inclusion of the word "vacana" (expression). Since the instrumental case here could have been established simply by saying "by the quality produced by that," the fact that he includes the word "vacana" serves this purpose: so that it may be understood that a "guṇavacana" is that which has expressed a quality—such as "khaṇḍa" being that which possesses the quality of being sugar-candy, or "pāṇḍu" being that which possesses the quality of being pale.

If this is so, then there is no purpose in including the mention of "produced by that" (*tatkṛta*), for indeed, curd possesses the capacity to produce a lump of dough; however, because it lacks such capacity in the case of "sharp with curd" (*dadhnā paṭuḥ*), the rule will not apply here. What, then, is the purpose of including "produced by that"? It is so that when a compound of a *kāraka* (participant in an action) with words denoting a substance is formed, an action corresponding to each [substance] must be supplied, as for example: "addicted to dice" (*akṣeṣu prasaktaḥ*) or "addicted to dice" (*akṣaśauṇḍaḥ*).

Now, if [the word] *dravya* (substance) denotes that which is expressed by a term ending in the suffix *kvin*, why is it necessary to say "by a word denoting a quality (*guṇavacana*) in a compound formed with it"? It is so that [the rule] might not apply here: *dhānyena dhanavān* ("wealthy by means of grain") or *gobhir vapāvān* ("possessing a hump by means of cows"). Furthermore, regarding the expression *aśrāddhabhojī* ("one who does not eat at a funeral feast"), what kind of compound is this? It is a negative (*nañ*) tatpuruṣa compound with an incompatible meaning (*asamartha*). But what is the incompatibility here? It is the mutual independence of the prior and subsequent members; for in the case of *aśrāddhabhojī*, the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with the action of eating, not with the "funeral feast" (*śrāddha*). Indeed, there is no such restriction for him that "one must not eat at a funeral feast."

Rather, it means "one should not eat with faith. For the capacity [of the negative particle] exists only where an action inherent in the substrate (vartipadārtha) is denoted or implied and is naturally manifested as being negated by the *nañ*, as in "non-cooker" (*apācakaḥ*) or "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇaḥ*).

However, where the *nañ* is connected to an external action, there is no such capacity; for example: "the king's wives do not even look at the sun" (*asūryampaśyā rājadārāḥ*), "verses that are not to be sung" (*apunar-geyāḥ ślokāḥ*), or "one who does not eat salt" (*alavaṇabhojī bhoktā*).

Now, if this is so, since there is no meaning of the whole distinct from the meanings of the parts, and thus a lack of meaningfulness (*arthavattva*), how can the designation of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*) apply? If you argue that it is due to the mention of "compound" (*samāsa*) [in the rule], then because the purpose has already been served by that [mention], the restrictive rule (*niyama*) would be untenable; consequently, even a sentence (*vākya*) possessing meaning would incur the undesirable consequence of being designated as a nominal stem.

Now, since the correctness of negative compounds (*nañ-samāsa*) that are not semantically connected is indicated by the rule "asūryalalāṭayor adṛṣṭatapolayoḥ," one might object: let there be no compounding even for forms such as *akiṃcitkurvāṇaḥ*, *amāṣaṃ haraṇaḥ*, or *agādhād utsṛptaḥ*. Thus, only four types—beginning with *asūryampaśya*—are enumerated as non-semantically connected compounds (*asamartha-samāsa*). By the force of this very enumeration, the designation of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika-saṃjñā*) will also apply [to these]. Nevertheless, because they are devoid of meaning, in the absence of a substratum, and consequently in the absence of number, object, and so forth, for them...

Or else, case endings—whether expressive of verbal action (*vācikā*) or indicative of grammatical relation (*dyotikā*)—would not arise at all. This is not so; for even though the aggregate (*samudāya*) is devoid of meaning, it necessarily requires a case ending due to the rule that "a base alone (*prakṛti*) should not be employed. However, because the constituent part (*avayava*) possesses meaning, it accepts that very specific case ending as the locus for number, object, and so forth. Consequently, just as when a sick person and a healthy person eat together, the healthy person also partakes in the meal of the sick ones.

In the same way, even though the aggregate [the compound] has the sense of following the meanings of its constituent parts (*avayavārtha*), it will nevertheless convey a specific case-ending (*vibhaktiviśeṣa*); thus, there is no fault whatsoever. Now, if there is no "integration into a single meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*), why do the properties of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*) not persist? What, then, are those [properties]? They are: connection with an adjective, as in "he does not eat at a *śrāddha*"; conjunction, as in "he eats, having been invited to a *śrāddha*"; and connection with a specific number, as in "he eats a *śrāddha*" or "he eats *śrāddhas*."

And these [grammatical operations] are observed only in the case of a sentence (*vākya*), not in a compound (*vṛtti*) such as *na-aśrāddhabhojī* (one who does not eat at a funeral feast), nor in expressions such as *nāśrāddhabhojī brāhmaṇasya śobhanam* (it is auspicious for a Brahmin who does not eat at a funeral feast). Why, then, is it said that there is no "integration of meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*) here? It is not so; for in this context, the word *aśrāddha* alone is incapable [of entering into syntactic relation], whereas the word *aśrāddhabhojin* is not. Furthermore, these applications of qualifiers and so forth are perceived as pertaining to the person who eats at a non-śrāddha, and not as pertaining to the non-śrāddha itself.

But surely, if the word *aśrāddha* is meaningless because it lacks a collective meaning, then the word *aśrāddhabhojin* would also follow as being meaningless, since it is a compound consisting of a meaningful and a meaningless element. Let it be meaningless.

The properties (*dharma*) will indeed pertain to the sentence, and that [objection regarding] their purposelessness must also be avoided. This is how it is avoided: this is the power of words (*śabda-śakti*) such that, even when the referent (*artha*) is not different, when it is denoted by one particular word, there occurs a connection with qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) and so forth, while by another word it does not. In that case, although the state of being an *asamartha-samāsa* (an irregular compound) does not exist in the sentence, it exists in the *vṛtti* (the compound formation) because of the difference in words; thus, there is the capacity to denote a single unified meaning.

But surely, if a compound occurs even when there is no semantic capacity [for composition] due to the force of usage (*vacanāt*), then why not in these cases: *kim adya te vastram nīlam* ("What is your garment today? It is blue"), *utpalam āli karṇe* ("O friend, a lotus on your ear"), *neha kaścit puruṣaḥ vyāghraḥ sarati pallīm* ("No man here; a tiger is prowling through the village"), *paśya sakhi kaṣṭam śritaḥ priyo me gurukusumam* ("Look, friend, alas! My beloved has taken refuge with heavy flowers"), *kim te śaṅkulayā khaṇḍo devadatta upalena* ("What use have you for a wedge? Devadatta is broken by a stone"), *gaccha tvam yūpāya dāru śobhanam śaile* ("Go, you need beautiful wood for a sacrificial post on the mountain"), *nivartasvavṛkād bhayam devadattasya yajñadattāt* ("Turn back from the wolf; Devadatta's fear is from Yajñadatta"), *bhāryā rājñaḥ puruṣo devadattasya* ("The king's wife; Devadatta's man"), and *saktaḥ*.

[Objection: Even in cases such as *tvamakṣeṣu śauṇḍaḥ* (“you are addicted to dice”) and *pibati pānāgāre* (“he drinks in the tavern”), a compound would result; for there too, by virtue of the specific rules—"the qualifier is compounded with the qualified" (*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*), "the accusative with words beginning with *śrita*" (*dvitīyā śritādibhiḥ*), "the instrumental with that which is produced by it" (*tṛtīyā tatkṛtena*), "the dative with that which is for its sake" (*caturthī tadarthena*), "the ablative with fear" (*pañcamī bhayena*), "the genitive with a nominal ending" (*ṣaṣṭhī subantena*), and "the locative with words beginning with *śauṇḍa*" (*saptamī śauṇḍādibhiḥ*)—compounding occurs. [Response: This is an unequal comparison; the enumerations and so forth are undertaken precisely because of a lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*) [in those other cases], for the purpose of compounding.

For instance, in the sense of "one who has previously made a mat," [the suffix] *ini* is applied by the rules "pūrvādiniḥ" and "sapūrvācca. However, rules such as "viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa bahulam" are adopted only when there is semantic compatibility (*sāmarthya*), according to the principle "an operation concerning words [applies] when there is a connection of meaning."

And precisely for the purpose of demonstrating the scope of its capacity (*sāmarthya*), the following is established: in the first [case], there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) according to the rule "the qualifier by the qualified" (*viśeṣaṇaṃ viśeṣyeṇa*); in the second, the prohibition of suffixes such as *śata*; in the third, the mention of "that which is produced by it" (*tatkṛta*) and so forth; in the fourth, the relation of material cause and effect (*prakṛtivikārabhāva*); in the fifth, the enumeration of "fear" (*bhaya*) and so on; in the sixth, the prohibition of ordinal numbers (*pūraṇa*) and the like; and in the seventh, the mention of the group beginning with *śauṇḍa*. Thus, it is logically consistent.

Therefore, where there is an absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth in the case of qualifiers and the like, no compound occurs due to a lack of semantic capacity (*asāmarthya*). What kind of compound is this in the expression "this is a non-Brāhmaṇa" (*abrāhmaṇa*)? It is a *nañ*-tatpuruṣa compound with semantic capacity. What is its predominant referent? It has the meaning of the final member as its predominant referent. When it is said, "Bring a non-Brāhmaṇa," the bringing of any Brāhmaṇa whatsoever would follow [if the compound were not interpreted correctly].

This is not a fault. First, this person should be asked: when it is said here, "Bring the king’s man," why does the bringing of a mere man not occur? The king is employed here as a qualifier; therefore, there will be the bringing of one qualified by the king. But who is he? He is the one whose individual substance has ceased [to be perceived independently].

When, however, this meaning of the word is negated, is that negation inherent (*svābhāvikī*) or is it based on verbal instruction (*vācanikī*)? What follows from this? If it were inherent, what would the negative particle (*nañ*) accomplish by being employed? In that case, it must be based on verbal instruction; furthermore, because of its counteracting nature (*pratikīlatvāt*). Just as a wedge being struck drives out a counter-wedge, so too the negative particle, when employed, negates the meaning of the word.

If this were not the greatness of the negative particle (*nañ*), kings would never maintain elephants and horses; they would simply say "no. In that case, the absence [of perception] is natural, while the perception is caused by the negative particle. It is just as when objects in pitch darkness are seen because of a lamp; yet the lamp does not become the cause of their cessation.

If, however, this negative particle (*nañ*) were devoid of a referent object (*padārtha*), for what purpose would the word "Brāhmaṇa" be employed? It is so that it may be understood that the meaning of this term has been negated. For if only "no" (*na*) were said, there would be doubt as to whose referent object is being negated; therefore, the word "Brāhmaṇa" is employed to eliminate such uncertainty. Alternatively, all these words—Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra—also apply to those who have fallen from their status (*avareṣu*).

“Asceticism, sacred learning, and birth—these are the causes of being a Brahmin. One who is devoid of asceticism and sacred learning is merely a Brahmin by birth. Thus, he also mentions these internal qualities for Brahminhood: being fair-complexioned, having a broad forehead, and having reddish-brown hair. Furthermore, words that function for a whole (samudāya) also apply to its parts; for example, "the Eastern Pañcālas" or "the Northern Kurus. In this way, the word *brāhmaṇa*, which functions for the whole, also applies to a part, whether to a quality (*guṇa*) or to the genus (*jāti*).

First, regarding quality (*guṇa*): "This is a non-Brahmin, for he urinates while standing," or "This is a non-Brahmin, for he eats while walking. Furthermore, having seen a man in the marketplace who is dark-complexioned, speckled, and has the color of a heap of beans, one concludes, "This is not a Brahmin; this is a non-Brahmin. Thus, there is the exclusion of the object based on its qualities. Now, regarding the genus (*jāti*): because of doubt arising from the deficiency of the genus, or due to difficulty in apprehension, another word—namely *brāhmaṇa*—is applied.

Due to doubt, one first perceives a person who is fair-complexioned, of pure conduct, with reddish-brown hair on his head, and determines, "This is a Brahmin. Thereafter, one subsequently realizes, "This is not a Brahmin; this is a non-Brahmin," and thus the determination regarding him occurs. In this case, the word "Brahmin" was applied due to doubt, while the exclusion of the object based on caste has taken place. Furthermore, due to faulty instruction, one may have been wrongly directed, thinking, "Bring a Brahmin to this spot."

Having gone there, even though he perceives someone and determines, "This is a Brāhmaṇa," he subsequently realizes, "This is not a Brāhmaṇa; this is a non-Brāhmaṇa. In that case, the word "Brāhmaṇa" is applied due to a false instruction, while the exclusion of the actual meaning is based on caste (*jāti*). [Objection: But surely, when words such as "Brāhmaṇa" are used with a negative particle (*nañ*) for the purpose of exclusion, it follows that the compound would have the first member as its predominant element (*pūrvapadapradhānatā*). [Response: This is not so, because it would result in the designation of an indeclinable (*avyaya*); for its first member is indeed an indeclinable.

This is not a fault; the designation of *avyaya* (indeclinable) is established by its inclusion in the list [of *avyayas*]. And the negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) is not included there. Let it not be read among the *avyayas*. Even so, the gender and number of a word follow those of its referent (*abhidheya*). Now, that which is denoted here [by the negative particle] has no connection with gender or number. This lack of gender and lack of number is not something based on an explicit rule (*vācanika*); rather, it is inherent (*svābhāvika*).

In this regard, what can we say? It is not that the negative particle (*nañ*) lacks connection with gender and number prior to compounding, but rather that such connection exists within the compound. Or rather, whatever gender and number belong to that [negation] apply to the compound just as they do to the quality (*guṇa*). It is said: absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), relative non-existence (*anatyantābhāva*), mutual non-existence (*anyatarābhāva*), non-existence of identity (*tādātmyābhāva*), non-existence of relation (*saṃbandhābhāva*), and non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*).

For example: "wind of such a kind," "a girl with no belly," "a man who does nothing," "a wall that is not a *piśāca*," "ground that is not a jar," and "Kāma who is bodiless. However, when the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is qualified by the meaning of the subsequent member, then the *tatpuruṣa* compound has the meaning of the prior member as its primary sense; and due to the limiting condition of the meaning of the negative particle, six distinct types of compound meanings arise: antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), absence of capacity (*sāmarthyābhāva*), absence of necessity (*āvaśyakatābhāva*), mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), absence of being (*sattābhāva*), and the negation of existence (*bhāvābhāva*). For instance: "a jar that has not been produced."

"An invincible warrior," "an unadorned lover," "a winter without rain," "the non-existent horn of a hare," and "an unburst sprout. However, when the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is qualified by the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), then that *tatpuruṣa* compound has the meaning of the subsequent member as its predominant element. And regarding the meaning of the word as conditioned by the sense of the negative, six varieties of compounds arise: namely, its absence (*tadabhāva*), something other than it (*tadanya*), its likeness (*tatsadṛśa*), its opposite (*tadviruddha*), its inferiority (*tadapakṛṣṭa*), and its superiority (*tadutkṛṣṭa*).

For example: *ananayaḥ* (one who is not a logician), *anatriḥ* (one who is not a singer), *abrāhmaṇaḥ* (one who is not a Brahmin), *asitaḥ* (one who is not white), *amanuṣyaḥ* (one who is not human), *amānuṣaḥ* (one who is not a man). Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*) is observed elsewhere even in Tatpuruṣas where another word-meaning is predominant, such as *abhakṣikaṃ* (absence of flies)? This is not a negative compound; what then? It is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) compounded in the sense of absence according to the rule beginning with "indeclinables [are compounded] with case-endings" (*avyayaṃ vibhakti*), and thus it becomes an Avyayībhāva compound, as in *nivātam* (absence of wind) and *niśītam* (absence of cold).

Furthermore, do these meanings of negative compounds (nañ-samāsa) remain restricted to categories such as the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*), or do they overlap? Some remain restricted, such as "non-existence through destruction" (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) and so forth; for example: "How could Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s army exist without Bhīṣma and Droṇa? If you, who are their equal, are not appointed here as the leader. And likewise: "The girl has no belly" (*anudarā kanyā*), or "the ewe has no wool" (*alomikā eḍakā*).

The [four] absences, such as prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the rest, coalesce with the word *eka*. For example: "A person who has not yet been born is, for that time, neither a man nor even a beast, so long as he does not perceive the object seen by a cowherd's daughter. And likewise, [the word] *aneka* [coalesces with its meaning]: "And many [are those who say], 'It is not one' (*aneka*). Now, the word *eka* has multiple meanings; for instance, in the phrase "That certain sage born from a jar," it has the sense of a specific individual (*ṛṣārtha*). In the expression "In this regard, some first say," it has the sense of an alternative position (*pakṣāntarārtha*). In the statement "This nature of ours is indeed one," it has the sense of identity (*tulyārtha*).

The word *eka* has several meanings: it signifies "without a companion" as in "one should not sleep alone"; it signifies "non-difference" as in "this Śabdabrahman is indeed one"; and it signifies "number" as in "one," "two," or "many. Which of these is intended here? It is the sense of number. Why does it not apply to [the senses of] excellence and so forth mentioned previously? Because there is no such conventional usage (*anabhidhānāt*). For example, when the word *amitra* is used, in a *tatpuruṣa* compound where the first member is predominant, only an "enemy" is understood, not "one who is not a friend. Likewise, when *aneka* is used, only "many" is understood, and not those possessing qualities such as non-excellence.

By this, the case where the *uttarapada* (the final member) is predominant in a *tatpuruṣa* compound is also explained by the rule "aneka. But how can there be a comprehension of many when there is a prohibition of only one? This [negation] applies to the action and the quality (*kriyāguṇa*) and subsequently effects their exclusion, just as in the examples: "Feed [many people] who are not seated," or "Have [many people] lie down who are not [already] lying down."

It might be argued: "Where action and quality are applicable, it is so; but where indeed they are not applicable, how can there be the notion of 'many' standing [there]? Even in such cases, when one is negated, there is still the cognition of many, as for example: "not not one beloved," or "not not one happiness. The base and the suffix are of three kinds each; likewise the case-endings of the upapadas and the nominal stems are of three kinds.

The subordinate element (*upasarjana*) is declared to be threefold, and compound (*samāsa*) is likewise said to be threefold. This word is now explained as that which conveys meaning; furthermore, it is stated that the word (*pada*) is here presented as being of three kinds, for the sentence (*vākya*) is indeed threefold. Indeed, linguistic usage is based upon words, since it rests upon both of these [the word and the sentence]. Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Nominal Stem (*prātipadika*) and Other Elements," in the *Śṛṅgāraprakāśa* composed by the Great King of Kings, Śrī Bhojadeva.

The Śṛṅgāraprakāśa, Third Prakāśa: The Third [Section], the Exposition of Words such as *prakṛti*. In this context, a *pada* (word) is that by which a meaning (*artha*) is expressed. It is threefold: the form of action (*kriyārūpa*), the form of the agent (*kārakarūpa*), and the form of embellishment (*upaskārarūpa*). Among these, the form of action denotes the object to be accomplished (*sādhya-artha*); the form of the agent denotes the means of accomplishment (*sādhana-artha*); and the form of embellishment consists of ornaments and the like for both the object to be accomplished and the means of accomplishment. Since each of these has six subdivisions, there are [six] forms of action, [six] forms of agents, and [six] forms of embellishments.

Since each of these has six varieties, there are eighteen varieties of the *pada*. Among them, the varieties of verbal forms (*kriyārūpa-pada*) are: the impersonal (*bhāva*), the active (*kartṛ*), the passive (*karman*), the impersonal-passive (*bhāvakarman*), the impersonal-active (*bhāvakartṛ*), and the passive-active (*karmakartr*).
