Among these, examples of the state-word (*bhāvapada*) are as follows: *pacyate*, *apāci*, *pakṣyate* by Devadatta; *āsyate*, *āsi*, *āsiṣyate* by you; *bhidyate*, *abhedi*, *bhetsyate* by a granary; *śrāyate*, *aśrāyi*, *śrāyiṣyate* by barley-gruel; likewise, *śrāyuṣīṣṭa*, *śaśre*, *āśrāyuṣyata* by rice; *ghāniṣīṣṭa*, *jaghno*, *aghāniṣyata* by an elephant; *grāhiṣīṣṭa*, *jagṛhe*, *āgrāhiṣyata* by a crocodile; *darśiṣīṣṭa*, *daddaśe*, *adarśiṣyata*; and *preyaset*.

Examples of the object (karmapada): "Rice is cooked by the cook" (*odanaḥ sūdena pacyate*); "A month is sat through by the laborer" (*māsaḥ bhṛtakena āsyate*); "The village is gone to by the traveler" (*grāmaḥ pānthena gamyate*); "A *krośa* is slept through by the child" (*krośaḥ śiśunā supyate*); "The mat was made by the skillful one" (*kaṭaḥ kuśalena akāri*); "The cow was restrained by the cowherd" (*gauḥ gopālakena arodhi*); "The milch-cow was milked by the calf-herder" (*dhenuḥ vallavena adohi*); "The earth was crossed by the king" (*pṛthivī rājñā atāri*); "The gambler was tormented by his own deed" (*kitavaḥ karmaṇā anvavātapta*); "The blanket was experienced by the hand" (*kambalaḥ kareṇa anubabhūve*); "Barley-gruel will be cooked by the physician" (*yavāgūḥ bhiṣajā pakṣyate*); "Alms were obtained by the ascetic" (*bhikṣā tāpasena alāniṣīṣṭa*).

Thus it will be done: *grāhitā*, *grāhiṣīṣṭa*, *grinthaḥ*; *darśiṣyate*, *darśitā*, *darśiṣīṣṭa*—these are examples of the agentive voice (*kartṛpada*). Examples are as follows: *pacati caitraḥ* (Caitra cooks), *āste maitraḥ* (Maitra sits), *tapati suparṇaṃ suvarṇakāraḥ* (the goldsmith heats the gold), *tapyate tapastāpasaḥ* (the ascetic performs penance), *sṛjati mālaṃ mālakaḥ* (the garland-maker weaves a garland), *sṛjate dharmaṃ dhārmikaḥ* (the righteous man practices dharma), *udasarji svaṃ vadānyaḥ* (the generous man gave away his wealth), *udapādi satyaṃ bhūpaḥ* (truth arose from the king), *pāripārayante vṛkṣaṃ karṇakāḥ* (the bees protect the tree), *śoṣayate vrīhīnātapaḥ* (the heat dries up the rice), *saṃyujyate*.

The householder cooks with his wife; the udumbara tree bears red fruit; likewise, the smoke blazed—it blazed (adīpi/adīpiṣṭa); the sleeping man woke—he woke (abodhi/abuddha); desire was fulfilled—it was fulfilled (apūriṣṭa); dharma spread—it spread (atāyi/atadīyiṣṭa); the world prospered—it prospered (āpyāyi/āpyayiṣṭa). Thus it is said.

Regarding the verb forms used for the sense of the agent (bhāva) or the object (karman): as I desire, "May he eat" (*bhuñjīta*); "I honor you, may you eat" (*saṃbhāvayāmi bhuñjīta bhavān*); "I consider it possible that you will eat" (*samarthayāmi bhokṣyate bhavān*); "I trust that you did not eat" (*śraddadhe nābhukta bhavān*); "I judge that you will not eat" (*avakalpayāmi nābhokṣyate bhavān*); "I do not trust that you would cause a low-born man to sacrifice" (*na śraddadhe nanu bhavān vṛṣalaṃ yājayet*); "I do not judge that your honor will cause a low-born man to sacrifice" (*nāvakalpayāmi tatrabhavān vṛṣalaṃ yājayiṣyati*); "I do not tolerate that your honor caused a low-born man to sacrifice" (*na marṣayāmi tatrabhavān vṛṣalam ayājiṣyat*); "I censure that your honor causes a low-born man to sacrifice" (*vigarhe api tatrabhavān vṛṣalaṃ yājayati*); "Do you remember, Devadatta? (*smarasi devadatta*).

"We shall dwell in Kaśmīra"; "Do you remember that we dwelt in Kaliṅga?"; "Do you remember that we dwelt constantly in Kaliṅga?"; "Do you remember that we shall dwell in Kaśmīra and there we shall eat rice?"; "Do you remember that we dwelt in Kaliṅga and there we ate rice?"; "Come, I think you will go by chariot"; "I know [you] slept and left"; "I am going"; "Look, the deer runs"; "Let us look here"—these are cited as examples for the dual and plural endings in the sense of the object (*karman*).

An example of a word with the agent as the object of the action (*bhāvakartṛpada*) is: *corasya rujati*, *corasya āmayati*, *corasya bādhate*, *corasya pīḍayati*, *corasya dahati*, *corasya ātakṣayati*, *corasya spṛśati*, *corasya śoṣayati*, *corasya mardayati*, *corasya moṭayati*, *coraṃ jvarayati*, *coraṃ saṃtāpayati*.

Likewise: *bhārati*, *pacati*, *pakṣyati*; *abhārṣīt*, *apākṣīt*; *bhavet* also *bhavet*; *syāt* also *syāt*; *nāsti rame*; *ayūyujas tvam asi*; *asit tvam īśiṣe*; *asti gacchāmo vayam*; *asty atra kāṃcid gāṃ paśyati*; *si bhavati gamyate*; *bhavatu sādhayāma iti*.

Examples of the *karmakartṛ* (object-agent) construction are as follows: *rajyati vastraṃ svayameva* ("the cloth colors itself"), *kukṣyati pādaḥ svayameva* ("the foot swells itself"), *avakirate hastī* ("the elephant scatters [musth]"), or *avākīryata svayameva* ("it was scattered by itself"); *granthīte mālā* ("the garland strings itself"), or *agrathiṣṭa svayameva* ("it was strung by itself"); *cikīrṣati kaṭaḥ* ("the mat wishes to be made"), or *acikīrṣata svayameva* ("it wished to be made by itself"); *ucchrayate daṇḍaḥ* ("the staff stands upright itself"), or *udaśiśrayata svayameva* ("it was made to stand upright by itself"); *anuruddhyate gauḥ svayameva* ("the cow submits itself"), and *akṛta kaṭaḥ svayameva* ("the mat made itself"). Others maintain that these also possess the status of object-agents.

The granary bursts of its own accord; the rope breaks of its own accord; the field is mown of its own accord; the fruit ripens of its own accord; the wood splits of its own accord; the foot swells of its own accord; the cow yields milk of its own accord; the cow is obstructed by itself; and the oblation is offered by itself.

Likewise: *bhūṣayate kanyā svayameva* (the maiden adorns herself), *maṇḍayate kanyā svayameva* (the maiden adorns herself), *dohayate gauḥ svayameva* (the cow milks itself), *ārohayate hastī svayameva* (the elephant mounts itself), *dadhayate rājā svayameva* (the king places himself), *maṇḍayate kanyā svayameva*, *dohayate gauḥ svayameva*, *ārohayate hastī svayameva*, *dadhayate rājā svayameva*, *abhivādayate guruḥ svayameva* (the teacher salutes himself), *lāvayate kedāraḥ svayameva* (the field reaps itself), *pācayate odanaḥ svayameva* (the rice cooks itself), *bhedayate*.

"The granary [opens] by itself; the troop [assembles] by itself; the forest-thicket smiles by itself. And they say: "That which has an object is treated like an object" (*karmavat karmaṇā tulyakryaḥ*). When there is a state [of the agent] similar to that of an object, regarding the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), the *ciṇ* affix, and the verbal states (*bhāva*), they say that for a root ending in a vowel where the agent is also the object, it is like the *ciṇ* affix (*ciṇvadbhāva*). And they say: "Not for roots beginning with *ru*" (*na rudhaḥ*); "For the roots *duh*, *snus*, and *nā*, neither *yak* nor *ciṇ*" (*naduhasnusnāmāṃ yak ciṇau*); "In the prohibition of *yak* and *ciṇ*, there is an addition for the roots *han*, *ṇi*, *śri*, and *bruñ*"; and "For the roots *bhūṣ*, *karmakṛ*, *kir*, etc. (*bhūṣākarmakirādīti*).

"An addition [to the rule] should be made for the roots *ni*, *śranthi*, *granthi*, and for those that are *ātmanepada* and intransitive. This, however, applies correctly; for instance, in examples such as "the granary opens itself" (*bhidyate kusūlaḥ svayameva*) and "the mat was made by itself" (*akāri kaṭaḥ svayameva*), the suffixes *yak* and *ciṇ* occur precisely when there is an object, while from the word *svayam* (itself), there is the understanding of the agent being the same as the object (*karmakartṛ*). As in "the cow blocked itself" (*arodhi gauḥ svayameva*). Even in the case of the root *rudh*, when the sequence [of action] is intended to be expressed, *ciṇ* indeed occurs: "the cow was blocked by itself" (*arodhi gaurātmanaiva*). The very same meaning as "by itself" (*ātmanaiva*) is the same as "by itself" (*svayameva*).

When it is said, "he causes [something] to be made," the status of being both object and agent (*karmakartṛtva*) is not understood unless another verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) expressive of the agent is heard. Therefore, here too, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) applies only to the object. However, in cases such as *bhūṣayate kanyā svayam eva* ("the maiden adorns herself"), the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) occurs because of the rule: "When there is no other agent (*aṇau*), that which is the object in the non-causative (*yatkarmaṇau*) becomes the agent in the causative (*sa kartā*), provided it is not a sentient being (*nādhyāne*). But how then is the well-known status of being both object and agent established in these instances? Listen: first, regarding the steps of the process (*kramapadeṣu*): "But when an action that was being performed as an object is accomplished by itself..."

It is easy for the agent to perform [the action] by means of its own qualities; therefore, they know him as the "agent of the sequence" (*kramakartṛ*). This is a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) based on the fact that he was previously the agent in the primary sense of the term "agent. For instance, maidens and others employ ornaments and the like for their own adornment due to their excellence of beauty and so forth. Likewise, great poets such as Māgha [wrote]: "The female elephant causes the rider to mount her, the sequence of which is determined by uncontracted love..."

"Free from pride, he displays a constant and virtuous kinship as if it were his own sovereign power. Thus, the fruit of these two is the delight of the world through their pleasant appearance. Otherwise, one might be oppressed by thorns and the other would be difficult to look upon; thus they would not be approached. Even in the case of non-animate things, when there is a desire to express the fruit of an action, we see such usage: "thorns surround the tree," or "the sun dries the rice."

By this very rule, it is not necessary to state that "an agent whose action is similar to that of the instrument (karaṇa) becomes like the object (karmavadbhavati)," as in: "men surround the tree with thorns" (*parivārayanti kaṇṭakaiḥ vṛkṣaṃ manuṣyāḥ*) and "the thorns surround themselves" (*parivārayante kaṇṭakāḥ svayameva*). Likewise, it is not necessary to state that "in the case of the transitive roots *duh* ('to milk') and *pac* ('to cook'), the agent frequently becomes like the object," as in: "the cow milks the milk itself" (*dugdhe gauḥ payaḥ svayameva*), from which it is understood that "the milk cooks [itself]" (*payaḥ pacati*).

Therefore, in the expression "the red fruit of the *udumbara* ripens," it is precisely the action (*karma*) itself that is intended as an adverbial modifier of the action. Here, the word *udumbara* refers to the fruit; the meaning is that the *udumbara* fruit ripens at that time with a red quality, such that it becomes connected with a red coloration. And when agency (*kartṛtva*) is intended, one says "the self cooks itself. Likewise, for the root *yuj*, both the passive (*karmavat*) and the active (*kartṛvat*) forms should be stated: "the student devotes himself for a month" (*māsaṃ yujyate brahmacārī*).

If there is an intention to express agency (*kartṛtva*), the status of being a root such as *div* (from which *devayate*) will not be established; however, if there is no intention to express the object (*karman*), then the status of being an object (*karmatva*) applies, just as agency is understood directly from the word itself. Enough of this digression.

Indeed, a verbal derivative (*kṛdanta*) exists there which possesses the form of an action, just as the state (*bhāva*) [is expressed] by them here: "gone by them," "sat by them," "eaten by them here," "purified by them here," "done by you," "asleep by you," "well-done by you," "well-watered by you," "become by you," "about to be by you," "being called by you," "to be by you," "to be produced by you," "fit to be by you," "necessarily to be by you," and "honoredly shown by you."

"By you, [it was] made somewhat wealthy, poorly wealthy, or well-wealthy; by you, there was a slight rising up; by you, it flowed well. As for the object (*karman*): "By you, the mat was begun; by you, it was made, is being made, or will be made; indeed, the mat must be made, it is to be made, it is fit to be made, it is to be done, it is to be performed, or it is to be easily performed by you; the Soma is to be drunk slightly by you, it is easy to drink, or difficult to drink; you are difficult to be governed by enemies."

Suyodhana, Duryodhana, Durmarṣaṇa, Durdharṣaṇa; you are easily obtained by people (*sulabhya*), yet difficult to see (*durdarśa*). Regarding the agent (*kartṛ*): as in "he who has made a mat" (*kṛtakaṭaḥ*), "one desiring to go to the village" (*upeyivān grāmam ākāmuḥ*), "one longing for a woman" (*yoṣām abhilāṣukaḥ*), "one wishing to eat rice" (*odanaṃ bubhukṣuḥ*), "one hoping for prosperity" (*śriyam āśaṃsuḥ*), "this one who gave cows" (*dadir gāḥ pavissaḥ ayam*), "one who does not bow" (*avandāyī*), "one who gives a hundred" (*śatadāyī*), "one going to the village" (*grāmagāmī*), "one going to the state of being a village" (*grāmatāṃ gāmī*), and "the maker of a mat walks" (*kaṭaṃ kārako vrajati*) or "the cooker of rice walks" (*odanaṃ pācako vrajati*).

The *bhavakarma* (resultant action) is like verbal actions (*kriyā*): they are performed, ordinances are enacted; "the camel-sitting is being sat," "the dead-man-laying is being laid"; "you deserve a sugar-cane-eating," "you owe me a sugar-cane-eating"; "they engage in joking," "they perform a threshing. [Examples of verbal nouns: "I invite you to a festival," "an invitation, two invitations," "to counsel"; "what kind of doing did you do? "what kind of doing, what kind of making, what kind of action, what kind of duty? "What was done? "I did all the doing," "all [the duties]."

[The suffix *kṛtya* is used] after all [roots] meaning "to do" (*karoti*), "to act" (*kriyā*), "to perform" (*kṛtya*), and "to make" (*kṛta*). For example, when the agent of the action exists as a state (*bhāva*): *brahmabhūyam vartate* ("he exists as becoming Brahman"), *brahmahatyā na bhavati* ("the killing of a Brahmin does not occur"); *pākaḥ vartate* ("cooking is taking place"), *tyāgaḥ bhavati* ("renunciation occurs"), *sāṃrāviṇam vartate* ("a general shout is occurring"), *ākhūtthaḥ bhavati* ("a gathering of rats occurs"), *anveṣaṇā vartate* ("searching is taking place"), *vyāvabhāṣī bhavati* ("there is mutual conversation"); *samajaḥ paśūnām* ("a gathering of animals"), *uṭajaḥ paśūnām* ("a hut for animals"), *gavām upasaraḥ* ("the gathering of cows"), *ṛtūnām paryāyaḥ* ("the succession of seasons"), *bhavata āsikā* ("your sitting"), *bhavataḥ śāyikā* ("your lying down"), *ābhyūṣakhādikā vartate* ("the eating of raw food is taking place").

"An itch has arisen; there is a headache, though no dysentery; a disease of the head afflicts the head, though no loss of appetite; you have been seized, you have been held back, you have been born [to misfortune], you have come into being, O low-born one—may it be so!"

The agent of the action (*karmakartṛ*) is as follows: "his feet have washed themselves," "the clarified butter has melted itself," "the rice ripens without being ploughed," "the beans are ready to cook," "the wood is ready to burn," "he who is about to eat," "he who is about to rule," "wood that is fragile," "an elephant mounting [its back]," "a field being reaped," "a story being told," "a girl adorning herself," "a garland being woven," "a garland being tied," "a mat being desired to be made," "an elephant being sprinkled," "a staff being held," "being raised up."

Examples include: *daṇḍhaḥ*, "a cow yielding milk" (*duhānā dhenuḥ*), "a cow obstructing" (*rundhānā gauḥ*), "a cow striking" (*āghnānā gauḥ*), "cloth being dyed" (*rajāyadvastram*), and "a foot being scratched" (*kuṣyan pādaḥ*). Others, however, maintain that even these possess the status of being the agent of the action in sequence.

"You have made a mat" (*prakṛtaḥ kaṭaṃ bhavān*), "a mat has been made by you" (*prakṛtaḥ kaṭo bhavatā*); "you have gone the path" (*yātaḥ panthānaṃ bhavān*), "the path has been gone by you" (*yātaḥ panthānaṃ bhavatā*); "you have sat for a month" (*āsīno māsaṃ bhavān*), "a month has been sat through by you" (*āsīno māso bhavatā*); "you eat rice" (*bhuṅkte odanaṃ bhavān*), "rice is being eaten by you" (*bhujyate odano bhavatā*); "you lie upon a bed" (*adhiśayīta khaṭvāṃ bhavān*), "a bed has been lain upon by you" (*adhiśayitā khaṭvā bhavatā*); "you have climbed a tree" (*āruḍho vṛkṣaṃ bhavān*), "a tree has been climbed by you" (*ārūḍho vṛkṣo bhavatā*); "you have embraced your beloved" (*āśliṣṭaḥ priyāṃ bhavān*), "your beloved has been embraced by you" (*āśliṣṭā priyā bhavatā*); "you have worshipped the sun" (*upāsitassūryaṃ bhavān*).

"The sun has risen for you" (upasthitaḥ sūryaḥ bhavatā), "the fire has been attended by you" (upāsitaḥ agniḥ bhavatā), "you have studied under the teacher" (anuṣitaḥ guruṃ bhavatā), "the teacher has been studied under by you" (anūṣitaḥ guruḥ bhavatā), "the boy has followed the girl" (anujātaḥ māṇavakaḥ māṇavikām), "the girl has followed the boy" (anujātā māṇavikā māṇavakena), "Devadatta has grown old after the low-caste man" (anujīrṇaḥ vṛṣalaṃ devadattaḥ), "Devadatta's wife has grown old after the low-caste woman" (anujīrṇā vṛṣalī devadattena)—this is not correct, as it arises from a confusion of sentence structures.

But surely, you [hold that] the agent is obtained through implication (*ākṣepa*) and is not denoted by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*); so how can it be said that there are "agent-words," namely "words for the agent of the action" (*bhāva-kartṛ-pada*) and "words for the agent as object" (*karman-kartṛ-pada*)? For indeed, the denotative power of a word is inferred through the methods of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*). And while the agent is understood through the implication of the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), no such agreement and difference of the suffix with respect to the agent is postulated; just as when an individual is understood through the implication of a universal (*jāti*), it is not logical to postulate a denotative power of the word directed toward that individual.

But how, when the agent is not denoted, is the distinction of number and person for the suffix appropriate? Just as it is not [appropriate] in the case of the *ātmanepada* endings, so too—under the view that the universal (*jāti*) is denoted—the gender and number belonging to the individual (*vyakti*) which serves as the substratum of that universal, even though the universal itself lacks gender and number, come to function; in exactly the same way, although there is no difference in the productive activity (*bhāvanā*), the distinction of number and person based on the agent will likewise be attained.

Nor should it be said that the *lakāra* (the verbal suffix marker) is not prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*), because [the following rules] are recorded: "The *kṛt* suffixes occur when the agent is expressed" (*kartari kṛt*); "The *la*s occur when the object is expressed, and also in the sense of the action (*bhāva*) for intransitive verbs" (*laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ*); "The *laṭ* occurs in the present tense" (*vartamāne laṭ*); "For *la*, there are *tiP* and the others"; "The *tiṅ*s have three triplets: first, middle, and last"; "These are each singular, dual, and plural"; and "In the second person... (*yuṣmadi...* etc.).

The rules such as “the middle [person] when [the agent is] ‘you’,” “the highest [person] when [the agent is] ‘I’,” “the first [person] in the remaining cases,” “the *ātmanepada* for roots ending in *bhū* and *kṛ*,” and “the *parasmaipada* for the remainder when [the agent is] the doer,” are explained as forming a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*) with the prescriptions of number—namely, “the dual and singular endings for two and one [respectively],” and “the plural ending for many”—due to the desire to express a single unified meaning. For it is precisely in expressions such as “one indeed cooks” that these words are analyzed; therein alone does the sentence-meaning reside.

Regarding the singular number of the agent: *kvip* and so forth denote the singular agent; *tiP* and so forth denote the agent; and *jhi* and so forth denote the plural number of the agent. Thus, it is traditionally taught (*smṛta*) that the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) denotes the number of the agent only as projected by the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), and not the agent himself. It is replied: If the *lakāra* were to express only the number of the agent as projected by the efficient force, then in the case of "devadattena pacyate" (it is cooked by Devadatta), where the suffix expresses the efficient force (*bhāva*), it would follow that it expresses the number of the agent as well, since the agent is present in both cases.

For by the very same reason that in expressions such as "he cooks" (*pacati*), the number belonging to the object (*karman*) alone is what is signified, by that same reason it would also be signified in other usages. Furthermore, how could it be logical for the number qualified by that [object] to be signified when the agent (*kartṛ*) is being signified?

Now, if it is argued that only the number is denoted and not the specific [agent], then the cognition of distinctions such as "the person" (puruṣa) and so forth would be untenable; furthermore, the denotation of that which is qualified by it is logically possible only through the simultaneous denotation of the qualifier itself, according to the maxim: "A cognition of the qualified does not occur when the qualifier has not been apprehended. Nor is it possible for an agent, who is not touched by the word, to qualify the number merely through proximity; for since number is of the nature of an attribute (dharma), its contact with the agent is appropriate only as a delimiting factor (avacchedaka) of that attribute.

Since instruments and the other factors also possess the property of proximity, it is logical that they too would be [the objects] of that [number]. Furthermore, after the number has been expressed by the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) in relation to the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), the time is subsequently obtained, and the agent is obtained as implied by the efficient force. Consequently, because this [agent] exists prior [to the restriction], there would follow a delimitation of all the case-factors (*kāraka*s) by the number expressed simultaneously with the efficient force, since there is no distinction [in their being expressed]. And how could the agent, being implied only later, restrict within itself the number expressed simultaneously with the efficient force?

Now, if the agent is perceived at the very same time as the cognition of the number and the bhāvanā, then it is not obtained through implication (ākṣepa); rather, like the number itself, it is indeed denoted by the lakāra suffix. Furthermore, because we observe grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) between words such as "Devadatta" and forms such as "pacati," it follows that the agent alone, possessing the number, is denoted by the lakāra suffix.

If, however, the *lakāra* were to express the number of the agent—such as singularity and so forth—then the usage would have to be "devadattasya pacati" (the cooking of Devadatta), just as one says "the singularity of Devadatta. Now, if it is argued that number is not expressed by the *lakāra*, but rather the numbered object itself, such as Devadatta, is denoted; and that in the expression "Devadatta cooks," the meaning is "he performs the act of cooking as delimited by the number one"—in this way, when the numbered object is being denoted, the agent itself becomes denoted.

Nor should it be argued that even when the agent is present, the coreferentiality [of the suffix] is untenable because the capacity (*śakti*) is the actual causal factor (*kāraka*). For even when the capacity is denoted by the verbal suffix (*lakāra*), it is denoted as being dependent upon a quality or a substance, just as in the cases "the cloth is white" (*śuklaḥ paṭaḥ*) or "the garment is white" (*śuklā śāṭī*). Furthermore, you yourselves accept that the object is expressed by the suffix; that is untenable. Just as the agent is not expressed because it is obtained through the implication of the two-fold productive activity (*bhāvanā*), so too it is possible for the object to be likewise unexpressed.

Now, since the action (*karman*) is not [already] implied, it must be expressed [by the suffix]. This being the case, it is also logical that the agent (*kartṛ*) should likewise be so [expressed]. For we do not perceive any difference between the agent and the object regarding their implication by the action; for just as the action is not perceived without an agent, so too is it not [perceived] without an object. If it is argued that "there is no connection with an object in every instance," [we reply] that there is such a connection in those cases where it exists. How so? Furthermore, since the object is also obtainable through the implication of the action, its very number is what is expressed by the *sakāra* (the suffix).

How, then, can there be a distinction such that the *lakāra* (verbal suffix), which does not denote either the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*), sometimes denotes a number residing in the agent and sometimes a number residing in the object? Nor should it be said that there is no such distinguishing factor; for in the case of *pacati*, a cognition arises through the manifested nature of the agent, whereas in the case of *pacyate*, a cognition arises through the apprehended form residing in the object. Furthermore, if the agent and object were not denoted by the *lakāra*, then when it is stated "Devadatta cooks" (*devadattaḥ pacati*), the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) would be required because the agent has already been expressed.

In the case of *odanaḥ pacyate* ("the rice is being cooked"), the second case ending (*dvitīyā*) would be expected [for the object]. Now, if it is argued that this will not occur because the number of the agent and the object has already been expressed (*uparabhihitatvāt*), then a difficulty arises regarding words ending in *kṛt* suffixes, since the number is not denoted by the *kṛt* formation. In that case, in the expression *pakva odanaḥ* ("the rice is cooked"), the second case ending would apply, and consequently, the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) would result. But surely both [number and the object-relation] are the meanings of the case ending, namely number, the object, and so forth?

In that regard, just as in the case of finite verbs (*ākhyāta*), because number is already expressed, the second and third cases do not occur for the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*); likewise, in the case of words ending in primary suffixes (*kṛdanta*), because the grammatical factor (*kāraka*) is already expressed, the second case and others will not occur for the number associated with that factor. This might be argued: if this were a prohibition regarding what is already expressed, then this would be a rule concerning what is not expressed; however, because of the force of the context and the unity of the sentence, it is understood as an exclusion (*paryudāsa*).

In that regard, although number is expressed by verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*), case endings for the object and so forth would still apply because the number remains unexpressed [by the primary suffix]. Furthermore, in forms such as *devadattaḥ pacan* and *devadattaḥ pacamānaḥ*, since the number is not expressed even when the agent is denoted by the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac*, the third case ending would fail to apply.

Now, if it is argued that the *kartṛ* (agent) is not denoted by the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac*, what wrong has been done by the *tiṅ* suffixes? If you say that those [suffixes] also denote the agent because they are substitutes (*ādeśa*) for the *l*-suffixes, and because of the rule "kṛt suffixes [denote] the agent" (*kartari kṛt*), then how is it that in the expression "the rice is being cooked" (*odanaṃ pacyamānaḥ*) the object (*karman*) is denoted? If you reply that the object is denoted because the original element (*sthānin*), the *l*-suffix, is prescribed for the object, and because *śānac* is its substitute, then consider this: Thus it is said:

By the rules "laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve cākarmakebhyaḥ" (Pāṇini 3.4.69) and "bhāvakarmaṇorātmanepadam" (Pāṇini 1.3.13), the *lakāra* suffixes are prescribed for the object (*karman*) as well as for the state (*bhāva*) in the case of intransitive verbs. This being so, even where the *tiṅ* suffixes are prescribed, they would also apply to the object. Consequently, how could [the rule] be restricted to the agent (*kartṛ*)? For there too, the *kṛt* suffixes apply to the agent by the rule "śeṣāt kartari parasmaipadam" (Pāṇini 1.3.78). Thus, it has been stated that in all cases, the *ātmanepada* form indeed applies to the object.

In that case, why should this *lakāra* not also occur in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*)? Nor is it appropriate to assume that the *tiṅ* affixes apply there according to the number [of the agent] that applies to the agent or the object; for there is no syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) between the rule "The *lakāras* are used in the sense of the object and in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) after intransitive roots" and the rules "The dual and singular endings are used for two and one [respectively]" and "The plural ending is used for many," because the *lakāra* is also prescribed in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*). And since the abstract action (*bhāva*) is something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), it cannot be connected with number.

Nor can there be syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) between the prescription of case-endings (*vibhakti-vidhāna*), such as *svaujasam*, and the prescription of number (*saṃkhyā-vidhāna*), because case-endings (*su*) are produced even from indeclinables (*avyaya*), which lack number. As the author of the Mahāvṛtti stated: "Because the rules for *su* and *tiṅ* are prescribed without distinction, and because their usage is observed [even without number], the statement is for the purpose of restriction (*niyama*). The author of the Mahābhāṣya also said: "*Su* and *tiṅ* are produced without distinction; for those that have been produced, there is restriction."

Therefore, it must be accepted that the rule for the *lakāra* suffixes does not apply to the number of the agent or the object, but rather to the agent and the object themselves. But how is it that, when all the *kārakas* (factors of action) are present, the *lakāra* denotes only the agent and the object? It is said: because of their preeminence. Among them, the agent is predominant because the instrument and the other factors function under his control; as for the object, its very existence is for the sake of that [agent], since its activity proceeds toward him.

Alternatively, the *lakāra* (verbal suffix) which arises after a verbal root (*dhātu*) denoting the operation of the agent or the object expresses only the agent and the object. Now, why does it not express time (*kāla*) and so forth as well, in the same way that it expresses the agent and the object? This is because their domains (*viṣaya*) differ. For instance, six factors are understood through a finite verb (*tiṅanta*): action (*kriyā*), time (*kāla*), voice (*upagraha*), grammatical relation (*kāraka*), person (*puruṣa*), and number (*saṃkhyā*).

Among these, the base denotes the action, time, the middle voice, and the conditions [for the middle voice]; the suffix denotes the instrument (sādhana), number, and person. Among those denoted by the base, the action is the primary element, while time and the voice (upagraha) are qualifiers. Among those denoted by the suffix, the instrument is the primary element, while time and the voice are qualifiers. Among those denoted by the suffix, the instrument is the primary element, while number and person are qualifiers.

But how is it that number is a qualifier of the *kāraka* alone, and not of the action (*kriyā*), the time (*kāla*), the voice (*upagraha*), or the person (*puruṣa*)? It is said: because the action, being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), is not yet fully established; because time is distinct from the action; and even if it were not distinct, it would be subordinate as a delimiting factor of the action. As for the voice (*upagraha*), such as the indicative (*gandhana*) and so on, since it is not fully established as the object of the action, it cannot be designated by "this" or "that," and thus there is no connection with number. The person (*puruṣa*), however, is simply the means of expressing the first [person] and so forth, and nothing else.

Therefore, number is connected only with the *kāraka*, and not with the action (*kriyā*) and so forth. Thus, what was stated—that because the agent is not denoted by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), there is the term "agent" (*kartṛpada*), the term "agent of the state" (*bhāvakartṛpada*), and the term "agent as object" (*karmakartṛpada*)—is indeed untenable. The distinctions of the forms of *kārakas* are: the term "agent" (*kartṛpada*), the term "object" (*karmapada*), the term "instrument" (*karaṇapada*), the term "recipient" (*saṃpradānapada*), the term "ablative" (*apādānapada*), and the term "locus" (*adhikaraṇapada*).

Among those, the agent (*kartṛ*) and others will be explained in detail later in the section on the grammatical factors (*kāraka*); however, they are here briefly illustrated for the sake of maintaining continuity in the discussion. Of these, the agent is threefold: independent (*svatantra*), dependent (*asvatantra*), and the agent-as-object (*karmakartṛ*). Among them, that which employs other factors such as the instrument (*karaṇa*) according to its own will in an action, and is not itself employed by them, is the independent agent. It is twofold: expressible by a primary case-ending (*svavibhaktivācya*) and expressible by a secondary case-ending (*paravibhaktivācya*).

The [agent] expressed by its own case-ending (*svavibhaktivācya*) is as follows: "By intoxication, which was skilled in shattering pride, which generated a desire for amorous play, which spread passion, and which suddenly suppressed internal hesitation, the women were won over, as if by a lover. The [agent] expressed by another case-ending (*paravibhaktivācya*) is as follows: "Beauty adorned their bodies; the union with full and fresh youth adorned that beauty; the splendor of the god of love (Cupid) adorned that [youth]; and intoxication, whose ornament is the company of a beloved, adorned that [splendor]. That which is employed by another in actions and is itself engaged in activity is the non-independent (*asvatantra*).

That [cause] is also of two kinds: one with manifested operation (*udbhūtavyāpāra*) and one with unmanifested operation (*anudbhūtavyāpāra*). Of these, an example of one with manifested operation is: "O Lord of Men, who else but you—being devoted to virtue, possessing loyal ministers, and proud of his lineage—could have wrested away from others the kingdom, which is like a beautiful wife, beloved by her virtues and born of noble family, as if she were his own spouse? An example of one with unmanifested operation is: "The love-god, the intoxication of spring, and the radiance of the moon, which produce a secluded tranquility of mind..."

They lead their beloveds to union and bring forth an indescribable state of passion in women. The agent of action (karmakartṛ) is also twofold: that whose portion of action is predominant (udriktakarmāṃśa) and that whose portion of action is not predominant (anudriktakarmāṃśa). Of these two, the one whose portion of action is predominant is as follows: The night-lotus, having drunk the lunar nectar through its various breaths, is unable to bear the essence of its own radiance; sprinkled with the humming of bees, it is severed from its stalk by the darkness.

The earth, milked by the virtues of this king—who is like Vasu himself, whose portion of action is not excessive, who possesses noble fame, who is compassionate, and who grants prosperity while warding off harm with his protection—yields its treasures effortlessly. When that which is to be accomplished is attained through an agent’s action performed for no other purpose, that is "action" (*karma*). That too is threefold: the produced (*nirvartya*), the modified (*vikārya*), and the reached (*prāpya*).

Among these, the object to be produced (*nirvartya*) is of two kinds: "that which is non-existent [before] is born, or that which is existent is made manifest by birth. Of these two, the first is as follows: "This Malaya breeze, shaking the sprouts of the full-grown sandalwood trees, produces joy for the world. The second is as follows: "The intoxication of spring, though already present, was not manifested for a long time because it was not its natural state; it now shines forth upon the limbs of young women, like a preposition (*upasarga*) revealing the meaning hidden within a verbal root (*dhātu*). The object to be modified (*vikārya*) is also of two kinds.

There is also the [transformation] consisting of the destruction of the original nature and the imposition of another quality. The first is as follows: "O Lord, withdraw, withdraw your wrath!"—while these words of the gods were still traveling through the sky, that fire born from the eye of Bhava reduced Madana to nothing but ashes. The second is as follows: Adorning her with *pāriḍāta* flowers fit for the curls of Puloma’s daughter, the Three-eyed One was gazed upon with longing by the celestial damsels for a long time in the Nandana grove. That which is to be attained is also of two kinds.

[The object] is either *kathita* (expressed) or *akathita* (unexpressed). Among these, that which is expressed by means of verbal roots having the sense of *kṛt*, *kt*, *khal*, and so forth, is *kathita*; that which is not expressed by them is *akathita*. An example of the first is: "The Ashoka branch, its clusters being drunk upon by bees and its young shoots trembling, was seen by the women as it emitted [pollen] while shaking its lips and hands with great force. An example of the second is: "For our sake, the Himalaya must be requested by you."

Relationships properly established do not lead to modification. That which functions as the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for the accomplishment of an action is the instrument (*karaṇa*). It is also threefold: internal (*brāhma*), external (*ābhyantara*), and both internal and external. Among these, the external is twofold: obstructive (*vyavadhāyaka*) and non-obstructive (*avyavadhāyaka*). Of those two, the first is, for example, the hair at the edge of the head, which has been deprived of its moisture by the heat of incense and contains flowers within it.

A certain maiden covered his broad waist with a pale, rising wreath of *dhūmaka* and *dūrvā* grass. Then, as if directed by the King of Vidarbha, the prince ascended the second platform by means of a constructed flight of stairs, just as a lion cub climbs a lofty mountain peak by means of a path of jagged rocks. The internal [space] is also twofold, divided into the distinct and the non-distinct. Of these, the distinct is exemplified thus: by the chest-regions of the sky-dwellers, solid as rocks, and by the expansive breasts of the brides.

The water, driven to the edge of the bank by waves breaking apart, assumed turbidity as if out of anger. O lady with the curved limbs, you ought to accept the second kind of guest-honor which one bestows upon oneself; for it is said by the wise that friendship is formed by walking seven steps together. It is also twofold, both external and internal: the former being outward-facing and the latter inward-facing. Of these, the first is like her who, having gone out, returns again through the window-opening, her heart filled with intense longing for her lover.

For a moment, the woman measured the state of the sun as it stood between her and the mountain; then, as if simultaneously, two things fell upon those filled with passion—her face, possessing an exceeding sweetness, and the fragrance of blue lotuses from her nostrils as they opened. That which one experiences through an action, whether by way of an object (*karman*) or by way of an activity (*kriyā*), is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). It is threefold: that which is pervaded by the object of the act of giving (*dadāti-karma-vyāpya*), that which is merely pervaded by the object (*karma-mātra-vyāpya*), and that which is pervaded by the activity (*kriyā-vyāpya*).

Among these, the object of the action of giving (*dadāti-karma*) is twofold: when the state of ownership (*svatva*) is not revoked, and when it is revoked. Of these two, the first is as follows: "Even Śaṅkara gave his eye born on the forehead—smeared with the powder of matted locks—from kissing, to the breeze from Pārvatī’s face, which possessed the fragrance of a blooming lotus. The second is as follows: "O tree, you are not able to give me away to another, nor even to take me away as a slave; for I am not your son, such that you should fear me in this way."

The object of the verb *dā* (to give) is twofold: that which is pervaded by the action (*kriyākarmavyāpya*) and that which is the objective domain of the meaning (*dadātyarthaviṣaya*). Regarding these, the first is as follows: "In this [hermitage], the creepers are like palaces, the medicinal herbs are like lamps, the beds are fresh sprouts of yellow sandalwood, and the breezes from the lotuses dispel fatigue; thus, O celestial beauties, they do not allow you to remember heaven. The second is as follows: "Having prostrated before him, Nandin announced that the daughter of the mountain had arrived, desiring to serve him."

And she caused her to enter, her entry permitted by a mere movement of her husband’s eyebrows. The object of an action (*kriyāvyāpya*) is also of two kinds: technical (*pāribhāṣika*) and non-technical (*apāribhāṣika*). Of these, the first is as follows: "Garlands did not please, nor sandal-pastes, nor wines, during separation from their beloveds; it is the joy of union alone that imparts beauty to the means [of adornment]. The second is as follows: "Thus, the bridegroom and the bride were attended with the rites of marriage by the family priest, who was skilled in the ritual procedures."

The two parents bowed to the Grandfather (Brahmā), who is seated upon a lotus throne and is the progenitor of all beings. In this context, *apādāna* (the ablative relation) is that which, through an action performed by an agent, enters into a state of fixedness (*dhrauvya*) produced by that very action. It is specified there as being of three kinds: having a stated object (*nirdiṣṭaviṣaya*), having an implied object (*upāttaviṣaya*), and having an action understood (*apekṣitakriya*). Among these, *nirdiṣṭaviṣaya* is further divided into two types: that which is abandoned (*ujjhita*) and that which is not abandoned (*anujjhita*). Of those two, the first is illustrated as follows: "On her forehead, marked with fresh nail-scratches moistened by perspiration, and on her cheeks where the tips of her hair were mostly bitten off..."

The *śirīṣa* flower, though fallen from the ears of the amorous women, did not drop even with their laughter—as if it were the second [day of the dawn], which, having hidden itself for fear of the sun’s heat, was now being overtaken by the darkness that more effectively brings an end to the luster of the day; as if descending slowly from the lowlands, the darkness gathered and filled the level plains. That which has been acquired as an object is twofold: the rejectable (*heya*) and the acceptable (*upādeya*). Of these two, the first is illustrated as follows: "O proud woman, shaking your hands which have the form of fresh sprouts, do not labor in vain."

How indeed could the swarm of bees not be bewildered, suspecting them to be wish-fulfilling creepers (*kalpalatā*) that have arrived? Just as Kumudvatī obtained from the descendant of Kakutstha a second son named Atithi, so did consciousness obtain clarity from the latter watch of the night. Even that which is devoid of action is twofold: dependent on the general and dependent on the particular. Of these two, the first is as follows: "May I never again, my mind deluded by intoxication, approach that wrongdoer."

"The young woman thus longed for wine; indeed, pride is difficult to abandon even when it is accompanied by pleasure. "How is it that you have not seen the second [Citrakūṭa] on the way? By whom was he of lovely and charming power seen? "O innocent one, what of him? During this festival of love, shall I have him painted at will upon the wall of your chamber? The locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the substratum of action, which is mediated by the agent and the object. It is threefold: objective (*vaiṣayika*), contactual (*aupaśleṣika*), and occasional (*naimittika*). Among these, the objective is twofold.

Of these two, the first is as follows: "Upon her broad hips, which were like the trunk of a plantain tree, the young woman fastened a great girdle of many strings, thereby adorning the elephant of the god whose banner is the makara. The second is as follows: "Fortitude in adversity, forbearance in prosperity, eloquence in the assembly, valor in battle, and a devotion to fame—this is indeed the innate nature of great souls, along with a love for sacred learning. The *aupacchandasika* meter is also of two kinds: partial (*ekadeśika*) and pervasive (*abhivyāpaka*).

Of these two, the first is as follows: When the deer-eyed women prepared for amorous sport upon their beloveds and their beds—which possessed a smooth luster and were fashioned with soft textures—their glances fell incessantly upon them, bowing down in devotion. The second is as follows: The beauty of intoxication was seen in all its fullness in the faces of the women—whose eyes were lovely with passion and whose cheeks were as red as coral—as if it were reflected in mirrors. The occasional (naimittika) [simile] is also of two kinds: pure and mixed.

Of these two, the first is as follows: "O you who are like smoke in a mass of fuel! O you who are like a flame without fire! O you who are like a painting on a wall! O you who are like a kiss upon a lotus-face! The second is as follows: "In this place, formerly the burden of the earth was borne by the Lord of Tortoises; here the words were recited by the Lord of Birds, the refuge of the mountains; and from here, the clouds—having removed the heat from their bodies—attained those whose secret essence is the constant utterance of 'Om', which is the primary source of sorrow for the wicked."

The specific cause that instigates an action is both the *hetu* (efficient cause) and the *kartṛ* (agent). That too is threefold: the impeller (*preraka*), the favorable one (*anukūla*), and the informer (*pratyayaka*). Among these, the impeller is twofold: the mediated (*vyavahita*) and the immediate (*avyavahita*). Of these two, the mediated is as follows: "And she, whose thighs were like the trunk of an elephant, fastened with her two hands that necklace, white as powdered camphor, upon the neck of the delight of the Raghus in its proper place, like affection incarnate."

The immediate [cause] (*avyavahita*) is as follows: "She whose speech was left unfinished, who was indifferent toward her garlands, garments, and ornaments, and who rose to go for no reason—she revealed the intoxication and its playful movements. The proximate cause (*anantara-kāraṇa*) is also twofold: the accomplished (*siddha*) and the to-be-accomplished (*sādhya*). The accomplished is as follows: "In the courtyards of the houses of the farmers, which were made fragrant by the scent of the scattering of grains of fresh rice, the young brides brought joy; their rows of bracelets jingling as they slipped from their hands while they threshed with upraised pestles."

The *sādhya* (the object to be accomplished) is, for example: "In an empty mountain village, the sun has set in the forest grove; O householder, your daughter-in-law, charming as a lotus, speaks thus to me. The *pratyāyaka* (the indicator) is twofold: that which involves a visible causal action (*dṛṣṭaprayojyakriya*) and that which involves an invisible causal action (*adṛṣṭaprayojyakriya*). Of these, examples such as "He causes Kaṃsa to be killed" or "He joins the moon with a flower" involve a visible causal action. An example of the former is: "Vālmīki joined the ocean together with mountains carried by monkeys."

Even though Vyāsa was [struck] by the arrows of Pārtha, no exaggeration is attributed to those two. Word and meaning are like two things held on a scale; likewise, this one, with mouth agape to find fault with our compositions, stands like a gourd [sinking] into the mud—salutations to him! He drives away the nights in Vārāṇasī, he makes the sun rise in Māhiṣmatī—such are the instances of *dṛṣṭayojya* (visible application). Just as the Lord of Life (Death), finding no space to lie down because obstructed by the expansive hips of a beautiful woman, [seeks elsewhere].

With sleepiness and lethargy dispelled by the experience of sexual pleasure, he somehow passes the night on his bed; what else could he do? Furthermore, regarding such instances as "the storyteller causes Kaṃsa to be killed" or "the singer causes Bali to be bound," it is said that the causative suffix (*ṇic*) arises from the operation of the instigator (*prayojaka*). Having reached the state of being objects of the intellect through forms infused with words, [the poet] regards Kaṃsa and others as if they were directly perceived, acting as the instruments of accomplishment.

And by describing their prosperity from the time of their birth until their destruction, he causes others to understand it in exactly the same way. For instance, speakers say: "Go, Kaṃsa is being killed," or "What is the use of going? Kaṃsa has already been killed. In the same way, one should understand that such communication occurs in cases like "He makes the night pass" (*rātriṃ vivāsayati*).

And this is the logical principle regarding the position that [the *sūtras*] are the commencement [of the action]; however, regarding the position that the *sūtras* are the commencement, it was cited previously: "Because of the narrative (*ākhyānāt*), one expresses the whole; there is elision of the *kṛt* suffix, restoration of the original form (*prakṛti-pratyāpatti*), and the grammatical relation (*kāraka*) is as in the original. Now, if this meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is not delimited as being the meaning of the verbal root itself, how could it be directly delimited? It must be so. For otherwise, it would not be obtainable; that [otherwise] is untenable. Since an action is not something already accomplished, its mutual connection with its own means of accomplishment occurs through mutual dependence.

Let it be then; however, this [objection] is untenable because of the intervention of the agent. For the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) consists in the activity of the agent; even though that agent is not directly perceived, the root-meaning implies him and qualifies the meaning of the suffix through him. And in this case, the instigation (*preraṇā*) is not purposeless, because one who suspects an interruption of the action instigates the agent even when he has already set out to act. Even where one is instigated while not yet having set out to act, there too, by virtue of suitability, the instigator employs the agent after apprehending a connection with the action as a mental object.

Even though not based on cognition (*buddhi*), the close connection between the action and its agent is established. Even then, whether by means of verbal suffixes (*ākhyāna*) or through the addition [of rules] such as "the *kṛt* suffix is used in the sense of the agent" (*kartari kṛt*), it remains a general [principle]. Since it is not distinguished from the cause of being "done" (*kṛtatva*), it is rejected precisely on the grounds that it is based on cognition. And in that case, by relying on the operation of an instigator (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*) directed toward an object of cognition such as "the intellect or the non-intellect is slain by Vāsudeva," a purely mental (*bauddha*) operation of the instigator is once again accepted.

Furthermore, there is a connection between the action denoted by the verbal root—which is linked to an agent implied by the sense—and the suffix-meaning, such as instigation (*preraṇā*). For this very reason, even when one has already begun acting, if one is being commanded, the suffixes such as *loṭ* arise; thus, the status of being an agent (*kartṛtva*) ceases [to apply to the previous state]. Now, one might object: "How can the status of being an agent belong to one who has not yet engaged in external activity? Moreover, how could the status of being an agent, which is to be accomplished through a command (*praiṣa*), possibly exist prior [to that command]? It is replied: This status of being an agent is not being designated here as something dependent upon the commencement of external activity.

However, when the agent is intended to be connected as being related to the action, his status as something to be accomplished [by that action] is established; for the agent—whose presence is obtained through the force of the action's own capacity and who is necessarily concomitant—is indeed already present, yet he is made the object of the instigator’s activity solely for the sake of accomplishing the external performance. Otherwise, if his agency were dependent upon the instigator’s activity, his agency would only come into existence after the instigator has acted; thus, in the absence of agency at the present time, the *loṭ* suffix and others based upon that agency would not be justified.

Therefore, by the expression "he cooks" (*pacati*) and so forth, what is stated is: "let him who cooks impel [others] toward the act of cooking. The verbal suffix (*lakāra*) applies itself to this agent—who is already determined through the power of the action—as being the object of an injunction (*praiṣya*), in its capacity as the denoted meaning. For they declare: "This very agent, understood through the power of the meaning of the verbal root such as 'cooking' (*pāka*), is designated by the verbal suffix when he is made the object of operations such as injunctions for the sake of accomplishing external application, which serves the purpose of providing the means (*sādhana*)."

Granted that the agent is brought into proximity by the action; however, how is it known that this agent is necessarily a person (*puruṣa*), such that it is said: "He who cooks for you, let him proceed with the cooking"? For this very reason, in the *Bhāṣya*, after stating the formation of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) when employing an agent who possesses an action, the production of the imperative (*loṭ*) is stated when employing a mere substance (*dravyamātra*): "May your honor ask," and "May your honor inquire."

It is said that even when a mere substance is being impelled, it is only that which is capable of accomplishing an action that is impelled, not something like wood or a wall. [Objection: In that case, there would result a confusion of the domains of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the imperative (*loṭ*). [Reply: There is no such confusion. Only that whose agency in an action has been repeatedly understood through other means of knowledge is the domain of the causative suffix when its capacity for action is merely potential. However, that which is merely capable, though its power to perform an action has not yet been observed, is indeed the domain of the imperative.

The mere substance [denoted by] "you" is incapable [of the action expressed by] "cook"; rather, you who are capable of cooking—fit for cooking, able in cooking—it is you who must set the cooking in motion. Thus, because one who is known to be fit through their status as the agent of the action is the one being impelled to act upon its employment, it is stated that the entitlement belongs to the agent alone. This very point is reinforced by various modes of expression such as, "Your Majesty is entitled to the kingdom because you are a learned, heroic, and noble-born agent."

If, then, the agent is not authorized, this intelligent person would not restrict the authorization in such a manner to a specific individual alone, but might employ just anyone. Alternatively, these [verbal suffixes] such as the *loṭ* have as their domain the issuing of commands (*praiṣa*) and so forth.

To whom do these [functions] belong as their inherent properties? They describe them as belonging to the *prayoktṛ* (the instigator) alone. For the *prayoktṛ*, by means of commands (*praiṣaṇa*) and so forth, impels the person toward his desires for the sake of accomplishing what has been expressed; he does so sometimes by commanding, sometimes by entreating, and sometimes by inviting. Others maintain that these are the operations (*vyāpāra*) of the word itself. Indeed, "commanding" (*preṣaṇā*) is a form common to all [types of] injunctions (*vidhi*) and the like. And this is the operation of the word, whereas "inviting" (*nimantraṇā*) and the rest are its specific varieties based on the [particular] means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and other factors.

For instance, it is understood from the context and other factors that "this is an invitation," "this is a permission," or "this is the appropriate time. According to another view, the specific operations of the person to be prompted (*prayojya*) are those [states], and they remain unperceived. Yet, through the employment of the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, that person considers himself to have reached a particular state regarding actions such as eating—thinking, "I am invited" or "I am requested. Others, however, say that the meaning of the suffix is solely *vidhi* (injunction); and in whatever form it is understood from expressions such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), it is exactly of that form.

"Make a mat!"—in this instance, because the meaning of the verb consists in the act of "doing," the connection of the *kārakas* (factors of action) follows the meaning of the verbal root according to the rule (*vidhi*). For it is observed that a specific state (*viśeṣa*) arises among the *kārakas* through the operation whose essence is the act of "doing"; indeed, one becomes a *kāraka* only by performing [an action]. Others, however, say: "This specific state, such as cooking and so forth, which is perceived through its mutual distinction from others and which produces a specific result..."

Since the instruments (*karaṇa*) operate precisely where there is the accomplishment of a result, and since that very [accomplishment] consists essentially in activity (*vyāpāra*), it necessarily also possesses the nature of action (*kriyā*). To distinguish this other view, one must consider whether the factors of action (*kāraka*) are active here or inactive. In a reality that possesses both natures, because a specific limiting condition (*upādhi*) has been determined, a factor of action, while operating in one respect, is perceived as if it were also operating in the other.

Now others say: indeed, an entity whose nature consists of both [substance and action] is brought about by the factors of action (*kārakas*). For this very reason, it is consistent even with the position of *bhāvanā* that "action" (*kriyā*) is a particular manifestation of the activity of the factors of action. Nor do we accept a *bhāvanā* in the form of the meaning of the root *√kṛ* (to do) that follows after all verbal roots; for thus they have studied: "The roots *√kṛ*, *√bhū*, and *√as* denote action in general, while roots such as *√pac* (to cook) and others denote specific actions."

However, its status as being denoted by the suffix (pratyaya) is drawn forward [from the previous discussion]. Nor is there an inconsistency regarding the plural number in "of the factors" (*kārakāṇām*) in the view that it is *bhāvanā* (productive activity); for *bhāvanā* is indeed the operation of the agent alone, and it is not said to belong to the causal instruments. It is the agent alone who is expressed by the word "factor" (*kāraka*), and not other instruments and so forth. As for the plural number, it refers to multiple agents due to the diversity of their actions. How, then, is this known? Because this is stated with reference to the act of eating.

The causal factors operate in one way toward dry rice and in another way toward rice with meat. Toward dry rice, the agent acts with slow movement; toward rice with meat, he acts with zeal. Therefore, it is understood that the manifestation of slowness and zeal belongs to the *kratu* (volition). It is the agent alone who is grasped [as the subject], because such activity proceeds from his mental attachment (*buddhy-anuṣaṅga*). But surely, in the case of dry rice and rice with meat, there will also be a plural number for the instruments, locations, and so forth, based on those distinctions?

It is not so; for even when other factors of action (*kāraka*) such as a bronze vessel or the like are present, [the action] proceeds either slowly or with intensity depending on whether it concerns dried meat or boiled rice. Even when the position is taken that the operation of all the *kārakas* occurs simultaneously, it is nevertheless the agent (*kartṛ*) alone who is designated by the term *kāraka*, because of its primacy and because it is the substratum of all specific actions, and because it is the cause for the application of the grammatical usage.

Furthermore, although action (*karman*) is primary because the activity is directed toward it, nevertheless, since it is not the object of the *kāraṇas* (factors of action), it is included by means of the plural number. If this is so, why was the word "agent" (*kartṛ*) itself not used, so that the exclusion of the *lakāras* (verbal suffixes) from the sense of the object might not occur? By that [use of the plural], wherever the object is possible, it is indeed accepted; however, the plural is employed with respect to that [object]. But surely, because of the demonstration of exertion (*saṃrambha*) and so forth, the status of "action" (*kriyātva*) would not apply to the operation of consciousness (*cetanā-vyāpāra*).

It is not so, because exertion (*saṃrambha*) and the like are distinct from the agent. Therefore, it is established that action (*kriyā*) is the operation of the agent. [Objection: If this is the case, the Bhāṣya is inconsistent; for it asks, "What is the primary meaning of the root *pac*? and answers, "It is that softening (*viklitti*) of the rice grains. [Response: There is no contradiction, for that Bhāṣya relies on the primacy of the purpose. That which is the solicitation or the entreaty for that purpose—that is the entire meaning of *pac*.

And thus, in the expression "he cooks" (*pacati*), the meaning of the verb (*ākhyāta*) consists of the act of moistening (*vikledana*), with the softening (*viklitti*) as a subordinate element. Others, however, explain the plural number in the phrase "of the factors" (*kārakāṇām*) as referring to the activity of all the factors, because it is observed that verbal roots denote the activities of all the factors.

And likewise, in such cases as "the cooker of Devadatta with wood on the stove for rice," all the *kārakas* are qualifiers of the verbal root's meaning; here, no subordinate or primary status of any one of them is perceived. Why, then, are the operations of all the *kārakas* not understood from the verb (*ākhyāta*)? Because the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) arises only for the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*) due to their predominance, it is only their operation that is cognized from the verb.

Furthermore, is there a single activity (*pravṛtti*) for all the causal factors (*kārakas*), or are there distinct activities for each factor? The first position is not tenable, because it is impossible for all [factors] to have one and the same activity; for it is not possible that the very activity of the wood is the same as that of Devadatta or the pot and so forth. Therefore, distinct activities belonging to each individual factor, which are denoted simultaneously by the verbal root (*dhātu*), are called "action" (*kriyā*).

Alternatively, there is only one activity (*pravṛtti*), namely action (*kriyā*), common to all factors of action (*kāraka*). For indeed, a single activity is produced by all the factors of action together. Or rather, let it be that there is only one [activity] among all the factors of action; however, because it produces something in a particular form, the designations such as "instrument" (*karaṇa*) and so forth arise due to internal differences. Furthermore, the occurrence of a single [activity] in many places is justified, just like a genus (*jāti*). Moreover, this [activity] is characterized by the production of a result, and not by forms such as placing [the pot on the fire] (*adhiśrayaṇa*) and so forth; thus, it is not of the nature of [mere] physical operations.

Those whose form consists of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) and so forth, those whose form consists of particles (*nipāta*) and so forth, those whose form consists of vocatives (*saṃbodhana*) and so forth, those whose form consists of relations (*saṃbandha*) and so forth, and those whose form consists of reasons (*hetu*) and so forth are the types of *upaskāra* (adornments). Since these will be described in detail later in the section on the meaning of adornment (*upaskāra-artha*), they are not elaborated upon here. However, they are cited briefly for the purpose of ensuring the continuity of the connection (*saṃbandha*). Among them, the qualifiers and so forth consist of adverbial qualifiers (*kriyā-viśeṣaṇa*), substantive qualifiers (*kāraka-viśeṣaṇa*), and prefixes (*upasarga*).

Just as in "he cooks well" (*śādhu pacati*), "he makes [the hair] formidable, noble, beautiful, or curly" (*bhīṣmam udāram darśanīyam kacam karoti*), and "others will go by chariot" (*evam anye rathena yāsyanti*); likewise, particles (*nipātāḥ*) that function as karmapravacanīyas and indeclinables (*avyayāni*), such as "O slayer of Vṛtra, it is not right for both you and me to conquer" (*yathāham ca tvam ca vṛtrahan asāmpratam jetum*); verbal roots (*ākhyātāni*), which are verbs; primary derivatives (*kṛtaḥ*) and secondary derivatives (*taddhitāḥ*), such as "O Devadatta, do you remember? We shall dwell in Kaśmīra" (*śmarasi devadatta kāśmīreṣu vatsyāmaḥ*), "he thrives with the nourishment of wealth" (*raipoṣam puṣyati*), and "he speaks like a Brahmin" (*brāhmavad bravīti*).

Addressing and so forth—namely, invocation, limit, state, and gender—are, for example: *he devadatta*, *bhuktvā vrajati* (having eaten, he goes), and *saḥ* (he). Relation and so forth are the "remainder" (*śeṣa*), which is the "governed word" (*upapada*). And the sense of "together with" (*sahārtha*) is, for example: *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* (the king's man), *kuśalaṃ devadattāya* (well-being to Devadatta), and *putreṇa sahāyātaḥ* (he has come with his son). Cause, characteristic, and purpose are, for example: *vidyayā ślāghyaḥ* (praiseworthy because of learning), *kamaṇḍalunā chātraḥ* (a student by virtue of a water-pot), and *yūpāya dāru* (wood for a sacrificial post).

How, then, is this *hetu* (cause) distinguished from the *kāraka* (agent/actor)? "The *hetu* has substance (*dravya*) and so forth as its object, while the *kāraka* has a fixed action. For example: "A crop [arises] by means of a seed," "He is emaciated by heat," "He is strong by means of food," "Brahminhood [is attained] by means of a vow. As for the *kāraka*, for example: "Devadatta gives a hundred gold *niṣkas* to a Brahmin at a sacred ford with faith. If it were thus, then by virtue of having substance and so forth as its object, the *hetu* would be non-fixed (*aniyata*) with respect to the action, as in: "The Brahmin together with his son."

It is not so; for it is not by means of the word that the exclusion of substance and the other categories from the meaning is expressed. On the contrary, the operation of the cause—even though it is dependent [on something else]—is prescribed by the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) and the others. If it is asked, "How then does the object of the action differ from the instrument (*karaṇa*)?", [the answer is: "The substitute for the instrument is seen to be that by which the action is performed; however, even when it serves as a cause, it is not a substitute for the cause of the action. If that is so, then there is non-difference because of having that same purpose (*tādathryāt*).

What is this so-called *tādārthya* (being-for-the-sake-of-that)? It is the state of being a motivator (*prayojakatva*) of the effect with respect to the cause; that is to say, it is a specific kind of causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). For whatever exists for the sake of something else, that [latter] must necessarily be produced by the former. How, then, is this not different from *hetu* (cause/reason)? Because the capacity of the cause to introduce the possibility of the effect is the state of being-for-the-sake-of-that, which consists in the effect’s being the motivator with respect to the cause.

And this is the distinction: the dative case occurs in the sense of "for the sake of that" (tādārthye) only when the word denotes the effect (*kārya*); however, for a cause (*hetu*) that denotes either the effect or the motive (*nimitta*), the instrumental case is used. If this were so, then by the rule for the instrumental denoting a cause, the instrumental would result [instead of the dative] in the expression *kanakāt prapnoti* ("he obtains from gold"). Nor can it be argued that both meanings—[the sense of "for the sake of"] and the relation of cause—will arise together. This is not the case; for the very meaning which is understood through the pronoun *tasmai* ("for that") in the expression *tadartham* ("for the sake of that") is precisely what is connected with the dative case, provided it possesses a distinction relative to its own cause.

Just as in the case of a mantra, it is only the referent of the pronoun that is connected with the action—namely, that "he has mastered that for which this mantra was intended"—so too here, the very object denoted by the word *tat* (that) is transformed into a purpose; thus, the word itself is not directly expressed [as the purpose]. Even when this word ends in an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), it expresses only a specific conventional form residing within the action: namely, the state of being a motivator toward a cause, which is its "being-for-that-purpose" (*tādathrya*).

How, then, could the dative case ending, which expresses purpose (*tādathrya*), be suspected for the agent (*kāraka*)? For even in the case of an effect (*kārya*), the dative is employed because the relationship residing in both [the cause and the effect] is understood; thus, from the word "cause" (*kāraṇa*), there arises [the dative] as non-different from the meaning of the base (*pratipadikārtha*), which is not distinct [from it], and not the instrumental (*tṛtīyā*) characterized by separation. And this is the domain of both "cause" (*hetu*) and "purpose" (*tādathrya*): as in *vāsena adhīte* ("he studies for the sake of lodging") and *adhyayanena vasati* ("he lodges for the sake of study"), and *yūpāya dāru* ("wood for a sacrificial post") and *adhyayanāya valate* ("he exerts himself for the sake of study").

However, for one who considers that "having that as its purpose" (*tad-arthitā*)—which consists in being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*)—is the capacity of a cause to produce an effect when it has no other purpose, and that this "being for that purpose" (*tādārthya*) belongs to that specific [cause], then the two qualifiers "of that" (*tad-viśeṣasya*) and "having no other purpose" (*ananyārthasya*) are redundant, because they make no difference in either case. If, first of all, "having that as its purpose" means the absence of any other purpose, then let it be so; yet the capacity of gold for bracelets and the like remains the same even in the cause of that [bracelet], by virtue of the property of denoting a composite whole.

For knowledge does not state that [the cause] possesses fitness for any other effect apart from being a cause of fame; nor should it be said that this consists in "being for the sake of another" (*pārārthya*), because that is already covered by the phrase "fitness for the production of an effect. Now, one might object: in expressions such as "he hears the actor," even though the actor and so forth are fit to produce an effect, they are "for the sake of another"; therefore, to ensure that they do not function as the *hetu* (cause/reason) when such a distinction is intended, the qualification is made.

It is not so. Just as in the expression "he studies from the preceptor" (*upādhyāyād adhīte*), the preceptor and others possess the status of a *kāraka* (participant in an action) by virtue of being for the sake of another, and their being "for that purpose" (*tādarthya*) consists precisely in their being the instigator (*prayojaka*). Now, what is the status of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*)? A defining characteristic is also simply a specific kind of cause (*hetu*), just like being "for that purpose. For a cause is established as being either an agent (*kāraka*) or a communicator (*jñāpaka*). Among these, when an agent does not rely upon its own operation, it is termed a "cause" (*hetu*); whereas for a communicator, it is a "defining characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*). Indeed, the meaning of a defining characteristic is the state of being a cause for the determination of a distinct category of entity.

In the case of operations that do not depend [on a substratum], a cause (*hetu*) is intended as the *nimitta* (motivating factor); however, the wise know that in the case of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic is that which has existence delimited by its substratum (*āśraya*). In some instances, even a cause is a defining characteristic. For example: "an ascetic by his matted hair" (*jaṭābhis tāpasaḥ*) is explained as a *itthambhūtalakṣaṇa* (characteristic of being in such a state); "blind in one eye" (*akṣṇā kāṇaḥ*) is a *vikāralakṣaṇa* (characteristic of a modification); "there was a flash of lightning" (*kapilā vidyut*) is a *utpātalakṣaṇa* (characteristic of an omen); "he departed while the cows were being milked" (*goṣu duhyamānāsu gataḥ*) is a *bhāvalakṣaṇa* (characteristic of an action/state); and "he sits while cooking" (*pacann āste*) is a *kriyālakṣaṇa* (characteristic of an activity). A sentence (*vākya*) is a collection of words directed toward a single meaning.

The refined language (*saṃskṛta*) is threefold: *prākṛta*, *apabhraṃśa*, and *brāhmaṇa*. Just as a man becomes impassioned, lustful, and deluded by women, so too there is sovereignty over others; thus, he is endowed with all human desires. This is the supreme bliss of men. The archaic language (*ārṣa*) is twofold: *smṛti* and *purāṇa*. Regarding these two, *smṛti* says: "A Śūdra woman alone is the wife of a Śūdra; she and a woman of his own [caste] are for a Vaiśya; those two and a woman of his own [caste] are for a Kṣatriya; and those three and a woman of his own [caste] are for one of the first-born [Brāhmaṇa]."

As in the *Purāṇa*: "In whatever direction the Daitya Hiraṇyakaśipu cast his gaze, the gods, bewildered by fear, offered salutations to that very direction. Worldly literature (*laukika*) is of two kinds: poetry (*kāvyam*) and science (*śāstram*). Of these two, an example of poetry is: "O charming girl, whose thirst does not agitate the mind? This lower lip of yours has the luster of coral, like a desert path. An example of science is: "Whose eye is white with collyrium and fringed with lashes reaching to the corners?"

Her abode of love becomes like fresh butter. Prakrit is threefold: *sahaja* (natural), *lakṣita* (characterized), and *śliṣṭa* (blended). Among these, *sahaja* is twofold: *saṃskṛtasama* (identical to Sanskrit) and *deśya* (regional). Of these two, an example of *saṃskṛtasama* is: "O girl with thighs like plantain stalks (*raṃbhoru*), abandon this rash passion; give up your agitation. Your heart is unable for me to bear such a fruitless and wearying burden. An example of *deśya* is: "Even though she was a woman, she attained forgiveness while laughing at the six seasons."

The *vāsaara* (Prakrit) is corrupted; it causes one to stumble. It is observed to be twofold: Mahārāṣṭrī and Śaurasenī. Mahārāṣṭrī is as follows: "Salute the slayer of Madhu (Viṣṇu), who is not increased, not lofty, not spreading, not extensive, not narrow, not deep, not light, not easily grasped, and whose feet are manifest without stumbling. Śaurasenī is as follows: "... [the] hand, and also not a little angry, O you who have no fear, having placed [it] at the feet... (Note: The provided fragments appear to be phonetic transcriptions of Prakrit verses. The first example illustrates the characteristics of Mahārāṣṭrī, while the second provides a fragment of a Śaurasenī verse.)

In these very tender fingernails, their sound is exceedingly thin—like the Magadha language, which destroys the peace of the heart, like food that cuts through the throat with a jar, and like blood constantly drunk by those with powerful fangs; let it be consumed with impurity. Apabhraṃśa is threefold: the highest, the middle, and the lowest. Among these, the Avanti, Lāṭa, Ṭakka, and others constitute the highest.

Among these, an example of the Avanti style is as follows: "O noble lady, you who are like a single moon, whose body is unblemished, whose ornaments are perfectly arranged, whose eyes are wide and clear, and whose face is stainless—alas, even though you are near, I do not perceive you; for you have been consumed by the fire of separation, and your very existence is being devoured by the heat of the day. An example of the Lāṭīya style is as follows: "When the sun, the thief of beauty, steals away the splendor of your arms, it is as if it were a wicked person speaking harsh words; yet even now, O lady with breasts like the peaks of Mount Gaṇa, your face is not pierced by the rays of the moon, for the moon's teeth are but the fragments of your own lips."

The Ābhīra, Gaurjara, and others are of the middle [class]. Of these two, the Ābhīra is as follows: "O son, you who are the support of my life, why do you go? Even if I were to die today, it would have been better for me. The Gaurjara is as follows: "The dice are won, the stake is gained; the daughter of the ocean is heavy with jewels. But this dull-witted man, alas, is being tormented by the gambling board. The Kāśmīra and Paurastya are of the lowest [class].

Of these two [styles], the Kāśmīra is as follows: "O Kaṃvalī, alas! One of your teeth is loose; this impurity must be removed by you. Alas, O you who are so lazy! All your limbs are afflicted by disease; having been weakened, you have become emaciated; alas, you have reached the state of old age! The Paurastya (Eastern) is as follows: "By the great lords, the Sāmavedins, and the Erāvatīs, let it be announced: 'Let the women of the household perform the rites of purification. Let the eyes be moistened with tears, and let the sounds of *huṃ* arise from the throats.'"
