The venerable Ācārya [Harivṛṣabha] has stated that there are eleven types of *upādhi* (limiting conditions) for the soul (*jīva*) in its various forms of existence (*bhavana*). All that collection of statements regarding them is proclaimed as being of eleven kinds. Namely: 1. *ekākhyāta* (single finite verb), 2. *anekākhyāta* (multiple finite verbs), 3. *āvṛttākhyāta* (repeated finite verb), 4. *anuvṛttākhyāta* (continued finite verb), 5. *vipariṇātākhyāta* (transformed finite verb), 6. *ekārthākhyāta* (single-meaning finite verb), 7. *samuccitākhyāta* (conjoined finite verb), 8. *kṛdabhihitākhyāta* (finite verb expressed by a nominal suffix), 9. *apekṣitākhyāta* (finite verb requiring supplementation), 10. *ekāntarākhyāta* (separated by one word), and 11. *nirantarākhyāta* (uninterrupted).

Among these, an example of a single verb (*ekākhyāta*) is as follows: "I salute Pārvatī and Parameśvara, the parents of the world, who are joined together like speech and its meaning for the sake of the comprehension of both speech and meaning. An example of multiple verbs (*anekākhyāta*) is as follows: "My beloved does exactly what pleases me; she knows this, yet she does not realize that which she does for my pleasure. An example of repeated verbs (*āvṛttākhyāta*) is as follows: "Victorious is Hari, whose stainless Kaustubha gem rests upon his broad shoulder; victorious are the fawn-eyed women with the movements of their glances and trembling side-long looks."

Then Mallikā triumphs; following that, victorious is the sound of the fifth [note], capable of destroying all worldly perception. An example of *anuvṛttākhyāta* (corresponding description) is as follows: "The elephants roam in the gardens on the shores of the four oceans, and your virtues, white as kunda flowers, reside in the hollows of the Cakravāla mountains and elsewhere. An example of *viparītākhyāta* (contrary description) is as follows: "Victorious is that fifth note of the five-arrowed god [Kāma] which is the very life-breath in this spring; and those winds, scattering the blossoms in Caitra, are indeed the playful sports of that season."

An example of a verb expressing a single meaning (*ekārthākhyāta*) is: "The *kadamba* trees bloom, the *kuṭaja* flowers burst open, the *kandalī* plants unfurl, and the *kakubha* trees blossom. An example of a verb expressing a cumulative action (*samuccitākhyāta*) is: "He helped his wife down from the chariot, and he himself descended. An example of a verb expressed through a *kṛt* suffix (*kṛdabhihitākhyāta*) is: "Then the eastern quarter was adorned by the moon—the lord of night-lotuses, white as the cheek of a passionate woman, and a delight to the eyes."

An example of *adhyāhṛtākhyāta* (supplying an implied verb) is: "He who [cuts] the neem tree with an axe, he who [anoints it] with honey and ghee, and he who [worships it] with perfumes and garlands—in all cases, it remains bitter. An example of *anapokṣitākhyāta* (omitting an expected verb) is: "O Brahmin, how much water is there? [It is only] knee-deep, O King. And yet such is your condition; for indeed, not everyone is like you. An example of *ekāntarākhyāta* (separated by one word) is: "By that [act], the ocean, bound to the mountain, increased; Rāma was gratified; the lord of monkeys rejoiced."

There the enemy was seen, Suvela was beheld, the water's edge was proclaimed, and those hoping for nectar rejoiced. Now, [the opponent argues that] syntactical variations such as the "successive verb" (*nirantarākhyāta*), the "cumulative verb" (*samuccitākhyāta*), the "single-meaning verb" (*ekārthākhyāta*), and the "repeated verb" (*āvṛttākhyāta*) are untenable; for the author of the *Vākyapadīya* maintains that there is no connection whatsoever between two finite verbs (*tiṅanta*).

And thus, regarding the rule *tiṅṅatiṅaḥ*, he rejects the mention of *atiṅ* (non-tiṅ) on the grounds that it is purposeless because of the governing principle of "being within the same sentence" (*samānavākyādhikāra*). For there cannot be two finite verbs (*tiṅanta*) in a single sentence. Accordingly, he states: "A sentence consists of a verb (*ākhyāta*) together with indeclinables (*avyaya*), case-words (*kāraka*), and qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*). In this context, the explicit mention of "verb" (*ākhyāta*) need not be made; for indeclinables, case-words, and qualifiers do not require the inclusion of a separate word [to define a sentence] without such a basis.

Where one finite verb (*ākhyātapada*) occurs together with indeclinables (*avyaya*), case-words (*kāraka*), and adjectives (*viśe�ṣaṇapada*), that constitutes a sentence (*vākya*). However, lest the designation "sentence" apply even when multiple finite verbs are employed, he begins another statement—namely, *ekatiṅ vākyam*—"a sentence consists of a single finite verb"—in order to exclude those cases where the portion consisting of a finite verb is not restricted to being singular.

In this regard, the following is considered: Is it that there is no connection whatsoever between two finite verbs (*tiṅanta*) within a single sentence, or is it that although such a connection exists, the second verb is not employed? [The author] says something regarding the rule "a sentence contains only one finite verb" (*ekatiṅvākyam*), which follows the convention of the ancient teachers: even though a connection between two finite verbs exists, the definition of a sentence as "containing only one finite verb" is established merely as a technical (*pāribhāṣika*) designation for the purpose of regulating grammatical operations such as the substitution of *ti*, the vocative (*āmantrita*), the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, and protracted vowels (*pluta*).

What is the reason? Because it is traditionally taught (*smṛta*) that there is a suppression of accent (*nighāta*) for two finite verbs (*tiṅ*) or vocatives following a word within a single sentence-meaning (*samānavākyārtha*). Furthermore, substitutions such as *vaṃ*, *nau*, and *vaḥ* are prescribed for the genitive, dative, and accusative cases of the pronouns *yuṣmad* and *asmad*. Also, by the rule "the final syllable (*ṭi*) of a sentence (*vākya*) is protracted (*pluta*) and acute," the protraction of the last syllable of a sentence is enjoined. And this [application of these rules] is only possible if the technical definition of a sentence is established as "a sentence consists of a single finite verb" (*ekatiṅ vākyam*).

Otherwise, according to the rule "a grammatical operation concerning words applies only when they are semantically connected" (*samarthaḥ padavidhiḥ*), since there would be no mutual semantic connection between the words and the sentence would remain incomplete, [the formation of compounds] would not be possible in any case. For example: *nadyāstiṣṭhanti kūle* (they stand by the river-bank), *vṛkṣasya lambate śākhāyām* (it hangs from the branch of the tree), *kaḥ priye mayi kopaḥ?* (what anger is there toward me, your beloved?), *kā subhaga priyā te?* (who, O fortunate one, is your beloved?), *śālīnām odanam dāsyāmīti me mātā bravīti* (my mother says she will give me rice-gruel), *āgaccha bho devadatta kugrāmaṃ gacchāvaḥ* (come, O Devadatta, let us go to the wretched village), and *grāmaṃ yadi yāsi re na mām api pratīkṣasva* (if you go to the village, O rogue, do not wait for me either).

In this case, [the meaning is determined as follows]: because of the connection with "not unfavorable" (nākūlam), it is not a river; because of the hanging down, it is a branch and not a tree; by the word "who" (ka) used with anger, it is the beloved; but by "who" (kā) used with affection, it is the beloved and not "your fortune" (subhagā te); by the sense of the second person pronoun "you" (yuṣmad) in "me" (me), it is a gift and not rice; by the sense of the first person pronoun "I" (asmat) in "me" (me), it is not the word for mother. In the two sentences, "Come, Devadatta, to the village" and "If you go, hey you!", the completion of the sentence occurs at these very words.

What then? [One might say: "Let us go; wait for me as well. In that case, there would be no occurrence of the *nighāta* (tonal suppression) and other such operations. However, if a collection of words containing a single finite verb (*ekatiṅ*) is considered a sentence, then—provided there is some kind of connection, whether direct or indirect—the *nighāta*, the substitutes for *yuṣmad* and *asmad*, and so forth, are appropriate. Regarding the rule "and an addition concerning what is joined with what is joined" (*yukteyukte copasaṅkhyānam*), it must be stated by means of the word "joined" (*yuktena*).

In this way, when a collection of words (*padakadambaka*) is perceived as a sentence (*vākya*) by means of the delimitation of a single finite verb (*ekatiṅ*), the rule "the *pluta* [protracted vowel] of the final syllable of a sentence" (*vākyasya ṭeḥ plutaḥ*) is established, whereby the final syllable of the sentence becomes acutely accented (*udātta*). However, some say that there is no connection at all between two finite verbs (*tiṅanta*). For if such a connection were to be postulated among finite verbs, it could only be conceived in six ways.

The relations are: the relation between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣya*), the relation between the probandum and the probans (*sādhyasādhana*), the relation between the object to be defined and the definition (*lakṣyalakṣaṇa*), the relation between cause and effect (*hetuhetumat*), the relation between limit and limited (*avadhyavadhi*), and the relation of conjunction (*samuccaya*) and so forth. Among these, the relation between qualifier and qualified may occur either through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) or through non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).

First of all, [the relation] cannot be one of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "cooks" and "reads," because their meanings are entirely distinct; for the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*) is not possible when word-meanings are either entirely different or entirely identical. Indeed, it is not the case that "the mango is a mango" or "the mango is a *aśvattha* tree"; however, where there is neither total difference nor total identity, it is appropriate, as in "the blue lotus."

Now, one might object: just as in expressions such as *prapacati* ("he cooks thoroughly") or *stokaṃ pacati* ("he cooks slightly"), the verb is qualified by a prefix (*pra-*) or by a word such as *stoka*, why is it not likewise qualified by another verb? This is not so; for in these cases, just as the words *nīla* ("blue") and *vīra* ("hero") denote blueness and heroism respectively as qualifiers, they simultaneously apprehend the lotus and the man in their general form.

Nor do the two universals, "form" (*rūpa*) and "man" (*puruṣa*), become restricted [to one another]. Even the words "lotus" and "man," while denoting the lotus and the man as the qualified subjects (*viśeṣya*), grasp blueness and manhood respectively as their qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) in a general sense; they do not, however, restrict their own nature to those two universals or their qualifiers. The relationship of qualifier and qualified arises through their mutual association.

And this [distinction] is not applicable to the pair "he cooks" (*pacati*) and "he reads" (*paṭhati*), for *pacati* cannot grasp *paṭhati*, nor can *paṭhati* grasp *pacati*, in the same way that [the word] "blue" grasps "lotus. Now, one observes the relationship of qualifier and qualified even between things whose meanings are entirely non-different; for example, between two words of non-different meaning as in "he studies" (*adhīte*) and "he learns" (*adhyeti*), and between two words of different meanings as in "he stands firm" (*pratiṣṭhate*) and "he forgets" (*prasmarati*).

It is not so. Although the verbal root (*dhātu*) does not deviate from its connection with the prefix (*upasarga*) in the cases of *adhīte* and *adhyeti*, the prefix certainly deviates from the root. Therefore, it is possible to determine a difference in meaning through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): whatever meaning this prefix *adhi* is seen to have elsewhere, that same meaning it ought to have here as well. Furthermore, this *adhi* is observed elsewhere to have the sense of "being above," as in *adhyāste* ("he sits upon") and *adhirohati* ("he climbs up"). We consider that its meaning here is also that very same one; therefore, the root *iṅ* (in *adhīte*) alone possesses both the action of speaking and the action of knowing.

The prefix *adhi*, however, qualifies this very same meaning by way of its sense of "above" (*uparibhāvena*). For meaningful words, their specific designation (*viśabdana*) is preceded by a rule, and likewise is the cognition whose object is the meaning already studied; it is only this much meaning that is differentiated by the prefix *adhi*. But how is it [used] here in cases such as *pratiṣṭhate* ("he stands") or *prasmarati* ("he forgets")?

For here, even though the roots *tiṣṭhati* or *smarati* are used alone, they do not denote a general action like the root *pacati*; rather, a contrary action is understood. Furthermore, the departure from the act of walking and the cessation of remembering are clearly indicated; by the word *pratiṣṭhate*, the commencement of staying is not expressed.

Rather, it is the act of going itself that is remembered; thus, even by virtue of this remembrance, the commencement [of the action] is not denoted. Since there is the commencement of the remembrance of the father, this is not a fault. This word [pacati], being known as a verbal root expressing an action through examples such as *prapacati*, has its status as expressing an initial action (*ādikarma*) inferred from the inference based on specific observation (*viśeṣato-dṛṣṭa*). Furthermore, the root *tiṣṭhati*—as in "Devadatta stands" (*devadattastiṣṭhati*)—is known as a verbal root because it expresses an action; therefore, its meaning as "going" (*gamana*) is also understood through the inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*).

Roots also possess multiple meanings; for instance, the root *vapi*, though seen in the sense of "covering," is also employed in the sense of "cutting," as in the expression *keśān vapati* ("he cuts his hair"). The root *īh*, though seen in the sense of "motion," is also employed in the sense of "impelling," as in *agnir vā itaḥ pravamīhe* ("the fire indeed impels from here"). The root *kṛ*, though seen in the sense of "the manifestation of something previously non-existent" (*apūrva-prādurbhāva*), also functions in the sense of "cleansing," as in *pādau kuru*, *pṛṣṭhaṃ kuru*, *mā kuru*; for it is understood that when one says "rub the feet," "rub the back," or "do not rub the belly"—as the oil diminishes—the meaning intended is "rub thoroughly" (*unmṛdāna*) or "rub well" (*mṛdonmṛdāna*).

Likewise, it is understood that [the root *kṛ*] means "make a mat" (*kaṭe kuru*), "bend with a stone" (*aśmanā namitaḥ kuru*), or "throw down and throw up" (*nikṣipa-avakṣipa*). This [root] also, being a verbal root (*dhātu*), is capable of having multiple meanings; by this, the root *smṛ* (to remember) is also explained. Nor is it unseen that two contradictory meanings are expressed by a word of identical form. For example, it is observed that the words *śan* (near) and *karṣa* (draw) are both expressed by the word *ārāt*: "drive away the enemy from afar" (*ārāc chatrum apabādhasva*) and "drive the enemies far, even further away" (*dūrād davīyaḥ apasedha śatrūn*).

Therefore, it is logical to say that *tiṣṭhati* (stands) has the sense of going, and *smarati* (remembers) is the action of the cessation of remembering, and that the prefix (*upasarga*) is a qualifier; for it has been rightly stated that the relationship of qualifier and qualified exists between two things whether they are absolutely different or identical, as in the rule: "A qualifier is meaningful when there is both possibility and deviation. Nor can a verbal root (*ākhyāta*) be a qualifier through a lack of coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), because when it possesses primacy, its meaning is not subordinate to the meaning of the verbal root.

In the expression "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), there is a distinction based on the causal relation to actions such as supporting, which constitutes a specific connection. And this [distinction] does not arise solely from the predominance of the meaning of the word "king," nor is such predominance possible for the meaning of the verb (*ākhyāta*) in the absence of a substantive entity (*sattva*).

Furthermore, even in cases where a verbal action is not explicitly heard—such as in "he remembers his mother" (*mātuḥ smarati*) or "he knows the ghee" (*sarpiṣo jānīte*)—there too, a distinction arises for the non-primary object such as the mother or the ghee, which exists as a substance (*sattvabhūta*) and is understood in the form of being that which is to be accomplished by the action (*kriyāsādhya*). This [distinction] serves as the cause for its connection with the specific action that is being heard. However, this is not possible for a verb (*ākhyāta*), because, precisely due to its being a substance, it cannot be designated as "of this" (*asya*) since it lacks the status of being a referent for a causal condition.

That which indeed possesses a fully established nature (*pariniṣṭhitasvabhāva*) is fit to be referred to by a pronoun (*sarvanāma*) as "this" or "that," and it may or may not be employed as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) for something else. However, how could that which is itself incomplete in form and remains unfulfilled ever attain the status of being a qualifier for another? [Objection: But surely, in examples such as *prapacati* ("he cooks thoroughly") and *stokaṃ pacati* ("he cooks slightly"), the words *pra-* and *stoka-* are said to function as qualifiers, even though they do not denote a substance (*asattvabhūta*).

It is not so, for it is established otherwise; for prepositions (*upasarga*) or qualifiers of action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), even though they are substantial entities (*satvabhūta*), possess the status of being subordinate (*guṇabhāva*) with respect to the action precisely by virtue of having no other object. To illustrate: the prefix *pra-* manifests that quality which constitutes the action—such as "commencement" (*prārambha*)—by denoting it as something that has entered into the action and is non-substantial (*asatvabhūta*), just like the purpose of the action itself.

Alternatively, just as the closing of the eyes and so forth indicate objects even without denoting them, in the same way, particles such as *pra* and others illuminate actions like "commencement" (*prārambha*) while indeed denoting them. It is observed that even when a meaning is not being expressed [by a suffix], its own inherent state is illuminated; for example, in the case of *daṇḍākrīḍaḥ*, the suffix *ṇa* is prescribed after the root *krīḍ* (to play) in the sense of "this is his weapon" (*tadasya praharaṇam*). Thus, while not expressing the act of playing, it illuminates the fact that the stick is the weapon used in that play.

Therefore, in the expression *pacati* ("he cooks"), even a word denoting a non-substance (*asattvārtha*) attains the status of a qualifier by establishing a specific quality that is itself uncertain, namely "cooking" (*paci*). In the same way, the word *stoka* ("little") also denotes a property such as "diminution" (*apakarṣa*), which is a mode of action, having entered into the action while being of the nature of a substance; thus, by conforming to the action, it assumes a non-substantial state and functions as a qualifier of the action.
However, a qualifier situated within one verb is neither able to manifest nor denote another verb, because both verbs are primary and independent of one another.

Let it be granted that even for a prefix (*upasarga*) and so forth, which lack a substantial referent (*asatvārtha*), there exists a relationship of qualifier and qualified through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), just as in the case of "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*). However, how could this possibly occur in the case of grammatical non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), where there is a requirement for distinction (*vyatireka*)? For indeed, in the case of a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*)—which is exhausted by the mere acquisition of its own form due to its non-substantiality and does not assist anything else—a distinction from the verbal base (*aṅga*) is not logical. Therefore, even through non-coreferentiality, no relationship of qualifier and qualified arises between two finite verbs.

The relationship of the proven and the means of proof (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) is also not tenable; for that [relationship] would exist only if there were agency or objecthood between two actions, since the *sādhya* (that which is to be accomplished) is indeed the object (*karman*) of the agent (*kartṛ*) by virtue of its being produced through the verbal suffix (*laṭ*). Yet neither of these two [agency nor objecthood] is applicable to one action with respect to another action. For by means of a finite verb (*tiṅanta*), an action whose nature is effort toward its own production is expressed as having its own form already established in its usage through its base (*prakṛti*), even while it requires factors of action (*kāraka*) directed toward that production.

Therefore, because action has not yet attained its own form and is dependent upon the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), it is subsumed by them; thus, since there is no connection with another "action-self," its status as an agent (*kartṛ*) is impossible. For the state of being a means of accomplishment is possible for that which has a fully established form, which is independent of the attainment of selfhood and possesses an already perfected nature, but not for that whose nature is the opposite of what was described.

And this is precisely the nature of action (*kriyā*): namely, that it is understood as having the nature of the object-to-be-accomplished (*sādhya*) by virtue of its dependence upon the means-of-accomplishment (*sādhana*). Now, how could that which has the nature of the object-to-be-accomplished enter into the state of being a means-of-accomplishment with respect to another object-to-be-accomplished, such that it is called the "agent" (*kartṛ*)? And how could that which has the nature of the object-to-be-accomplished by virtue of its dependence upon the means-of-accomplishment be accomplished as an action, such that it is called the "object" (*karman*)? Furthermore, if it were [an entity], it would have to be designated as such like a substance (*dravya*) whose form is fully established (*pariniṣpanna*). Yet, even though it is not so designated, it is nonetheless not a non-means-of-accomplishment.

Furthermore, the property of the means (*sādhanadharma*), which consists of a state and is denoted by the word "operation" (*vyāpāra*), is itself an action (*kriyā*). How could such an action require another property of that same kind for its own establishment? And if they do not require one another, how can a mutual relationship between them be possible? Moreover, there remains nothing of the first action that has not been accomplished by the means which could serve as the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) by a subsequent action. Thus, since their forms are not dependent upon each other, there is simply no connection between these two actions.

Furthermore, an entity that has acquired its own nature through the process of ceasing cannot enter into a relationship with another without a negating factor. For things whose natures are bound by the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary, how could there be a loss of their capacity to benefit if they have already acquired their nature through mutual connection? Moreover, since an action lacks such a form [of mutual dependence], and since it depends upon its own means of accomplishment for its very arising, how could it possibly enter into a relationship with another action that is not of that same nature? Therefore, because it is restricted by its own means of accomplishment, an action possesses a nature that consists solely in being in the process of being accomplished.

In the case of agency (*kartṛtva*), there is no connection with another action. Now, one might object: just as in the expressions "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*) and "cooking occurs" (*pāko vartate*), a relationship of means and end (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) is observed between two actions expressed by a *tiṅ* suffix and a *kṛt* suffix respectively, why does such a relationship not also occur between the two [verbs] *paṭhati* and *pacati*? This is not so; for it has been stated in the *Bhāṣya*: "There is indeed a distinction between an action expressed by a *tiṅ* suffix and an action expressed by a *kṛt* suffix. For an action expressed by a *kṛt* suffix, appearing like a substance (*dravyavat*), [is connected] with an action..."

"It goes to a state of inherence. For it is not the case that, in expressions such as "he cooks" (*pacati*) or "he reads" (*paṭhati*), there can be a relationship of characterized and characteristic (*lakṣya-lakṣaṇa-bhāva*) between two actions denoted by verbal suffixes, even if they share the same instrument (*sādhana*). This is untenable in either way: because the self (*ātman*), which is proceeding as something to be accomplished (*sādhyamāna*) and is devoid of an instrument, lacks the demonstrative quality of "this-ness" (*anidantā*), and thus cannot logically function as a characteristic like an instrument.

But surely, even if there be no accomplishment of an action (*kriyāsādhana*), a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is seen in both ways, as in *pācakaḥ paṭhati* ("the cook recites") and *rudataḥ prāvrājīt* ("he went forth while [someone] was weeping"). Therefore, in the case of the two verbal forms in *yaḥ pacati sa paṭhati* ("whoever cooks, he recites") and *sa roditi ayaṃ pravrajati* ("he weeps, this person goes forth"), there will be a relationship of the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). [Objection: "Live long! You have reminded me. [Response: Because of the lack of connection between two verbal forms by way of being the characterized and the characteristic, the rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.126) is remembered, whereby the suffixes *śatṛ* and *śānac* are prescribed after a verbal root when followed by another finite verb (*tiṅ*) or a word ending in a nominal suffix (*apratyaya*).

Therefore, if one action were to depend upon another action for its definition (*lakṣaṇatva*), then in the case of "He went forth while cooking and weeping," it would have to be expressed as *pacan rudataḥ prāvrājīt*. But surely, [one might object]: "He who cooks, he reads; he weeps, this man goes forth. How, then, can there be a connection? By this, the causal relationship (*hetuhetumadbhāva*) between two finite verbs is refuted, because that relationship also occurs in two ways: either the cause is directed toward the effect, or the effect is directed toward the cause.

In that regard, when a cause (*hetu*) refers to its effect (*hetumat*), it must be expressed by means of the suffixes *śatṛ* or *śānac*, since the effect refers back to its own cause; or it must be expressed by means of the infinitive suffixes (*tumun*) and so forth. For example: *pacan bhuṅkte* (while cooking, he eats), *adhīyamāno vasati* (while studying, he dwells), *bhoktuṃ pacati* (he cooks in order to eat), and *bhojako vrajati* (the eater goes). But [one might object]: in cases such as *pacati*, *bhuṅkte*, and *vrajati*, what is the connection between which [action] and which [agent]? Furthermore, there can be no relation of "limit" (*avadhi*) and "limited" (*avadhimat*) between two verbal forms ending in *tiṅ* suffixes, for such a relation would have to be either spatial or temporal.

It cannot be [simultaneous] in terms of space, because that [space] has as its object only material things; however, it is possible in terms of time. But in that case, since the suffix *ktavatu* is prescribed for a prior time, one would have to say "having cooked, he breaks," (*paktvā bhinatti*), and not "he cooks and breaks" (*pacati bhinatti*) with the two actions connected by conjunction.

That [conjunction] is indeed of two kinds: either in the performance of the means (*sādhana*), as in "Let the cow and the horse be taken," or in the accomplishment of actions (*kriyā*), as in "He cooks and he reads. It is not, however, [the case] of actions being accomplished by means, as in "He cooks and he reads"—for that would be merely the conjunction of actions with an action. Now, since an action is a single entity, even if there is no connection with multiple actions when there is a conjunction of means, nevertheless, this will be a conjunction of actions by virtue of having a single object.

For instance, in the case of "he who cooks is the same as he who reads," a connection is indeed possible because they share a common substratum (*ekādhikaraṇya*). But this is not the case here; for the two things to be accomplished (*sādhya*), which have not yet attained their own nature and are revolving toward the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), are mutually independent in their action. Indeed, a substratum cannot produce a sense of expectation (*apekṣā*) for those whose natures are unconnected. Therefore, like the left and right horns of a cow, the two actions, being entirely unrelated to one another, are merely conjoined with respect to the means of accomplishment.

Furthermore, when things are being conjoined (*samuccīyamāna*), they do not relate to one another; for if that were the case, upon the occurrence of either a collective whole (*samāhāra*) or a mutual connection (*itaretara*), the very notion of conjunction would be absent. By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [it is shown that] *anva* and the like likewise lack connection between two actions. Therefore, there is indeed no mutual relation between two finite verbs (*ākhyāta*). But surely, in such cases as "He exists and it pleases him" (*asti sa bhe rocate*), "You exist and you rule" (*asti tvam īśiṣe*), or "I do not delight in this" (*nāham ramemiṃsmin*), there occurs a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

"pacati" (he cooks), "bhavati" (he is), "pakṣyati" (he will cook), "bhavatyapākṣīt" (he was), "bhavedapi bhavet" (perhaps he might be), and "syādapi syāt" (it might be)—regard these as the agent, as in "the deer runs. In the case of the object, dual and plural forms are illustrated: "iha paśyāmaḥ" (here we see). Regarding the relationship between the goal and the means (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*), examples are given with the sense of the object: "ehi manye rathena yāsyāsi" (come, I think you will go by chariot); "smarasi devadatta kāśmīreṣu vatsyāmastatraudanaṃ bhokṣyāmahe" (do you remember, Devadatta, that we shall dwell in Kashmir and there we shall eat rice?); and "na marṣayāmi yattatra bhavān vṛṣalaṃ yājayet" (I do not tolerate that your honor should cause a low-born man to sacrifice there).

The relationship between the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) occurs through both non-differentiation and differentiation of the means (*sādhana*). For instance, in "He who eats, let him be seized" (*yo bhuṅkte sa gṛhyatām*) and "He who studies, he cooks" (*yo'dhīte sa pacati*), there is non-differentiation of the means; whereas in "He sleeps, this one wakes," "That one rises, this one sets," there is differentiation of the means. Furthermore, in "He runs because he is struck" (*hantīti palāyate*) and "He runs because it rains" (*varṣatīti dhāvati*), there is the relation of cause and effect (*hetu-hetumat*) by virtue of the cause being subordinate to the effect. Likewise, in "He goes because he will speak" (*vakṣyāmīti vrajati*) and "He sits because he will eat" (*bhokṣyate ity āste*), there is the relation of cause and effect by virtue of the cause being subordinate to the cause itself.

In such cases as "he goes as far as he eats," "he studies what he eats," or "having eaten, he goes"—this is indeed *adhīta* (studied/learned); thus, there exists the relationship of limit and that which is limited (*avadhyavadhimadbhāva*). Furthermore, in the case of verbal endings (*tiṅanta*), we observe the following: "Drink the groats, taste the parched grains, eat the rice"—this constitutes a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of actions; and "Boy, beg alms and [bring] a cow"—this is seen as a secondary conjunction (*anvācaya*).

How then can it be said that there is no connection between two verbs? It is not so, for such a connection is established through syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) and other means. For instance, in the following cases, syntactical splits are logically justified: *asti sa sa me rocate* ("He exists; he is pleasing to me"), *asi tvaṃ tvam īśiṣe* ("You exist; you rule"), *asmy aham ahaṃ rame* ("I exist; I rejoice"), *asti yad nacchamo vayam* ("That we do not desire exists"), *bhavatu evaṃ tat* ("Let it be so"), *payasodhayāmayatvam amithyeva asi* ("By milk, [you] become free from disease, indeed not falsely"), and *yan murajito stavaṃ apūpujaḥ* ("Since you have worshipped the hymn of Murajit"). In these instances, syntactical splits are appropriate.

Or rather, particles such as *asti* and so forth, although they are meaningless and resemble verbal forms (*ākhyāta*), are employed like *kam*, *im*, *id*, and others for the sake of completing a sentence; however, they do not undergo the relationship of qualifier and qualified with verbal actions. In expressions such as *bhavati pacati* ("he exists while cooking"), the meaning that is expressed by *pacati*, *pakṣyati*, or *apākṣīt* is precisely the meaning of *asti*. Now, one might object: "In cases such as *pacati*, there is a relationship of means and end (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) between the agent and the action; likewise, it could be *bhavet* or *syāt*. [This is true, but the particle remains distinct.]

Now, it must necessarily be admitted that actions such as "cooking" have the action of "becoming" (*bhavati*) as their agent. For if this [action of becoming] were not present, then [the action of cooking] would be an established entity by virtue of having that as its agent; it would not be expressed by the verbal suffix (*lakāra*). Nor does that which already exists attain the state of being established [merely by existing]. Furthermore, without the expression of that [action of becoming] as something established by the verbal suffix, the suffix is not capable of conveying this [action of cooking] through its status as an agent.

Consequently, the agent would not be identical to that by which the action is performed, nor would the action be identical to that by which it is accomplished as the object; thus, it would follow that the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) expresses a distinct entity as the agent. Furthermore, in the case of "Devadatta cooks," Devadatta is made known through this [suffix] just like the action itself, because he is the one who performs the act of cooking; however, in the case of "existence occurs" (*bhavati*), existence is presented in an unknown form, because it is the experiencer of the act of coming into being.

Furthermore, it is not logical for the same substratum to simultaneously possess both the state of being a knower and the state of being an unknown; therefore, it does not attain the status of being both the action and the agent. As for the expression "Look, the deer runs," the word *paśya* is not a finite verb ending in *-ti*. What then? It is a particle (*nipāta*) used in the sense of "this is wonderful"; its meaning is "Look [at this] while eating. Some consider the words *paśya* and *paśyata*, which resemble verbal forms, to mean "this action is not fit to be seen. Alternatively, in the phrase "Look, the deer runs," it means: "Do not direct that very act of seeing toward the running of the deer."

What then? [The meaning is: "Fix your eye; do not be heedless. When someone whose eye is not fixed upon a present object pursues a deer or something else, or having seen one form, says "Look! Look!"—therefore, even by saying "look," he determines that much. Since the act of seeing is already completed, there is no connection between the act of seeing and the pursuit. Thus, when the object is identified by the name of the pursuit as "the deer that is running, look at it," then the action (the verb) functions merely as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for that object.

When one who runs perceives the runner, this meaning—that "see, he runs"—is understood through *śrutārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is heard) due to the lack of syntactic connection between the two words; it is not, however, contained within the verbal form itself. Alternatively, we observe that the very meaning of the sentence "the deer is running," which is concluded by the particle *iti* and is understood precisely through *śrutārthāpatti*, serves as the object of the act of seeing (*dṛśi*). Thus, these are cited as examples.

Now, these are two sentences; we see here one sentence ending with *akarma* (intransitive), and a second beginning with *yasmāt* (since). Regarding the example *ehi manye rathena yāsyasi*, according to the rule "In jest, when *manya-* is the attendant word, the third person singular is used for *manya-*" (*prahāse ca manyopapade manyateruttama ekavacca*), the meaning is either: "Come, I think you will go by chariot," or alternatively: "Come, I think I shall go by chariot."

Alternatively, if one adopts the position that the prohibition [of the suffix] applies to the *sūtra* itself, then "middle" (*madhya*) and "highest" (*uttama*) refer to their own respective domains; in that case, the external object alone—conveyed by the words *gamyā* and *anehi*—functions as the grammatical object (*karman*). Furthermore, *ehi* is a particle (*nipāta*) in the form of a verb (*ākhyāta-svarūpa*) used for the purpose of addressing someone in a playful manner. And particles in the form of verbs deviate from [the rules governing] person (*puruṣa*) and number (*saṃkhyā*); for it is not the case that one says *tvam asti* or *vyam asti*. Moreover, even the verb *asti* is a particle, as in the example *astikṣīrā gauḥ* ("a cow whose milk is available").

For it has been stated there, under the heading of *sub*-affixes, that "the mention of *astikṣīrā* and so forth is made because [the word] is a verb (*ākhyāta*)," and the resolution is that this particle (*nipāta*) does not possess the nature of an indeclinable (*avyaya*). Now, one might object: "If he is mocking the number, how can the word *eka* express plurality when mocking many? It is not so; it is many people who mock one, not one person who mocks many. For when many are mocking one, under the view that the rule prohibits [the suffix], [the example is]: "Come, I think I shall go by chariot."

Or rather, even in the view that [the particle] *vā* functions as a prohibition of the verbal suffix (*sūtrapratiṣedhapakṣe*), how could it be that the entity which exists does not undergo the relationship between the probandum, the means of proof, and the proof itself? In the sentence "Let him who eats be apprehended," there too there are indeed two distinct statements. Nor is there here a relationship of indicator and indicated (*lakṣyalakṣaṇabhāva*) between two actions, because an action serves merely to indicate its factors (*kāraka*). In the case of "He who eats is Devadatta," the existence of Devadatta is the indicator; this is one sentence-meaning. "Let him who is thus constituted be apprehended" expresses his connection with apprehension; this is the second [sentence-meaning], namely, the act of seeing.

Nor can it be said that, because one remembers [the agent] as denoting its form according to its actual existence, the primacy of the agent—while being expressed—expresses the action's status as a qualifier (*lakṣaṇa*) with respect to another action; for the nominal suffix (*kṛt-pratyaya*) is not capable of expressing that. Rather, since that action is displaced from its state of being something to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and is brought into a subordinate position as a means (*sādhana*), it serves to characterize Devadatta who is grasped by it; and he, being thus characterized, is connected with another action.

For it is not possible for a single activity to both indicate its own means and be connected with another action. Now, one might argue that this very indication of another’s means is precisely what constitutes its connection with that other action. This is not so; for while this activity proceeds by indicating its own means, it can only indicate that upon which its own arising depends, and not anything else merely through a connection with it.

But surely, Devadatta himself is the means (*sādhana*) for this [action], and he is characterized (*upalakṣita*) by her; so how can there be a difference in sentences? It is not so. While it is true that Devadatta serves as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇatva*) for her, he does not characterize her as "Devadatta," but rather as his own means (*svasādhana*). Therefore, while Devadatta is indeed the accomplisher of his own [action], his primary resting point is elsewhere at first; and Devadatta’s connection with her must also be understood through that very [action].

For it is not possible for [the same object] to simultaneously attain the status of being characterized (*lakṣyamāṇatva*) and primary (*prādhānya*), while also maintaining a subordinate status (*guṇabhāva*) toward another action, as that would lead to a contradiction. Nor is the connection of the [object] delimited by the act of eating with other actions intended, because that would result in two simultaneous actions being enjoined. Since the activity proceeds with a single flavor—namely, "let him who eats be grasped"—due to proximity, the sacrifice (*satra*) is distinct from that alone; however, since its purpose is precisely of such a nature, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in that case.

By this, the statement "he who studies cooks" is also refuted. Furthermore, in cases such as "he sleeps, this one wakes," or "that one rises, this one sets," there is all the less a relationship of indicator and indicated (*lakṣya-lakṣaṇa-bhāva*) because they function as means (*sādhana*). In the case of "he runs because he strikes," however, the word "because" (*iti*), by indicating a causal relationship (*hetu-hetumat-bhāva*), establishes the independence (*svātantrya*) of the agent.

The word *dṛṣṭam* (seen) generates the independence of the referent; for in the rule *“tasminniti nirdiṣṭe pūrvasya”* (when that which is designated by ‘in this’ [is mentioned], [an operation applies] to what precedes it), the word *tasmin* refers to a locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Since it functions as a qualifying condition (*upādhi*) with respect to actions inherent in the agent or the object, there arises an expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) for that in which the action resides. Because there would otherwise be no establishment of its own nature within that [locus], if there were no delimitation (*avaccheda*) provided by the word, there could be no connection with the grammatical effect (*kārya*).

When it is stated, "when that [word] is specified," and "of the preceding," there would be the understanding that [the rule applies] to that which was specified as the thing to be placed [in the preceding]. Therefore, when there is a specification of the locative sense (*saptamyartha*), the word *eva* is employed for the sake of ensuring the understanding of the preceding operation; so it is here as well. Furthermore, the word *vā* does not produce independence for that [preceding element], as in the case of "because this man kills, therefore this man flees. The same should be applied to examples such as *varṣati* ("it rains") and so on; and in this context, the phrase "of the two finite verbs" (*tiṅantayoḥ*) [is used].

The relationship of cause and effect is inferred from the power of the words themselves, and not as something inherent in the arrangement of the words. Furthermore, in cases such as "he goes as far as that" (*yāvad bhaktas tato vrajati*), even though there is a difference in sentence structure, the relationship between the limit and that which is limited is understood through the power of the particles *yāvat* and *tataḥ* (meaning "prior to that"), and not as something inherent in the arrangement of the verbal forms.

Even in cases such as "saktūn piba" (drink the barley-meal), the specific meanings of the qualifying clauses—namely, "drink the barley-meal," "eat the parched grains," and "eat the cooked rice"—are concluded by the word *iti*. It is solely through the power of that word *iti* that these [specifics] are expressed by the subsequent sentence, "this person is consuming," which denotes them in their general sense. Similarly, "pacati cāyaṃ paṭhati ca" (he cooks and he reads) consists of two distinct sentences; likewise, "bhikṣāmaṭa, gāṃ cānaya" (go for alms and bring the cow).

Thus, according to the opinion of Kātyāyana, there is no such connection between two finite verbs; however, in the opinion of the author of the Sūtras, there is indeed a connection between two finite verbs by virtue of their constituting multiple sentences. This is because he prescribes the *nighāta* (elision of accent) for a finite verb following another finite verb within the scope of the rule governing "a single sentence" (*samānavākya*).

Regarding the statement on the *abhijñā* (cognition of past events), [Pāṇini] prescribes the *lṛṭ* (future tense) even for the past time when used with words expressing memory or narration, as in "he remembers that... (*yat*); yet, by the rule "optionally when there is expectancy" (*vibhāṣā sākāṅkṣe*), he permits it optionally when there is such expectancy. Furthermore, by the rule "not with *na*, *yat*, or when there is no expectancy" (*nayadyanākāṅkṣye*), he prohibits the suffixes *ktvā* and *ṇamul* in a sentence lacking expectancy and allows only the *laṭ* (present tense) and others. What, then, is the justification for this? It is said in reply: for the form ending in *ktvā*, which shares the same grammatical properties as a finite verb (*ākhyāta*), is observed to have a connection with multiple finite verbs (*tiṅanta*) as well.

"Having bathed, having drunk, having begged, he goes"—thus, first he bathes, eats, drinks, and then goes. In that regard, just as there is syntactic unity (*ekavākyatva*) between a word ending in the suffix *ktvā* and one ending in the personal endings (*tib*), so too it occurs for all finite verbs (*ākhyāta*) expressing prior actions, because they function as adverbs (*kriyāviśeṣaṇaka*) to the main action. And it has been said: "Just as even multiple words ending in *ktvā* are qualifiers of a word ending in *tiṅ*, so too they say that a word ending in *tiṅ* is a qualifier of another word ending in *tiṅ*."

The fourth [section] is the illumination of the fourfold objects, beginning with action (*kriyā*). In that regard, there are twelve divisions, which consist of the meanings of roots and so forth as expressed by words, and which function as the meanings of verbal suffixes, the primary meanings of nominal stems, and the meanings of words and sentences—namely: action, time, case-role (*kāraka*), substance, attribute, embellishment, the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika-artha*), the meaning of the suffix (*vṛtti-artha*), the meaning of the word (*pada-artha*), and the meaning of the sentence (*vākya-artha*). Among these, action is the specific manifestation of the activity of the case-roles; the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is what the grammarians designate as that [action]. And verbal roots are of three kinds: those whose meaning is "to be" (*astyartha*), those whose meaning is "to become" (*bhavatyartha*), and those whose meaning is "to do" (*karotyartha*).

In this regard, those [roots] whose agent remains indifferent are "those having the sense of 'is'" (*astyarthāḥ*), such as *asti*, *vidyate*, *dhriyate*, *tiṣṭhati*, *āste*, *vartate*, and so forth. Those whose agent undergoes transformation are "those having the sense of 'becoming'" (*bhavatyarthāḥ*), such as *bhavati*, *saṃjāyate*, *vardhate*, *dhriyate*, *tiṣṭhati*, *āste*, *vartate*, and so forth. Those whose agent exerts effort are "those having the sense of 'doing'" (*karotyarthāḥ*), such as *karoti*, *vidhatte*, *janayati*, *nirvartayati*, *sādhayati*, *utpādayati*, and so forth.

In that regard, because the roots *asti*, *karoti*, and *bhavati* abide in a state of equilibrium, they call it the "Sound-Brahman" (*śabdabrahman*), which is changeless and without beginning or end. Likewise, they designate the root *bhavati* alone as "Om," since it expresses many such meanings. When its first modification—caused by ignorance (*avidyā*), yet not consisting of a transformation of its own nature—arises in the form of "existence" (*asti*), then, because "existence" is the counter-correlative of "non-existence" (*nāsti*), this single reality manifests itself in both ways as "it exists."

When there is the expectation that "that which does not exist comes into being," then from the state of its becoming, its name arises; this is called the second transformation, which fluctuates. Then, regarding each thing that comes into being, because of a false attachment (*mithyābhiniveśa*) to one thing arising from another, he imagines a relationship of mutual agent and object; this is designated as performing the third transformation.

And thus, when ignorance—which has spread far through egoism, desire, and attachment—is driven far away by these [means], then knowledge (*vidyā*) arises; from it, the verbal roots *vid*, *jan*, *pac*, and so forth, manifest. Regarding this, it is said: "The roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* express action in general, while *pac* and others express specific actions. All these various meanings of verbal roots intermingle and exceed one another in their mutual connection, yet they do not transcend the nature of *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as*.

But surely, the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is action (*kriyā*), and that is a specific kind of activity of the factors of action (*kāraka*). Among the factors of action, the independent one is the agent (*kartṛ*); that which is most desired by the agent is the object (*karman*); that which is the most effective means is the instrument (*karaṇa*); the locus is the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*); that which one intends through the object is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*); that which remains fixed when there is a separation is the point of departure (*apādāna*); and anything other than these, or that which is not intended to be expressed as such, is the residual relation (*śeṣa*). Furthermore, the instigator of the agent is the cause (*hetu*). Thus, no distinct entity separate from the agent and the other factors is perceived that could be recognized as "action."

It is said: action exists, but it cannot be described as separate from the agent and so forth, because its state of being has not yet been attained. Just as a blade of *darbha* grass that has not yet emerged cannot be described as distinct from its source while in the state of a *kalala* (embryonic stage), even though it is not yet manifest; so too, action cannot be described as distinct from the instruments of accomplishment while it remains in the state of being accomplished. For example: "the light shines" (*jyotir prakāśate*) or "the sound resounds" (*śabdo dhvanati*).

How, then, is it known that [the action] exists? Even when the factors of action (kāraka) are present, one observes the presence or absence of the verbal expression "he cooks" (pacati). Indeed, in this world, when the presence or absence of one thing depends on the presence or absence of another, it is observed that the former requires a cause other than that [latter].

Just as in the case of the conjunction of fire and a pot, the qualities produced by cooking (*pākaja*) depend upon that conjunction—whether it exists or not—and since the agent and so forth exist when there is conjunction, it is observed that sometimes [the action] occurs and sometimes one sees "he does not cook"; therefore we consider that there must certainly be a power (*śakti*), a property distinct from the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), by whose presence these two—the manifestation and the non-manifestation—proceed, and by whose absence they would not proceed. Thus, the existence of action (*kriyā*) is established.

For this reason as well, a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is untenable without that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) through the act of existence (*astikriyā*). That which is to be accomplished is the action (*kriyā*). As it has been said: "The single object that is brought into being by the factors of action (*kāraka*) when they are combined—that is action."

A *kāraka* is that which is the cause of an action (*kriyā*). Thus, he who employs the *kārakas* and so forth in actions according to his own will, and is not employed by them, is the agent (*kartṛ*). That which is obtained by the agent through an action other than [his own] is the object (*karman*). That which functions as the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for the accomplishment of an action, being immediate [to it], is the instrument (*karaṇa*). The locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is the substratum of the action that is separated from the agent or the object. That which, being determined as an effect of the action, experiences contact with the object is the recipient (*saṃpradāna*).

That which, by means of an action or through its very arising as an action, remains fixed while undergoing separation is the *apādāna* (ablative). This is a specific type of relation between factors (*kāraka*)—whether they are expressed as such by a verbal root or not—which is brought about by an action that is either explicitly heard or implied. That which, by giving commands and so forth, directs one who is already acting toward an action is the *hetu* (causal agent), and it is also considered a *kartṛ* (agent).

And thus, just as wood and other materials experience their mutual fitness for connection only by depending upon lac and so forth, in that same way, neither conjunction nor disjunction would occur. As it has been said: "Insofar as Devadatta, having been here, comes to be in Pāṭaliputra, that is surely action. Let it be called action; however, how can there be a distinction between that [action] and the factors of action (*kāraka*)? Nor do you yourselves fail to acknowledge a distinction between action and the factors of action.

For example, one says, "the thief is ill" (*corasya rujati*) or "the thief is afflicted" (*corasyāmayati*). It is said that the action (*kriyā*) is indeed distinct from the factors of action (*kāraka*s), because it is the cause for the designation of many as one. Here, whatever is the cause for the designation of many is other than them; just as the universal (*jāti*) is other than the individual (*vyakti*), so too is the action the cause for the designation of many—such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and so forth—as "the factor of action" (*kāraka*). Therefore, it is understood to be other than those [factors], because it is what is followed through [them].

In this world, that which is approached and followed by certain things is other than those things; for example, a king is approached and followed by men. Therefore, [the effect] must be led away from its causes and conditions, because it is perceived as something produced. Whatever is perceived as being produced from something else is other than that thing.

Just as a son is perceived as distinct from his father by virtue of being produced through the action of an agent, so too [the sun] is other than that [the earth], because it is not perceived when that [earth] is perceived; for in this world, when one thing is not perceived while another is, the former is other than the latter—just as taste is other than color, and the perception of the sun's upward motion is other than [the perception of the earth]. And this [motion] exists in it due to its reaching another location, and that too is observed, since it is seen upon returning from the western ocean. This is because it is apprehensible by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

In this context, whatever is apprehended by a means of valid cognition other than [the one under discussion] is distinct from that; for example, the self is distinct from the body. Furthermore, motion is apprehended by another means of valid cognition when it pertains to eternal entities (sadāgati); therefore, it is distinct from them. Because it is designated as being distinct from many, whatever is designated here as a unity while being distinct from many is distinct from those; for example, a cloth is distinct from its threads. Motion, although it rests upon many [entities], is designated as a unity through its distinction [from them]; for example, "the Brahmins are sitting. Therefore, it is distinct from them.

Because there is a recurrence [of the term] despite the absence of a [literal] recurrence: in this case, when something does not recur, that which recurs must be different from it—just as the genus (*jāti*) is distinct from the individual elephant, or as the action (*kriyā*) is the cause for the singular designation of multiple factors such as the agent (*kartṛ*). Therefore, because it is understood as being distinct from them, that which is followed by certain things here is different from those things; just as a king is approached and followed by men, so too is action different from the factors of action (*kāraka*), since it is perceived as having the nature of an object of cognition (*jñeya*).

That which is perceived as being produced from something else is distinct from that thing. For example, a son is perceived as being produced from a father by way of the production of an action; therefore, he is perceived as distinct from him, because he is not perceived when [the father] is not perceived. In this case, when one thing is not perceived while another is perceived, the former is distinct from the latter. Taste is distinct from color, and motion is distinct from the sun, because it is perceived even when the sun is not perceived. Furthermore, this [motion] exists as the reaching of a different location; it is likewise seen when one who did not see [the object] turns back and sees it again.

Because it is perceivable by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). In this context, whatever is perceived by a different means of valid cognition from something else is distinct from that thing, just as the self (*ātman*) is distinct from the body. Furthermore, motion (*gati*) in the case of the wind (*sadāgati*) is perceivable by another means of valid cognition; therefore, it is distinct from that [wind]. Because it is designated as being distinct from many: in this context, whatever is designated as a unity while being distinct from many things is distinct from them, just as a cloth is distinct from its threads.

It is stated that even though an action (*kriyā*) depends upon many factors, it is designated as a single unit through its isolation (*praviveka*), just as when one says "the Brāhmaṇas are sitting. Therefore, [the action] is distinct from those [factors]. Because of non-return in the case of returning: here, when something does not return, that which returns is distinct from it, just as a mosquito is distinct from an elephant. And an action returns even while the agent who does not return remains constant—as in the expression "he cooks five times"—therefore, it is distinct from him. Furthermore, because both are the causes for doubt and certainty: here, when there is doubt regarding both, that which is the cause of certainty for a person—such as the action of moving—is therefore distinct from that [doubt].

Because it is expressed after having been expressed: here, when something is expressed that is intended as a different meaning without [intending] another referent, it is distinct from that; for example, "cow" and "horse. And since the agent (kāraka) is expressed—such as "the student studies" (*adhīte*) or "the goer goes" (*gacchati*)—and then the action is expressed, therefore the action is distinct from that agent, because no synonymy is established between them. For in this world, those things for which synonymy is established are not distinct from one another, as in the case of "potter" (*nirvartī*).

Furthermore, "he cooks while he studies" (*pacann adhīte*) and "he studies while cooking" (*pacaty adhīte*) do not imply that the words *pacan* and *pacati* are synonyms. Rather, in the expression "he studies while cooking," the agent (*kartṛ*) is designated by *pacan*, whereas in *pacati*, the action (*kriyā*) is designated; thus, they are distinct. Even when expressed by non-different words, there is a distinction between them due to the difference in gender and number.

In this world, although the action (*kriyā*) and the agent (*kartṛ*) are denoted by non-different words, a difference in gender and number is observed among their qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), as in: *śobhanaṃ pacati* (he cooks well), *śobhanaṃ pacataḥ* (the two cook well), *śobhanaṃ pacanti* (they cook well). Such a difference in gender and number is seen only when there is a difference in the referent (*artha*) and the word used is distinct; for example: *taṭaḥ*, *taṭī*, *taṭam*; *puṣyaḥ*, *tārakā*, *nakṣatram*; *rasaḥ*, *apaḥ*, *jalam*; *dārāḥ*, *kalatram*, *bhāryā*. However, this is not the case with examples similar to those cited [where the action and agent are identical]; thus, the action is other than the agent.

Because there is a difference in cognition due to the difference in the recurrence of words. Indeed, a difference in cognition is observed in the recurrence of words for both action (*kriyā*) and its factors (*kāraka*): "the student reads, reads," and "the goer goes, goes. In the former pair, there is repetition (*vīpsā*), while in the latter, there is frequency (*ābhīkṣṇya*). And that which has a difference in cognition from something else is distinct from it, just as the sound of a cloud is distinct from clay and a pot, and cloth and so forth are distinct from pots and so forth; thus, action is distinct from its factors.

Once this [non-difference] is established, it should be understood that the perception of difference and the exclusion of non-difference arise solely from a lack of discrimination (*aviveka*); and indeed, such is observed. A contrary current—the nature of sound (*śabda-śarīra*)—proceeds as a uniform cognition (*abhinnapratyaya*) with respect to things differentiated by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), knowledge (*jñāna*), pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*duḥkha*), desire (*icchā*), aversion (*dveṣa*), effort (*prayatna*), color-form (*rūpa*), and so forth; and there is a corresponding designation for them precisely as non-different. However, in the case of "the thief's pain" (*corasya rujati*), because the agent (*kratu*) who effects the pain is absent, the *lakāra* suffix, though residing in the agent, functions [there] as "it pains him" (*rujāti*).

This is its meaning: [the example] "pain arises for the thief" (*caurasya rug utpadyate*) has been cited. But what, then, is this distinction between the *kāraka* (participant) and the action (*kriyā*), such that in one case there is *vīpsā* (repetition/distribution) and in the other *abhīkṣṇam* (frequency)? For *vīpsā* is not perceived through the oneness of an action; rather, *vīpsā* is the speaker’s desire to simultaneously pervade many actions by means of qualities (*guṇa*) or substances (*dravya*). That [desire], however, is not possible when the action is a single unity. But surely, the oneness of an action is not tenable, because it is designated as being simultaneously connected with the three times, which are absolutely contradictory?

In this world, indeed, an expression based on the connection with all three times is observed for action at any given time, as in: "Devadatta cooks," "Yajñadatta cooked," and "Viṣṇumitra will cook. And since that [connection with three times] is not possible if there were only one single action, there must be multiple actions, based on their differentiation; for they are joined with comparative suffixes such as *tara* and *tam*. Indeed, here the comparative suffixes are seen applied to action, as in "he cooks better" (*pacatitarām*) and "he cooks best" (*pacatitamām*).

And since that [distinction] is established as occurring in the excellence of two or many, there is a plurality of actions because a single agent simultaneously distinguishes multiple substrates. Here, when that which resides in multiple loci at a single time is determined as distinct, it is "multiple," just as nails are distinguished among fingers. And since movement is simultaneously determined by one who has multiple substrates, there is a plurality of actions; for this is observed even in the case of past time.

In this context, the suffix *ktvā* is observed after two actions performed by a single agent when one occurs at a prior time, as in "having eaten, he eats" (*bhuktvā bhuṅkte*) or "having cooked, he cooks" (*paktvā pacati*). Furthermore, duality is the opposite of unity; thus, there are multiple actions because of the simultaneous connection of the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Here, a connection between the characterized and the characteristic is seen among actions that do not occur at different times. For instance, even while the cow is being milked (*duhyamānāyām*), one says "he milks" (*dogdhi*); since this would be untenable if there were only a single action, there must be multiple actions, given that the suffix is observed even for the earlier [action].

In this world, the suffix *ktvā* is observed after two actions performed by the same agent when they occur in a prior time, as in "having eaten, he eats" (*bhuktvā bhuṅkte*) or "having cooked, he cooks" (*paktvā pacati*), because there is no absence of a causal relationship between the cause and the result. Indeed, here the distinction between cause and effect is well-established. And that [distinction] is seen in actions, such as "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*), "he cooks vegetables" (*śākaṃ pacati*), and "eating, he eats rice" (*bhuñjāna odanaṃ bhuṅkte*). Furthermore, since the Veda prescribes unity [of action], multiple actions arise through the production of suffixes such as *tumun* and others, which have another action as their purpose (*kriyārtha-kriyā-upapada*).

In this context, those suffixes such as *tumun* which are prescribed when a word denoting an action is the object of another action—such as in "he goes to eat" (*bhoktuṃ gacchati*), "he goes for cooking" (*pākāya vrajati*), or "he cooks [thinking] 'I shall eat'" (*bhokṣyāmi iti pacati*)—are observed even though they are expressed by different verbal roots. For example: "he goes to go" (*gantuṃ gacchati*), "he eats for the sake of eating" (*bhojanāya bhuṅkte*), or "he cooks [thinking] 'I shall cook'" (*pakṣyāmīti pacati*). And this [usage] is possible only if there is oneness through the state of having that [subsequent action] as its fruit; for it is based on the manifestation of the power [of the action], whether that power is already expressed or not, through various actions.

In this world, we observe the appearance of case endings and verbal suffixes in such instances as: *dhātrīṃ dhayati* (he sucks the nurse), *dātreṇa dāti* (he cuts with a sickle), *dāśāya dāśate* (he gives to the servant), *bhīmād bibheti* (he fears Bhīma), *āsate āste* (they sit), *śayane śete* (he lies on the bed), *sthāne tiṣṭhati* (he stands in his place), and *prāsāde prasīdati* (he is pleased in the palace). From this observation of suffixes and case endings, we perceive the manifestation of powers that are both expressed and unexpressed. Since this multiplicity cannot be accounted for without a diversity of actions, there must be multiple actions even when a single entity is denoted; thus, dual and plural endings are observed even from words like *yantra* (machine) and others.

Indeed, even when the action (*bhāva*) is singular, we observe dual and plural endings in such cases as *yantrādibhyaḥ pākau pākāḥ* ("from the machines, two or many cookings"), *uṣṭrāsikā āsyante* ("the camel-sittings are being sat"), and *hataśāyikāḥ śayyante* ("the dead-lying-downs are being lain"). This would not be logical if the action were one; therefore, there must be multiple actions denoted by the primary suffix (*kṛt*) or the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). Alternatively, if the action denoted by the primary or verbal suffix were one, then the observation of all numbers through the plural ending would be consistent with that unity of action, because of its coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with all the numbers.

In this context, it is observed that both action expressed by a *kṛt* suffix and action expressed by a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) exhibit grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words denoting number, even though these words express distinct meanings. For example: *ekaḥ pākaḥ* (one cooking), *dvau pākau* (two cookings), *bahavaḥ pākāḥ* (many cookings); likewise, *ekā uṣṭrāsikā āsyate* (a single camel-sitting posture is assumed), *dve āsyete* (two are assumed), *bahvya āsyante* (many are assumed).

And since that [simultaneity] is not possible if the action were a single unity, there must be multiple actions here, because the accomplishment of the effects—such as the cutting of wood and so forth—depends upon distinct movements of the axe and other instruments. In this regard, there is no dispute concerning the multiplicity of those actions which possess distinctness due to the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the meanings of the verbal roots (*dhātu*) that delimit them; and among these, there are well-known properties (*dharma*) based on their distinctions.

For example: *bhoktum icchati* (he wishes to eat), *bhavati* (he is), *pacati* (he cooks), *bhavati* (he will cook), *bhavaty apākṣīt* (he has cooked), and "I invite the assembly, I invite to the festival"—these are seen even in cases expressed by the same verbal root (*samāna-dhātu*). Also: *eṣitum icchati* (he wishes to seek), *bhaved api bhavet* (let it be, let it be), *syād api syāt* (let it be, let it be), and "I invite for the purpose of inviting, I address for the purpose of addressing. Therefore, there must be a relationship with the grammatical operation based on the distinction [between the roots].

Multiplicity [of action] arises through differentiation everywhere by means of manifold elements; thus, action is manifold because of the relationship between the goal (sādhya) and the means (sādhana). Here, a well-known distinction between the goal and the means is observed. The state of being goal and means regarding actions is seen, for example, in "He nourished these people" (*sa imān poṣānapuṣat*) and "The ascetic performs penance" (*tapyate tapas tāpasaḥ*). And since that [relationship] is not possible if there were oneness, action is manifold.

Thus, if action were manifold, all this would be untenable; for if it were one, its diversity could be accounted for solely through the diversity of its instruments. Furthermore, even for things that are not distinct, we observe the designation of different locations based on differences in their substrata and the perception of them as having different forms.

Just as there is moonlight in the waters, a mass of moonlight in the clouds, the quarters of the sky in their fixed positions, distinctness in objects, and the flash of lightning in the clouds; and just as there is ripened barley among barley, the Śuka tree among Turuṣkas, the ruined Surāda among Īṣṭras, the beautiful breast of Indrasenā, eyes in Kaliṅga, you were clever [among the clever], this well on the path was more clever [than others], the well will be [there], "Your honor is dear to us, but we are not dear," Maithilī is the wife of Rāma—Ah! (Note: This passage consists of a series of examples illustrating various types of *vṛtti* (grammatical compounds) and *samāsa* (compounds), including those where the case endings are elided or retained, and where the relationship between members is expressed through specific syntactic markers.)

Just as there is a designation based on differentiation for distinct objects of meaning—such as "the sacred city of Varaṇā," "Śirūṣāḥ," "Rāma," or "the Pañcāla regions"—even though [the action] is not different from the genus (*jāti*) and so forth, so too will there be distinctions such as the connection with time for an action due to the difference in its means (*sādhana*). Furthermore, the simultaneous apprehension by a single word of an action inhering in multiple substrata is possible, just like a genus (*jāti*). However, in the case of pure actions denoted by *kṛt*-suffixes, the imposition of their properties [onto the action] is improper, because they lack the distinction between identity and difference that exists in the case of actions expressed by finite verbs (*ākhyāta*) which behave like substances.

For a state of being (bhāva) expressed by a *kṛt* suffix, appearing as if it were a substance (*dravya*), becomes the locus for the powers of gender, number, object, and so forth; however, this is not the case for those expressed by a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). This is because it is impossible for that [verbal action] to be a locus, since it is not yet fully accomplished (*pariniṣpanna*) at that time. To illustrate: just as in the cases "cooking occurs" (*pāko vartate*) and "he cooks" (*pacati*), the connection with powers, number, and so on is observed in words ending in *kṛt* suffixes, but never in those ending in *tiṅ* suffixes.

It is not the case that [the following] do not occur: *bhavati*, *pacati*, *vartate*, *pacati paśyati*. But surely they do occur: *paśyati*, *mṛgo dhāvati*, and "I clearly see" (*utpaśyāmi*). Since dual and plural forms are cited for the object (*karman*), the running deer (*dhāvat*) is indeed the object of the act of seeing (*dṛś*); however, because it is not a nominal stem (*prātipadika*), there is no production of case endings (*sup*). That is not so; for just as an action is seen to exist by virtue of being performed—such as *pacati*, *pakṣyati*, *bhavati*, and *apākṣīt*—so too does it exist naturally.

In cases such as *pacati* ("he cooks"), the agency (*kartṛtva*) belongs to the root *bhū* (to become); it is observed that [the agent] "becomes" while "seeing. In cases such as *paśyati* ("he sees"), the objecthood (*karmatva*) is observed; it is understood through the sequence of adverbial qualifiers that [the agent] "becomes" while "seeing. Therefore, because it is in the very process of arising, the agency in the act of going is likewise inherent. In examples such as *mṛgo dhāvati* ("the deer runs"), the objecthood belongs to the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) as conveyed by the implied word *iti*, not to the verbal action (*kriyā*) itself.

Therefore, since it is not to be doubted that the action possesses the capacity for both agent and object, and given the presence or absence of the connection with instruments and so forth, the mutual difference between the state denoted by a *kṛt*-suffix and that denoted by a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is indeed manifest. Consequently, because there is no intention to express a distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) regarding multiple objects, the unity of the action is established.

And because of the non-difference between the word and the cognition: where there is absolute non-difference between the denotation and the knowledge [of it], its unity is established, as in the case of a genus or of individual particulars taken one by one; and space and time are seen to be non-distinct even when there is a difference in action, as in the cases "he cooks" (*pacati*) and "they cook" (*pacanti*). Therefore, action is a single entity which is the cause of both the word and the cognition.

But surely, regarding the examples such as the moon in water, there is doubt concerning the usage of difference: are the grammatical suffixes and designations—such as the connection with the three times of action—which are effects of difference, based on non-difference as their cause, or rather are they based on that very difference? To this it is replied: even though there is no difference in the action itself, doubt must be entertained because dual and plural suffixes arise due to the difference in the means (the substrates).

In this context, since differentiation is preceded by non-differentiation, one who accepts differentiation must necessarily accept non-differentiation as well. It is observed that for an action whose unity is accepted, there occurs the application of dual and plural endings based on the plurality of its instruments (*sādhana*). For example: *paramāṇuṃ pacati* (he cooks a single atom), *paramāṇuṃ pacanti* (they cook many atoms). Conversely, when plurality is accepted, if the instrument is non-differentiated, only the singular ending is observed; thus, there is a change in verbal expression, as in *bhinatti kusūlam* (he splits the granary).

Therefore, because action conforms to the diversity of its instruments (*sādhana*), and because the instruments conform to the diversity of the action, the differentiating effects reside in the instruments which serve as the substratum of the action, and not in the action itself with respect to its own substratum. How then is it that there is a difference in verbal number (*vacanabheda*) due to a difference in the agent (*kartṛbheda*), as in "two pots are being cooked" (*pacyete odanau*) or "the rice-porridges are being cooked" (*pacyante odanāḥ*) by Devadatta? [The answer is: those verbal suffixes (*lādi*) which denote the instrument—do they not conform to its diversity? It should not be doubted that the actions conform to the diversity of the instruments, or that the instruments conform to the diversity of the action.

Since difference and non-difference are not absolute in cases such as "pratīpa" and the like, there is no deviation [from the rule] even when cognition and designation are likewise [non-absolute]. Furthermore, because there is a repetition of multiple actions, the suffixes *kṛtvasuc* and *ādac* are prescribed by tradition for counting the repetition of many actions, as in "he eats five times" (*pañcakṛtvo bhuṅkte*) or "he drinks four times" (*catuṣpacati*); and this is only possible where there is non-difference. Indeed, when Devadatta has gone and Yajñadatta has arrived, one does not observe the designation "it has returned" (*punarāvṛta*).

In that very case, the statement "he has come" constitutes a single action because there is no accumulation (*samuccaya*) of actions. Here, an accumulation is observed when distinct things converge upon a single object, as in: "Devadatta’s cow, horse, and man," or "the cow belonging to Devadatta, Yajñadatta, and Viṣṇumitra.
