The relationship of connection (*saṃbandha*) and non-connection (*asaṃbandha*) occurs as follows: *pacati* (he cooks), *pakṣyati* (he will cook), *apākṣīt* (he cooked), *bhavate* (it becomes), and *syāt* (it may be). The instigator (*prayojaka*) is of five types: the instigator of the object (*karma*), the instigator of the agent (*kartṛ*), the instigator of the cause (*hetu*), the instigator of that which is not a cause (*ahetu*), and the instigator of both cause and non-cause (*hetvāhetu*). Among these, the instigator of the object is illustrated as follows: *gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ* (he milks milk from the cow), *pauravaṃ gāṃ yācate* (he begs a cow from the Paurava), *gargāñchataṃ daṇḍayati* (he fines the Gargas a hundred [pieces]), and *kāśān kaṭaṃ karoti* (he makes a mat from *kāśa* grass).

The instigator of the agent (*kartṛprayojaka*) is as follows: *yajñadattaḥ pācayati* (Yajñadatta causes [someone] to cook), *māṭharaḥ pāṭhayati* (Māṭhara causes [someone] to teach), *bhikṣā vāsayati* (the alms cause [someone] to dwell), *kārīṣo'gniḥ adhyāpayati* (a fire of dried cow-dung causes [someone] to study). The instigator of both the object and the agent (*karmakartṛprayojaka*) is as follows: *ārohayati hastinaṃ hāstipakaḥ* (the elephant-driver makes the elephant mount [himself]), *ārohayate hastinaṃ hāstipakaḥ* (the elephant-driver causes himself to be mounted by the elephant), *ārohayate hastī* (the elephant causes itself to be mounted), *niṣādayati kramelakam auṣṭrikaḥ* (the camel-driver makes the camel sit down), *śrapayati yavāgūṃ yajñadattaḥ* (Yajñadatta causes the gruel to be cooked), *sādhayati odanaṃ sūpakāraḥ* (the cook causes the rice to be prepared).

But how is it that [the roots] *śrāti* and *sidhyati* are established as having both object and agent (*karmakartṛ*)? The status of being both object and agent is appropriate for the two roots *yavāgū*. The roots *śrāti* and *sidhyati*, being intransitive (*akarmaka*), function in the sense of the root *paci* when it has an object-agent as its domain. Furthermore, these two express the original (prākṛta) meaning of the verbal action.

The causal agent (*hetu-prayojaka*) is illustrated as follows: *yathā vīṇāṃ pravīṇo vīṇāṃ parivādakena* (just as a skilled lute-player [causes] another to play the lute), *apīpaṭhat kaṭho māṇavakaṃ māṭhareṇa* (Kaṭha caused the young student to study with Māṭhara), *ajighrapat priyaḥ kusumaṃ kāntayā* (the lover caused his beloved to smell the flower), *adūduhat gāṃ balīvardaḥ gopālakena* (the bull caused the cow to be milked by the cowherd). But how can the agent of the root *duh* (to milk) be the causal agent (*hetu*) of the prompter? Because the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is included within the root itself; for it will be stated that roots such as *duh*, which have the causative sense inherent in them, are treated like those ending in the causative suffix (*ṇijanta*). Thus, the status of being an object (*karman*) is established by the preceding rule [Pāṇini 1.4.52], while the restriction regarding the causative applies only to those [roots] where the causative suffix is explicitly present.

Thus [it is said]. An agent without a cause (*ahetu-prayojaka*) is as follows: *saṃparmayati*, *atihastamayati*, *abhiṣeṇayati*, *upaślokayati*. An agent with both a cause and no cause (*hetvahetu-prayojaka*) is as follows: "The son causes the teacher to teach" (*putra upādhyāyam adhyāpayati*); "The girl causes the river not to flow" (*kanyā nadīm na vartayati*); "He causes the sacrificer and the priest to sacrifice" (*yājyayājakau yājayati*); "He causes the bridegroom and the bride to marry" (*kanyāvarau vivāhayati*). Furthermore, there are: the agent as object (*karma-kartṛ*), the agent of the reverse action (*vikarma-kartṛ*), the causal agent (*prayojya-kartṛ*), the agent who is both object and causal agent (*karma-prayojya-kartṛ*), the agent of the original material (*prakṛti-kartṛ*), the agent of the transformation (*vikāra-kartṛ*), and the agent of both the original material and its transformation (*prakṛti-vikāra-kartṛ*).

Among these, the agent of the action itself (*vikarmakartṛ*) is as follows: "the elephant scatters," "the garland is being woven," "the cow yields milk," and "the mat desires to be made. The prompted agent (*prayojyakartṛ*) is as follows: "he causes Devadatta to cook," "he causes Viṣṇumitra to read," "he causes the porter to carry the load," and "he causes the mat-maker to weave the mat. The prompted object-agent (*karmaprayojyakartṛ*) is as follows: "the elephant causes the hunter to mount it," "the field causes the peasant to reap it," "the king causes his servants to see [him]," and "the teacher causes Devadatta to salute him."

An agent of primary nature (*prakṛti-kartṛ*) is as follows: "The pieces of wood become ashes; the moon becomes me; the castes become you; the heirs become me. An agent of transformation (*vikāra-kartṛ*) is as follows: "The gruel turns into urine; the barley is fit for making *abhyuṣa*; the two potsherds become a jar; a lump of gold becomes a pair of earrings."

The agent is the performer of the modification of the material cause (*prakṛti-vikāra-kartṛ*). For example: "the Brahmins become Śaṅkhas," "the cows form into herds," "the calf becomes a bull," or "the child becomes bold. Although this agent is of eighteen types, it occurs in many ways through various distinctions such as: being expressed (*abhihita*) or unexpressed (*anabhihita*), being employed (*prayujyamāna*) or not employed (*aprayujyamāna*), being conventional (*prasiddha*), depending on the material cause (*prakṛtāpekṣita*), metaphorical (*aupacārika*), imagined (*prakalpita*), continuous (*anusyūta*), and so forth, including generalities (*sāmānya*). Among these, an example of the expressed agent is: "it was done by you" (*bhavatā kṛtam*), or "he sleeps by means of that" (*tena supyate*).

The *prayujyamāna* (employed) is, for example: "you cook," "I cook. The *aprayujyamāna* (unemployed) is, for example: "you cook," "I cook" [where the agent is not explicitly stated]. The *prasiddha* (well-known) is, for example: "it rains," "it neighs. The *prakṛta* (contextual) is, for example: "they wandered," "they leaped. The *apekṣita* (expected) is, for example: "so they say," "whom he employed. The *upacarita* (metaphorical) is, for example: "the bow shoots," "the platforms cry out. The *prakalpita* (conceptualized) is, for example: "even of the self, no selves are born," "the self alone knows the non-self."

The conceptualized (*vikalpita*) is, for example, "I go" or "another goes," or "I am another who goes. The continuous (*anusyūta*) is, for example, "you and he both cook," or "you and I both cook. The common (*sāmānya*) is, for example, "he cooks" or "he reads. These distinctions should also be inferred as applicable to objects (*karman*) and so forth, according to the circumstances. As for the divided [categories], the object (*karman*) is that which is to be reached by the action; as it is said: "The object is that which is most desired by the agent. That, moreover, is of three kinds: that which is to be produced (*nirvartya*), that which is to be modified (*vikārya*), and that which is to be attained (*prāpya*).

In this regard, that which is non-existent and brought into being, or that which already exists and is manifested through birth and so forth, is the *nirvartya* (that which is produced). That which, though already accomplished, undergoes modification through the destruction of its nature or the addition of another quality, is the *vikārya* (the modified). That for which no distinctions produced by action are perceived in any way is the *prāpya* (the attained). Furthermore, that which is brought into being as something non-existent, or that which, being existent, is manifested through birth, is the *nirvartya*. Thus, the object of the root *√kṛ* (to make) is established as being twofold.

Some [products] arise from the destruction of their original nature (*prakṛti*), like the ash of wood and the like; others arise through the acquisition of different qualities, like the modification of gold and the like. Where the accomplishment of specific changes is not perceived either through direct observation (*darśana*) or through inference (*anumāna*), that is said to be "attainable" (*prāpya*). In this context, the properties of the "to-be-produced" (*nirvartya*), the "to-be-modified" (*vikārya*), and the "attainable" (*prāpya*)—as well as the inherent properties of each—are as follows: in the case of the *vikārya*, there are both the properties of being modified and its own inherent properties; in the case of the *prāpya*, however, there are only its own inherent properties.

What, then, is this manifestation (*ābhāsa*), comprehension (*avagama*), clarity (*vyakti*), or firmness (*sodhatva*)? These are the specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) established for the object being attained (*prāpyamāṇa*) when the action is accomplished. However, in the case of the produced (*nirvartya*) and the modified (*vikārya*), there are only two effects: cessation (*nivṛtti*) and transformation (*kārya*). As it is said: "Having first experienced independence regarding the produced objects and so forth, it subsequently becomes an object (*karman*) in relation to the operation of other agents. Among these, the produced (*nirvartya*) is that which is to be brought into existence, manifested, subordinate, qualifying, remote, or unattainable.

Among these, that which is produced is "the producible" (*utpādya*); for example: "he effects conjunction," "he produces pleasure," "he effects separation," or "he generates pain. That which already exists but becomes manifest through the removal of an obscuration is "the manifestable" (*prakāśya*); for example: "he fathers a son," "she gives birth to a son," "they produce oil," or "he milks the cow."

That which has become non-primary is the *upasarjana* (subordinate), as in: "he begins to make a mat" (*kaṭaṃ kartumārabhate*), "the village is desired to be inhabited" (*grāmo vāsayitumiṣyate*), "cooked rice is eaten" (*pakvaudano bhujyate*), and "rice is intended to be cooked" (*paktumodanaścintyate*). That which generates its own inherent cognition is the *viśeṣaṇa* (qualifier), as in: "he makes a mat that is beautiful and noble" (*bhūṣmamudāraṃ kaṭaṃ karoti*), "he utters a sound that is great and indistinct" (*mahāntamavyaktaṃ śabdamuccarati*), "she gives birth to a son who is long-lived and virtuous" (*dīrghāyuṣaṃ guṇinamātmajaṃ prasūte*), and "he weaves a cloth that is variegated and clear" (*citramacchapaṭaṃ vayati*).

An action is considered "separated" (*vyavahita*) when it is intervened by another action, as in: *māsam āste* ("he sits for a month"), *godoham pacati* ("he cooks while the cows are being milked"), *krośam adhīte* ("he studies for the distance of a *krośa*"), and *kurūn gacchan svapiti* ("he sleeps while going through the land of the Kurus"). Time, distance, state, and location are [treated as objects] when they are internalized along with other intervening actions; when joined with all intransitive verbs, the status of an object (*karmatva*) arises. Even a transitive verb is restricted to substances and the like as its objects; however, in the case of time and the like as objects, as in *māsam odanam pacati* ("he cooks rice for a month") and *krośam anuvākam adhīte* ("he studies a section of the Veda for the distance of a *krośa*"), [the time and distance become the primary objects].

Having attained, as it were, the status of a substratum (*ādhāra*) with respect to the substances and actions, time and the other factors—occupying a distinct level—subsequently attain the status of an object (*karman*). An adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), while not being something to be produced (*aprāpya*), expresses happiness, brings about the cessation of suffering, [expresses] "he goes slowly," or "he comes quickly. But how can there be a state of being produced (*nirvartyamānatā*) for things such as qualifiers (*upasarjana*)? Just as in the case of that which is being produced—for instance, when one produces a mat (*kaṭa*)—so too does one produce the qualities inherent in it, such as its beauty or excellence.

The same applies to the word *odana* in the expression "cooked rice is being eaten" (*pakkodano bhujyate*). Although the rice is produced by the act of cooking, that [production] is merely its potentiality (*śakti*). When the primary capacity for being the object of the action of eating is present, the mention of the subordinate act of cooking—by means of a verbal suffix expressing the primary capacity—manifests as if it were already expressed.

In the case of the expression *paktum odanaś cintyate* ("The rice is intended to be cooked"), although the act of cooking is in reality subordinate to the act of intending—since "intending" (*cintā*) is the meaning of the verbal root here—the intention is expressed as the primary element by the suffix of the gerundive (*tumun*). Consequently, the action of cooking becomes subordinate to that intention. Therefore, the objective force (*karma-śakti*) directed toward that [cooking] is considered "expressed" (*abhihita*) when the primary force is expressed. By this same reasoning, the examples *kaṭaḥ kartum ārabhyate* ("The mat is begun to be made") and *grāmo gantum iṣyate* ("The village is desired to be gone to") are also explained.

[Objection: But in the case of *gam* (to go), there are two objects for the root *iṣ* (to desire); so which one here has the status of a subordinate object (*upasarjana*)? [Response: It is not so. What is stated—that there are two objects for *iṣ*—should be understood as being intended merely to demonstrate the semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*). One desires the village; for what purpose? To go. Whether it is expressed as "the village" or "to the village," it is not the case that both objects of *iṣ* occur simultaneously. Even when this is stated, the fact that months and the like are brought about by sitting and so forth is understood just as in the case of a mat (*kaṭa*) and other such things.

For instance, there are those who cook, thinking, "He who stays here completes [the cooking] in a month. Likewise, while cooking, one studies for the duration of a cow's milking; while sleeping, they traverse a *krośa*. Thus, it is precisely the distances to be traversed—such as a *kurukrośa*—that possess the status of an object (*karman*). As it has been said: "Time, distance, and the path to be traversed are designated as objects (*karman*) even when [the action] is otherwise intransitive (*akarmaṇām*)."

If it is asked: "How can that which is unattainable (*aprāpya*)—because it functions as a qualifier of an action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*)—be something to be accomplished (*nirvartya*) like the action itself? [The answer is: Because it takes recourse to the general nature of human activity (*puruṣavyāpāra*). Its unattainability, moreover, is with respect to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*); for it is not attained by the meaning of the verbal root, but rather by human activity. The meaning of the verbal root, however, serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*) therein.

In such injunctions as "one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," the instrumental case is observed for the verbal roots and names, such as *viśvajit* and others; furthermore, the commencement of the sūtra "yajeta" (one should sacrifice) in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) is for the purpose of establishing [the status of] "one who has sacrificed with the Agniṣṭoma" and so forth. For the Agniṣṭoma and other rites are indeed the instruments in the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) directed toward results such as heaven. The object (*karman*) is that which is not to be destroyed, that which is to be destroyed, that which is desired, that which is undesired, and that which is undertaken by the agent.

In that regard, that which is indestructible (*avināśya*) is, for example: he fashions gold into a bowl, he splits a stalk, he causes his beloved to sit down, he causes his friend to sit down. That which is destructible (*vināśya*) is, for example: he breaks a water-jar, he burns wood, he drinks grains, he grinds [them] with water. That which is desired (*īpsita*) is, for example: he goes to a woman, he drinks milk. That which is undesired (*anīpsita*) is, for example: he sees thieves, he abandons wealth, he eats poison, he leaps over a snake.

What, then, is their modification (*vikāra*)? It is the alteration of the original nature (*prakṛti*); for thieves and the like do not become objects of perception and so forth. One who has set out goes along the path, crosses a river, ascends a mountain, or climbs over a pit. What, then, is the distinction between this [action] and others? It is said: "When one has reached that which is to be abandoned—such as the act of seeing—the action performed therein assumes a dual form."

The agent and the object are as follows: "the field cuts itself," "the rice cooks itself," and "the granary splits itself. Furthermore, there are objects that are reached (*prāpya*), those that are employed (*prayojya*), those that are to be avoided (*parihārya*), those that are expressed (*abhihita*), those that are unexpressed (*anabhihita*), and those that are unspecified (*atathita*). Among these, an example of an object that is reached is: "he sees the sun," "he hears the Himalayas," "he studies the Veda," and "he completes the recitations. An example of an object that is employed is: "he causes the boy to go," "he awakens the disciple," "he brings the Brahmin," and "he makes the soldier lie down."

But is it not the case that [the object] is merely the effect (*kārya*)? No, for it is the motivator (*prayojaka*), since only the mere activity is intended to be expressed; moreover, the "object to be modified" (*vikārya*) is based upon its own action. This is unavoidable, as in: while producing separation, one destroys conjunction; while making a mat, one gathers *kāśa* grass; while going to the village, one approaches the roots of trees; while eating the *āmikṣā*, one obtains the whey (*vājina*).

That which is expressed (*abhihita*) is as follows: "the camel-like sitting is being sat," "the dead-like lying is being lain," "he nourishes with wealth-nourishment," or "he grinds with water-grinding. That which is unexpressed (*anabhihita*) is as follows: "see, the deer runs," "remember, Devadatta, we shall dwell in Kashmir," or "I cannot tolerate that your honor should cause a low-born man to sacrifice there. The wise know that action in the form of a state (*bhāvarūpa*) is what is expressed here; however, they consider action in the form of an activity (*kriyārūpa*) to be unexpressed.

Now, the "unspecified" (akathita) [object], such as: he milks the cow for milk; he begs a cow from the descendant of Puru; he shuts the cow into the pen; he asks the boy the way; he eats the cow from the descendant of Puru; he gathers fruits from the tree; he tells the boy the Dharma; he instructs the boy in the Dharma; he conquers Śatānīka; he fines the Gargas a hundred; he nourishes the horse with fodder; he churns nectar from the ocean; he drags the branch to the village; [he milks] the goat...

"He leads the village," "He carries wood to the village," "He carries the load to the village," likewise, "He carries the load to the city," "The collector takes ten thousand," "He makes a mat from *kāśa* grass. But what here is the "unexpressed" (*akathita*) [object]? Milk and so forth. By what is it unexpressed? By the *la*-affixes, the *kṛt*, *ktvā*, *lyap*, *tṛc*, *artha*, and so on. For milk and the like are not expressed by the *la*-affixes and so forth; rather, it is cows and the like—as in: "The cow is milked for milk" (*duhyate gauḥ payaḥ*) or "The cow is easy to milk for milk" (*suduhā gauḥ payaḥ*).

As for that which is designated by them as the "most desired" (*īpsitatama*) primary object (*pradhānakarma*), it exists even prior to its connection with the action. As it has been said: "Since the word 'cow' (*go*) is connected with the verb *duh* (to milk) first, whereas the word 'milk' (*payas*) is connected with the agent who milks the cow [only later], therefore the *l*-suffixes and so forth apply to the former; likewise, in the case of *sara* and other such objects, since they are connected with the verb *nī* (to lead) and so forth even before their connection with the act of bringing water and so on, it should be understood that when these are expressed by *l*-suffixes and the like, secondary nominal suffixes (*taddhita*) arise. And that which is expressed through verbal description is called "kathita" (expressed), while that which is the opposite of that is "akathita" (unexpressed).

Regarding the rule *druhi-yāci-kathi-pracchi-bhikṣi-ci-ām* and so forth, as well as for the roots *cit*, *daṇḍ*, *ḍip*, *mukh*, *masj*, and those meaning "to go" (*gaty-artha*), it is desired that there be an extension (*upasaṃkhyāna*) for *nīvṛt*, *pra-hṛ*, *vṛh*, and others. The meaning of this is as follows: when the application (*upayoga*) of roots such as *druh*—such as the filling [of milk] and so on—has a cause (*nimitta*) such as milk (*payaḥ*), and when that which is connected by inherence (*samavāya*) to the action of the roots *brū* and *śās* (such as dharma and the like), then, since the technical designations (*saṃjñā*) of *apādāna* and so forth have not been prescribed, that which is to be expressed in the accusative case is called the "principal object" (*pradhāna-karman*) or the "designated object" (*kathita*).

Regarding the statement that "there is an addition [to the rule] for the non-primary object (*apradhānakarman*) of roots such as *ji* (to conquer) and others," others, however, maintain that "use" (*upayoga*) refers to things such as milk; they declare that which is connected with that cause—such as a cow—and with the primary object (*pradhānakarman*) such as Dharma through the secondary action (*guṇa*) of speaking or instructing, such as a student (*māṇavaka*), is called "unspoken" (*akathita*). In that view, the primacy of cows and other such objects expressed by the *l*-suffixes (*la-ādi*) would be contradicted, and the designation "unspoken" (*akathita-saṃjñā*) would become polysemous.

The *l*-affixes and others apply to these [verbs] as well only when the primary object (*pradhānakarman*) is expressed, as in "the goat is led to the village" (*ajā nīyate grāmam*). As it has been said: "They say that for two-object verbs (*dvikarman*), the *l*-affixes and others denote the primary object; for verbs such as *duh* (to milk), they denote the non-primary object; and for causatives (*ṇyanta*), they denote the agent who is not an object. Because these [rules] contradict one another in their meaning, this leads to the conclusion that these very authorities are speaking without due reflection.

How is it that, while the security and acquisition (*yogakṣema*) are identical, cattle and the like are subordinate (*aprādhānya*), whereas goats and the like are primary (*prādhānya*); or how is it that the primary [object], such as cattle, is expressed by [verbs] like *duh* (to milk) in the same way as goats and the like? Furthermore, since [verbs] like *duh* have the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) included within them, their status as an object is established by the preceding rule, just as in the case of a causative verb; likewise, there is a restriction regarding the causative. On this view, because cattle and the like are clearly the things being employed (*prayojya*), they possess the status of the primary object (*pradhānakarman*) precisely by the previous sūtra.

And likewise, in the expression "he milks the cow for milk" (*gāṃ dogdhi payaḥ*), the meaning is "he causes the milk to flow from the cow. For the root *duh* signifies filling; filling is nourishment, whereas "filling forth" (*prapūraṇa*) is actually evacuation, because it effects a reversal of purpose, as in the case of [the root] *sthā* when used in the sense of "to urge" (*preraṇa*).

As for the initiation of the designation *karman* (object) for roots such as those ending in the causative suffix (*ṇic*), by means of the rule *gatibuddhipratyavasānārthaśabdakarmākarmakāṇām aṇikartā sa ṇau*, that will serve a restrictive purpose (*niyamārtha*)—precluding the designation *karman* for the prompted agent (*prayojya-kartṛ*) in cases such as *pācayati devadattena* ("he causes Devadatta to cook")—and thus it is stated that "the divided object is called the instrument" (*vibhaktaṃ karma karaṇam ucyate*). In that context, among the factors such as the object (*karman*) whose operations are employed toward an action, that factor whose operation immediately precedes the accomplishment of the action when so intended is the most effective causal factor (*sādhakatama*) and is called the instrument (*karaṇa*).

As it has been said: "When the accomplishment of an action is intended to be expressed as occurring immediately after the operation of something, that thing is then traditionally regarded as the instrument (*karaṇa*). That [instrument] is also threefold: external, internal, and both external and internal. Among these, the external [instrument] is of four types: that which has the form of the agent, that which is based on the agent, that which has the form of the object, and that which is based on the object. It is also [fourfold as] based on the action or not based on anything. Among those, an example of that which has the form of the agent is: *edhaiḥ pacati* (he cooks with fuel), *senayā jayati* (he conquers with an army), *aśvena gacchati* (he goes by horse), and *nāvā tarati* (he crosses by boat).

That which is dependent on an instrument (*karaṇāśrita*) is as follows: he plays with dice, he cuts with a sickle, he pierces with a bow, he chops with an axe. That which has the nature of an object (*karmarūpa*) is as follows: he goes by way of a path, he goes near, he eats with milk, he drinks barley-gruel. That which is dependent on an object (*karmāśrita*) is as follows: he eats rice with milk, he goes to the village by way of a path, he buys grain for two *droṇas*, he binds animals for five [coins].

That which is dependent on action (*kriyāśrita*) is, for example: "he studies in a month," "he studies for a *krośa*," "he sacrifices with the *Viśvajit*," or "he performs according to the rule. That which is non-dependent (*anāśrita*) is, for example: "released with ease," "obtained with difficulty," "he goes by light," or "he goes by means of a lamp. Internal (*ābhyantara*) is also [divided into]: internal (*āntara*), intermediate (*avāntara*), internal (*ābhyantara*), immediate (*anantara*), closely following (*samanantara*), immediately preceding (*pratyanantara*), and external-internal (*bāhyābhyantara*).

Therein, the internal [state] is as follows: it is perceived by itself, it initiates itself, it manifests from itself, and it knows through mutual relation. The intermediate [state] is as follows: a person by birth, handsome by nature, noble by origin, and fortunate by disposition. The internal-internal [state] is as follows: one boasts by means of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*), endures by means of goodness (*sattva*), is colored by passion (*rajas*), and is deluded by darkness (*tamas*).

Immediately after, as one rejoices with the mind, acts within, perceives with apprehension, and recollects through mental formations; immediately following that, as one undertakes with effort, knows with the intellect, sleeps in comfort, and studies with difficulty; subsequently, as one prospers through dharma, falls through adharma, crosses over death through ignorance, and attains immortality through knowledge.

There is also that which is external-internal, outward-facing, inward-facing, mouthless, characterized by external predominance, characterized by internal predominance, and devoid of predominance. Among these, the outward-facing is, for example, when one attains immortality through knowledge (*vidyā*). The external-internal is, for example, when one sees with the eye, speaks with speech, communicates by gesture, or makes known by facial expression. The inward-facing is, for example, when one smells with the nose, tastes with the tongue, perceives by touch, or hears with the ear.

The *nirmikha* (unmasked) type is as follows: he moves about with fearlessness, he moves about with intrepidity, he is liberated by his lack of possessions, and he is slain by his lack of weapons. The *bahurudreka* (excessively outward) type is as follows: he walks on his feet, he touches with his hands, he communicates by signs, and he gratifies others through virility. The *antarudreka* (excessively inward) type is as follows: he rains by means of strength, he cooks by means of skill, he studies through application, and he retains [knowledge] through practice.

For example, as in the case of a sacrificer who is generally *nirudreka* (without surplus), [specified] by his lineage as a Gārgya, by his ancestry as a Sauhya, and by his Vedic branch as a Chāndoga. If it is argued that [the qualifiers] such as "smallness" (*stoka*) and so forth are not effective [as causes] because they are non-existent or of the nature of absence (*asat*), that is not so. For just as that [smallness] is present when it exists, so too is it present even when it is absent; the accomplishment of an action is understood through the existence of a thing functioning as an instrument (*karaṇa*). This is because of the production of smallness or the non-production of it.

They declare that the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is established for things such as *stokaka* (a small amount). Furthermore, there is no real, intrinsic nature (*vāstavam rūpam*) to an instrument, because it is dependent upon the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*). As it has been said: "In reality, it cannot be designated; for it does not reside in the object itself, since we observe even this usage: 'The food is cooked by the pot' (*sthālyā pacyate')."

Furthermore, it is not the case that "the fuel cooks," "the bow pierces," "the eye sees," or "the mind knows"—for these are spoken of as instruments (*karaṇa*). Next, the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is mentioned; this [recipient] is threefold: that which is reached by the act of giving (*dadāti-karmāpya*), that which is reached by the mere object (*karma-mātrāpya*), and that which is reached by the action (*kriyāpya*). Among these, it is called "recipient" (*saṃpradāna*) because of the application of this significant technical term.

When something is correctly bestowed upon someone by means of an act of giving—such as the gift of a cow or the like—that recipient who is to be reached through the act of giving (*dadāti-karman*) receives the designation of "recipient" (*saṃpradāna*). This [status] unfolds in six ways: in the cessation of one's own ownership, in the acquisition of another's ownership, in the conjunction of both, in the application of one's own [effort], and in the application of both. Regarding the cessation of one's own ownership: for example, "he imparts knowledge to the pupil," "he bestows a maiden upon the groom," "he gives instruction to a trusted person," or "he offers himself to his teachers."

Just as one gives fear to enemies when transferring ownership to another, one delivers a blow to a foe, gives a reply to a disputant, offers a prayer to a deity, or gives one's body to a beloved; one gives one's eye to the wind, exposes one's back to the heat of the sun, gives one's ear to music, and offers one's heart to what has been heard.

Regarding utility for another (*paropayoga*): as when one bestows a blessing upon a son, gives a bamboo staff to a student, grants fearlessness to one who is afraid, or gives medicine to one who is afflicted. Regarding utility for both (*ubhayopayoga*): as when one gives a razor to a barber, a staff to the Maitrāvaruṇa priest, offers the lower lip to one’s most beloved, or gives an embrace to a lover.

By the technical definition (paribhāṣā), "that which one intends through an action is the recipient" (*saṃpradāna*), that which is characterized as the mere object of attainment (*karmamātrāpya*) is also sixfold: the instigator (*preraka*), the consenter (*anumantṛ*), the rejector (*nirākartṛ*), the non-rejector (*anirākartṛ*), the one who hands over (*pratyarpaṇaka*), and the non-acceptor (*apratigrāhaka*). Among these, the instigator is, for example: giving food to a beggar, granting interest to a creditor, providing hospitality to a guest, or assigning a share of inheritance to an heir.

The *anumantṛ* (consenter/approver) is as when one presents a cow to a teacher, assigns a village to a servant, shows a bridegroom to a maiden choosing her own husband, or bestows a garment upon a maidservant. The *nirākartṛ* (rejecter/offerer) is as when one casts a flower before a deity, offers an oblation to Kubera, sacrifices an animal to Rudra, or gives curdled milk to Soma. The *anirākṛta* (not rejected/not excluded) is as when one prescribes medicine for a madman, gives a refutation to a debater, strikes a coin with a hammer, scatters fodder for a horse, or sends meat to a Śākyan.

An example of one who returns [what is received] is as follows: he points out a horse to the groom, hands over a treasury to the treasurer, reports the kingdom to the collector-general, and presents a seal to the minister. An example of one who does not receive [anything in return] is as follows: he gives leftover food to the gods, offers the remains of a meal to the ancestors, shows forms to the blind, and teaches the scriptures to the deaf.

Since action (*kriyā*) is also included by the term "object" (*karman*), that which is obtained through action is also a recipient (*saṃpradāna*), and thus becomes "pervaded by action. If it is asked, "What is the distinction between this [recipient] and the object? the answer is: it is called the "most desired" (*īpsitatama*). Even then, the remainder (*śeṣa*) is sixfold: the remainder of the object, the object mediated by an object, the cause that is an object, and the cause that is a motive (*nimitta-hetu*). As it has been said: "In cases such as those involving the roots meaning 'to please' (*rucy-artha*), the grammatical treatise designates a *kāraka* as 'recipient' (*saṃpradāna*), whether it possesses the status of a cause, the technical name of 'object,' or even the status of a remainder."

In that regard, the remaining cases (*śeṣa*) are as follows: *devadattāya rocate*, *devadattāya svadate*, *devadattāya tiṣṭhate*, *devadattāya namate*. The remaining case for the object (*karmaśeṣa*) is as follows: *devadattāya gāṃ pratiśṛṇoti*, *devadattāya santaṃ dhārayati*, *devadattāya daivam īkṣate*. The case for the object (*karman*) is as follows: *devadattāya rādhyati*, *puṣpāya spṛhayati*, *grāmāya gacchati*, *devebhyo namati*.

An example of a remote object (*vyavahita-karman*) is: *chātrasya ślāghate* (he praises the student), *caitrāya śapate* (he curses Caitra), *hotre pratigṛhṇāti* (he receives from the Hotṛ priest), *potrē anugṛhṇāti* (he favors the Potṛ priest). An example of a cause (*hetu*) is: *devadattāya krudhyati* (he is angry with Devadatta), *devadattāya druhyati* (he bears malice toward Devadatta), *devadattāyērṣyati* (he is envious of Devadatta), *devadattāyāsūyati* (he finds fault with Devadatta). An example of a motive-cause (*nimitta-hetu*) is: *edhebhyo vrajati* (he goes for fuel), *śrāddhāya nigadate* (he speaks for the sake of a funeral rite), *yuddhāya saṃnahyati* (he prepares for battle), *patye śete* (she lies down for her husband).

By this [rule], the following statements are explained: "In the case of roots meaning 'to please,' the one being pleased; in the case of *ślāgh*, *huṅ*, *sthā*, *śā*, and *jñīps*, the one desiring to praise; in the case of *dhāri*, the creditor; in the case of *spṛhi*, the desired object; in the case of roots meaning 'to be angry,' 'to hate,' 'to envy,' or 'to be jealous,' the one toward whom the anger is directed; in the case of *rādhi* and *īkṣi*, the one who is the object of the inquiry; in the case of *śru* preceded by *prati* or *āṅ*, the agent of the preceding action; likewise for *anu-prati-gṛ*; in the case of the object of a root meaning 'to go,' both the second and fourth cases [are used] provided there is physical movement and the word does not mean 'path'; in the case of a root used as a complement to express another action, the object of the stationary [agent]"—and so forth. [This applies to] that which is [the object] by means of an action (*karmaṇā*).

It has been stated that the rule "that which one intends [to give] is the recipient" (*saṃpradāna*) is for the purpose of elaborating upon the very same principle; thus, the section on the recipient is concluded. Now, the ablative (*apādāna*) is being discussed: "In separation (*apāya*), that which is fixed (*dhruva*) is the ablative. When there is a separation—whether preceded by physical contact or preceded by mental contact—that which is intended as the fixed point of reference is designated by the technical term "ablative. As it is said: "In separation, whether that which is indifferent or moving, If it is fixed through its involvement [in the action], it is called the ablative."

That [ablative] is also taught as being threefold: having a specified object (*nirdiṣṭaviṣaya*), having an implied object (*upāttaviṣaya*), and having an expected action (*apekṣitākriya*). As it has been said: "The ablative is said to be threefold: some have a specified object, likewise some have an implied object, and some have an expected action. Among these, where the departure (*apāya*) is understood through the ablative itself because the action is implied, that is "having a specified object. That [specified object] is sixfold: abandoned (*ujjhita*), not abandoned (*anujjhita*), desired (*īpsita*), intended to be avoided (*jihāsita*), transformed (*pariṇata*), and ceased (*nivṛtta*).

Among these, *ujjhita* (abandoned) is as follows: he comes from the village; a leaf falls from the tree; this one runs away from the ram; he was thrown down from the galloping horse. *Anujjhita* (not abandoned) is as follows: the reed grows from the horn; the Gaṅgā originates from the Himavat; a sprout hangs down from the banyan tree; smoke rises from the fire. *Īpsita* (desired) is as follows: he keeps the cow away from the barley; he restrains the buffaloes from the beans; he wards off the blind man from the well; he moves the boy away from the fire.

That which is abandoned (*jihāsita*) is, for example, when one goes out from a forest, crosses over a pit, descends from a mountain, or falls from the sky. That which is transformed (*pariṇata*) is, for example, when a scorpion is born from cow dung, durva grass arises from cow-hair and goat-hair, a bowl is produced from gold, or a mat is made from kasha grass. That which ceases (*nivṛtta*) is, for example, when one is deprived of power, falls away from wisdom, departs from justice, or deviates from one's true nature.

If it is asked how there is stability in the powers (*prabhāva*), [the answer is: it is due to the adherence to the means through the operation of words. Where, through the capacity of the action already undertaken, there is the cognition of a departure (*apāya*) by means of a word expressing that action, [that power] has that as its object which is undertaken. That too is sixfold: established (*siddha*), to-be-accomplished (*sādhya*), attainable (*prāpya*), unattainable (*aprāpya*), to-be-avoided (*parihartavya*), and to-be-removed (*nihartavya*).

Among these, the form of the accomplished (*siddharūpa*) is as follows: he falls from the family, he cooks from the granary, he eats from two bronze vessels, he chants like a Brāhmaṇa, he studies from the teacher. The form of the object to be accomplished (*sādhyarūpa*) is as follows: he is defeated by study, he neglects dharma, he feels aversion toward adharma, he desists from what ought not to be done. The form of the attained (*prāptarūpa*) is as follows: he looks from the seat, he gazes down from the palace, it flashes from the cloud, he transforms himself from youth.

The form of the goal (*prāpyarūpa*) is as follows: "He will eat food from Dyūṅga," "He desires prosperity until death," "He pierces a target a hundred thousand *krośas* away," or "It has rained as far as Pāṭaliputra. The form of what is to be avoided (*parihartavya*) is as follows: "He fears thieves," "He dreads wicked people," "He hides from his teacher," or "He conceals himself from his fellow students. The form of what is to be protected (*nihartavya*) is as follows: "He protects a secret from thieves," "He guards the sick man from diseases," "He shields the curd from crows," or "He protects himself from untruth."

In cases where, based on the meaning, context, and so forth, one extracts a verbal action from what is understood, that [sentence] also possesses six varieties, depending on whether it requires a general action, a specific action, an existent entity, a non-existent entity, a removal of a fixed form, or a removal of an unfixed form.

Among these, [comparison] with respect to general action (*sāmānyakriyā*) is as follows: "The gods are wiser than the Dānavas; the Asuras are more knowledgeable than the Suras; the Suhmas are wealthier than those of Brahmottara; and they are more delicate than the people of Pāṭaliputra. [Comparison] with respect to specific action (*viśeṣakriyā*) is as follows: "A jewel [is distinguished] by its brilliance; [a cloud] from a rain-cloud; 'Where are you from? 'From Pāṭaliputra. [Comparison] with respect to being distinct from another (*stavabhītāpekṣam*) is as follows: "Different from Devadatta," "other than Devadatta," "separate from Devadatta," or "distinct from Devadatta."

[The ablative] depending on eight types of entities, as in: *yathārte devadattāt* (as in the season from Devadatta); [expressing separation] without Devadatta, *ārād devadattāt*, *dūrodevadattāt*. [Expressing the loss of a fixed form: as in *kaumudyāḥ kṣarātruḥ* (the day after the Kaumudī), or in the alternative, *kārtikyā āgrahāyaṇī māse* (from the Kārtikī to the Āgrahāyaṇī month); *gavodhumataḥ sāṃkāśyaś caturṣu yojaneṣu* (Sāṃkāśya is four *yojanas* from Gavodhuma); *pāṭaliputrād rājagṛhaṃ sapta yojanāni* (Rājagṛha is seven *yojanas* from Pāṭaliputra). [Expressing an indefinite form: as in *prāg grāmāt* (east of the village), *dakṣiṇā grāmāt* (south of the village), *tata uparuṣṭāt* (higher than that).

Others, however, maintain that the rule *dhruvam apāye 'pādānam* (A 1.4.24) has a restricted scope (*nirdiṣṭaviṣaya*), while the rules taught in such *yoga*s as “the cause of fear for roots meaning ‘to be’,” “that which is not endured in the case of *parā-ji*,” “that by whom one desires non-perception in the case of disappearance (*antardhi*)”, “in the case of instruction (*upayoga*) following a verb of speaking,” “the source (*prakṛti*) of the agent of birth,” “the point of origin (*prabhava*) of the root *bhū*,” “the addition [of the designation *apādāna*] regarding the object when a *lyap*-affix is elided,” and “the locative and ablative cases [are used] when between two causal factors (*kāraka*)” have a restricted scope (*upāttaviṣaya*).

"When there is a separation (*vibhakta*), [the fifth case is used] after words for directions (*dik-śabda*) preceded by *anādi* or *rati*, when joined with a word ending in *añcu* as the final member of a compound, or with *āc* and *āhi*; *prati* is used in the sense of a representative (*pratinidhi*) or an exchange (*pratidāna*); and [the fifth case is used] for that from which there is a counter-measure (*pratividhi*) or an exchange (*pratidāna*)—such rules, however, involve an action dependent upon the state of being a limit (*avadhi-bhāva*). Thus, they consider the *apādāna* (ablative/point of departure) to be threefold. And they say: 'The rule regarding separation (*vibhakta*) in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), and the rule regarding those beginning with fear (*bhī-trādi*), as well as the loss (*apāya*) expected from a calamity (*utpāta*)—this is understood as the fixed (*dhruva*) [point of departure]. "

The locus (*ādhāra*) has been explained; now the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) is being discussed. "The substratum is the locus" (*ādhāro'dhikaraṇam*): that which serves as the support for the agent or the object with respect to the action—that is the substratum. As it has been said: "That which, while remaining unperceived, supports the action indirectly through its mediation by the agent or the object, and thereby assists in the accomplishment of the action, is traditionally known in the grammatical treatise as the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*). This is threefold: the domain-based (*vaiṣayika*), the contact-based (*aupaśleṣika*), and the conditional (*naimittika*).

In this context, the "object" (*viṣaya*) is that which disciplines (*vinoti*) the threefold [categories] in their many forms; it is the substratum for names based on genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), and so forth. That which pertains to the object is "objective" (*vaiṣayika*), according to the rule *vinayādibhyaṣṭhak*. This is sixfold: objective by genus, objective by quality, objective by action, objective by substance (*dravya*), and objective by name (*saṃjñā*). Among these, an example of the objective by genus is: "gods in heaven," "humans on earth," "fish in water," and "serpents in the netherworld."

The locative based on quality (*guṇavaiṣayika*) is as follows: "He is skilled in making mats" (*kaṭakaraṇe kuśalaḥ*), "he is proficient in making mats" (*kaṭakaraṇe sādhuḥ*), "he is clever toward his mother" (*mātari nipuṇaḥ*), or "he is expert in cooking" (*pāke pravīṇaḥ*). The locative based on action (*kriyāvaiṣayika*) is as follows: "The sun rises in the east" (*prācyām āditya udeti*), "Agastya is seen in the south" (*dakṣiṇasyām agastyo dṛśyate*), "birds fly in the sky" (*ākāśe śakunāḥ patanti*), or "the ears and other senses are directed toward sound and the rest" (*śabdādiṣu śrotrādayo 'bhiniviśante*). The locative based on substance (*dravyavaiṣayika*) is as follows: "The master is among the cows" (*goṣu svāmī*), "the heir is among the cows" (*goṣu dāyādaḥ*), "the Pañcālas are under Brahmadatta" (*adhibrahmadatte pāñcālāḥ*), or "Brahmadatta is over the Pañcālas" (*adhipāñcāleṣu brahmadattaḥ*).

That which pertains to a name (*saṃjñā*) is, for example: Pitāmaha in reference to Brahmā, Puruṣottama in reference to Viṣṇu, Maheśvara in reference to Rudra, and Śakra in reference to Indra. That which pertains to a convention (*saṅketa*) is, for example: the acute accent (*udātta*) is on the middle of the index finger, the grave accent (*anudātta*) is on the middle of the little finger, the circumflex accent (*svarita*) is on the middle of the ring finger, and the *pracaya* is on the middle of the middle finger. *Upaśleṣa* means contact; that which is capable of [producing an effect] through such contact is *aupaśleṣika*.

That [locus] is also sixfold: partitive (*ekadeśika*), pervasive (*abhivyāpaka*), proximate (*sāmīpyaka*), contiguous (*aupaśleṣika*), near-by (*aupaśalyaka*), and metaphorical (*aupacārika*). Among these, the partitive is, for example: "He stays in the house," "He cooks in the pot," "He sleeps on the couch," or "It hangs from the branch. The pervasive is, for example: "Oil in sesame seeds," "Color in crystals," "Cowness in a cow," or "A cloth in its threads. The proximate is, for example: "He dwells near the teacher," "He dwells near the sacred ford," "The hamlet is on the Ganges," or "Garga’s family is at the well."

The *aupaśleṣika* [locus] is as follows: "He will eat in two days," "From the Kārttikī full moon to the Āgrahāyaṇī full moon is a month," "This distrustful man is standing here," "He hits the target at the distance of a *krośa*," and "Rājagṛha is seven *yojanas* from Pāṭaliputra."

The term *aupacārika* (metaphorical) is illustrated as follows: "A *droṇa* [of grain] is in the vicinity of the *upakhāryā*"; "a *kārṣāpaṇa* is in the vicinity of the *upaniṣka*"; "a *vitasti* is in the vicinity of the *upavyāma*"; "fifty is in the vicinity of one hundred. Furthermore, it is metaphorical when one says: "He who is dear to someone dwells in that person's heart"; "he who is hateful to someone dwells in that person's eyes"; "the whole [army] stands within the middle of a single fist"; or "a hundred herds of elephants are on the tip of a finger."

The sign (*nimitta*) itself is the "occasioned" (*naimittika*); that too is sixfold: occasioned by place, occasioned by time, occasioned by disposition, occasioned by substance, occasioned by action, and occasioned by the yoga of action. Among these, that which is occasioned by place is as follows: one rejoices in the house, fears in the forest, and falls into a pit in the water. That which is occasioned by time is as follows: the *kāśa* grasses flower at the end of the rainy season; the cuckoos intoxicate themselves in spring; one should eat milk-rice under the asterism Puṣya, and meat-rice under Maghā.

That which is caused by mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is as follows: one feels confidence upon seeing [something], feels dejection toward a boar, rejoices at the acquisition of wealth, and is gratified by the destruction of an enemy. That which is caused by an object (*vastu*) is as follows: one becomes weary in the heat, finds relief in the shade, is repelled by defects, and is attracted to virtues. That which is caused by sequence (*krama*) is as follows: one is proficient in the sacrificial ritual (*yajñiya*), learned in the Vedic meters (*chandas*), and studied in grammar (*vyākaraṇa*).

The occasional cause (*naimittika*) according to sequential application (*kramayoga*) is as follows: "One kills the leopard for its skin; one kills the elephant for its tusks; one kills the yak for its hair; the musk deer is killed for its scent-gland. Now, an objection may be raised: since a causal factor (*nimitta-hetu*) is itself an agent (*kāraka*), and an agent is dependent upon a prompter (*prayojaka*), how can it be considered an agent here? It is said in reply: there are two kinds of causal agents: those that impel what is already active (*pravṛtta-preraka*) and those that impel what is not yet active (*apravṛtta-preraka*). Of these, the former falls within the domain of the causative suffix *ṇic*; the latter, however, consists of injunctions (*vidhi*) and the like, as well as occasional causes (*nimitta*).

Of these two, the first is expressed by the suffixes *liṅ*, *loṭ*, *tavya*, and so forth. As it has been said: "The suffixes *loṭ* and *liṅ* are prescribed for verbs such as *praṣ* (to ask) and *pracch* (to inquire) when they denote a mere substance; however, when they are used with an action (*sakriya*), that is the domain of the causative suffix *ṇic*. But because the cause (*nimitta*) is essentially identical with the action (*kriyāśrayatva*), the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) is expressed by the seventh case (*saptamī*) as the locus of the effect (*naimittika*); thus the substratum is distinguished [from the other kārakas].

But surely, in examples such as *upakhāryo droṇaḥ* ("A drona-measure [is] near") and *adhipāñcāleṣu brahmadattaḥ* ("Brahmadatta [is] over the Pañcālas"), if the locative case (*saptamī*) denotes only the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), then what is that locus? It is said: "The locative occurs there where there is that which is superior (*adhika*) and that which expresses the lord (*īśvara*). It is replied: This is stated so that the accusative (*dvitīyā*) prescribed for connection with words having the sense of "kramapravacanīya" (words expressing sequence) may not be sublated. Objection: But surely, according to the rule "the case-ending of the *kāraka* is stronger than the case-ending of the *upapada*," the accusative will not occur; as in the examples *gosvāmī vrajati* ("The owner of the cow goes") and *devānāṃ namaskaroti* ("He pays homage to the gods").

It is not so; this is not a derivative case-ending (*upapada-vibhakti*), but rather a serial case-ending (*krama-vibhakti*) connected with an implicit intermediate action. For example, in the expression *śākalyasya saṃhitāmanu prāvarṣati*, the meaning is "having followed the *saṃhitā* of Śākalya [in its recitation], it rained. What then? For what purpose is this prescribed? So that it may also apply when there is another *kāraka* (participant in an action). Thus, in the phrase *te upārjanam yoddhāraḥ* ("those warriors are for the sake of acquisition"), the fifth case (*pañcamī*) prevails even in the sense of the ablative (*apādāna*). For this very reason, it is stated: "The fifth case is employed after *apa*, *āṅ*, and *pari*, even in the sense of the ablative."

By this, examples such as *adhītī vyākaraṇe* ("learned in grammar") and *edhebhyo vrajati* ("he goes for fuel"), which concern the case-endings of the *kāraka*s, as well as examples such as *goṣu svāmī* ("owner of cows") and *prāg grāmāt* ("east of the village"), which concern the case-endings of relation (*saṃbandha*), are illuminated by the absence of *kāraka*-case-endings. Now, it may be objected: "Power (*śakti*) is the means (*sādhana*), because it is by virtue of that power that a substance (*dravya*) is connected to actions."

Furthermore, even if one assumes that substance (*dravya*) is the means (*sādhana*), one must still postulate powers (*śakti*) that are not to be resorted to again because of the difference between the means; these very powers, being real distinctions, are then imagined to be the means. Nor is there any need for a substratum-substance (*adhikaraṇa-dravya*) for those powers, since their status as means would thus be independent of substance; for substance itself has its birth dependent on its own inherent nature, and thus the fault is equal when considering it in relation to them. Moreover, if the powers alone are the means, then the subsequent employment of words denoting substance is appropriate when the powers have been expressed by the suffixes.

In the case of "Devadatta grows" (*vardhate devadattaḥ*), where the reality of the object is fully understood, if the substance were the means (*sādhana*), its expression would already have been stated [by the verb], and thus the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) would not apply. Furthermore, it is only among the capacities (*śakti*) that the status of being a *kāraka* is found. Since a substance such as Devadatta is a single entity, a temporal sequence such as "before" or "after" is not possible within it. Moreover, if capacities alone constitute the means, then in the example "he sits in the palace" (*prāsāde āste*), the locus (*adhikaraṇa*)—the domain of the suffix *-ghañ* and others—is expressed [by the noun], whereas the locus in relation to the root *ās* (to sit) is not; thus, the locative case (*saptamī*) is obtained by virtue of the definition of the "unexpressed" (*anabhihita*).

Because [the substance] is expressed as persisting (*staya*), this distinction of means (*sādhanabheda*)—which is heard of as being based on multiple substances (*ekadravyādhikaraṇa*)—is applicable only when the potencies themselves (*śakti*) are the means. For instance, it is said: "He fell with speed," "He broke from the tree," or "He shone forth. This would not be possible if it were based on the substance, because that [substance] is a single entity. If one were to argue that it must be based on a distinction in action (*kriyābheda*), then the rule regarding [the suffixes] *karma* and so forth would be subverted, and there would be no difference in cognition, since in that case the action would be something distinct [from the potency].

For the Veda of one person does not differ from that of another. Furthermore, if the substance were a single entity, how could there be a distinction between actions, instruments, and effects, given the non-distinction of the result? Moreover, if it is only powers (*śakti*) that constitute the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), then case-endings are appropriately joined to the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). If, however, the substance were denoted by the nominal stem, then case-endings would not arise because their purpose would already be served; if you argue they arise as *svārthika* suffixes due to specific rules, then the restriction regarding objects (*karman*) and so forth would be sublated, and the difference in perception (*pratīti*) would not occur.

In the expression *vṁkṣaṃ vṛkṣeṇa* ("tree by tree"), since that [repetition] occurs even when the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is not distinct, it follows that the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) is a different meaning from the meaning of the nominal stem; namely, the *kāraka*. This is not so; for the substance (*dravya*) possessing power (*śaktimat*) is the *kāraka*, because its operation (*vyāpāra*) is employed for the accomplishment of the action. Nor does the fact that no action is accomplished from what lacks power constitute a deficiency in that [substance's] capacity for power; for if power itself were dependent on a substance, the same fault would apply.

Furthermore, dependence on other factors does not contradict the causal agency (*kārakatva*) of causal factors, because their status as causes is understood precisely through the presence and absence (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the effect. For when an effect occurs, even if it were possible for it to arise from something else, that which has not previously obtained its existence and subsequently obtains it—having acquired a specific excellence (*atiśaya*) through the presence of another entity—is recognized as the cause. This is observed in the case of a sprout: although the seed may be present in a granary, the sprout is not perceived; however, when the seed is brought together with the collection of auxiliary factors (*sahakāri-grāma*) such as soil and so forth, the sprout’s form is seen. Thus, the causal agency belongs to the seed in conjunction with the auxiliaries, as established by the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the effect.

It is perceived [as such]. Rather, it is understood that this very seed, when accompanied by auxiliary conditions (*sahakārakāri-pratyaya*) such as soil and so forth, is its producer, and not otherwise. Since the substance (*dravya*) is one, how can there be a distinction in the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*)? If this is asked: powers (*śakti*) residing in a single substance have distinct forms; by manifesting a difference in their substrates through a difference in their own nature, they demonstrate the non-difference of the substrate. Just as for a single person such as Devadatta, designations such as "carpenter" or "blacksmith" function to establish a distinction in meaning based on the difference in his crafts.

That has been stated: when the *sādhana* (the means of accomplishment) is the object to be expressed (*sādhya*), because it is already denoted by the suffix (*pratyaya*), there would be no subsequent employment (*anuprayoga*) of that [root]. In that case, the general property (*sāmānya*) is denoted, while the specific instance (*viśeṣa*) would not be employed. It should not be argued: "How can a suffix prescribed for a *sādhana* denote the *sādhana* as a general property? For a general property depends upon specific instances; rather, it is the specific instance itself that is denoted by the suffix, which possesses a single form, even though it requires subsequent employment—just as the word "cow" (*go-śabda*), depending on context and so forth, denotes the meaning "ox" (*gavādi*).

But surely, when a suffix expresses a distinction in relation to something else, how is there no obstruction to the expressive power of the word? For example, the expressive power of the word *go* (cow) is not obstructed when it expresses [the specific] *gaurī* and so forth; this is the same in the case of the power of the means (*sādhana*). [Objection: There is an obstruction to the expressive power of the word regarding the distinction of the powers of the means. [Reply: It is not so. Only a distinction in power is expressed, because the suffix arises precisely from the verbal root’s expression of a particular action (*kriyā*). And that [distinction] is determined by the difference between the basis and the specific effect.

In that case, the distinction of the action (*kāryabheda*) is expressed by the verbal root itself, whereas the distinction of the substratum (*āśrayabheda*), being unperceived, is stated by another word, such as "Caitra" or "Maitra. Nevertheless, the dependence on another factor remains exactly the same. Furthermore, there can be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the supported (*āśrita*) and the support (*āśraya*); therefore, one would not say "Caitra increases," but rather "Caitra grows."

Furthermore, since a verbal root (*dhātu*) denotes a specific action, how is it that [the general] increases up to the point where it must be increased by this? In such instances as "you should perform this action," "he follows the conduct of a city-dweller," or "this does not flourish in a general sense," a particular is understood from the general. As for the claim that, just as there is oneness for Devadatta and others, a dual or plural time cannot occur within a single [action], that too is incorrect, because a distinction based on the conditions (*upādhi*) that are resorted to is logically possible.

For instance, speakers say: "You are clever," "You were clever," "You are more clever," "You are the best," or "Today you have become quite another. Thus, by distinguishing the substratum—which is inherently undivided—into parts based on the difference in capacities (*sāmarthya*), the differentiation of the means (*sādhana*) is postulated, which in turn brings about the notion of a middle state. Furthermore, even in the view that [the agent] is a capacity (*śakti*), a direct middle state is impossible; for at the time of the prior capacity, the subsequent one does not exist, and at the time of the subsequent capacity, the prior one has ceased to be.

Alternatively, if the ablative in *bhoktā* (eater) expresses the limit (*avadhi*), then the fifth case in *abhoktṛtvāt* (due to not being an eater) would likewise express the limit; and that [limit] would be severed at the final meal. If, however, for the sake of establishing the intermediate state, a difference in substance and a difference in capacity are postulated, then, because of the difference in agents, the suffix *ktavatu* in *bhuktvā* (having eaten)—which applies when two actions have the same agent and the first occurs earlier—would not be valid. If it is argued that this [suffix] rests upon a superimposed non-difference, then the intermediate state is not established.

Furthermore, because [the agent] is one, there would be no distinction between the factors (kārakas) based on the difference in time for the single act of eating, as in the case of "the man goes" (*sattvo vrajati*). Moreover, since there is a difference between the acts of bathing and departing, there would also be a difference between the two capacities of the agent (*kartṛ-śakti*) caused by those acts; consequently, due to the absence of a common agent (*samānakartṛkatva*), the rule would not apply. But surely, even here, the means (*sādhana*) is a substance that has acquired multiplicity through the distinctions among the capacities residing within it; thus, this same fault remains.

Furthermore, for one who maintains that the capacity is inherent (*ādheya-śakti-vādin*), it can be said that because the two capacities reside in different substrates (*bhinnadhāra-vartitayā*), they are identical as to their locus. However, for one for whom the substrate is differentiated by the distinctness of the capacities, even the unity [of the substrate] that has been stated would not exist as a basis; moreover, a difference in the substrate must be required for a difference in action characterized by temporal sequence, since such a sequence is expected. To this it is replied: the identity of the two capacities is asserted on the basis of the unity of the substance.

If the multiplicity of a substance is established through the multiplicity of its powers (*śakti*), yet the ultimate unity of the substance itself is not tolerated—oh, what a state of arbitrary whimsy! Furthermore, regarding the power (*śakti*) as the means (*sādhana*), the animal (*paśu*) as the agent (*kartṛ*), and the elephant and the door-panel as the agents (*kartṛ*), how can the designation "power" be understood as being delimited by a substratum? I ask about the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of that which is to be expressed: if you say that the one who is the agent resides in the animal, which is the substance, then [the rule] *upamānāt kartuḥ* does not apply.

Now, as for the claim that the scriptural designations such as "agent" (*kartṛ*) and so forth have the various powers (*śakti*) as their instruments, even that cause is understood through its connection with the effect; for instance, [the statement] "white and so forth are the substrata of specific colors" is justified by grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). In that case, you have been defeated! The distinction between power and the possessor of power is established, because the scriptural designations such as "agent" denote the substratum which possesses the power. Furthermore, in the view that the power is the *kāraka*, there would be no basis for the rule: "When the object (*karman*) is dual or plural, the number of the case-ending follows that," because [the power itself] would not be the object.

For a connection with number is not observed in the case of a quality, as in the cases: "five actions," "four states of action," "three conjunctions," "two universals," or "one inherence. Nor is this a mere figurative usage, because there is no difference in the resulting cognition; likewise, powers (śaktayaḥ) too will experience a distinction of number based on the distinctions among their effects.

It is true that there is a distinction among powers (*śakti*), yet even in that case, there is no difference in their verbal expression; for although the powers are distinct due to the difference in actions such as seeing and praising—as in "he sees the sun" and "he praises [it]"—the plural number is not observed [to be used]. If it is argued that powers are not connected with actions through synonymous expressions, we say no; for even when actions are not fully accomplished in each individual instance, they bring about a difference in verbal expression when expressed collectively.

Just as one is said to "discharge five arrows," "pierce with both the left and right hands," or "lie upon two couches. Furthermore, perception and the other [mental functions] do not occur merely in succession, because they also exist simultaneously. Therefore, the difference in verbal expression is based on the maintenance of distinct capacities (*sāmarthya*), and not on a difference in the underlying powers (*śakti*). For this very reason, power (*śakti*) is not denoted even by a separate case-ending (*vibhakti*) due to its independence.

For if the case-ending were to denote an independent power (*śakti*), then it would denote the number as already residing [in that power], because they are conveyed by the same word; but this is not the case. Therefore, that which the case-ending takes up as its number is precisely the factor of action (*kāraka*) endowed with power.

As for the claim that only an indeclinable (*avyaya*) which possesses the capacity to function in the sense of a case-ending is compounded—that is incorrect. For even when a *kāraka* possesses such capacity, since indeclinables also denote a substance (*sattva*), they express that [substance] alone. How, then, could a substance existing as a real entity (*satvabhūta*) be denoted by an indeclinable whose meaning is non-substantial (*asatvārtha*)? As for the argument that the locative case ending (*saptamī*) characterized by the rule of "non-expression" (*anabhihitatva*) is not observed in the example "he sits on the palace" (*prāsāde āste*), in that case, just as in the domain of *ghañ*-affixes and the like a substance possessing capacity is expressed, but the substance possessing capacity in the domain of the root *ās* (to sit) is not, so too here there is no such [inconsistency].

By what is the locative case (saptamī) prevented? And if suffixes such as *ghañ* were to denote a power (*śakti*), then, since a power denoted by the word "sword" (*asi*) could not possess another power, let alone the locative case, even the accusative (*dvitīyā*) and other cases would not arise. Furthermore, how can he say this: "The words 'prasāda' and so forth express the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) and other [kārakas]"?

For these designations and words are indeed conventional (*rūḍha*) with respect to certain specific objects, just like the word "tree" and others; they merely possess either a restriction of properties (*dharmaniyama*) or some manner of derivation, such as in the case of [the expression] "falling with this speed. Furthermore, even that hearing of a difference in the means (*sādhana*) which resides in the same substance (*ekadravyādhikaraṇa*), as in the aforementioned examples, has already been refuted. Nor does this much imply that nominal stems (*prātipadika*) and so forth would not be produced for the grammatical factors (*kāraka*).

For substance (*dravya*) indeed receives case-endings, gender, capacity, number, and grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*), just like the suffixes themselves; therefore, it is established that substance is the possessor of capacity (*śaktimat*) and the factor (*kāra*). The person (*puruṣa*) is a specific factor denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta-pratyaya*); it is threefold: first, middle, and last. Among these, that which is denoted by the first triad of *parasmaipada* and *ātmanepada* endings is the first person; that denoted by the middle triad is the middle person; and that denoted by the final triad is the last person.

And in that regard, if the upādhi (condition) of the agent and the object consists in their having distinct temporal states (*pratyuktāparabhāva*), then the middle and the highest [persons] denote them respectively by virtue of specific scriptural injunctions. Thus it is said: "The middle person is used for *yuṣmad* (the second person), the highest for *asmad* (the first person), and the first for the remainder. In that context, the application of persons regarding the agent is as follows: "As he has declared, Maheśvara is known; you, seeking this and that, have been present right before him. Having reflected upon your delight in the practice of inauspiciousness, I do not venture to grant you permission."

Regarding the matter at hand: if you think that he might be pleased by you in such a way, then why, O messenger, do you not rely on anger? We shall provide it. Or rather, if among these [options] you two should adopt even the first one, we shall take it into account.

In some cases, it occurs only in the middle [person], as in the case of the intensive repetition (*kriyāsamabhihāra*) through the three [persons]: for example, in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*): "Lunīhi lunīhi" (Cut! cut! — thus he cuts; "alāvīt" (he has cut) or "laviṣyati" (he will cut); "adhīṣvādhīṣva" (Study! study! — thus they two study; "adhyaiṣātām" (they two have studied) or "adhyeṣyete" (they two will study); "rāṣṭram aṭa, maṭham aṭa, khadūram aṭa" (Go to the kingdom, go to the monastery, go to Khadūra) — thus we two wander; "aṭiṣva" (you have wandered) or "aṭiṣyāvaḥ" (we two will wander); "chando 'dhīṣva, vyākaraṇam adhīṣva, niruktam adhīṣva" (Study the Veda, study grammar, study etymology) — thus we two study; "adhyagīṣmahi" (we two have studied) or "adhyeṣyāvahe" (we two will study); "saktūn... (barley meal...).

"Drink! Eat the parched grains! Consume the boiled rice!"—in this manner you have conversed, or you have conversed with, or you will converse with [someone]. In some cases, however, they consider that the *uttama* (first person) is used in jest, as in: "Come, I think you will go by chariot," "She will milk [the cow] for you," "Your father has gone," "Come, I think you will eat rice," "Indeed, you shall not eat," or "He has already eaten with his guests."

But you may think that even in the case of the highest person (*uttamapuruṣa*), it remains only the middle (*madhyama*). In that regard, the meaning here is as follows: "Come, you two think [this], 'O sir, you shall eat rice. However, when there is simultaneous expression (*yugapadvacana*) of multiple persons, the highest person occurs; for example: *sa ca tvaṃ ca pacathaḥ* ("he and you two cook"), *tvaṃ cāhaṃ ca pacāvaḥ* ("you and I cook"), and *sa ca tvaṃ cāhaṃ ca pacāmaḥ* ("he, you, and I cook"). Furthermore, the simultaneous expression of the *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) is understood to pertain only to the domain of meaning (*arthaviṣaya*) because it shares the same referent as a *dvandva* compound, and not to the domain of the word-form itself (*śabdaviṣaya*).

Therefore, he said: "Whether it be I, or Kumbhakarṇa, or you, O bull among Rākṣasas, or Indrajit, or Nikumbha—whoever shall carry such a burden. [The opponent objects: "In that case, since there is no simultaneous expression when the sense is 'or,' the plural form 'vaheyuḥ' (they shall carry) is not appropriate. [The author replies: "It is not so; for in certain instances involving the sense of 'or,' simultaneous expression is observed."

Just as one says "two or three" (*dvitrāḥ*), so too the author of the *Mahābhāṣya* has said: "When 'two' is employed, 'three' is understood; when 'three' is stated, 'two' is understood. This is the speech concerning the five bases (*pañcādhiṣṭhānavāk*). In that case, the plural number is appropriate, or rather, the plural is based on the generality [of the group], just as in the examples: "How many sons do you have? or "How many wives do you have?"—wherein plurality is established with respect to that which is the referent of the pronoun *yuṣmad*, even if it is not explicitly expressed.

The activity of the person (puruṣa) exists [within] primordial nature (prakṛti), and that [activity] is prescribed as follows: "He becomes one with 'you' (tvad-bhāvati)," meaning he becomes entirely you; "they become you" (yuṣmad-bhavanti), meaning they become you. This is an illustrative example. For the purpose of determining the relationship between the person who is the substratum of both the material cause and its modification, it is established that the person is the substratum of the material cause alone, not the substratum of the modification.

By this [rule], *anahaṃ* becoming *ahaṃ* results in *madbhavati*; *avayam* becoming *vayam* results in *asmadbhavanti*; *asaḥ* becoming *saḥ* results in *tadbhavati*; and *anahaṃ* becoming *ahaṃ* results in *madbhavasī*—such forms are also established. What, then, is the justification here? When there is a transformation from one state to another (*abhūtatadbhāve*), there is freedom of usage (*kāmacāraḥ*) regarding whether one intends to express the agency of the material cause (*prakṛti*) or the effect (*vikṛti*). For instance, in some cases, the agency of the effect is intended to be expressed.

Just as gruel is transformed into urine, and just as a lump of gold, when combined with another form, becomes a sacrificial vessel (kuṇḍa) the color of acacia charcoal; for indeed, when the root *klṛp* is used in the sense of "becoming" (*saṃpadyamāna*), the dative case denotes the product (*vikāra*). In the case of the lump of gold, which is the material cause (*prakṛti*), the expression refers to the basis of the vessel. However, in some cases it refers to the material cause itself, as in "the Brahmins become conches" or "the moon has become great."

In this context, if the agency of the *prakṛti* were not intended to be expressed, then since agency would belong solely to the modification (*vikṛti*), namely the assembly (*saṅgha*), the plural number in the word "bhavanti" would not be applicable. Furthermore, in the word "mahadbhūtaḥ," because the word "mahat" would be used in its primary sense, the substitution of *ā* (as prescribed by the rule *ānmahataḥ samānādhikaraṇajātīyayoḥ*) would occur. For the *prakṛti* is sometimes figuratively treated as having the form of a modification, as in the cases: "Indra is the pillar," "Upendra is the pressing-stone."

One [type of modification] is transformative (*pariṇāminī*), such as milk becoming curds. Since that which has fallen away from its prior state and attained a subsequent state possesses activity (*savyāpāratva*) in relation to both the prior and subsequent states, there is an intention to express agency (*kartṛtva*) with respect to the prior state. Consequently, it is understood that terms expressing modification—such as "the aggregate" (*saṅgha*) or "the Great One" (*mahat*)—which take the primal nature (*prakṛti*) as their substrate, are used figuratively (*gauṇatva*). As it has been said: "The Primal Nature attains both magnitude (*mahattva*) and the state of being an aggregate."

"But that [expectation] when required by way of distinction is the establisher of its secondary status. If this is so, then in the case of *atimahatī*, *mahatī saṃpannā*, or *mahadbhūtā brāhmaṇī*, the substitution of the masculine form (*puvadbhāva*) would not apply; for this occurs based on the meaning (*arthāśraya*). However, the substitution of the masculine form is based on the word-form (*śabdāśraya*), as in the rules *goto ṇit* and *autoṃśasoḥ* regarding the word *bāhyīkā*. In the case of the word *go* being present—as in *gostiṣṭhati* or *gāmānaya*—the *vṛddhi* and the substitution of *ā* (ātvam) take place.

These four categories—action (*kriyā*), time (*kāla*), the agent (*kāraka*), and the person (*puruṣa*)—have been declared, each accompanied by its own respective subdivisions. Furthermore, time, which is essentially a substance (*dravya*), has also been mentioned here incidentally; for it is generally employed in various contexts throughout the treatises. Time is included within action, and the person is included in the term "agent" (*kāraka*). Both of these, along with their respective adjuncts, are subsumed under the primary category. They call that the "primary" (*pradhāna*) which is expressed by suffixes such as *ghañ* and others.

"But it resides in the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) along with the meanings of the suffixes. Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Fourfold Meanings beginning with Action," in the *Śṛṅgāraprakāśa* composed by the Great Emperor, the illustrious Bhojadeva.

The fifth [section], the Illumination of the Fourfold Meaning of the Upādhi, etc.: Action (*kriyā*) is the specific activity of the *kārakas* with respect to the meanings of the base (*prakṛti*), the suffix (*pratyaya*), and the defects; the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* express that [action] when it is unconditioned (*anupahita*). Through their mutual non-intermixture, twelve distinct types of action arise as the meanings of the verbal roots (*dhātvartha*), produced by [the variations of] equality, excellence, and deficiency.
