Namely: those without an object (*akarmaka*), those with an internal object (*antaḥkarmaka*), those with a different object (*arthāntarakarmaka*), those with an unmanifested object (*avivakṣitakarmaka*), those with a well-known object (*prasiddhakarmaka*), those with two objects (*dvikarmaka*), those with a well-known agent (*prasiddhakartṛka*), those with an abstract agent (*bhāvakartṛka*), those with an object-agent (*karmakartṛka*), those whose action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthakriya*), those whose action resides in the object (*karmasthakriya*), and those whose action resides in both (*ubhayasthakriya*). These, being each divided into two according to the distinction between non-motion (*aparispanda*) and motion (*parispanda*), become twenty-four in total.

In this regard, it is established that *asti* (to be) is without motion because its agent is indifferent (*udāsīna*); *karoti* (to do) is with motion because its agent is one who instigates (*prayuñjāna*); and *bhavati* (to become) is both with and without motion because its agent is one who undergoes transformation (*vikurvāṇa*). Therefore, roots whose meanings are "being" (*astyartha*), as well as those whose meanings are "subordinate" (*nyagbhūta*) or "downward" (*nyaga*), are intransitive (*akarmaka*). Among these, the former—those without motion—are: *yāti* (he goes), *bhidyate* (it is split), *svadate* (it tastes good), *vartate* (it exists/continues), and *prīyate* (he is pleased).

The latter [verbs] involve physical motion (*saparispanda*), such as "is born," "grows," and "spreads. Those very same [verbs] with internal objects (*antah-karmaka*) lack motion; among them, the former are without motion, such as "lives," "dies," "desires a son" (*putrīyati*), and "breathes" (*prāṇiti*). The latter involve motion, such as "dances," "sighs," "steams," and "weeps. Verbs whose meaning is "to exist" (*asti-karoti-arthāḥ*) and those whose meaning is "to do" or "to become" (*karoti-bhavati-arthāḥ*) have objects that are distinct from their own meanings.

Among these, the former are without physical motion (*aparispanda*), such as: "the wood floats," "he crosses over misfortune," "he crosses over a perverted mind," or "he moves his hand. The latter are with physical motion (*saparispanda*), such as: "it carries a load," "the leaf falls," or "he travels the road. For this very reason, even those [verbs] that do not denote upward movement (*anutkaroti*) can have an intended object (*vivakṣitakarmaka*). Among these, the former are without physical motion, such as: "the name (*saṃjñā*) settles upon the named object (*saṃjñin*)," "the intellect (*buddhi*) settles upon reality (*tattva*)," "he fasts at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*)," or "he fasts for three nights (*trirātra*)."

The latter [actions] involve physical motion (*saparispanda*), such as "Caitra laughs," "Maitra laughs," "the wheel revolves," or "he moves from one place. However, those that are *utkṣepaṇa* (upward throwing) and so forth are purely mental actions (*prasiddhakarmaka*). Among these, the former are without physical motion; for instance, when "he sows" is said, it is understood to mean "seed," and when "he marries" is said, it is understood to mean "a maiden. The latter involve physical motion; for instance, when "he plows" is said, it is understood to mean "a field," and when "he gives birth" is said, it is understood to mean "an embryo."

When there is elevation (*utkaroti*), those [verbs] that possess the quality of being directed downward (*nyagbhāva*) and those that possess the quality of becoming downward (*nyagbhavati*) are precisely the *dvikarmaka* (two-object) verbs. Among these, the former are devoid of motion (*aparispaṇda*), such as: "the mark makes the possessor of the mark known to the knower," or "he conquers a hundred horses for Aśvasena. The latter involve motion (*saparispaṇda*), such as: "he milks milk from the cow," or "he gathers fruits from the tree. Thus, these six varieties of *viyoga* (separation) further result in six varieties of *triyoga* (threefold connection).

In that regard, the roots *ud-asti* and *ud-bhavati* have well-known agents (*prasiddha-kartṛkā*). Among these, the former are devoid of motion (*aparis-pandā*), as when "he burns" is said, fire is understood [as the agent]. The latter involve motion (*saparis-pandā*), as when "he coos" is said, a pigeon is understood; and when "it neighs" is said, a horse is understood. The roots *ni-gam-bhavati*, *karoti*, *ni-gam-asti*, and *karoti* have the abstract state (*bhāva*) as their agent.

Among these, the former are motionless (*aparispanda*), such as *cerasya rujati*, *corasyāmayati*, *coraṃ jvarayati*, and *coraṃ saṃtāpayati*. The latter are characterized by motion (*saparispanda*), such as *bhavati*, *pakṣyati*, *abhavat*, *apakṣīt*, *bhaved api bhavet*, and *syād api syāt*. These [latter] have both object and agent (*karmakartṛka*) and involve either upward movement or downward movement.

Among these, the former are devoid of motion (*aparispanda*), such as "the cow milks itself," "the cow gives birth herself," and "the maiden chooses [a husband] herself. The latter involve motion (*saparispanda*), such as "the elephant scatters [itself]," "the staff raises itself," "the staff bends itself," and "the elephant mounts itself. These are *udastakarotayaḥ* or *udbhavatikarotayaḥ*, wherein the action resides in the agent (*kartṛsthakriyā*).

Among these, the former are those without physical motion (*aparispanda*), such as: "he offers worship as is fitting," "he knows the color," "he sees the form," or "he hears the sound. The latter are those with physical motion (*saparispanda*), such as: "he goes to the village" or "he mounts the horse. The actions residing in the object (*karmastha-kriyā*) consist of either *nyagbhavana* (becoming humble/subordinate) or *utkarṣaṇa* (being raised/exalted). Among these, the former are those without physical motion, such as: "he harms the enemy," "he pleases the friend," "he gladdens the well-wisher," or "he makes the companion happy."

The latter [actions] involve physical motion (*saparispanda*), such as: "he cooks rice," "he splits a granary," "he sharpens or polishes a weapon," or "he whets it"—these involve actions situated on both sides [of the agent]. Among these, the former are those without physical motion (*aparispanda*), such as: "he receives honor" or "he attains merit. The latter are those with physical motion (*saparispanda*), such as: "he eats rice," "he studies his lesson," "he performs penance," or "he accomplishes heaven."

But surely, [forms such as] *bhavati*, *pakṣyati*, *abhavat*, *apākṣīt*, *bhavet*, *api bhavet*, *syāt*, and *api syāt*—these do not have the meaning of "to exist" (*asti*) or "to become" (*bhavati*), but rather they are directly [expressions of] "to exist" and "to become. And since those two denote an action that is not superimposed [upon another], they ought not to function as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). It is replied: because of the root-list (*dhātupāṭha*) stating "as- is in the sense of non-existence" (*asa-bhuvi*) and "bhū- is in the sense of existence" (*bhū-sattāyām*), and because *bhū* is prescribed in place of *as* before an ārdhadhātuka suffix (with the exception of the subsequent application, *anuprayoga*), it is understood that there is indeed a commingling (*saṅkara*) [of the two roots]. Even so, the entry of the meaning of the root *kṛ* ("to do") remains difficult to justify.

This [usage] is also justified because the connection with agency (*kartṛtva*) would otherwise be untenable. But surely, in cases such as *bhavati*, *pakṣyati*, and *apākṣīt*, this is merely the use of the present indicative (*laṭ*). Furthermore, even the use of the verb *as* is seen in instances where the agent is an abstract state (*bhāva*), as in "we exist" (*asti gacchāmo vayam*). This is not so; for we do not say that *as* and *bhū* have abstract states as their agents. Rather, it is the verbs *as*, *bhū*, *pac*, and so forth, that are the agents of existence and cooking. For these, like the class of verbs beginning with *ruj* (to break), become agents of existence (*asti*) even when they are themselves adjuncts (*upādhi*).

However, this much is the distinction: the agency of roots such as *ruj* (to suffer) is expressed by the verbal suffix (*lakāra*) itself, whereas for roots such as *pac* (to cook), it is expressed by a suffix following the verb *bhavati* or *asti*. And just as the meaning of the verbal root has action as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), so too does time. As it has been said: "The past, future, and present states are limiting adjuncts of action; they are understood along with their capacities for the purpose of distinguishing priority and posteriority. That [time], through its divisions into the past and so forth, is twelvefold.

Now, [the past tense] is: *bhūta* (past), *bhūtānadyatana* (past not of today), *bhaviṣyat* (future), *bhaviṣyadanadyatana* (future not of today), *vartamāna* (present), *vartamānānadyatana* (present not of today), *parokṣa* (remote past), *atipanna* (elapsed), *avyakta* (unmanifested), *saṅkīrṇa* (mixed), *prakīrṇa* (scattered), and *viprakīrṇa* (dispersed). Regarding the scope of the *luṅ* (aorist) and other [moods/tenses], the *bhūta* (past) refers merely to what has passed; that *bhūta* is sixfold: *bhūta*, *prakarṣabhūta* (intensive past), *bhūtānadyatana* (past not of today), *abhimānādyatana* (past by convention), *prabandhādyatana* (continuous past), and *sāmīpyādyatana* (proximate past).

Among these, when the specific temporal qualification is not determined, it is simply "become" (*bhūta*), as in: "he drew," "he sat down," "he dwelt," "he heard," "he cooked," or "he has cooked. When excellence is understood from another word, the cognition of [tenses such as] non-recent, remote past, and so forth is disregarded, resulting in a state of excellence; for example: "In this place, formerly, there were students" (*vātsuriha purā chātrāḥ*). When a specific limit is intended to be expressed, it is "recently past" (*anadyatana*); for example: "He went from the other cow-pen" (*anyām agāt maghoṣāt*).

The remainder of the night (*rātriśeṣa*) is considered "present" (*adyatana*) when there is a continuous state of wakefulness (*jāgaraṇasaṃtati*), due to the speaker's identification [with that state], as in: "I have been awake all this night"; because the night has not yet ended, one considers the time to be present. When the cessation of an action is not intended to be expressed, it is "present" by virtue of its continuity (*prabandha*), as in: "He gave food abundantly for as long as he lived. When there is an intended immediate succession of actions, it is "present" by virtue of proximity (*sāmīpya*), as in: "On this very full moon day that has passed, the teacher shall establish the sacred fires."

In this regard, it is traditionally taught that for the two immediately following [conditions], the *laṅ* is not used when there is continuity of action (*kriyāprabandha*) or proximity (*sāmīpya*). Thus, the condition for *laṅ* is a past time that is not "immediate" (*avidyamānādyatana*). That is sixfold: general non-immediate (*sāmānyānadyatana*), specific non-immediate (*viśeṣānadyatana*), non-immediate with recognition (*abhijñānadyatana*), well-known non-evident (*prasiddhāparokṣa*), non-evident in response to a question (*praśnāparokṣa*), and non-evident with the particle *ha* or *śaśvat*. Among these, the "general non-immediate" is that in which the quality of being non-evident (*aparokṣatva*) and so forth is not intended to be expressed. For example: *yāvajjīvaṃ bhūśam annam adāt* ("Throughout his life, he gave food abundantly").

The immediate past (anadyatana) is that which follows immediately upon the action intended to be expressed; for example: "On this very full moon day, the teacher shall establish the sacred fires. Here, it is traditionally taught that the two [past tenses] may function like the immediate past when there is either continuity of action or proximity. Similarly, the cause for the *laṅ* (imperfect) tense is the past non-immediate (bhūtānadyatana). That is sixfold: the general non-immediate, the specific non-immediate, the non-immediate with recognition (*abhijñā*), the well-known unperceived (*praśiddhaparokṣa*), the unperceived in response to a question (*praśnāparokṣa*), and the unperceived with *ha* or *śaśvat* (*haśaśvadaparokṣa*).

Among these, that in which the quality of being remote (*parokṣatva*) and so forth is not intended to be expressed is the "general non-recent past" (*sāmānyānadyatana*). For example: *akarot* (he did), *aśṛṇot* (he heard), *nyaṣīdat* (he sat down), *amutrāvasam* (I lived there), *āsīd idaṃ tamo bhūtam* (this was once darkness), and *rāmo vanam agacchat* (Rāma went to the forest). That in which specific qualities such as remoteness are understood from other words is the "specific non-recent past" (*viśeṣāvadyatana*). For example: *purā chātrā avasan iha* (formerly students lived here). The expression of recognition using *na yadi* and so forth is an exception to the [use of] the *lṛṅ* and *luṅ* suffixes; it is the "non-recent past of recognition" (*abhijñānadyatana*). For example: *smarasi devadatta kāśmīreṣu yad avasāma* (Do you remember, Devadatta, where we lived in Kaśmīra?).

That which is well-known in the world (*lokaprasiddhi*) yet possesses a superimposed notion of immediacy (*āparokṣābhimāna*), while being actually known as remote (*parokṣa*), is "remote-as-though-immediate" (*prasiddhaparokṣa*); for example: *jayajjayanto hūṇān* ("Jayanta conquered the Hūṇas"). That which has its remoteness consumed by a question (*praśna*) is "immediate-by-question" (*praśnāparokṣa*); for example: *kim agacchad Devadattaḥ?* ("Did Devadatta go?"). When the sense of immediacy is subsumed under the meanings of *ha* and *śaśvat*, it is "immediate-by-*ha*-and-*śaśvat*" (*haśaśvadaparokṣa*); for example: *iti hākarot* ("Thus he did") and *śaśvad akarot* ("He did repeatedly"). The future (*anāgata*) alone is the domain of the *lṛṭ* suffix and others; it is divided into "continuous future" (*bhaviṣyat-prabandha*), "recent past" (*adyatana*), "proximate" (*sāmīpya*), and "distinguished recent past" (*pravibhāgādyatana*).

Among these, the general future tense (*sāmānyabhaviṣyat*) has the non-determination of [specific times] such as "today" and so forth; for example: *kariṣyati* ("he will do"), *balir indro bhaviṣyati* ("Bali will become Indra"), *kadā gamiṣyati?* ("When will he go?"), *eṣa gamiṣyāmi* ("I am going here"), *pakṣyan vrajati* ("he goes while intending to cook"), and *pācako vrajati* ("the cook goes"). The specific future tense (*viśeṣabhaviṣyat*) has the determination of a particular [time] such as "today"; for example: *adya gamiṣyāmi* ("I will go today"). The continuous present (*prabandhādyatana*) is that in which the cessation of the action is not intended to be expressed; for example: *yāvajjīvaṃ bhṛśam annaṃ dāsyati* ("He will give food abundantly for as long as he lives").

The "immediate" (*anadyatana*) [past] refers to that which follows the action intended to be expressed, such as immediacy (*sāmūpya*), as in: "On this coming full moon day, the teacher will establish the sacred fires. When there is a statement of a limit (*maryādā*) regarding the future, and when there is a division of time other than days and nights, the "non-immediate" (*anadyatana*) is used optionally for the subsequent division, as in: "On that part of the road which is to be traveled toward Pāṭaliputra, which lies beyond Kauśāmbī, we shall eat rice."

Regarding this coming year, that which precedes the full moon of Āgrahāyaṇī, we shall study there with diligence. In the same way, it should be understood that the option (*vibhāṣā*) applies to the subsequent [period] as well. Only the future that is not of the current day (*avidyamānādyatana*) is the cause for the *luṅ* suffix; thus, the "future not of the current day" (*bhaviṣyadanadyatana*) is sixfold: the general future not of the current day, the future not of the current day involving desire (*lipsā*), and the future not of the current day involving lamentation (*paridevana*). For example: *kartā*, *kartārau*, *kartāraḥ*; *kāritā*, *kāritārau*, *kāritāraḥ*.

The "non-recent" (*anadyatana*) [tense] refers to a distinction understood from another word, as in: "you are a cooker" (*yatā tvaṃ paktā*). The "non-recent" [tense] conditioned by desire (*lipsopādhika*) is as follows: "whoever is going to me, whoever places his feet thus"—this one shall study grammar (*ayaṃ me kālādhyetā*), provided he is not already diligent. Regarding the division of time, the phrase "not including days and nights" (*cānahorātrāṇām*) refers to a distinction of priority and posteriority concerning days and nights. For example: "In that which is the coming year, in the period prior to the Āgrahāyaṇī festival, we shall go to Pāṭaliputra."

That very same [topic] concerning the specification of time-periods (*adhvavibhāṣā*) is the "pertaining to the specification of time-periods" (*adhvāvibhāṣīya*). This refers to a time-period yet to be traversed, such as: "Pāṭaliputra is to be gone to; beyond Kauśāmbī, we shall drink flour-water there. The present tense (*vartamāna*), which is the cause for the *laṭ* suffix and others, has as its object an action that has been attained but not yet ceased. It is sixfold: the general present (*sāmānyavartamāna*), the specific present (*viśeṣavartamāna*), the non-interrupted present (*avipāmavartamāna*), the present of what has begun but not yet ended (*pravṛttoparata*), the present of what has occurred and not yet ceased (*vṛttāvirata*), and the eternally occurring present (*nityavṛtta*).

Among these, the "general present" (*sāmānya-vartamāna*) disregards distinctions such as the cessation of an action; for example: *asti* (he is), *bhavan* (being), *kurvāṇāḥ* (doing), *pacyamānaḥ* (being cooked), *pavamānaḥ* (purifying), *patram udvahamānaḥ* (carrying a leaf). The "particular present" (*viśeṣa-vartamāna*) concerns specific actions, such as: *porakṣāt* (he protects) or *ajīvat* (he lived). The "present of continuity" (*avirāma-vartamāna*) refers to the uninterrupted persistence of an intended action, as in: *prāsādaṃ karoti* (he is building a palace). The "present of interrupted activity" (*pravṛttoparata*) refers to the cessation of an intended undertaking, as in: *jīvantaṃ mārayati* (he kills one who is already living).

That which has no intended cessation of its activity is "uninterrupted in its occurrence" (*vṛttāvirata*), as in: "Just as boys play. That which possesses an uninterrupted continuity of activity is "perpetually occurring" (*nityapravṛtta*), as in: "The mountain stands. Even in the case of actions that have not yet occurred or have already passed, the present tense (*laṭ*) is applicable because the state of being present is brought about by the employment of another word; thus, the condition for the present tense is "the present time not belonging to the current day" (*anadyatana*). However, [in the specific context of the *nityapravṛtta*], it is the "present time belonging to the current day" (*adyatana*).

That [subject] is sixfold: the object of desire (*lipsā-viṣaya*), the object of hope (*āśaṃsā-viṣaya*), that which is connected with *pura*, that which is connected with *snā*, that which is connected with both, and that which is connected with neither. Among these, the object of desire is, for example: "He who gives me alms goes to heaven; who gives me alms goes to the world? Likewise, which one among them gives me alms? Which one gives me alms? The object of hope is, for example: "If it rains, the rice will flourish. That which is connected with *pura* is, for example: "The students lived here formerly."

The *smayogīya* (that which pertains to memory) is, as our teacher says, like [the statement]: "Thus it was said by the preceptor. The *ubhayayogīya* (that which pertains to both) is, for example, as in the phrase: "In Naḍeḍḍhattha, the city was studied. The *anubhayayogīya* (that which pertains to neither) is, for example, as Rāghava speaks: "Then... That which is real (*bhūta*) is the object of the indicative mood (*liṅ*). It is beyond the senses; thus, it is "beyond perception" (*parokṣa*). It is sixfold: self-beyond-perception (*svaparokṣa*), other-beyond-perception (*paraparokṣa*), self-and-other-beyond-perception (*svaparaparokṣa*), mind-beyond-perception (*manaḥparokṣa*), means-of-knowledge-beyond-perception (*pramāṇaparokṣa*), and determination-beyond-perception (*nirṇayaparokṣa*).

Among these, *svaparokṣa* (the speaker's own indirect past) is as follows: *cakāra*, *cakāra*, *cakāsāñcakāra*, or "students lived here in the past. *Paraparokṣa* (the other's indirect past) with respect to another is as follows: "Who conquered the Kaliṅgas?", "Who saw the Brāhmaṇas?", or "I did not go to the Kaliṅgas. *Svaparaparokṣa* (the indirect past of both self and other) with respect to both is as follows: "Vāsudeva slew Kaṃsa," "Hara burnt Tripura," or "Mādhava crushed Vṛtra."

The particle *yathā* is used when there is an expectation of recollection (*smaraṇāpekṣayā*) and the action was not witnessed by the speaker, as in: *śaśvac cakāra*, *iti ha*, or *śaśvac cakāra iti*. Furthermore, when a question concerns a recent time, it is treated as if it were not witnessed, as in: "Did she go to his side? What did she say appropriately? Did he hear her words? I ask, 'What [did you do], O friend? The conditional (*lṛṅ*) is the indicator (*nimitta*) for the non-occurrence (*atipatti*) of an action in the future, past, or present.

It is sixfold, due to the distinction between pure and mixed forms of the future, the past, and the conditional (bhaviṣyat-bhūta-vartamāna-kriyātipatti). Among these, one employs [the conditional] having understood through some sign that the action is purely future and conditional; for example: "If it had not been struck by the thunderbolt, it would have fallen"; "How indeed would His Honor have caused the Vṛṣala to sacrifice?"; or "If he had gone by the right-hand road, the cart would not have overturned."

And had you conducted yourselves according to the path pointed out by the virtuous, they would not have failed to conduct themselves properly, nor would there have been a lack of prosperity at the end of their journey. Likewise, even though it was a mixed marriage, Sītā would surely have become the wife of Rāma—that moon among the sons of Daśaratha, who possessed a merit-glorious splendor worthy of her—had the noble Lord of Tryambaka, the wielder of the bow, not made the wager irrevocable by the stringing of the bow. Some, perceiving the conditional past tense (*kriyātipatti*) as being purely conveyed by the suffix alone, employ it [in this way].

I cannot believe that you would have caused a *vṛṣala* to perform a sacrifice; nor do I think it possible that you would not have sprinkled the oblation there. And as for that which is difficult to speak of: may he who acted with such power against you not become a deer; had the Lord of the Host not swiftly repelled him with a sharp-winged arrow? Thus, even though they were mixed together, this pair—which possesses a mutually desirable splendor—would not have been brought about [if you had not acted].

In this pair [of past tenses], the Lord’s effort to prescribe the form would have been in vain for his subjects. Even when there is a pure *kriyātipatti* (past conditional) established by some means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), he employs it; as in: *utākariṣyat*, *apyakariṣyat*. And as in: "How could the elephant not have supported the earth with hoods as soft as lotus-stalks, had you not held it from the very base of the netherworld? Likewise, even in the case of a mixed [form], as in: "The earth, its bond to the king of mountains severed, would have sunk into the water."

"O Nārāyaṇa, had you not been weary, you would not have been overcome. Thus, the unmanifest (*avyakta*) is that in which the distinctions of past, future, and so forth are concealed. It is sixfold, being the object of the *liṅ* (optative), the *loṭ* (imperative), the *laṭ* (present indicative), the *lṛṭ* (future indicative), the suffixes beginning with *tavya*, and the suffixes beginning with *tumun*.

Among those [moods], examples of *liṅ* and *lṛt* are as follows: "He might make a mat" (*kaṭaṃ kuryāt*), "May he live long" (*ciraṃ jīyāt*), "How could His Honor cause a low-born man to sacrifice? (*kathaṃ tatrabhāvān vṛṣalaṃ yajayet*), "Would he even split a mountain with his head? (*api śirasā parvataṃ bhidyāt*), "I expect that Your Honor will eat" (*saṃbhāvayāmi bhuñjīta bhavān*), and "It is time for Your Honor to eat" (*kālo 'yaṃ yad bhūñjīta bhavān*). Examples of *loṭ* and *lṛt* are as follows: "If the teacher comes" (*upādhyāyaśced āgacchati*), or "he will come" (*āgantā* or *āgamiṣyati*), then you should study the Veda in this manner (*atha tvaivaṃ chando 'dhīṣva*).

"Prepare the mat; the time has come for you to prepare the mat. May you live long! What can you do here? Cut it, cut it!"—thus he cuts, or [the forms] *alāvīt* (he has cut) or *laviṣyati* (he will cut). Regarding the suffixes *laṭ*, *liṭ*, and *luṅ*: as in "When does he eat? (*kadā bhuṅkte*), "At what time does he eat? (*karhi bhuṅkte*); "Does His Honor officiate at the sacrifice for a Śūdra? (*api nāma bhavān vṛṣalaṃ yājayati*); "Does His Honor ever officiate at the sacrifice for a Śūdra? (*jātu tatrabhavān vṛṣalaṃ yājayati*); "Is my mother alive? (*kañcijjīvati me mātā*); or "Whom do riches not delight? (*kaṃ vā vibhūtayo na madayanti*).

"Will a blind man indeed climb a mountain? Or will a staff indeed fall [of its own accord]? Who indeed is that *vṛṣala* whom your honor intends to cause to sacrifice? I do not tolerate it, I do not believe it, I do not conceive it—that your honor will cause a *vṛṣala* to sacrifice; having applied your soul to each [task] individually, how, O Lord, would you not know?"

The domain of [suffixes] such as *tavya* is, for example: "The Veda is to be studied" (*svādhyāyo 'dhyetavyaḥ*), "A Brahmin is not to be killed" (*brāhmaṇo na hantavyaḥ*), "Ancestors are to be saluted" (*pitaro vandanīyāḥ*), "Teachers are to be honored" (*guravo mānanīyāḥ*), "One should not neglect one's duty" (*kṛtyaṃ na bāvayet*), and "One should not do what ought not to be done" (*kāryaṃ na kuryāt*).

The domain of [suffixes] such as *tumun* is, for example: "He desired/wishes/will desire to eat" (*bhoktum aicchat*, *icchati*, *eṣiṣyati vā*); "Having eaten, he went/is going/has gone" (*bhuktvā abrajīt*, *vrajati*, *vrajiṣyati vā*); "Having studied, he sat/is sitting/will sit" (*adhītyāsnāsīt*, *sīdati*, *satsyati vā*); "He reviled him with the cry 'thief! (*coraṅkāram ākrukṣat*, *ākrośati*, *ākokṣyati vā*); "He desires to sit, drinking repeatedly" (*pāyaṃpāyam āsisīṣṭa*, *āste*, *āsiṣyate vā*); and "He nourished/is nourishing/has nourished with wealth" (*rai-poṣam apuṣat*, *puṣyati*, *pokṣyati vā*).

That which is mixed with another point of time is "confused" (*saṅkīrṇa*). Because it possesses multiple forms, it cannot be pointed out [as a single category], yet it is illustrated as being sixfold for the sake of completing the classification. An example of the past and future non-proximate (bhūta-bhaviṣyad-anadyatana) is: "He will have begotten two sons who will sacrifice at the Agniṣṭoma. An example of the past and future proximate (bhūta-bhaviṣyad-adya-tana) is: "He will go either today or tomorrow. An example of the past and future non-proximate is: "He will have begotten two sons who will sacrifice at the Agniṣṭoma. [Note: The phrase *yathānyebhyo vā* refers to other such combinations, and *abūkṣmabi* appears to be a corruption; the intended meaning concerns the various temporal mixtures.]

An example of the past non-remote future (*bhūtānadyatana-bhaviṣyat*) is: "It was as if the task were already accomplished. An example of the present remote (*vartamāna-parokṣa*) is: "O Lord, restrain your anger, restrain it!"—while these words were still traveling through the air of the gods, that fire born from the eye of Bhava reduced Madana to nothing but ashes. An example of the future, present, and remote past is: "Those [rivers], roaring incessantly upon the earth with their embankments, by which they will flood everything on all sides..."

He saw those waters from a certain spot as they were being drunk by clouds from the ocean that was drinking them in. Thus, there is a "scattered" (prakīrṇa) usage when the present tense is used for the future or the past. Regarding the entry into the future: in the sense of hope (*āśaṃsā*), as in, "If the teacher comes, we shall study grammar. In the sense of desire (*lipsā*), as in, "He feeds [the guest] while he is still angry. In connection with *purā*, as in, "He goes away before [he] eats," or "before [he] departs."

Regarding proximity (*sāmīpya*): for example, "When will you go to the village? [The reply is: "I am going now; know me as one who is indeed going. Likewise, regarding the entry of the past into the present (*bhūtānupraveśa*), there is proximity to the past, as in: "When did you come from the village? [The reply is: "I am coming now; know me as one who is indeed coming. Regarding the response to a question (*pṛṣṭāprativacana*): for example, "O sir, have you made the mat? [The reply is: "O Devadatta, I am indeed making the mat," or "I am indeed making it. There is a confusion (*viprakīrṇa*) of the future entering the past and the past entering the future.

It occurs when a future event enters into the past, as for example: "Do you remember, Devadatta, how we were to dwell in Kashmir? Do you recall that we were to dwell in Kaliṅga and eat rice there? Do you remember that we were to dwell in Kashmir and that we were to eat rice there? Or, for instance, as one remembers: "When you were the son of Daśaratha, you will slay that abductor of my wife at the very gates of Laṅkā, after crossing the ocean turbid with surging waves."

The penetration of the future into the present is as follows: "Do not do it," "Do not have done," or "If it had rained, the rice would have ripened. Or, for example: "Let there be no fear in your mind that 'I am the one who will kill him,' nor should any woman named Samīntinī give birth to such a son; yet this one born from your face has become a lover of frowns, and the lineage of Vasudeva has been reduced to nothing but its name."

Now, how is it that even when [the action] is eternally present, one employs linguistic usage pertaining to the past and future—such as "the mountains stood" (*tasthuḥ*) or "they will stand" (*sthāsyanti*), or "there was a well on the path" (*mārge kūpo 'bhūt*) and "there will be a well" (*kūpo bhaviṣyati*)? It is said in reply: regarding those kings who existed in the realms of the Haihayas and others, because their actions have passed away, one employs a suffix denoting the past time when there is a desire to express a connection with them, such as "even in the kingdom of the Haihayas, the mountains stood" (*hehayarājye 'pi parvatā iti tasthuḥ*).

Likewise, regarding those kings who will exist in future manvantaras, because their actions will belong to the future, he employs a verbal suffix denoting the future time with the intention of expressing that connection: "When Bali shall become Indra, then the mountains will likewise remain standing. In this way, since even a well is connected to the acts of seeing [water] in the past and future, its connection with the verbs "it was" (*abhūt*) and "it will be" (*bhaviṣyati*) is not contradictory.

Even the *upagraha* (voice) is merely an adjunct (*upādhi*) to the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*). What, then, is this? It is a specific meaning that serves as the cause for the application of the *parasmaipada*, *ātmanepada*, or both; it is the distinction between the *ātmanepada* and *parasmaipada*. As it has been said: "That distinction of meaning which is sometimes perceived from the *ātmanepada* or even from the *parasmaipada*, they consider that to be the *upagraha*. For example: *nāthati* vs. *nāthate*, *śapati* vs. *śapate*, *āhvayati* vs. *āhvayate*, and *pratijānāti* vs. *pratijānīte*.

In these cases, there are differences in meaning: *nāth* is used in the sense of a blessing (*āśis*), *śap* in the sense of reproaching (*upālambhana*), *āṅ-ḍīp* in the sense of rivalry (*spardhā*), and with *sam* and *prati* it takes the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) when not expressing reflection (*anādhyāna*); otherwise, the root *jñā* takes the middle voice, while in the remaining cases it takes the active voice (*parasmaipada*). Similarly: *miṇḍo bhīṣayate* (the eunuch terrifies himself), *kuñcikayainaṃ bhāyayati* (he frightens him with a key); *jaṭilo vismāpayate* (the matted-haired ascetic astonishes himself), *matyainaṃ vismāpayati* (he astonishes him with intelligence). Also: *śyeno vartikāmullāpayate* (the hawk makes the quail cry out), *kastvāmullāpayati* (who makes you cry out?); *saṃpravadante grāmyāḥ* (the villagers converse together), *saṃprapadanti śakunayaḥ* (the birds fly together).

In this regard, there is a distinction in meaning: for the roots *bhī* (to fear) and *smi* (to smile), the *ātmanepada* is used when expressing fear caused by a cause; for the root *lī*, when expressing honoring or making firm; and for the root *vad*, when expressing the simultaneous utterance of articulate speech. In these cases, the *ātmanepada* is employed, whereas in the remaining instances, the *parasmaipada* is used. This should be inferred in other cases as well. Now, one might ask: regarding the statement, "In some cases, a difference in meaning is understood from the *ātmanepada*," what is the purpose of the inclusion of the word "in some cases" (*kvacit*)? It is said in reply: [The remainder of the passage would follow here.]

The application of the *parasmaipada*, *ātmanepada*, and both sets of endings (*ubhayapada*) occurs in six ways: caused by the verbal root (*prakṛti*), caused by the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha*), caused by the suffix (*pratyaya*), caused by the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*), caused by an augment (*upaskāra*), and caused by the meaning of an augment (*upaskārārtha*). Among these, the status of being a cause for the comprehension of meaning exists as appropriate in those cases where the meaning is the cause; however, it does not exist in the remaining cases. In some instances, [the author] indicates this by means of non-mention (*anagrahaṇa*).

In this regard, the application of the *ātmanepada* [middle voice] is based on the original root (*prakṛti*) as follows: "The *ātmanepada* occurs after roots marked with an indicatory low-pitched vowel (*anudātta*) or the suffix *ṅit*; also after the desideratives of *jñā*, *śru*, *smṛ*, and *dṛś*"—as in *edhate*, *cyavate*, *susmūrṣate*, and *didṛkṣate*. The application is based on the meaning of the root (*prakṛtyartha*) as follows: "Also in the senses of 'making manifest' and 'consenting'; *bhuja* except in the sense of 'protecting'; *pralambhate* after the roots *gṛdh* and *vañc*; and in the sense of reciprocal action (*karmavyatīhāra*)"—as in *tiṣṭhate*, *bhuṅkte*, *gandhāyate*, and *vyatilunīte*.

An example conditioned by a prefix (*pratyaya*) is as follows: *jeḥ* after *vi* and *pari*; *sthaḥ* after *sam*, *ava*, and *pra-vi*; *sam* when joined with the third case; *kṛñaḥ* after *mithyā* when meaning repetition; *vijayate*, *parājayate*; *saṃtiṣṭhate*, *avatiṣṭhate*, *pratiṣṭhate*, *vitiṣṭhate*; *aśvena sañcarate*; *padaṃ mithyākārayati*.

An example caused by an accessory meaning (*upaskāra-artha*) is as follows: *vi-* in the sense of moving the feet (*pādaviharaṇa*), *āṅ-* in the sense of lifting up (*udbhramaṇa*), *upa-* in the sense of performing a mantra (*mantrakaraṇa*), and *dāṇ-* with *saṃ* and *pra* in the sense of the fourth case (*caturthyarthe*). For instance: *vī gacchati*, *ākramate jyotiḥ*, *sāvitrīm upatiṣṭhate*, and *dāsyā saṃyacchate*. An example caused by the verbal root itself (*prakṛti-nimitta*) in the case of the *parasmaipada* (active voice) is as follows: "The *parasmaipada* occurs after the remaining roots when used in the sense of the agent" (*śeṣātkartari parasmaipadam*). For instance: *bhavati*, *vyatihasanti*, *vyatiharanti*, and *parasparasya vyati-*.

An example caused by the meaning of a suffix (*pratyayārtha-nimitta*) is as follows: for the roots *kuṣ* and *rañj*, the suffix *śyan* is applied and the *parasmaipada* (active voice) occurs according to the rule "for those in the eastern [tradition]"; and for the remaining [roots], the *parasmaipada* occurs in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), as in: "the cloth colors itself" (*rajyati vastraṃ svayameva*), "the foot pains itself" (*kuṣyati pādaḥ svayameva*), and "the cloth is colored" (*rajyate vastram*), "the foot is pained" (*kuṣyate pādaḥ*). An example caused by an augment (*upaskāra-nimitta*) is as follows: after the prefixes *anu* and *parā* with the root *kṛ*; and when *itaretara* or *anyonya* are used as accompanying words (*upapada*), as in: "he imitates" (*anukaroti*), "he overcomes" (*parākaroti*), "they cut each other's [hair]" (*itaretarasya vyatilunanti*), and "they cut one another's [hair]" (*anyonyasya vyatilunanti*).

An example caused by the meaning of an *upaskāra* (auxiliary) is as follows: *śam-* [is used] when there is no sound; *āṅ-ud-* when there is no moving of the mouth; *ud-* when there is no upward action; *pra-* and others [are used] with *yaj-* when it refers to things other than those beginning with *aja-* or *antara-*, provided they are not sacrificial vessels—as in "the carts move along together" (*saṃkrīḍanti śakaṭāḥ*), "the tiger opens its mouth" (*vyāghro mukhaṃ vyādadāti*), "he rises from his seat" (*āsanād uttiṣṭhati*), and "he employs the sacrificial vessels" (*yajñapātrāṇi prayunakti*). An example caused by the root itself in connection with both voices (*ubhayapada*) is as follows: *vākyaṣ-*; or, when not preceded by a prefix (*anupasarga*), as in *lohitāyati* or *lohitāyate*, and *krāmati* or *kramate*.

An example caused by the meaning of the root (*prakṛtyartha*) is as follows: "optionally after an intransitive verb" (*vibhāṣākarmakāt*), and "optionally in the sense of idle chatter" (*vibhāṣā vipralāpe*): *uparamati* / *uparamate*; "the astrologers speak together" (*saṃpravadanti mauhūrtāḥ*) / "the astrologers speak together" (*saṃpravadante mauhūrtāḥ*). An example caused by the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) is as follows: "he becomes attached" (*rajāyati*) / "he is attached" (*rajyate*); "he is angry" (*kuṣyati*) / "he is angry" (*kuṣyate*). [This is] because of the rule: "The suffix *śyan* and the Parasmaipada endings are used for the roots *kuṣ* and *rañj* in the sense of the agent-as-object (*karmakartṛ*) among the Eastern grammarians. An example caused by an augment (*upasarga*) is as follows: "after the prefix *ud*, optionally with the roots *as* and *ūh*" (*upasargādasyatyūhyor vā*): *udasyati* / *udasyate*; *samūhati* / *samūhate*.

An example caused by the sense of "accessory" (*upaskāra*) occurs, for instance, in the case of elision (*lup*): when the meaning is understood through a co-occurring word (*upapada*), one says *bhikṣuko brāhmaṇākulam upatiṣṭhati* or *upatiṣṭhate*, and *brāhmaṇaḥ svaṃ yajñaṃ yajati* or *yajate*. In this way, other specific adjuncts to the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛtyartha-upādhi*) are to be understood, such as cause (*hetu*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), repetition (*abhīkṣṇya*), intensity (*bhṛśārtha*), censure (*garhā*), crookedness (*kauṭilya*), totality (*sākalya*), priority in time (*pūrvakālatā*), purpose (*tādarthya*), and so forth.

For example: *adhīyānaḥ* (while studying), *vasitaḥ* (having dwelt), *pacann āste* (he sits while cooking), *punaḥ-punaḥ paṭhati* (he recites again and again), *pāpaṭhyate* (he recites repeatedly), *punaḥ-punaḥ pacati* (he cooks again and again), *pāpacyate* (he cooks repeatedly), *garhitaṃ dahati* (he burns contemptibly), *dandahyate* (he burns intensely), *kuṭilaṃ krāmati* (he moves crookedly), *caṅkramyate* (he walks to and fro), *kanyā-darśaṃ varayati* (he chooses [a bride] while looking at a girl), *bhuktvā vrajati* (having eaten, he goes), and *bhoktuṃ vrajanti* (they go in order to eat). In this way, these forms of verbal roots—which are adjuncts to the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*)—become adjuncts precisely to the meaning of their own suffixes (*pratyaya*), which are themselves forms of suffixes.

In the case of nominal stems (*prātipadika*), however, there exist qualifiers (*upādhi*) such as gender, number, measure, grammatical relation (*kāraka*), vocative, concomitance, purpose, cause, indication, and so forth, which are distinct even from their own primary meaning. Since these will be described immediately following [the discussion of] the meanings of suffixes, the meanings of nominal stems, and the meanings of the stems themselves, they are not elaborated upon here. Now, regarding the qualifiers of the meaning of suffixes: among those, the persons (*puruṣa*) have been stated under the qualifiers of *kāraka*, and number (*saṅkhyā*) will be explained first.

Furthermore, there are other conditions for this [optative suffix], namely: injunction (*vidhi*), invitation (*nimantraṇa*), request (*adhīṣṭa*), inquiry (*saṃpraśna*), entreaty (*prārthana*), command (*praiṣa*), permission (*atisarga*), proper time (*prāptakāla*), capability (*śakti*), worthiness (*arha*), and censure (*garhā*).

For example: *agnihotraṃ juhuyāt* (one should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice); *iha bhuñjīta* (one should eat here); *iha bhāvān āstām* (let the two of you, Bhāva and [the other], sit here); *bhāvaṃ māṇavakam adhyāpayet* (one should teach the young student Bhāva); *kiṃ nu khalu vyākaraṇam adhīyīya* (what indeed should I study? grammar!); *itaś chando labheya ahaṃ bhikṣām* (from here may I obtain alms for the sake of Vedic study); *ārśasanaṃ api prārthanaiva* (even the act of requesting is a form of prayer); *ciraṃ jīvyāḥ* (may you live long!); *grāmaṃ gaccha* (go to the village); *gacchānujñāto 'si* (you are permitted to go); *kuru kaṭam* (make a mat); *prāptaḥ te kālaḥ kaṭakaraṇe* (the time has come for you to make a mat); *bhavān khalu śatruṃ hanyāt* (your honor should indeed slay the enemy); *khalu tatrabhavān bhāraṃ vahet* (surely your honor would carry the burden); *kathaṃ nu vāma* (how indeed shall we speak?).

"In that case, let his honor officiate at the sacrifice for a *vṛṣala*. In this manner, other [suffixes] are also to be understood as denoting: habit (*tacchīla*), duty (*taddharma*), performing an action well (*tatsādhukārin*), cause (*hetu*), favorability (*ānulomya*), ability (*śakti*), age (*vayas*), speaking (*vacana*), difficulty (*kṛcchra*), undertaking (*anudyamana*), artisan (*śilpin*), characteristic mark (*lakṣaṇa*), gender (*liṅga*), and so forth.

For example, [the following are] due to public censure: "The Śrāviṣṭhāyanas are shaven-headed ascetics"; "He adorned the bride with ornaments"; "Knowledge that brings fame"; "A wife who obeys commands"; "An elephant-killer soldier"; "A prince wearing armor"; "One who maintains the Upaniṣad"; "A son who inherits a share"; "A dancing girl is a courtesan"; "A sectarian mark that kills its owner"; "The speech of a fool"; "The etymology of Pāṇini"; "The composition of Kālidāsa. This is the iron-like metaphorical adjunct (*ayomayopādhi*).

That [suffix] is also of infinite varieties due to its divisions such as name (*saṃjñā*), genus (*jāti*), appearance (*prabhāsa*), measure (*parimāṇa*), gambling (*dyūta*), non-failure (*abhreṣa*), language (*bhāṣā*), meter (*chandas*), mantra, Brāhmaṇa, benediction (*āśis*), and treasury (*utkośa*). For example: *ticūka* and *ca* in the sense of a name, as in *bhadrabhūti* and *devadatta*; *hastā* and *puroḍā* [in the sense of a genus]; the second case ending in the Brāhmaṇa, as in "on that day they should gamble with their companions" (*tadahassahāyān dīvyeyuḥ*) and "he gambles for a four-year-old mare" (*praṣṭhauhīṃ dīvyati*); the suffix *-vun* in the sense of a benediction, as in *jīvatāt* → *jīvakaḥ* and *nandatāt* → *nandakaḥ*.

In the case of *māṅcākrośe* (the prohibition of abuse), the suffix *ṇyani* is applied after the verb *ā-kruś* (to revile): "May he not live—he who lives even while consumed by the pain of being despised by others. [As it is said: "Let there be no birth at all for that one who causes distress to his mother. In this way, other instances such as envy (*asūyā*), consent (*saṃmati*), anger (*kopana*), reproach (*kutsana*), censure (*bhartsana*), affliction (*vādhā*), modes (*prakāra*), hardship (*kṛcchra*), synonyms (*paryāya*), worthiness (*arhaṇa*), and origin (*utpatti*) are to be understood. Regarding envy in verbal expressions, for example: "O student, O student! You are handsome, O handsome one! Your handsomeness is empty!"

*Saṃmati* (agreement/approbation) is, for example: "O young man, O young man, you are handsome, truly handsome; you are indeed beautiful. *Kopa* (anger) is, for example: "O young man, O young man, you ill-mannered one, you ill-mannered one! Now you shall know, you fool! *Kutsana* (reproach) is, for example: "O spear-bearer, O spear-bearer! O staff-bearer, O staff-bearer! Your spear is empty. *Bhartsana* (threatening abuse) is, for example: "Thief, thief! Wretch, wretch! I shall kill you!"

*Ābādha* (affliction) is, for example, as in *gatagatā naṣṭanaṣṭā*, where someone, being tormented by the departure and so forth of a beloved or an unbeloved, employs [the repetition]. *Prakāra* (manner) is, for example, as in *paṭupaṭu* or *bhītabhīta*; this occurs when an inferior quality is compared to a quality that is fully perfected. *Akṛcchra* (absence of difficulty) is, for example, as in *sukhaduḥkhena dadāti* or *priyāpriyeṇa dadāti*, which means he gives without being afflicted.

Examples such as *pāramparya* (tradition), *ādi* (beginning), and so forth are as follows: *bhavataḥ śāyikā* (your lying down), *arhati bhavān ikṣubhakṣikām* (you deserve a meal of sugarcane), *ukṣubhakṣikāṃ me dhārayasi* (you owe me a meal of sugarcane), and *udapādīkṣubhikṣikā* (a meal of sugarcane was provided). Furthermore, this entire elaboration of secondary meanings (*upādhiprapañca*) is explained in three ways: the qualifier of the action (*dhamryupādhi*), the qualifier of the property (*dharmopādhi*), and the miscellaneous qualifier (*prakīrṇopādhi*). Among these, [the suffix] *in* is applied after the root *kṛ* when combined with *stamba* and *śakṛt* to denote rice and a calf respectively; [the suffixes] *amu* and *ap* are applied after *stamba* and *karṇa* to denote a bamboo thicket and an ear-ring respectively; and [the suffix *ṭak*] is applied to denote an elephant and a spy, and so forth.

Just as a rice plant causes a stalk in the field, a calf produces dung in the house, a slanderer causes trouble in the kingdom, or a rutting elephant causes havoc in the forest; so too, when a quality is conditioned by its context (*dharmyupādhi*), it is said: "The root *sṛ* takes the suffix *ap* in the sense of procreation (*prajane*)," and "the root *aj* takes the suffix *ap* after *sam* and *ud* in the sense of cattle (*paśuṣ*"). An example of a quality conditioned by its context (*dharmopādhi*) is: "The cowherd’s assembly (*samajas*) is with the cows, and the driving out (*udaja*) is with the bulls. This is my "excellent cow" (*gomatallikā*), which occurs at the right moment and for whom there is a place [to roam].

[The rule] "In the sense of contempt regarding the object of the verb *man* (to think), [the sixth case is used optionally] with reference to living beings; and when there is an indication of a state (*bhāva-lakṣaṇa*) involving excessive contempt, the sixth case is also used. An example of a scattered (*prakīrṇa*) qualifier is as follows: "Hara does not consider you even as much as a blade of grass while he looks at the boat; even while the world-protectors look on, he drinks the oblation at the sacrifice. The meaning of the suffixes expressed by *tiṅ*, *kṛt*, and *taddhita* is primary (*pradhāna*). That [primary meaning] is threefold: its own meaning (*svārtha*), the relation (*sambandhin*), and the factor of action (*kāraka*). Among these, the meaning of the base (*prakṛtyartha*) itself is its own meaning (*svārtha*).

That [meaning] is threefold: the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), and the suffix-meaning (*pratyayārtha*). Among these, the meaning of the verbal root is threefold: state (*bhāva*), action (*kriyā*), and the factor of action (*kāraka*). Of those, state is twofold: substantial (*sattvabhūta*) and non-substantial (*asattvabhūta*). Of these two, that which is connected with gender and number is substantial; for example, the word *vacana* (speech) is so called because it is not seen even when one is in close proximity to speech. Furthermore, the covering of a limb by means of a piece of cloth is the "offering of a limb" (*aṅgasamarpaṇa*).

It is devoid of gender and number, and is not a substantive entity; for instance, as you were permitted by the serene Great Sage after being duly instructed—"O you who have been duly instructed, it is time for you to go home. For this is the time to transition to your second refuge, which is capable of providing all assistance. Action is twofold: pure (*śuddhā*) and mixed (*saṅkīrṇā*). Of these two, the pure is that which is unassociated with a *kāraka* (participant in action), as in: "The young woman’s bud-like lower lip, having been bitten by her beloved—which was like a rival in its freshness—chirped out shrilly with her hand, whose trembling bangles were like aching [limbs]."

How does it not cause anguish in the hearts of young women, O slender one, when this pair of breasts—possessing the form of the goal [of beauty] yet having attained the state of being the agent [of comparison]—bears a resemblance to the frontal globes of a pair of elephant calves? Or how does it not fever the youth here, as your pair of thighs, possessing the luster of molten, beautiful gold, draws away the heat [from his body]? The *kāraka* (grammatical participant) is of two kinds: that which pertains to a restricted verbal root (*dhātu*) and that which pertains to unrestricted verbal roots.

Regarding those two [types of *dhvani*], that which has a fixed word-meaning as its object is illustrated by: "Though her emotion was not concealed, she was unable to close her eyes when looking at him; for, fearing the destruction of the auspiciousness [of her marriage], her eyes were filled with tears like blue lotuses disturbed by a few grains of husk. That which has an unfixed word-meaning as its object is illustrated by: "When I stood before her, her gaze was withdrawn; her smile arose under some other pretext; her conduct was restrained by modesty; thus, she neither revealed her passion nor did she conceal it. The meaning of the nominal stem (*pratipadikārtha*) is threefold: explicit (*vyakta*), implicit (*avyakta*), and doubtful (*saṃdigdha*).

Among these, the production and non-production of a derivative (*pratyaya*) are indistinguishable [from the primary]; that [derivative] is of two kinds: having the same gender as it (*talliṅga*) and having a different gender (*anyaliṅga*). Of these two, an example of having the same gender is: *mana eva mānasam* (the mind itself is "mental"), *bandhureva bāndhavaḥ* (a kinsman is "related"), and *yava eva yāvakaḥ* (barley is "barley-gruel"). An example of having a different gender is: *upāya eva aupayikam* (a means is "suitable"), *deva eva devatāḥ* (a god is "deity"), and *devataiva daivatam* (a deity is "divine object"). The unmanifest (*avyakta*) is of two kinds: that which has abandoned its own form (*ujjhitasvarūpa*) and that which has not abandoned its own form (*anujjhitasvarūpa*).

In this regard, an example of one whose own form (*svarūpa*) is abandoned is as follows: *veśāla-chaṅkaṭac-au*, *saṃ-prod-aś-ca kaṭat*, and *upādhibhyāṃ tyakan-nāsannārūḍhayoḥ*. For instance: *viśālam*, *viśaṅkaṭam*, *prakaṭam*, *vikaṭam*, *upatyakā*, and *adhityakā*. Here, by means of the prefixes (*upasarga*), the original form—such as "immeasurability" and so forth—is abandoned. An example of one whose own form is not abandoned is as follows: *vatsokṣāśvarṣabhebhyastanutve*, *kāsūgoṇībhyāṃ ṣṭarac*, and *kimettiṅavyayaghādāmb-dravyaprakarṣe*.

The suffixes *nā* and *añ* do not occur together with the words *vinā* and *nānā*; for example: *vatsataraḥ*, *ukṣataraḥ*, *nitarām*, *atīvataram*, *vinā*, and *nānā*. A word whose function is based on a metaphorical meaning (*upacaritārthavṛtti*) is ambiguous (*saṃdigdha*). It is of two kinds: that which has a numerable sense (*saṅkhyāvān*) and that which has a non-numerable sense (*asaṅkhyaka*). Of these two, an example of the meaning of a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) is *pacatitarām* and *pacatakī*. An example of the meaning of a nominal suffix (*subanta*) is *tvayakā* and *uñcakair*. The meaning of a suffix (*pratyayārtha*) is twofold: the meaning of a *kṛt* suffix and the meaning of a *taddhita* suffix. Of these two, an example of the meaning of a *kṛt* suffix is *nyāvakrośī* and *sāṃrāviṇam*.

The meaning of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) is, for example, *abhijityaḥ* or *kauḍhjāyanyaḥ*. The meaning of a compound (*samāsa*) is twofold: that which is the cause of compounding (*samāsyanimitta*) and that which is the cause of the compound itself (*samāsanimitta*). Among these, that depending upon which the compound occurs is called "the meaning of a secondary derivative. That which is the cause of compounding is, for example, *dvaimāturaḥ* or *pañcakapālaḥ*. However, that whose relation is the cause of the compound ending [in a suffix] is "the cause of the compound," as in *devarājaḥ* or *pratyurasām*. This relation is threefold: action (*kriyā*), substance (*dravya*), and quality (*guṇa*).

Among these, the action (*kriyā*) is threefold: that which relates to the action itself, and that which relates to both. Of those, the one relating to the action itself is twofold: of different form (*bhinnarūpā*) and of identical form (*abhinnarūpā*). An example of the former is *cikīrṣati* (he wishes to do) from *kartum icchati*, and *jugupsiṣate* (he wishes to loathe) from *jugupsitum icchati*. An example of the latter is *atyarthaṃ pāpacyate* (he cooks excessively) and *punaḥ punaḥ pāpaṭhyate* (he recites repeatedly). That which relates to the grammatical factor (*kāraka*) is also twofold: expectant (*sākāṅkṣā*) and non-expectant (*nirākāṅkṣā*).

[The suffix *kyac*] is used with expectancy (*sākāṅkṣa*), as in: "the blanket acts like a cloth" (*paṭīyati kambalam*) or "the hut acts like a palace" (*prāsādīyati kuṭīm*). It is used without expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣa*), as in: "he desires a son" (*putrīyati*) or "he wags his tail" (*utpucchayate*). That which relates to both [expectancy and non-expectancy] is twofold: relating to action and agent (*kriyākāraka-sambandhinī*), and relating to agent and action (*kārakakriyā-sambandhinī*). Of these, the first is exemplified as follows: "Devadatta causes [someone] who is cooking to cook" (*pācayati devadattaḥ*) or "the fire of dried cow-dung causes [someone] who is studying to study" (*adhyāpayati kārīṣo 'gniḥ*).

The second [type of compound] is as follows: *kaṃsavadham ācaṣṭe* becomes *kaṃsaṃ ghātayati*; *ārātrivivāsam ācaṣṭe* becomes *rātriṃ vivāsayati*. Substance (*dravya*) is also threefold: the qualified (*viśeṣya*), the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), and the remote (*vyavahita*). Among these, the qualified is twofold: dependent (*sāpekṣa*) and independent (*anapekṣa*). An example of the dependent is: *yuṣmākam ayaṃ* becomes *yauṣmākaḥ gauḥ* ("this cow belongs to you"), and *vatsabhyo hitaḥ* becomes *vatsīyaḥ godhuk* ("the cowherd who is beneficial to the calves"). An example of the independent is: *vasiṣṭhasya apatyam* becomes *vāsiṣṭhaḥ* ("the descendant of Vasiṣṭha"), and *pṛthivyā īśvaraḥ* becomes *pārthivaḥ* ("the lord of the earth").

The qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is of two kinds: that which resides in the substrate (*dharmin*) and that which resides in the attribute (*dharma*). An example of the former is "one who possesses cows" (*gomān*), [meaning] "he has cows"; an example of the latter is "wood suitable for a palace" (*prāsādīyaṃ dāru*), [meaning] "there should be a palace for him. An example of [the qualifier] residing in the attribute is "one who holds the view 'it exists'" (*āstikaḥ*), [meaning] "he has the view that it exists," and "one who holds the view 'it does not exist'" (*nāstikaḥ*), [meaning] "he has the view that it does not exist. The mediated (*vyavahita*) [qualifier] is of two kinds: that which takes the form of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) and that which takes the form of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). An example of the former is "barley measured by two *udaśvin* measures" (*dvimayā yavāḥ*), [meaning] "the barley is measured by two *udaśvin*s. An example of the latter is "barley measured by two *udaśvin*s" (*dvimayā yavāḥ*), [meaning] "the *udaśvin*s are measured by two [units]."

The form of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇarūpa*) is as follows: "the fifth month of this [child] born" (*pañcamo māso 'sya jātasya*), resulting in *pañcamī bālakaḥ*; "the sixth [instance of] grasping the *Rūpāvatāra* text by him" (*ṣaṣṭhaṃ rūpagranthagrahaṇam asya*), resulting in *ṣaṭko vaṭuḥ*. Quality (*guṇa*) is also threefold: inherent (*āśrita*), the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), and the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Among these, the inherent is twofold: non-distinct in form (*abhinnarūpa*) and distinct in form (*bhinnarūpa*). Of these two, an example of the non-distinct in form is: "a collection of alms" (*bhikṣāṇāṃ samūho bhaikṣam*), and "the enmity of the crow and the owl" (*kākolūkasya vairaṃ kākolūkikā*).

The form [of the suffix] varies, as in the case of the *ṛtvij* priests' *karmatva* (the state of being an officiant), or the cooking of *pīlu* seeds, which is called *pīlukaṇa*. The ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is twofold: that which is concomitant (*anurañjaka*) and that which is non-concomitant (*ananurañjaka*). Among these, the concomitant is genus (*jāti*) and so forth, as in "the state of a Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇya*) or "the state of a straight person" (*ārjava*). The non-concomitant is relation (*saṃbandha*) and so forth, as in "the state of one possessing a staff" (*daṇḍitva*) or "the state of a cook" (*pācakatā*). An adjunct (*upādhi*) is a qualifier of either the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) or the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*).

It is twofold: separate (vyasta) and combined (samasta). As separate, when applied to the meaning of the base (prakṛti), for example: *śivo devatāsya iti śevam* ("He whose deity is Śiva is a Śaiva"), or *lavaṇaṃ paṇyamasyeti sāvaṇikaḥ* ("He whose merchandise is salt is a salt-merchant"). When applied to the meaning of the suffix (pratyaya), for example: *gārgikayā ślāghate* ("He praises by means of being a Gārgya"), or *kāṭhikayā adhikṣipati* ("He reviles by means of being a Kāṭhaka"). Here, "deity," "merchandise," "praising," and "reviling" are the limiting conditions (upādhi). As combined, for example: *daṇḍāḥ praharaṇamasyāṃ krīḍāyām iti dāṇḍā* ("In this game, sticks are the weapons; thus it is a 'stick-game'").

In this case, from the word *daṇḍa*, a suffix is prescribed in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) according to the rule *tad asyām* [Pāṇini 4.2.55], forming *daṇḍā*. This conveys both the state of being a weapon (*praharaṇatva*) residing in that locus and the fact that it constitutes a game (*krīḍātva*). Similarly, *hyogodoha-vikāraḥ* is *haiyaṅgavīnam*, which is fresh butter. Here, a suffix is prescribed after the word *hyogodoha* in the sense of a modification (*vikāra*); thus, it conveys the milking (*doha*), which is the adjunct of the base meaning (*prakṛtyarthopādhi*), and the name (*saṃjñā*), which is the adjunct of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārthopādhi*).

The *kāraka* (grammatical participant) is threefold: active (*sakriya*), having distinct actions (*bhinnakriya*), and having non-distinct actions (*abhinnakriya*). Among these, the active is threefold: in the form of an agent (*kartṛ*), in the form of an object (*karman*), and as an underlying thread (*anusyūta*). The form of the agent is twofold: residing in a specific action (*kriyāviśeṣastha*) and residing in a specific *kāraka* (*kārakaviśeṣastha*). Of these two, that which resides in a specific action is as follows: one who asks about a good bath is called a *sausnātika*; likewise, a *sukhaśāyanika* (one who asks about a comfortable sleep); one who speaks much is a *prābhūmāha*, a *prabhūtika*; likewise, a *māśabdika* (one who speaks "no"); one who acts in opposition is a *prātīpika*; and one who behaves contrarily is a *prātikūlika*.

An example of that which resides in a specific *kāraka* (grammatical participant) is as follows: "one who knows or studies grammar" (*vaiyākaraṇaḥ*), "she who gives birth every year" (*samāṃsamīnā*), "one who plays with dice" (*ākṣikaḥ*), "one who is capable of causing distress" (*sāntāpikaḥ*), "that which has come from a father" (*pitryam*), and "one who has lain in the same womb" (*sodaryaḥ*). The form of the object (*karman*) is twofold: residing in a homogeneous [category] and residing in a heterogeneous [category].

That which resides in a similar category should be understood according to its respective application: a *śāra* die that lasts for a day is called *āyānayīna*; a servant hired for a month is *māsika*; a teacher appointed for a year is *vārṣika*; a fixed tax of one hundred [coins] for a fortnight is *pākṣika*; a slave purchased for six months is *ṣāṇmāsika*; and a practice performed for a year is *sāṃvatsarika*.

An example of [a suffix] standing for that which is not of the same class (*asajātīyastha*) is: the *vāmadevya* chant as seen by Vāmadeva; a cloth dyed with lac is *lākṣika*; an oblation to be given to a god is *daivya*; a cloth recently taken from the loom is *tantraka*; a man appointed at the gate is *dauvārika*; and a demon seen on the fourteenth day is *cāturdaśya*. The connection with another meaning (*arthāntarānubandhana*) is what is meant by "pervasion" (*anusyūta*). That is of two kinds: pervasion by action (*kriyānusyūta*) and pervasion by the grammatical factor (*kārakānusyūta*).

In these two cases, the suffix is applied based on the action connected to them; for example, a treatise composed concerning the search for Sītā is called *sītānveṣaṇīyaḥ*, and likewise *kirātārjunīyaḥ* and *vākyapadīyaḥ*. Similarly, a month in which the full moon occurs in the month of Pauṣa is called *pauṣaḥ*, and likewise *āgrahāyaṇikaḥ* and *aśvatthikaḥ*.

Just as those students who know or study the Veda as taught by Tittiri are called *Taittirīyas*, so too are there the *Vāratantavīyas*, the *Āgaleginas*, the *Aitareyiṇas*, as well as the mendicants (*bhikṣus*) who are *Pārāśariṇas* and the actors (*naṭas*) who are *Śailālins*. The [nouns] based on action (*kriyā*) are of three kinds: those characterized by an expressed action (*lakṣitakriya*), those requiring an implied action (*apekṣitakriya*), and those whose action is merely permitted (*anumatākriya*). Among these, those characterized by an expressed action are of two types: residing in the agent (*kartṛstha*) and residing in the object (*karmastha*).

Of these two, that which resides in the agent (*kartṛstha*) is as follows: *mudgā bhavanti asmin* [the field] is *maudgīnam*; *daṇḍinaḥ santi asyām* [the hall] is *daṇḍimatī*. That which resides in the object (*karmastha*) is as follows: *śrāddham anena bhuktam* [he has eaten the funeral feast] is *śrāddhikaḥ*; *agrabhojanam asmai dīyate* [the first portion of food is given to him] is *āgrabhojanikaḥ*; *padam asmin dṛśyam* [a footprint is visible in it] is *padyaḥ kardamaḥ* [muddy ground]. That which requires an implied action (*apekṣitakriya*) is twofold: separated (*vyavahita*) and unseparated (*avyavahita*).

The [kāraka] separated by another is, for example: *grāmād āgacchati* (he comes from the village), *brāhmaṇāya dadāti* (he gives to the Brahmin), and *paryaṅke śete* (he sleeps on the couch). The non-separated is, for example: *kaṭaṃ karoti* (he makes a mat), *dātreṇa lunāti* (he cuts with a sickle), and *devadattenāsyate* (it is eaten by Devadatta). The "action with a transferred force" (*anuśaktakriya*) is twofold: that which has the same locus (*tulyādhikaraṇa*) and that which has a different locus (*atulyādhikaraṇa*). Of these two, the one with the same locus is, for example: *śuklībhavati* (it becomes white), *unmanīsyāt* (may he become free from mental distress), and *bhasmasāt saṃpadyate* (it turns into ashes).

An example of a non-identical substratum (*atulyādhikaraṇa*) is: *paṭapaṭākaroti* ("he makes it crackle"), *devatrāgacchati* ("he goes to the gods"), and *manuṣyatrāvasati* ("he dwells among men"). The non-differentiated action (*abhinnakriya*) is threefold: that expressed by a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), that expressed by a primary derivative (*kṛt*), and that expressed by a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). Among these, that expressed by a verbal suffix is twofold: having the form of an agent (*kartṛ*) and having the form of an object (*karman*). Of these two, an example of the form of an agent is: *pacati devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta cooks"), *dugdhe gauḥ* ("the cow yields milk"), and *corasyārurujati rogaḥ* ("the disease afflicts the thief").

The form of the action (*karmarūpa*) is illustrated by: "the rice is being cooked," "the granary is being split," and "they are sitting like camels. That which is expressed by a *kṛt* suffix is twofold: the qualified (*viśeṣya*) and the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Of these, the qualified is exemplified by: "reaper" (*dātra*), "palace" (*prāsāda*), and "potter" (*kumbhakāra*). The qualifier is exemplified by: "to be done" (*kartavya*), "cook" (*pācaka*), and "easy to understand" (*subodha*). That which is expressed by a *taddhita* suffix is twofold: that whose action is dependent (*sāpekṣakriya*) and that whose action is independent (*anapekṣitakriya*). Of these, the dependent-action type is exemplified by: "one who performs the *iṣṭi* sacrifice," "one who is versed in the sacrificial rites," "one who has studied the Veda," "one who has studied grammar," and "one who previously made a mat" (*kṛtapūrvī kaṭam*).

That which is produced by cooking without looking [at the process] is *pākima*; that produced by sprinkling is *sekima*; that produced by pounding is *kuṭṭima*; that produced by artifice is *kṛtrima*. In the sense "the act of falcon-flying" (*śyenapāka*) occurs in this [act], or "sesame-cooking" (*tilapāka*) occurs in this [act], one says *śyainaṃpātā* or *tailaṃpātā*. An embellishment (*upaskāra*) is a qualifier of the word-meaning that functions through both the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*). It is threefold: functioning through the base, functioning through the suffix, and functioning through both.

Among these, that which pertains to the *prakṛti* (base) is sixfold, distinguished by elision (*lopa*), augmentation (*āgama*), assimilation (*savarṇa*), substitution (*vikāra-ādeśa*), restoration (*pratyāpatti*), and the embellishment of a subordinate word (*apapada-upaskāra*). Among these, for example, there is elision [of the nasal] in the case of the root *rañj* when followed by the suffix *ṇic*, due to the "sporting of deer" (*mṛgaramaṇa*) rule, and so forth. The purpose of the embellishment by elision is as follows: "Though bearing a weapon, he did not follow a crooked course; though supporting the earth with his weighty deeds, he was free from passion (*virajaḥ*). He caused the kings to rejoice—what indeed could virtues not accomplish? [In this verse, the root *raj* (to color/passion) takes the suffix *ṇic*, resulting in *rañjayati*. By the rule of elision, the nasal *ṇ* is dropped, yielding *rajāyāñcakāra*. This illustrates the use of elision as an embellishment.]

The phrase "when there is a desire for sexual union between a stallion and a mare," and so forth, serves as an embellishment (*upaskāra*) for the *Āgama* [grammatical augment]. For example: "She who lives through many ages, whose thirteenth day has arrived—that cow, longing for the bull, felt no shame while suckling her calf. And the rule "the sound *ve* [is substituted] for [the root *bhuj*] in the sense of eating, with a cerebral [nasal]" and so forth, serves as an embellishment for the modification of phonemes (*varṇavikāra*). For example: "Having drunk blood to awaken his hunger and thirst, the jackal—his indigestion remaining—made a 'svāduṅkāra' sound while devouring pieces of meat as a side-dish, and let out a loud, piercing cry."

The purpose of the suffix *ādi* in expressions such as *mātarmātaḥ putre ślāghyaḥ* is for the sake of the grammatical ornamentation of the injunction (*ādeśopaskārārtha*). For example: *gaurī mā tasya tasyaitāḥ kārtikeyasya kīrtayaḥ | kīrtitāsu na kīrtyante yāsu kasyāpi kīrtayaḥ ||* The suffix *ākhyā* expresses the sense of "having done" (*kṛta*). There is the elision of the *kṛt*-suffix and the restoration of the original base (*prakṛti*), along with the rule that the case-role (*kāraka*) remains as it was in the original base; this is for the sake of the restoration of the suffixes. For example: *śailairbandhayati sma vānarahṛtairvālmīkirambhonidhim |*

"Vyāsa [was struck] by the arrows of Pārtha; nevertheless, no exaggeration (*atiśaya*) is attributed to those two. In rules such as *apādāne parīpsāyāṃ ṇamul*, the root *sthā* and others serve to embellish the *upapada*; for example: "In the courtyard of the house, the children of the plowmen go out from their beds toward the *kukūla* fire, which is sweet to the touch due to the remaining frost of the night. The suffix-based (*pratyayadvāraka*) [exaggeration] is also sixfold, distinguished by elision (*lopa*), augmentation (*āgama*), modification of a letter (*varṇavikāra*), insertion (*vikaraṇa*), substitution (*ādeśa*), and change of voice (*upagraha*).

Among these, the purpose of elision (*lopārtha*) is the dropping (*luk*) of the suffixes for fruit and flower, as in: "When the excellence of color is present, the mind is pained by the lack of fragrance. The purpose of augment (*āgamārtha*) is as in *hṛṣerlomasu*: "He blossomed with faces," and "He was embraced by the beloved’s face, which was slightly bent. The purpose of vowel modification (*varṇavikārārtha*) is the substitution of *ṇatva* for the final letter of the root *div* when expressing the desire to win: "Being a gambler, he was mostly supported by his wife alone, as if by a staff. The purpose of the verbal suffix (*vikaraṇārtha*) is as in *śaaliṣaḥ*, where the suffix *śa* is added to form a word meaning "many" when referring to the limbs of living beings.

As in: "The newlywed bride, her eyes trembling with fear, clung to her husband; she was not censured in that misfortune because of her great splendor. The *ātmanepada* suffix *tāt* is used for the sense of an injunction (*ādeśa*) or a benediction (*āśis*). For example: "May your intellect be auspicious! May you be victorious, O Lord of the Earth! The *ātmanepada* suffix is used for the sense of subordination (*upagraha*) when the root *adhi* is used in the sense of overcoming (*prasahana*). For example: "If those like you were to exert themselves toward pleasure that is without support, alas, they would be destroyed by their own pride."

The *ubhayadvāraka* (dependent on both) is twelvefold, distinguished by the following types: limit (*avadhi*), address (*saṃbodhana*), action (*kriyā*), qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), agent (*kartṛ*), qualifier of the agent (*kartṛviśeṣaṇa*), remainder (*śeṣa*), further remainder (*pariśeṣa*), conjunction (*sahārtha*), purpose (*tādathrya*), cause (*hetu*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and miscellaneous (*prakīrṇa*). Among these, a limit (*avadhi*) is a mutual boundary between actions and so forth. It is of many kinds, based on distinctions such as prior time (*pūrvakāla*), interval (*vyatihāra*), posterior connection (*parāyoga*), simultaneous time (*samakāla*), and inferiority (*adhaḥ*). Among those, an example of prior time (*pūrvakāla*) is: "Having gradually formed ripples, the water slowly became slackened in its flow."

He took delight in gazing upon the sandy shore of the ocean-maiden, white as the foam of her waves; the night passed away like the exchange of two young lovers who, having embraced and kissed each other closely, speak incessantly and restlessly to one another, while they both beg and give back their respective senses. As for the union with another [the mountain]: Having traversed those various features on the slopes of the snowy mountain (Himalaya), he reached Haṃsadvāra—the path to the fame of Bhṛgupati (Bhṛgu’s son, Paraśurāma)—which is the Krauñca pass.

Therefore, you should proceed toward the northern direction, which is dark with the beauty of its horizontal expanse, like the foot of Viṣṇu raised for the purpose of crushing Bali. As for the application [of time]: having reached this mountain, the breezes from the waves of the celestial river (Gaṅgā) will remove the mass of your sins and the fatigue of your journey as you traverse these forest regions where Lodhra, Bakula, and Nīpa trees have withered before you. As for the conjunction of circumstances (*kālayoga*): by following the path of sensual pleasure, your passion has been further inflamed.

The bull-bannered Lord (Śiva) dwelt for one month with Umā in the palace of the King of Śailas. Just as the path of the sun [is traversed]—[the verse continues]: "The traveler Pūṣan always counts the measure of the sky. Thus, the states of worldly existence are closed by the seal of manifesting artifice; yet, the dawning of wisdom in the virtuous triumphs, reaching the very limit of the ocean of milk. Addressing (*sambodhana*) is the act of making a perfected being face toward a task to be performed. It is sixfold, according to its purpose: command, prohibition, permission, reproach, inquiry, and narration.

Regarding those matters, please command me as you see fit what must be done by me among the worlds of men who have come to know your excellence. Remembering your favor which has not yet been fully enacted, I desire to increase it through your command. As for the purpose of prohibition: O playful lady, since your face is naturally lovely, fragrant with the essence of wine, and possesses eyes that are intoxicated, what further quality could intoxication add to it once it has taken up residence there?

An example of [the particle *nu*] used for the sake of consent (*anumatyartha*) is as follows: "O friend, all this is appropriate in you: both my two weapons, the thunderbolt and my own powers; and previously, their power was spent upon the great [asuras], while you are all-pervading and effective. An example of [the particle *nu*] used for the sake of reproach (*upālambhārtha*) is as follows: "How indeed will this hand of yours, with its marriage-thread still bound, endure that first offense of Śambhu’s hand, which has the serpent coiled around it as a bracelet?"

An example for the purpose of inquiry (*praśnārtha*): "Who are you, O auspicious one? Whose wife are you? Or what is the reason for your coming to me? Speak, considering that the minds of the self-controlled Raghus are naturally averse to the wives of others. An example for the purpose of narration (*ākhyānārtha*): "Surely the Lord of Sacrificers is rising to dispel the darkness of night, since the face of the eastern quarter is struck by the pollen of ketaka flowers from the breasts of the lotus-faced women."

An adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*) is that which differentiates the aggregate of base and suffix by way of the portion consisting of the meaning of the base. For even when a suffix is produced in the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*), the aggregate is sometimes qualified by way of the suffix, as in *tīvraḥ pākaḥ* ("intense cooking") or *tīvraṃ pākaḥ* ("an intense cooking"). [The types of adverbs include] those in the form of nouns, indeclinables, verbal roots (*dhātu*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), compounds (*samāsa*), and prefixes (*upasarga*), among others.

In them, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is as if gently pushed by a mild breeze that is favorable to you; this sweet-sounding *cātaka* bird on your left coos melodiously; and the cranes (*valākā*), having formed a line through their familiarity with the moment of conception, will surely serve you—who are so pleasing to the eyes—in the sky. An example of the indeclinable form (*avyayarūpa*): "With the affliction of his peaceful nature gradually subsiding, and having had the lotuses rubbed away [of their pollen] by playful women..."

The wind, moving within the rows of waves and bearing spray as if it were a supporting arm, gave [relief] to those resting there. Just as travelers, having sat down in the shade of trees along the road, lie down in the form of a *kṛt* (a posture), so too do the pious people sit in the *uṣṭrāsikā* (camel-sitting) posture in the temples of Śrīkaṇṭha. O friend, at midday in the summer, when the forest of lotuses is empty, this moment has arrived for those prepared for the act of meeting their lovers.

An example of a derivative form (*taddhita*) is as follows: "O dear friend, though spoken to with very harsh words a hundred times, though shaken off a thousand times, though he fell at my feet and was struck with kicks, and though I knit my brows against him countless times—I do not even know how many—yet this insolent man torments me; he does not stop for even a moment. An example of a compound form (*samāsa*) is as follows: "Be appeased! O Hero, let the thunderbolt rest; who among your enemies is to be slain by my arrows?"

Let him whose prowess of arms has been rendered futile [be humbled] even by women whose lips quiver with anger. Among the [six] specific case-relations (*kāraka*) beginning with the agent (*kartṛ*), there are qualifiers belonging to each; these too are sixfold: the qualifier of the agent, the qualifier of the object (*karman*), the qualifier of the instrument (*karaṇa*), the qualifier of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*), the qualifier of the source (*apādāna*), and the qualifier of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Among these, an example of a qualifier of the agent is: "She, her limbs purified by a propitious bath, took up the garment for ascending."

She shone like the earth when the heat has ceased, when the waters of the rivers have been poured out, and when the *kāśa* grass is in full bloom; she bore the floral ornaments of spring, characterized by *karṇikāra* flowers that mocked the luster of rubies, drew away the golden splendor [of the sun], and surpassed the *sindhuvāra* with their clusters of pearls. An example of an adverbial modifier (*karmaviśeṣaṇa*) is as follows: "She bore the floral ornaments of spring, which mocked the rubies, drew away the golden brilliance, and surpassed the *sindhuvāra* with their pearl-like clusters. An example of an instrumental modifier (*karaṇaviśeṣaṇa*) is as follows: "By night, with her lotus-fragrant face, adorned by trembling lower-lip petals, she made the mass of water-lilies—which had been withered by the fall of frost—appear as if they were merely a row of reflections."
