An example of a qualifier of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) is as follows: "Strive to win for that self-restrained one the daughter of the Himalaya, who is devoted to him; for among women, only she is fit to be the ground for the sowing of his seed," so it was instructed by the Self-born [Brahmā]. An example of a qualifier of the point of departure (*apādāna*) is as follows: "Her hand has been made a friend to the rosary, its fingers scarred by the picking up of *kuśa* sprouts, having turned away from the red lac-dye on her feet and from the ball reddened by the cosmetic ointment of her limbs. A qualifier of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is as follows: "The remainder [of the verse] serves the purpose of a subsequent application (*anuprayoga*)."

It is sixfold: for the purpose of using a *liṭ* [perfect] suffix, for the purpose of using a *loṭ* [imperative] suffix, for the purpose of using a *kṛt* [primary derivative] suffix, for the purpose of using a suffix according to its specific rule (*yathāvidhi*), for the purpose of using an additional suffix (*adhika*), and for the purpose of using a reduplicated form (*dvirvacana*). An example of the purpose of using a *liṭ* suffix is as follows: "His hooves did not strike the heads of the great people, nor did he reach the height of arrogance; the dust of the golden ground, struck by his hooves, acted in a manner befitting his majesty. (aceṣṭata) In this verse, the root *ceṣṭ* takes the *liṭ* suffix (*aṭ*) in the sense of "acting" or "behaving," which serves as the subsequent verb (*anuprayoga*) following the past passive participle *aṣṭāpadabhūmireṇuḥ*. This illustrates the use of the *liṭ* suffix for the purpose of providing a subsequent verbal action.

An example of the purpose of employing a verb (*loḍ-anuprayoga*) is as follows: "Attack the city! Reap the Nandana grove! Steal the jewels! Carry off the celestial nymphs!"—it was by thus inflicting such distress day and night that the powerful enemy of Namuci (Indra) performed his service. An example of the purpose of employing a *kṛt* suffix (*kṛd-anuprayoga*) is as follows: "While one woman was playfully placing a floral ornament upon her ear, its decoration being a whirling stick attached to it, another stout woman pushed her aside with her hip, pressing against her breasts."

An example of the sense of "subsequent application according to the rule" (*yathāvidhy-anuprayoga*) is as follows: "O fortunate one, if he is dear to you, there is no fruit in these anxieties you have devised through obstructions; for the offense against a beloved, when brooded over, seems to tear the heart out by its very roots. An example of the sense of "subsequent application with a beneficial purpose" (*taddhitānuprayoga*) is as follows: "Falling from the sky, cooled by the embrace of her beloved, she will be scratched by the tusks of elephants; yet the Mandāra garland does not diminish the delusion of those who commit such rash acts toward their beloveds."

The purpose of employing a word twice is as follows: "Speak, speak the truth! Such a form was never seen before, nor such a face and so forth, by anyone other than you, O ascetic. In this world, where the entire host of enemies has been conquered... [this] like [something] has not been seen by you through my grace. The particle *ca* and others indicate a residual category of sentence-meaning (*padārtha-dharma*), such as conjunction (*samuccaya*) and so on. Although it is of infinite varieties, six types are illustrated here.

Aggregation (*samuccaya*), option (*vikalpa*), simile (*upamā*), injunction (*niyoga*), restriction (*vinigraha*), and prohibition (*pratiṣedha*). Among these, aggregation is as follows: "She set out, saying 'I shall go from here' or 'I shall stay,' and her bark garment was torn asunder; and having mounted his bull, he whose banner is the king of bulls, smiling, took hold of her. Option (*vikalpa*) is as follows: "Does his body shine with ornaments or is it bound by serpents? Does it wear an elephant hide or does it wear fine silk? Is it bearing a skull or is it crowned by the moon? The form of the Universal Being (*viśvamūrti*) cannot be definitively determined."

*Upamā* (Simile) is illustrated as follows: "Just as a mango tree shines intensely when grasping the hand of its bride with its own hand, having obtained the sprouts of a nearby *aśoka* creeper through the arrival of new shoots. *Niyoga* (Injunction/Identity) is illustrated as follows: "That same vigorous form, that same heroism, and that same natural loftiness—the prince did not differ from his source, just as a lamp lit from another lamp does not differ from it. *Vinigraha* (Restriction) is illustrated as follows: "O day, destroy the proud women [as you do the night]; for the lover separated from his beloved, the night is unbearable..."

Thus the arrival of the clouds uttered a speech that seemed to follow the melody of the *kalāpa* ornament. As for prohibition (*niṣedha*), it is as follows: "The sky was not brought to its customary clarity; the darkness was not extracted from the best of mountains; nor was radiance scattered across the quarters of the horizon; yet the night was adorned by the cold-rayed moon. If there is the acquisition of an auxiliary cause at the time of production, then the sense of "together" (*saha*) is threefold: expressed (*abhidhīyamāna*), implied (*pratīyamāna*), and mediated (*vyavadhīyamāna*). Among these, the expressed is twofold: by means of the word *saha* and by means of a synonym (*paryāya*).

Of these two, the first is as follows: "O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, do you perhaps have a desire in your heart to sport with this youth in the succession of gardens shaken by the breezes from the waves of the Śiprā? The second is as follows: "Together with him, on the shores of the sporting-lake, rustling with groves of *tālī* palms, may the breezes—having removed every drop of perspiration with the clove blossoms brought from other islands—[serve you]. The implied meaning (*pratīyamāna*) is also twofold: through syntactical division (*vibhakti*) and through particles (*nipāta*).

Of these two, the first is as follows: Having reflected upon the affairs of the citizens at the proper time, he took delight with the daughter of the Lord of Videha, as if with the Goddess Lakṣmī herself, who had assumed her beautiful form out of eagerness for enjoyment. The second is as follows: O King, the Creator followed him, and the Person (Viṣṇu) accompanied him in person, both increasing his greatness with the cry of "Victory!", just as fire is increased by the oblation.

The [action] being performed is also twofold: by way of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) and by way of division (*bhāga*). For indeed, actions are intended by the agent to be pervaded simultaneously only when accompanied by qualities and substances; and they are divided only when so accompanied. Furthermore, the word *artha* may also signify cessation (*nivṛtti*), as in the expression "smoke for the sake of mosquitoes" (*maśakārtho dhūmaḥ*). In that regard, an example of distributive repetition is: "the bee moving near the bimba-lip, its thirst increased by the fragrant breath [of the woman]."

Warding me off with a lotus held in a gaze trembling with agitation at every moment—though her limbs are adorned with ornaments suited to her lineage, she does not shine in my eyes as long as she does not carry that head, which is truly proud in the company of women, like the wife of a hero. *Tādārthya* (purposefulness) is the state of being an instrument (*prayojakatva*) toward a cause, whether it be the effect itself or the agent of the action.

That [subordination] is sixfold: subordination to action (*kriyātādathrya*), subordination to substance (*dravyatādathrya*), subordination to both action and substance, subordination to both substance and action, subordination to modification of parts (*prakṛtivikāratādathrya*), and subordination to the relation between action and its factors (*kriyākārakatādathrya*). Among these, an example of subordination to action is as follows: "By her, who was established in a vow to take them back again, the two were deposited as if in a double receptacle: graceful gestures in slender creepers, and tremulous glances in the female deer."

An example of the subservience of substance (*dravyatādathrya*) is as follows: "With the quarters clear, the wind free from dust, and an endless rain of flowers falling like conch shells, that day of his birth became for the sake of the happiness of all embodied beings, both stationary and moving. An example of the subservience of action to substance (*kriyādravyatādathrya*) is as follows: "Though he was exceedingly pleasing to behold, that lord of the earth did not bring her delight, just as the full moon, when its progress is obstructed by clouds entered during the autumn, does not please the lotus."

The identity with the substance and the action (*dravyakriyātādathrya*) is as follows: "O fair-browed one, how could there be this humiliation, this grief that overcomes even what is obtainable? Where is such contempt in your father’s house? There is no assault by another for you; who would stretch out his hand toward the jewel on the crest of a serpent? The identity with the modification of nature (*prakṛtivikāratādathrya*) is as follows: "The daughters of the sages, of noble speech, gathering wild seasonal fruits and roots growing unplowed, shall console you when you are afflicted by new sorrows."

The relationship of action, agent, and purpose is as follows: "O Rādhā, you who went to the river from your home, desiring to fetch water, yet instead took refuge in the houses on the banks of the Yamunā; you who give milk to the cows, yet enter only the forests of Govardhana Hill—why have you been cast into the sight of the Son of Devakī? Among the specific types of causes (*hetu*), the *prayojaka* (instigator) is indeed a *kāraka* (participant in an action), whereas the non-*kāraka* cause is now explained in detail.

In this context, the causal factors capable of producing an effect are sixfold: that which is expressed by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth, that which is expressed by the verb "to be" (*sat*), that which is expressed by particles (*nipāta*) and the like, that which is expressed by the instrumental case, that which is expressed by the ablative case, and that which is expressed by the nominative case and so forth. Among these, an example of that expressed by the optative suffix and so forth is as follows: "If a flower were placed upon a sprout, or a pearl were set within a bright coral, then it might resemble her bright smile, with its radiance spreading across her cloud-like lips."

An example of what is expressed by the particle *sad* (the prefix *sa-*): Like a creeper with blossoming flowers, like the night with shimmering stars, or like a river with birds settling upon it, she shone, never casting off her ornaments. An example of what is expressed by the particle *nipāta* (the prefix *ni-*): "Her pair of shanks, as if naturally [long]... "...thus, as it were, her pair of shanks [seemed to] ascend the tips of the scales [of comparison]."

An example of the third case (instrumental) as the expressed meaning (*vācya*): "By that daughter, whose circle of radiance was shimmering, the mother shone even more intensely; like the ground of Mount Vidūra by a sprout of jewels bursting forth at the sound of a new cloud. An example of the fifth case (ablative) as the expressed meaning: "Therefore, O lady rich in asceticism, this person—whose fickleness is justified by his status as a twice-born—desires to ask you something, for you are very patient; provided it is not a secret, please grant me an answer."

Just as the words "first" and so forth denote [the fingers], where even when the snow on the road has become solid, the horse-faced goddesses (Aśvamukhyas)—though pained by their heavy hips and breasts—do not break their slow gait; [in this context] the indicator (*jñapaka*) is indeed the cause (*hetu*), and that is sixfold: the definition of substance (*dravyalakṣaṇa*), the definition of state (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*), the definition of modification (*vikāralakṣaṇa*), the definition of accident (*utpātalakṣaṇa*), the definition of existence (*bhāvalakṣaṇa*), and the definition of action (*kriyālakṣaṇa*).

Among these, an illustration of the *dravyalakṣaṇa* (characterization by substance) is as follows: "The various amorous gestures of the kings, whose desires were fully manifested toward her, became like the forerunners of their affection; they were like the beauty of young shoots belonging to trees. An illustration of the *itthambhūtalakṣaṇa* (characterization of one who has already attained a state) is as follows: "A pigeon, intent on wandering with its beak filled with soft cooing, circles about and kisses its mate, desiring to sport."

An example of the characteristic of transformation (*vikāra-lakṣaṇa*): "By virtue of his childhood, he has three eyes with a face like the full moon and four arms; as a youth, he uproots mountains with the tips of his hands; undoubtedly, he is now the Sun by his splendor. An example of the characteristic of portents (*utpāta-lakṣaṇa*): "Applying medicinal dust to the *gonāsa* snake, binding herbs against the serpent, holding water for the poison residing in his throat, and bearing jewels in his hand to ward off great danger..."

May the Daughter of the Mountain protect you—she who, at the time of her marriage, was both bashful and afraid, and who uttered the syllables of the mantra prescribed by the elderly women of her clan for her husband’s host of spirits. An example of indication by state (*bhāvalakṣaṇa*): A friend, out of jest, said to her companion—who was already [blushing] while holding a cane—"Noble lady, let us go elsewhere. Then, the bride looked at her with a frown of resentment. An example of indication by action (*kriyālakṣaṇa*): "Causing horripilation on my limbs and producing bliss in my mind..."

Without closing his eyes, he proceeds to touch his beloved. A *upapada* (prepositional adjunct) is of six kinds: the form of a verb (*kriyārūpa*), the form of a noun (*nāmarūpa*), the form of a noun-meaning (*nāmārtharūpa*), the form of an affix (*pratyayarūpa*), the form of a particle (*nipātarūpa*), and the form of a *karmapravacanīya* (governing preposition). Among these, an example of the form of a verb is: "For the sake of the satisfaction arising from the possibility of your presence, [my heart] faints. Another example: "Even my limbs, though they pervade the ends of the quarters, are not capable [of reaching you]. An example of the form of a noun is: "From those nights [comes] happiness; from those [nights], the day is always beneficial."

For those whose peerless love does not leave the side of their beloved; as the name, meaning, and form [of a thing]—for example, the splendor of a forest ablaze with the fire of a sacrificial oblation is a substitute for a golden ornament; young women wore that flower placed in their hair, which was delicate with its petals and filaments. As for the form of the suffix (pratyaya)—for example, [the beauty] of a maiden filled with passion standing near the prince, her slender body concealed by the garments of her attendants.

The desire of the bride became clearly manifest, for concealment itself speaks of one's longings. As an example of the *nipāta* (indeclinable) form: "Salutation to that beast of a king, who has fallen under the power of the beloved’s face, with its long, dark eyes and eyebrows playfully arched. An example of the *karmapravacanīya* form: "Turning her ears toward that pure speech of the Guru from the corners of her eyes, she [received it] like the earth first receives the rain of Indra when the heat of summer is intense."

The association with other words (*sāhacarya*), contradiction (*virodha*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), accent (*svara*), gesture (*abhinaya*), and so forth, constitute miscellaneous [means of determining meaning]. Among these, *sāhacarya* (association) is as follows: "The forest of your enemies is filled with intoxication for the sake of pleasure, possesses the luster of beautiful *campaka* flowers like a woman adorned with a forehead-mark (*tilaka*), and is overrun by thick sandalwood trees like a woman embraced by a lover. *Sāhacarya* is also illustrated thus: "Rāma, followed by Lakṣmaṇa, is like another Rāma who is generous; the sky bears a splendor radiant with its coronation, just as Kausalyā does."

**Contradiction (virodha):** "Like Rāma and Arjuna in battle, these two heroes, Hari and Bāṇa, both having taken up their weapons out of wrath, are prepared to strike. **Indicative Mark (liṅga):** "This sun causes my friend to swell; his friend is the ocean. Yet that moon has become my enemy; therefore, O friend, today I suffer from a lack of friendship. **Tone (svara):** "If my beloved’s messenger is dear to me, then her lover is also dear to me. If the words she speaks are dear to him, then those words are dear to me as well."

"Having bowed, [he said]: 'As these are my brothers, this wife, and this maiden who is the very life of the Rāghava clan—tell me what business you have here, for one should not place reliance on insubstantial things. The meaning of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is threefold: its own meaning (*svārtha*), substance (*dravya*), and gender (*liṅga*). Among these, the "own meaning" is the essence of the word itself. It is twofold: the word's own form (*svarūpa*) and that which is to be imitated (*anukārya*). Of those two, the word's own form is twofold: capable of being expressed as a substantive (*sattvavacanārha*) and incapable of being expressed as a substantive (*asattvavacanārha*). Regarding the former, an example is: "Cīḍāmaṇis at the ends of the head; Karalas in the middle of the necklace."

"The *paryaṅka* is prescribed for lying down, and the *āveśa* for a dwelling. The poetic figure *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is expressed by words such as *yathā*, *manye*, *śaṅke*, *dhruvam*, *prāyaḥ*, *nūnam*, and so forth; the word *iva* is also of that same nature. The object of imitation (*anukārya*) is twofold: meaningful and meaningless. Of these, the meaningful is as follows: "When the beloved forcibly lifts her face by the hair and kisses it, the soft murmuring of the proud women—'Hum! Hum! Let go! Mine!'—is victorious."

It is as useless as a pale, arrogant pigeon that, having climbed to the top of a mountain tree, utters shrill, long, and drawn-out "ghū" cries at dawn while intoxicated by its own broad neck and ruffled feathers. That which is heard, understood, or expressed through either an expressed cause (*upātta-nimitta*) or an unexpressed cause (*anupātta-nimitta*) is *dravya* (substance). It is of two kinds: that which has the form of a substratum (*āśraya-rūpa*) and that which does not have the form of a substratum (*anāśraya-rūpa*).

In that regard, that which is based upon bases such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth is the "based form" (*āśrayarūpa*); for example: *gauḥ* (cow), *aśvaḥ* (horse), *śuklaḥ* (white), *ekaḥ* (one), *prastham* (a measure), *palam* (a weight), *ṛjuḥ* (straight), *pūrvaḥ* (prior), *pācakaḥ* (cook), *daṇḍī* (staff-bearer), *rājapuruṣaḥ* (king’s man), and *caitraḥ* (Caitra). The opposite of that is the "non-based form" (*anāśrayarūpa*), which is the meaning of particles (*nipāta*), indeclinables (*avyaya*), prefixes (*upasarga*), verbs (*gati*), and adverbial particles (*karmapravacanīya*), etc.; for example: *ahaṃ ca tvaṃ ca vṛtrahan* (I and you, O slayer of Vṛtra), *kastvāmūrīkariṣyati* (who will accept you?), *kastaṃ prati nayāsyati* (who will lead him back?), and *svayaṃ prayetumicchati* (he wishes to go by himself).

The *liṅga* (grammatical gender) is twofold: the gender of words (*śabda-liṅga*) and the gender of meanings (*artha-liṅga*). Of these two, that which is the cause for the designation of meaning as "this" or "that," and the cause for the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the word as "this"—namely, the masculine [gender]—is the cause for the designation of meaning as "neuter" according to the rule *puṃ-napuṃsakasya jhal-acaḥ*. It is the cause for the designation of meaning as "neuter" because it serves as the basis for such a designation. Thus, this [gender] expands into six types through distinctions such as pure (*śuddha*), mixed (*miśra*), and so forth: namely, the pure, the mixed, the confused (*saṅkīrṇa*), the subordinate (*upasarjana*), the permeated (*āviṣṭa*), and the unmanifest (*avyakta*).

Among these, the *śuddha* (pure) has a single grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*): *khaṭvā*, *vṛkṣaḥ*, *kuṇḍam*, *strī*, *pumān*, and *napuṃsakam*. That which possesses two refinements is *miśra* (mixed): *marīciḥ*, *ūrmiḥ*, *artiḥ*, *chardiḥ*, *kaṣāyaḥ*, and *kavāṭam*. That which is associated with three refinements is *saṅkīrṇa* (blended): *taṭī*, *taṭaḥ*, *taṭam*; *śṛṅkhalā*, *śṛṅkhalaḥ*, *śṛṅkhalam*. That which has the form of an invariant qualifier relative to a word to be qualified (*viśeṣya*) is *upasarjana* (subordinate): *śuklā*, *śuklaḥ*, *śuklam*; *paṭvī*, *paṭuḥ*, *paṭu*.

Even when functioning as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), it is manifested as that which is fit for the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of a specific word: *prakṛtiḥ*, *viṣayaḥ*, *pradhānam*, *bhāryā*, *dārāḥ*, and *kalatram*. That which is unfit for the grammatical refinement of a word based on gender (*liṅga*) is unmanifest (*avyakta*): *pañca*, *ṣaṭ*, *kati*, and *uñcaiḥ*. That by which a substance (*dravya*) is qualified or delimited is called the "ground for the application" (*pravṛttinimitta*) of a word; it is a property of the object (*arthadharma*), a qualifier of the object's gender (*arthaliṅgaviśeṣaṇa*), and is designated as a quality (*guṇa*) or an abstract state (*bhāva*). This is threefold: quality (*guṇa*), ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), and relation (*saṃbandha*).

In that regard, with respect to a substance (*dravya*) already mentioned by its own name, a quality (*guṇa*) that generates a cognition is a "class" (*jāti*); [other qualities include] number (*saṅkhyā*), configuration (*saṃsthāna*), state (*avasthāna*), and so forth. For example: *gauḥ* (cow), *brāhmaṇaḥ* (Brahmin), *paṭuḥ* (clever), *gauraḥ* (fair-skinned), *ekaḥ* (one), *anekaḥ* (many), *hanūmān* (Hanumān), *vāsudevaḥ* (Vāsudeva), *yuvā* (young), *vṛddhaḥ* (old), *ṛjuḥ* (straight), *pūrvaḥ* (eastern). That which is denoted merely as a non-coloring factor (*ananurañjaka*) is a delimiting measure (*avacchedaka-parimāṇa*); it is of many kinds, distinguished by distance (*adhvan*), weight (*gaurava*), number (*saṅkhyā*), collection (*saṅghāta*), space (*kṣetra*), and so on.

For example: a mountain measuring a *yojana*, a fruit, a *suparṇa* bird, an ancient [text], cowrie shells, an *akṣauhiṇī* army, rice measured in a *khārī*, or land measured by a *nivartana*. In the meanings of primary derivatives (*kṛt*), secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), compounds (*samāsa*), and nominal bases (*pratipadika*), the basis for their application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is a relation (*sambandha*). That [relation] is threefold: relation with an action (*kriyāsambandha*), relation with a substance (*dravyasambandha*), and relation with both action and substance (*kriyādravyasambandha*). Among these, an example of relation with an action is "cook" (*pācaka*). An example of relation with a substance is "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) or "king’s man" (*rājapuruṣa*).

The relationship between action and substance is, for example, as in "akṣika" (one who plays with dice) or "niṣeka-auśāmbi" (one who has performed the *niṣeka* rite at Ośāmvi). However, when words denoting genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), measure (*parimāṇa*), and so forth, are expressed primarily or are conveyed by abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*), then these possess only the status of substance (*dravyatva*) and not the status of gender (*liṅgatva*). For an abstract suffix denotes a genus from a word expressing genus, a quality from a word expressing quality; it denotes a relationship from a compound, a primary derivative (*kṛt*), or a secondary derivative (*taddhita*); it denotes its own form (*svarūpa*) [as in the case of feminine suffixes like] *ṅī*, *ḍī*, *ttha*, etc.; and it denotes a collection of genus from words such as "dhava" and "khadira."

Others, however, maintain that the meaning of the word itself (*svārtha*) is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the substance (*dravya*) is the qualified (*viśeṣya*), and gender (*liṅga*) consists of feminine, masculine, and neuter. Furthermore, they state that particles (*nipāta*), prepositions (*gati*), prefixes (*upasarga*), adverbial particles (*karmapravacanīya*), and so forth, have the sense of direction (*prātipadikārtha*). For particles and the like do not function with respect to entities that have become existent (*sattvabhūta*)—which are fit to be designated as "this" or "that"—by taking up a basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). Rather, by means of grasping the basis for application, they enter into meanings that have not become existent (*asattvabhūta*), such as conjunction (*samuccaya*) and the like.

Regarding this, it is said: "Because they function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) for those [substantives], and because they are seen to be connected with everything, their status as denoting entities (*sattvārtha*) is stated to be due to their arising as dependent on another. Now, are these [particles] denoters (*vācaka*) or indicators (*dyotaka*)? On this point, some explain: "Since they are to be determined through the cognition of that [substantive], they are denoted by them, just as 'cow' and so forth are for others. For the determination of the denotation of words is based upon positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)."

Furthermore, how could the nature of the meaning—such as conjunction (*samuccaya*) or option (*vikalpa*)—which is determined through beginningless linguistic usage, not be the denotable object (*vācya*) of these words? For conjunction is indeed understood from the word, as in "I and you, O slayer of Vṛtra" (*ahaṃ ca tvaṃ ca vṛtrahan*); or option is understood from the word, as in "Come, I shall place this earth within my mouth" (*hantāha pṛthivīmimāṃ nidadhāni havehave*). In this way, since comparisons (*upamāna*) and so forth are understood from beginningless [usage], they become denotable by those words. Others, however, say: "Because of the absence of the genitive case, there is no [denotation] of conjunction and option."

"And by these [terms], their status as indicators is well-established. For instance: when the sentence "the conjunction of the *plakṣa* and the *nyagrodha*" is employed, the genitive case is used; it is not the case that one says "the *plakṣa-nyagrodha-s*. And just as when the expression "let there be an option between rice and barley" is used, the word-meaning "option"—which has become a substantial entity (*sattvabhūta*)—is connected with the action, it is not the case that one says "between rice and barley."

Furthermore, just as the object possessing branches and so forth is understood by the single denotative word "tree," it is not the case for conjunction (*samuccaya*) or option (*vikalpa*). And just as there is freedom in the sequential application of denotative words such as "give alms" or "alms," it is not the case for "tree and tree. And just as the connection with an adjective is observed in the case of the denotative word "the beautiful tree," it is not the case for "and beautiful. Thus, because of this difference from denotative words, it is determined that these [particles] are indicators (*dyotaka*).

And the author of the *Sūtras* states that "ca" and so forth are non-substantives (*asattva*). The author of the *Nirukta* also says: "A verb has being as its primary meaning, while nouns have substance as their primary meaning; particles (*nipātas*) are those which fall upon various high and low meanings. Now, the high and low, manifold meaning of these [particles], whose nature is not understood from themselves, is determined by means of the connection with other words, the context, and so forth.

Therefore, since the meaning is not understood even by the mere form [of the word] due to the dependence upon the employment of others, these [suffixes] are merely indicators (*dyotaka*), not expressers (*vācaka*). However, some maintain that all of this is subject to deviation (*savyabhicāra*). For instance: even by an expresser, namely a verb (*ākhyāta*), that which is indicated—the meaning existing as a substance (*sattvabhūta*)—is itself an expresser; for example, in "it is sat" (*āsyate*) or "you sit" (*bhavadbhir āsyate*), the verb is indeed an expresser. Furthermore, even though they are expressers, a base (*prakṛti*) and a suffix (*pratyaya*) are never employed in isolation. The word *juhoti*, which is a transformation of an expresser, remains fixed according to the rule of priority and posteriority (*paurvāparyaniyama*).

As for what is said—that it is because of the traditional usage (smṛti) of the term *rājapuruṣa*—that too is incorrect. For meanings are not explicitly taught in grammar; rather, the author of the Nirukta considers [the particle] to be expressive (*vācaka*), not indicative (*dyotaka*). Therefore, since we observe instances of deviation, how can this [argument] be tenable? It is replied: Because of its expressiveness (*vācakatva*), when a verb is used and there is a desire to express a residual relation (*śeṣa*), the genitive case is indeed seen, as in "one should not eat beans" (*māṣāṇām aśnīyāt*). However, when particles such as *ca* are used, the genitive does not occur at all.

Nor is there a relationship consisting in the non-existence of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), for a form is perceived in order to be understood; it is that very [form] which causes one to understand the mere object as being non-existent. Furthermore, the meaning is expressed even by the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) alone, as in *dadhi*, *madhu*, *iyān*, and *adhunā*. But particles such as *ca* and so forth do not denote that [meaning] when they are used alone. Now, if it is argued that these words like *dadhi* and so on, which occur in actual usage, are simply other words [distinct from the base and suffix], then neither the base nor the suffix would exist at all.

How is it stated that even the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) do not express meaning when isolated? Furthermore, the usage of words in reverse order is also observed, as in *āhitāgni* and *agnyāhita*. Nor is such a phenomenon a different word altogether or a compound (*samāsa*). Moreover, the mention of the option (*vā*) is redundant because [the reverse order] is established by its very nature.

If, by the rule "the subordinate member [comes] first" (*upasarjanaṃ pūrvaṃ*) and so forth, there is a restriction on the usage of both base and suffix—since it is stated that [the suffix] comes after [the base]—then for prefixes and prepositions, there is a restriction on usage by the rule "they [come] before the verbal root" (*te prāg dhātoḥ*). Indeed, even among restrictions on usage, a further restriction on usage is observed; therefore, there is no deviation. Furthermore, the connection of a qualifier is seen even in the case of subordinate members, as in the example: "Devadatta’s teacher’s house" (*devadattasya gurukulam*).

But for particles such as *ca* and so forth, this [capacity for denotation] never exists; for how could their meanings be taught in grammar? As it is said: "The words *śālīna* and *kaupīna* denote 'timid' and 'that which should not be done,' respectively; and *praghaṇa* and *praghāṇa* denote a portion of a house. Furthermore, in the *Nirukta*, since a wide variety of meanings is not perceived from a particle alone, but rather the meaning is manifested through the employment of another word, the particle is shown to be merely indicative (*dyotaka*) and not expressive (*vācaka*). Thus, particles such as *ca* and so forth are indeed indicators, not denoters.

Now, what is the status of *gatis*, *upasargas*, and *karmapravacanīyas*? It is said: first, regarding *gatis* such as *sadasat* and so forth, since their designation as *gatis* is established by the very indication of the meanings they express—such as respect or disrespect—it follows that even for those like *ūry-ādi*, which are indicated meanings, their function is strictly that of denoters (*vācaka*). However, *upasargas* may be denoters (*vācaka*), illuminators (*dyotaka*), qualifiers (*viśeṣaka*), co-expressers (*sahābhidhāyaka*), or they may be devoid of meaning (*nirarthaka*) when serving a specific grammatical purpose. Furthermore, *karmapravacanīyas* are, like particles (*nipāta*), exclusively illuminators (*dyotaka*).

Regarding this, it is said: "In the manifestation of relations produced by specific actions, how could the status of being an object (*karmatva*) and the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) be resorted to as distinct [categories]? For here, since relations are preceded by action, they depend upon a *kāraka* (participant in an action) whose specific character is revealed by that action, rather than being established independently of instruments.

And in that case, since things of the same class can be expressed simultaneously by a single case-ending, at the time of denoting the remaining relation (*śeṣasaṃbandha*), the relationship between action and its factors (*kriyākārakasaṃbandha*)—which is not directly expressed by words—remains present as something inferred through the proximity of the verbally expressed remaining relation. Furthermore, that inference regarding the remaining relation, by virtue of the specific capacity of its own form, has as its object both restricted actions and unrestricted actions. An example of one with a restricted action is as follows...

People do not produce a relationship characterized as "subsidiary" (śeṣa)—such as the relationship between father and son—when a specific agent required for an action is present; rather, that very [relationship] is inferred from it. Similarly, in the case of "the branch of the tree," the stability based on the connection between locus and located establishes a subsidiary relationship characterized by part and whole when a specific agent required for the action is present; thus, that very [relationship] is perceived.

An example of a case where the scope of action (*kriyā*) is indefinite is "the king’s man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*). Here, the relationship between owner and owned (*svasvāmisambandha*), which is designated as the "agent" (*kartṛ*) of a variety of indefinite and manifold actions—such as providing, adorning, buying, or defeating—is established. Since this [relationship] is preceded by indefinite and manifold actions, it is insufficient to infer a specific action; rather, it brings about only the general action that serves as its own cause. In such a case, *karmapravacanīyas* are employed to illuminate the specific nature of that action.

Just as in the case of Śākalya’s *saṃhitā*, the causal relationship between "having rained" (*uprāvarṣat*) and "it rained" (*avarṣat*)—which is preceded by action—is regulated; this is what is being demonstrated here. For it is impossible to conceive of a case-ending for a verb that would express a specific action, since even the manifestation of a specific action depends upon the proximity of a verbal form; in the absence of a verbal form, such [expression] is not appropriate. Furthermore, the relationship itself is not its denotation, because that [relationship] is dependent upon the suffix of the case-ending.

Furthermore, if the *karmapravacanīya* were to denote [the relation] itself, there would be no emergence of a distinction from the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), as in the case of "the king's master" (*rājasvāmī*). Yet, in common usage, the connection with a *karmapravacanīya* is understood to be the delimitation of a specific cause for the relation. Therefore, it is concluded that it is the indicator (*dyotaka*) of its application. As it has been said: "This [particle] is not a denoter (*vācaka*) of action, nor is it a denoter of the relation; nor does it imply a verbal root (*kriyāpada*), but rather it is the differentiator (*bhedaka*) of the relation."

But surely, as long as the act of hearing (*niśamayati*) is not understood, it is impossible to effect the delimitation of its connection [with other words]. Therefore, it is illogical to say that a word, without conveying an action, delimits a connection. Now, if it is argued that the manifestation of this action is not postulated because it is not observed elsewhere, then let the delimitation of the connection also not be postulated, for the same reason—that it is not observed elsewhere. To this, it is replied:

The particle *anu* is the cause of the suffix [in *anugata*] by making known, through the power of its meaning, a specific action that is connected to a particular excellence of the self (*ātma-atiśaya*) as understood from the distinction of the actions themselves. Therefore, its status as denoting an action is not postulated because the action is already perceived from another source. Alternatively, the *karmapravacanīyas* make known the distinction in the relation by disregarding the specific differences imposed by the various causes.

Just as the Pañcālas [are subordinate] to Brahmadatta, or Abhimanyu [is subordinate] to Arjuna, so too the relationship of master and servant (*svasvāmibhāva*) and similarity (*sādṛśya*) are understood from the *karmapravacanīya* [preposition] *prati*. However, the relations that serve to delimit a specific substratum convey a distinction in the action through the excellence of their own essential nature.

Just as the protection of the Pañcālas, the collection of taxes, and so forth are duties to be performed by Brahmadatta, while the leading of the army, determination, and striking are similar to Arjuna—these being understood through the force of their established connection—so too this [author] Āpastamba defines the relationship between *saṃhitā* and *pravacana* as that of cause and effect; for *saṃhitā* consists specifically in the form of study.

And because of its capacity to manifest a preeminence of sound (*śabdātiśaya*), "listening" (*niśamana*) is understood here from the meaning itself, and is not something to be apprehended through a *karmapravacanīya* particle. However, regarding its "seeing" (*darśana*), since the power [of the prefix] *anu* is well-known in the sense of denoting a state of being subsequent (*paścādbhāva*), as in the expression *anurūpādāna* ("taking what is suitable"), it ought to have that very same meaning here as well. Therefore, by virtue of the rule prescribing its application in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), its function is postulated in the sense of a cause; yet there is no contradiction even in the sense of posteriority, because here the sequence of priority and posteriority pertains to the relationship between cause and effect.

In that case, then, it is precisely this delimitation of the relation (*saṃbandhāvaccheda*) that is the cause for the designation *karmapravacanīya* being applied to particles (*nipāta*) as the basis for their distinct treatment. But how is it then that *adhi* and *pari* are "meaningless" (*anarthaka*), *su* is used in the sense of "praise" (*pūjā*), *ati* in the sense of "transgression" (*atikramaṇa*), and *api* in the senses of "possibility of a word-meaning," "permission," "reproach," and "conjunction"—yet these are still designated as *karmapravacanīyas*? For indeed, no relation whatsoever is delimited by these. This is true.

However, for the sake of grammatical function, even these [words] which do not possess that property [of denoting substances] are stated in the treatise to have the status of *karmapravacanīya* by virtue of scriptural injunction. Now, it might be argued: "Words such as 'tree' (*vṛkṣa*) are denoters of substances (*sattvavacana*), because they apprehend bases of application such as genus (*jāti*); whereas words such as 'ca' (*ca-ādi*) are denoters of non-substances (*asattvavacana*), being the opposite of those. But there is no such thing as a "genus" that exists as an object of knowledge (*prameya*) perceivable through perception or other means of valid cognition.

For indeed, that [universal] is not perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) lacks a continuity between prior and subsequent moments, whereas a universal (*jāti*) possesses a nature that extends through prior and subsequent moments. As it has been said: "How can a cognition born of the senses—which is independent—touch upon the universal's 'subsistence in common' with respect to particulars, which is dependent? Furthermore, the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) arising subsequently are incapable of establishing a universal, because by their very nature they have non-real entities as their objects. Neither inference (*anumāna*) nor verbal testimony (*śabda*) establishes a universal either.

Because that [universal], being an object of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), is incapable of establishing the reality of the thing itself. As for the attainment of the real thing, it will occur through the determination of its existence based on the non-determination of its difference [from the individual]. Furthermore, there is no universal distinct from the individual, because it is not perceived as distinct—unlike a water-lily, a myrobalan, or a wood-apple—and because its spatial distinction is not grasped—unlike a jar or a cloth. Nor can it be argued that it is not perceived because the individual is not perceived, since the universal subsists in the individual; for if the individual is not perceived, the universal is likewise not perceived. This is not so.

Because the mode of subsistence is untenable: does the universal subsist in each individual in its entirety, or by way of parts? If the universal "cowness" were present in its entirety in one individual, it would not exist anywhere else; thus, how could the cognition of "cow" arise with respect to every individual? Furthermore, since it is partless, there are no constituent parts [of the universal]. Nor is any mode of subsistence observed where it exists in one individual by way of completion that exists by way of completion in another individual as well. Nor is its subsistence of the nature of inherence (*samavāya*).

For that [inherence] occurs between things that are not established separately (*ayutasiddha*). However, "not being established separately" and "connection" are contradictory. If it is argued that this is not so because a connection is observed even between substance and quality which are not established separately, we say no; for even there, the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*) is not established as distinct from the qualities themselves. Furthermore, there is no connection between part and whole either, due to the absence of separate establishment. Nor should it be said that the connection will be characterized by the relation of form (*rūpa*) and the bearer of form (*rūpin*), because the meaning of "form" cannot be defined.

Is this word "form" (rūpa) a term denoting qualities such as white and so forth, or is it a term denoting intrinsic nature (svabhāva)? If it denotes qualities such as white and so forth, then substances such as air and the mind, which lack color, would be devoid of universals (sāmānya). Even if it denotes shape (ākāra), those same [substances] that are devoid of spatial configuration would likewise result in being devoid of universals. However, if it denotes intrinsic nature, there would be no distinction at all between the universal and the possessor of the universal. For it is said: "The intrinsic nature does not appear as distinct from the possessor of the intrinsic nature."

“This is merely an excess of words, not an excess of reality. Furthermore, this universal (*jāti*) must either be omnipresent (*sarvasarvagatā*) or present only in its individual instances (*piṇḍasarvagatā*). If it were omnipresent, there would be the cognition of "cow-ness" even in a white horse (*karka*), the cognition of "horse" in a brindled cow (*śābaleya*), and the cognition of "camel" in elephants and the like. In this way, a total confusion of categories (*padārthasaṅkara*) would result. Now, if it is argued that this confusion does not occur because of the restriction of the capacity for manifestation (*abhivyakti-sāmarthya*), [then we reply: only those individuals such as the white horse possess the skill for manifesting "cow-ness."

Let it not be so; for even if the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) were manifested by individual instances such as Khaṇḍā and others, it would either be perceived everywhere or else it would not be omnipresent. There is indeed no restrictive factor for its apprehension in specific parts. The individual instance (*piṇḍa*) is the manifester like a lamp, but that [universal] does not reside within that individual instance. And who could say that something exists everywhere when it is not being apprehended everywhere? Thus, the universal "cowness" cannot logically be omnipresent in every respect. However, if it were omnipresent within each individual instance, then this objection would indeed be invalid.

However, there is no cognition of "cow" with respect to a cow that has only just been born. The universal (jāti) did not exist in the body [of the cow] before it was born, yet it exists once it is born; moreover, being inactive, it does not migrate from one body to another. Nor does it arrive at that body having abandoned its previous one, nor does it subsist by means of parts. What kind of succession of calamities is this? Therefore, the universal, being of the nature of exclusion (apoha), is merely false and not ultimately real. Consequently, because of its non-existence, that which possesses it (tadvat) is untenable.

To this it is replied: Is the position regarding *apoha* based on the non-existence of external objects such as universals (*jāti*) and so forth, or is it based on the force of cognition? It cannot be based on the force of cognition, because cognition has as its object a form that is inclusive in nature, and thus stands as an adversary to *apoha*. Nor is the non-existence of the universal established by perception, for its own nature is revealed precisely like that of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*). Indeed, only the first moment of visual consciousness is in contact with the object; there is no subsequent [moment]. What kind of royal edict is this?

Let that [particular] alone be the means of valid cognition; however, by that [means], only the form of the object as excluded [from others] is apprehended, not a recurring [universal]. What proof is there for this? If non-conceptual perception had only the particular as its object, how could this determination of a universal arise all of a sudden? Nor is this [determination] of the nature of verbal knowledge; for one perceives the recurring form even when the denotative word is unknown, just as a Southerner suddenly sees a succession of camels.

Furthermore, for one who has previously perceived the individual body of a *śābaleya* (spotted cow), upon subsequently seeing the individual body of a *bāhuleya* (black cow) at different times, the recollection of the *śābaleya* body arises. This would not be possible in the absence of a commonality (*sāmānya*). For there is no basis for the recollection of one thing when another is seen; this is only possible if an underlying, recurring form (*anugatarūpa*) is admitted, and not otherwise. Moreover, even when seeing a different individual, there is recognition in the form: "This is that very same cow."

That too is not tenable if the recurring form is not apprehended; nor can it be denied, because the difference between individuals is established by perception. Furthermore, in cases where there is no uninterrupted apprehension of individual characteristics due to the proximity of a heap of very small objects such as mustard seeds or lentils, it is precisely the recurring form that is grasped by the sense organ. Therefore, the denial of the universal, which possesses its own specific character, is not logical. Consequently, at the initial contact with the eye, both the commonality and the difference are perceived, like [the balance of] a scale; thus, both the universal and the particular are real.

In that case, there would be no apprehension [of the universal] in the form "this is common," nor would there be cognition of the particular in the form "this is excluded. Furthermore, the cognition of a universal does not depend upon a common occurrence; therefore, because it is present there, it should not fail to be apprehended, just like the individual instance. If the universal is not apprehended because it depends upon a common occurrence, then the particular should likewise not be grasped, for it too depends upon exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). For what means could there be for the apprehension of those things in which its persistence (*anuvṛtti*) resides?

If it is asked: "What is the means of apprehending those things from which this [object] is excluded?"—if, on the other hand, the object itself is apprehended independently of both continuity (*anuvṛtti*) and exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), then let it be; however, it must be told what kind of thing that is. It cannot be pointed out at the time of indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*); yet the determinate cognitions (*niścaya*) arising from it provide testimony for both cases. Furthermore, whatever refutation was described there regarding the alternatives concerning its functioning (*vṛtti-vikalpa*) and so forth—all of that is countered by the very power of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

As for what was stated—that [the universal] does not appear because it is not perceived like a blue lotus or an amalaka fruit—the difference in cognition has already been demonstrated there. As for the argument that it is not perceived due to a difference in location, and that when the locus is not grasped, the cognition of the [universal] is absent, the reason for this is that the universal resides in those loci (*jātes tadāśritatvam*), not that it is non-existent. Furthermore, regarding the claim that its mode of subsistence (*vṛtti*) is untenable, it is replied: the universal subsists in its entirety within each individual; therefore, its perception in another individual is indeed possible. For universals have no parts whatsoever.

If you have seen this elsewhere, oh, how clever you are! For you ask for what has already been seen, as if employing inference even when something is directly perceived. If you ask, "What is the name of this mode of existence? we do not know its name; we simply designate it as the "universal inherent in the individual" (*piṇḍasamavetā jātiḥ*). [Objection: But surely inherence (*samavāya*) is the relation between two things that are inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*); that [definition] is refuted precisely by the contradiction [of the opponent's position]. [Reply: It cannot be so refuted. Let there be a distinction based on a difference in cognition (*pratītibheda*), but a difference in location (*deśabheda*) is not admitted.

Therefore, subsistence (*vṛtti*) is logically possible, and inherence (*samavāya*) is indeed asserted. This very mode of subsistence applies to both the part and the whole, as well as to the quality and the possessor of the quality. Furthermore, their being distinct entities is established by the same reasoning that applies to the case of a genus and its instances. Since there is no difference in location between them, their inseparability (*ayutasiddhatva*) is perfectly clear. As for the objection that "there can be no relation for that which is not yet produced, and once it is produced, there would be separateness" (*yutasiddhatā*), that too has been refuted by the Teachers (*Ācāryas*).

Furthermore, for those who assert that there is only one time [for both the universal and its relation], it is argued: "The occurrence of universals and the like in the throat and other locations where the word is produced is distinct from their occurrence in the individual objects (piṇḍa), because they do not constitute parts of those objects. Therefore, the objection regarding the impossibility of such an occurrence is not a valid refutation. As for the criticism based on the dilemma of whether the universal is omnipresent everywhere or only present in the individual object—that too is trivial, because we accept the universal as being omnipresent exactly as it is perceived. Thus, it is accepted that the universal is indeed all-pervading.

Its apprehension occurs everywhere because of the proximity of the manifestor that reveals it; an individual becomes a manifestor only when the universal is already perceived, not otherwise. Where there is the perception of the individual, there alone is the cognition of that [universal]. The universal exists everywhere, yet it is not seen everywhere. It is seen only where the individual that manifests it exists. If its existence elsewhere than in the individual were asserted, what proof is there for that? Even here, when a cow is being brought in, there is the perception of "cowness."

Furthermore, it is impossible for a single entity to arrive together with a physical body (*piṇḍa*); therefore, just as the self exists apart from the body, its existence here [in this location] must likewise be admitted. Its manifestation, however, is restricted to that specific time at which its manifestation is perceived; thus, once manifested, it is not perceived at any other time. Moreover, its manifestation is restricted to that specific place where the manifestation is observed; therefore, manifested in this place, it is not seen in another place. Even though [the universal] is omnipresent, according to some of our own school, it is dependent upon a particular individual body.

There will be the cognition of "cow" regarding a cow born at a later time because of its apprehension by that [same] [cognition]. For the individual being born is born already endowed with the universal (*jāti*). Indeed, the time for this [individual] is one and the same for both its birth and its connection with the universal. Here, there is no prior existence of the universal, nor is there a transfer of it from another. Rather, that individual arises from its own causes as being precisely such [as to possess the universal]. As for the question, "How is this so?", it is answered as follows:

Furthermore, alas, let this other matter be questioned by him: "The bull is tawny, the cow is black, and she eats green grass; how is it that the calf produced from those two is pale-white? Just as an individual is perceived through its connection with color and other qualities, so too is it [perceived] as being endowed with a universal (*jāti*); what is this endless obsession of yours? Moreover, if [the universal were defined merely as] the exclusion of non-cows (*agovyāvṛtti*), this question would not cease. Therefore, that which is excluded from non-cows is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) belonging to another genus.

Therefore, having understood that the intrinsic nature of things is subject to inquiry, one should abandon frivolity and examine the correct practice (*pratipatti*). And this practice has already been shown to be without exception, whether with respect to particulars or even universals (*sāmānya*). Therefore, like particulars, this universal is not to be rejected. The qualifier (*upādhi*) alone is threefold, the primary [meaning] (*pradhāna*) is also threefold, and the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*) is described as possessing a threefold embellishment. It is established that particles (*nipāta*) possess both denotative power (*vācakatva*) and indicative power (*dyotakatva*).

The connection regarding the relationship expressed by the *karmapravacanīya* particles has been stated. Now, the determination of the meaning of case-endings (*vibhakti*) is declared in three ways, and likewise, the determination of the meanings of words (*pada*) through their functions (*vṛtti*) is threefold. Following that, the comprehension of the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*), by way of resolving [the meanings of] actions and so forth, is elaborated in exactly three ways. Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Four Meanings Beginning with the Upādhi," in the *Śṛṅgāraprakāśa* composed by the Great Emperor, the illustrious Bhojadeva.

The sixth [chapter], the *Vibhaktyarthādicatuṣṭayaprakāśa*: The meaning of case-endings (*vibhaktyartha*) is threefold—number (*saṅkhyā*), grammatical relation (*kāraka*), and the residual (*śeṣa*). Among these, number consists of the singular, dual, and plural forms pertaining to grammatical relations and their connections. It is sixfold: denotative (*ābhidhānikī*), intentional (*vaivakṣikī*), conditional (*naimittikī*), technical (*pāribhāṣikī*), optional (*vaibhāṣikī*), and residual (*pāriśeṣikī*). Among these, the denotative is as follows: *apaḥ*, *dārāḥ*, *lājāḥ*, *dvayam*, *anekam*, and *niyutam*.

In this context, that which arises from the nature of the word itself is the *ābhidhānikī* (lexical), such as the dual and singular endings [in the case of *rodasī*, etc.]. The *vaivakṣikī* (intentional) is as follows: *rodasī* / *rodasyau*, *kabarī* / *kabaryaḥ*, *stanau* / *stanāḥ*, *viśākhā* / *viśākhe* / *viśākhāḥ*, *dṛke* / *dṛśau* / *dṛśāḥ*, *jagat* / *jagatī* / *jaganti*. Here, singularity, duality, and plurality are determined by the speaker's intention; thus, it is *vaivakṣikī*. The *naimittikī* (conditional) is as follows: *vṛkṣaḥ*, *śobhanaḥ*, *dampatī*, *pitarau*, *akṣāḥ*, *gabhastayaḥ*.

In this context, because the cause (*nimitta*) exists as a real entity (*vastu*), the [number] is derivative (*naumittikī*). The technical (*pāribhāṣikī*) is as follows: *mārdaṅgikapāṇavikaṃ* (the drummers and lute-players), *puruṣau* (two men), *khalatikaṃ* (the ridge of the forest), *vanāni* (forests), *gaudau* (two Gaudas), *grāmaḥ* (the village), *tiṣyapunarvasū* (the two stars Tiṣya and Punarvasu), *tārakāḥ* (the stars), *pañcālā janapadaḥ* (the country of Pañcāla), and "he and I cook. Here, the application of singularity and so forth to duality, plurality, and so on is technical.

The *vaibhāṣikī* [type of derivation] is as follows: *aśvabaḍaḍḍatdhba*, *aśvabaḍaḍḍatdhbau*, *plakṣanyagrodhaṃ*, *plakṣanyagrodhāḥ*, *pūrvaphalgunyau*, and *pūrvāḥ phalgunyaḥ*. Here, the *vaibhāṣikī* refers to the fact that, according to the *vibhāṣā* (optional rule), there are singular, dual, and plural forms. The *pāriśeṣikī* [type of derivation] is as follows: *ekaḥ*, *dvau*, *bahavaḥ*, *ubhau*, *dvitrāḥ*, and *ardhatṛtīyāḥ*. Here, the *pāriśeṣikī* refers to the fact that when the numbers mentioned—such as "one" (*eka*) and so forth—are exhausted, the case endings (*svādayaḥ*) apply by way of remainder (*pariśeṣa*).

It has been stated in this regard that "the cause is one," and here it should be understood as referring to those [kārakas] that have been divided. However, the oneness belonging to that which possesses them resides in the case-ending (*vibhakti*). The *kāraka*—which was previously explained as having six types—is extended here into six distinct varieties according to its not being expressed by the second through the ninth case-endings. Among these, the object (*karman*) is expressed by the second case, as in *kaṭaṃ karoti* ("he makes a mat"). That which is expressed by the third case is, for example, *mātrā sañjānīte* ("he agrees with his mother"). That which is expressed by the fourth case is, for example, *na tvā śune manye* ("I do not consider you equal to a dog").

The meaning of the fifth case (ablative) is expressed as: "It has rained outside the Trigartas. The meaning of the sixth case (genitive) is expressed as: "He remembers his mother. The meaning of the seventh case (locative) is expressed as: "He is proficient in grammar" (*adhītī vyākaraṇe*). The meaning of the second case (accusative) is expressed by the agent (*kartā*): "He causes Devadatta to go to the village" (*gamayati grāmaṃ devadattam*). The meaning of the third case (instrumental) is expressed as: "Done by Caitra" (*caitreṇa kṛtam*). The meaning of the fourth case (dative) is expressed as: "The barley-gruel serves for urine" (*mūtrāya kalpate yavāguḥ*). The meaning of the fifth case is expressed as: "He studies from the teacher" (*upādhyāyād adhīte*). The meaning of the sixth case is expressed as: "The composition of Vyasa" (*vyāsasya kṛtiḥ*). The meaning of the seventh case is expressed as: "While the Brahmins are eating, the Śūdras sit" (*brāhmaṇeṣu bhuñjāneṣu vṛṣalā āsate*).

The *karaṇa* (instrument) may be expressed by the second case, as in *akṣān dīvyati* ("he plays with dice"). It may be expressed by the third case, as in *dātreṇa lunāti* ("he cuts with a sickle"). It may be expressed by the fourth case, as in *śatāya parikrītaḥ* ("bought for a hundred"). It may be expressed by the fifth case, as in *stokān muktaḥ* ("released from a little"). It may be expressed by the sixth case, as in *sarpiṣo jānīte* ("he knows [the way] through ghee"). It may be expressed by the seventh case, as in *akṣeṣu dīvyati* ("he plays at dice"). The *sampradāna* (recipient) may be expressed by the second case, as in *devadattam abhyasūyati* ("he finds fault with Devadatta"). It may be expressed by the third case, as in *dāsyā saṃprayacchate* ("he gives with the slave woman"). It may be expressed by the fourth case, as in *devāya dadati* ("he gives to the god").

The meaning of the fifth case is expressed [by the verb]: "He gives cows starting from his teacher" (*guror ārabhya gāḥ prayacchati*). The meaning of the sixth case is expressed [by the verb]: "He gives the back to the one who strikes" (*ghnataḥ pṛṣṭhaṃ dadāti*). The meaning of the seventh case is expressed [by the verb]: "He desires flowers" (*puṣpeṣu spṛhayati*). The meaning of the ablative (*apādāna*) is expressed by the second case: "The warriors [flee] from Arjuna" (*arjunam yoddhāraḥ*). The meaning of the third case is expressed [by the verb]: "He pierces with a bow" (*dhanuṣā vidhyati*). The meaning of the fourth case is expressed [by the verb]: "They accept out of faith" (*śraddhāya nigṛhṇate*). The meaning of the fifth case is expressed [by the verb]: "He comes from the village" (*grāmād āgacchati*). The meaning of the sixth case is expressed [by the adjective]: "Kṛṣṇā is the most abundant in milk among cows" (*kṛṣṇā gavāṃ saṃpannakṣīratamā*).

The locative case is expressed [by the verb]: "He has eaten rice in a bronze vessel" (*bhukta odanaḥ kaṃsapātryām*). The locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is expressed by the accusative: "He dwells in the village" (*grāmam adhivasati*). It is expressed by the instrumental: "He runs on level ground" (*samena dhāvati*). It is expressed by the dative: "He arms himself for battle" (*yuddhāya saṃnahyati*). It is expressed by the ablative: "He wakes up from a *krośa* away" (*krośād budhyate*). It is expressed by the genitive: "The lord of the people" (*janānām īśvaraḥ*). It is expressed by the locative: "He fasts at the sacred bathing place" (*tīrthe upavasati*). A relation distinct from the [standard] *kārakas*, which is preceded by an action and a *kāraka*, is a specific type of connection.

It is threefold: that which is other than what has been stated (*uktādanya*), that which is other than the *kārakas*, and the non-intentionality (*avivakṣā*) of the *kārakas*. Among these, under the category of "other than what has been stated," there is that which depends on a distinct correlate and that which depends on a non-distinct correlate. Of these two, the first is exemplified by "the king's servant" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*). For instance, when a female friend, out of jest, says to her, "Touch the moon-digit on your husband’s head with this [garland]," she, having colored his feet and offered her blessing, struck her silently with the garland.

The second [type] is "the head of Rāhu," as in: "The face of the deer-eyed one, obscured by the weight of her crest-ornaments, parasol, and mass of falling hair, shone like the orb of the moon (the Lord of Constellations) as it prepared to attack the face of Rāhu. [This occurs] when there is a difference from the grammatical factors (*kāraka*s), whether the action is expressed or unexpressed. Of these two, the first is exemplified by: "He dwells for the sake of food" (*annasya hetor vasati*). As in: "Sovereignty over the world under a single umbrella, fresh youth, and this lovely body..."

"Desiring to sacrifice much for the sake of little, you appear to me to be deluded in your judgment. You are the second [son] of this Brahmin, equal to him in lineage, in beauty, in youth, and in those various virtues preeminent in humility. Choose him as your own equal; let him unite with Kāñcanā. [In this context, there is] dependence on a substance and dependence on an action when there is an intention to express a grammatical case-role (*kāraka*).

Of these two, the first is: "The wealth of a virtuous man is pleasing," as when the wine offered by her lover was filled with an extraordinary flavor; it tasted sweet to the women, and though its name was already established, it was also [newly] produced. The second is: "One should not eat beans," as in: "Friend, let this boy be stopped from saying something; his lower lip quivers with a desire to speak again. Not only does he who speaks to the great incur sin, but he who merely listens to him also shares in that guilt."

However, since specific types of relations—such as accompaniment (*saha-artha*), purpose (*tādarthya*), cause (*hetu*), definition (*lakṣaṇa*), secondary word (*upapada*), and vocative (*sambodhana*)—have already been discussed under the section on "Enhancement" (*upaskāra-adhikāra*), they are not elaborated upon here. Now, one might object: since a relation is preceded by the action and its factors (*kāraka*), the residual relation (*śeṣa-sambandha*) must also be included among the *kārakas*; thus, the case endings (*vibhakti*) would express both number and the capacity for action (*saṅkhyā-śakti*). In that case, a connection between a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) expressing a universal (*jāti*) and a case ending expressing number and *kāraka* would not be possible.

For it is not possible for a genus (jāti) to be connected with number or agency. It is argued in reply: since the individual (vyakti) is indicated by its inseparable connection (avinābhāva) with the genus, there will be a relationship characterized by inherence in a single substrate (ekārthasamavāya) through its connection with number and agency. This is not so; for, because of the faults of infinite regress (ānantya) and deviation (vyabhicāra), verbal roots (prakṛti) are unable to denote the individual as possessing distinctions, and thus they express the genus, which is undifferentiated and non-deviating.

Since case-endings are incapable of expressing both power (*śakti*) and number (*saṅkhyā*) because they differ in their substrates and due to the faults of infinity and deviation, the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of stem and suffix is untenable, as there would be no connection between the power and number residing in those respective substrates. It is not untenable, however, for it is established through inherence in a single unified object (*ekārthasamaveta-samavāya*). But how can there be a mutual relationship between number and substance when they are expressed by denoting their generalities? [It is] just as when they are being expressed [directly].

Just as two objects expressed by words revolve in the intellect and become mutually related, so too two objects perceived from meanings expressed by words will experience a mutual relationship. But does this number or power necessarily delimit the universal (*jāti*)? No, he says; for the singular number heard in the injunction "One should wipe the cup" (*grahaṃ sammārṣṭi*) does not convey the number one as a constituent part of the ritual action.

Nor does the accusative hearing in "he offers the groats" (*saktūn juhoti*) denote the capacity of the groats as the object (*karman*) in relation to the act of offering; rather, as in the case of "he plays with dice" (*akṣān dīvyati*), it enjoins the groats as the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*) in the act of offering, while the specific form of the object is obscured by the general relation [of the accusative]. However, in some instances, the status of number, object, and other capacities as auxiliaries to the action is understood through the hearing of the case-ending in its very form, as in "one should sacrifice an animal" (*paśum ālabheta*) and "one should thresh rice-grains" (*vrīhīn avahanti*).

But why, even when the number and the power are both mentioned by direct audition (*śruti*), is the number alone sometimes intended to be significant? In that regard, concerning the number, it is heard that this entity—which is a substantial thing (*sattvabhūta*) capable of being designated as "this" or "that"—cannot be denoted by words without a number, because only words associated with numbers denote substantial entities. Therefore, since the inclusion of the number is an inseparable concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*) [of the substance], the number is not intended to be significant when there is a reference to a substantial entity.

Just as in the case of the statement "a Brahmin is not to be killed," so too, even in the absence of a genus (*jāti*), because it is impossible to designate a mere object without confusion, the mention of the genus is an inseparable concomitant; thus, it follows that the genus itself is not intended to be expressed. Another says: where number is denoted by words for numbers such as "one" and so forth, there it is necessarily intended to be expressed as a constituent part of the ritual action (*karmāṅga*). For example: "He gives one cow," "He digs with two," and "He sacrifices three animals."

For when that [number] is perceived from the form of a word such as *eka* ("one") and so forth, it cannot be disregarded. However, in other cases, because the intention is solely toward the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the word, the singular number and so forth may be disregarded, as in: "A cow must not be touched with the foot. But even this is not the case, since we observe that disregard does not occur even when words like *ubhaya* ("both") are employed, as in: "If both of one's sacrificial offerings (*havir*) should meet with ruin," and so on. Others hold that, based on the indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) in the rule "In the expression of a genus, when there is a single individual, either [the singular or plural] may be used," both the singular and the plural numbers are not intended to be significant.

"But the dual number is intended to be significant," as in the case of "the two Sarasvatīs. That too is incorrect, because we observe that even the dual number may not be intended to be significant, as in: "If these two should fall ill, this medicine should be given. Since that medicine is capable of pacifying disorders such as wind (vāta) even when given to only one person, then, in cases where a genus (*jāti*) is prescribed as a subordinate element (*parāṅgatayā*), the number is indeed intended to be significant.

However, where something is restated for the sake of its own refinement (*saṃskāra*), it is not intended to be emphasized. For example: "One should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*) and "One should wipe the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*). Since it is impossible to understand both of these through mere examples alone, a logical argument must be stated; that is now being expressed. In the case of "one should sacrifice with an animal," because the sacrifice possesses a fruit, it is primary, and the animal is its subsidiary (*aṅga*); and a subsidiary is that which assists the primary.

Since the benefit for the primary rite (*pradhāna*) is accomplished by a single animal alone, a second one is not required. For if it were assumed that as many animals as one possesses must all be employed, then other sacrifices would have to be performed so that the original sacrifice—having been completed with only one animal—would not render the others useless, and the non-primary sacrifice would be prompted by the accessory substance. However, this is not the correct principle: that an accessory should prompt the primary.

Furthermore, in such injunctions as "one should immolate an animal" (*paśumālabheta*) or "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), this [derivative] sentence is produced in order to manifest the status of the animal as a means (*sādhana*), a status which was previously unknown as being merely a subordinate factor (*aṅga*) of the action. Since the meaning [of a word] is to be determined through the observation of the word itself, the object is accepted exactly as the word expresses it. Through the methods of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is determined that just as the genus (*jāti*) is the denotation of the nominal stem (*prakṛti*), number is the denotation of the case-ending (*vibhakti*).

If the meaning of the word were not completed without the inclusion of a second animal, or if the ritual action were not fulfilled, then a second one might indeed be included. However, because the universal property of "otherness" (paratva) is non-conceptual with respect to each individual and is fully realized through the sacrifice of a single animal, the ritual action is accomplished; thus, a second animal is not required. Furthermore, there exists no number mentioned in the originative injunction that would contradict the singular number in the rule "one should sacrifice with an animal."

That on account of which this [singular number] would have to be abandoned—namely, because this very [singular] is the originative statement (*utpattivākya*) regarding the animal, and because it possesses the status of a word (*śabdatvāt*), and because it is not understood through another number—in cases such as "one should sacrifice with an animal" (*paśunā yajeta*), the number is intended to be significant (*vivakṣyate*). However, in the case of "he wipes the cup" (*grahaṃ sammārṣṭi*), it is not intended to be significant. This is because in the originative statement for the cups, such as "there are nine cups for Prajāpati," the plurality that exists there pertains to the primary element (*pradhāna*), since the cups are being enjoined therein.

However, in the case of the statement "He cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*), the number one (*ekatva*) is subordinate (*śeṣa*), because it is the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) that is being enjoined, and the word "cup" (*graha*) is intended for the purpose of providing a locus for that injunction. It is not logical that a number connected to the primary element (*pradhāna*) should sublate the number belonging to the subordinate element. But surely, by the force of the original productive injunction (*utpattivākya*), several cups are indeed taken; yet, from the singular ending in the word "cup," only one should be cleansed.

What would be contradicted here? If that is the case, then in the sentence concerning the cleaning (*vidāna*), since the absence of the constituent parts (*aṅga*) has already been established previously, the act of cleaning is enjoined as something new (*apūrva*). Consequently, by the word "cup" (*graha*) alone, they are brought together in the ritual recollection (*smṛti*). And since the recollection of the cup arises through the power of prior experience, it presents only those objects exactly as they were experienced; thus, it does not cause one to remember only a single cup, but rather all cups. Likewise, in the presence of multiple cups, the singular number would not cause one to remember only one, but rather [all] the cups, chalices (*camasa*), and so forth.

For by that person by whom many have been experienced, even one has indeed been experienced. This is true; however, although this numerical distinction is perceived, it is incapable [of being enjoined] with respect to the action because it is not being enjoined. The sentence culminates in establishing the action in a single entity. Furthermore, there is no word for "one" (*eka*) by which that [action] might be enjoined for a single [entity]. Nor can a single word enjoin both, because of the difference in their modes of operation: [the word] would have to enjoin the cleansing (*saṃmārjana*) of the unknown [entities] and the connection with the known singleness.

Now, it might be argued that the cleansing (*saṃmārga*) is enjoined as qualified by both the cup (*graha*) and the singularity (*ekatva*); thus, there would be no difference in the performance of the action. However, this is not the case, because the cleansing is for the sake of the cup, since it serves its purpose. Furthermore, the specific case-ending indicates primacy [of the cup]. Therefore, the number is not enjoined.

In that case, how is it that in the sentence "He binds the brindled cow" (*citragavīm badhnāti*), the quality of being brindled (*citro guṇaḥ*) is enjoined? For here too, there is a distinct mode of operation (*bhidyate pravṛttiḥ*), since the making of the cow dependent [on another] and the fact that it is the brindled one are expressed by the direct audition (*śruti*) itself; and because the connection between the quality and the substance is the very object of that [audition]. If it is argued that there is no fault here regarding the action, [we reply: it is like the word *graham* (the cup). Direct audition alone expresses the status of the number and its substratum, the substance, as being auxiliary members (*aṅga*) of the action.

Likewise, one should apply the word *śoṇa* (red), whereby there is the acceptance of both genus (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*) through the employment of a single term. If that is so, then since it is impossible to enjoin a distinction of number when the word functions according to its own primary meaning, the number is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). This is as in the case of "he cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*). Here, because the cleansing is for the sake of the cup, the cups are the primary element (*pradhāna*), and the cleansing is their subordinate member (*aṅga*).

In cases such as "one should sacrifice with an animal," "one should yoke a red [horse]," or "one binds a brindled cow," since the animal and so forth are subordinate to the purpose of the sacrifice and other rites, it is intended that they are enjoined as qualified entities—possessing number, qualities, and so on; thus, both the number and the quality are intended to be significant. The conduct of the Teacher (Pāṇini) also indicates this very point: that number is not intended to be significant when applied to the principal element, but it is intended to be significant when applied to a subordinate quality. For instance:

In the rule *sarūpāṇām ekaśeṣaḥ* ("of those having the same form, there is a single remainder"), when the word *śe� substance* is used as a passive derivative (*karmasādhana*), the substance denoted by the word *śeṣa* possesses primacy because it is expressed through the grammatical refinement (*saṃskāra*) of being the "remainder.
