Therefore, since that which functions according to its own meaning does not intend to express number, the employment of the singular term "one" is made in the sense that "one [substance] remains. Thus, this is the indicator that the number of the primary element is not intended to be expressed.

Thus, because it is accepted that a word ending in a case-suffix (subanta) is compounded with another word ending in a case-suffix (subantena), there is no compound of numerals, such as in the expression *mahatkaṣṭaṃ śritaḥ* ("he has resorted to great hardship"). For in this case, the aggregate (*samudāya*)—as delimited by such an arrangement of constituent parts—is what is grammatically explained as being correct.

Therefore, in the process of imparting refinement (*saṃskāra*) to a whole by means of the individual consideration of its parts, the parts—functioning with reference to that primary whole—proceed by accepting a specific number that has been prescribed. However, where another effort is undertaken, there it applies even to many; as in the rule "time [is compounded] with a measure," and from the plural usage [we derive examples] such as *dvyahnajātaḥ* ("born after two days").

And just as in the formulation of *bahuvrīhi* and *dvandva* compounds, the inclusion of the term "multiple" (*aneka*) results in examples such as "the forest with many intoxicated elephants" (*mattabahumātaṅgaṃ vanam*) and "dhava, khadira, and palāśa trees" (*dhavakhadirapalāśāḥ*). In some cases, even when a quality (*guṇa*) is expressed, the number is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*), where by that non-intentionality the formation of the primary member (*pradhāna*) is established; for example, in the rule: "The object most desired by the agent is the *karman*."

For here, when the designation of *karman* (object) is prescribed for that which is most desired (*īpsitatama*), if the agent were understood as being restricted by the number one—since the desire itself is being specified—the object that is desired by many would lose its connection with the designation of *karman*. Therefore, in order to avoid obstructing or overriding the refinement of the primary factor (*pradhāna*), the agent is resorted to without regard for any specific number. But surely this purpose is merely the establishment of another primary factor; therefore, an argument must be stated for why the number is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣā*).

This is what is said: because the term *īpsitatama* (that which is most desired) is based on a general property, it is capable of applying without distinction to all related factors. Therefore, the mention of the *kartṛ* (agent) is made in order to exclude other means (*sādhana*). Since that [mention of the agent] is exhausted merely by negating its opposite and is incapable of accepting a distinction in number, the capacity (*śakti*), whether residing in a subordinate or a principal factor that possesses number, when enjoined by a case-ending (*vibhakti*), follows only the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*).

And thus, just as in the case of animals and the like, a specific number is associated with them, so too do the means of action (sādhana-bhāva) belong to the sacrifices and the like, even though they are themselves innumerable. But how is it that the number residing in the animal and the like is understood as a means of accomplishment? For, while the status of being a means belongs to a relative of the nominal stem’s meaning—either directly or indirectly—and the number is enjoined by the case-ending (vibhakti), there is no mutual connection between the number and the status of being a means.

In that case, then, the individual object (*vyakti*) is connected with number first; however, number, having attained its excellence through association, functions as the means (*sādhanabhāva*). This very status of being a means, falling upon the qualified [object], indicates that the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is also a means, just as in the expression "victory was achieved by one armed with weapons. But how can there be a connection between number and the status of being a means—which have different bases when expressed by a single word—given the difference in their time of relation? For this is not possible.

Since a number, failing to enter into a relation [with the action], is unable to attain the status of an instrument (*sādhana*), the individual entity (*vyakti*) is thus connected with both number and the status of being an instrument. The case-ending (*vibhakti*) of the verb, having its essence enhanced by these two, employs that [individual] in actions; since that [individual] experiences a connection with the action as qualified [by number and instrumentality], the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is also perceived as connected with the action.

But surely, the agent, instrument, and so forth—the *kārakas*—are the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*), and since they possess an operation (*vyāpāra*) employed for the accomplishment of the action, they are indeed substances (*dravya*) endowed with power (*śaktimat*). Now, if that [substance] is already expressed by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) alone, what is it that is expressed by the case-ending? We reply: it is "power" (*śakti*). For substance is twofold: that which has become an entity (*sattvabhūta*) and that which has not become an entity (*asattvabhūta*). Of these two, the referent of stems such as *vṛkṣa* ("tree") is that which has become an entity, being the substratum of power and number; whereas that which has not become an entity, being the referent of indeclinables (*avyaya*), is not such a substratum.

Both of these [the base and its meaning] are expressed by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself without any adjuncts; however, the adjuncts consisting of gender, number, and relation are conveyed by the case-ending (*vibhakti*). Now, an effect arising from the essential nature of a thing is augmented by its own effects; it is not possible to postulate a separate power (*śakti*) that is beyond the senses. For if such a power were to be postulated, it would have to be either eternal, like the essential nature of the object, or...

Alternatively, if that [capacity] were eternal, there would be the undesirable consequence of the effect being produced eternally. As for the dependence on auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), let it belong to the essential nature itself; what is the use of a capacity? If, however, the effect is [itself] a thing, then if the effect were merely the essential nature of the object, the effect would be produced at all times because the capacity is always present. Let the effect, then, simply be the result of the causal totality (*sāmagrī*).

What is the use of a power (*śakti*) in the interval? If it is argued that no effect is produced from an agent (*kāraka*) that lacks power, then power itself must be an effect; in that case, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) due to the postulation of another power for the production of that [first] power, or else there would be a contradiction of one's own accepted tenets. [The opponent] says: "Indeed, the unperceived is postulated for the sake of establishing what is perceived. The postulation of further powers results only in the creation of a chain of powers, because [powers] are momentary (*kṣaṇika*). Therefore, to prevent a failure of the effect by the agents, only a single power is postulated."

Why, then, this infinite regress? It is not so, for that [effect] is possible otherwise as well. For if the reality of the object were obstructed in its actions, then it would be reasonable to postulate a power distinct from it. However, objects manifest as effects through the acquisition of auxiliary causes (sahakārin) without being obstructed; so why postulate a power in vain? But surely, without power, there could be no causal factor (kāraka), because the very nature of an entity is obstructed in its actions.

For it is form alone that is seen, not taste and so forth; the visual faculty sees, not the gustatory faculty and so forth; taste alone is tasted, not form and so forth; the gustatory faculty tastes, not the visual faculty and so forth; water alone removes thirst, not fire; and fire alone quenches cold, not water. For if there were non-obstruction, since there would be no distinction in the essential nature of things, it would follow that every effect could arise from everything. Consequently, the gustatory faculty would see just as the visual faculty does, and taste would be seen just as form is.

The eye would taste even as the tongue tastes; flavor would be tasted even as form is perceived. Fire would quench thirst even as water does; and water would allay cold even as fire does. Just as sesame seeds are gathered by one seeking oil, so too would sand be gathered; and just as an axe is raised by one intending to cut down a tree, so too would a wooden shoe be raised.

Furthermore, when the power of fire and wind to kill and burn is not admitted [to be absent], yet they remain indifferent toward their own effects because they are restrained by a mantra—what is the reasoning for that? Or, regarding the eyes and ears, what is the justification for their failure to perform their own functions, such as seeing and hearing, due to disease and so forth? For neither by means of a mantra nor by means of disease are their essential natures or their auxiliary causes obstructed, since they are perceived precisely in those forms.

However, since powers (*śaktayaḥ*) are obstructed, it is logical that the effect does not arise even when the essential nature and auxiliary factors are present. Therefore, just as the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) inferred from effects such as pleasure, or the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) which is the cause of memory and cognition based on excellence, or momentum (*vega*) produced by a specific action and conducive to the production of another action—these and others are postulated as being entirely beyond the senses (*atīndriya*)—so too, you must postulate that power (*śakti*) is also beyond the senses, as it is the cause of the excellence of the effect.

That is untenable, because actions, obstructions, and so forth are possible even in the absence of a power (*śakti*). Since tastes and other qualities possess a specific nature determined by their own causal series and are thus distinct in nature from colors and other qualities, how could they—being of such a different nature—accomplish the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) to be accomplished by color and the like? This must necessarily be admitted, for the same objection applies equally even if one postulates a "power."

How is it that these powers have fixed substrata, such that power pervades only the male body? If you say it is due to a specific excellence in the nature of the object itself, then the distinction between effects will also be established from that very same cause.

Moreover, if there is a difference in the substratum (*āśraya*), how can there be a difference in the capacities (*śakti*)? For if capacities possess distinct forms, then the distinction in effects is established by that very distinction in the form of the substratum; what, then, is the use of postulating a difference in capacities? How, then, is it explained in the case of individual instances (*vyakti*) that have identical forms but produce dissimilar effects? For example: water-courses flow by the rays of the moon, but not the sun-stones; hailstones melt by the rays of the sun, but not pearl-jewels; and internal light sees, but external light does not.

Just as the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is wind residing in a living being but not the diffused breath (*vyāna*), the space of the ear hears but the space of the mouth does not, and the learned man is qualified for ritual actions but the ignorant man is not—even though these belong to the same class of entities—there is a restriction based on unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), and the distinction caused by contact with other substances establishes the difference in their effects.

Regarding those individual manifestations of that [universal] which accomplish their respective effects, how is it that—just as that very same fire burns, illuminates, and dispels cold; and those very same waters flood and remove fatigue—there exists such a specific excellence of form (*rūpātiśaya*) in fire or water? It is like the suitability for conjunction, velocity, and disjunction-velocity in the case of action, or like the causality toward pleasure, knowledge, and liberation in the case of *dharma*.

In the determination of causal relations (*upādānaniyama*), however, we do not produce any new or novel relationship of cause and effect through mental construction (*bhāvanā*). Rather, we act by following what is already established. In that regard, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) or from the usage of elders, we understand that sesame seeds and axes alone are the causes for the production of oil and the felling of trees, respectively. Therefore, those who desire such results take up only those [causes], and not sand, shoes, or the like.

Furthermore, even though the nature of sesame seeds or axes remains constant, their effects do not arise at all times; for, just like their own nature, the presence of auxiliary causes (sahakārin) must also be depended upon, and such presence cannot be established as existing at all times. Moreover, factors such as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are included within the class of auxiliary causes; if the production of an effect depends upon these, how could everything possibly arise from everything? Indeed, the postulation of merit and so forth is unavoidable, as it is necessitated by the force of observed effects such as the diversity of the world.

Furthermore, even when poison and fire are present, the fact that their effect is not produced due to the employment of a mantra is not caused by the obstruction of their power; rather, it is caused by the introduction of another causal complex (*sāmagrī*). But what is done by the mantra as it enters [into the complex]? Nothing at all is done; rather, another causal complex is brought about.

If it is argued that a particular causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is the cause of a certain effect and its nature remains exactly as it was [before], then why would poison not kill even when it has not been consumed? In that case, other factors such as contact must also be considered. Furthermore, let the absence of a mantra also be taken into account; just as merit (*dharma*) enters into the matter at the time of a divine rite, so too does the mantra enter and obstruct the effect. Even on the view that there is a potency (*śakti*), what is the function of the mantra? For by means of the mantra, either the destruction or the obstruction of the potency is effected.

It is not, first of all, destruction [of the capacity], because the effect is observed again once the mantra has been removed. Let it be, then, that there is an obstruction of the very nature [of the cause]. But what has happened to the nature itself? And what has happened to the capacity (*śakti*)? If you say it is "indifference toward the effect," that is equally true for the other case as well; the nature certainly exists, since it is perceived. The capacity also exists, since it is inferable from the subsequent observation of the effect. By this, the dilemma regarding the destruction or obstruction of the capacities of sight and hearing due to disease and so forth is also explained.

Furthermore, you yourselves maintain that even the operation (*vyāpāra*) is beyond the reach of the senses, just like the capacity (*śakti*). Since the effect can be accounted for by the assumption of either one alone, why resort to the cumbersome assumption of both? If it is argued that a cause is not a causal factor (*kāraka*) unless it possesses capacity and is also operating, then how is its capacity known? If it is said to be known from the observation of the effect, then the effect will be established by the operation alone; yet I do not see the severing of a foot resulting from the mere operation of a sandal.

In that case, [the causal capacity] would not be beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), because one would know its state of being active even prior to the observation of the effect. For activity is indeed inferable from the effect; it could not be known at all without the effect. However, since an effect can be accounted for by some other cause, it is impossible for it to necessitate the postulation of both [the agent and the capacity]. If it is argued that this refers to "capacity" (*śakti*), it is said in response:

Regarding what you say, "the essential nature (svarūpa), the essential nature," what is this so-called essential nature? It cannot be substance (dravya), because it is designated separately as "the essential nature of substance. Furthermore, is it not the case that there is no logical argument [against it] being the property that distinguishes [an object] from its own kind and from other kinds? For even you describe it using an abstract suffix (bhāvapratyaya) as "the reality of the object" (arthatattva) or "the reality of the entity" (bhāvatattva).

And it is traditionally taught that when a word is applied to a substance because of the presence of a certain quality (*guṇa*), the suffixes *tva* and *tal* are used to denote that quality. Quality, property (*dharma*), capacity (*sāmarthya*), the state of performing a purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*), and power (*śakti*) are one and the same thing. That [quality] is either distinct from the substance or the very self of the substance; nevertheless, by resorting to a conceptual distinction (*vyatireka*), it functions as a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).

For how could the various instruments and other means of accomplishment—which possess bodies that are mutually distinct—fail to become confused when they attain the nature of a single substance? Or, if there is no confusion, how is it possible for these to have the nature of a single substance? Therefore, it is precisely the exclusion of being an instrument (the state of being non-instrumental) residing in a single substance that brings about the distinction of this [substance] from other substances. Furthermore, let it be understood from the rule regarding *avyayībhāva* compounds concerning the meaning of case-endings (*vibhaktyartha*): "The meaning of a case-ending, which is distinct from the substance, is expressed by an indeclinable. To illustrate:

An indeclinable (*avyaya*) occurring in the sense of a case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*) is compounded with a subsequent word. Now, if by the phrase "in the sense of a case-ending" what is meant is a substance (*dravya*) that has become a real entity (*sattvabhūta*) as the locus of power (*śaktyāśraya*), then that would not be denoted by an indeclinable which expresses non-existence (*asattva*). Since that meaning is already expressed by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) itself, the indeclinable—which denotes that [meaning]—undergoes compounding with the subsequent word while expressing [it]. By this, it is determined that the case-ending denotes a power (*śakti*) distinct from the substance.

What you say is indeed correct. [We] do not consider *śakti* (power) to be something other than the substance itself, such as its causal capacity (*kārakatva*) or its essential nature (*svarūpa*). Rather, we maintain that the manifestations of objects are capable of producing effects; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of every effect arising from everything. We do not understand how things possess a restricted nature derived from a succession of their own causes. If it is argued that *śakti* is a pre-eminent quality of an object arising from the qualities of its causes, [we reply: so be it.

However, the conceptualization of that [power] as either eternal or non-eternal is not applicable; because it exists as long as the substance itself, it is—like the substance—either eternal or non-eternal. Consequently, the production of an effect occurs at all times, since power manifests precisely at the time of action. Furthermore, factors such as unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) or specific auxiliary causes are the triggers for the manifestation of power; these too are not denied by us until the very moment of action.

However, regarding the restriction of the material cause (*upādāna*), both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are rooted solely in the capacity (*śakti*) ascertained through the observation of effects, even within hundreds of usages by elders; for even the elders express positive and negative concomitance based on that [capacity]. Furthermore, the alternative views—that there is no obstruction to destruction, or that [obstruction] is caused by mantras and the like—are already refuted once it is established that the essential nature (*svarūpa*) itself constitutes the capacity. As for the operation (*vyāpāra*), it is indeed denoted by the verbal root (*dhātu*) and is supersensible (*atīndriya*), not something real in its own right; for it is precisely through those two [the essential nature and the operation] that causality is understood in such a manner.

A power (*śakti*) postulated because the manifestation of an effect cannot otherwise be explained is indeed more appropriately regarded as being beyond the reach of the senses. The meaning of a word (*vṛttyartha*) is threefold: that which is not the meaning of a single word (*apadārtha*), that which is the meaning of one word (*ekapadārtha*), and that which is the meaning of multiple words (*anekapadārtha*). Among these, that which is not the meaning of a single word (*apadārtha*) is threefold: pertaining to the meaning of a verbal root and an affix (*dhātupratyayārthīya*), pertaining to the meaning of an affix and an affix (*pratyayapratyayārthīya*), and pertaining to the meaning of a nominal stem and an affix (*prātipadikapratyayārthīya*). Of these, that which pertains to the meaning of a verbal root and an affix (*dhātupratyayārthīya*) is twofold: having the form of an action (*kriyārūpa*) and having the form of a factor of action (*kārakarūpa*).

The form of *kriyā* (action) in these two [types of compounds] is as follows: *cikīrṣati* ("he wishes to do"), where one desires to act; *kārayati* ("he causes to do"), where one employs another who is acting; and *pāpacyate* ("he cooks excessively" or "he cooks repeatedly"). The form of the *kāraka* (participant in action) is as follows: *pacati* ("he cooks"), where he performs the cooking (*pāka*); *pacyate* ("it is cooked"), where it is performed by means of cooking; and *pācakaḥ* ("the cooker") or *paktavyam* ("that which is to be cooked"). The relation between the suffix and the meaning of the suffix is twofold: obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*vaivakṣika*). Of these, the obligatory is exemplified by: *kṛtrimaṃ sāṃrāviṇam* ("artificial shouting together"); *vyāvakrośī bhidā* ("mutual reviling" or "splitting"); and *ābhijityaḥ kauñjāyanyaḥ* ("descendant of Kauñjāyana, born from Abhijit").

The *vaivakṣika* (intentional) [meaning] is, for example: *cikīrṣuḥ* (one who wishes to act), *kāraṇā* (a female descendant of Karaṇa), *gārgyāyaṇaḥ* (a male descendant of Garga), *kālyāṇineyaḥ* (the son of Kalyāṇī), *mālāyāḥ* (of the garland), and *kumāryāḥ* (of the maiden). The meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) is twofold: in the form of an individual (*vyakti*) and in the form of a capacity (*śakti*). Of these two, the form of the individual is, for example: *ajā* (goat), *kumāra* (boy), *brahmabandhuḥ* (one who is a Brahmin in name only), *vṛkṣaḥ* (tree), *vṛkṣau* (two trees), *vṛkṣāḥ* (trees). The form of the capacity is, for example: *vṛkṣam* (the tree [as object]), *vṛkṣeṇa* (by the tree), *vṛkṣāya* (for the tree), *vṛkṣāt* (from the tree), *vṛkṣe* (in the tree), *vṛkṣasya* (of the tree).

A single word-meaning is threefold: consisting of a substance (*vasturūpa*), consisting of a non-substance (*avasturūpa*), and consisting of an action (*kriyārūpa*). Among these, that which consists of a substance is twofold: a meaning denoting a sentient being (*sattvabhūta*) and a meaning denoting a non-sentient thing (*asattvabhūta*). Of these, an example of a meaning denoting a sentient being is: *aupagavaḥ* (the son of Upagu), *chāndasaḥ* (one who knows the Veda), *lākṣikaḥ* (one who dyes with lac), and *yauṣmakaḥ* (belonging to you). An example of a meaning denoting a non-sentient thing is: *āstikaḥ* (a believer), *upatyakā* (the land at the foot of a mountain), *prakaṭam* (manifestly), and *tatratyaḥ* (situated there). That which consists of a non-substance is likewise twofold, as previously described.

The meaning that has become a sentient being (*sattvabhūta*) is, for example: *pañcakṛtvaḥ*, *karvadā*, *bahuśaḥ*—like fire. The meaning that has not become a sentient being (*asattvabhūta*) is, for example: *nātarām*, *prāha tarām*, *pacatitarām*, *pacatirūpam*. The form of action (*kriyārūpa*) is twofold: contracted (*saṃkṣipta*) and expanded (*vitripta*). Of these two, the contracted is, for example: *putriyati* (he desires a son) from *putram icchati*; *śyenāyate* (he acts like a hawk); *bhṛśāyate* (he becomes intense); and *abhiṣeṇayati* (he marches with an army).

The *vikṣipta* [type of compound] is as follows: one says "he causes Kaṃsa to be killed" (*kaṃsaṃ ghātayati*) when describing the slaying of Kaṃsa; "he causes the night to pass" (*rātriṃ vivāsayati*) when describing the passing of the night; "he knows the conjunction of the moon with Puṣya" (*puṣyeṇa candraṃ yojayati*) when knowing the conjunction of the moon with the asterism Puṣya; and "having set out from Ujjayinī, he reaches the sunrise at Māhiṣmatī" (*māhiṣmatyāṃ sūryam udgamatīti*) when describing reaching the sunrise at Māhiṣmatī. The *anekapadārtha* [compound] is threefold: that which rests on the meaning of a single word, that which rests on the meaning of both words, and that which rests on the meaning of another word.

In that regard, the compound based on the meaning of a single word is of two kinds; the compound based on the meaning of the first member is of three kinds: based on the meaning of the first member, based on the meaning of both members, and based on the meaning of another member. Among those, the compound based on the meaning of the first member is of two kinds: based on the meaning of the prior member and based on the meaning of the subsequent member. Of these, the one based on the meaning of the prior member is exemplified by: *upakumbham*, *paruṣavyāghraḥ*, *gomatallikā*, *pūrvakāyaḥ*, *rājadantaḥ*, and *prāptajīvikaḥ*.

An example of that which relies on the meaning of the final member [of a compound] is: *rājapuruṣaḥ* (the king’s man), *yūpādāru* (wood for a sacrificial post), *kaṣṭāśritaḥ* (one who has resorted to hardship), *śvalebhyaḥ* (from dogs and jackals), *dvyāhnajātaḥ* (born after two days), and *prāptajīvikaḥ* (one who has attained a livelihood). That which relies on the meaning of the final member is of two kinds: having a single substratum (*ekadhikaraṇa*) and having different substrata (*bhinnadhikaraṇa*). Of these two, an example of that with a single substratum is: *nīlotpalam* (a blue lotus), *agnistokaḥ* (a small fire), *puruṣottamaḥ* (the best of men), *sarvaśvetaḥ* (all-white), *saptarṣayaḥ* (the seven seers), and *khajekuṇḍaḥ*.

Examples of [compounds] with distinct substrata (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*) are: *dhava-khadirau* (the dhava and khadira trees), *asva-baḍabau* (a horse and a mare), *dadhi-payasī* (curd and milk), *dhava-khadira-palāśāḥ* (the dhava, khadira, and palāśa trees), *kāka-ulūkau* (a crow and an owl), and *go-aśvam* (a cow and a horse). The compound based on another word-meaning (*anyapadārtha-āśraya*) is twofold: that which possesses its quality (*satadguṇa*) and that which does not possess its quality (*atadguṇa*). Of these, an example of *satadguṇa* is: *unmatta-gaṅgām* (the "Mad-Ganges," i.e., a river whose banks are inhabited by madmen), *śastrī-śyāmā* (dark like a knife, i.e., a woman as dark as a knife), *sahasrākṣaḥ* (thousand-eyed, i.e., Indra), *śūla-pāṇiḥ* (trident-handed, i.e., Śiva), *dvitrāḥ* (two or three), and *ardha-tṛtīyāḥ* (two and a half).

An example of that which does not possess the quality [of its parts] (*atadguṇa*) is: *uḍharatha* (one who has brought a chariot), *citragu* (one who has variegated cows), *dakṣiṇapūrvā* (southeast), *uṣṭramukha* (camel-faced), *guḍadhātṛpriya* (fond of one who places molasses), and *priyaguḍa* (fond of molasses). Now, those who maintain the theory of *vṛtti* (compound formation) ask: "What do they mean by saying that *vṛtti* is the expression of another's meaning (*parārthābhidhāna*)? What, then, is the meaning of this? Does it mean the expression of something that is for the sake of another, or is it an expression that is itself for the sake of another? There is no fault in either case. First, when the view is that even a single word conveys a manifold meaning, then in the state of a sentence (*vākya-avasthā*),...

The function (*vṛtti*) takes up that nature of the object which is already cognized as being denotable by another word; it presents that [object] as a subordinate element within its own domain through the mode of being a denotation. Thus, because the power of denotation is obstructed when the word exists in its state of being divided [into stem and suffix], the denotation of the meaning of another [word] during the *vṛtti* is called "the denotation of the meaning of another" (*parārthābhidhāna*).

Furthermore, when this position holds—that a single word conveys multiple meanings—then, regarding the object present before one, those subordinate words (*upasarjana*) assume their objects for the sake of another [meaning]. In this view, the denotation of another’s purpose is quite evident. In that regard, there are two possibilities: either the subordinate words, setting aside their well-known connection with their own meaning, would take up a different meaning; or, while remaining fixed in their original sense, they would denote an additional meaning.

Indeed, both [possibilities] are observed elsewhere. For example, in the case of a curd-pot, after the curd has been removed, milk is placed inside; however, in the case of a water-jar made of sand, the water remains together with the sand and other constituents. Thus it is asked: for those who maintain that the function (*vṛtti*) of words is the expression of another meaning (*parārthābhidhāna*), is this function one that abandons its own meaning (*jahatsvārthā*) or one that does not abandon its own meaning (*ajahatsvārthā*)? What follows from this? If it were one that abandons its own meaning, then when it is said, "Let the king’s man be brought," the bringing of the mere man would result.

In the command "Bring the son of Upagu" (*aupagavam ānaya*), [if the secondary term were to denote] the offspring alone, there would be a problem. Alternatively, if it is argued that the secondary term does not abandon its own primary meaning (*ajahatsvārthā*), then since both meanings—each having its own distinct sense—are present, the dual number (*dvivacana*) would apply to the two [meanings], and thus the dual form would result. Thus, because faults are seen in both cases, neither [interpretation] is accepted. Regarding this, some hold the following view: secondary terms (*upasarjanapada*) introduce a different meaning by abandoning the meaning they have already assumed; for it is impossible for a word that was previously independent [of another] to express a different meaning while being made subordinate to another meaning.

Therefore, by one who expresses a different meaning, the original referent (arthavastu) that was previously adopted must be abandoned. To this he says: "Which mode of operation (vṛtti) is then logical? It is proper that it be 'abandoning its own meaning' (jahatsvārthā). Indeed, it is proper. For it is observed thus in the world: when a person engages in the work of another, he abandons his own work. Just as, for example, a carpenter, when engaged in the king's work, abandons his own work.

And thus, if the king, while engaged in the service of a man, or Upagu, while engaged in the service of his offspring, were to abandon their own purpose; would it not be just as when a carpenter, occupied with the king’s business such as the fetching and placing of tools, abandons his own work of cutting wood and shaping it because it is impossible to perform the king’s task without abandoning his own? In the same way, even if a subordinate element (*upasarjana*) is engaged in the service of another, such as the communication of a different meaning (*arthāntara*), it [would abandon its own purpose] without abandoning its own purpose.

If it were impossible to express the meaning for the sake of another, one would have to abandon previously established meanings such as "masculinity" and so forth; consequently, in the two examples mentioned, there would result the bringing of any mere male person and any mere offspring. This is not a fault.

Although subordinate words enter into their own meanings, nevertheless, having imparted a distinction of form to the principal word—which serves as the basis for grasping an excellence of meaning—they subsequently abandon their own meanings. Therefore, at that time, the human purpose (puruṣārtha) accompanied by that distinction of form is perceived as qualified, even though the meaning of the subordinate word has ceased [to function]. For the specific qualities imparted by those [subordinate words] do not merely persist as long as the presence of the cause that brings about the excellence; rather, they continue to persist even when the cause has been removed.
In this regard, just as the internal bodily heat, produced by the intense heat of the autumnal sun's rays, cannot be countered merely by avoiding the touch of the sun's glare;

or just as the specific qualities of form, taste, smell, and touch—which arise from contact with a blazing fire—persist for as long as the fuel lasts even after the fire itself has been driven far away; so too, the excellence of the primary form, when conditioned by subordinate factors, serves as the cause for delimiting the specific nature of the word-meaning even when those subordinate factors have ceased.

Alternatively, for one who has ascertained that the mention of the subordinate element possesses the capacity to denote a specific meaning, there arises—through the activation of latent impressions (saṃskāra) produced by that ascertainment—a determination of that meaning. Even though the verbal expression has abandoned its primary sense, the cognition is carried away by the similarity of form; thus, for one who has not realized the abandonment of the original meaning, activity proceeds. Consequently, it is the principal element itself that is qualified by that [subordinate].

But surely, if one understands that very same meaning through the power of repeated practice in observing its usage, what abandonment of its own meaning is there? For in that heard [word], the specific implements or objects are not established as being physically situated within a bellows; rather, they are to be inferred from the observation of the form of the word. Since it is the same here as well, what is lost of its own meaning? It is not so; for even when its own primary meaning has ceased, meanings are understood through syntactic connection (*anvaya*).

For example, "a jar of ghee" (*ghṛtaghaṭa*) or "a jar of oil" (*tailaghaṭa*). Even when the ghee or the oil has been poured out, "ghee" or "oil" remains as the qualifier of these jars, such that one says, "this is a jar of ghee" or "this is a jar of oil. Thus, the object serves as the secondary designation (*upanyāsa*). In this regard, whatever portion of the meaning constitutes the constituent part—that which cannot be removed from the fire of existence even after being heated, like a tuft of grass that cannot be washed away—that is the specific distinction (*viśeṣa*). For instance, [one speaks of] a "māllika-fragrance jar" (*mallikāpuṭa*) or a "campaka-fragrance jar" (*campakāpuṭa*).

Even when the flowers have been removed, designations such as "this is a jasmine-bundle" or "this is a campaka-bundle" continue to apply because the specific fragrance produced by contact with them persists; thus, these designations are perceived. Likewise, in this case as well, due to positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the qualifying attribute will remain even when the subordinate object has been discarded. Alternatively, although the word *rājan* abandons its own primary meaning, it does not abandon it entirely; for only a certain portion of its own meaning is relinquished.

How does this [subordinate purpose] abandon its own purpose due to contradiction? To that extent that there is a contradiction with the application of the primary purpose, to that same extent it should abandon the purpose. Thus it is said: "That which is one's own purpose if it contradicts the purpose of another, that one abandons. For there is no instance of abandoning one's own purpose when it serves the primary purpose; for a carpenter engaged in the king’s business does not abandon the king’s business itself, nor indeed his laughter, joking, scratching, and yawning.

Nor is this meaning what is called "having a qualifier that contradicts the purpose of another. Therefore, it does not abandon its status as a qualifier. Now, it is said that prefixes (*upasarga*) and subordinate words (*napada*) possess an engagement in the function of delimiting the meaning of the principal word; they do not abandon their state of being qualifiers that assist the principal. And this is precisely the function of the meanings of subordinate words: that they cause one to understand the principal word as having its form fully realized. For instance:

In the expression *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king's man"), the referent "man" is understood as being qualified by a distinction conditioned by its relation to a specific possessor; however, in the expression *rājapuruṣaḥ*, this is not the case. Furthermore, it is not the case that the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) merely conveys its own meaning—which would otherwise not be conveyed—while the primary distinction (which is not itself a word-meaning) is what is to be established. Why, then, is it said that "in a compound, the members abandon their own meanings" (*jahatsvārthā vṛttiḥ*)? It is thought thus: when a word brings about the cognition of its own specific excellence, it possesses independence; by the abandonment of that [excellence], there is the relinquishing of its own meaning.

Furthermore, if the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) were not to benefit the principal member through its own meaning, its very nature would be lost; for its status as a subordinate is caused precisely by its being subservient to another. Moreover, the subordinate member would result in a useless employment (*prayogavaiyarthyam*), since the principal member would already be understood by the subsequent word alone. Nor can a connection with another [word] be established for that which is meaningless, and the designation of a compound (*samāsa-saṃjñā*), which is dependent upon semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*), would be untenable. Therefore, there is no abandonment of the entire meaning.

Rather, what is lost is merely the capacity to convey a specific excellence of form that would otherwise be presented as a qualifier (*viśe�ṣaṇa*) within its own word. But [one might object]: even when it has abandoned its entire meaning, will not the aggregate [of phonemes] that expresses the particularity of the subordinate word-meaning attain the status of a subordinate factor (*aṅga*), just like a phoneme? It is not so; for if it were understood in this way, the primary meaning, being incompatible with the word-meaning [thus reduced], would end up being abandoned.

Nor is a distinction of the principal [meaning], delimited by the qualifier and the qualified, or a composite [meaning] understood from subordinate words that have abandoned their own individual referents; and it is not reasonable to postulate a word-meaning that is not being perceived—thus, this [objection] is trivial. Furthermore, although this very composite, whose prior and posterior parts are unexpressed, appears as if followed by a division of parts, it denotes a referent in which the difference is superimposed by the two word-meanings related [to it].

Nevertheless, the means for attaining that [understanding] is the demonstration of the distinction between the preceding and the subsequent. And in that regard, within the *vṛtti* (the compound), the qualification of capacity (*samarthādhikāra*) is established; [this refers to] the difference in meaning through the difference in names of the capable [words], or their combination (*saṃsarga*). Here, when "the king's" (*rājñaḥ*) is said with the singular suffix (*ekavacana*), all [his] property is implicated. When "man" (*puruṣaḥ*) is said with the singular suffix, every master is implicated. Now, here, when "the king’s man" (*rājapuruṣam*) is said with the singular suffix, it excludes [the king's man] from other masters.

The man [is also protected] from the king and from others among his own kin; thus, when he is excluded from both sides, if he should abandon [the woman], let him do so at will. There shall never be the abduction of a mere man. But surely, when "man" is mentioned, there must be an understanding that it is not a woman? This is true; however, this is said with reference to a man who has been specifically identified through a particular form or through connection with another substance as being independent.

For when a king, having ascertained his own purpose, engages in activity for the sake of another, there arises a distinction from the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadika) whose object is the general relation [of ownership]. However, a person, being determined through the connection with a specific owner from that which has already ascertained its own purpose, initially possesses a nominal stem meaning that is not distinct [from the person]; thus, ending in the nominative case, he experiences a relation residing in a specific owner. When that [person] has obtained the case-ending, the subsequent distinction that arises constitutes the sentence-meaning (vākyārtha).

Now, in this case, the king turns back a man from other masters. In that situation, there is a certain distinction, its capacity, and the activity caused by it; and when such activity, which is caused by distinction, exists, the king’s own purpose is accomplished by creating a distinction in the person who is oriented toward that activity. Even for that man whose [purpose] does not turn back, he too creates a distinction between himself and his master.

Thus, when these two [terms] are mutually established, once the specific person has been determined through exclusion on both sides, and no other meaning for the aggregate has appeared—if the meaning of "king" were to cease, let it cease as it pleases. However, if there were a cessation of that which has not yet achieved its purpose prior to the formation of the compound, then the formation itself would not occur; and cessation is dependent upon the cause for formation. Therefore, there is no fault. Another says: indeed, the "king's man" (*rājapuruṣa*) is simply a person, just like a "Brahmin and so forth" person (*brāhmaṇādipuruṣa*).

In that case, the king merely effects the cessation of one master; he does not, however, cause the person to cease from being a servant altogether. Once the cessation of the previous master has been effected, the person himself performs the duties of a royal servant. Now, according to another view, a word does not assume a different meaning by abandoning its established meaning. For words whose meanings are fixed by a non-human (apauruṣeya) relationship are not capable of uttering a meaning other than their own, nor are they able to forfeit their established security and well-being (yogakṣema).

For water does not abandon its own inherent moisture, even when its touch is intensified through contact with fire. However, when a specific cause is present, these [words] may optionally possess the capacity to denote a distinct meaning; therefore, it is precisely through this accumulation that subordinate words provide an excellence of assistance to the principal word in its function. The assistance to the principal, however, consists in the delimitation of the specific owner regarding the human purpose (puruṣārtha). And that [assistance] can be accomplished only by not abandoning one's own primary meaning.

For it is not possible to apply a specific excellence of the word-form (*śabdarūpātiśaya*)—whose own meaning has been completely discarded—to another meaning. Since the application of a specific excellence of form is dependent upon the primary object, those subordinate words (*upasarjana*) that do not admit their own meaning and instead reside in the meaning of the principal (*pradhāna*) merely express that very same meaning through another word; they do not convey any excellence of the principal. Consequently, when it is said, "Bring the king's man" (*rājapuruṣam ānaya*), it would follow that one brings any man at all.

Regarding the example "Bring the son of Upagu" (*aupagavam ānaya*), it refers to the offspring in general. Having determined this, he says: "Alternatively, let the compound formation (*vṛtti*) be one that does not abandon its own meaning (*ajahatsvārthā*). But is it logical that there should be such a thing as a compound formation that does not abandon its own meaning? "Certainly it is logical; for it is observed thus in the world: when this beggar obtains a second alms, he does not abandon the previous alms, but rather strives for the sake of accumulation. [Objection: But was it not already stated that since both meanings are present, the dual number would apply because "the dual occurs for two things"?

But why does the dual number apply to the *kaṣāya*s? It applies to the nominative (*prathamā*). [Objection: But the king is not in apposition with the nominative. [Reply: Then it would apply to the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*). [Objection: But the man is not in apposition with the genitive. [Reply: Then it must indeed apply to the nominative. [Objection: Was it not already stated that the king, being expressed by the word, is not in apposition with the nominative? That meaning has been internalized and has become the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). In that case, since the nominative occurs when the meaning of the nominal stem is present, the dual number would necessarily apply to the nominative alone.

In that regard, just as in the case of the expression "dhava and khadira," where the addition of another object-entity gives rise to a distinction in number, causing the singular number to be applied [to each], so too here in the case of "rājapuruṣa" (king's man), one might argue that the dual number would apply to the word *puruṣa*. But it is not so; for in the case of "dhava and khadira," the specific number is inherent in the meanings of the individual components, and therefore it is the cause for the case-ending following those components. Here, however, since there is only one person who is the referent of the single word *puruṣa*, the singular number alone is logically appropriate for the word *puruṣa*.

For a case-ending that is not connected with the word *rājan* does not require number as its expressed meaning when that number is inherent in the meaning of that [word]. However, in the case of the members of a *dvandva*, because they possess the capacity to express multiple meanings, the use of the singular suffix is not contradictory. If it is argued that this would then apply even to words that are not subsequent members [of a compound], let it so; the elision will occur by the rule "supo dhātuprātipadikayoḥ. Now, if this is the intended meaning:

The case-ending follows the aggregate; therefore, it denotes the number inherent in the meaning of that aggregate. Since an aggregate consists of its constituent parts, the distinction in number is based on the distinction between those parts; this is the cause for the plural number. Where, then, is this applicable? It is where a collection of meanings is conveyed by a collection of words, as in the case of a *dvandva* compound.

But where a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), delimited by the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), is the denotation to be taken up by the parts as a whole—as in the case of *bahuvrīhi* compounds such as *lohitavasanaḥ* ("red-clad") or *cetraveṣṭanaḥ* ("encircled by a mat")—there, because the word-meaning, which possesses a distinction imparted by the meanings of the parts, is denoted by the whole, the subsequent case-ending takes up a number that resides in the meaning of the whole. Thus it is said: "Because the aggregate has a single unified meaning (*ekārthya*), there is no production of a case-ending based on the number of the parts."

For in this case, the case-ending must arise from the whole expression "rājapuruṣa" (king’s man). By that very whole, which constitutes a single unified meaning supported by the powers of its constituent parts, the power of the constituents—which cannot be designated separately—is expressed. And since unity inheres in that collective meaning, which is delimited by a specific owner and whose connection with other owners has ceased, the case-ending will not arise based on the number of the constituents, even though such a number exists.

Thus, in a compound (*vṛtti*) that does not abandon its own meaning (*ajahatsvārthā*), that subordinate member (*upasarjana*) denotes the principal meaning as qualified by an excellence of its own meaning. Consequently, in the compound, there occurs the denotation of two meanings standing in the relation of qualifier and qualificand (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya*) for the subordinate member. However, that which was a qualifier possible for the principal meaning—such as "inhabitant of Pāṭaliputra" (*pāṭaliputraka*)—is excluded from it. Therefore, in the domain of the compound, the meaning of the king is not delimited by those qualifiers.

But when, in the state of the sentence, the meaning of the subordinate word remains entirely distinct from contact with the principal element, then it is indeed appropriate that it experiences the absence of qualification, as in the case of "the man of Pāṭaliputra, [who is] the king's. Or, if diversity arises merely from the means [of expression], the aggregate itself is one; however, the conceptualization of distinction or connection occurs through either option (*vikalpa*) or combination (*abhyuccaya*).

In that regard, in the case of a *vṛtti* (compound) where the individual meanings are not entirely abandoned (*atyantājahatsvārthā*), there is only a relation of distinction (*bheda*) as the capacity (*sāmarthya*) between the word *puruṣa*, which denotes the "person," and the words *sarva*, which are intent upon their respective specific objects. However, in the case of a *vṛtti* where the individual meanings are not abandoned (*ajahatsvārthā*), there is only a relation of connection (*saṃsarga*) as the capacity between the word *puruṣa*, which denotes the person alone, and the words *sarva*, which are intent upon their respective specific objects.

In a compound where the constituent words do not completely abandon their own meanings—as in the case of *puruṣa* and other relative terms—and given the admission that all words have their origin in what is semantically incapable [of independent syntactic function], it is explained that when the compound is completed, "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) consists in the relation between difference and connection. This is stated by those who employ such formations for the sake of the comprehension of the unlearned; for there are various means of communication regarding persons that are not fixed.

For, when an object endowed with excellence is denoted by a composite [word] that, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*), does not touch upon the distinction between prior and posterior parts, there is no occasion whatsoever for the perception of a connection between distinct elements. Therefore, it is precisely through the non-real perception of distinction and connection that the real meaning of the aggregate is determined. The referent of a word (*padārtha*) is threefold: genus (*jāti*), individual (*vyakti*), and configuration (*ākṛti*). Among these, the genus is the cause of the cognition of non-difference among things that are different. That [genus] is threefold: substance-genus (*dravyajāti*), quality-genus (*guṇajāti*), and action-genus (*kriyājāti*).

Among these, the genus of substance (*dravyajāti*) is twofold: that manifested by configuration (*saṃsthāna*) and that manifested by instruction (*upadeśa*). Of these, the first is, for example: "A cow must not be touched with the foot," or "Rice, when fully ripened, brings about an abundance of food. The second is, for example: "A Brāhmaṇa must not be killed," or "The Kaṭha is a reciter [of the Veda]. The genus of quality (*guṇajāti*) is twofold: perceptible (*pratyakṣā*) and inferable (*anumeyā*). Of these, the first is, for example: "One should sacrifice a white goat," or "Sourness is digestive and appetizing."

The second [type of accusative] is as follows: "the skillful man attains prosperity," or "the lover becomes fond of ornaments. *Kriyā* (action) and *jāti* (genus) are each twofold: having the form of a general property (*sāmānya-rūpā*) and having the form of a particular property (*viśeṣa-rūpā*). Of these two, the first is exemplified by: "he nourishes his wealth," or "he should conduct himself according to the conduct of a city-dweller. The second is exemplified by: "the *Aṣṭakā* sacrifice has been performed," or "one should sacrifice with the *Viśvajit* [rite]. The individual (*vyakti*) is the substratum of the genus; it is threefold: the individuality of substance (*dravya-vyakti*), the individuality of quality (*guṇa-vyakti*), and the individuality of action (*kriyā-vyakti*).

Among these, the manifestation of substance (*dravyavyakti*) is twofold: pure (*śuddhā*) and mixed (*miśrā*). Of these, the first is, for example: "Bind the cow," "He milks the cow," "You cook," "I cook. The second is, for example: "In Magadha the breasts are full; in Kaliṅga the eyes are beautiful; in Aṅga the arms are long; in Vaṅga the feet are soft. The manifestation of quality (*guṇavyakti*) is twofold: primary (*mukhyā*) and secondary (*gauṇī*).

Of these two, the first is, for example: "I see white color," "I taste sweet flavor," "I smell fragrant odor," or "I experience cold touch. The second is, for example: "His majesty is intense; his fame is sweet, new, and pure; his nature is fragrant. The manifestation of action (*kriyāvyakti*) is twofold: that which resides in the agent (*kartṛ-āśrita*) and that which resides in the object (*karman-āśrita*). Of these, the first is, for example: "Devadatta sits," or "The cow itself yields milk."

The second [type of *ākṛti*] is, for example: "the rice is being cooked," "the field is being harvested," or "he himself. *Vyakta-pratirūpa-ākṛti* (manifested form) is threefold: *dravya-ākṛti* (substantial form), *guṇa-ākṛti* (qualitative form), and *kriyā-ākṛti* (actional form). Among these, *dravya-ākṛti* is twofold: the state of hearing (*śruta-daśā*) and the state of seeing (*dṛṣṭa-daśā*). Examples of the former include: "Let Vāsudeva be fashioned upon this stone," "Let Krāmadeva be painted on this wall," and "Let Hanūmān be carved here on the banner."

The second [type] is as follows: "Let these lumps of flour be made into lions," "This is the moon in the well," or "This is the path of the gods in the sky. The form of qualities (*guṇākṛti*) is twofold: based on perception and based on inference. Of these two, the first is as follows: "The *vandhrīka* bird is handsome," "The puppet is beautiful"—this is like a character carved by a woodworm (*ghuṇākṣara*). The second is as follows: "Oh, how painful is the appearance of a painting," "The disposition of the mind is clever," or "The form of the statue is serene."

Action (*kriyā*) is twofold: that which has the body as its basis and that which has the mind as its basis. Of these two, the first is, for example, a painting depicting a figure standing upright; it includes the position of the face, the turning of the head, and the placement of the face itself. The second is, for example, a frightened gaze, a terrified expression, or a form characterized by emotional transformation. But surely the followers of Jaimini maintain that "form" (*ākṛti*) is simply the universal (*jāti*). For Jaimini said: "The universal alone is called 'form,' by which the individual (*vyakti*) is implied; and that is the commonality of individual objects which serves as the basis for a single unified cognition."

But surely, the configuration (*sanniveśa*) of the dewlap and so forth is the "form" (*ākṛti*). And this does not fail to exist as a distinct entity even in the system of Jaimini. As the author of the *Bhāṣya* says: "Now, regarding the word 'cow,' what is the meaning of the word? It is the form characterized by the dewlap and so forth. Consequently, that very form would be the meaning of the word. It is not so. For if that were the case, since the configuration differs with each individual instance, it would be impossible to grasp the relationship [between the word and its meaning] due to the faults of infinity (*ānantya*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

Furthermore, even though the form (*ākṛti*) exists, when someone says "bring a cow," one does not bring a cow made of painted cloth. Now, one might object: even on the view that the universal (*jāti*) is the word-meaning, since the universal is omnipresent, why does it not follow that a clay cow should be brought? [The answer is: because only a living being possessing a dewlap and so forth serves as the manifestor (*abhivyañjaka*) of "cowness" (*gotva*). Therefore, the form is not a meaning of the word distinct from the universal. Nor is the individual (*vyakti*) the word-meaning; for that would have to be either the individual in general or a qualified individual.

It cannot be the individual alone, because that would entail the occurrence of the cognition and designation "cow" even with respect to an individual such as a horse. As for the comprehension [of the universal], it must arise either from the word or from another means of knowledge (pramāṇa). It cannot be from another means of knowledge, because such a means is not present. Rather, when there is comprehension of cowness (*gotva*) from the word, the word denotes that very universal first, according to the logical principle that "there is no cognition of a qualified object without its qualifier having been apprehended."

But surely, the word "cow" (go-śabda) will express both the genus (*jāti*) as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the individual (*vyakti*) as the qualified (*viśeṣya*). It cannot do so because of an excessive burden. Thus it is said: "The denotative power (*abhidhā*), its capacity exhausted by the qualifier, cannot reach the qualified. But surely, we shall understand the qualifier from words such as "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) and the individual as the qualified from the word "cow" itself; what then is this excessive burden for it? This is an unequal comparison.

For in that case [of verbal suffixes], by means of the distinction between stem and suffix, the meaning of the suffix is understood as qualified by the meaning of the stem; however, this is not the case with the word "cow" (*go*). Nor is there any other way to apprehend the individual (*vyakti*) such that one would have to postulate the denotation of both [the universal and the individual]; for even when the universal (*jāti*) is cognized through the force of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), the cognition of the individual is thereby established.

If the individual were the meaning of the word, the word "cow" would not be applied to another individual; yet it is not the case that it is not so applied. Therefore, its meaning is the genus (*jāti*) common to all individuals, not the individual itself. [Objection: But surely another individual is also just an individual; thus, this word "cow" is applied to the individual and not to the universal (*sāmānya*). [Reply: It is not so. For if that were the case, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the word would apply even to individuals such as a white horse (*karka*).

If it is argued that [a word] is employed only where its application has been observed, then [the word "cow"] was applied today to a cow born this very day. Furthermore, if the individual were the meaning of the word, the cognition would be "this is a cow" or "that is a cow," rather than "this and that [are cows]. Moreover, as in the case of the universal (*ākṛti*), the apprehension of the relationship [between word and meaning] is impossible in the case of the individual due to infinity (*ānantya*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*). How, then, could previous universals have bodies that are mutually distinct?

For it is their form alone that is differentiated from one another. And the cognition, conforming to the form of the object, delimits it through its own distinct aspect. And the words, following that [cognition], take up the object in exactly that same way. If this were so, then because they are eternal, the cognition of their form would be employed at all times. This is not so, because those [sounds] which are restricted to our organs of hearing are not manifested. If, on the other hand, the determination of them were due to the power of the manifesters, then they would be denoted by words along with their manifesters. But that is not the case.

Just as the object such as a face, which appears with distinctions in glass, mirrors, water, and so forth, is not perceived as it truly is when dependent upon the perception of the glass and other media; and just as words that denote an object shown by glass and the like do not themselves incorporate the glass and such media—so too, universals (*jāti*), whose specific forms are displayed by individuals (*vyakti*), are conveyed by words precisely as they are, without being touched by those individuals. But how is it that the substrata (*āśraya*), even though their distinctions are not directly touched by the word, serve to bring about the comprehension of the distinction between universals?

Just as the eyes and other sense organs, though themselves imperceptible, serve to apprehend specific objects such as form; as it has been said: "Just as the face itself is designated when manifested by water and the like, so too is the universal (jāti) alone designated when manifested by substances. Just as a distinction residing in the sense organ, though invisible within the objects of the senses, serves to differentiate cognitions even without being perceived, so too do individual manifestations (vyaktis), which manifest [the universal] without being grasped in their own form, become the cause for the differentiation of cognitions regarding the universal.

Thus [it is said]. The followers of Vyāḍi maintain that the individual (vyakti) alone is the meaning of a word. For a word is a *pada* (an inflected form), and that consists of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) plus an inflection (*vibhakti*), not the nominal stem alone. An inflection, when uttered after a nominal stem, expresses its own meaning as residing precisely within the meaning of that nominal stem. Furthermore, the threefold meaning of an inflection—namely gender, number, and grammatical relation (*kāraka*)—is expressed simultaneously. This triad does not connect with the universal (*jāti*) which is the meaning of the nominal stem; for a universal cannot possess the status of a *kāraka*, because it is formless (*amūrta*).

It does not possess a relation to number because it is non-differentiated; nor is there a connection with universals such as femininity and so forth, because it is devoid of universals (*niḥsāmānyatvāt*). [Objection: But surely, even in the absence of its own universal, it will possess the status of a *kāraka* (grammatical participant). [Reply: This syntactic connection expressed by case-endings is properly understood as being mediated by an intermediate level. This is not sound. For even though the Self is incorporeal, its status as a *kāraka* is established through its association with cognition, effort, and so forth. A universal, however, has no contact with activity whatsoever, even in the slightest degree. [Objection: But surely, the occurrence of the word is possible through the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the individual (*vyakti*).

This is not so; for *lakṣaṇā* (indication) occurs only where a word, having been employed once to denote a certain meaning, subsequently indicates another meaning that is otherwise untenable, and then applies properties such as number and gender to that indicated meaning. Here, however, no such necessity (*anyathānupapatti*) or similar factor is perceived. Furthermore, some maintain that the cognition of the individual (*vyakti*) is not mediated [by the universal]. We observe that it is the individual itself—colored by number and gender—that is connected to the action.

For this very reason, acts such as touching, sprinkling, and slaughtering are not prescribed with respect to the genus (*jāti*). Nor is the genus connected with a numerical distinction, as in "six should be given," "twelve should be given," or "twenty-four should be given"; rather, it is the individual (*vyakti*) alone that bears this burden. Furthermore, if the referent of the word were the genus, the statement "if the sacrificial animal should run away while being prepared, one should sacrifice another of the same age" would be untenable, because there can be no substitution of one genus for another due to its lack of differentiation. Moreover, [if the genus were the referent], notions such as increase, decrease, aggregation, and individual ownership could not be conceived.

In the view that the genus (*jāti*) is the denotation of a word, [the word] does not directly possess logical consistency [with ritual acts]. By this, it is also stated that the form (*ākṛti*) cannot be the meaning of a word, as its status is identical [to that of the genus], since it too is incapable of being the means for performing actions such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). Indeed, the configuration (*saṃniveśa*) is not sprinkled, nor is it sacrificed to, nor is it slaughtered. Furthermore, those [properties] such as connection with number, or increase and decrease, which apply to the genus, do not apply to the form either.

Furthermore, if the word *go* (cow) were to denote the generic form (*ākṛti*), it could not achieve grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with other words denoting qualities such as "white" and so forth; for qualities like whiteness do not reside in the generic form, but rather reside in the individual (*vyakti*). Nor can it be argued that this [coreferentiality] will occur by means of the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the individual, for indication functions only in the absence of a primary sense (*mukhya*).

Indeed, when the straight path is being traversed, one should not resort to a crooked way. Nor should it be said that the relationship [between word and object] cannot be grasped due to infinity and variability; for that [grasping] will occur by relying on a genus (*jāti*) or a configuration (*ākṛti*) as a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*). If it is argued that the word, having denoted the genus or configuration which serve as the defining characteristic, then denotes the individual (*vyakti*), this is not so; for a defining characteristic, even while being denoted, serves merely as a pointer toward what is actually present.

For example, as in the case of "Devadatta’s house, where this crow is. Here, the word "Devadatta’s house" does not denote the object "crow" by way of characterizing the crow's specific characteristics; nor does it abandon its application to the object delimited by that [crow] once the connection with the crow has ceased. In the same way, a word functioning toward an individual by way of characterizing a genus will neither denote the genus itself, nor will it abandon its application to the individual cow delimited by that [genus].

By this same reasoning, it is observed that even a form (*ākṛti*), though not directly denoted by the word, indicates the individual (*vyakti*); for example, as in the case of "Which is the gold? That which is the *rucaka*, the *svastika*, or the *vardhamānaka*. For here, the word "gold" (*suvarṇa*), though applied by way of the forms such as the *rucaka* and so forth, does not denote the form of the *rucaka* itself. When the forms of the *rucaka* and so forth cease, the word relinquishes its focus on the gold as delimited by those forms. As it has been said: "Just as Devadatta’s house is indicated by a transient sign..."

That which is grasped by the word "house" is denoted as pure [in itself], just as gold and other substances, though associated with their own forms and limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as bracelets and the like, are denoted as pure by words such as "bracelet. Likewise, when the universal (jāti), the class-characteristic (ākṛti), or the secondary indicator (upalakṣaṇa) is relied upon, individual instances (vyakti) become the pure objects of expression for words. By this, the argument that was stated—that if the individual were not denoted, words would apply to all things—is also refuted.

For instance, just as the capacity of words such as "eye" (*cakṣus*) and so forth to manifest all forms and other objects is restricted by the passage through the hollow of the eye-socket and the like, and because their vision is obstructed by the specific forms situated within that space, it does not extend to other objects; in the same way, the denotative power of words such as "cow" (*go*), whose referents are already delimited by genus (*jāti*) and configuration (*ākṛti*), does not over-extend (*atiprasajyate*) to horses and other animals. And it has been said: "By means of the spokes [of a wheel], its universal capacity is obstructed."

Just as the capacity of the eyes and other sense organs is [enhanced] by means of tubes and such; and as it has been stated by the proponents of the "as-it-is" (yathāvādin) view that the moon and other objects, when reflected in mirrors and the like, are denoted by the very words "moon" and so forth; and just as there occurs a distinction in the cognition of objects such as color-form even without the perception of a difference in the sense organs, so too it is held that universals (jāti) alone, as qualified by individuals, are denoted by words such as "cow. And upon the perception of the individual, the universal, being manifested by that individual, will be perceived. That also is not correct.

When, first of all, the view is held that a reflection is indeed a distinct entity produced in water and other media, then why should words—which follow the distinctions of form—apply to the water and such? For at that time, the water and so forth do not manifest the moon and other objects, but rather serve as the cause for the production of a form; and words do not experience contact with the cause merely by virtue of denoting the effect.

But when there is a distortion of perception such that one has the cognition "it is seen as such," then the relationship between the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) is completely set aside. However, this [distortion] will be possible when the eye, having been turned back by reflection from water or a mirror, perceives even one's own face, the moon, and so forth. For in that case, the proximate manifestor—like the belly and other parts—reveals the genus whose form is manifested through a distinction of color-form (*rūpa-bheda*), and it is precisely that which the word denotes.

This [argument] is also highly fallacious due to the objection: "How can the types of perceptions (*jāti*), which have specific secondary characteristics (*upavyañjana*) as their inseparable adjuncts, be cognized without those secondary characteristics? For the perception of the moon and other such objects is possible even otherwise. Likewise, although the apprehension of the distinction between types occurs, the determinations of objects such as blue—which arise dependent upon the sense organs like sight—conform to the difference in their causes. It is not so, however, with the delimitations of types (*jātipariccheda*), because these arise in connection with the form of the individual (*vyakti*); therefore, they would have to follow its differences.

Consequently, even "cowness" and other universals would not be mutually distinguishable from one another. Furthermore, how can it be accepted that a category whose difference is being perceived is suddenly one? Therefore, let it be admitted that the individual (*vyakti*) alone is the referent of the word; in this way, the cognition of the word heard arises with respect to that very [individual]. For those, however, for whom a universal is not possible in certain objects, the individual alone is said to be the referent, as in the case of words such as "space" (*ākāśa*).

Thus, for words such as *ḍittha*, whose nature as proper names (*saṃjñā*) is not recognized, the denotation is the individual (*vyakti*), because the thing to be expressed lacks a universal (*sāmānya*). Furthermore, those who declare that the word's function resides in various imagined universals—even there, they cause a universal to be grasped excessively. Indeed, no universal such as "ḍitthatva" is perceived, just like "sky-ness" (*gaganatva*); yet for the wise, there is no ground whatsoever for mere imagination. Thus, those who follow the scent of the view of Binda and Āsima maintain that the form alone (*ākṛti*) is the meaning of the word.

In this context, by the term *ākṛti* (form), the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) is denoted, because it is observed both in common usage and in the technical treatises (*śāstra*), and not as a genus (*jāti*) as in the system of Jaimini. As it is said in common usage: "Where there is form, there qualities reside"; and in the treatise: "The genus is grasped through form, and it does not possess all genders. In both cases, the word *ākṛti* refers to a specific arrangement of parts. And whatever meaning an elder uses a word for when engaging in linguistic practice, that becomes its meaning.

In this regard, when this word "cow" is applied to that which possesses a dewlap and so forth, and not to that which possesses a mane and so forth, it indicates that its object is a specific configuration (*sanniveśa*). Furthermore, words such as "cow" are employed with respect to the object of perception (*pratyakṣa*), and perception has configuration as its object. For the configuration of a cow-individual is perceived by the sense organ as distinct from the configuration of a horse-individual; this distinction among entities is indeed produced by that [configuration].

Therefore, a word such as "cow" (gauh), when applied to an object of perception, is capable of functioning only with respect to the configuration (ākṛti). Furthermore, in the injunction "one should build the fire-altar in the shape of a hawk" (śyenacitaṃ cinvīta), neither the genus nor the individual is built; rather, it is the configuration alone that is built. Moreover, for words such as "lamp," "stream," and so forth, the meaning must be accepted as the configuration alone; for in their referents, there exists no fixed form of either genus or individual.

Furthermore, if the form (*ākṛti*) were not the meaning of a word, how could words such as "cow" produce a cognition that possesses precisely the form of a cow and so forth? Moreover, such conventional usage as "We are wearing those very same cloths that [were worn] in Pāṭaliputra," or "We are eating those very same rice-grains that [were eaten] in Mathurā," is entirely appropriate; it is consistent only when the referent of the word is the form.

When a ritual is completed using *nīvāra* rice and the like in the absence of the primary material such as *vrīhi* rice, that [completion] would result in being fruitless even though the rite was finished, because the generic form (*ākṛti*) is not the meaning of the word, since the genus and individuality of *vrīhi* and the like are absent in *nīvāra* and the like. Furthermore, this application of words such as "Vāsudeva" to an image or representation is also appropriate only if the word's referent is the generic form. Moreover, it is observed that even with respect to objects never before perceived, a cognition whose object is a form arises from a word.

For example, [the words] "Indra," "Skanda," and "Vaiśravaṇa. And it is precisely the form (ākṛti) that is logically established as the meaning of the word. Furthermore, the grasping of its relationship [to the word] will be possible for this [form], just as it is for a genus (jāti). Since the configuration of a cow (go-saṃsthāna) is uniform across all individual cows, the distinction between primary and secondary usage will be determined by common usage and non-usage. Moreover, actions such as sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and the connection with qualities such as whiteness will be possible for the form through the medium of the individual.

Nor does the fact that the generic form (*ākṛti*) is incorporeal mean it cannot be a subordinate factor in action, because even incorporeal qualities are subordinate factors in ritual acts—as seen in such injunctions as "one buys [the cow] with a red one" and "one offers while stepping forward. Furthermore, just as an action is intended to have a self as its agent produced by the senses as they actually exist, so too is it said to be accomplished by and dependent upon the individual (*vyakti*) characterized by that form. Therefore, the generic form is the meaning of the word.

How, then, is there no contradiction with the opinion of the Teachers (Ācāryas) that the referent of a word (*padārtha*) consists of genus (*jāti*), individual (*vyakti*), and configuration (*ākṛti*), given that words such as "cow" denote that which possesses these [three]? But what is this so-called "possessor of that" (*tadvān*)? It is called "possessor of that" because "that belongs to it"; thus, it is the particular (*viśeṣa*) itself that is said to possess the form of the universal (*sāmānya*). However, if the particular were the denoted object, the faults of infinity (*ānantya*) and ambiguity (*vyabhicāra*) would remain as they were. Furthermore, a universal that is not expressed by the word cannot serve as a defining characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*). And it has already been stated that for a word to denote both [the universal and the particular] would be an excessive burden (*atibhāra*).

It is said: the particular, such as a brindled cow (*śābaleya*) and so forth, being indicated by its specific identity, is not what possesses that [universal].
