Rather, something indefinable, which is the substratum of the universal and does not specify particulars such as the brindled cow, is said to possess it. And because it is the substratum of the universal, there is no room for the faults of infinite regress (*anantyam*) or deviation (*vyabhicāraḥ*) therein. Nor do we accept that a word denotes the qualified (*viśeṣya*) after having denoted the qualifier (*viśeṣa*); for if we did, we would be oppressed by this excessive burden.

Since the convention is grasped merely through the fact that [the word] has the universal as its substratum, what excessive burden does a word incur when it expresses only that much? Furthermore, perception is not established as being restricted solely to the abstracted portion of the universal; and how could a word, which functions within the domain of that [perception], express it? Surely, the simultaneous cognition of the qualifier and the qualified is neither observed even in perception, nor is it accepted by you. For, in your view, that indeed constitutes the relationship of cause and effect.

Therefore, regarding the universal as the qualifier, the cognition produced by the sense organ arises first; even from a word, which requires the knowledge of a relationship dependent upon that [universal], the cognition occurs with respect to that very [universal]. Thus, the individual is not the denotable object either. It is replied: In perception, both the qualifier and the qualified are objects of the senses. When the sense organ operates through conjunction or inherence toward the universal, it grasps the qualified just as it grasps the qualifier.

Nor is there a conventional usage such that "the universal is perceived and the particular is to be inferred. For if this were so, then when a sense organ perceives only a quality (*guṇa*), the possessor of the quality (*guṇin*) would have to be inferred; yet this is not the case. Therefore, it is logical that perception extends up to the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), and likewise, the word has the same object as that [perception] and does not rest upon the universal alone. As for the statement, "The word functions by extracting [its meaning] from the universal aspect," this is said out of fear of infinite regress and deviation (*anantya-vyabhicāra*) if one were to maintain that the word denotes the individual (*vyakti*) exclusively.

However, since neither of those two [defects] exists when the word denotes that [universal], the operation of the word need not be restricted to having the bare universal as its denotation. [Objection: If the word were to have an object identical in every respect to that of perception, it would follow that there is an identity of cognition. Yet, cognitions arising from a word and from a sense-organ are not identical. As it has been said: "The burning is conceived by one who is actually burned through contact with fire in one way; the meaning of 'burning' is understood through the word 'burning' in quite another way."

It is replied: this has already been answered by the fact that the distinction in cognition is established through the apprehension or non-apprehension of all particular features. It does not follow from this that words have as their sole object the universal alone. Furthermore, if they were to express only the abstracted portion of the universal, then the cognitions produced by the word *go* (cow) and the word *gotva* (cowness) would be identical; and just as one says "the cow is white," one would likewise have the notion "cowness is white. Moreover, just as in the case of the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*), the suffixes denoting abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*), such as *-tva* and *-tal*, would be applied to the word *go* itself to denote its own meaning.

Now, you might think that the word "cow" expresses the universal (*jāti*) as one whose individuals are not excluded, whereas a suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) expresses it as extracted [from its substrate]. That is untenable, because a universal that does not exclude individuals is never observed anywhere. Furthermore, at the time of hearing the word "cow," the universal is not apprehended as being devoid of contact with individuals.

If it is argued that when the word *go* (cow) is heard at the end of an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*), it is understood as pure (*śuddhā*) because of its connection with that [suffix], then if the universal (*jāti*) is said to possess a substratum (*āśrayavatī*), the substratum of the universal has already been stated; otherwise, it would not be described as possessing a substratum. However, when there is a desire to express merely the generality of the possessor of the substratum by excluding the specific substratum itself, suffixes such as *-tva* and *-tal* are employed.

And so they have said: "When a word is applied to a substance because of the presence of a certain quality, the suffixes *tva* and *tal* denote that quality. These very words are witnesses to our position, for they state that the application of a word to a substance occurs due to the existence of a quality. Furthermore, it has already been stated that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is possible only in that case. Therefore, just as the operation of the sentence is held to extend as far as the specific ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*), so too should the operation of the word be held to extend as far as the individual (*vyakti*).

Since that [meaning] is understood while the word’s own operation is still unceased, he who maintains that words denote things as already connected must, all the more, admit that the cognition extends as far as the individual (vyakti). It is an established principle that there is no mutual connection or denotation of universals (jāti) that are independent of individuals; for instance, in cases such as "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā," there is a secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) based on proximity, but in cases such as "the cow is white," there is no such indication of an individual. This is determined from usage and comprehension by means of the elders (vṛddha).

Therefore, it is established that the meaning of words such as "cow" (gavādi) is that which possesses the universal (tadvat). Furthermore, in practical applications regarding objects—such as in the expression "milk the cow" (gāṃ dogdhi)—since the capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyā) belongs to that which possesses the universal, it is that very thing which constitutes the referent of the word. The word directly denotes the object as possessing the universal; there is no intervening cognition, nor is there any excessive burden on the word. Moreover, linguistic usages such as grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) and the like, being possible through this primary mode of signification (mukhyā vṛtti), shall not be interpreted otherwise.

This was stated by the Blessed Akṣapāda: "The individual, the configuration, and the genus are the meanings of a word. Here, the word *tu* (but/however) serves to specify; what is specified? That the status of being the primary or secondary meaning of a word is not fixed. Therefore, even though that which possesses [the genus] (*tadvat*) is the ultimate referent, in certain usages the genus is primary and the individual is subordinate. For example, in the injunction "A cow must not be touched with the foot," the prohibition is understood to apply to all cows.

In some cases, the individual (vyakti) is primary and the class-character (ākṛti) is subordinate, as in "Release the cow," "Bind the cow"; these are employed with reference to a specific, determined individual. In other cases, the class-character is primary and the individual is subordinate; however, the universal (jāti) itself does not exist [as a separate entity]. For example, in "Let cows be fattened," the expression is used with the desire to bring about a particular state of their physical arrangement. Furthermore, certain quality-words (guṇaśabda), having denoted a quality delimited by its own universal, cease their operation right there.

Some, however, having denoted a quality, also imply the substance, because usage is observed through their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). First, qualities such as odor, color, and taste are restricted solely to qualities; they denote qualities like odor that are distinguished by the universal of "odor-ness" (*gandhatva*) and so forth. Their application is never seen to extend to the substance. There is no cognition of coreferentiality such as "the odor is a lotus. But words like "white" and others, while expressing a quality, [also] express its substratum.

Even [words denoting] substances necessarily imply [an action], as seen in the expression "a white horse. Verbal roots (*kriyāśabda*), however, are of various kinds; some are employed in reference to the agent (*kartṛ*), the object (*karman*), or the instrument (*karaṇa*), while others are used in reference to the abstract state (*bhāva*) or even the limit (*avadhi*). Words such as *pācaka* ("cook") and the like, having taken up some particular action as their basis, denote a substance that is connected with it. Even in cases where the connection with that specific action is not perceived at that moment, virtuous speakers employ the word by observing its inherent capacity (*yogyatā*).

Others maintain that verbal actions such as "cooking" (*pāka*) and the like are established as having a completed form, by way of abandoning their nature as a sequence of prior and posterior stages. In this regard, there is a first position: the basis for the application of a word is understood to be one thing, while its denotation (*abhidheya*) is another. For in words such as "cook" (*pācaka*), the action is the basis for the word's application, whereas the agent and so forth are what is denoted. However, in some cases, that which serves as the very ground for the word's application is itself the denotation, as is the case with words ending in abstract suffixes (*bhāvapratyaya*).

Thus, this function of nouns has been briefly illustrated by name. As for verbs, their expressed meaning was described previously; however, the division of prefixes and particles is not [described] here as it was for nouns. Through usage and comprehension, a manifold meaning is understood. By the power of a prefix, a verbal root brings about a variation in its meaning, as in the cases of *vihāra* (wandering), *āhāra* (eating), *saṃhāra* (withdrawal), *prahāra* (striking), and *parihāra* (avoidance). That meaning is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): because when that [prefix] is present, there is the cognition of that [meaning], and in its absence, that [meaning] is not apprehended.

Or what is the use of deliberating whether "this is the meaning of this word"? The established rule is that whatever meaning is understood from something, that is its meaning. The meaning of a sentence is threefold: *bhāvanā* (productive operation), *vidhi* (injunction), and *pratibhā* (intuition). Among these, *bhāvanā* is said to be the human activity in the sense of "doing" (*karoti*), which impels a person toward becoming something conducive to the production of another state. Since it cannot be carried out if it remains undefined, it requires—by virtue of proximity—the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) presented within the same word as its defining delimiter.

In such cases as "he cooks rice" (*odanaṃ pacati*), although [the fuel] is expressed by the same word [as the agent], it falls away from being the object (*sādhya*) due to its lack of fitness; instead, it settles into the role of the instrument (*karaṇa*). Thus, it brings about the primary action which has rice as its fruit. Furthermore, an instrument is never observed to produce an action on its own if it lacks the capacity to be effective. Therefore, wood and other such factors enter into the process as the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) so that the status of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*) may be established. As for their entry into the result, it occurs because the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) proceeds precisely with that result as its aim.

Therefore, due to the delimitation of the result (*phala*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the procedure (*itikartavyatā*), the *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) becomes incomplete with respect to its three factors, requiring [the answers to] "what," "by what," and "how. In that regard, in examples such as "Devadatta cooks rice with firewood using a pot," the rice is the result, the cooking is the instrument, and the cycle of causal factors beginning with the firewood constitutes the procedure. As it has been said: "When the rice is being accomplished, the cooking is held to be the instrument; the pot, the fire, the ladle, and the firewood are considered the procedure."

And that human activity, characterized by effort and movement yet observed as a state of indifference [on the part of the self], is the meaning of "doing" (*karoti*), namely *bhāvanā*. How, then, is there the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) for pieces of wood? Because the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is an action (*kriyā*). However, since the meaning of the verbal root serves as the instrument toward the *bhāvanā*, and because when the instrumental case is employed it cannot connect with another primary element [if it were not itself the primary].

It is said in reply: because of its connection with *bhāvanā* (the efficient force), even the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is understood as having a sequential nature consisting of a process of becoming; thus, in relation to that, the firewood (*kāṣṭha*) possesses the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*). Therefore, it is established that the sentence-meaning is the *bhāvanā* complete in its three constituent parts. An injunction (*vidhi*) is the operation of the word expressed by the optative (*liṅ*), imperative (*loṭ*), and other such suffixes, which impels toward engagement or cessation and is assisted by explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and the like. For by means of that, a person is either incited to act or restrained from acting within the context of the *bhāvanā*.

For example: "One should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice as long as one lives," "One should not kill a Brāhmaṇa," "Recite the *prauga*," "Do not speak falsely," "The *aṣṭakā* rites must be performed by the *hotṛ* priest," "Liquor must not be drunk," "The ancestors are to be honored," "Teachers are to be respected," "May it be well with you," and "May the hawk not strike you down. And this is the meaning of all such sentences; for every sentence ultimately culminates in either an injunction or a prohibition.

Furthermore, even where optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and the like are not heard, they are understood as being part of the remainder of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣa*), since all sentences have the purpose of enjoining or prohibiting. For example, when it is said, "In this region there is plenty of food," it is understood that "one should stay right here"; when it is said, "There is poison here," it is understood that "one should not eat right here"; when it is said, "The path has robbers," it is understood that "one should not go [there]"; and when it is said, "There are crocodiles in this river," it is understood that "one should not bathe. Moreover, this very point is elucidated by great epics such as the *Rāmāyaṇa* and others.

Even for Rāma, who was dwelling in the forest while obeying his father’s command, such prosperity came to pass; whereas for Rāvaṇa, though he was the conqueror of the three worlds, such destruction occurred because he lusted after another's wife. Therefore, one should obey the command of one’s father and not lust after another’s wife; one should behave like Rāma and not like Rāvaṇa. Now, it might be argued that it has been stated that *bhāvanā* (the efficient force) alone is the injunction (*vidhi*), as it is the meaning expressed by the verbal suffix.

And how can it be the instigator (*pravartaka*) of that very [action] in itself, given the contradiction of an action acting upon its own self? That is not so, because *bhāvanā* is twofold due to the distinction between the word and its meaning. As it has been said: "The optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and others express one *bhāvanā* alone, namely the verbal expression (*abhidhā-bhāvanā*); another, consisting of the object (*artha-ātmā*), is understood in all finite verbs (*ākhyāta*). In this context, the *śabda-bhāvanā* consists of instigation (*preraṇā*); it is the denotation and the injunction of the word. As it has been said: "It denotes and it effects."

The cultivation of the efficient-force (*bhāvanā*) has as its object two parts: the means (*upāya*) and the fruit (*phala*). Regarding the fruit-part, the suffixes such as the optative (*liṅ*) are not injunctive; for by their own inherent power, they express only the injunction itself. Thus it has been said: "With respect to the fruit-part of the *bhāvanā*, the suffix is not an enjoiner; for the optative and other suffixes denote only the injunction through their own capacity."

And when there arises the expectation regarding that [efficient force] as to "what," "by what," and "how," the person's activity directed toward the objective-efficient-force (*arthabhāvanā*) constitutes the object; the knowledge of the impulsion (*preraṇājñāna*) constitutes the instrumental part; and the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and so forth constitute the procedural part. Thus, there is a fulfillment of these three parts. Furthermore, that [efficient force], by making known the relationship of the means and the end—which is the relationship between the instrument and the fruit where the latter was previously unknown—becomes a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is a communicator of truth. Now, one might object: "The definition of an injunction (*vidhi*) is simply this: the instigation of one who has not yet acted. For in this way, every injunction would indeed be merely the making known of what was previously unknown."

For instance, the relationship between the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) exists in all verbal forms (*ākhyāta*). And since the verbal form exists in injunctive sentences (*pravavākya*), it satisfies the requirement of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*). Nor is it the case that the capacity to incite action (*pravartakatva*) is not established without the comprehension of the relationship between the goal and the means; therefore, the comprehension of this relationship must necessarily be postulated. If it is asked, "Since its capacity to incite action arises solely from its being the generator of the knowledge of an instigation (*preraṇā*), why does one engage in an action that is fruitless? we reply: "Because it is indeed an injunction (*vidhi*)."

An injunction impels a person toward an action, whether that action be fruitful or fruitless; thus, when persons do not engage in sacrifices and the like, their lack of authority [to compel them] is indeed unavoidable. For those who are free from passion and loathe sensual pleasure do not engage in action even when a result is imagined; yet those whose passion is more intense do not desist from it. It is said in response: in such injunctions as "one desiring heaven should sacrifice," the injunction impels the person toward the *bhāvanā* (productive activity). A *bhāvanā* is an operation whose essential nature consists in having something to be brought about (*bhāvya*) as its object.

And that [action], being devoid of the nature of the "to-be-accomplished" (sādhya) and so forth, would be entirely without logical justification. Furthermore, when there arises a doubt—whether the state of being the "to-be-accomplished" belongs to the meaning of the verbal root due to its proximity with the employment of a single word, or rather to heaven and the like mentioned by the word *kāma* because they are desired—the conclusion is that it belongs to heaven alone on account of its suitability, and not to the meaning of the verbal root. As it has been said: "When an injunction (*vidhi*) is not accepted, a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) as the object to be accomplished is not obtained; thus, by setting aside the heard heaven and so forth, the meaning of the verbal root would become the object to be accomplished."

Having set aside the [Vedic] injunction (*vidhi*), it is maintained that heaven and so forth are what is to be accomplished; and this being the case, it follows that the means of accomplishing those [ends] is indeed *dharma*. For regarding matters beyond the reach of perception, the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) alone is the authority. Indeed, only the injunction is capable of making known an object—whether past, present, future, subtle, or concealed; no other sense organ can do so.

By this, it is stated that the Vedic sentence—whether by virtue of its being non-human in origin (*apauruṣeya*) or by virtue of being composed by a trustworthy person (*āpta*) who conveys the matter as it truly is—is inherently authoritative (*prāmāṇya*), provided its defective portions have been eliminated and it is free from subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*). Thus, the meaning of a sentence is an injunction (*vidhi*). When words have ceased their activity after denoting their respective individual meanings, there subsequently arises a cognition that follows upon the comprehension of those word-meanings; this cognition is designated as "this is that," is established even without explicit instruction, serves as the cause for the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful, and is conducive to purposeful action. This cognition is *pratibhā*.

For instance, when the mere manifestations of meaning—whether based on whole words or based on word-components—proceed without interruption, the individual manifestation (*prītibhā*) unfolds within each person as something inferable from the production of the fruit of activity, being of the same genus as that [manifestation]. This is just as, in the case of liquors, poisons, and elixirs, where various substances whose prior contact with unseen portions was not observed are seen to produce functional effects such as intoxication, death, or gold once they have reached full maturation.

Likewise, it is observed that distinct words are uttered at every step; and this is its distinction from the [ordinary] states of being and so forth. For as long as one does not investigate how the form of the meaning spoken by me here is apprehended or how it is synthesized by another, so long does this [intuition] effect the synthesis of these preceding and succeeding elements through an inexpressible means.

Even regarding the objects of perception and inference, as long as there is a synthesis of preceding and succeeding cognitions accompanied by verbal expression, all means of valid cognition attain the status of being valid cognitions. For the world proceeds toward its duties through intuition and observation.

But is it not the case that intuition (*pratibhā*) is not the meaning of a sentence? For it is observed that intuition arises naturally even without hearing a sentence in the following instances: in infants’ drinking of breast milk and so forth; in swans’ discriminating milk from water; in creatures such as ants building their nests and so forth; in newborn animals, deer, snakes, and reptiles crossing over water; in those who have just awakened from sleep; and in a young girl’s knowledge that "my brother will come tomorrow."

Likewise, intuitive knowledge (*prātibha*) is observed even from ordinary causes: from a specific time, in the case of the change in the song of the male cuckoo; from a specific practice, in the case of jewel-examiners’ knowledge of the defects and qualities of gems and the like; from spirits such as *rakṣas*, *pitaras*, and *piśācas* who have not been seen before, in the case of possession and invisibility; from yoga, in the case of yogis’ comprehension of another’s intention; from the cessation of the activity of the external senses, in the case of Vasiṣṭha and others’ knowledge beyond the senses; and from the recitation of the *Anuśāsana* by Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana and others, in the case of the Śrinjayas’ hearing of things difficult to see.

Just as, when a person is directly instructed by a sentence regarding the construction of a chariot, the intuition (*pratibhā*) of the listeners—which had been withdrawn through the operation of the word—manifests itself; in exactly the same way, for infants and others, in acts such as suckling at the breast, an intuition arises that is no different from the comprehension of sentence-meanings, due to the persistence of the latent impressions (*bhāvanā*) of previous words.

Furthermore, even those whose linguistic usage is based on words that are not conventionally established—such as elephants, horses, and so forth—undertake all their activities by following intuition (*pratibhā*), which consists of present verbal cognitions arising through the force of the latent impressions (*bhāvanā*) of words from previous births. Moreover, because they follow upon the experience of words from the past, an intuition arises in cuckoos and other such creatures regarding the modification of their notes and the like, even when directed toward their own names, despite the absence of any manifest operation of words.

The means for awakening the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by hearing words in previous births, however, are other practices such as repetition over time, the conjunction with unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), yoga, meditation (*dhyāna*), and so forth. This, however, is the distinction: in some cases, a sentence, merely upon being uttered, illuminates its own meaning—that which is not yet designated, which has not yet become an object of existence, and which is denoted by the term "intuition" (*prātibha*).

However, in some cases, even when a long time has elapsed, that very same sentence—due to the infusion of the cultivation of the seed of a particular intuition (*pratibhā*) and the presence of other auxiliary causes—manifests its own meaning through a traditional succession as an object of intuition; thus, the meaning of a sentence is intuition (*pratibhā*). But surely, action (*kriyā*) is also said to be the meaning of a sentence, and that too must be explained? It is not so; action is the meaning of a word (*padārtha*), not the meaning of a sentence. Rather, the meaning of a sentence is that surplus (*ādhikya*) which arises when the meanings of words are mutually combined.

To this he says: "That which is the surplus here is the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). This [surplus] is sometimes the *bhāvanā*, consisting of human activity; sometimes it is the injunction (*vidhi*), consisting of the operation of the word; sometimes it is the intuition (*pratibhā*), consisting of the operation of the intellect. Now, one might object: even the *bhāvanā*, being understood from either the verbal root or the suffix, does not deviate from being a word-meaning (*padārthatva*). Or, if it were argued that the *bhāvanā* is not merely a word-meaning...

Furthermore, it is argued that human activities—which are distinct from the nature of the meanings of verbal roots such as injunctions (*vidhi*) and so forth, which are observed to possess prior and posterior states—do not qualify as the meaning of the *pada* (word-meaning), whether they are expressed by the verbal root or by the suffix. In cases such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*), the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is the action in the form of the sacrifice and so forth, while the meaning of the suffix is the instigation in the form of an injunction and so forth. Apart from these, no human activity called "efficient force" (*bhāvanā*) is perceived; nor is there any case-ending (*vibhakti*) that expresses such an efficient force.

Pāṇini remembers [the suffixes] *siḍ* and so forth in the context of injunctions (*vidhi*) and the like. This is not so; let alone the word of injunction, even from present-tense statements such as "he cuts" (*chinatti*) and so forth, that bhāvanā is understood. For just as the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), such as cooking, is perceived from words like "he cooks" (*pacati*), so too is the agent's activity—the meaning of the root *kṛ* (to do)—perceived. This is because that perception does not fail even in the absence of qualifiers such as cooking.

For just as in the case of "Aupagavaḥ," "Kāpaṭavaḥ," and "Aupamanyavaḥ"—where even when Upagu and the others are added or removed, the meaning of the suffix, namely "his offspring" (*tasyāpatyam*), persists—so too in cases such as "he cooks," "he reads," and "he goes," the meaning of "he does" (*karoti*) is seen to persist. Thus it has been said: when the verb "he cooks" (*pacati*) is uttered, commentators employ the sentence "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*) as its explanation.

In this context, they explain that by the word *pāka* (cooking), ending in the accusative case, the base-meaning (*prakṛtyartha*)—which is the object to be accomplished—is expressed, while the word *karoti* (does) expresses the performance of the agent's activity. Furthermore, when asked "What is Devadatta doing?", there are two types of speakers who respond: "He cooks" (*pacati*) or "Cooking" (*pākam*). Both of these forms, though differing in expression, convey the same meaning; otherwise, the questioner would not be informed by the answer. Therefore, he says: the meaning of the two words "he cooks cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*) is identical to the meaning of the single word "he cooks" (*pacati*).

A verbal root-meaning distinct from the action [of the suffix] would not be perceived as separate from the agent-number [denoted by the suffix], were it not for the suffix; and if it were so perceived, it would likewise be perceived in the case of the word *karoti* ("he does"). As it has been said: "Just as there is the common usage 'he performs cooking' (*pākaṃ karoti*) through a distinction [between the object and the action], there is no such worldly cognition as 'he performs doing' (*kāraṃ karoti*). If one asks what the basis for this [distinction] is, it is that the roots *kṛ*, *bhū*, and *as* denote the general notion of action (*kriyāsāmānya*).

Furthermore, universals do not reside in universals; for instance, while in the injunctions "one should sacrifice," "one should give," and "one should offer oblations," the universal of "acting" (*karoti*) is understood, it is not the case that [the verb] "exists" (*bhavati*) functions in the same way as "acts" (*karoti*). But how is it that the meaning of "acting" is not understood from the word "acts"? It is not that it is not understood; however, it remains unqualified by specific acts such as sacrifice and thus is not fit for performance. If that is so, let it then not be the meaning of the suffix; it will be the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*).

For just as, in the case of the *śābaleya* (the spotted cow) and others, the universal form of "cowness" (*gotva*) appears as something continuous, while the specific forms such as the *śābaleya* appear as excluded [from one another], so too, in the case of actions such as sacrifice (*yāga*), a form consisting of "activity" (*vyāpāra*) appears as continuous, while the specific forms such as sacrifice appear as mutually distinct. In that context, that which is continuous—the universal of "doing" (*karoti-sāmānya*)—is "being-ness" (*bhāvatā*); that which is excluded—the specific acts such as sacrifice—is the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). And just as it is impossible to point out "cowness" separately from the *śābaleya* and other individuals, even so, "effort" (*bhāvanā*) cannot be pointed out separately from the sacrifice and other actions.

Because it is always perceived as being colored by that [object], one cannot say that the object does not exist merely on this account. For when one asks, "What does non-existence do to it?"—a question regarding the activity of a subject whose specific nature is not understood—the answers "it cooks" or "it reads" are simply no answers at all. Furthermore, when a person remains in a state of indifference, he is impelled to act; that effort toward sacrifice, oblation, and so forth, is studied in the scriptures as *bhāvanā* (the creative urge).

And although it has a general form, this action—unlike "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like—is not something that appears as already accomplished anywhere, such that it would not be something to be enjoined (*vidheya*). Or rather, this internal operation of the knower is indeed a specific kind of action; it is distinct from the moments of external action consisting of physical movement (*spanda*). And it is certainly accepted that action is a word-meaning (*padārtha*); for even if it is a word-meaning, it is logical that action constitutes the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), since word-meanings attain the status of sentence-meaning when they are combined.

[The meanings of words] are distinguished by a specific mutual interconnection corresponding to their respective expectations; and this interconnection occurs when there exists a relationship of primary and subordinate elements. Furthermore, that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is understood as the primary element because it is the object being accomplished. Since [the word-meaning] does not extend beyond the action (*kriyā*), the meaning of the sentence is therefore the unity of purpose centered on the action. When one is enjoined with such commands as "one should sacrifice," "one should give," "one should offer oblations," or "one should study," one understands the action as something to be accomplished, and the world proceeds to perform it.

Even the status of the person qualified for the sacrifice, such as "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*), is consistent as it serves to provide the agent required by the efficient force (*bhāvanā*). [This is understood as: "In this action, this person is the agent; by means of this [agent], this action is to be accomplished. Nor does the primacy of the action thereby lapse here. For the action does not reside in the agent; rather, the agent exists for the sake of the action, since he is perceived as being the one who brings that action to completion. Even the verbal expression teaches it in exactly the same way: "this person should do this."

If it is asked, "For what purpose, then, does this action perform another action?", we reply: "Simply from the word [of the Veda]. Indeed, the venerable Bādari perceived this very point: there is no status as a subordinate element (*śeṣatā*) apart from substances, qualities, and purificatory acts. Whether through the Veda, through the instruction of a teacher, or through the command of a king, no conscious person performs any action that is fruitless.

To this it is replied: we take scripture as our authority; whatever the scripture says is authoritative for us. Now, the term *svargakāma* (one who desires heaven) is also indeed a word. Therefore, its syntactical connection (*anvaya*) here must also be stated. [Objection: But surely the term *kartṛpada* (agent-word) is singular, and the agent exists for the sake of the action. [Reply: It is not so. The term *svargakāma* is not an agent-word, but rather an *adhikāripada* (word denoting the qualified person). One whose desire is for heaven, or one who desires heaven—such a person, distinguished by the desire for heaven, is understood from this word.

In this context, how is the desired heaven connected with the act of sacrifice? Since heaven consists of unsurpassed bliss (*prīti*), and since bliss, being non-substantial (*adravyatva*), cannot function as a constituent part of an action; furthermore, it is not logical for bliss to be for the sake of an action. For everything else is for the sake of bliss, but bliss is not for the sake of anything else. Thus, because no means for accomplishing the action is taught, the word "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*) is not connected [to the injunction] by way of designating the agent (*kartṛ*); rather, it is connected by way of designating the qualified person (*adhikārin*).

Now, who is this so-called "eligible person" (*adhikārī*)? It is the owner (*svāmī*) of the ritual action. But surely the agent alone is the owner of the action. Not so; he is not simply the owner. He is the agent, but not its owner. [Objection: Apart from the relationship between the action and its factors (*kāraka*), what other relationship could there be between the action and the person? [Response: It is said: having first conceived the relationship of ownership in the form "this is my duty" and "I am the owner here"—a relationship which cannot be otherwise imagined—the subsequent relationship between the action and its factors is understood.

If it is asked what the proof is for the term "westerner" (pāścātya), it is the designation of a person characterized by an unacceptable qualification; therefore, the agency belongs to the one who is authorized, not the authorization to the agent. And in this way, the authorization of the "one who desires heaven" (svargakāma) is fulfilled if that ritual action is for the sake of heaven, and heaven itself must be something to be experienced. One is called "desirous of heaven" when, desiring heaven as a goal to be accomplished, one thinks, "How may I attain heaven?"

Furthermore, if ritual action were not a means for attaining heaven, this contradiction would ensue: one desires heaven but performs a sacrifice; one intends one thing but does another. Therefore, since the ritual action is being performed as a means toward that which is desired, the one who desires heaven is not at all qualified [for it]. And one who is not qualified has no connection with it.

Thus, since the person desiring heaven (*svargakāma*) is the qualified agent (*adhikṛta*) in relation to the ritual action, and since the status of being a qualified agent cannot be sustained without understanding the relationship of means and end between the sacrifice and heaven, one must necessarily admit that the action is the means and heaven itself is the end. Consequently, because the action is subordinate (*guṇabhāva*) with respect to the fruit, it lacks primacy; and due to this lack of primacy, it does not constitute the primary meaning of the sentence. As it has been said: "Jaimini [maintains] that even ritual actions are for the sake of the fruit."

And what is this "action" (kriyā)? It is said to be the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*). Is it that which is expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*) as the sense of being (*bhāvārtha*), such as sacrifice and the like; or is it the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*); or is it something additional [to both]? In this regard, since the sense of being is the means for attaining that which is desired, its lack of primacy has already been stated. However, the meaning of the suffix attains the status of the sentence-meaning precisely without abandoning the relationship between the goal and the means inherent in the sense of being that is desired. Therefore, the sentence-meaning does not terminate in mere action alone.

Should we now maintain that the fruit alone is the meaning of the sentence? For that [fruit] is the primary goal and the object to be accomplished; indeed, all effort is for its sake. This is not so. Just as an action lacks primacy because it exists for the sake of the fruit, so too the fruit lacks primacy because it exists for the sake of the person (*puruṣa*). A person does not strive so that heaven might attain existence independently; rather, he desires it as something to be enjoyed by himself. Thus it is said: "And the fruit [is subordinate], because it exists for the sake of the person."

In that case, let the person alone be the meaning of the sentence. Not so; for even he is a subordinate member of the action, as in the statement, "The *audumbarī* post is equal in size to the sacrificer. Thus it is said: "And the person is for the sake of the ritual act. Alas! If the action is for the sake of the fruit, the fruit is for the sake of the person, and the person is for the sake of the action, we have fallen into a circle. Whose fall is this? Whose primacy do we maintain?

It might be argued: first of all, the person (*puruṣa*) is not the meaning of the sentence, because even when word-meanings are mutually connected, it is the meaning of the verb alone—qualified by the meanings of indeclinables, kārakas, and adjectives—that constitutes the primary sense of the sentence. But surely, even in verbal forms such as *yajeta* ("one should sacrifice"), the *lakāra* suffix denotes the agent (*kartṛ*)?

It is not so. For this element called *lakāra* (the verbal suffix) is indeed employed for the sake of that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*); thus, even the agent, as the meaning of the suffix, becomes subordinate to the action, which is the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). Furthermore, the result (*phala*) is not the sentence-meaning, because the dilemma of whether it is already established (*siddha*) or yet to be accomplished (*asiddha*) is untenable. First, there is no denotation at all of a result that is already established, since it is indicated as something being desired (*kāmyamāna*). On the other hand, in the case where it is being accomplished, its establishment is not directly perceived. Therefore, it is logical that the sentence-meaning is the activity itself, or rather, that which is centered upon it.

For this very reason, they maintain that the meaning of a sentence is *bhāvanā* (the creative urge), which is adorned by its connection to the three factors and possesses a corresponding fruit. For *bhāvanā* is the activity of the bringer-into-being (*bhāvaka*) which has the object-to-be-brought-about (*bhāvya*) as its goal. This very meaning, consisting of action and so forth, is proclaimed to have twelve varieties; it is accepted as the primary denotation of a word, the qualificand, and the object to be conveyed.

Nor should it be said that the capacity to convey meaning belongs to the sentence alone and not to the words, because just as the word *guḍa* denotes the substance *guḍa*, it also causes one to understand its inseparable quality of sweetness; or else, it may be that the words themselves, when combined, denote the meaning within the sentence. There are also views according to which the verb (*ākhyāta-śabda*) is the sentence, or that the sentence is a collection of words (*pada-saṅghāta*). Furthermore, action (*kriyā*) and the other categories of meaning are included within the very meaning of the words.

For instance, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is action (*kriyā*), which time (*kāla*) qualifies; the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) is the factor of action (*kāraka*), which the *tatpuruṣa* compound qualifies. Both of these have adjuncts (*upādhi*) that serve as delimiters (*avacchedaka*). Together, the base (*prakṛti*) and the suffix (*pratyaya*) express the meaning of the suffix. That which they declare to be the primary element receives the designation of a distinct meaning qualified by the meanings of the embellishments (*upaskāra*), through both difference and non-difference.

For the manifestation of its number and gender, there is an inflection (*vibhakti*); that which ends in an inflection is a "word" (*pada*). The operation (*vṛtti*) occurs when words—whether they are [simple] words or non-words—are in a state of semantic expectancy (*sāmarthya*). Furthermore, for those [complex formations] such as *kṛt*-derivatives, *taddhita*-derivatives, and compounds, there is again the designation of "nominal stem" (*prātipadika*), and from the subsequent arising of an inflection, they receive the designation of "word. Thus, in the view where the sentence-meaning is indivisible (*akhaṇḍa-vākyārtha-pakṣa*), the sentence itself also becomes the expressive unit. In this context, the capacity of a word to denote an object is "expressiveness" (*vācakatā*). That is threefold: primary (*mukhyā*), secondary (*gauṇī*), and indicative (*lakṣaṇā*).

For example: "the cow goes," "the Vāhīka is a cow," and "he dwells among cows. We shall explain the distinctions between these cases in detail later on. For when those [meanings] have been awakened—that is, when they have been understood through the usage of elders, the instruction of grammarians, and the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with well-known words—then, by the force of the relationship between the name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*), the word, remaining entirely external, causes the meaning "cowness" (*gotva*) to be conveyed. As it has been said: "It is understood through coreferentiality with a well-known word."

Just as the meaning of the word "cūta" (mango tree) is not well-known [to a child], yet one hears "the *pika* cries," so too there arises the certainty: "That which cries in the *cūta* is the *pika*. Through instruction, this true meaning becomes manifest as the designation of the term "pavasā" (the mango). However, the relationship between word and meaning is established through usage and is based on three means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). One perceives directly (*pratyakṣa*) the objects denoted by the words of the elders; one perceives the understanding of the listener through inference from their activity (*ceṣṭā*); and when no other explanation is possible, one cognizes the basis of the two-fold capacity [of the word] to denote both the object and its name. Thus it is said.

The state of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) consists in being the cause of a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) by means of its own delimitation (*svāvacchedena*). In this regard, it is threefold: the differentiator (*bhedaka*), the conformer (*anurañjaka*), and the indicator (*upalakṣaka*). For example: "One should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," "One should immolate a white goat," and "The priests proceed wearing red turbans. Furthermore, universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*) never attain the status of being objects of a cognition that is devoid of the superimposition of words (*śabdānuvedha*).

For instance, just as in a determinate cognition (*savikalpaka*)—such as "This spotted cow has stepped forth," where the object does not appear as delimited by a genus, quality, or action—the object likewise flashes forth in indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) as qualified by a word. As it is said: "There is no cognition in the world that is without the accompaniment of words; every cognition is understood as if permeated by speech. Nor should it be argued that there first exists an indeterminate, non-conceptualizing awareness of the mere "is-ness" (*astitva*).

It is similar to the cognition of infants, the mute, and others, arising from a pure object; for infants and the like, possessing a multitude of various latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by experiences in previous births, perceive each respective object solely through the exclusion of its genus (*jātyapoha*). Thus, even before an infant born on that very day, clever women do not place a lamp down, thinking, "He might become a crab."

Now, since being the cause for the ascertainment of "as-it-is-ness" (*tathātva*) and "not-as-it-is-ness" (*atathātva*) constitutes the nature of a means of cognition (*pratyaya*), how does a word convey an object that is not as it is? It is through the greatness of the word's own power (*śakti*). For cognitions produced by the power of a word, arising with specific forms due to the maturation of their own seeds, manifest difference even when there is no difference in the actual thing (*vastu*). This is just as in the cases of "Rāhu’s head" or "the body of a stone statue."

Thus it has been said: "This distinction is conceived as being like a magical illusion or a juggler's trick, produced solely by the power of the word's capacity (*śabda-śakti*), even though the reality (*vastu*) is without division. Others, however, say: "The object does not possess a form exceeding [what is denoted], nor does the word have an additional referent. Yet, through the adjunct (*upādhi*) of another word, the word is perceived as having an additional referent. For example, the word *puruṣaḥ* (man) denotes merely a man; but when the word *rājñaḥ* (of the king) is in proximity, that very same person is perceived as qualified—namely, as "the king's man" (*rājapuruṣaḥ*). This is a specific kind of man.

In the same way, in expressions such as *bhavati* and *pacati*, there is the cognition of the mere action (*kriyā*) in the word *pacati*, whereas in *bhavati*, the cognition is produced by the power of the agent (*kartṛśakti*), which is conditioned by the word itself. Others, however, hold that even with respect to an object that is devoid of the delineation of all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), words—by their own inherent power alone—become the cause for the arising of various cognitions and project [them] onto it; on account of this, an object, though possessing a non-differentiated nature, appears otherwise.

For instance, when it is said, "The narrator causes Kaṃsa to be killed," it is understood that he describes the slaying of Kaṃsa. However, when the usage is "Indra causes Kaṃsa to be killed," then it means that Indra employs Upendra (Viṣṇu), who is the slayer of Kaṃsa. Others, however, maintain that even in the case of "The narrator causes Kaṃsa to be killed," one expresses the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka*), because: "Those [objects] whose forms are presented by words, having become objects of the intellect..."

"One regards Kaṃsa and others as if they were directly present, taking them to be the means [of the action]. And from their initial arising until their destruction, one who describes their growth causes even others to understand it in that very same way. Thus people say: 'Go, Kaṃsa is being killed,' 'What is the use of going? Kaṃsa has been killed. Now, according to the view of others: 'Words have conceptual construction as their source, and conceptual constructions have words as their source. There is no mutual connection between them; words do not touch upon the object at all.'"

For example: "By the fame spreading through its attachment to virtues, as if by saffron-juice, a sudden half-saffron mark has appeared upon the faces of the quarters, who are like brides. Here, by the expression "half-saffron mark," the metaphorical application (*rūpaka*) of fragrance and other qualities to fame, and of passion to fame, is understood. Furthermore, by the word "bride" (*vadhū*), the status of the quarters as heroines (*nāyikā*) is perceived; yet, not even a scent of a real relationship exists between them. And this common worldly usage originates from that very [metaphorical] conception.

Even when it is not [directly] brought forth, but remains as it is within the heart, that particular meaning is understood; for speech has the nature of being a means of communication regarding specific objects. Let it be granted that a word possesses denotative power even with respect to a die, and thus conveys its meaning despite the [die's] lack of actual movement. But how can this be justified in the case of a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*)? For a qualifier must follow the principal (*pradhāna*), whereas the principal remains fixed in its own inherent meaning.

It is not so; for even a qualifier, by virtue of being an adjunct (*anurañjaka*), superimposes itself upon the object. Appearing otherwise due to some limiting condition (*upādhi*), it causes its own substratum to appear otherwise as well. For example: "In Magadha the breasts are full; in Kaliṅga the eyes are beautiful; in Aṅga the arms are long; in Vaṅga the feet are soft. Thus [it is said].

In this context, genus-words (*jātiśabda*) such as "breast" and so forth—though associated with unity because they inhere in a single substratum that possesses the two genera of "leftness" and "rightness"—appear as dual; thus, they cause their own substrata to appear in the same way. By this, the appearance of duality even for many [individuals] when the individual (*vyakti*) is the word-meaning is explained. For example: "The young women surrounded him, their breasts possessing the qualities of luster and firmness through wounds that had attained the state of ornaments upon the nails of the Lord of the Daityas, which robbed him of his life."

In this case, because specific ornaments such as distinct nail-marks are mentioned, the denotative function (*vyaktyarthatā*) of the word "breasts" is indeed clearly manifest. Similarly, in the expression "When [are] the Pūrvaphalgunīs joined with the moon?", when plurality is intended, both [stars] appear in the plural. In the expression "When [are] Tiṣya and Punarvasu?", when the duality of the two constellations is intended independently of the individual stars, even many [stars] appear in the dual.

Thus, if the intention were to express both the conjunction with the Moon and the number of stars, the usage *tiṣyapunarvasavaḥ* would not be appropriate. For such an intention does not exist in common worldly usage; and intention, like a virtuous wife, does not overstep the bounds of worldly convention. As it is said: "When the attendants of the harem announced to the people the birth of the prince in words as sweet as nectar, they said: 'O King, these two—the moon-bright umbrella and the two fly-whisks—were indeed not to be given away.'"

Indeed, even when an object possesses its own specific attributes, it is seen to appear otherwise. For example: "May that Lord, who assumed the form of Trivikrama to slay the Daityas, protect you—He whose body grew suddenly so vast that the orb of the sun became like a mere speck upon His crown; the luster of jewels on His head was surpassed by the radiance of His earrings; the Kaustubha gem appeared like a mere spot on His chest; and His navel became like a lotus. In this verse, although the Lord’s body actually possessed its own inherent attributes, it is described as appearing otherwise (smaller than the sun, etc. due to the influence of the intended meaning (*arthopādhi*). Thus, an object may be perceived differently from its actual state because of the context or purpose of the description.

Consequently, it is not known whether this appearance of an object otherwise is based on the adjunct (*upādhi*) of the object itself, or based on the adjunct of the word. Live long! Since that which appears as if it has descended into the path of the objects to be expressed is seen, I ask the venerable one: what is this so-called "object"? Do you say it is that which is expressed by a word? Now, in the case of the word "cow" (*gauh*), what is the word-meaning? Do you say it is the horned animal with dewlaps and so forth? How is it that, even when asked about its own nature (*svarūpa*), you designate it by means of a word alone?

What has been said? Whose nature, colored by the specific qualification called "word," cannot be described otherwise? And I experience it through that very experience whose manifestation is obtained without abandoning the word. Therefore, since it is impossible to designate or experience the reality of the object as separate from the word, we perceive this so-called "object" as either a superimposition (*adhyāsa*) or a transformation (*vipariṇāma*) of the word itself. Others also say thus: "Though the nature of consciousness is undivided, it is [seen as such] by those whose vision is perverted."

"We bow to Sarasvatī, whose form is the light of supreme bliss, who has transcended the path of illusion consisting of the grasper, the grasping, and the grasped, yet appears as if possessing the distinctions of the perceived, the perceiver, and consciousness. What, then, is this so-called *vivarta* (illusory manifestation)? It is said: *Vivarta* is the assumption by a single reality—which does not deviate from its own essence—of other unreal, differentiated forms due to specific arrangements and the like.

In this regard, just as water and the like manifest (*vivartante*) in the form of waves and so forth, serpents and the like in the form of coils and so forth, and blue and other colors in the form of variegated patterns and so forth, so too does the reality of sound (*śabdatattva*), conditioned by ignorance (*avidyopādhi*), manifest in various ways as the forms of diverse objects. As it is said: "The expanse of the sky, whose body resembles a motionless ocean when the mass of clouds has vanished, [is now filled with] the darkness of night, dark as a heap of powdered collyrium."

Now, if it were the case that just as the meaning is a transformation (*vivarta*) of the word, so too the word is a transformation of the meaning, what fault would there be? None at all. However: "If the eternal nature of speech were to depart from cognition, nothing would be manifested; for it is that [speech] which makes things manifest and is itself the object of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśana*). This entire triple world would become blinding darkness if the light called 'word' did not shine throughout the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). Furthermore, the status of being "cognized" exists as a property of the sentence-meaning, just like the state of being "denoted."

And as it is said: "In the compositions of great poets, there exists a certain reality that is perceived as something distinct; it shines forth as something exceeding the well-known constituent parts, like the *lāvaṇya* (grace) in women."

And since its comprehension occurs at a time subsequent to the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the meaning of the sentence, how can this be logically established under either the theory of superimposition (*adhyāsa*) or the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivarta*)? It is said: transformation (*vipariṇāma*) is the transition of a real entity into another state; in that regard, just as clay and the like transform into the form of a jar, milk and the like into the form of curds, and Caitra and others into the form of youth and so forth, so too does this Śabda-Brahman, through the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of ignorance, transform itself into various forms of objects in their respective ways.

For example: "I have five sons; my mother is currently performing austerities on the banks of the Ganges. In this case, there is no inconsistency whether the sentence-meaning is expressed (*abhidhīyamānatā*) or suggested (*pratīyamānatā*), as word and meaning appear separately. Nor does the function of the word cease at this point, because the specific nature of *tātparya* (the final purport) will be explained further below. An illustration of that [purport] is: "He has already attained sovereignty; why then would he again cause me the exhaustion of churning?"

O enemy of sleep, I do not even imagine that the ocean, which possesses a brilliance like fire, would ever break its dam; yet, why does it appear to tremble as if harboring doubts now that you have arrived here, followed by the lords of all the islands? May the ocean protect you!

In this case, while the literal meaning of the sentence as heard—which describes the specific king under discussion who has conquered the quarters—is being expressed, there exists an implicit superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of Viṣṇu upon the word "Being" (*sat*), just as there is in the phrase "the descent of Viṣṇu. This is perceived because of the connection of other incarnations with defects such as sluggishness due to sleep, whereas this [king] is free from those. Consequently, the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is the demonstration of his distinction; it is this which is renowned in poetry as *dhvani*.

Thus it has been said: "In speech, it is *tātparya* (intended meaning) alone; in poetry, it is *dhvani* (suggestion) alone; in the perfection of virtues, it is *saubhāgya* (grace) alone, according to Vallabha; in the body of a woman, it is *lāvaṇya* (loveliness) alone; and in the heart of a passionate person, it is *śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment) alone. But what is the distinction between poetry and speech, or between *dhvani* and *tātparya*? It is said: That which is straightforward (*avakra*) is merely speech in both scripture and the world; that which is indirect (*vakra*), as found in arthavāda and the like, is traditionally known as poetry (*kāvya*).

If the entire essence of the speaker’s intention is understood from the sentence, then *tātparya* (intention) is a property of the meaning (*artha-dharma*), whereas *dhvani* (suggestion) is a property of the word (*śabda-dharma*). Intention is held to be an internal quality, like the grace of the Goddess of Speech; suggestion is an external quality, like her physical beauty. Because they are not far removed from one another, the two [terms] are used for both [meanings], just as the months of Āśvina and Kārtika are designated by the names Madhu and Mādhava. Thus, the meaning of case-endings (*vibhakty-artha*), the meaning of verbal function (*vṛtty-artha*), and the meaning of the word (*padārtha*) have been described.

The meaning of a sentence has been proclaimed through its various divisions, such as *bhāvanā* (productive activity) and others. Because action (*kriyā*) constitutes the sense of the verbal root (*dhātu*), it is presented as the meaning of the sentence; and the status of *bhāvanā* as the meaning of the word is established on the grounds that it is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*). Action and the rest have been stated to be the denotata (*vācyāḥ*), the qualificands (*viśeṣyāḥ*), and the objects conveyed (*pratyāyyāḥ*) by the word. With respect to these [denotata], there occur their non-existence (*adhāya*), transformation (*vipariṇāma*), and modification (*vivarta*). The meaning of a word is held to be the substratum (*dhāma*) for both the primary elements—the case-ending (*vibhakti*) and the verbal base (*vṛti*)—which possess their respective meanings, and for their mutual embellishment (*upaskriyā*).

"Since the meaning of a word is not within the scope of a sentence, that meaning is therefore defined here. Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Fourfold Meaning of Case Endings," in the *Śṛṅgāraprakāśa* composed by the Great Emperor, the illustrious Bhojadeva.

The seventh [chapter] is the exposition of the power of the relationship between word and meaning alone. In that regard, the twelvefold capacity of word and meaning—consisting of denotation (*abhidhā*), intention (*vivakṣā*), purport (*tātparya*), expectancy (*apekṣā*), semantic competency (*sāmarthya*), syntactic connection (*anvaya*), unification of meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), the elimination of defects (*doṣahāna*), the adoption of excellences (*guṇopādāna*), and the inseparability of figures of speech and aesthetic flavor (*alaṃkāra-rasāviyoga*)—is called *sāhitya* (literature). Among these, what is the power of the word that expresses the meaning? It is denotation (*abhidhā*).

A word, functioning toward its denoted object as if toward its own form, operates through three modes of function (*vṛtti*); these are the primary (*mukhyā*), the secondary (*gauṇī*), and the indicative (*lakṣaṇā*). Among these, the primary is that which directly denotes an object without mediation. The secondary is that which denotes an object mediated by the connection with qualities such as swiftness that are understood [through association]. The indicative, however, is that which indicates another object invariably connected with its own primary meaning.

For instance, this word "cow" (go) denotes an object possessing a dewlap and so forth by means of its primary function (mukhyā vṛtti). However, when that same word is applied to a "Bāhīka" (a person from the Punjab) with reference to his possession of qualities such as stoutness and fatness, it follows a secondary function (gauṇī vṛtti). Thus it has been said: "A word which, through conventional usage (rūḍhi), is established in common worldly usage for a specific meaning is 'primary' (mukhya) in that context; elsewhere, it is 'secondary' (gauṇa) because of its similarity to that [primary] meaning."

But when words are incapable of becoming the means for the accomplishment of an action through their own primary meanings, they then indicate another meaning that is invariably connected with the expressed meaning; at that time, that function is called *lakṣaṇā* (indication). For example, in the expression "a hamlet on the Gaṅgā," the word "Gaṅgā" is incapable of becoming the locus for the action of dwelling, and thus it indicates the bank, which is invariably connected with its own primary meaning. As it has been said: "Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is the cognition of something invariably connected with the expressed meaning."

This very mode of expression is held to be the lifeblood of clever, witty speech (*vidagdhavakrokti*). Each of these three modes is further divided into two, and thus separately they are distinguished into six types. Among them, the primary [mode] is twofold: *tathābhūtārthā* (the thing as it is) and *tadbhāvāpatti* (attaining the state of that). Of those two, *tathābhūtārthā* is sixfold: pertaining to genus (*jāti*), pertaining to individual (*vyakti*), pertaining to configuration (*ākṛti*), pertaining to quality (*guṇa*), pertaining to action (*kriyā*), and pertaining to relation (*saṃbandha*).

Among these, [the cognition] "This person is a fair-complexioned Brahmin" and so forth has the universal class (*jāti*) as its object. For example: "Whose mouth possesses words that are gracious, captivating, and skilled in various modes of address, and whose home possesses women—[all this] occurs through whose merits? Or, for example: "In whose house there is a single wife who is plump-bodied, having many female companions, gentle in her disposition, and beautiful with eyes like those of a *kora* bird. And, for example: "A certain woman was repeatedly deceived by the reflections of her own eyes in the water..."

The flower-gatherer reaches out her hand to touch the blue lotuses, yet she hesitates; for objects such as the *iṅgudī* fruit possess forms that defy thought, like the initial objects of a visual illusion or a reflection. This is that very place in the city of Śṛṅgavera, where in ancient times he had a meeting with the affectionate chief of the Niṣādas. Objects pertaining to qualities are illustrated by such descriptions as "white," "rough," "thin," or "thick"—just as the quarters of the sky are darkened by rows of clouds in the rainy season, and the earth is made lush by fresh streaks of young grass.

Or, for example: "The young lip, intensely red from much betel-chewing, turned grey after being enjoyed by his beloved, and now, with its edges fading, it resembles the luster of a *kāñcanāra* flower. Regarding the application of verbal suffixes (*kṛt-pratyaya*) to express the agent (*kartṛ*), the object (*karman*), or other grammatical roles such as the instrument (*karaṇa*), locus (*adhikaraṇa*), and so forth—just as in the case of the roots *pac* (to cook), *sthā* (to stand), *yaj* (to sacrifice), and *tṛp* (to satisfy)—one might ask: "Why do you grieve for the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, who was a giver, a sustainer, a sacrificer at the head of the rite, a gratifier of the ancestors, and one who fought, broke, and perished? [Note: The examples provided illustrate the technical application of Pāṇinian grammar to poetic expression.]

Or, for example: "The women of Ucchanna, though sitting quietly with downcast faces, laugh as they carry away their lovers exactly as they were seized. Regarding the subject of relationship, there is the verse beginning: "Father, mother, enemy, brother-in-law, son-in-law," and so forth; and: "He whose maternal and paternal grandfathers were the Sun and the Moon; he who was [the father] of Urvashi by his own choice and of the Earth through his wife. Or, for example: "Here, in order to protect those suffering from separation, their friends secretly break [the branches]."

The first knots of the emerging buds on the mango clusters [are like this]. The imposition of a state of being upon an object through superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is what constitutes "becoming that" (*tathābhāvāpatti*). That too is sixfold: consisting of superimposition (*adhyāsātmikā*), consisting of imagination (*kalpanātmikā*), consisting of illusory appearance (*vivartātmikā*), consisting of transformation (*vipariṇāmātmikā*), consisting of error (*viparyayātmikā*), and consisting of conventional discourse (*pravādātmikā*). Among these, *adhyāsa* is the attribution of "this is that" even by one who knows it is not so. For example: "Why do you not look at the mango? Why do you gaze at the sky? *Indira kiṃ na pekkhasi āāsaṃ kim uṇa puloesi |* (Prākṛt)

The sequence of the arrangement of the *miadvaaṇda* (the *madavṛnda*) occurs at the base of the arms. Or, for example: "The lotus is not in water; the blue lilies are in the lotus; these are upon a golden creeper; and she [the creeper] is delicate and beautiful—what is this succession of marvels? An imaginative construction (*utprekṣākalpanā*) even of that which does not exist is as follows: "By your fame, mingled with affection for your virtues, the faces of the women of the quarters have suddenly become half-smeared with saffron. Or, for example: "Having cast aside the wealth of asceticism, abandoned by flowers because of its lack of fruit..."

How could a wise person approach a wicked person who dwells in wickedness? Through a particular arrangement of things, there occurs a transformation of states; just as the pollen produced from the lotuses of this blooming forest of land-lotuses, when wafted up and whirled about in the sky by whirlwinds on all sides, assumes the splendor of a golden parasol.

Just as in this [forest], the smoke of the forest fire—tossed by the force of the wind, uneven, slightly interrupted, and curved; somewhat subsided, bent over the woods, heaped up, and then rising again; dark as the shoulder of a young buffalo—creates, as it flows freely through the sky, fleeting patterns like the decorative lines on leaves. Transformation (*vipariṇāma*) is the passage of an entity into another state. For example: "Those who were performers of sacrifice, whose great luster was renowned; those who were lords of the earth; and these fawn-eyed women—for whom all talk of further worldly existence has ceased."

Oh, how even those trees that bend their branches with fruits and flowers appear so magnificent on this earth because of this divine lady! Or rather, may he protect us—he whose face was smiling as the daughter of the mountain, having gathered together the crescent moon fallen from his head and the bracelet broken in a lovers’ quarrel, said, "Look at this!"—and may she, Girijā, and that playful moon, its body filled with rays of light, likewise protect us. False knowledge is error (*viparyaya*).

"Without doubt, this breast-cloth, dark as the belly of a parrot, has fallen from her breast—marked by the teardrops falling from her eyes as she sank down to her navel when her lover departed in anger, his gait broken. Or as in another example: "Do not fear, O Moon! There is no Rahu in my drink. Rohini dwells in the sky; why, O coward, do you fear? What is so surprising in this—that the minds of men waver during the secret trysts with clever women?"

Even regarding non-existent things, there is a flow of false establishment as if they were real entities, such as the forms of a city of Gandharvas, a celestial weapon, a deer in a mirage, and darkness. These occurrences are difficult to attain and defiled by the grasping of the unreal and the untrue; or rather, like the intermingling of the luster of jewels, this is seen before one as a fragment of a rainbow emerging from the tip of an anthill.

By means of which [quality], your dark body shall attain a splendor surpassing that of Viṣṇu in his cowherd guise, with the shimmering luster of a peacock feather. Secondary indication (*gauṇī*) is twofold: based on similarity (*sādṛśyanimittā*) and based on metaphorical application (*upacāranimittā*). In this regard, when there is a usage of two words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇya*) or in different grammatical cases (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), a relationship arises—mediated by either an implied or an expressed quality—because the status of qualifier and qualified would otherwise be untenable.

That [quality] has as its object a thing delimited by a quality, and it is independent of any other cause. In that context, whatever distinguishes the associated [substance] is understood as a quality (*guṇa*). Because it is subordinate (*paratantra*), its nature as a quality is illustrated in the treatise. "Quality" means its own referent, a qualifier, and the ground for the application [of a word]; these are one and the same meaning. That [quality] is infinite due to the distinctions of property (*dharma*), quality, action, form, genus (*jāti*), color, and so forth.

Although, in relation to that connection, an infinite variety of functions (vṛtti) based upon it may be conceived, nevertheless, there are six types of its conceptualizations (vikalpa): having the primary [meaning] as its object, having the non-primary [meaning] as its object, having difference as its object, having non-difference as its object, and having no qualification as its object. Among these, when both meanings—the primary qualificandum and the [other] meaning—have attributes (*dharma*) and so forth as their basis, such that one becomes the qualifier of the other, that is the case "having the primary [meaning] as its object."

An example of a compound based on a quality (*dharmanimitta*) is as follows: "Homage to that beast of a king who has fallen under the power of her lovely face, with its eyes darkened by collyrium and brows arched in playful grace. The same [expression], when not a compound, is as follows: "The wise remember that the word 'cow' (*go*), when properly employed, is a wish-fulfilling cow; but when wrongly employed, that very same word becomes a mere cow. An example of a compound based on an action (*kriyānimitta*) is as follows: "Even at night, which is the time for union with my beloved friend, I am distressed..."

That which proceeds by taking both the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the object (*karman*) is called *caṇḍāla*. An example of this compound is: "O wretched god, why have you at the door raised this wicked poison-tree along with its root? When even the slightest change occurs in it through blossoming, terrifying complications of the fever of love arise within me. Where, between the qualifier and the qualified, one is initially non-primary (*amukhya*), that is the scope of the non-primary (*amukhyaviṣaya*).

When the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) is not primary, [the figure] based on a common substratum (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is caused by an attribute (*dharma*), as in: "By some chance, the young bride’s two jar-like breasts were touched by the youth with trembling hands, while he was removing the drops of perspiration from her face, which resembled a *himālaba* flower. The same [figure], when caused by an action (*kriyā*), is as follows: "O friend, in this lotus-face of yours, the dancer that is the creeper-like eyebrow gracefully wards off the glances of young men with the movements of its limbs."

When the particular (viśeṣa) is primary, there is a case of different grammatical substrata (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) based on form (*ākṛti*), as in: "O you whose breasts are like jars of loveliness, like the frontal globes of the elephant of Love, supported by the hearts of men—why do you sigh? The same [type of figure] is based on action (*kriyā*), as in: "The time of autumn is the enemy of the season of resolve, the firm binding chain for the elephant of anger, and the cage for the lion of the moon-like face of Dāsarathi."* *Note: This verse is from the *Gāthāsaptaśatī* (or similar Prakrit anthology). The commentary explains that "autumn" is metaphorically identified with various things through its specific actions.*

That [metaphor] is one whose object is difference (*bhedaviṣaya*) wherein a single word, through the conceptualization of a distinction, undergoes the relationship of qualifier and qualified based on a quality (*guṇanimitta*). This occurs between the secondary (*gauṇa*) and the primary (*mukhya*), where it is caused by a quality, and between two primary things, where it is caused by a genus (*jātinimitta*). For example: "O lotus-eyed one, moon-faced one, your face is the moon; the lotus is indeed a lotus, and the moon is truly the moon. An example of [the metaphor] between two primary things caused by a quality is: "Qualities arise from the palm tree; those which are grasped by the hand are the ones that are useful."

The rays of the sun favor the lotuses, making them truly lotuses. An example of the cause being the action of the two principal [words] is as follows: "He is a true man, he alone is a man, whose name—even his enemies—rejoice in pronouncing, as if it were swallowing the very vigor of the assembly through its gravity. An example of the cause being the essential nature [of the words] is as follows: "Nectar is indeed nectar, the moon is indeed the moon, the lotus is indeed a lotus, Rati is indeed Rati, Kāma is indeed Kāma, and honey is indeed honey."

Thus, since things generally do not possess a mutual commingling of natures, how can this woman possess states of being that consist of all [of them] at once? When, through the establishment of similarity and so forth, the standard of comparison itself causes the object of comparison to be understood, that is the domain of non-difference (*abheda*). This other type occurs in speech as follows: "Behold! As a bee drinks honey at will from a blossoming lotus, it kisses even a bud that lacks fragrance. The twilight is full of passion; the day is the courtesan of that city."

Oh, how strange is the course of destiny! And yet, there is no meeting. O travelers, as you have been instructed by both of us, go once more to that Tilaka tree on the road, which is the very ornament of the path; having reached it, sport at your pleasure, your burden of fatigue dissolved. But from here, within the belly of the salt ocean filled with the caustic bile of sea-monsters, there is only a beautiful cessation, never again an emergence, however difficult it may be.

An example of the statement of neither [the object nor the subject] is as follows: "This act, committed by the hand-convulsing [Rāvaṇa] under the pretext of a golden deer, terrifies even the wicked when it is recounted; for in the empty Janasthāna, even a stone weeps at the noble one’s deeds performed with piteous gestures, and even the heart of diamond shatters. In this context, where a name that serves as a qualifier, or a pronoun, takes up the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*)—such as a specific quality or attribute—that is called the "domain of the qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇaviṣaya*).

Let it be that a name is caused by specific qualities; however, the deer-eyed woman is both firm and lovely, for these transformations are the essence of unconditioned sweetness. Water, though hard-natured, takes refuge in oyster shells; yet it is those waters, highly esteemed by noble families, that become pearls.
