Does even a mere designation arise from refinement and the like? As for that [name], it is like a cloud with shimmering cranes, which coats the sky with its glossy, dark luster.

May the winds be full of spray, the cries of joy of the peacocks—the friends of the clouds—be timely, and may the seasons be mild; for I, Rāma, am of a firm and hard heart and can endure everything. But what will become of Vaidehī? Alas, alas! O Queen, be steadfast. As an example of a universal term (*sarvanāman*) being used as the cause for the manifestation of specific qualities: "That king, that happiness, that retinue, and those horses—all of this has appeared today in your memory, O friend, now that you are seen."

"Indeed, your friend was not at all deluded regarding this terrible consequence; for the heart of city-dwellers is as delicate as a flower. In this case, even though it is a secondary (gauṇa) attribute, its qualification [of the subject] is indeed a qualification of that [subject] itself, provided that the pronoun there functions solely on the basis of the excellence of qualities (*guṇasampatti*). As in: "...O you who possess long eyes, O you who are the abode of the world, O you whose face is like the moon, O you who are the very life of others! (Chadā... valaa dīhiahimaṃghallahini adeha | annajīdiharaloaṇahotahomuhaaṃdahoreva ||)

The "perversion of the non-qualifier" (*aviśeṣaṇaviparyāsa*) occurs where that which is a non-qualifier—being non-deviant—is applied by virtue of its association with qualities such as those [of the qualifier]. ... "The Halāhala poison kills; who could live by eating a *koṇa*? Having heard this, even he died. The *riṣṭha* is truly a dear ox. As an example regarding the nature of sentient beings (*cetana-prakṛti*): "Truly, the Lord of Gods is made of stone, since by his lotus-petal-soft hands, Citta was not made to sprout [with love] for the daughter of the plowman."

"O pestle, it is known that you are indeed wood; this is the truth. What more can I say? You were raised in the forest. Yet, at this festival of contact with the hand of the lotus-eyed maiden, you have become a sprout in an instant—this is due to the power of the insentient itself. O Lord, if those who seek wealth could somehow find it after a long search, they would eventually obtain it; but you, on the other hand, seek out those who seek [your favor] every day with great effort."

If this wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*) does not shatter upon seeing you—who bestows more than what was even imagined when it was merely thought of—then it is no wish-fulfilling gem at all. Metaphorical transference (*upacāra*) is the attribution of a qualifier belonging to one thing to another, whether primary (*mukhya*) or secondary (*gauṇī*). That [transference] which has that [attribution] as its cause is "metaphorical" (*aupacārikī*); however, because its meaning is mediated by a secondary sense, it is called "secondary" (*gauṇī*). Even for that [secondary type], there are various grounds for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*), such as properties (*dharma*), qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*kriyā*), essential nature (*svarūpa*), and genus (*jāti*), according to their respective distinctions.

That [suggestion] also is of six types: based on a property (*dharmanimitta*), based on a quality (*guṇanimitta*), based on a shape (*ākṛtinimitta*), based on an action (*kriyānimitta*), based on an essential nature (*svarūpanimitta*), and based on a genus (*jātinimitta*). Among these, an example of that based on a property is: "May she be hollow, hard, yet beautiful—this deer-eyed woman... and "...danced by my beloved with her arms, charming with jingling bracelets... [etc.].

In this instance, the words *kaṭhoka* ("thicket") and *subhaga* ("fortunate") are conventionally established as denoting specific types of corporeal substances and living beings respectively; however, when superimposed upon *roṣa* ("wrath") and *valaya* ("bracelet"), they come to function as adjectives for *trāyikā* ("female protector") and *kāla* ("time") by virtue of that connection. An example based on qualities (*guṇanimittā*) is as follows: "Indeed, what is there that is not a source of joy for those who are sweet-natured? This sound of the drum, though its conclusion is unpleasant, was heard by the one with the wine. Here, the words *madhura* ("sweet") and *virasa* ("unpleasant") are conventionally established as adjectives for other things [such as flavors or sounds].

By means of that [quality] being concealed, through the method of description, the words *ākṛti* (form), *valaya* (bracelet), and so forth, undergo the state of being superimposed as qualifiers. An example where the cause is form (*ākṛtinimitta*) is: "In the mango tree, it has sprouted, put forth leaves, formed buds, and blossomed; likewise, in my heart, Love has sprouted, put forth leaves, formed buds, and blossomed. Or, for example: "The lady’s loveliness is as if in bloom with her hands like tender shoots, as if in full flower with her eyes, and as if bearing fruit with her full breasts."

In this context, terms such as "sprouted" (*aṅkurita*) and "leafed" (*pallavita*), which are conventionally established as qualifiers for embodied objects like trees based on their specific forms, undergo a figurative state of being qualifiers when they are superimposed upon the formless [states] of Madana and loveliness through that mediation. An example based on action (*kriyā*) is: "The East gave birth to the moon; Madana dances; even the quarters laugh; and the wind scatters the pollen of night-lotuses like fine powder in the courtyard of the sky. Or, for example: "He who has brought forth the moon with its blossoming flowers at the onset of evening, like the descent of the Ganges..."

"O Queen, when the moon has set out toward the western quarter of the night... Here, because actions such as "embracing" (sevopagūḍha) and others are transferred elsewhere through that intervention [of another action], they function as adjectives (*viśeṣaṇa*). But how is this variety distinct from the secondary (*gauṇī*) [metaphor]? For where the well-known relationship between the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) is understood, they describe that as *anyokti* or *samāsokti*, which is non-secondary (*agauṇī*) because its meaning is mediated by qualities (*guṇa*).

Furthermore, when the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) is understood through its similarity in quality with the object of comparison (*upameya*), that is *gauṇī* (secondary) with an unmediated meaning; they call this *samādhi*. As it has been said: "When the subject is non-contextual, it is called *samāsokti*; when it is contextual, it is *samādhi*. An example based on the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is as follows: "To whom would wretchedness, the mother of misery, not cause dejection? Or whom would this Fortune, the kinswoman of intoxication, not exhilarate?"

"Her body is, as it were, an ornament to ornaments, a special refinement of adornment; O friend, even for a standard of comparison, it is a counter-standard. Here, because poverty is the cause of wretchedness, there is a metaphorical superimposition (*upacāra*) of motherhood upon poverty; thus, the relationship between poverty and wretchedness is mediated by the status of being an offspring—the sentence-meaning being that "poverty produces wretchedness. And the justification for this metaphorical usage is established, just as in the verse beginning with "The East gave birth to the moon. This same principle should be applied to subsequent examples as well.

Those characterized by their birth are as follows: fortitude, forbearance, self-restraint, purity, capability, propriety (this is the reading in the root text), eloquence, and lack of malice toward living beings—these seven are the fuel for prosperity. Or, conversely: those for whom the killing of living beings is a sport, whose words cut to the quick, and whose duty is the torment of others—they are death upon death.

In this context, when the properties of fire and fuel are superimposed upon the properties of death and the mortal, as well as upon prosperity, fortitude, and so forth—along with death and wicked people—the status of being a subordinate factor (guṇabhāva) belongs only to the fuel and death by virtue of their respective classes (*jāti*), and not to fire and the mortal themselves. Since these [latter] have no direct connection [to the subordinate factors], a metaphorical transfer (*upacāra*) mediated by the properties of "blazing" and "destruction" is employed to establish that connection. By this, the following meaning is established: "Fortitude and the rest nourish prosperity (*śrī*)," and "wicked people even kill death itself."

And this very action, having been performed by one form, is superimposed upon another; thus, it constitutes a figurative application (*upacāra-vṛtti*). As it has been said: "The night-lotuses close and the day-lotuses open"— through the superimposition of the action of the eyes, the word expressing that [closing and opening] is obtained. In the same way, "Pārtha is he who experiences joy... and "Joy does not leave a living man even after a hundred years," and so forth, should be understood.

If this is so, why is this [comparison] not based on an action (*kriyā*)? Because the action itself undergoes a transformation into the form of a substance-class (*dravyajāti*), just as in expressions such as *dainyamātā* ("motherly wretchedness"), where it takes the form of a state (*vṛtti*). But then, why is this also not a secondary metaphor (*gauṇī*), just as in "a cow-like cow" (*gauriva gauḥ*) or "fuel-sticks [are like cows]" (*samidhaḥ*)? It would be so if the word *samidhaḥ* were not dependent on the word *śriyaḥ* (glories), or if the word *vahni* (fire) were used in the sense of "the fire of Śrī," as in: "The time for the purification of the body through penance is the fuel for the pot of the god of love."

Thus, by this it is stated that even for [words] such as *dainyamātā* ("mother of wretchedness") and *daridratā* ("poverty"), which are "the death of even death," there is no lack of figurative status (*gauṇatva*). By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*), it is meant that even in the case of pronouns and the like, when there is metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) based on both difference (*bheda*) and non-difference (*abheda*), the figurative sense arises through a mediated meaning. That [metaphorical usage] occurs through the superimposition of a name in the case of difference, as in: "O right hand, release the sword upon the Śūdra ascetic for the sake of the life of the deceased Brahmin boy!"

"You are the very body of Rāma, who was capable of banishing Sītā when she was exhausted by her heavy pregnancy; how could there be compassion in you? Or as it is said: 'O scion of Raghu, it is only fitting that you despair; what ill-omened mark has the Creator observed upon your limbs? O Hanumān, you still live even today; why this waiting for an enemy standing right before you? "

By means of metaphorical identification (*abhedopacāra*), there is the superimposition of all names; for example: On a sandy bank made bright by the moonlight of the moon, two young Siddhas once played a game of dice for a very long time. One says, "Kaiṭabha was killed first," while the other says, "Kaṃsa. "Tell me the truth of the matter: which of those two was killed by you first?"

Or rather, why would he—who has already attained sovereign glory—direct that same exhaustion from churning the ocean toward me again? Nor do I imagine that his sleep, which was previously so effortless, could possibly recur for one whose mind is so restless. And why does he build a bridge once more? (In another reading: "And how is it that... As you approach, the ocean, followed by the lords of all the islands, appears as if it were trembling, harboring such doubts.

In the first two examples here, the names Rāma and Hanumān are conventionally established as specific designations for two distinct physical forms who are respectively exceedingly merciless and unable to endure humiliation; through that mediation, they are applied by metaphorical transfer to two other distinct physical forms possessing qualities opposite to those [original ones], thereby assuming a figurative status as qualifiers. Thus, this is a case of *gauṇī* (secondary) [metaphor] based on the occasion of a figurative application of a mediated meaning.

However, where there is no metaphorical attribution of difference (*bhedopacāra*), the figurative usage (*gauṇī*) occurs solely on account of the quality as the cause, because there is an absence of any intervening factor—as in: "I am Rāma, the endurer of all," or "Even that Tārkṣya knows me, Rāvaṇa, as distinct from himself. But how, when there is non-difference between word and meaning, can there be a designation of difference? For in such cases as "the head of Rāhu," "the cow is the cow," or "the wish-granting [cow]," a difference between word and meaning is indeed observed.

It is said: in general, metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) proceeds only when there is a primary referent (*mukhya*), and when a purpose (*prayojana*) and a cause (*nimitta*) exist. This [metaphor] serves as the basis for designating difference among things that are non-different, and it serves as the basis for designating non-difference among things that are different. In this regard, the designation of difference among non-different things is as follows: "You know yourself by yourself; you create yourself by yourself; and through your own creative power, you dissolve back into yourself alone."

In this context, because there is no other entity apart from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and because actions such as knowing are impossible without the various causal factors (*kāraka*) such as the object of action (*karman*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*), the One alone appears differentiated through the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the roles of agent, object, instrument, and so forth. Once this differentiation is established, the conventional usage of "standard of comparison" (*upamāna*) and "object of comparison" (*upameya*) proceeds based on similarity, whether the terms are used in their primary sense or in a metaphorical one. For example: "Your face is like your face; your eyes are like your eyes; your form is like your form; you are like yourself, O slender-waisted one."

However, a distinction (*vyatireka*) arises based on a perceived difference (*vaisādṛśya*). For example: "He is truly a man whom even his enemies revere; lotuses are truly lotuses when touched by the rays of the sun. Furthermore, from this [distinction], there arises the production of a connection that suggests a different meaning, as in: "O Hanuman, you are the very limb of Rama. By this, metaphors such as simile (*upamā*) and poetic fancy (*rūpaka*)—whether primary (*mukhya*) or secondary (*gauṇa*)—are also explained. For example: "This moon-like face, with its red luster, is full of intoxication."

It rivals the moon when its rising glow has been fully prepared. The [celestial] moon is drunk by the gods; but by me, the moon of your face is drunk. For this [celestial] moon is always incomplete, while this one possesses a full orb. While this moon of your face exists—consisting of nectar, hating the lotuses, and possessing radiant stars—what is the use of the other moon? It does not cause the lotuses to close, nor does it traverse the sky; your moon-like face exerts itself solely for the snatching away of my life-breaths.

The metaphorical application of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*) occurs as in the two subsequent examples; for there, several qualifiers of the object of comparison—which possess qualities equal to those of the implied or explicitly stated standard of comparison—are employed with respect to the subject of comparison, separated by the pronoun and the standard of comparison, thereby superimposing excellence through the metaphorical application of non-difference.

Now, one might ask: why is this not considered *anyokti* (indirect expression), *samāsokti* (condensed expression), or *ubhayokti* (expression of both)? For indeed, when the excellences of the implied (*pratīyamāna*) and the expressed (*abhidhīyamāna*) objects of comparison are present, these three—*anyokti*, *samāsokti*, and *ubhayokti*—are observed even when there is the superimposition of a pronoun (*sarvanāmādhyāsa*). Among them, an example of *anyokti* is as follows: "Alas, O sandalwood! Where is that fragrance of yours? Alas, where is that coolness of yours which dispels all torment? You have fallen into the hands of one who treats you like charcoal! Fie upon fate!"

*Samāsokti* (Abridged Expression) is as follows: "O bee, why do you distress the young *navāmalikā* bud, which is unripe and has not yet developed its flavor out of season? For now, divert your restless mind toward other flowering creepers that can endure being crushed. *Ubhayokti* (Expression of Both) is as follows: "By what merciless person have you been seated comfortably, having had your true nature extracted from your form? Or by whom have you been sought after in this foreign land?"

"Since there is no brother capable of bearing the burden of the cost of acquisition, let alone one capable of examining a sapphire like yours. It is said in reply: "Where the very standard of comparison (*upamāna*), when employed, makes the object of comparison (*upameya*) understood through its implied or expressed qualities, only there do figures such as *anyokti* (indirect expression) and others occur. But here, no standard of comparison is employed. What then? It is a pronoun serving as its qualifier; therefore, in the first example, it is not *anyokti*, while in the second example, it is not *samāsokti* (condensed expression)."

If this is so, why does the attainment of that state (*tadbhāvāpatti*)—which consists of superimposition—not occur? For example, as when one says, "The young moon is at the root of the boy's arm," or "O kings! Alas! Why do you not kill this victim together with these five sons of paramours, and take this slave along with this aged princess? It is replied: it is not only pronouns (*sarvanāman*) that are used here; rather, since the use of adjectives (*viśeṣya*) is also appropriate, the attainment of that state is logically possible.

In cases such as "the moonlight" (*candrajyotsnā*), however, because there is a connection with the defining characteristic of superimposition (*samādhi*) upon the superimposition of names, this is *gauṇī* (secondary) based on metaphorical usage (*upacāra*). Furthermore, we shall explain later how superimposition is also possible even when the substratum (*dharmin*) itself is superimposed. Metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is of two kinds: *lakṣaṇā* and *lakṣitalakṣaṇā*.

Of these two, when the meaning of a word employed [in a sentence] cannot function as a means (*sādhana*) for the accomplishment of an action, it indicates another meaning that is invariably concomitant (*avinābhūta*) with its own primary sense, yet remains mediated; this is *lakṣaṇā*. That which is distinct from this, and which will be described in various forms, is called *lakṣitalakṣaṇā*. In this regard, *lakṣaṇā* is sixfold: indication based on proximity (*sāmīpya-lakṣaṇā*), indication based on accompaniment (*sāhacarya-lakṣaṇā*), indication based on association (*sahacarita-lakṣaṇā*), indication based on cause (*hetu-lakṣaṇā*), indication based on purpose (*tādathrya-lakṣaṇā*), and indication based on measure (*parimāṇa-lakṣaṇā*).

In this regard, in examples such as "the cattle station on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*) or "the platforms are shouting" (*mañcāḥ krośanti*), there is indication based on proximity (*sāmīpyalakṣaṇā*), which is the cause for the cognition of another meaning—namely, proximity—which is invariably connected with the primary sense. As in: "That face, pale like the ripening of a palm leaf; those cheeks, as beautiful as a fresh slice of elephant tusk."

In this case, because the acts of "ripening" and "cutting" are immaterial as actions, it is impossible for them to possess paleness or whiteness; therefore, they indicate nearby ripe palm leaves and a freshly cut elephant tusk. In expressions such as "the umbrella-bearers are going" or "bring in the spears," the cause for the cognition of another meaning—based on the perceived association with the primary sense—is indication based on association (*sāhacarya-lakṣaṇā*). For example: "Having appointed all the mountains as the calf, while Meru stood as the milker skilled in the art of milking..."

They milked the earth, as directed by the King, for radiant jewels and great medicinal herbs. Here, due to the association with the "milkers" (the subjects), the verb *duduhuḥ* ("they milked") is used even with reference to the mountains. Or, for example: "At every step, at every chariot, at every elephant, at every horse, and at every steed, Śatakratu stationed hundreds upon hundreds of chariots, hundreds of rutting elephants, hundreds of horses, and hundreds of spears. Where another property is indicated through its association with a stated property, that is the figure of speech known as *sahacaritalakṣaṇā*.

For example: "Like drops of honey, tawny like milk, with broad hips like golden planks. Here, the tawny color and the broadness, along with their substrata—the shape and so forth—are indicated through *lakṣaṇā*. In such cases as "Food is indeed the vital breaths" (*annaṃ vai prāṇāḥ*) or "Clarified butter is life" (*āyur ghṛtam*), there is the *hetu-lakṣaṇā* (causal indication), which is the cause for the cognition of an internal purpose that is inseparably connected to its own literal meaning. For example: "You are my life, you are my second heart."

In this context, by the words *jīvita* (life) and *hṛdaya* (heart), that which is dear—the cause of the consciousness of life—is expressed. In examples such as "the pillar of Indra," "the jasmine," and "the lamp," there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on identity with that purpose (*tādarthya*), which serves as the cause for the cognition of that meaning. For instance: "O King, lion among men, Lord of Siṃhala, you who brandish the staff of your arm like the Malaya mountain to shatter the vast fame of the ocean's far shore. Here, by the word *daṇḍa* (staff), the people dispatched by the staff-bearer are expressed.

In expressions such as *prastha*, *pala*, and *krośa*, there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) characterized by measure, which serves as the cause for the cognition of another object that functions as the means of measurement. For example: "Because priceless, lofty [jewels] were repeatedly carried away in no small measure by many *prasthas*, the people constantly took up immeasurable gems, as if from a wealthy guest. In this verse, by the word *prastha*, what is meant is a measuring vessel made of wood or other materials, which serves as the instrument for measuring a *prastha*.

Indirect indication by means of what is indicated (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*) is also of six kinds: conventional indication (*rūḍhalakṣaṇā*), indicative indication (*pratīkalakṣaṇā*), intended indication (*vivakṣitalakṣaṇā*), contradictory indication (*viruddhalakṣaṇā*), indication of something other than that (*tadanyalakṣaṇā*), and miscellaneous indication (*prakīrṇalakṣaṇā*). Among these, when an object is indicated by a name that has been indicated through some kind of etymological derivation, it is conventional indication (*rūḍhalakṣaṇā*). Examples are *durodara* (dice-player), *cakravāka* (ruddy goose), and *dvirepha* (bee). As in: "The bee (*dvirepha*), following his own beloved, drank honey from the single vessel of the flower."

In this case, the state of being a gambler (*durodaratva*) and the state of being a bee (*dvirephatva*) can also apply to a curlew (*kurara*); however, there is no conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) here that would constitute indication (*lakṣaṇā*). This is not indication. Where a whole is indicated by means of a part—that is, by a synonym for a portion of the name—it is indeed indication; it is not any random instance. This is called *pratikalakṣaṇā*. For example: "Bhīma is one of terrible prowess," or "She too has become one whose sight is difficult to obtain."

In this context, because of the hearing of the partial forms of the words *bhīma* and *bhīmasatya*, there is indicated a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of the previously characterized names *Bhīmasena* and *Satyabhāmā*. It does not occur as "the elder, the elder" or "the wet, the wet. Wherever, upon the employment of a word in any manner whatsoever, that which is intended to be expressed is indicated in accordance with the indicated meaning, that is *vivakṣitalakṣaṇā* (indication of the intended). For example: "The half-eye, the victorious chariot of the mind-born [Cupid]"; "The third part of the eye, captivating like a startled doe."

Thus [it is said]. Here, the meaning is not that of the word *ardha* (half) or the word *tribhāga* (one-third); rather, by those two words, incomplete vision is indicated (*lakṣyate*). For it does not occur that "one-fourth of the eye" or "one-sixth of the eye" [is meant]. When a word, either in isolation or in proximity to another, indicates a meaning that is contrary to what was directly expressed, that is *viruddhalakṣaṇā* (indication of the contrary). For example: "The seat is auspicious," "Mars is Mangala," and "I am meritorious, since you, my husband, are such as this."

In this context, the words *bhadrā* (auspicious) and *maṅgala* (mangala), as well as the word *puṇya* (meritorious), indicate by means of indication (*lakṣaṇā*) precisely the lack of auspiciousness and the lack of merit (*apuṇyatva*). Or, for example, in the *Ratnāvalī*, the King says to Vidūṣaka: "You are a great Brahmin; who else is so conversant with the *ṛcs*? Here, by the term "great Brahmin" and by the phrase "conversant with the *ṛcs*," his status as lower even than a *vṛṣala* (outcaste) and his stupidity (*vaidheyatva*) are indicated. And likewise, in the *Mālatīmādhava*, Lavaṅgikā addresses Madayantikā.

"How indeed will my dear friend endure, having approached her husband—who is skilled in the means of winning the confidence of a new bride, who speaks with sweet and charming words, and who is free from anger—after [you have acted] thus? Here, the qualities such as being "skilled in the means of winning the confidence of a new bride" suggest a meaning contrary to that literal sense. Similarly, there are others as well, for example: "O friend, this fresh nail-mark upon the slope of your breast, which has not yet faded—let it be covered by your upper garment."

The women of Utsanna, though angry, yet gracious; though weeping, yet smiling—just as they were seized, they steal the hearts of men. "We are indeed such as you say. What can I say? For suddenly, in the midst of conversation, I am overwhelmed. How could the women of noble families be so pure and innocent as to take on the form of a *kadamba* bud? In these verses, by the word *amlāna-māna* ("unfading pride"), the breaking of pride (*mānabhaṅga*) is indicated; by the word *utsanna* ("fallen" or "ruined"), a blessing for non-extinction (*anucchedāśīḥ*) is indicated; and by the word *viśuddha-mugdha* ("pure and innocent"), the absence of impurity and lack of innocence (*aviśuddhi-amaugdhya*) are indicated.

That [type of indication] in which another meaning is indicated by setting aside the literal meaning of the words used is *tadanyalakṣaṇā* (indication other than that). For example: "Three types of men gather golden flowers: the brave, the learned, and he who knows how to serve. Here, neither the literal meaning of the word "gold" (*suvarṇa*) nor the literal meaning of the word "flower" (*puṣpa*) is intended; rather, by the word "gold," gold as the root of all human goals is indicated, and by the word "flower," the sense of "fruit" or "attainment" is indicated.

And when those two [names] are observed, it indicates that the earth (*vasumatī*) has produced all the desired objects for those distinguished men who are industrious. Any other [name] than those mentioned is of miscellaneous characteristics (*prakīrṇalakṣaṇā*). For example: "The wise know him whose splendor is like ten hundred rays, who is heard of in fame throughout the ten directions, who possesses ten chariots as his predecessors, and who is the preceptor of the enemy of the Ten-Necked One (Rāvaṇa). They call him Hiraṇyakaśipu; having abandoned the water like a lotus stalk, he blossomed forth from the fire of the breath of the beloved of the horse (Hayagrīva). Thus [it is said].

Others, however, explain *lakṣitalakṣaṇā* differently: where another meaning is indicated by means of a secondary application (*upacaritavṛtti*), that is to say, through a figurative function (*gauṇī*) based on the expressed meaning, it is called *lakṣitalakṣaṇā*. For example, in the cases of *rathāvayavāyudhaḥ*, *paṅktirathaḥ*, and *rathāṅganāmā*, the word *rathāvayava* (chariot-part) indicates the number ten; and through those two [words], because of the proximity to the word "weapon" (*āyudha*), the specific deity and king known as Cakrāyudha and Dalāratha are indicated.

By the term *rathāṅga* (chariot-part), a single part of a chariot is indicated, by which the word *cakra* (wheel) is meant. By the word *nāma* (name), the act of naming is the indicated meaning. Through the mutual proximity of these two, the specific bird called *cakranāka* is indicated. Furthermore, this usage is frequently found in literary compositions. For example: "By the upward-moving wind, which was scattering the pollen of the *sūrpa* flowers, he was seen even from a distance, though he had been living in a single village."

In this case, the entry of a pestle through a needle-hole is impossible; however, by the fact that people do indeed perform even such a feat, it is indicated that the speaker has uttered something seemingly impossible. For example: "Kissing is done a hundred times, pushing away a thousand times; one plays and then stops again—there is no repetition in the company of a beloved. Here, although the word *punarukta* (repetition) is semantically meaningful, its power is restricted to a specific usage; it indicates the general concept of performing an action again.

[The author] defines [this] for the sake of distinguishing it from its opposite (*vipakṣin*): "In this way, the nights, like you, O Queen, though harsh toward the new moon, steal away the pride of the deer-marked one, just as blue [clouds] [steal the light]. Here, the words *matta* ("intoxicated") and *nirahaṅkāra* ("devoid of pride"), while signifying the state of being "mountain-like" (*anibhṛtatva*), are employed in reference to non-sentient things; being already conventional (*rūḍha*) in their application to sentient beings, they indicate that those [non-sentient things] also possess such a quality. Furthermore: "The sweetness of the cheeks is one thing, and the luster of the growth of the limbs is quite another."

"In the phrase *sāmāsāmaṇṇavaā paissarehañcihaṇahoi*, the word *rekhā* (line) indicates *citrālekhyam* (painted drawing), and not the creation of a specific form. Furthermore, in the phrase *agaṇia naaṇāāsā māliṣuloijjatajaṃkatako hosi maaṇassa*, by the expression *ko bhavasi madanasya* (who are you to Madana?), his being a kinsman (*sanābhitvam*) is indicated; and through that, a comparison with him is established."

Thus, the lower lip of the slender-limbed maiden receives the transformation of an ashoka bud; her cheek, through its paleness, descends into the state of a palmyra leaf; and her gaze, nearly withered, imitates the lotus. Thus triumphs the passion of love! Here, by means of the attributes of sentient beings—namely, "receiving," "descending," and "imitating"—applied to insentient objects, the states of "holding," "attaining," and "following" are indicated. Through the transformation of the ashoka bud, her sighing and pallor are suggested.

Because of its proximity to that [lotus], it bears a resemblance to an *aśoka* sprout; thus, through the withering of the palm leaf and the fading of the lotus stalk, the intensity of her separation is revealed, and by that, the excess of her affection. In this way, the bed of lotus leaves speaks of the torment of the slender-limbed woman: having failed to reach the center of her waist—which was green from being pressed on both sides by her full breasts and hips—it has become withered. It tells of her distress through the tossing and turning of her slackened vine-like arms as she shifts her position.

In this context, by the phrase "he speaks," it is indicated through metaphorical function (*upacāra-vṛtti*) that he makes known; and by such qualities as "faded" and so forth, the excellence of the beauty of its form and arrangement is implied. Furthermore: "The lotus is the discarded offering (*nirmālya*) of the eye’s splendor, the moon is the servant of the face, and the bow-staff of Kandarpa—what more need be said? It is held at the gateway of the eyebrows. Here, by the words "discarded offering" and "servant," which imply inferiority through metaphorical function, the excellence of the eyes and the face is implied.

Moreover, by the very indication that the entrance of the bow-creeper of Kandarpa has been withdrawn, he speaks all the more clearly of their own deficiency: "The face is as pale as the ripening of a palm leaf; the eyes are overcast like a rainy day; and the breaths rush forth like dancing lotus petals."

In this context, regarding the phrase "a storm for the eyes," the word *durdina*—which has acquired its conventional denotation through its application to a day whose beauty is struck by clouds raining hundreds of times—indicates a torrent of water that is invariably concomitant with its own literal meaning; since such a torrent is impossible for the eyes, it thereby indicates a torrent of tears. Furthermore: "Times when happiness has passed are present; days are perpetually more wretched; the earth has lost its youth. (In this verse, there are alternative readings: *śvaśśvaḥpā* and *pṛthivī*).

If it is argued that this is because [the quality] has transcended pleasure, then by means of mental attributes superimposed upon non-conscious entities such as time and so forth—which are impossible in those [entities] themselves—the life-breaths (*prāṇa*) and other qualities residing therein and inseparable from them are indicated. Thus, there is "disgust with the self" (*ātmanirveda*). Furthermore: "This entire triple world would become blinding darkness; like a mirror blinded by its own breath, the moon does not shine."

In this context, just as the manifestation of specific forms is not possible for one who is blind, so too in darkness where the manifestation of specific forms is impossible due to its density, that is called "pitch black" (*andhatamas*). Likewise, just as a blind person is incapable of perceiving form, so too is a mirror. One who is incapable of perceiving form is called "blind. In that case, according to a figurative application (*upacarita-vṛtti*), he who does not see like a blind person is himself called "blind."

In this context, even where nothing is actually seen, the word "blind" (*andha*) is applied there as well through a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) characterized by its conventional usage. Similarly, other cases may occur; for instance, even with very little liquid, wood is not burned [by it]. [As in the verse: "Friend, you too are being soothed by a mere drop of sandalwood juice. Here, in the former case, the literal meaning of the word *atha* is possible regarding the subject to be described; it indicates that just as Vikramāditya was, so too is this person a distinguished great soul.

By means of these very few words, one perceives the gravity of the majesty and other qualities of both [the speaker and the listener], which otherwise could not be expressed. However, later on, that same meaning is conveyed through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by way of inversion; thus, this infinite operation of "indication of the indicated" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*) is to be observed in literary compositions (*prabandha*). For example: "One day, two days, three days, not Bhadrapada; the month of Mādhava, the great lady, the path... the beginning of the spring. "In the limbs, the house, the good gait, the *ḍiḍḍat* [?]—in the salt-ocean, the path, the mountain, the head...
