The dust, rising from the mountain and reaching the sky, momentarily blinded the eyes of the Yadava forces; it was as if the mountain itself had risen up. It was soiled by a mass of frost, making the eyelashes of the womenfolk appear doubly thick. Regarding words, their application to objects consists of denotation (*abhidhāna*), giving (*dāna*), intention (*abhiprāya*), and the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*). As it has been said: "The employment of words is preceded by the speaker's desire to speak. Indeed, speech is threefold: non-human (*apauruṣeya*), inspired (*ārṣa*), and human (*pauruṣeya*).

Among these, that which is primarily concerned with sound (*śabda-pradhāna*) and is of non-human origin consists of the *mantras* and the *brāhmaṇas*. Because there is no speaker therein, the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) is not applicable. That which is primarily concerned with meaning (*artha-pradhāna*) consists of the *ārṣa*, the *smṛti*, and the *itihāsa*. In those cases, it proceeds merely according to the intention to speak; for while the speech of ordinary people or even of the virtuous follows the [conventional] word, the meaning follows the speech of the primordial seers (*ṛṣis*). (There is an alternative reading: “*dhāvati*”. Thus it is said.

Both the primary [cause] (*pradhāna*) and that which pertains to the person (*pauruṣeya*) arise from specific intentions for those whose intellects are attached to them. For example, grammatical factors (*kāraka*) arise from intention: one says *akṣān dīvyati* (he plays with the dice), *akṣair dīvyati* (he plays with the dice), or *akṣeṣu dīvyati* (he plays upon the dice); likewise, one says *valāhako vidyotate* (the cloud flashes) or *valāhakasya vidyotate* (it flashes from the cloud). Because the collection of all things, consisting of mere potencies and possessing manifold properties, does not exist at all times or in every way, something is intended to be expressed in some particular manner in some particular place.

Even regarding factors of action (*kāraka*), there is the intention to express them as non-factors (*akāraka*). For example: *mātuḥ smarati* ("he remembers his mother"), *sarpiṣo jānīte* ("he knows [the use of] ghee"), and *na māṣāṇām aśnīyāt* ("one should not eat beans"). Also: *naite sukhasya jānanti yena vatsyanti nandane* ("these do not know happiness by which they will dwell in the Nandana grove"). Here, when the objects and other factors are intended to be expressed as residual relations (*śeṣa*), the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used for the mere relation; thus, even in the cases of object, instrument, and agent, it is not a case-ending expressing a factor of action. Regarding non-factors, there is the intention to express them as factors, as in: *bhavati pacati*, *bhavati pakṣyati*, *bhavaty apākṣīt*.

"Let us go," [he says]. Likewise: "Do you remember? We shall dwell in Kaśmīra. "Come, I think you will not go. "Look, the deer runs. "Let us look here. Thus, dual and plural forms are cited even for the object (*karman*). Furthermore, there is the desire to express a factor of action (*kāraka*) even with respect to an action (*kriyā*), as in: "It pains the thief" (*corasya rujati*), "He causes the thief to suffer" (*corasya armayati*), "It burns the thief" (*coraṃ jvayati*), or "He torments the thief" (*coraṃ saṃtāpayati*).

In this context, regarding verbs meaning "to cause pain" (*rujārtha*), as in: *corasya rujati* (he causes pain to the thief), *corasyāmayati* (he makes the thief ill), *coraṃ jvarayati* (he fevers the thief), or *tac-coraṃ santāpayati* (he torments that thief). Here, for verbs meaning "to cause pain" that express a state (*bhāvavacana*), according to the rule *aḍaḍḍatdhjvarisantāpyoḥ*, the state itself functions as the agent. An instance where an action is intended to be expressed despite there being no actual activity is: *nīlati vanam* (the forest turns blue) or *śvetate prāsādaḥ* (the palace becomes white). Also: *viṣavṛkṣo 'pi saṃvardhya svayaṃ chettum asāmpratam* (Even a poisonous tree, having been nurtured, is not fit to be cut down by oneself).

The desire for another action within an action is seen, for example, in *aisitum icchati* ("he wishes to wish"), *kamitum kāmayate* ("he desires to love"), *bhaved api bhavet* ("might he perhaps be"), and *sāyad api syāt* ("perhaps it might be"). Likewise, the desire for an action is expressed even with respect to a *kāraka* (participant in an action), as in *draṣṭuṃ cakṣuḥ* ("the eye for seeing"), *yoddhuṃ dhṛṣṇuḥ* ("bold for fighting"), and *gantumanāḥ gantukāmaḥ* ("intent on going, desirous of going"). In these cases, the suffix *tumun* is prescribed when an action is intended as the purpose of another action; this would not be established without the intention of an action on the part of the eyes and so forth.

The desire to express a relationship where no relationship exists is, for example: "He saw the clouds drinking the waters from a single region of the ocean—those waters which, roaring incessantly, will inundate the entire earth. The desire to express sentience in insentient things is, for example: "The riverbank wishes to fall," or "The stone desires to split the mountain. The desire to express insentience in sentient beings is, for example: "The horse-rider wishes to fall. The desire to express a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) when the primary subject (*pradhāna*) is intended is, for example: "the whiteness of the crane" or "the blackness of the crow."

The intention to express the subordinate as primary is, for example, "the sweet taste nourishes" or "the sour [taste] stimulates digestion. The intention to express the whole when referring to a part is, for example, "the village is burnt," "the cloth is burnt," "blind in one eye," or "lame in one foot."

The intention to express a part within a whole is as follows: when the bow, which is capable of bearing the fierce weight of his staff-like arms, was present, Lakṣmaṇa said to the noble lord, "May your ladyship consider even me, this Vikukṣi by name, to be among the foremost servants of that very deity whose name is auspiciously invoked. The intention to express difference within non-difference is as follows: "You were eloquent; you were clever; this one is even more clever"; or "he was quite another person"; or "the head of Rāhu," or "the body of the stone-statue."

The intention to express non-difference despite actual difference is, for example: "We eat those very same rice-grains that are in Madhurā; we wear those very same garments that are in Pāṭaliputra. The intention to express what is non-existent is, for example: "The ocean is a water-pot; the Vindhya mountains are a mustard seed. The non-intention to express what is existent is, for example: "The girl is waistless" (meaning she has a slender waist); "the ewe is hairless" (meaning she has very fine wool). The intention to express both the existent and the non-existent is, for example: "This year is a non-rainy year"; "death with breath remaining."

The non-intention of expressing either existence or non-existence is, for example: "The daughter of the mountain-king neither went nor stayed. The intention of expressing censure through praise is, for example: "It is solely due to the wickedness of his virtues that the leader is yoked to the burden; the Gaur-gali bull, whose shoulders have not yet developed calluses, sleeps soundly. The intention of expressing praise through censure is, for example: "That person is fickle and merciless; what does he matter to me, my friend?"

By whom flatteries have been learned solely for the purpose of wiping away offenses. An example of an injunction intended through a prohibition (*niṣedha-vivakṣā*): "Go, my dear, if you must go; may your paths be auspicious. May my birth also occur in that very place where you have gone. An example of a prohibition intended through an injunction (*niṣedha-vivakṣā*): "Do not come, O lover of women! You have already been told so by me many times with hundreds of endearments. Yet, by your arrival at the courtyard, this young girl has reached a state beyond [endurance]."

Moreover, because her breasts press so heavily, our house is daily deprived of its threads as the seams of her bodice burst despite her most strenuous efforts. Thus, this intention of hers spreads out in manifold ways; such is the worldly proverb: "In this shoreless ocean of poetry, the poet alone is the creator of the world. As it pleases him, so does the universe transform. (Alternatively, following another reading: "In this shoreless world... In this shoreless world, the poet is the sole sovereign; as it pleases him, so does this universe revolve.

Moreover, what is stable appears unstable, and even that which is stable appears as if it were falling; likewise, what is well-composed is censured by poets—these are the ways of poets. Furthermore: sometimes there is composition with abundant words even for a very small meaning; sometimes the subject matter is radiant with only a few words. Or, just as words placed on a scale may be equalized by three syllables alone, such is the rule of composition for the bull among poets.

In both worldly discourse and poetic discourse, the intention (*vivakṣā*)—as inferred by the wise—is understood to be threefold: that which is suggested by intonation (*kāku*) and so forth, that which is suggested by context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth, and that which is suggested by dramatic gesture (*abhinaya*) and so forth. Among these, *kāku* refers to a change in tone or a break in the voice; thus, "intonation" (*kāku*) and its like are defined. Among those, it is designated as *kāku* by the learned because it is a sound produced from a modified throat. It is threefold: with a fixed connection, with an unfixed connection, and without connection.

Among those, the *niyatapratibandha* (restricted connection) is of two kinds: *sākāṅkṣā* (expectant) and *nirākāṅkṣā* (non-expectant). Of these two, that which requires another sentence is *sākāṅkṣā*. It is threefold: containing an implication (*ākṣepagarbhā*), containing a question (*praśnagarbhā*), and containing a deliberation (*vitarkagarbhā*). That which occurs within a single sentence is *nirākāṅkṣā*. That too is threefold: positive (*vidhirūpā*), negative (*uttararūpā*), and conclusive (*nirṇayarūpā*). Indeed, the same sentence may be expectant through one particular intonation (*kāku*) and non-expectant through another intonation.

Among these, an example of the *ākṣepagarbhā* (pregnant with an implied objection) is as follows: "If she is dear to me as a messenger, then I too am dear to her; if her words are pleasing to him, then they are also pleasing to my beloved. This very same [verse] is an example of the *nirdiṣṭa-vidhirūpā* (stated in the form of a positive injunction). An example of the *praśnagarbhā* (pregnant with a question) is as follows: "Gone is that time when pearls were born from the creepers of living beings; nowadays, their causes—the oyster shells—merely exist [as their source]."

This very [verse] is the *uttara-rūpa* (the form of a reply) for the instructor: "This is a cloud, not a bold night-stalker; this is a bow drawn far back, not his [Rāvaṇa’s] bow. This too is a sharp downpour of rain, not a succession of arrows; this lightning, glistening like gold on a touchstone, is my beloved, not Urvaśī. This very [verse] is the *nirbhaya-rūpa* (the fearless form) for the instructor. In the same way, there are others as well: "O Lord of all kings, such a woman, beautiful in every limb, has been seen by me in this lovely forest, yet she is separated from you."

These and others are to be understood in this manner. These three types of reasons possess a necessary connection (*niyatapratibandha*); however, those with an uncertain connection (*aniyatapratibandha*) are infinite. Among these, an example of *abhyupagama-anunaya-kāku* (persuasion through the intonation of an admission) is as follows: "By me, who am indeed submerged in the sin of transgressing your command, even among those of noble standing who have attained freedom from reproach, I remain [only] as a younger brother. Today, as I destroy the Kauravas with a mace reddened by blood tossed up in fury, for a single day you are no longer my elder, nor am I subject to your will."

An example of a gesture of derision (*kākuryathā*) through permission (*abhyanujñā*) is as follows: "Shall I not, out of anger, crush a hundred Kauravas in battle? Shall I not drink the blood from Duhshasana’s chest? Shall I not shatter Suyodhana’s thighs with my mace? Let the king settle this by means of a wager for you all. An example of a gesture of derision (*kākuryathā*) through the offering of poisoned food (*viṣānnādya*) is as follows: "Having struck at our lives and our accumulated wealth through the fire of the lacquer house, the poisoned food, and the entry into the assembly hall..."

"Having seized the hair of the wives of the Pāṇḍavas as they were being stripped of their garments, let the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra remain at ease while I yet live! Other such [examples] are also to be seen; for instance, even a poisoned arrow with flashing teeth might be endured by the steadfast, but not the false and wicked speech of a villain provoked without cause. The *apratibandhā* (uninterrupted) [metaphor], however, is of one, two, or three qualities.

Among these, examples of those with a single attribute (*ekaguṇā*) are as follows: "A frown was drawn, the gaze was turned away, and then the face was withdrawn; or else, something unkind was said. Yet even so, this lordship is exercised by force, for a person who is not angry acts as if he were angry. Examples of those with two attributes (*dviguṇā*) are as follows: "What did the hunter do by drawing his arrows? And what does the hunter do by drawing his arrows? (The answer is: nothing at all).

"Three qualities [of delusion]: 'She sees thus; it is not the doe's frightened glance; this is her hand, not a leaf trembling in the wind; she weeps loudly, yet this is not a flute being blown by the breeze; this is my beloved speaking to me, not the warbling of a cuckoo. Furthermore, regarding the four qualities [of delusion], let it be said: "O friend, tell her the whole of what must be said; she is a virtuous woman, not a master over a man."

"Bring him here after conciliating him; or else, how could he be followed while causing you displeasure? What is the use of going? It is not right to approach him. O beloved one who considers yourself so fortunate, what is this pride?"—in such conversations among women, lovers assumed a resolve rich in manifold sentiments. Here, the *kāku* (intonation) resides in the speech of either the female friend or the heroine, or in the speech of the friend and the hero, or even in the speech of many friends. In this manner, other instances such as "Who am I? and so forth are also to be understood.

The vowels include the *pluta* (protracted) and others; the accents include the *udātta* (acute) and others; and there are the *pragṛhya* (non-sandhi) vowels and so forth. Among these, regarding the *pluta* and others, as in the verse: "O passionate one, your anger has been cast aside by the sight of me bowing before you; please be gracious now. You have abandoned eating, you have given up talk with women, and fragrant garlands, perfumes, incense, and the like have been avoided from afar. O beloved, when you look upon me thus humbled, release your wrath; for because of your absence, all the directions have become blind to me. In this example, the *pluta* vowel is used to express the intensity of the emotion. Furthermore, the *udātta* and other accents are employed to convey specific nuances of meaning within the poetic expression. The *pragṛhya* vowels prevent the application of sandhi rules to maintain the integrity of certain words. Thus, these phonetic elements serve to enhance the aesthetic and emotional impact of the composition.

This very sentence, though primarily intended to appease one’s most beloved, becomes instead intent on appeasing an angry glance due to the *pluta* (protracted) accent on the vocative particle *dṛṣṭe*. By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), short, long, and nasalized vowels are comprised. For in those cases, a difference in meaning arises from the use of a short vowel, as in the address "aśva-vat," which is understood as a form of address; or a difference in meaning arises from the use of a long vowel, as in "viśvāmitraḥ" and "viśvānaraḥ," where they are understood respectively as a sage and a proper name.

A difference in meaning arises from the nasalization (*anunāsika*), as for example in *gambhīrā apaḥ*; because of the rule *āṅo 'nunāsikaś chandasi*, the sense of "slightly" (*īṣat*) is understood, not "a pillar" (*sthāṇuḥ*). Regarding the vowel length (*dīrgha*), as in *yathājñātam*: "That Jaṭāyu, afflicted by old age, desires death among these [trees]. Regarding the accents such as the acute (*udātta*), as in *kalaravaḥ* (meaning "one whose sound is sweet") and *ekaputraḥ* (meaning "one who has one son"). In a compound, the accent of a *bahuvrīhi* occurs, and that is the acute accent on the final syllable of the first member.

In the compound *kalaśca asau ravaśca* (that sound which is black) and *ekaśca asau putraśca* (that son who is one), the accent of the *karmadhāraya* [compound] occurs. And by the rule *sa ca samāsasya*, the end of the compound becomes udātta. Through these two, the meaning of the other word (*anyapadārtha*) and the meaning of the final member (*uttarapadārtha*) are understood. As it has been said: "Regarding an action that possesses a similar form for two compounds whose results are vastly different, those learned in the science of grammar determined the analysis (*vigraha*) of the two compounds by means of the accent."

By the inclusion of the term "etc. (*ādi*), the *an-udātta*, *svarita*, and *ekaśruti* accents are comprised. Among these, the difference in meaning resulting from the *anudātta* is as follows: in the two previously mentioned examples, the meaning of the external compound member (*anyapadārtha*) is understood, and not the meaning of the final member (*uttarapadārtha*). The difference in meaning resulting from the *svarita* is as follows: in the case of *bhrātṛvya* (with *svarita* on the first syllable) versus *bhrātr-vya* (with *anudātta* on the first syllable), the meaning "offspring of a brother" is understood as the external compound member, and not "rival" (*sapatna*). The difference in meaning resulting from the *ekaśruti* is as follows: "Come, O boy Devadatta! (*āgaccha bho māṇavaka devadattā*).

"Agni is the head of heaven, the summit, the lord of this earth; he quickens the seeds of the waters... [The mantra] "putraika" [is cited]. Just as in the case of "āśruteḥ," when there is a distant invocation in a sacrifice, [the word] is joined [with the following vowel]. Its accent also, by virtue of occupying that position, is called *pragṛhya*. Consequently, there is a difference in meaning: for instance, in the phrase "alīka āgacchāmi tām itaḥ," the sense understood from the two female friends is "one must come here."

It is not [the case] for adventitious [words], because of the mention of *piṅktarasmarāt*; by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), those that are euphonically combined (*sandheya*), contracted (*saṃvṛta*), and augmented (*vṛddha*) are included. Among these, an example of a difference in meaning due to euphonic combination (*sandheya*) is "Aṅgirasaḥ. A pause (*viccheda*) is threefold: the pause between words (*padaviccheda*). Among these, an example of a "chain" (*śṛṅkhalā*) is: "kāntāratarutalāsitamṛgayuvaracitāntarāharatyaṭavī. Here, when the word-division is *kāntārāḥ*, *tarutalaḥ*, *āntarāḥ*, it means "in the midst of a forest filled with hunters who were delighted by the amorous cries of their beloveds."

This is like a chain (śṛṅkhalā) because of its mutual interlocking. As for *bhaṅga* (breakage), it occurs when a sentence is split [in two] for the purpose of censure; this is *bhaṅga* as the bifurcation of words (*padadvaidhībhāva*). For example, in the case of *parivartaka*, the phrase “the censuring of the bee-like buds” (*kalikāmadhugarhaṇā*) is split exactly as it stands, yet the understanding of the meaning arises as “the flow of nectar from the buds” (*kuṭamalakarandaniṣyanda*). However, when it is read as *kalikāmadhuk-arhaṇā*, then it means “worship indeed,” as in “the wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmadhenu*) in the Kali age. This is *parivartaka* because of the transposition of the letters *ga* and *ka*.

"Observe the powder-like [foam] of the ocean's water, from which oysters and fish have long since departed"—the meaning is: "Behold the water of the ocean, which is dear to the fish. However, when it is read as *dūrasam-unmukta-śukti-mīnāṅkāntam*, then it means: "Behold the water that is difficult to taste (*duḥkha-rasanīyam*), from which the receptacles of pearls have been vomited out (*udvānta-mauktika-ādhāram*), and whose boundaries are marked by fish. This is called *cūrṇaka* because of the "powdering" (*cūrṇa*) of the conjunct consonant *kṣ* in *akṣa* (oyster) and the letter *r* in *dūrasam*.

The interruption of a sentence (*vākyaviccheda*) is also fourfold: *vākyasambheda*, *vākyāsambheda*, *vākyāsambheda*, *vākyānyathātva*, and *vākyāsamāpti*, as well as *vākyānuccāraṇa*. Among these, *vākyasambheda* (the breaking off of a sentence) is as follows: "The earth, with its four boundaries divided by the herds of elephants of the quarters, is being won; even while we are merely speaking of it as already won, look, our hair stands on end! What more can be said? Salutations to that Rāma!"

"Since this wonderful story appeared [here], and right here it has come to its end; even as we speak of this, our hair stands on end—look! This exclamation of the sentence demonstrates the speaker’s excellence in discerning specific qualities through his capacity for evoking aesthetic emotion (*bhāvakatva*). An example of the deviation of the sentence (*vākyānyathātva*) is as follows: "Together with his host of servants, his kinsmen, his friends, his army, and his followers, the son of Pāṇḍu will before long slay Suyodhana in battle by his own strength."

In this context, where it ought to have been said "Suyodhana [said] to the son of Pāṇḍu," the statement "the son of Pāṇḍu [said] to Suyodhana" indicates that the words of Suyodhana—uttered while distressed by separation from Bhānumatī—were otherwise than they appeared, thereby making known the truth of what was yet to come. An example of the non-completion of a sentence (vākyāsamāpti) is as follows: "You are my life; you are my second heart; you are the moonlight to my eyes; you are nectar to my limbs."

"By means of hundreds of such endearments, having won over that simple girl—be silent, or rather, what is the use of more? Here, the phrase "be silent, or rather, what is the use of more" indicates that Vāsantī’s speech remains unfinished, conveying the principle that one should not utter inauspicious words regarding a friend. An example of the non-utterance of a sentence is as follows: "The glances of [Arjuna], whose intense anger was aroused by the slaughter of Abhimanyu at the hands of the enemy of the Kṣatriyas, fall upon his bow, drenched with teardrops and paralyzed by shame."

As Pārtha, unable to retaliate against his enemy and bewildered by inner grief, utters the words "Alas, my son! they quiver in his throat but do not emerge from it. Here, the failure to utter the phrase "Alas, my son! indicates that such lamentation is unbecoming of great souls who have failed to take revenge upon their foe. *Virāma* is the pause (*yati*). It is fourfold: at the word, at the foot of the verse, at the half-verse, and at the appropriate place. The violation of this is known as *yativiccheda*.

In that verse: "Wealth is as flickering as waves upon the water; youth lasts but three or four days; life is as transient as an autumn cloud—what is the use of riches? Perform deeds for the benefit of others" (or with the reading *tanudhvaṃ*). Here, in the word *kiṃ dhanaiḥ* ("what is the use of riches"), a righteous meaning is perceived. However, when [the line] is read as *ājñāsiddhāni catvāri na* ("the four [goals] are not accomplished by command"), having transgressed the metrical foot, then it is unrighteous (*anyāyya*).

"Tell me the rest of what is to be said in the first half [of the verse]; O friend, harshness toward the Lord is not proper. Bring him back after conciliating him; or rather, how can one who produces unpleasantness be brought back? In this case, when there is a pause (*yati*) at the middle of the line, it is understood that this is the speech of only one person, and thus another meaning is perceived. However, when the pause is made at the end of each quarter-verse (*pāda*) instead of breaking the middle, then it is understood that this is the speech of two, many, or even one person.

May that Mādhava—who, in a fitting manner, formerly transformed the body of the conqueror of Bala into a woman by means of his power over the mind; who, the destroyer of Andhaka, assumed the form of a peacock; and whose praiseworthy name the immortals call "Hara" because he bears the moon upon his head—protect you, he who always wears serpents as necklaces, bracelets, and earrings.

In this regard, among these twelve syllables, there is a point of caesura; by transgressing that [fixed] position, when the caesura is applied in the phrases *balijitkāyaḥ* and *śaśimacchiroharaḥ*, the respective meanings "Umā’s husband" and "Mādhava" are understood in succession. Context (*prakaraṇa*), meaning (*artha*), indicative mark (*liṅga*), propriety (*aucitya*), place (*deśa*), and time (*kāla*)—these are the factors beginning with context.

In this regard, based on context (*prakaraṇa*) and so forth: for example, the word *saindhava*, which generally applies to salt, a horse, and a person, becomes the cause for the comprehension of a specific meaning through the influence of a context such as eating. In the phrase "the god rains," the word "god" (*deva*) by implication denotes the cloud; in "Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa," the word "Rāma" refers to the son of Daśaratha due to the presence of Lakṣmaṇa; and in "the lady with the lotus-face," the word "lotus" (*puṇḍarīka*) denotes a water-lily (*kamala*) due to propriety (*aucitya*).

In Amarāvatī, the word *hari* denotes Indra by virtue of place; at night, one sees a *pataṅga*, here the word *pataṅga* signifies a moth by virtue of time. Other examples are likewise found. For instance: "Let it be known that words indicate the speaker's intended meaning. And so it is remembered: when a lover forcibly embraces his beloved, her words—"Nanana! Mama! Māmāmā! Do not touch me!"—are utterances intent on prohibition once the knot of pride has loosened, yet those very same words become prescriptive [of the act].

Thus: *Abhinaya* (gesticulation), *apadeśa* (pretext), *nirdeśa* (direct statement), *saṃjñā* (sign), *iṅgita* (hint), and *ākāra* (expression)—these are the types of *abhinaya* and so forth. Among these, *abhinaya* is as follows: "She has breasts of such a size, eyes of such a length, and a state [of pregnancy] of such a degree, in just so many days. *Apadeśa* is as follows: "That Daitya has attained prosperity; he does not deserve ruin from this [source]. Even a poison-tree, having been nurtured by oneself, is unfit to be cut down by one's own hand."

*Direct statement* (*nirdeśa*) is as follows: "By good fortune we are prospering, since here someone is staying for someone else," thus they informed me by the playful movement of their fingers. *Symbolic indication* (*saṃjñā*) is as follows: Although the matter was unreal, for the sake of initiating a conversation, Pārvatī—seeing that the Destroyer of Smara (Śiva) was intent on questioning her—accepted his gaze and gave an answer consisting of a nod of her head. *Gesture* (*iṅgita*) is as follows: Perceiving that her lover was unable to speak because the place was crowded when she asked, "When will our union take place?", the frail woman closed her play-lotus.

The outward appearance is as previously described by her warm sighs, yet my mind plunges into doubt alone. Is it not the case that what you desire to seek will surely exist, though it may be difficult to obtain once sought? So it is with others as well; for instance, when the heart has first been won, and then the offering of the lower lip, and then the stake in the game of dice—when the beloved asks his lover again about his beloved woman.

With cheeks quivering from the bursting forth of the rasa accumulated and restrained by suppressed laughter, her hand—filled with perspiration—is placed silently to ward off the gaze of the spectators. The intended meaning is that whatever word is beyond [the literal] is the "meaning of the word" (śabdārtha). And this is possible only in a sentence, because an intention cannot be manifested by a single word alone. Furthermore, that reality conveyed by the sentence is threefold: the expressed (abhidhīyamāna), the implied (pratīyamāna), and the nature of suggestion (dhvanirūpa).

That which is denoted (*abhidhīyamāna*) is that wherein, when words have been employed, their own respective meanings have been expressed through the powers of words—namely, the primary (*mukhya*), secondary (*gauṇī*), and indicative (*lakṣaṇā*)—and their operations have ceased, only the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is expressed by means of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and compatibility (*yogyatā*). That which is suggested (*pratīyamāna*) is that which, subsequent to the comprehension of the sentence-meaning—as in the case of the sentence "The cow goes"—is conveyed by the sentence-meaning itself, aided by factors such as the context (*artha*), the topic (*prakaraṇa*), and the disposition (*aucitya*), whether that [meaning] is logically consistent (*upapadyamāna*) or inconsistent (*anupapadyamāna*) with it.

For example, when it is said, "Eat poison, but do not eat in his house," it is understood that eating poison is preferable to eating in his house. Because the word *artha* (meaning) is employed as a means, it subordinates all other meanings; immediately following the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, it manifests itself either in the form of a resonance (*anuraṇana*) or in the form of a non-verbal [impression]. This is what constitutes *dhvani*. Furthermore, this is not universal.

For instance, just as when a sound has ceased, an after-sound (*anunāda*) arises from certain substances such as bronze, or an echo (*pratiśabda*) from certain places such as mountain caves; and just as, immediately following the comprehension of the expressed meaning of a certain sentence, a resonance (*dhvani*) is perceived—whereby, when it is said "this one blinks," the blinking of the eyes is expressed, while it is understood that she is not a goddess, and an excellence of form is resonating.

Now, regarding their application, that which is being stated therein is fourfold: positive in form, negative in form, both positive and negative in form, and neither positive nor negative in form. Among these, an example of the positive form is: "One should extract the essence from what is essenceless: generosity from wealth, truthfulness from speech, fame and merit from life, and service to others from the body. An example of the negative form is: "One should not dwell with one in whom these are not found: worldly conduct, fear of censure, modesty, courtesy, and a virtuous character."

In the form of a positive injunction and a negative prohibition, as for example: "O King of kings, women are common property to all, like cooked food; therefore, one should neither feel anger toward them, nor passion for them, yet one may enjoy them. In the form of neither injunction nor prohibition, as for example: "Neither by gifts, nor by honor, nor by guile, nor by service, nor by sacred scripture are they won over; in every way, what indeed can be done with women? The implied meaning (*pratīyamāna*), moreover, is manifold. In some cases, there is a prohibition within an injunction, as in: "O pious man, beware! That dog has been killed by him today."

"By the fierce lion dwelling in the thickets on the banks of the Golā river... Here, in the injunction "wander with confidence," the prohibition is understood: "A lion stays in that bower; you are afraid even of a dog; therefore, you must not go there. In some cases, an injunction is implied within a prohibition, as in: "She is immersing herself in water there; look here for me during the day. O heartless one, blinded by passion, do not immerse yourself in my bed at night!"

In this prohibitive statement, "Do not stay on this bed," there is understood an injunction: "This is my mother-in-law’s bed, this is my bed; you should come here at night after having observed [the distinction] during the day. Sometimes, within one injunction, another injunction is implied, as in: "O woman with thick, dark hair, tonight the husband has gone abroad and the house is empty; therefore, O friend, close the door so that we may not be robbed."

In this context, when there is a statement of an injunction such as "Be vigilant so that we do not suffer loss," another injunction is implied: "The night is pitch black, the husband has gone abroad, and the house is empty; therefore, come to my side without fear. Sometimes, within a prohibition, another prohibition is implied, as in: "Only as much as is necessary for the sake of the body should be bound by a waist-cloth; O son of a virtuous woman, desist from further [tightening], lest your hips be deformed."

In this instance, within a prohibitive statement intended to ward off wicked bulls from the householder’s field, the warding off of a lover is understood as another prohibition. An example of a positive injunction within a prohibition is as follows: "O Mahua flower, why do you entreat me? As for my modesty, it belongs to my mother-in-law. Whom shall I lead into the forest? The village is far away, and I am all alone. Here, although neither a positive injunction nor a prohibition is explicitly stated, the injunction "my secluded dwelling is also desirable" is understood from the instruction regarding the secluded place—namely, that she is alone and the village is distant.

In some cases, there is a prohibition even when there is no injunction, as in: "The hope for life is strong; the hope for wealth is weak for me. Go, or stay, O beloved; my own condition has been made known. Here, because there is neither an injunction nor a prohibition such as "go" or "stay," the prohibition of departure is understood through the implication that "I am unable to live without you," based on the statement, "The hope for life is strong; the hope for wealth is weak for me."

In some cases, there is another injunction within an injunction and a prohibition, as for example: *“By another path, O traveler, go—[you who have] made your own wife’s beauty a virtue; otherwise, by this road, you will see the daughter of the householder, whose form is to be beheld.”* Here, while the expression “go by another path” conveys both an injunction and a prohibition, another injunction is understood: “O traveler, you who boast of the beauty of your own beloved, here in this village the daughter of the householder is one whose form must be seen.”

In some cases, there is a further negation within a prescription or a prohibition, as in: *ucchinna-paḍia-kusumaṃ mādhava sehaāliaṃ halia-putte | esa avasāṇā-viraso sasureṇa suo valaa-saddo ||* Here, while the expressions "pluck the fallen flower" (*ucchinnapaḍiakusumaṃ*) and "do not shake the *śephālikā*" (*mā dhunīhi śephālikām*) constitute a prescription and a prohibition respectively, another negation is implied: "O friend, you must not make the sound of your bracelets (*valayaśabdaḥ*), lest it be heard by your father-in-law. This occurs because she is engaged in secret amorous play (*cauryarata*).

In some cases, there is neither [an injunction nor a prohibition], as in: "Go slowly, O you whose heart is deceived by the news of your husband's journey; you have been fashioned by Fate with a sorrow that will not break. Here, in the expression of the injunction "go slowly," there is neither an injunction nor a prohibition; rather, mere description (*varṇanā*) is perceived. In some cases, there is neither [an injunction nor a prohibition] within a prohibition, as in: "O friend, desist from speaking; the mass of darkness has been dispelled by the moonlight of your face. You create an obstacle for the female messengers who are exhausted from their daytime wandering."

In this case, although there is the expression of a prohibition—"Turn back here"—there is neither a prohibition nor a prescription; rather, only the description of the moon-like beauty of her face is perceived. In some instances, there is neither a prescription nor a prohibition, as in: "O deceitful one, let her alone remain weeping with sobs; let her not become the object of your compassion when she is without you."

In this case, regarding the expression of both injunction and prohibition—“Let sighs and weeping belong to me alone; let them not arise for you as well without her”—there is neither injunction nor prohibition; rather, only a reproach directed at the beloved who has committed an offense is perceived. In some instances, where there is neither injunction nor prohibition, there is "neither" (*anubhaya*), as in: “The cries of the cranes on the bank of the Godāvarī river have ceased. Here, neither injunction nor prohibition is expressed. Nor is it the case that...

It is understood that he has come to the lofty peak of Ranyaketu and has not departed; thus, it is perceived. Because the meanings of both the expressed (*abhidhīyamāna*) and the implied (*pratīyamāna*) sentences are infinite, *dhvani* (suggestion) is likewise of many kinds. *Dhvani* is twofold: *arthadhvani* (suggestion of meaning) and *śabdadhvani* (suggestion of word). Of these two, *arthadhvani* takes the form of a resonance (*anunāda*) and the form of an echo (*pratiśabda*). Among these, that which is interwoven with the expressed sentence-meaning itself, like the resonance of a bell, is another meaning...

"O Śikhariṇī, who indeed is he, how long has he practiced penance, and what was his name, by which this young parrotling now bites the bimba-fruit as red as your lower lip? Here, while the literal meaning of the sentence is being expressed, the description "the lower lip red as a bimba-fruit" serves as an indicator that conveys an excess of passion; furthermore, through the flattering remark that "one of little merit even kisses a mere substitute for your lip," the speaker reveals his own affection for the woman being described—this is *dhvani*.

And this is perceived as a continuous resonance in the form of an echo, like the sound of a bronze bell; thus it is called *anunādadhvani*. Likewise, may there be peace for you: "The attendants (*gaṇas*) read here and there, word by word, the inscription of the Lord of the worlds, whose syllables are not very well known: 'He will create the universe, he will protect the earth, he will rule over the waters, he will be taught by the Nāgas, he will sport with those full of passion... he will enjoy the world...'"

In this context, the sentence-meaning expressed as "the Gaṇas are reciting the Kapāla-script with its well-known syllables one by one" suggests that those skulls belong to Brahmā and the other gods; thus, it resonates with the suggestion (*dhvani*) of the Lord’s solitary abiding, his power unimpaired, at the conclusion of the Great Path (*mahādhvopasaṃhāra*). And since this is perceived as echoing the very meaning of the words "he will create that universe" and so forth, which are already interwoven [with the literal sense], it is called *anunāda-dhvani* (echo-suggestion). Likewise: "O young thief, why do you look at me with such longing?"

"Thus it is for those who are afraid of their wives; there is no ford for those who are thirsty. [The reading is: "O young man, go elsewhere! Why do you look around at the *kīsa* reeds as if they were your wife? Thus it is for those who are afraid of their wives; there is no ford for those who are thirsty."]

In this context, by saying, "Why do you gaze at me as I am sinking? Go elsewhere; this is not a bathing place for those who fear their wives," he conveys the reproach: "You fear your wife, and therefore you do not desire me. By making this understood, he suggests through *dhvani* that young women become jealous even without actual affection. Furthermore, because he expresses this form of respect—which is not overly intense—in order to evoke her passion, it is called *anunāddhavani*.

In this way, in a sentence such as "Thus one sinks here [into the pit]," the prohibitive injunction being perceived might sometimes lead one to suspect that [the speaker] has mistaken a mother-in-law for a dog in the darkness; thus, even the mention of the term "night-blind" (*rātryandha*), which serves as a correction for a slip of the tongue, suggests the cleverness (*vaidagdhyam*) of the young woman. And since that is perceived through the continuous thread (*anusyūta*) of both the expressed and the implied, it is called the "resonance" (*anunāda-dhvani*).

Likewise, in such passages as "O traveler, what is the use of *mahua* flowers? and so forth, a positive injunction is perceived within a prohibition; this suggests the cleverness (*vaidagdhyam*) of a woman who is skillful in gathering *madhuka* flowers. And since that [cleverness] is perceived here as a resonance (*anunāda*) inextricably woven into the suggested meaning, it is called "resonant suggestion" (*anunādadhvani*). Furthermore, in a sentence such as "O farmer, the flowers have been gathered and placed upon the high ground, and the bees have been driven away," a prohibition is perceived within the context of an injunction and a prohibition; this suggests the cleverness of a female friend (*sakhī*) in concealing her lover.

Under the pretext of gathering *śephālikā* flowers, he approached the back of the garden; there, as the daughter-in-law of a plowman was engaged in a clandestine amorous quarrel with her lover, he—intent on silencing the charming sound of the bracelets being struck by his father-in-law’s hand (which was hidden behind a wall)—continued the shaking of the *śephālikā* branches that were intertwined with the daughter-in-law, and the shaking of the hands with their bracelets, producing a resonant sound like that of a bronze vessel.

By conveying [this meaning], it attains the designation of "reverberating sound" (*anunādadhvani*). Furthermore, that which, as if distinct from the meaning of the sentence being expressed, conveys another meaning corresponding to an echo in a cave or similar place, and thus "resounds," is "echo-sound" (*pratiśabdadhvani*). For example: "What indeed is this other ocean of loveliness here, wherein lotuses float together with the moon; wherein the temples of elephants emerge, and wherein there are other stalks of plantain trees and lotus-stems?"

In a cave, echoes of words such as "pauruṣa" arise, and these are perceived as generating further sound. Likewise, in the case of this object expressed by the phrase "lāvaṇyasindhu" (ocean of beauty), echoes of words such as "utpala" arise according to their respective denotable meanings—such as splendor and so forth—and these are perceived as generating a resonance of other meanings.

In this context, when the meaning of words such as "lotus" (*utpala*) heard here is expressed, it conveys a similarity with objects such as the eyes; this necessarily brings about the perception of the excellence of the beauty of the subject being described. Since that [beauty] is perceived as if distinct from those [objects], it is considered a *pratiśabdadhvani* (echo-sound). Thus it should be understood: "One should desire many sons, even if only one should go to Gayā, or perform the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*), or set free a dark-colored bull."

Here, the meaning of the sentence "many sons are to be desired," while being expressed, conveys that they must be produced through the designation of them as "sons" (by the father); this suggests that the fulfillment of the desires of the ancestors is the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*). And that [sentence], having proceeded by way of the designation of them as "sons," is perceived as if it were distinct, echoing back within the activities directed toward those sons; thus, it is called an "echo-sound" (*pratiśabdadhvani*). Likewise: "Who would not feel resentment upon seeing the bitten lip of his beloved?"... [text fragment] ...is an example of *virodhadhvani* (the suggestion of contradiction). In the verse beginning with *kassa va ṇa hoi roso*, the word *piāe* ("of the beloved") is used in the sense of "beloved woman" (*priyā*), which is its primary denotation (*abhidhā*). However, because the context is one where the husband's anger is expected, the word *piāe* is understood through *lakṣaṇā* (secondary indication) to mean "beloved man" (*priya*). This is because the primary meaning is obstructed by the context, and there is a relationship of proximity between the two meanings. Thus, the word *piāe* possesses two powers: the power of primary denotation and the power of secondary indication. Through these two powers, the word *piāe* simultaneously expresses both "beloved woman" and "beloved man. Consequently, the sentence "Who would not feel resentment upon seeing the bitten lip of the beloved" appears to express two contradictory meanings at once: "Who would not feel resentment upon seeing the bitten lip of the beloved woman? and "Who would not feel resentment upon seeing the bitten lip of the beloved man? Therefore, this is an instance of *virodhadhvani*. "O you who are dripping with nectar, O destroyer of the village of water-lilies, endure this!"—here, while the purpose of the friend’s reproach is being expressed, it serves to pacify the husband's jealousy by making him understand that her lower lip was bitten by a bee and not by a paramour; thus, it suggests the cleverness of the friend in concealing a slip. Furthermore, as this [speech] was directed toward one person but has been reflected in the mind of another, it constitutes the resonance of an echo (*pratiśabdadhvani*).

Thus, in the sentence beginning with *evaṃ bhamadhasmi avīsaddho* ("I wander thus without confidence"), a negation perceived within an injunction suggests, by means of the river-bower, a secret rendezvous with someone; appearing as if distinct from the literal meaning of the sentence, this is the "resonance of the echo" (*pratiśabdadhvani*). In the sentence beginning with *āsāiaṃ aṇāe ṇajhattiam* ("She has been reached by her mother-in-law..."), a negation intended to ward off the bull, while conveying the warding off of a lover, suggests the wit of the speaker; this is the "resonance of the suggestion" (*dhvani*).

Just as when one expresses one thing by means of another expression, the echo is perceived as if distinct from it; likewise, in the case of "golāṇaīatūhe cakkantorāi āevattai" (the girl at the Gola river-ford is calling out), this too is an echo-sound. Thus, sound-echo is also of two kinds. Among these, that which consists of resonance (*anunāda*) is as follows: those [rays] who, desiring to attract Lakṣmī—who plays within the hollows of the buds of the *pucakuṭī*—to one prostrate with devotion, perform the opening of the lotus groves as if they were eager to draw her forth.

"May those rays of the Sun—which are like the luster of young sprouts, which are capable of destroying the terror of the world fallen into the darkness that has the form of saliva, and which bring about your welfare—grant you prosperity! Here, the sentence-meaning is "May the rays of the Sun grant you welfare"; yet, due to the inherent power of the word *kara* (which means both 'ray' and 'hand') and because of its connection with the shared epithets such as "having the luster of young sprouts," the word generates a resonance (*anunāda*) regarding the hands, thereby suggesting both the Lord's nature as light and his nature as a person.

Since both of these are described here as being permeated by that [reality], there is the term *anunādhvani* (the path of resonance). Thus: May the rays of the sun protect you—rays which, at the commencement and at the conclusion of the day, fall equally upon the lotuses in their wombs and upon the sharp peaks of mountains; which proceed without alternation across the courtyard of the mansion of the three worlds; and which bear intensely a heat like that born of the fatigue of a long journey.

In this context, everything should be applied according to the inherent nature of the word *pāda* (foot/quarter). However, there is this distinction: whereas in the previous case it was by way of similarity (*sādharmya*), here it is by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). And here, the resonance of the word *apratigha* (unimpeded) is as follows: "Bringing joy to all beings with waters produced effortlessly at the appropriate time, scattered in every direction during the forenoon, they gather together as the day comes to an end."

May the rays of the Sun—the boat for crossing the ocean of fear arising from long-lasting suffering—generate in you an immeasurable and supreme joy, O cows, who are the most purifying of all things. Here, everything is to be construed by virtue of the inherent nature of the word *pāda* (which means both "quarter-verse" and "ray"); however, this is the distinction: in the previous instance it was by way of similarity (*sādharmya*), whereas here it is by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).

And here is an example of the sound *apra* (the *apratiśabda*): May the cows—the ships for crossing the ocean of worldly existence (*bhava*), which is the source of long-lasting suffering—produce for you supreme and boundless purifying joy. These cows bring delight to all creatures with their milk, produced without effort at the appropriate time; scattered in every direction during the forenoon, they gather together as the day comes to an end. They belong to the Lord of Radiant Rays (*dīptāṃśu*). *atra cāpratiśabdadhvaniryathā...* (In this instance, the sound *apra* is as follows... [The verse continues as above].

Here, the rays—the "cows" of the sun whose parts are blazing—are being praised; by the inherent nature of the power of words and through the employment of identical epithets, they produce echoes in the form of actual cows, and in those cows as well, they resonate with a further, distinguished greatness.

Thus, with eyes closed, ears dulled and deafened, the function of the nose suppressed, the skin rendered incapable of its own activity, the mind stolen away, and nothing remaining but breath; with limbs relaxed, having fallen and deprived of his own station—may the Sun-born Prāktāpa protect you, raising up the world devoured by the serpent of Time like a medicine, as he rescues those who have taken refuge in him. Here, the meaning of the sentence is: "May the Sun-born Prāktāpa, raising up the world devoured by the serpent of Time, protect you who have sought refuge in him."

Due to the inherent power of the word *arka* and its connection with words for similar actions and so forth, the word *arka*—signifying a medicinal herb born from the *arka* tree that can revive even one bitten by the serpent of Time (*kāla-vyāla*)—arouses a resonance in the form of a secondary meaning (*pratiśabdarūpa-dhvani*) that conveys: "The *arka* is the best among those that destroy poison. Thus, as it has been stated, other specific types of resonance (*dhvani*) within the compositions of great poets are to be sought, such as the claim that "in speech, the intended meaning itself is the resonance; this alone is poetry," and so forth.

What, then, is the distinction between *dhvani* (suggestion) and *tātparya* (implication) in poetic speech? Has this not already been stated previously: "That which is spoken in both the technical treatises (*śāstra*) and in common worldly usage is merely 'speech' (*vaca*). That which is indirect (*vakra*), as found in explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) and the like, is traditionally known as 'poetry' (*kāvya*). If the entire essence of the speaker's intention is perceived from the sentence, that is *tātparya*; it is a property of the meaning (*artha-dharma*). *Dhvani*, however, is a property of the word (*śabda-dharma*). Like charm (*saubhāgya*), *tātparya* is held to be an internal quality.

"The external resonance (*dhvani*) of those two is like the loveliness of the Goddess of Speech; however, because they are not far removed from one another, each pair is spoken of as a single unit, just as the months of *surabhi* and *vaiśākha* are designated by the name *madhumādhava*. This has been well said. However, it is not yet established through an illustrative example. Then listen, for we shall now demonstrate this: let it be understood that whatever was just mentioned as being "internal" is entirely *dhvani* in poetry.

The intended meaning (*tātparya*) in the treatise (*śāstra*) and in poetry (*sloka*) is twofold. Regarding that, in the treatise, for example: "The excellence of the qualities residing in the self of the egoistic one," and so forth. Here, the authoritative tradition (*āgama*) in the form of an instruction from a reliable person (*āpta*) is: "They call the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), which is the excellence of the qualities residing in the self of the egoistic one, the life-breath of the self-born [poetry]. Its status as *rasa* (flavor) consists in its being relishable through the power of the self; this is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) to be individually experienced, which conforms to the meaning of its designation.

For instance, that unimpeachable worldly report—“this man has taste,” “this man is a connoisseur”—regarding certain specific individuals, which occurs without reference to sweet flavors and the like, is not possible without a connection to an object of aesthetic relish (*rasāhvaya-vastu*) that is to be personally experienced within oneself. Thus, when the meaning intended to be expressed is set forth by means of the three types of valid cognition, the person who is both the speaker and the one being addressed becomes threefold according to the nature of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).

Regarding the terms "one who has not understood," "one who has misunderstood," and "one who is doubtful": just as food is prescribed for both the sick and the healthy, yet it is the non-sick person who partakes of it, so too is it conceived here. Thus, in accordance with those who have not understood, the scripture itself is presented first for the other two as well. In that regard, the one who has misunderstood or the one who is doubtful does not accept the scripture.

Therefore, for that purpose, perception—which is more powerful than all other means of knowledge—ought to be presented; yet, out of audacity, one who is mistaken does not accept even that. Consequently, in order to instruct him, a reasoning that is like the Brahma-missile (Brahmāstra) and universally accepted is set forth. This very intention of the speaker, which is perceived as the reason for presenting the three means of knowledge, manifests itself as the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), being based on the Sāṅkhya system through the presentation of the three means of knowledge and so forth.

The intended meaning is to demonstrate that what is non-existent does not arise, and that [the existent] is of three kinds, which is not conducive to the highest good (*aśreyas*). For the Sāṅkhyas say this: "Only the existent arises; *prakṛti* alone is the agent; the *puruṣa*, however, remains indifferent; and yet, even though he is indifferent, *prakṛti* approaches him for the sake of producing experience. Now, one might object: the Sāṅkhyas' sequence for presenting the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is "perception, inference, and authoritative testimony."

What is the purpose of introducing scripture (*āgama*) first here? It has already been stated that this is done out of consideration for those who have not yet attained realization. Furthermore, another reason is given: objects perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) do not provide such satisfaction as when they are communicated by the words of eloquent speakers; thus, the author indicates this by placing scripture at the outset. Moreover, he demonstrates the inversion of the usual order of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to show that we do not rely exclusively on the Sāṅkhya system, since literary composition (*sāhitya*) is intended for all audiences.

Now, by means of the next verse, he points out the causes of manifestation and the effects of that *śṛṅgāra*—which exists in the self through the medium of being reflected therein as a specific quality of *ahaṃkāra*, whose life is the third human goal consisting of the fruits of dharma and artha, and which has the name "self-conceit" (*abhimāna*)—beginning with the words: "Born from a specific birth of stainless nature," and so forth.

In this regard, this [self] arises from specific merits that follow it; once arisen, the self becomes the cause for the emergence of the perfection of its own qualities, which are characterized by being manifest. Furthermore, it excels due to the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of many births; and when it has thus excelled, it becomes the cause for the excellence of the very perfection of its own qualities.

And this very same single entity, consisting of such conceit (abhimāna) and being a modification of primordial nature (prakṛti), awakens as if from sleep in the form of a reflection within the locations of the various distinctions of the self that are characterized by darkness; this is the meaning of the sentence as it is being stated. Furthermore, by the phrase "the sole cause," [the author] demonstrates the absence of any other cause for the perfection of the qualities of the self, and makes it known that this alone is the cause of the fourfold aims of human life (caturvarga).

By the phrase "he keeps watch," and by means of the analogy of awakening from sleep, he refutes the notion that [the ego] is non-existent even in its unmanifest state, since it persists in a latent form. By the word "some" (*kaścit*), through the demonstration of its wonder, he proclaims its excellence—that it cannot be described even in a thousand of its own births. And by the phrase "consisting of pride" (*mānamaya*), he shows that its root is indeed the self-conceit of the Self itself, thereby refuting any dependence on other supports.

Thus, this kind of sentence-meaning, being perceived as such, is the very thing for which we are prepared to speak; therefore, the intention (*tātparya*) of this speech lies in encouraging the audience by saying, "May even those who seek the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*) proceed [to act]. In this way, even in worldly speech, the expressed meaning (*abhidhīyamāna*), the suggested meaning (*pratīyamāna*), and the intention (*tātparya*) must be carefully considered. By this, the occasional convergence (*samplava*) of the expressed and suggested meanings in poetic speech is also explained.

For example: "With the girdle unloosed, yet not having attained a firm embrace," and so forth. Here, the meaning of the poem is as follows: the body of Purāri (Śiva), though mixed with his beloved, is described through the application of qualifiers such as "with the girdle unloosed" and so on; this body, which brings about friendship between separation (*vipralambha*) and union (*saṃbhoga*), is conceived as being "new. Thus, the sentence-meaning expressed is: "May it protect [you]. By the phrase "the body of him whose form is mixed with his beloved," it is made known that it is his physical form alone that is authorized for worldly activities, and not his *ātman* (self).

While one could have simply said "mūrti" (form), the use of the word "vapuḥ" (body) indicates that he is not only engaged in the protection of the universe, but is also constantly active in its creation and withdrawal. For the root *vap* is seen to apply to both creation and withdrawal, as in "he sows the seed" (*bījaṃ vapati*) and "he shaves the hair" (*keśānvapati*). Furthermore, by the phrase "as if having established a friendship between separation and union," it is made known that he brings together even those things that are mutually incompatible—such as those that cannot coexist—into a single state.

And by the word "of Purāri," it is established that even though his body is mingled with his beloved, he is indeed capable of such activities as the slaying of enemies; this is the kind of sentence-meaning that is perceived as suggested (pratīyamāna).

Thus, the essential meaning is that he alone whose sovereignty is of such a nature—boundless and not shared by others—is worthy of salutation, and no other. Similarly, in the following verse as well, while the literal meaning of the sentence is being stated, the phrase "upon those [beings] who have been cleansed by the dust of his lotus-feet" indicates the activity of the agent; by showing this, he instructs that Gaṇapati should be brought before the mind through meditation and established there.

By the phrase "the surfaces of their minds having attained the stainlessness of a mirror's surface," he declares that even by the dust of his feet, when applied with mindfulness, their minds become pure, just as a mirror's surface is cleansed by ashes. By the phrase "the most exalted riches of word and meaning flash forth," he makes known that within these [minds], which are as stainless as mirror-surfaces, all objects of experience flash forth as if in mirrors.

By the phrase "May that Lord of the Gaṇas be the cutter of obstacles," he demonstrates the Lord’s possession of qualities that cause one to approach Him (abhigāmika-guṇa) according to the principle restated here; thus, through this prayer for the removal of obstacles, he sets forth his own great undertaking which he intends to perform. This is the meaning of the sentence as it is perceived: "If even the mere remembrance of whose lotus-feet yields such a fruit, what then can be said of his direct worship and the like? This is the underlying purport (tātparya).

Now, these very two verses at the beginning of the treatise are explained in the form of speech, extending to their ultimate purport (*tātparya*). In this regard, it is the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) that one’s chosen deity (*abhīṣṭadevatā*) should be praised; for from that, through the attainment of distinguished merit (*adṛṣṭa*), the desired fruit is obtained. Furthermore, the chosen deity is of two kinds: the qualified (*adhikṛta*) and the unqualified (*anadhikṛta*). Between these two—the qualified and the unqualified—recognition of the qualified is more significant; thus, the qualified deity is praised.

In this treatise, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is the subject matter. And therein, just as the Lord Maheśvara is authorized by virtue of his omniscience, his good fortune, his status as the beloved of [the Goddess], his sovereignty, his supreme perfection, and his capability—so it is not with others, such as Śakra and the like, whose power is subordinate to him. Among these, that which was previously mentioned is the suggested sense; however, that which consists of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is now being defined. In this treatise, the erotic sentiment is to be discussed. It is twofold: union (*sambhoga*) and separation (*vipralambha*).

In this regard, since enjoyment (*sambhoga*) does not reach its highest excellence without separation (*vipralambha*), it is separation itself that must be described first. This [separation] is fourfold: love at first sight (*prathamānurāga*), jealousy (*māna*), separation due to distance (*pravāsa*), and separation through death (*karuṇa*). Furthermore, this is said to be more varied than enjoyment; thus it is explained in detail. And there are four stages of this [separation]: existence (*sattā*), birth (*janma*), continuity (*anubandha*), and culmination (*prakarpa*).

He indicates by the first half-verse this [love], which is fourfold, exists in four stages, and is diverse, as it will be described hereafter. In that context, by the phrase "with the girdle unloosed," he indicates *prathamānurāga* (the first stage of love), for *prathamānurāga* is defined as lasting until the girdle is loosened. By the phrase "not yet having attained a firm embrace," he indicates *māna* (the stage of jealous anger), for in *māna*, a firm embrace is not obtained. By the phrase "not having reached a kiss," he indicates *karuṇa* (the stage of separation/pain), for in *karuṇa*, the beauty of the face is no longer seen. Now, these very same words apply even to these [subsequent] stages.

In that context, "with the girdle unbroken" refers to the state of separation (*vipralambha*). For separation necessarily occurs for one who desires union as long as the girdle remains unbroken; this is its first stage.

"Not having obtained a firm embrace" refers to the arising of *vipralambha* (love-in-separation). For one who possesses *vipralambha*, not attaining union due to the cutting of the girdle, entreats his beloved: "O most beloved, if you do not permit the cutting of my girdle, then grant me even a firm embrace. When she does not consent to this, *vipralambha* arises for him; this is its second stage.

"Not having attained a kiss" refers to the persistence of *vipralambha* (love-in-separation). For one who is deceived by separation, not obtaining the embrace of his beloved with all his limbs, longs even for the contact of her face alone. When even that is not obtained, this state of deception persists; this is its third stage. "Not having beheld the beauty of her face" refers to the culmination of *vipralambha*. Indeed, when the desired embrace and other such acts are unattainable, lovers hold even the mere sight of their beloved’s face in high regard.

Even for those who do not attain that [union], this separation (*vipralambha*) is intensified; it is its fourth state. This fourfold and four-staged separation, being described individually according to its four types and four stages, is called "variegated" (*vicitra*). Union (*sambhoga*) is likewise of exactly four kinds: following initial passion, following anger (*māna*), following separation due to travel (*pravāsa*), and following grief (*karuṇa*).

For that [rasa] as well, there are those same four stages: existence (*sattā*), birth (*janman*), continuity (*anubandha*), and excellence (*prakarṣa*). This [rasa], which possesses four divisions and four stages, is also indicated in brief by the phrase "of the body intermingled with the beloved," because of its variegated nature (*citrātva*).

In this context, because the prefix *vyupa-* denotes a qualifier of the action (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*), by whichever specific quality the union with the beloved occurs—whether immediately following the first passion (*prathamānurāga*), following the stage of jealous anger (*māna*), or following the stage of pathos (*karuṇā*)—it arises accompanied by trembling from fear, tinged with jealousy, impetuous with longing, and filled with joy and wonder. All of these are indicated; thus, by the word *vimiśra* (mixed), all four types of *sambhoga* (enjoyment) are implied. Furthermore, by the word *kāntā* (beloved), its four stages are established.

In this regard, when the word *kāntā* is a synonym for "woman," then even the name "woman" is delightful and indeed agitates the mind; thus, the first stage of sexual enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*), known as "existence" (*sattā*), is perceived. But when the word *kāntā* is a synonym for "charming," then, according to the maxim, "What is the sight of her, whose eyebrows quiver with playful grace?", the second stage of sexual enjoyment, known as "birth" (*janman*), is perceived.

Furthermore, when the word *kāntā* is a synonym for a woman longing for her lover (*vṛṣasyantī*), then, according to the maxim: "Indeed, a young man who is devoted to penance and easily found is not obtained as a suitable match," the third stage of sexual union, known as *anubandha*, is understood. And according to the maxim: "The beloved does exactly what pleases me; she does not know that which is dear to her because of what she does," the fourth stage of sexual union, known as *prakarṣa*, is recognized.

The intended meaning is this: this manifestation of the Brahman, which is fourfold and possesses four states, has been introduced here as a mere indication of its direction (*diṅmātra*), whereas its enjoyment (*sambhoga*) will be described specifically and in detail further on. Now, what is the status of those specific qualifications that determine the particular eligibility for this [enjoyment]? Even they have indeed been indicated here by way of a double entendre (*tantra*) within the phrase "for the sake of those who desire to drink the nectar of the beloved."

For in that context, the interpretation is: "May [the Lord] protect men and women whose bodies are mingled with their beloveds, as if providing assistance to the Blessed One’s *vibhu* (all-pervading) and *vipula* (vast) *pralamba* (long) *saṃbhoga* (enjoyment). And by the word *vimiśra* ("mingled"), those who are separated are expressed just like those who are united, because the prefix *vi-* is observed to signify the reversal of an action just as it signifies a particularization of an action.

For example: "Separated and yet united, both types of male characters who are the subjects of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) [are described]; women with lovely and unmixed forms, both united and separated, are likewise perceived as the specific types of female characters who are the subjects of the erotic sentiment. Furthermore, by the word *vapuḥ* (form/body) here, even in the context of qualifying the Enemy of Tripura (*purāri*), the body is meant—which is the locus of the excellence of all personal qualities and possesses the beauty of loveliness budding forth with youth.

However, unlike the case of the Creator of the gods and others, whose body is seen during both creation and destruction, [the body] is seen here even during the state of *kānti* (beauty). For example: "The particular *apsaras* named Vapuṣṭamā was endowed with beauty by means of her rays (*gobhiḥ*). In that context, phrases such as "with an unbroken girdle" (*acchinnamekhalam*) function as qualifiers because they provide the necessary indication (*gamakatva*) through the case-endings and the verbal action contained within the compound term "body mixed with beauty" (*kāntāvimiśravapuṣaḥ*). This is just as in the cases: "intending to make a mat" (*kartumanāḥ kaṭam*) or "desiring to go to the village" (*gantukāmo grāmam*).

Now, regarding the aspect of enjoyment (*sambhogapakṣa*), how are [the verses] beginning with "unbroken girdle" (*acchinnamekhalam*) connected? It is said: because they are so united with their lovers due to being blinded by passion for such names, they—immersed in supreme bliss—are unable to perform the cutting of the girdle, the embrace, the kiss, or the gazing; just as one embraced by a beloved woman knows nothing external nor internal; and as it is said: "Blessed are you who speak even during union with the beloved."

"I swear by my friends that I do not recall even the slightest thing, though hundreds of confident endearments were exchanged during our lovemakes—once my beloved had placed his hand upon the earth. Thus is the first verse explained according to the view that a sentence expresses its meaning through the combination of word-endings. Now, it is explained according to the view that the sentence-meaning is indivisible (*akhaṇḍavākyārtha*). In that case, the syntactical connection of the words here is as follows: What is to be protected? The universe (*viśva*). From what? From calamities (*apāyebhyaḥ*). What is that [which is to be protected]? The body (*vapuḥ*).

Of whom? Of Purāri (Śiva). Of what sort? One whose wine was mixed with his beloved. How characterized [is the waistband]? Unsevered from its girdle, not having attained a firm embrace, not having reached a kiss, and not having beheld the beauty of her face. How is it being imagined? As if it had formed a friendship with both the state of separation and the enjoyment of union.

And here, this compound "acchinna" (uninterrupted) and the *bahuvrīhi* compound, along with two supplied words, constitute a twelve-word *nāndī*. It contains a specific mention of the non-separation of words (*padāviśleṣa*), is pregnant with a particular statement (*viśeṣokti*), and possesses poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*); it is an ornament of benediction (*āśīralaṅkāra*) intended for auspiciousness. These four [elements], all serving the purpose of auspiciousness, when employed at the beginning of a treatise, bring about prosperity for the author, the listener, the student, and the teacher.

As it has been said: "Treatises that begin with auspiciousness, have auspiciousness in their middle, and end with auspiciousness, proceed without obstruction and possess long-lived listeners. Now, one might object: "But here, there is no mention of 'the world' as the source (*apādāna*) from which [beings] are rescued from misfortunes (*apāya*)."

How, then, is this *nāndī* said to consist of twelve words? It is explained as follows: the word *pātu* is a scriptural term (*śrutipada*). Now, the meaning of a single word—such as an injunction (*vidhi*) and so forth—is based upon multiple words; and since that meaning cannot be established otherwise, it implies (*ākṣipati*) for its own realization the object, the instrument, the agent, the locus, and so on, which are likewise based upon multiple words. That [implication]...

The meaning of all words in the Veda becomes [determined] in this way: therein, whether the agent, the object, and so forth are explicitly mentioned (*upādīyamāna*) for the sake of restriction (*niyamāya*), or they are understood without being explicitly mentioned, it is as follows. When a general term implies [a specific], a particular word being explicitly mentioned serves for restriction; for example, "May the Supreme Light protect you. When a specific term implies [a general], it is understood there even without being explicitly mentioned, as in "The god rains water."

In this context, just as from the injunction "one should initiate a Brahmin at eight years of age and teach him," the phrase "by a twice-born [student] from a teacher" is necessarily supplied—even though unstated—to the rule "the Veda is to be studied"; likewise here, because the meaning of the root *pā* (to protect) consists in the removal of misfortunes (*apāya*), and because its object is the entire universe—just as in the case of creation and dissolution performed by the Lord—the two words "from misfortunes" (*apāyebhyaḥ*) and "the universe" (*viśvam*) are necessarily supplied, even though they are not explicitly mentioned.

Now, one might object: even if it is accepted that the bodiless Maheśvara is the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe, how can it be said, "May his body protect [us]"? This is because, despite being bodiless, such a description is possible through his universal form (*vaiśvarūpya*). Indeed, he is praised thus by those who know the truth: "The root-nature, the network of elements, the enjoyer, consciousness, the powers, and the aggregate of your enjoyers; knowledge, and this multitude of presiding deities—all these appear simultaneously in the remembrance of you."

For this very reason, the epithet *kāntavimiśravapuṣaḥ* ("whose body is mixed with his beloved") is applied to Purāri (Śiva) in the *Tantra*, and it is interpreted in another way through *tantra* (multiple meanings). That is to say: "She whose end (*anta*) is water (*ka*)" is the Earth (*pṛthvī*), who is the beloved (*kāntā*); "those whose ends are happiness (*ka*)" are the Waters (*āpaḥ*), who are the beloveds (*kāntāḥ*); "he whose end is air (*ka*)" is Fire (*vahni*), who is the beloved (*kānta*); and "he whose interior is water (*ka*)" is Air (*vāyu*), who is the beloved (*kānta*).

That which has *kaṃ* (pleasure) as its *brahman* at the end is *kānta*, meaning space (*ākāśa*). *Kānti* is radiance; that which possesses an excellence of this is *kānta*, the sun. *Kānti* is loveliness; that which possesses an excellence of this is *kānta*, the moon. Or, *kānti* is endearment; that which possesses an excellence of this is *kānta*, the Self (*ātman*). Thus, by the word *kānta*, all eight forms of the Lord are expressed. Those whose nature it is to protect these [forms]—namely Ugra, Bhīma, and the others—are the lords of the forms, the *kāntavinas*. The word *miśra* is a term of honor.

Therefore, this is a compound [formed] with words of praise for these [qualities], like *cetyārtha-miśra* and others; then, it means "one whose body is mixed with a beloved. Since the formation of a *bahuvrīhi* establishes a manifold nature (*vaiśvarūpya*), the intended meaning is established. Now, how is there a syntactical connection (*anvaya*) here for phrases such as "with an unbroken girdle" (*acchinna-mekhalam*)? These too are qualifiers of the body. Among them, by the phrase "with an unbroken girdle," the following is expressed: for a girdle (*mekhalā*) is a cord that encircles the hips; thus, it refers to one for whom that [girdle] is not broken.

By the phrase "not having obtained a firm embrace" (*alabdhadṛḍhopagūḍham*), the unfathomable depth (*agādhatva*) of [the ocean] is expressed; for "firm" (*dṛḍha*) means a support that is difficult to grasp, and its "embrace" (*upagūḍham*) is its contact—that is, its foundation—and that which has not obtained such is so described. By the phrase "not having reached a foothold" (*aprāptayumbanam*), the extreme subtlety (*parisūkṣmatva*) of its height (*uñcaiṣṭva*) is stated.

He whose splendor is such that it is not known from where he comes, who his speaker is, or what his face is like; and who, by the phrase "as if having established a friendship through both separation and union," appears as if deceiving because his ultimate reality is unknown, yet appears as if being enjoyed and as if enjoying because of his well-known forms as earth and the other elements—that very one is described thus: "They say of you: 'You alone are the oblation and the offerer, the food and the eater, eternal; you are the object of knowledge and the knower, the meditator and the object of meditation, the Supreme.'"

He too said: "It is known to you that none of my activities are for my own sake; indeed, such a one as I am indicated here by these eight forms. Thus, by this group of five adjectives, the following is expressed: "I bow to the slayer of Madhu—[him who is] unvanquished, exceedingly lofty, non-diffusive, non-expansive, non-shallow, non-light, non-measurable, and manifest as the supreme reality. Now, the optative suffix *pātu* (in the sense of "may he protect") is not used here in the sense of a command (*vidhi*), but rather in the sense of a benediction (*āśis*).

And since that [consciousness], in the absence of any specific [object] being heard, abides as having itself as its object by virtue of its very nature, how can it have the universe as its object?
