Let the meaning of that which always functions in combination be as much as it is, but only to the extent that its denotative power (*śakti*) extends.

And how great is its denotative power? It is that which, when conjoined with or disjoined from as much meaning as is required, compatible, and proximate, does not abandon either mere action or mere factors of action (kārakas). Therefore, by means of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), its denotative power is determined to extend only that far. As it has been said: "Because of non-deviation, only that much is its meaning; nothing more, because of deviation."

Surely, in this case, the defect characterized by the complexity of postulating three powers arises. For the distinctness of word-meanings is established by valid means of knowledge; thus, one must postulate for those meanings denoted by words the power of making them known. Furthermore, in the production of that power, it must be accepted that contact with the word itself is the cause.

For it is observed in common usage that a word is employed for the purpose of conveying a specific meaning; and since it is not capable of directly conveying the meaning of a sentence, it makes the meanings of the individual words its intermediate operation (*avāntaravyāpāra*). And if those word-meanings are capable of bringing about the cognition of the mutual connection [of the word-meanings], then they may constitute such an intermediate operation, but not otherwise.

Even for word-meanings, their power manifests at that time through contact with words intended to convey a specific composite meaning; thus, it must be admitted that the word also possesses the power to impart power to the word-meanings. This would be so, provided that the capacity of word-meanings—ascertainable through other means of knowledge—to bring about the mutual connection [of those meanings] is not determined.

And the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) "a white horse is running" is apprehended [as follows]: there is a whiteness whose specific substrate has not been determined; there is a horse perceived non-perceptually (*apratyakṣopalabdha*) whose specific quality has not been cognized; and there is [the horse] inferred from the sound of neighing. Thus it is said: "For one who sees the form of whiteness and hears the sound of neighing, and also the sound of the placing of footsteps, there arises the cognition: 'A white horse is running. The phrase "seen apart from a sentence" means that the form is unmanifest (*arūpam*).

By this it is stated that the specific quality (*guṇaviśeṣa*) is not determined by perception. Here, the following objection is raised: Is it the case that the determination of the substratum [of the horse] occurs for that person by whom the two sounds—the neighing and the sound of footsteps—have been perceived as having the same locus as whiteness? What follows from this? If you say that it belongs to one who has not yet reflected upon the neighing and the noise of the movement of the feet, then there is a contradiction with experience; for such a person understands: "In this place, there must surely be a horse; someone is certainly running."

Now, when one perceives the sound of the clatter of hooves belonging specifically to a horse—as if by virtue of the proficiency gained through practice—one infers the swift motion residing in that horse; one does not, however, become aware of it by understanding the motion alone and then reflecting upon it. Even for one who has ascertained that there is no other horse in this place, and thus lacks a definitive determination of the source [of the sound] despite the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the "horseness" of the neighing sound—which is co-located with whiteness—is a case of presumption (*arthāpatti*), just as the sight of something inside a house leads to the understanding of its existence outside.

The cognition that "that which is white is indeed a horse" is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). However, for one who superimposes [the property of] neighing, the sound of the hooves striking the ground, and so forth—which are not co-referential with the act of whitening—upon a horse, there arises a single inference regarding the horse-nature and the swift motion residing in the white substance. For those who have understood the object through its connection [to the mark], it is never observed that [such a mark] conveys a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) except through inference or presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

Furthermore, if the comprehension of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) arises from the mere comprehension of the word-meanings alone, then it must be stated in what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) this [comprehension] is included. It cannot be included in verbal testimony (*śabda*), because that [relation] is absent in the word itself; for according to the established doctrine of the proponents of "the relation of the expressed" (*abhihitānvayavādinaḥ*), the knowledge of the relation derived from the word—by virtue of the intermediate operation of the denotation of word-meanings—is not "verbal" (*śābda*). Thus, how could it be included within verbal testimony? If, however, another means of valid cognition is admitted, then verbal testimony would be abolished, since the verbal [cognition] has been established as having only word-meanings as its object.

Because it would result in [the absurdity of] all words being authoritative. Therefore, one must postulate that even for word-meanings not denoted by words, there exists a capacity to convey the sentence-meaning—a capacity never observed elsewhere. Furthermore, since the power to instill that [capacity] resides in words as well, it is more reasonable—on account of parsimony of hypothesis (*kalpanālāghava*)—to postulate that words themselves possess the mere capacity to convey their own meanings as already related (*anvita*). Now, it might be argued: "It is the word-meanings themselves, provided they possess expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and semantic competency (*yogyatā*), that constitute the sentence-meaning; they do not, however, convey the sentence-meaning."

That is extremely weak, because it would result in the absence of any cause for the comprehension of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). For if words were not the cause for the cognition of syntactic connection (*anvaya*), then even if word-meanings (*padārtha*) were present, the cognition of connection would become causeless. It might be argued: "When a meaning has been previously expressed by a verb (*kriyāpada*) or a noun denoting an agent (*kārakapada*) and is thus expectancy-laden (*sākāṅkṣa*), whatever other suitable counter-correlative meaning (*pratiyogipadārthāntara*) is brought into proximity by another word, that alone remains there as its correlate."

This is true; however, it must be stated what the basis for its connection with that [other word-meaning] is. Now, when another word-meaning is uttered while the meaning of the preceding word is still expectant, it presents and conveys its own meaning precisely as being connected to that [preceding one]. Just as an affix, being uttered after the meaning of the base has already been cognized, denotes its own meaning as qualified by that [base], so too does another word-meaning. As it has been said: "The base and the affix together express the meaning of the affix."

The meaning is that the *prakṛti* (base), presenting its own meaning as a qualifier for the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), expresses that meaning together with the suffix. Thus it has been said: "A suffix is always employed to qualify an object; therefore, for one who understands it immediately following [the base], it serves as a qualifier for the meaning of the *prakṛti*. If it is argued, "In that case, you have admitted that the second [word] functions through *anvitābhidhāna* (expression of the related), yet this does not apply to the first," we say no, because in a sentence there is no fixed rule regarding the order of the employment of words.

Since that which is sometimes the first [word] is at other times the second, it follows that all words must express their meanings as already connected (*anvitābhidhāna*). Furthermore, if the suffix (*pratyaya*) were to express the meaning as connected, then, given the lack of distinction between them, why would one not accept that all words express their meanings as connected? Why resort to this partial mutilation [of the theory]? To this, it is replied: all sentence-meanings are indeed secondary (*lākṣaṇika*); consequently, there is no burden of assuming a further expressive power (*śakti*) for words to bring about the cognition of the connection of word-meanings.

For a word denotes its meaning in an unconnected state, which then indicates its own related connected state. Since there is a relationship between a state and that which possesses the state, when the possessor of the state is understood, the state itself becomes present to the mind. It is established everywhere that when a related entity is perceived, a cognition arises regarding another related factor. Therefore, it is unnecessary to postulate a power (*śakti*) in word-meanings for the cognition of a connected sense. As it has been said: "The sentence-meaning is indeed indicated (*lakṣyamāṇa*) in every case. Thus it is concluded.

But how, then, does this indication (*lakṣaṇā*) function? It is said: "Indication is defined as the connection (*anvaya*) with the sentence-meaning of that which is reached by virtue of its relation to the expressed meaning, due to the impossibility of the expressed meaning itself being connected to the sentence-meaning. For example, in the statement "A hamlet dwells on the Gaṅgā," because the literal sense of the word *gaṅgā* cannot be connected to the sentence-meaning, one sets that aside and understands the bank (*kūla*), which is in proximity and possesses a relation to it, as being connected to the sentence-meaning. For this very reason, they say: "Indication occurs through [the expressed meaning's] impossibility [of connection] and through [its] relation [to something else]."

Furthermore, in cases such as "bring the cow," the listener lacks the capacity for further syntactic connection (*anvaya-yogyatva*), nor does the already connected meaning possess the fitness for connection with another, because there is no further connection possible for that which is already connected. Moreover, if all sentence-meanings were merely metaphorical (*lākṣaṇika*), it would result in the abandonment of the primary sense itself. Now, suppose it is argued: "Let this not be metaphorical; rather, the cognition of the action brings about the understanding of the state of the self (the agent) as being connected with the factors of action (*kāraka*), due to their inseparable relationship (*avinābhāvitva*). In this way, the verbal nature (*śābdatva*) of that which is understood by this [process] is effectively discarded.

However, it would follow that [the word] falls within the scope of inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭānumāna*). And in that case, the comprehension of a specific [meaning] would result in being without a valid basis. Now, if it is argued that because linguistic usage is impossible without a connection to a specific [meaning], the utterance of a word would be purposeless, and therefore one must resort to that [specific meaning], even so—for those who act with foresight, since words possess meaningfulness as their sole quality, and because there would otherwise be a lack of purpose for the reason [for speaking], it is not possible to state a connection to a specific [meaning] due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Nor does it follow that [the cognition] would be purposeless even in the world; for this reason alone, it is not logical to conclude a specific [object] even without the means [of knowledge]. For it is not the case that because the employment of fuel by one desiring to burn is purposeless, the power to burn manifests in water. While it may well be that [the fuel] is purposeless, the general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*) does not possess a connection with a specific [object]. Now, if it is argued that through the usage of elders (*vṛddha-vyavahāra*), words are understood to have as their primary function a connection with what is required, proximate, and capable—then there is the comprehension of that connection.

That is not so. We consider that the inquiry—how, in the absence of any other means, can the words in the usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*) alone convey that [intended] meaning—is untenable without the postulation of either a power (*śakti*) in the words or a power in the word-meanings (*padārtha*). And we hold that this [power] belongs to the words alone. As it has been said: "Because they are primary, because they are the denoters, and because the intention is understood from them, let it be understood that this power belongs to the words alone; what else could it be?"

For words that occur first lack the capacity to convey the meaning of a sentence when their referents have already been transcended; therefore, since their power of denotation (*abhidhāna-śakti*) is universally accepted, it is easy to assume that this very power extends as far as the syntactic relation (*anvaya*). However, the power of the word-meanings themselves consists only in being cognized. Consequently, since the postulation of a property (*dharma*) is simpler than the postulation of a substratum (*dharmin*), it is more appropriate to assume that the power of denoting the syntactic relation belongs to the words alone. Moreover, words are held to be denotative.

In that regard, if they were to produce a cognition whose object is merely the word's own form (svarūpa), its capacity to denote [an object] would be lost; for, since that cognition arises from the grasping of a relationship, one must necessarily admit a residual impression (saṃskāra) common to the objects that constitute the related entities, in order to establish the recollection of the relationship.

Therefore, since the capacity of words to denote is accepted precisely as the communication of meanings that were not previously understood at the time of grasping the relationship [between word and object], one who accepts this must resort to the theory that words denote meanings as already connected (*anvitābhidhāna*). As for the one who, on the grounds that "a word does not differ from its recollection because there is no additional element," and observing the case of verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*) which, like in common worldly usage, cause the *bhāvanā* to be remembered, considers that the denotative power of words consists merely in their being reminders (*smāraka*), just like their power of denotation (*abhidhāna-śakti*).

Nor, for the time being, should it be admitted that words have the sentence-meaning as their primary referent, because otherwise it would follow that the sentence-meaning is not verbal (*aśābda*). If this is the case, let it be that the words themselves possess the power to directly convey the sentence-meaning; what is the use of resorting to an indirect process? Thus, for those who claim that words possess a denotative function (*abhidhā*) toward word-meanings in addition to their function as reminders (*smāraka*), there is the postulation of three distinct powers.

First, there is one power of words, namely the power of denotation (*abhidhāna-śakti*), and another power, the power of making known the syntactic relation (*anvaya-jñāpana-śakti*) of word-meanings. This is according to those who maintain that words are merely reminders (*smārakatva-vādin*), who thus postulate two powers. However, in the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*), there is only a single power; because this involves a parsimony of postulated powers (*śakti-kalpanā-lāghava*), it is logical that words express only what is already related, and not that there is a subsequent relation of meanings already expressed.

To this it is replied: as for the claim that there is the fault of conceptualizing a triple potency (*śakti*) in the capacity of word-meanings to convey syntactic connection (*anvaya*), that is not correct; for it is observed that word-meanings understood through other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) do indeed convey syntactic connection. As it is said: "For one who sees the white color and hears the sound of neighing, and also hears the sound of the hoof-beats, the cognition arises: 'A white horse is running.'"* *This verse is cited from Śālikanātha’s *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, 1.23.*

Nor should it be said that this is the operation of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) or inference (*anumāna*), because what is intended here is the cognition whose object is that [sentence-meaning]. For where the word-meanings themselves, endowed with the triad of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth, bring about mutual syntactic connection (*anvaya*), there the operation of presumptive testimony, inference, and the like does not apply. This is as in the cases: "Fragrant sandalwood" and "Sweet mango."

Furthermore, in this case of the cognition of a qualified object (*viśiṣṭapratipatti*), perception alone does not operate, because the eyes and other senses are restricted to their respective objects such as color-form (*rūpa*) and are not known to cognize one another's domains. For instance, the eye does not operate in the apprehension of odor and so forth, nor does the nose operate in the apprehension of color-form and so forth. Yet, there is indeed the cognition of a qualified object in cases such as "fragrant sandalwood. The same should be understood for the case of "a white horse is running."

As for what was asked here—“In which means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is this included?”—it is not included in any [of the established] means of valid cognition; rather, it is the fruit (*phala*) of a means of valid cognition. Alternatively, the object itself (*padārtha*) is the means of valid cognition in this case; and since these objects are included within verbal testimony (*śabda*), there is no emergence of a seventh means of valid cognition. For objects—whether apprehended from verbal testimony or from another means of valid cognition—when they are perceived in the form of action, agent, and so forth, through the requirements of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and semantic competency (*yogyatā*), generate the cognition of their mutual relation (*saṃsarga*).

This is merely a verbal [objection]. Furthermore, as for the point raised and refuted—that it is the word-meanings themselves, possessing expectancy, proximity, and compatibility, that become the sentence-meaning—we do not say that the word-meanings themselves become the sentence-meaning. Rather, what do they do? They cause [the sentence-meaning] to be understood.

Furthermore, as for the objection that there is a partial contradiction regarding the second word's capacity to express the related meaning by means of the analogy of the suffix (*pratyaya*), that too is not the case. For even in the instance of a base (*prakṛti*) and a suffix, just as in the case of a word, their distinct powers are determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); thus, the theory of "expression of the related" (*abhihitānvaya*) is indeed appropriate. For it is said: "The root *pac* alone expresses the act of cooking (*pāka*), and the suffix also expresses the agent (*kartṛ*). However, the agent as connected with the act of cooking is not the denotation of either one [of them] alone. Furthermore, the base and the suffix together express the meaning of the suffix. Thus, the theory of *abhihitānvaya* is established.

Even though they are designated as distinct, it is stated thus because of their predominance. However, regarding the referent of a sentence-meaning that is metaphorical (*lākṣaṇika*), we have been mistaken; for we do not admit metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in cases such as "Bring the cow," nor is it denied in cases such as "The hamlet on the Gaṅgā. Therefore, there is no inconsistency in the distinction between the primary and the metaphorical sentence-meanings.

As for the objection raised against the position that an action, once understood, makes known its own state as being connected with a *kāraka* because of their inseparable relationship (*avinābhāvitva*)—namely, that this involves the faults of failing to determine a specific [relation] and of not being verbal—that too is indeed accepted by us. For we do not maintain that the cognition of the sentence-meaning arises from a specific [relation] through inseparable concomitance; rather, it arises by the force of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and semantic competency (*yogyatā*). And when expectancy and the other factors are present, the status of being verbal (*śābdatva*) certainly obtains, as has been stated previously.

As for the argument that the words themselves possess the power to convey the relational connection (*anvaya*) by virtue of their primacy and so forth—that is not so; for while the denotative power (*abhidhāna-śakti*) of words is indeed accepted here, its extension to the relational connection is not accepted, because the cognition of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) can be accounted for otherwise. Indeed, it is the power of intentionality (*tātparya-śakti*) that is attributed to words regarding the sentence-meaning, not the denotative power. And you, by wishing to describe that initial stage, have admitted *anvitābhidhāna* (the denotation of the related); yet that is not tenable.

Since the denotative power (*abhidhātrī śakti*) operates everywhere without distinction, if there were no determination of the specific meaning of a word, the fault of rendering the utterance of other words redundant and so forth would necessarily follow. If other words are not uttered, it is impossible to maintain that "the word *go* denotes an object as connected with the triad [of relations], yet that [object] itself is not denoted while its connection is denoted"—for this is a contradiction. Furthermore, if that were denoted, it would involve the denotation of the relationship between the cognition and its object; thus, the single word *go* would come to signify everything.

Therefore, it is not tenable that a word possesses a denotative power (*abhidhātrī śakti*) with respect to everything; thus, there is no such thing as "denotation of the related" (*anvitābhidhāna*). By this, the following argument is also refuted: that one should merely postulate the power to convey the meanings of word-meanings (*padārtha*), whereas for words whose existence is already established, their capacity extends up to the relation (*anvaya*); since the postulation of a property (*dharma*) is simpler than the postulation of a substratum (*dharmī*), "denotation of the related" alone is logical.

As for the claim that the denotative power (*abhidhāna-śakti*) must have as its object a related meaning (*anvitārtha*), established through the cognition of the relata understood via the recollection of the relation—that too is untenable. This is because a word’s capacity to denote depends upon the recollection of its relation; yet, no such recollection of the relation occurs with respect to a related meaning. This is because, due to the infinity of possible correlates (*pratiyogin*), it is impossible to grasp the relation. Therefore, one must simply accept that the scope [of the word] is restricted solely to the isolated word-meaning (*niṣkṛṣṭa-padārtha*).

As for the objection raised regarding the fact that [words] have objects already apprehended, that is indeed true; for this very reason, a word is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to its own meaning, because its object is already apprehended. For a means of valid cognition is that which makes known an object not yet apprehended. Nor is it the case that a word merely recalls its own meaning. As it has been said: "A word does not differ from a mere recaller (of what is already known) because there is no additional [information]. However, it does not become a mere recaller. Therefore, it is logical that the connection of meanings through the denotation of words (*abhihitānvaya*) alone is correct.

The proponents of both views, however, maintain this: general denotation of the related (sāmānyato 'nvitābhidhāna) and specific denotation of the related (viśeṣato 'bhihitānvaya). For the word "cow" denotes its own referent as related to universals of qualities and actions whose particulars have not yet been apprehended; this is the general denotation of the related. But the specific quality such as "white" is understood from another word; this is the specific denotation of the related.

Moreover, the meaning of a sentence consists in the relation between action and its factors (kāraka), because the status of being a factor is not possible without a connection to an action. Furthermore, since there are defects such as infinite regress and deviation regarding specific instances, [the meaning] must be connected only with the general form of action. There is no apprehension of a relation between the words for the factors themselves; rather, they are denoted in accordance with that relation. Thus, it is only logical that they are denoted as connected with the general [action]. And at the time of linguistic usage, it is only the factors as connected with specific actions that are perceived.

Furthermore, since actions are also perceived as being associated with specific factors of action (*kāraka*), and because the function of the word is fully accomplished by denoting the connection with the general [category], it is logical that the connection occurs specifically with those particulars not already expressed. In this way, the utterance of other words is not rendered useless, for they possess meaning by providing the specific actions and factors of action required [by the general]. And although, in this context, the denotation of the connection between mere action and mere factor of action intends the connection with the general category of action and factor of action;

For instance, there is a capacity toward all particularities for that which grasps only its own object; that alone is the "mere conformity" (*anuguṇyamātra*) which constitutes the universal (*sāmānya*). Indeed, there is no such thing as a universal with a fixed form—neither as this, nor otherwise, nor in every way; all of those are merely particulars (*viśeṣa*).

In its state as a universal (*sāmānyāvasthā*), because no particular differentiation can be determined and because it has not yet abandoned anything, there exists a conceptualization of an object that fluctuates due to its capacity to encompass all particularities. Relation (*sambandha*) restricts this by delimiting it from other objects, confining it to each specific qualified object. As it has been said: "Others know the universal to be that which is compatible with all particularities; through its connection with other objects, it assumes the form of particulars. Its state of fluctuation arises from the absence of a desire for [specific] particulars."

It delimits the relation by situating it within a specific [referent]. For this very reason, there is no cognition of multiple sentence-meanings, because all *kārakas* (grammatical factors) are connected to the action only after they have been established in their respective roles as objects (*karman*) and so forth. Nor is there a cognition of the meaning of the sentence based on the nominative case alone, since even an existing syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is not perceived without the apprehension of the relation. Furthermore, the entire meaning of the sentence is not cognized at the time of the utterance of a single word, because at that time it would be improper to employ words that convey specific details.

If this is so, let there simply be the theory of the expression of what is already connected (*anvitābhidhāna*) in a general sense; why resort to the particular theory of the connection of what has been expressed (*abhihitānvaya*)? For a word is the designator of an object only when its relationship [to that object] is established through the linguistic usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*). Furthermore, the determination of that relationship occurs through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). And those two [concomitances] are not possible with respect to a specific connection. For a verb (*kriyāpada*) undergoes positive and negative concomitance with an action (*kriyā*) that does not deviate from the generality of being a factor (*kārakatā*), whereas in the case of a specific connection, there would be a deviation from other specific factors.

The same applies to the case of the word denoting the agent (*kāraka*). That is not so; for even when there is a connection with a particular (*viśeṣa*), it is easy to grasp the relation by virtue of the conditions of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and semantic competency (*yogyatā*); therefore, it is logical that words denote those [particulars]. If this were not accepted, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning would be impossible, because the sentence-meaning consists precisely in the connection with particulars. But surely, the connection with the universal (*sāmānya*) has already been denoted, since a particular is incapable of being understood as anything other than a universal? Not so.

Just as a genus, although it implies an individual, does not imply a specific individual, so too here, due to the absence of a restricted particular, the cognition of a sentence-meaning consisting of a restricted particular is not established. [Objection: Even when there is only a general implication of particulars, that very particular which is required, proximate, and capable, and which is supplied by another word, is what is grasped; for there is no evidence for bypassing this. [Response: This also is not correct.

For according to the view of those who maintain that words denote [their meanings] as already associated with a universal (*sāmānyānvitābhidhānavāda*), words possess a power that terminates only in that [universal], and it is not admitted that word-meanings themselves have the power to bring about the cognition of a mutual relation (*anvaya*). Furthermore, even the implication (*ākṣepa*) of a universal does not reach a specific instance (*viśeṣa*) determined [by context]. Therefore, since there is no means for bringing about the cognition of the relation when a specific [meaning]—which is required (*ākāṅkṣita*), capable (*yogya*), and presented by another word (*sannidhāpita*)—is lacking, no relation is perceived. Consequently, expectancy, proximity, and capability are indeed useless [as conditions for verbal comprehension].

However, in the view of the proponents of the theory that words denote [objects] as qualified by particulars (*viśeṣānvitābhidhānavādin*), those factors which enter as conditions for the apprehension of the relation are what serve in the comprehension of the sentence-meaning. Regarding the linguistic convention that "from a word, the word-meaning—namely, a relation with another word-meaning—is to be understood," the author refutes the position of the *viśeṣānvitābhidhānavādins*, in whose view factors such as semantic competency (*yogyatā*) enter as conditions, but not the position of the proponents of the theory that words denote generalities (*sāmānyābhidhānavādins*).

Furthermore, even by examining the nature of action and its factors (*kāraka*), since the connection is established through the mere factor itself, it is futile to accept that a word expresses a connection with the mere universal (*sāmānya*). Therefore, the logic stated therein is superior: namely, that there is expression of connection through the universal, while the connection occurs through the particular (*viśeṣa*). And this is logical because a word consists of both stem (*prakṛti*) and suffix (*pratyaya*). For in a word such as *pacati* ("he cooks"), the meaning of the stem and the meaning of the suffix—which consist of the apprehension of the universal and the particular respectively—are perceived as mutually connected.

In this context, the verbal root *pac* denotes a mere universal of "cooking" (*pāka-sāmānya-mātra*), which is devoid of properties such as being already accomplished or yet to be accomplished, and is capable of being construed solely with the meaning of the suffix. However, the suffix, due to its restriction by the rule of temporal sequence (the priority of the root), does not, like the root, independently instill a cognition of a mere universal; rather, while expressing its own meaning, it presents that very meaning as a particular in dependence upon the meaning of the root.

The proponents of the theory of experience (*anubhavavādins*), however, justify it in this way: there is no denotation of related meanings (*anvitābhidhāna*); rather, a single sentence-meaning is conveyed by the words acting in concert, and that meaning is simply a certain word-meaning itself as connected with the other word-meanings functioning as subordinate elements. Now, is it intended to revive the position of *anvitābhidhāna* once again? Not so; this is not *anvitābhidhāna*. What then? It is the state of the words acting in combination (*saṃhatyakāratā*). It is said: the state of acting in combination does indeed exist, yet it is not *anvitābhidhāna*.

Words, having come together, bring about the meaning as already possessed by the relation [of expectancy], but they do not denote that which is related. What, then, do words do with respect to the sentence-meaning? Do they produce it, like clay and other materials produce a jar? This is not the case, because their function is that of indicators (jñāpaka).

What, then, is the logic of this statement? [The opponent claims: "Words function collectively, yet they do not denote the related [meaning]; these words cause the related meaning to be understood, but they do not denote it. Thus, the denotative power (*abhidhā-śakti*) does not have the related meaning as its object; rather, it has as its object only the isolated individual meanings known through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). However, their *tātparya-śakti* (the power of intentionality) extends up to the comprehension of the related meaning, because they function together, and because their function culminates in the production of a cognition that is free from further expectancy regarding that [related meaning].

For indeed, perceptions arising from direct experience manifest in one way, presenting an object—whether previously known or unknown—as standing before one; whereas verbal expression manifests in quite another way regarding its objects, extending until it produces in the cognizer a cognition that leaves no further desire for more. For this very reason, a single word is never used alone in common usage, for by means of a single word, the listener’s mind would not be rendered free from expectancy.

Now, what other operation of a word—distinct from denotation (*abhidhāna*)—is there that consists in conveying the meaning up to its complete result? There is indeed one such [operation] which cannot be denied by any proponents of the theory of relation (*saṃsarga*). For it is not the case that the relation is denoted; yet it is perceived through the sentence. [Objection: But surely, the relation is perceived only when there is the denotation of related things, and not otherwise. [Reply: This is not so, because the comprehension of the relation is established precisely through the fact that [the words] act in combination (*saṃhatyākāritva*).

For nowhere is an effect seen that is not touched by its cause of conjunction. Furthermore, the base (prakṛti) and the suffix (pratyaya) denote their meaning only through mutual dependence. The meaning of the suffix is not denoted by the base, because it is to be expressed by the verbal root (dhātu). Nor is the meaning of the base denoted by the suffix, because [otherwise] the meaning of the optative suffix (liṅ) and so forth would be incompatible with the root *yaj* and others. And yet, those two do not produce their respective effects separately.

In this way, words as well, being mutually dependent, will perform their function by combining together; yet they will not express the meaning of one another. Sentences that fall within a specific context (prakaraṇa) function in exactly the same manner. As it has been said: "Just as a base (prakṛti) and a suffix (pratyaya) depend upon each other, so too does one word depend on another word, and likewise a sentence on another sentence. And this very position is the most excellent, because it accounts for the collective action of word-meanings and their mutual intermingling.

In the theory of independent expression (*nirapekṣaprayoga*), whatever conceptualization might arise, if one were to express [the meaning] as already connected (*anvitābhidhāna*), then the final word would be rendered meaningless. However, in the view that words act in combination (*saṃhatyakāripakṣa*), not a single fault is applicable; therefore, this path should be accepted as free from thorns. The expressive power (*abhidhātrī śakti*) of words is considered to reside in their own individual meanings; however, their power of intention (*tātparyaśakti*) extends until the comprehension of the mutual connection [of those meanings]. Therefore, we do not accept here the doctrine of "expression of the connected" (*anvitābhidhāna*).

The cognition of the related [meaning] (anvitapratipatti), however, is certainly accepted. Because words function through cooperation (saṃhatyakāritva), their utterance is not for the sake of their own individual meanings alone, but rather to accomplish the primary task. As it has been said: "In their activity toward the comprehension of the sentence-meaning, the communication of word-meanings is an inseparable byproduct, just as the flame is to wood in the process of cooking. Therefore, there is neither the expression of the related (anvitābhidhāna) nor the relation of those already expressed (abhihitānvaya); rather, the position previously set forth is indeed the best.

Thus, word-meanings possessing expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and compatibility (*yogyatā*) become the sentence-meaning by undergoing a fourfold type of syntactic connection (*anvaya*). Now, one might object: "But even in cases of incompatibility (*ayogyatā*), a connection is observed, as in the expression: 'Look, the deer is running. For it is not logical that something whose sole nature is that of an effect (*sādhya*) could simultaneously possess both the state of being an effect and the state of being a cause (*sādhana*). This is not so; for it is precisely through its status as an effect that it possesses the status of a cause. Having the nature of coming-into-being (*bhavana*) in the form of the accomplishment of an action (*kriyābhyupapatti*), it exists in the form of a sequence precisely by virtue of its nature as an effect.

If it is asked: "Since its state of being is indeed non-toothed (inarticulate), indefinable, and unestablished—having the form of that which is yet to be accomplished (sādhya)—how can it appear as established (siddha) when it attains the status of an object to be accomplished (sādhya-bhāva) in this context? [The answer is: The *lakāra* suffix produced for the agent causes it to appear as established. Just as in the case of *corasya rujati* ("the thief suffers"): the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) characterized by suffering appears as established even while experiencing the state of an agent in the form of something to be accomplished, because no other agent is heard.

Alternatively, if there is no additional meaning in the word itself, from what then does it arise? It arises from the form of the sentence. For example, at the time of the word "man" (*puruṣa*), a man is expressed as distinct [from others]. But when there is proximity to a qualifier, such as "the king's man," then its distinction becomes manifest; this is a specific kind of man, namely "the king's man. In the same way, in the case of "he cooks" (*pacati*), the additional meaning does not arise from the form of the word alone.

But when there is the proximity of another word such as *bhavati*, then at the time of the sentence, a distinction (*vyatireka*) arises, just as it does for a person [as a distinct agent]. Or rather, there is never another action of "becoming" (*bhavana*) that exceeds this [inherent activity], nor is there any other agent who could serve as a cause of contradiction. On the contrary, that very [activity] shines forth, displaying both the nature of an action and the state of being the locus of becoming (*bhavitṛtva*), according to the principle of "behaving like that which possesses a designation" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*).

Moreover, even for a single entity, a dual nature is observed due to the difference in its relations (*viṣaya*), as in the case of "the king's man" or "the man's son. Here, the man is both the *śeṣin* (the principal) and the *śeṣa* (the subordinate); with respect to the king, he is the *śeṣin*. While his own status as "son"—which does not waver from its own meaning—is fixed, he attains the state of being a *śeṣa* by wavering from his own primary status. In the same way, in the expression "he cooks" (*pacati*), there will be for the agent (*bhavat*) both non-agency and the state of being that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*).

And observe that in the expression "the deer runs" (*mṛgo dhāvati*), the deer, without abandoning its status as the agent (*kartṛ*), its state of being the goal (*sādhyabhāva*), or its predominance (*prādhānya*), will attain the status of an accessory (*aṅgatva*) and an instrument (*sādhanatva*) with respect to the act of seeing. Therefore, this distinction that "this is the means" and "this is the goal" is merely a conventional designation (*prasiddhimātra*). Just as in a word one says "this is the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*)" and "this is the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*"), even though that single meaning is perceived either as qualified or as a distinct part—just as in the cases of *muṇḍayati* (he shaves) or *carcayati* (he recites).

In this context, the word *muṇḍayati* in the expression *muṇḍayati māṇavakam* signifies the cutting of hair. Its etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) is "he makes [the boy] bald" (*muṇḍaṃ karoti*). The word *muṇḍa*, which applies generally, restricts the verb *karoti* (to do/make) to this specific sense. This is a specific instance of "doing" (*karoti-viśeṣa*), for which the suffix *ṇic* is produced, and not merely "doing" in its general sense. In the same way, one says *carcayati* in the sense of "he performs a discussion" (*carcāṃ karoti*).

Therefore, some read *muṇḍ*, *carca*, and so forth among the roots beginning with *ciri* [DhP 6.127], deriving [the forms] from the sense of shaving (*miṇḍ*) or cutting hair (*keśakhaṇḍana*), as in "he shaves" (*muṇḍayati*) or "he recites" (*carcayati*). Likewise, in the example "look, the deer runs," this is merely a mental construction where one considers this to be the word expressing the means (*sādhana*) and that to be the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*). However, this is the true nature of the meaning: here there is no running, no seeing, and no deer. Rather, the sentence-meaning is this specific act of running, which has the deer as its agent and is the object of the verb "to see."

By this, forms such as *putrīyati* ("he desires a son") are also explained. The state of becoming inseparable—like sesame and rice, like milk and water, or like dust and sugar—in the case of word-meanings that are mutually expectant (*vyapekṣāvat*), semantically competent (*samartha*), and possess a connected meaning (*anvitārtha*), is what constitutes *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning). This definition applies both collectively and individually; therefore, it includes compounds where there is mutual expectancy or where the parts are not semantically independent (*asamartha*).

What is the difference [between *vyapekṣā*] and a compound (*samāsa*)? It is said: in the case of *vyapekṣā*, there is the expression of a specific number, the qualification of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*), conjunction (*ca-yoga*), lack of restriction regarding word order (*krama*), intervention (*vyavadhāna*), the optional application of singular status (*ekavadbhāva*) as desired, and the formation of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*). Furthermore, there is the unification of various types [of meanings] and the non-unification of a single type. For example, in the case of *vyapekṣā*, there is a specific number: "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), "the king’s man" (*rājño puruṣaḥ*), or "the men of the kings" (*rājñāṃ puruṣaḥ*). But in the case of *ekārthībhāva* (integration into a single meaning), that [specificity] is absent: "king-man" (*rājapuruṣaḥ*).

In the state of mutual expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), there is the explicit mention of individual words, as in "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*); but in the state of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), as in *rājapuruṣaḥ*, there is neither the suffix for the second person singular nor the elision of the case-ending, and thus there is no explicit mention of the individual words. In the state of mutual expectancy, there is qualification of the subordinate member (*upasarjana*), as in "the man of a wealthy king" (*ṛddhasya rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*); in the state of unified meaning, that [qualification] is absent, as in *rājapuruṣaḥ*. Furthermore, in the state of mutual expectancy, there is a connection [with other words], as in "the man of the king and of the Brahmin" (*rājñaḥ puruṣo brāhmaṇasya ca*).

In the case of *ekārthībhāva* (integration into a single meaning), however, we have "rājapuruṣaḥ" (the king’s man); whereas in the case of *vyapekṣā* (mutual expectancy), there is no fixed order: "rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ" (the king’s man) or "puruṣaḥ rājñaḥ" (the man of the king). In *ekārthībhāva*, however, it is only "rājapuruṣaḥ ayam" (this is the king’s man). In *vyapekṣā*, there is a connection with other words as desired: "rājñaḥ puruṣo vā bhāryā vā" (the king’s man or the king’s wife). In *ekārthībhāva*, however, by rule, the connection is only with the man, not with the wife. In *vyapekṣā*, there is the employment of other words: "dadhnopasiktam" (sprinkled with curd), "pariglāno 'dhyayanāya" (exhausted for study).

But this is not the case when there is *ekārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning), as in *dadhyodanam* (curd-rice) or *paryadhyayanam* (cessation of study). In *ekārthībhāva*, there is: 1. *Aikapadya* (being a single word), as in *ātmanā tṛtīyaḥ* (the third with himself) or *kaṇṭhe kālaḥ* (one whose throat is black). 2. *Aikaśabdhya* (having a single accent), as in *pitarau* (parents) or *bhrātarau* (brothers). 3. *Aikasvaryam* (having a single tone), as in *citraguḥ* (one who has brindled cows) or *brāhmaṇakambalaḥ* (a Brahmin’s blanket). 4. *Ekavibhaktitvam* (having a single case-ending), as in *nīlotpalam* (blue lotus) or *rājapuruṣaḥ* (king’s man). 5. *Ekavadbhāvaḥ* (behaving as a singular), as in *gavāśvam* (cows and horses) or *plakṣanyagrodhaḥ* (the *plakṣa* and *nyagrodha* trees).

The formation of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*) is as in the examples *akṣāḥ* (dice) and *vṛkṣāḥ* (trees). The unification of multiple distinct things is as in *putrīyati* (he wishes for a son for himself), derived from *putram icchati*, and *muṇḍayati* (he makes [someone] bald), derived from *muṇḍaṃ karoti*. The non-unification of identical things is as in *kaṃsaṃ ghātayati* (he causes Kaṃsa to be killed), derived from *kaṃsavadham ācaṣṭe* (he narrates the killing of Kaṃsa), and *candreṇa yojayati* (he joins with the moon), derived from *puṣyacandrayogaṃ jānāti* (he knows the conjunction of the Puṣya asterism and the moon). However, in the case of syntactic expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), this is not so.

This very state of unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*), manifesting as distinct from syntactic expectancy (*vyapekṣā*), is known as "sameness" (*sāmānya*) and is proclaimed in three ways across the three categories of compounds, secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), and verbal forms: namely, having a meaning equal to the sentence (*vākyatulyārtha*), having a meaning exceeding the sentence (*vākyādhikārtha*), and having a meaning different from the sentence (*vākyānyārtha*). An example of having a meaning equal to the sentence is *vīraḥ puruṣaḥ* (a brave man) becoming *vīrapuruṣaḥ* (a brave man), or *kaṣṭaṃ śritaḥ* (one who has resorted to hardship) becoming *kaṣṭaśritaḥ* (one who has resorted to hardship).

An example of the meaning of a sentence (*vākyādhikārtha*) is "grains mixed with molasses" (*guḍadhānāḥ*), or "a piece cut by a saw" (*śaṅkulākhaṇḍaḥ*). An example of the meaning other than the sentence (*vākyanyārtha*) is "one who gathers *kuśa* grass" (*kuśalaḥ*), or "one who is pre-eminent" (*pravīṇaḥ*). Now, this [compound] is divided in many ways, even though it consists of these three types.

Namely: obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*), non-obligatory compound (*anityasamāsa*), non-cohesive compound (*asamarthasamāsa*), non-elided compound (*aluksamāsa*), dependent compound (*sāpekṣasamāsa*), independent compound (*nirapekṣasamāsa*), that which has the prior member as the predominant element (*pūrvapadapradhāna*), that which has the posterior member as the predominant element (*uttarapadapradhāna*), that which has both members as the predominant elements (*ubhayapadapradhāna*), that which has neither member as the predominant element (*anubhayapadapradhāna*), that which has its secondary member [in a different way] (*anyathopasarjana*), verbal compound (*tiṅsamāsa*), nominal-stem compound (*prātipadikasamāsa*), compound with an accompanying word (*upapadasamāsa*), compound beginning with *pra* and other prefixes (*prādisamāsa*), negative compound (*nañsamāsa*), partitive compound (*ekadeśisamāsa*), general compound (*sāmānyasamāsa*), specific compound (*viśeṣasamāsa*), and coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa*).

There are three types: those with different substrata (*bhinnādhikaraṇa*), compounds based on comparison (*upamānasamāsa*), and compounds based on the object of comparison (*upameyasamāsa*). Among these, an obligatory compound (*nityasamāsa*) is, for example: *lobhitaśāliḥ* (one who has eaten rice), *gaurakharaḥ* (a wild ass), *uddālapuṣpabhañjikā* (the game of breaking *uddāla* flowers), and *dantalekhakaḥ* (a tooth-scratcher). An obligatory non-compound (*nityāsamāsa*) is, for example: *kiñcitkurvāṇaḥ* (doing something), *amāṣaṃ haramāṇaḥ* (taking without beans), *agādham utsṛptāḥ* (slipped into the deep), and *chātrāṇāṃ pañcamaḥ* (the fifth of the students). A compound of incapacity (*asamarthasamāsa*) is, for example: *sūryampaśyā rājadārāḥ* (the king's wives who do not look at the sun), *apunargeyāḥ ślokāḥ* (verses not to be sung again), *aśrāddhabhojī brāhmaṇaḥ* (a Brahmin who does not eat at a funeral feast), and *alavaṇabhojī bhikṣuḥ* (a mendicant who does not eat salt).

An example of an *aluk* compound (where the case-ending is not elided) is: *stokānmuktaḥ* ("freed with little effort"), *ātmanā tṛtīyaḥ* ("the third person himself"), *paśyato haraḥ* ("the thief while [he] was looking"), and *kaṇṭhe kālaḥ* ("Kāla [Death] upon the neck"). An example of a compound involving a relative dependency (*sāpekṣasamāsa*) is: *yajñadattasya bhrātṛbhāryā* ("the wife of Yajñadatta’s brother"), *viṣṇumitrasya gurukulam* ("the teacher’s family of Viṣṇumitra"), *cūtasya phalarasaḥ* ("the juice of the mango fruit"), and *priyāyāḥ stanaparśaḥ* ("the touch of the beloved’s breast").

An example of an independent compound (*nirapekṣasamāsa*) is: "one whose lifespan is a hundred years" as *śatāyuḥ*; "a king for whom vegetables are the primary [food]" as *śākapārthivaḥ*; "a chariot yoked with horses" as *aśvarathaḥ*; and "those who were not guilds made into guilds" as *śreṇīkṛtāḥ*. An example of a compound where the first member is predominant (*pūrvapadapradhāna*) is: *upakumbham* (near the jar), *nirmakṣikam* (free from flies), *bahirgrāmam* (outside the village), and *pārogaṅgam* (beyond the Gaṅgā). An example of a compound where the second member is predominant (*uttarapadapradhāna*) is: "a tree on which a monkey has climbed" as *ārūḍhavānaro vṛkṣaḥ*; "a cart-puller who is not a horse" as *ūḍharatho'naḍvān*; "Devadatta who has crossed over three [stages]" as *titra-gur devadattaḥ*; and "a forest containing intoxicated elephants" as *mattamātaṅgaṃ vanam*.

A case where the primary member (*pradhāna*) is otherwise [than its usual position] is, for example: *unmattagaṅgam*, *pañcakapālaḥ*, *dvitrāḥ*, and *kṛṣṇaśāraḥ*. A case where the subordinate member (*upasarjana*) is otherwise is, for example: *śākaprati*, *prāptajīvikaḥ*, *gogarbhiṇī*, and *agnistokaḥ*. An example of a *tiṅ*-compound (verbal compound) is: *astikṣīrā*, *ehivāṇijā*, *aśnītapibatā*, and *svādatamodatā*. An example of a nominal-stem compound (*prātipadika-samāsa*) is: *dadhiseka* and *carmakrīti*. An example of a derivative-object compound (*upapada-samāsa*) is: *kumbhakāraḥ*, *paṅkajam*, *uṣṭrakrośī*, and *sahayudhvā*.

An example of a *prādi* compound (prepositional compound) is: *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* (one who has departed from Kauśāmbī), *utpaśyaḥ* (looking up), *durāsadaḥ* (difficult to approach), and *suprabodhaḥ* (easy to awaken). An example of a *nañ* compound (negative compound) is: *abrāhmaṇaḥ* (a non-Brahmin), *anekaḥ* (not one), *abhāryaḥ* (one without a wife), and *apacasīti* (one who does not cook). An example of an *ekadeśin* compound (part-whole compound) is: *candramukhī* (she whose face is like the moon), *mṛgacapalā* (fickle as a deer), *śastraśyāmā* (dark as a sword-blade), and *ananyasadṛśī* (having no equal).

An example of a compound with the object of comparison (*upameya*) as the first member is: "a man like a tiger" (*puruṣavyāghraḥ*), "a young elephant like an elephant" (*karikalabhaḥ*), "a king like a tiger" (*rājaśārdūlaḥ*), and "a face like the moon" (*mukhacandraḥ*). Now, what is the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and what is the object of comparison (*upameya*)? Is that which is the standard of comparison also the object of comparison, or is the standard of comparison one thing and the object of comparison another? What follows from this? If that which is the standard of comparison were also the object of comparison, the purpose of comparison would not be established.

For it is not the case that "a cow is like a cow," since the object of comparison must be one thing and the object compared another; nevertheless, the purpose of the comparison does not hold. Nor is it the case that "a horse is like a cow. If this is so, then the object of comparison and the object compared exist only where there is some commonality and some distinction. Is this something that needs to be stated? For it is never understood from what has not been stated; indeed, a means of knowledge (*māna*) is employed for the purpose of making known what was previously unknown.

Just as a measure such as a *prastha* is employed for the sake of the absolute determination of a measurable object like grain that has not yet been determined, and it does not measure it absolutely in its proximity—that is *upamāna*, as in "the *gavaya* is like a cow. If the cow is already known, then for one who knows the *gavaya* but does not know the cow, the cow must be made known by means of the statement, "The cow is like the *gavaya*."

Certainly, it must be done in such a way that entities whose forms are superimposed with difference and similarity attain the relationship of standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and object of comparison (*upameya*) through mutual determination. For example: "the face of the beloved is like the moon" at night, or "the moon is like the face of the beloved" during the day. However, where there is no superimposition of forms characterized by difference and similarity, there is also no relationship of standard and object of comparison; as in "a cow is like a cow," or "a cow is like a horse."

[Objection: Surely, these entities which are superimposed with difference and similarity cannot exist without a contradiction produced by factors such as place, time, and action; thus, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would be untenable. [Response: It is not so. Although the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) are ultimately distinct, nevertheless, words denoting the standard of comparison, by resorting to a secondary function (*gauṇī vṛtti*), operate upon the object of comparison and thereby conceal their difference.

For instance, when [words such as] *vyāghra* (tiger) and so forth, having experienced a relationship between a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and an object of comparison (*upameya*) based on an excellence of qualities such as bravery, subsequently apply the superimposed distinctions arising from that relationship of comparison and contrasted object to the object of comparison—as in "this man is like a tiger" or "he is a tiger"—then they are compounded with words such as *puruṣa* (man) when they share a common locus (*abhinnādhikaraṇa*). Now, does the cognition of similarity arise only from those words which are the basis for the cognition of the standard and object of comparison, or does it arise from both those and others?

What follows from this? If [the second view were correct], then even in the case of "Look at the man as a tiger" (*puruṣaṃ vyāghraṃ ca vīkṣasva*), there would be the same result; furthermore, the use of the particle *iva* would be redundant. If, on the other hand, the second position were true, one would have to say simply "The man is like a tiger" (*puruṣo vyāghra iva*), and not "Man-tiger" (*puruṣavyāghra*). Let it be as you wish. For now, let us assume the first position. But was it not already stated that even in the case of "Look at the man as a tiger," there would be a comprehension of similarity?

For here, it is merely the coincidence of the two tigers among men in their act of looking that is intended to be expressed, not similarity. Now, one might object: even if it is intended [as such], the employment of the word *iva* would be useless, since the cognition of similarity occurs regardless. It is only in cases where words denoting a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) are applied to specific objects of comparison (*upameya*) by resorting to a secondary (*gauṇī*) function through a departure from their primary function (*mukhyavṛtti*), that they convey similarity even when devoid of words such as *iva*.

Just as when someone says of a man who is not a tiger, "He is a tiger," we understand from this that this man is similar to a tiger; and consequently, through the word "tiger," there will be a cognition in the man of the qualities of a tiger, such as bravery, strength, and so forth.

Furthermore, when the words denoting the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*)—in sentences where the intended relationship of comparison is to be expressed—are unable to convey the sense of similarity because they are incapable of abandoning their own primary meanings, they require the employment of a second word such as *iva*. What, then, is an example of this? It is: "śastrīva śyāmā" (dark like a knife) or "śastrīśyāmā" (knife-dark). But surely, in this case, the word *iva* is employed precisely to illuminate the equality of the quality conveyed by the word "śyāmā" between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison.

But in the case of "a man like a tiger" (*vyāghra iva puruṣaḥ*), since there is no application of a common property (*sāmānya*), of what is the similarity between the man and the tiger manifested by the word *iva*? It is said: a word conveys a meaning sometimes through the function of direct denotation (*abhidhā-vṛtti*), as the word *guḍa* [conveys] the substance molasses; and sometimes through the function of indication (*gamaka-vṛtti*), as [the word *guḍa* conveys] the sweetness which is invariably concomitant with the substance molasses.

Thus, in this case, by the word "tiger" (*vyāghra*), the quality of courage (*śaurya*) which is invariably concomitant with a tiger is indicated; then, the use of the suffix *-iva* is employed to illuminate the fact that both [the tiger and the man] share a common substratum, for the purpose of establishing the similarity between the tiger and the man. By this, the expression *śastrī-śyāmā* ("dark as a knife") is also explained. Here too, although not explicitly mentioned, "Devadatta" is understood. But where does this word "dark" (*śyāmā*) reside? He says: it resides in the knife. If so, how is Devadatta understood now? It is understood through the compound (*samāsa*).

When it is stated that "similes are compounded with words expressing commonality," and that this commonality can only exist when there is a shared quality, yet that [shared quality] is not possible without Devadatta, then the expression *śastrīśyāmo devadattaḥ* ("Devadatta is dark like a sword-blade") would not be established. [Objection: The shortening of the vowel will occur by the rule *upasarjanasya*. [Reply: If that is so, then even such items as these would be considered *upasarjana*s (subordinate members). Consequently, in the case of *tattirikalmaṣīkumbhakapālalohinī*, the long vowel *ī*—which is the characteristic mark of what is not an *upasarjana*—would not be obtained.

In that case, the word *śastrī* refers only to the knife, while the word *śyāmā* refers to Devadattā. Even so, the quality (*guṇa*) is indicated; for there are many qualities in the knife: it is fine, smooth, sharp, broad, and dark-blue (*śyāmā*). Even when a quality is not explicitly mentioned, it is understood in common usage, as in the expression "Devadattā has a moon-like face" (*candramukhī devadattā*). Although there are many qualities in the moon, that specific quality which consists of being pleasant to behold is what is understood.

And just as in the expression "this man is a tiger," even though there are many qualities of a tiger, it is specifically valor or strength that is perceived; so too, the term "by means of a coordinate [term]" (*samānādhikaraṇena*) continues to apply here. Because the terms are not in apposition (*vyadhikaraṇatvāt*), the compound does not obtain. For why would it not occur by virtue of an explicit rule? Even if the compound were to occur by virtue of such a rule, in the case of *mṛgacapalā* ("fickle as a deer"), where [the analysis is] "fickle like a female deer" (*mṛgīva capalā*), the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāvaḥ*)—which is characterized by coordination—would not obtain. Therefore, in this very case, both [conditions] are present.

And this is the logical conclusion here: that both [qualities] reside in that very same [Devadatta]; for otherwise, there would be a dependence on too many factors. When the analysis (*vigraha*) is performed in this way—namely, "Devadatta is dark like a sword-woman" (*śastrīśyāmā*)—then the quality of being dark would depend upon the sword-woman. But when the analysis is "she is both a sword-woman who is dark and she is dark herself" (*śastrīśyāmā cāsau śyāmā ca śastrīśyāmā*), then nothing is depended upon, and there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

If this is so, then the ground for the application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word "sword-bearer" (*śastrin*) with respect to Devadatta would remain undetermined. If you say that it will be understood through implication, I ask: what is it? If it is simply "darkness" (*śyāmatva*), then because the meaning has already been expressed by the word "dark" (*śyāma*), the use of the former would result in redundancy. For when qualities have already been conveyed through figurative application (*guṇavṛtti*), a word denoting that quality (*guṇavacana*) is not employed to express them again; for one does not say, "This man is a tiger-hero" (*vyāghraśūra*).

Now, if the word *śastrī* (knife) applies to Devadattā by taking up unexpressed qualities such as sharpness and so forth, then—in the case of a compound with two words expressing the quality of sharpness—the rule "comparisons [are compounded] with words expressing common properties" (*upamānāni sāmānyavacanaiḥ*) would be contradicted, and the usage *śyāma-śastrī* (a dark knife) would result. [Objection: Since faults are seen in all three positions and there is no other alternative, must it not necessarily be that the comparison-compound (*upamāna-samāsa*) occurs?

However, having set aside the two previously mentioned positions, in the middle position—just as in the case of "Devadatta is dark like a female rhinoceros" (*śastrīva śyāmā devadattā*)—the transformation to the masculine form (*puṃvadbhāva*) occurs by the force of the statement itself, even though there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*avaiyadhikaraṇye*). Now, it was argued that in the example "a deer-like woman" (*mṛgacapalā*), the masculine transformation required by the definition of coreferential compounds does not apply. This is not so. Here, the first member of the compound is not intended to be expressed as a female rhinoceros (*śastrī*), but rather merely by way of the genus "deer" (*mṛgatva*), just as in the cases of "deer-milk" (*mṛgakṣīram*) and "hen-egg" (*kukkuṭāṇḍam*).

In a comparative compound (*upamāna-samāsa*), because the word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*) functions as a specific term (*viśeṣavacana*), its status as a general term (*sāmānyavacana*) is not established. This is because this word "dark" (*śyāma*), when connected with the word "dagger" (*śastrī*) for the sake of establishing a similarity, is connected as a specific term. Consequently, since the quality of darkness exists in both [the dagger and the woman] and the word expresses that [quality], the status of the word as a general term is established. Furthermore, it is not necessarily the case that only that [word] is a general term.

He who states the commonality (*sāmānya*) of many, and he who states the commonality of even two—both are "denoters of the general" (*sāmānyavacana*). Alternatively, by the term *sāmānyavacanaiḥ*, the word *srava* itself, when connected with another [word], becomes a "denoter of the particular" (*viśeṣavacana*). Therefore, we shall understand it thus: that which is a denoter of the general prior to its connection [with another word]. But if this is the case, then in the rule *upamitaṃ vyāghrādibhiḥ* (P. 2.1.56), the inclusion of the phrase *sāmānyāprayoge* ("when there is no employment of the general") would be redundant.

Even when words such as "tiger" (*vyāghra*) are employed based on a distinction [between the subject and the object], if they function solely as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), they require the employment of a general term [expressing the common property]. For example: "This man is brave like a tiger; he is powerful like a lion. However, when the expression begins with non-difference (*abheda*), since the basis for the relationship is already included within the words denoting the standard of comparison themselves, there is no employment of a general term. And even in the absence of such a term, the determination of the common property will occur just as it does in the case of "moon-face" (*candramukha*).

It has been stated that "siṃho vyāghraḥ" (a lion-like tiger) is used for praise, while "svā kākāḥ" (one's own crows) is used for contempt; however, this is not so. Even if, in order to express the meanings of internalized comparison and contempt, words such as "vyāghra" (tiger) are employed to denote the object of comparison—such as a person—for the sake of praise, nevertheless, because there is no restriction regarding the multiplicity of those causes, it is not contradicted when words such as "śaurya" (valor), ending in the instrumental case to indicate the cause, are employed.

In the expression "This man is a tiger" (*puruṣo 'yaṃ vyāghraḥ*) on account of his heroism, there is indeed a metaphorical attribution of non-difference (*abhedopacāraḥ*) to distinct entities; this conveys merely a similarity of form (*sārūpyamātram*), but not the actual excellence of the self (*tasyātmātiśayam*). For instance, in cases such as *sumanāyate*, *durmanāyate*, and *abhimanāyate*—where *su*, *duḥ*, and *abhi* function as qualifiers of the root meaning—the prefix is employed to delimit the meaning of the preposition (*upasarga*), since the distinction between the meanings conveyed by the suffixes cannot be determined due to the lack of difference in the form of the suffix itself.

How is it that, when various specific causes for that honorific usage are possible—as in the case of "puruṣavyāghra" (tiger among men) and so forth—a word is employed that brings about a similar application in order to establish a restriction? In this way, this single unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) should be understood as having infinitely many varieties even in the case of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) and verbal suffixes (*ākhyāta*). Among those, in the case of secondary derivatives, it is generally threefold: pertaining to relations (*sambandha*), pertaining to grammatical factors (*kāraka*), and pertaining to the inherent meaning (*svārtha*). Within these, relation is twofold: primary and secondary.

When primary, as in: "he has cows" (*gāvaḥ asya santi*) [becomes] *gavya*; "his birthplace is Sālātura" [becomes] *sālāturīya*. When secondary, as in: "an enemy to be killed with poison" [becomes] *viṣayaḥ śatruḥ*; "mud in which a foot is seen" [becomes] *padyaḥ kardamaḥ*. When secondary, as in: "one who knows or studies grammar" [becomes] *vaiyākaraṇaḥ*; "one who plays with dice" [becomes] *ākṣikaḥ*. The primary sense is twofold: literal (*mukhya*) and figurative (*upacarita*). The literal is, for example: "barley itself is *yāvaka*"; "a gem itself is *māṇika*."

It is used figuratively (upacarita), as in "the intellect of Ruśāgrīya" (*ruśāgrīyā buddhiḥ*) and "the maxim of the crow and the palm fruit" (*kākatālīyo nyāyaḥ*), which is like the "crow-and-palm-fruit" occurrence (*kākātālīyam*). It is also used in three ways when applied to a verb (*ākhyāta*): by means of a kāraka, by means of a related noun (*sambandhin*), and by means of prefixes (*prādi*). By means of a kāraka, for example: *bhṛśo bhṛśo bhavati* becomes *bhṛśāyate*; "he makes a sound" becomes *śabdāyate*; "he passes by with an elephant" becomes *atihastayati*; "he exerts himself toward a difficult task" becomes *kaṣṭāyate*; "he releases from bonds" becomes *vipāśayati*; and "he acts like a palace" becomes *prāsādīyati*.

As for [the use of] a related term (*sambandhin*): one composes the aphorisms of grammar, i.e., "he aphorizes grammar" (*vyākaraṇaṃ sūtrayati*); one narrates the slaying of Kaṃsa, i.e., "he causes Kaṃsa to be slain" (*kaṃsaṃ ghātayati*); he remains until the end of the night, i.e., "he causes the night to pass away" (*rātriṃ vivāsayati*); he knows the conjunction of the moon with the asterism Puṣya, i.e., "he joins the moon with Puṣya" (*puṣyeṇa candraṃ yojayati*); he reaches sunrise at Māhiṣmatī, i.e., "he causes the sun to rise at Māhiṣmatī" (*māhiṣmatyāṃ sūryam udgamayati*); sitting down, he awaits the passing of time, i.e., "he causes time to pass" (*kālaṃ gamayati*).

Furthermore, particles (*prādayaḥ*) are of six types: denoters (*vācakāḥ*), indicators (*dyotakāḥ*), co-expressers (*sahābhidhāyakāḥ*), qualifiers (*viśeṣakāḥ*), and meaningless (*nirarthakāḥ*). And when they are connected with a verb, because the verb is predominant, they receive that designation [of "verb"]. Among these, the denotative function of prefixes (*upasargāṇām*) is as follows: *pra* and others denote meanings such as "gone" (*gata*) through the first case, as in *prācāryaḥ* (one who has gone before the teacher) and *prāntevāsī* (one who has gone before the resident pupil). *Ati* and others denote meanings such as "surpassed" (*krānta*) through the second case, as in *atikhaṭvaḥ* (one who has surpassed the bed) and *atamālaḥ* (one who has surpassed the *tamāla* tree).

The group beginning with *ava* (avādayaḥ) is compounded with a word in the third case when meaning "calling out" (*kruṣṭa*) and so forth; for example, *avakokilam* ("called out to by the cuckoo") and *avamayūram* ("called out to by the peacock"). The group beginning with *pari* (paryādayaḥ) is compounded with a word in the fourth case when meaning "weariness" (*glāna*) and so forth; for example, *paryadhyayanam* ("weary of study") and *paripravacanam* ("weary of speaking"). The group beginning with *nis* (nirādayaḥ) is compounded with a word in the fifth case when meaning "gone beyond" (*krānta*) and so forth; for example, *nirvārāṇasī* ("gone beyond Vārāṇasī") and *niṣkauśāmbiḥ* ("departed from Kauśāmbī"). Similarly, a leaf that has fallen off is *praparṇaḥ*, as in *prācīnapalāśaḥ* ("one whose leaves have fallen forward"); and because the waters have come together in it, it is *samāpam*; and because it is joined with the axle, it is *samakṣam*.

The capacity to illuminate a specific meaning belonging to a verbal root (*dhātu*) is "indicative power" (*dyotakatva*). And that which is indicated (*dyotya*) is other than [the root itself]. It occurs in six ways: as similar to it, opposed to it, its absence, its excellence, and its deficiency. Among these, "other than it" (*tadanya*) is, for example, *patīkṣate* (he looks at) and *upakramate* (he undertakes). "Similar to it" (*tatsadṛśa*) is, for example, *saṃvadati* (he speaks in agreement) and *anukaroti* (he imitates). "Opposed to it" (*tadviruddha*) is, for example, *pratiṣṭhate* (he stands firm) and *unmajjati* (he emerges). "Its absence" (*tadabhāva*) is, for example, *viyujyante* (they are separated) and *prasrapati* (he stretches out).

The excellence (*utkarṣa*) of that [action] is as in "he advances" (*pragalbhate*), "he oversteps" (*atikrāmati*); its deficiency (*apakarṣa*) is as in "he laughs at" (*vihasati*), "he eats up" (*prāśnāti*). And here, that property which constitutes the essence of the action, such as the taking of time and so forth, is already expressed by the verbal root (*dhātu*); the preposition (*prādi*) merely illuminates it without denoting it as a substance (*asattvabhūta*). Just as the closing of the eyes and so forth manifest their objects without themselves being denotative, in the same way, the prepositions (*prādayaḥ*) illuminate the stages of the action, such as the beginning and so forth, without themselves expressing them.

Regarding the fact that verbal roots (*dhātu*) alone lack the capacity to express specific actions and thus require auxiliary elements (*sahakārin*), there are various types of auxiliaries that express [the action] together with the root: the internal (*antaraṅga*), the external (*bāhya*), the non-deviating (*avyabhicārī*), the deviating (*vyabhicārī*), the remote (*vyavahita*), and the qualified (*saviśeṣa*). Among these, an example of the internal is *saṅgrāmayate* (he causes to fight) and *asaṅgrāmayata* (he was causing to fight). An example of the external is *anurudhyate* (he conforms to) and *anvarudhyata* (he was conforming to). An example of the non-deviating is *adhīte* (he studies) and *adhyeti* (he studies). An example of the deviating is *ācāmati* (he sips water) and *saṃdhukṣayati* (he kindles).

An example of a [verbal root] being separated [from its prefix] is *utpucchayate*, as in "he wags his tail" (*puccham udasyati*). An example of one with a specific modification is *abhiṣeṇayati*, as in "he marches against the army" (*senāyā abhiyāti*), and *upavīṇayati*, as in "he sings accompanied by the lute" (*vīṇayopagāyati*). But how is the distinction between prefixes understood when they express a meaning that is already inherent [in the root]? Even though a verbal root does not deviate from its prefix, a prefix certainly deviates from its root; therefore, the distinction can be established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Whatever kind of prefix (*samādi*) or affix (*upasarga*) is observed elsewhere, it occurs here as well to that same extent. Furthermore, it is a delimiter (*avacchedaka*) and a differentiator (*viśeṣaka*) from its own class (*sajātīya*). It is sixfold: a differentiator of the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), a differentiator of the meaning of the suffix (*pratyaya*), a differentiator of both, and a differentiator of the meanings of both. Among these, an example of a differentiator of the base is *vijayate* (he conquers) and *parājayate* (he is defeated). An example of a differentiator of the meaning of the base is *saṅkrīḍati* (he plays together) and *saṅkrīḍate* (he plays together).

An example of one that qualifies the suffix (*pratyaya*) is *viśālam* or *viśaṅkaṭam*. An example of one that qualifies the meaning of the suffix (*pratyayārtha*) is *abhimanāyate* or *durmanāyate*. An example of one that qualifies both is *upatuṣṭhati* or *upatuṣṭhate*. In these cases, the prefix (*prādi*), expressing meanings such as intensity (*prakarpa*) and so forth, grasps the action in a general sense; it does not restrict itself to either the action in general or its specific instance. However, when the two are in close conjunction, the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) arises between them, just as in the case of "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*).

Regarding their having a functional purpose (*kāryārthatva*): as in *prayuṅkte*, *parākaroti*, *abhiṣuṇoti*, *praṇamati*, *vittaṃ*, and *samīpam*. The middle voice (*ātmanepada*), the active voice (*parasmaipada*), the substitution of *ṣ* (*ṣatva*), the substitution of *ṇ* (*ṇatva*), the substitution of *t* (*tatva*), and the substitution of *ī* (*ītva*)—these grammatical operations occur when a prefix (*upasarga*) is present. Regarding their being devoid of meaning (*nirarthakatva*): as in *nihnute*, *niravjanti*, *pralambate*, and *saṃśrayati*. In these cases, the prefix is employed merely for the sake of increasing the word-form (*padopacaya*), and thus it is devoid of meaning.

And they say: "That [prefix] may be a qualifier (*viśeṣaka*) of specific meanings, or it may not even be an indicator (*dyotaka*); or it is employed as an auxiliary (*sahakārī*) for the root to impart its power (*śakti*); or it may be a specifier of the action (*kriyāviśeṣaka*), or it is taught for the sake of poetic meaning (*kāvyārtha*); or it is considered meaningless (*anarthaka*) when there is merely an accumulation of words (*padopacaya*). Thus, this *padaikārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning within a word) has many forms. Likewise, *vākyārthībhāva* (the unification of meaning within a sentence) also exists; in that regard, there are various options such as: a sentence is a verb accompanied by its auxiliaries, its factors (*kāraka*s), and its qualifiers; or a sentence is that which contains a single finite verb (*ekatiṅvākya*)," and so forth.

And therein, there is the *nighāta* (tonal suppression) of two *tiṅ*-inflected words or vocative words following a word within the same sentence; furthermore, the substitutes *na*, *nu*, and so forth, replace the forms of *yuṣmad* and *asmad*.
