Moreover, purposes such as "the final syllable of a sentence is *pluta* and acute" (*vākyasya ṭeḥ pluta udāttaḥ*) are stated. And the sentence-meanings—whether they be the *bhāvanā*, the injunction (*vidhi*), or the intuition (*pratibhā*)—manifest through the mutual relationship of benefactor and beneficiary among the meanings of the words, namely the action, the factors of action (*kāraka*), their relations, and the qualifiers.

In this way, even for sentences, when words such as *iva* (like) are employed due to the relationship of mutual comparison (*upamāna-upameya-bhāva*) and so forth, a state of syntactic unity (*ekārthībhāva*) occurs in *muktaka* and other forms. By this, various types of sentence complexes—such as the *yugalaka*, *sandānitaka*, *kīlāpaka*, and *kulaka*, which involve the simultaneous application of a single action or grammatical factor—are explained. Among these, the technical designations are established as follows: a *yugalaka* consists of two four-line stanzas; a *sandānitaka* of three; a *kīlāpaka* of four; and a *kulaka* of five or more.

By this, it is also explained that a *saṅghāta* is a collection of well-spoken verses (*subhāṣita*) composed within a single section (*praghaṭṭaka*), whereas a *kośa* consists of those composed across many sections. Furthermore, descriptions such as the city of Nāgara, the moon, the sun, or the ocean, which are collections of sentences belonging to the interior of a larger composition and taking the form of a *saṅghāta*, receive the designation of a "section" (*prakaraṇa*) and attain the status of intermediate units. And their meanings undergo a state of unified sense (*ekārthībhāva*).

That great sentence-meaning (*mahāvākyārtha*), however, which is assisted by them—being aided in works such as epic poems (*sargabandha*) or narratives (*ākhyāyikā*) through the five junctures (*sandhi*) known as the introduction (*mukha*), the sequel (*pratimukha*), the development (*garbha*), the pause (*vimarśa*), and the conclusion (*nirvahaṇa*); through the sixty-four members of the junctures (*sandhyaṅga*) beginning with the *upakṣepa* and *parikara*; and through the four styles (*vṛtti*) such as the *Bhāratī*, which consist of sixteen types of limbs—is joined with them so that they stand in a mutual relationship of qualifier and qualified, and it thus manifests in the form of a great sentence-meaning such as "The Abduction of Subhadrā" or "The Abduction of Jānakī. That [is what is meant].

The state of being a single unified meaning within a literary composition (*prabandha*) is designated as "the other" (*apara*). However, that specific intuition of injunctions and prohibitions—such as "one should behave like Rāma, not like Rāvaṇa"—which arises for one whose mental impressions have been refined by the ascertainment of the meanings of such compositions as the *Rāmāyaṇa*, is called the "Supreme" (*para*) Great Sentence-meaning (*mahāvākyaikārtha*). It pervades the entire universe, is the sole cause of the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*), and is the "Word-Brahman" (*śabdabrahman*), which is beginningless and endless, partless, and transformed from the root-meaning.

This very meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), being indivisible, is celebrated as the "Word-Brahman" (*śabdabrahman*). One who is proficient in the Word-Brahman attains the Supreme Brahman. This is the primary station for the steps of the ladder of spiritual accomplishments; this is that straight royal road for those seeking liberation. The fourfold distinctions between word, meaning, and their relationship have been stated again in sequence. Now, we shall describe those same four which reside in the specific varieties of speech.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Illumination of the Power of Words with Indifference," in the Śṛṅgāraprakāśa composed by the illustrious Bhojadeva, the Emperor of Great Kings.

The wise declare that the *bhūṣaṇa* (ornament) is speech endowed with conciliation, gifts, and so forth. As in the *Ratnāvalī*: "O Queen, Vasubhūti, you truly deserve the title of 'Queen' (*devī*). And as in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*, Bhīma says: "Where is that wretched follower of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, that base-born creature by whom this great mental agitation was caused for my noble brother? That evil-souled one has been captured by Nakula! Furthermore, the *punarvākya* (repeated statement) should be understood as the manifestation of a contradiction (*ākṣepa*) as previously described.

As in the *Ratnāvalī*: "O Queen, Bābhravya, I have now become one whose labor has borne fruit. And as in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*: "O Blessed One, Yudhiṣṭhira, have we indeed been deceived by the Cārvāka demon? Or what of Kṛṣṇa? The attainment of a boon is desired as the conclusion of a poetic work.

As it is said in the *Ratnāvalī*: "O King, Yaugandharāyaṇa says: 'Tell me, what further favor may I perform for you? The King replies: 'What favor could there be beyond this? For, Vikramabāhu has been brought to equality with myself; Sāgarikā, the very essence of the earth, has been obtained; and my beloved, the sole cause for the conquest of the world, has been won. The Queen has attained joy through the recovery of her sister, and Kosala has been conquered. When you, the bull among ministers, are present, what is there that one might desire?"* Thus it is said.

As in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*: Kṛṣṇa says, "O Great King, tell me this: what do you desire from us as a favor? Yudhiṣṭhira replies, "Indeed, it is not possible to request anything more than this. Let Your Majesty behold: the entire host of enemies has been slain by those blinded by wrath; we five remain unharmed; and the ocean of humiliation born of my own misconduct toward the Princess of Pañcāla has been crossed."

"O God, Supreme Person, you do not speak to a virtuous man with anything other than conciliation; what else, therefore, may I ask of the gracious Lord? Thus is *praśasti* (eulogy) defined as the power of kings, gods, and so forth. As in the *Ratnāvalī*: "May Indra, shedding his desired rain, produce a land of abundant crops; may the foremost of Brahmins duly gratify those worthy of offerings with their favorite oblations."

"And may there be an unending union with accumulated happiness for virtuous people; may the words of wicked men, which are difficult to overcome and like adamantine glue, vanish entirely into silence. As it is said in the *Veṇīsaṃhāra*: "Nevertheless, if the Blessed One is even more pleased, then let this be: May Jaja, whose mind is free from meanness, live out the full span of a human life; O Blessed One, may he possess devotion toward Puruṣottama that is untainted by duality."

May the King—whose realm is beloved, who is a kinsman to the learned, a connoisseur of virtues, ever virtuous, and who has adorned the entire earth—prosper. The sixty-four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) which were previously mentioned will now be analyzed clearly, starting with the *nāṭaka* (drama) and other forms. These are: ornament (*bhūṣaṇa*), concatenation of syllables (*akṣarasaṅghāta*), beauty (*śobhā*), illustration (*udāharaṇa*), as well as cause (*hetu*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), example (*dṛṣṭānta*), attainment (*prāpti*), apprehension (*āśaṅkā*), illustration by comparison (*nidarśana*), etymological explanation (*nirukta*), conjunction (*sandhi*), and qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Excellence (guṇātipāta), Distinction (atiśaya), Equal Reasoning (tulyatarka), Accumulation of Words (padoccaya); the Enjoined (diṣṭa) and the Instructed (upadiṣṭa), Investigation (vicāra), and then Contradiction (viparyaya); Falling Away (bhraṃśa), Conciliation (anunīti), Garland (mālā), Civility (dākṣiṇya), and Censure (garhaṇa); Presumption (arthāpatti), Notoriety (prasiddhi), Inquiry (pṛcchā), and Similarity (sārūpya); Wishful Thinking (manoratha), A Glimmer (leśa), Begging (yācñā), Encouragement (protsāhana), and Longing (spṛhā); Remorse (paścāttāpa), Compliance (anuvṛtti), Argumentation (yukti), Illumination (nirbhāsana), Forbearance (kṣamā); Praise of Virtues (guṇānuvāda), Lamentation (ākranda), Deceit (kapaṭa), and Slander (parivādana).

Birth, effect, negation, false speech, equivocation, change of voice, madness, derision, boasting, chance, connection, disparity, engagement in what was promised, benediction, accomplishment, and pleasant speech—these sixty-four characteristics one should point out in poetic works. And therein, that which is observed through many ornaments and qualities...

As in the first act of the *Ratnāvalī*: "Yaugandharāyaṇa, having set aside talk of war, dwelling in the hearts of the people with delight, and accompanied by his dear Vasantaka, the Lord of Vatsa approaches like the flower-bowed god [Kāma], eager to witness his own great festival. Here, one should observe the presence of figures of speech such as *śleṣa* (paronomasia), *upamā* (simile), and *pratyakṣa* (direct perception), as well as qualities (*guṇas*) such as *śleṣa*, *prasāda* (clarity), and *saukumārya* (gentleness). In the same way, the figures of speech and qualities in the passages to be cited below should also be inferred according to their occurrence.

And playwrights do not observe a fixed rule [regarding these]. However, in the *sandhyaṅgas* (subdivisions of the junctures), the employment of poetic qualities (*guṇas*) and ornaments (*alaṅkāras*) is not required. Where there is a description of various meanings through words that are phonetically or semantically punned (*śliṣṭa*), one should know that collection of syllables here as being designated by the term "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*). For example, in the seventh act of the *Abhijñānaśākuntalam*: (Entering with a clay peacock in her hand, the female ascetic says: "Śārṅgarava, look at the beauty of Śakuntalā!"

(Sarvadamana, behold the beauty of Śakuntalā! The Boy (casting a glance): Where is my noble mother? Both (smiling): You have been deceived by the similarity of the name, you who are so devoted to your mother! The King (to himself): Is "Śakuntalā" the name of her mother? When a meaning that is not yet established is established by means of meanings already established, that [figure of speech], being both allusive (*śliṣṭā*) and smooth (*ślakṣṇā*), with its manifold sense, is called *śobhā*.

As it is said in the *Ratnāvalī*, in the first act: "Whether from another island, from the midst of the ocean, or even from the ends of the quarters, Fate, having become favorable, suddenly brings [the object] and unites one with what is desired."

Otherwise, how could there have been the landing upon a plank of the daughter of the King of Siṃhala—who was sought by a perfected seer (*siddhādeśa*)—after her ship was wrecked in the ocean; and how could there have been the recognition of her in that state by a merchant from Kauśāmbī returning from Siṃhala, and her subsequent bringing here due to the identifying mark of the jewel-garland? In every way, prosperity touches our master, as it is demonstrated by this statement endowed with a corresponding meaning.

The accomplishment of the objectives by skillful means is known as *udāharaṇa* (illustration). For example, in the second act of the *Ratnāvalī*, the King and the Vidūṣaka overhear the words of a śārikā bird. Then the Vidūṣaka (to the air): "Why are you angry at the very beginning? Just as this Kāmadeva was painted by you, so too has Rati been painted by me. "O friend, what is this? The King: "Friend, I conjecture thus:"

A certain woman, out of affection, drew her heart’s beloved and concealed him under the pretext of being the god Kāmadeva; his friend, having recognized him, skillfully countered this by drawing that [deity] in that very same place. That which, through the power of its purpose, accomplishes a desired object and is captivating to the mind is designated as *hetu* (the causal figure).
